[h1]Plot[/h1]

The city of Dubai has been devastated by multiple major sandstorms ; Killing a lot of inhabitants from the city. After coming back from the War of Afghanistan, an american colonel named "John Konrad", and his regiment, the [b][u]33rd[/u][/b], made a rescue operation in the city to save the civilians. However, they will be asked to retire from Dubai, and they actually defy the orders of the US army and stay in the city, deserting with his regiment.

6 months later, a radio signal has been capted and reveals to be John Konrad himself, stating that the operation was a failure. Two weeks after the signal, the US army sends the [b]Delta Team[/b] into reconnaissance, led by Captain Martin Walker (Protagonist controlled by the player), First lieutenant Alphonso Adams, and the Chief sergeant John Lugo.

[h1]Good Qualities[/h1]

1. Really good story, implying the Delta Team going to Dubai to search for survivors and civilians, the city being completely ravaged by sandstorms. But is actually revealed that the city became also a total [b]War zone[/b] between the [spoiler]CIA and the 33rd.[/spoiler]

2. Another success of the game is how [u]it shows the real horrors of war.[/u] Unlike some few other games and series, this game completely shows how horrible and degrading a war can be. The game also shows and makes you explore things other games don't usually do. Like making moral choices, bloody damages, war crimes, and even [u]traumas[/u], which will also impact a lot Walker's mental health, to the point he will start to hallucinate a lot during [spoiler] the middle of the game[/spoiler], as stated in GQ#5.

3. Unlike most of the other games of the same genre, the game constantly makes you think that everything you do during the story is right. Until the end of the game, where Walker and his team realise that [spoiler]they caused a lot of terrible things, such has killing innocent people with white phosphorus, stole all the water of Dubai, and more, causing more harm than good.[/spoiler]

4. The scene where Walker and his team use the white phosphorus during [spoiler]Chapter 8[/spoiler] is one of the most tragics and best scenes in video games.[spoiler] When Delta team uses the white phosphorus to kill a lot of 33rd soldiers blocking their path, they after notice, with lot of shock, that they [b]also killed lot of civilians.[/b][/spoiler]

5. Speaking of that scene, after passing this one, Walker's actions, dialogs, etc, will gradually change in many ways, which makes the game very interesting and darker :

* Walker's executions (When he executes an enemy on the ground) will be more brutal and gore.

* His dialogs (during gunfights) will also change with a lot of curse and insults.

* Walker will often hallucinate, and sometimes, some of these hallucinations break the fourth wall.

6. Unlike some other TPS games where your teammates are immortal and mostly can't be given orders, your teammates in the game can be given orders, and each of them has his own arsenal depending of your order, which is interesting idea! Both of them can also be downed if they get damaged enough, and you'll have to save them, which gives a good challenge and makes you caring for your teammates.

7. The AI from the enemies is smart and challenging, they will usually plan to make strategies to bypass you and make profitable shots against you and your allies. The game has also few specials enemies, with their own tactics.

* Bayonet Runners are enemies who use a knife and charge towards you, they are fast and are able to dodge when you are shooting at them.

* Heavy Troopers are slow enemies, but heavily armored and mostly equipped with powerful weapons. 

* Zulu Squads are enemies who are very tactical and smart, they will mostly try to kill you by going around you.

8. The game has intels (Like in Call of Duty 4), but these are interesting since it explains the situation when the sandstorm occured (6 months before the game starts) about the city, as well as Konrad and the Radioman.

9. You can use your environment at your advantage, such as shooting glasses (containing sand) behind the enemies, which is a nice addition, especially to spare ammo.

10. Great graphics for its time, fitting well the environment of the desert and the city of Dubai!

11. Really good voice acting.

12. Great soundtrack, both for gunfights and the story! Composed by the Czech composer [u]Elia Cmiral[/u].

[h1]Bad Qualities[/h1]

1. Despite the game being well received by players, the game was a [b]commercial failure[/b]. According to the devs, the game was sold with [u]770 000[/u] copies one year after the release of the game.

* Because of that reason, a DLC that was planned to be released (named "Long Way Home") got cancelled, as well as any possibility for the game to have a sequel.

2. Some sequences in the game can be really hard, especially if you play the game in difficulty "FUBAR", which is needed to unlock an achievement :

* The beginning of chapter 6 is an example, you lose all your weapons (Except a Desert Eagle with few bullets), and you must survive against the 33rd while you have to wait for Adams and Lugo to save you. This can be pretty hard, especially if an enemy is charging at you.

* Chapter 14 is considered as the hardest chapter in the game, during the middle of the chapter, you must fight through a lot of enemies (And few Zulu Squads), half of these enemies usually camp near the 2 turrets and they are very well covered, which means that you can easily get killed if you are in plain sight of theirs shots.

3. The Multiplayer mode of the game hasn't been focused that much compared to the campaign.

* There is also no any achievement for multiplayer.

4. [b]Major Plot Hole[/b] : Why Adams and Lugo kept following Walker when they clearly saw that something wasn't right about Walker hallucinating and that he was losing his mind? Or just not making any comment to Walker about it?

* In chapter 9, it's revealed that, in the end of the game, the two hanged people (Where you have to choose who to kill, or simply kill the snipers) [spoiler]were actually corpses from all the beginning. And as stated above, Adams and Lugo never make any word to Walker about it and kept following him, which doesn't make sense.[/spoiler]

[h1]Tips[/h1]

1. Throwing a sticky grenade to an enemy (Except heavy troopers) will make the latter to run in panic to his allies before exploding, making a nice combo.

2. Doing executions gives you ammo for your weapons (Even for the rarest weapons), sometimes grenades. This tactic can be vital in FUBAR, since you get less ammo from enemies in general.

3. Try to often give priorities to your allies with the tactic mode, Lugo can easily kill the snipers from afar. And Adams can throw flashbangs to enemies who are entrenched.

4. The possible environmental damages (Where you can use them to kill your enemies with advantage) are displayed with a red skull icon when you are in tactic mode.

[h1]Trivia[/h1]

1. There is a high theory made by players that Walker and his team died at the end of chapter 12. And all the rest after said chapter are just hallucinations of [b]Walker being in hell[/b].

2. At the beginning of chapter 9, when you and your team rappel down, you can briefly see a red hanging man behind the window as a hallucination. [spoiler]This is actually Lugo, as he dies in the same way at the end of chapter 13.[/spoiler]

Spec Ops: The Line is the punctuation mark of a console generation that was dominated by shooters chasing after Call of Duty 4 and Gears of War. In the late 2000's and early 2010's - still buoyed by post 9/11 jingoism and imperialism guised as peacekeeping - both of those franchises and the titles that followed produced game after game that conveyed the dissonant ideas of "conflict is messy, but we need these brave few to cleave the darkness" and "conflict is cool an empowering, and don't think about the consequences" without ever resolving that dissonance.

Spec Ops: The Line is that resolution. It loosely adapts the classic novel Heart of Darkness to indict the video game industry for its paucity of sharp, incisive writing that led to the glut of unthinking Call of Duty clones; to indict the American Military Industrial Complex which engaged in the whole war on terror purely to drain developing nations of resources and protect their interests; and to indict players, who just need to feel like a hero, no matter how large the butcher's bill is or how much suffering they inflict.

It is a functional shooter, representative of its era but probably better than the median of its contemporaries. Would it be "better" if it was a better shooter, or would it undermine its message? I don't think it's particularly important: the shooting is a necessary component of the story, and the game is short enough that it doesn't outstay its welcome. It makes its point, then drops the mic. It is not a game you should come to for the shooting; it's a game you should come to as a sicko who likes de-constructive narratives; so that you understand how much of a rut that generation was and why everyone complained about grey, grimey shooters thay conflated a loose, naive notion of realism and grittyness for depth; and how the online gaming critique and discourse we have today was shaped in part by this game.

Total side bar, but it also came out within a twelve month window of both Mass Effect 3 and Bioshock Infinite and did both of their ending schticks better than them. The endings of both Spec Ops and Infinite are about whether a man who has done terrible things can forgive himself or accept responsibility for the things he's done, but where Infinite uses that as a gotcha twist that is largely unrelated to 90% of the game, Spec Ops is built around it and better for it. It also does Mass Effect 3's "sad, half dead walk to go shoot something at the end" better.

It might seem petty to suggest that if I were looking for a better anti-war or anti-violence narrative, I'd turn to films like Apocalypse Now, Come and See, or the works of Michael Haneke. These movies set a high bar for thematic depth and storytelling that many games still struggle to reach. This isn't to diminish the artistic potential of video games, but to acknowledge the challenges they face in these areas.

Spec Ops: The Line attempts to engage players with moral dilemmas and a deeper narrative, but it often falls short. The game tries to subvert typical shooter tropes and present complex choices, yet it doesn't provide the player with enough agency to truly feel the consequences of Walker's actions. The moral choices feel forced and lack the depth needed to make the narrative impactful.

Comparing games to movies might seem simplistic, but it's hard not to think of how Hideo Kojima has explored anti-war themes more effectively in some of his work. Spec Ops: The Line stands out from games like Call of Duty, but it isn't inherently better just because it's different.

In summary, while Spec Ops: The Line makes a effort to tackle serious themes, it ultimately doesn't provide the tools necessary for players to fully engage with its intended message. Video games have the potential for profound storytelling, but they still have some ground to cover to match the narrative depth found in the best anti-war films and books.

In a sandstorm-riddled Dubai, you play as the leader of Delta Squad, Captain Martin Walker, who's tasked with performing reconnaissance before being evacuated from the city. However, one horrifying discovery after another leads Delta Squad into an escalating hellscape of their own creation, with no other option other than trudging forward. Gameplay consists of typical third-person cover shooting fare, along with issuing commands to Walker's two companions, Adams and Lugo. The sandstorms that desolated Dubai play an occasional role in changing up combat scenarios, whether you can use mounds of sand to eliminate enemies or how sandstorms block you from giving commands. 

The game does a nice job in telling it's story through traditional methods and through subtle visual changes. Walker's appearance changes as the game goes on, reflecting his current mental state. Orders that were given professionally turn to ragged screams laden with curses. If you have a sharp eye, you can even tell when the game is playing tricks on you. A lot of care was put into the single-player campaign, and many would argue that its bare-bones nature serves as a critique of military-themed shooters that were popular at the time of the game's release. While it may not necessarily compare to games released nowadays, I'd say it's worth experiencing at least once if you're into that sort of thing. Supposedly, Nolan North -- who voiced Captain Walker -- has claimed that this is the performance he is most proud of. It shows. Visually, "Spec Ops: The Line" is stunning. The desolate beauty of Dubai provides a unique setting that's both opulent and apocalyptic. The attention to detail in the environments is remarkable, making the city itself a character in the story.
In conclusion, "Spec Ops: The Line" is a bold and innovative title that dares to explore the darker side of war. I loathe this game so much. One of the worst keyboard setup I have ever seen in a game. Several actions bind to one button is frustrating when playing and creates a clumsy experience. Also one of the worst achievements I had the displeasure to get is MFWIC. The story is like a fight club psychological war movie. It is a very effective story and entertaining. Why am I recommending it? The story is actually good and some parts of the game play are very good at times.

-Cover system: It's both the worst and best feature of the game. Basically cover is your worst enemy if you have the wrong weapon and it will make enemies throw grenades at you, forcing you to run to another cover and in the process probably killing you. Also shooting + aiming from cover is usually instant death. The best part of cover is shooting without revealing yourself, basically you are unkillable and no repercussions at all except lack of accuracy. Getting yourself X1014 or any shotgun allows you to shoot from cover and kill almost anything close by. This is how you beat FUBAR difficulty as you need to abuse this mechanic to be able to kill heavy's without them killing you. Most of the game, I was out of cover and crouched. Why? The AI can't shoot you in certain angles but you can shoot them. Hugging a wall while they are peaking is free kills and safer than cover. Also abusing certain holes through cover or debris works as well.

-Story: It carries the entire game. It is very intriguing and extremely effective but ultimately the story makes a classic twist which detracts completely from the intensity of your actions and in my opinion, ruins somewhat parts of the game. My problem with the story is that it is a gruesome inception-like war movie in which you are forced to make gruesome decisions and pay/experience the consequences. Sounds exactly what you want in a war game, right? If you are sensitive, emotional or never experienced a story like this, it will hit you like a truck but, if you are like me, you see a cheap gimmick that you have seen before several times in movies. I knew how the game was going to end from a mile away because it was hitting all the basic tropes. Obviously the Meta story in the game is very good and one of the best narratives I have ever experienced, but it could have been a movie instead of a game with clunky game play mechanics which detracts from the story.

-Soundtrack: Pleasantly rocking and it knew exactly when to enter to make an emotional toll and effectively adding to the story/game play. You will get goose bumps at times.

-Controls: Mediocre at best, mostly buggy and clunky. 2 hotkeys that have each 3 different actions bind to them which really makes no sense and halts game play quite a bit. Several times I wanted to get out of cover and was unable to because the game does not register well the actions you want to do and once you do, it is probably too late. Getting in and out of cover is a mess, trying to run away but there is cover nearby is also a mess. Shooting feels great in general but sometimes it seems the hit boxes are off even though you are on point with the targeting which usually happens with rifles and pistols. Could be because of debris, cover or other doodads but I do not know.

-FUBAR: This is very hard not because the difficulty is quite high but, It is very hard and extremely tedious because the controls are baffling awful at times. From forced scripted montages in the campaign to being one shot-ed, you require the game to respond to your commands with ease so that it is an enjoyable experience, not infuriating and have the ability to beat the game. The game does a piss poor job of giving you a smooth experience and is probably the only reason why I dislike this game so much. The difficulty itself is fantastic and more realistic, even though you have regenerative health and the AI is very trash. The biggest negative of FUBAR has to be scripted montages. I probably wasted 30 minutes on just running away from the helicopter fire which only last about 5 seconds. At one point I thought I would not be able to beat this trivial yet incomprehensible part of the game which kept killing me. I beat it accidentally by running into a crate and the helicopter miraculously disappeared. How stupid is that? Also the best weapons in the game are M1014 which kills heavy's in two reloads, M-99 that one shots regardless where it hits, AA-12 as it does insane damage, M249 SAW which has hilariously almost pin point accuracy, Everything else is lacklustre, including AK and M4A1.

-AI: Absolute garbage. The game is obviously old and I am playing it until now but, the AI would reload in the open in front of me on FUBAR difficulty. Sometimes it would take cover where it was not covering itself from incoming fire. Heavy's will stop right outside your cover continuously shooting and missing you, giving you the chance to shoot at them freely every 15 seconds when they have to reload. Hell, I was shooting without aiming and killing heavy's without repercussions. Like I said before, the game is not hard at all because the AI is so easily abused. If you are in cover the AI is scripted to throw grenades ever so often so how do you mitigate that? DO NOT GET INTO COVER. Crouch and get out of line of sight of the enemy, usually behind a wall or higher cover and slowly but surely start sniping away at them one by one. FUBAR was a cake walk yet extremely tedious because AI was not challenging at all except for the fact that they can one-shot you and have very good aim.

Spec Ops: The Line is a game developed by YAGER Development GmbH, previously known for Xbox Original Exclusive "Yager" (hah) and then later known for games like Dreadnought and The Cycle: Frontier, two games I've never played nor heard of. It was developed as the tenth entry in the Spec Ops franchise as well as a reboot and having NEVER played those other games I don't know how well those match up to them. However, I can tell you how this game matches up to other third person shooters in general and my thoughts are "It's pretty f u c king good". This game is VERY well known for it's violent "war is bad" story inspired by Heart of Darkness by Joseph Conrad (of which a favorite game of mine, Far Cry 2, also took inspiration from), and having both watched a friend of mine play this game, and then played it myself for my own merit I have my thoughts. Shoutout to Bad Ghosts for the copy!

The story starts with Martin Walker and his squad mates Lugo and Adams landing down in Dubai to try to find out where the 33rd Battalion and their leader, John Konrad. You fight your way through insurgents (which CIA coverups) and the 33rd Battalion itself as you try to figure out what's going on. It's a simple story, but with interesting meta narrative and strange moral choices. Spoilers Ahead: [Spoiler]One thing I enjoyed is that when you first start the game, you start out on a helicopter mini gun shooting people, of which when you later do this in Chapter 12 Walker questions as to why this shootout feels so familiar. Another revolves around a main conflict: In order to charge a gate in Chapter 7, you're forced to use White Phosphorus to clear out the 33rd Battalion surrounding it before you accidentally kill innocent civilians while using it. Lugo tells you it's an awful idea and that there's always a choice, whereas Walker tells him there is NO choices, of which of course the game won't let you move along unless you use it.[/spoiler] This sort of thing is intriguing to me, blurring the lines between narrative and game in a sense and I enjoy moments like this when done well. There is the whole CIA thing mentioned where they [Spoiler] Commit horrible acts in order to get everyone killed and cover up that Konrad and the 33rd war crimed the city because of threat of retaliation and world war [/spoiler] but while that sounds good it just sort of kinda feels like some side thing I forget about sometimes because the CIA guys aren't fleshed out. To me, the main characters you know are Walker and Konrad himself, whereas I feel your squad mates are ok but kind of just average? But your soldiers are supposed to be just that, average soldiers caught up in war so I kinda feel the need to give that a pass and since Walker is so focused on the mission it sorta makes sense that it doesn't really focus on them. The one thing I definitely wanna bring up is the final twist [Spoiler] Konrad's been dead the whole time, you imagined him up as an enemy to make yourself feel better for killing innocent civilians. This ultimately culminates in either shooting yourself or shooting him in your mind and having reinforcements come pick you up, where you can choose to go with them or kill them and retreat back into Dubai. [/Spoiler] Whereas I do like this twist, it feels underwhelming in a sense; there's foreshadowing stuff but it's also structured in a way where it's very artificial and delivered in a weird way? Like it works well, but it just doesn't do it to it's fullest potential. And that's something that was in the regular choices as well, whereas it doesn't really change anything in the story. It feels mixed to me because they don't have an impact on your character and there are no branching paths; but that is also kind of a highlight of the story because it was made to immerse you in the messed up atmosphere; I just wish it made an impact personally. Like they don't matter, because the situations will always be awful and it kind of speaks to Walker's mindset and his narrow minded perspective on always deciding his way as how he sees it. It's ultimately Walker's game, his story; you're just controlling him which in another meta narrative sense it reminds me of other war games where you go through, do your usual cleanup and then move along and nothing happens even if you used really messed up methods. In this game, you're similarly railroaded but it makes a point of it and whereas I'm mixed on that stuff in general it makes it's point really loud and f u c king clear. Another thing that also interests me is that throughout the game you go through hell and the further you get into and the worse your mental state goes the worse your off your character is: your outfit and skin is burned, shot grazed with bullets, your executions become more bloodthirsty (what would amount to shooting them once in the beginning of the game would amount to smashing a dude's face with the butt of your shotgun in the latter), as well as the game's loading screen tips becoming more and more insane and demeaning towards your actions. Speaking of.

The game play is basically that of an average cover shooter Gears of War type, if you played or seen games like that you'll see what this game is about. It's short, you can beat it in six hours, and it's kind of average as a cover shooter. Like it's not bad, it's serviceable and it's not the highlight of the game obviously but it's fine. The only detail I can add really is that you can shoot certain windows of sand and that it'll stun or kill enemies. Also, when playing through myself as well as my buddy playing through the first time; you can command your squad to take out certain enemies and such and we didn't really use it too often? It's certainly useful in FUBAR modes and such but I don't know I didn't end up using it that much so it just felt kinda...there.

The sound design/atmosphere of it is it's really brutal, it's good and feeding into the story like it's brutal, with miles of empty sand and destroyed buildings; it's depressing and oppressive and I hate it but I love it because of that. Again the details are great, and how your characters look over time as you go through this war is amazing, like I can't say anything bad about the atmosphere. The sound design is also good, with the notable likes of Nolan North and Jake Busey being the two big names behind it. The only one that doesn't fit in for me is Nolan North kind of? Like he's a bit too recognizable and takes me out of it but overall I can't complain about that, nor will I complain about the atmospheric music pieces of songs like "Nowhere to Run" by Martha and the Vandellas and Jimi Hendrix's "Star Spangled Banner". I think overall, the atmosphere/sound design really works well in tandem with the game's story and truth be told I have nothing to say other than that.

Final point, it's good! It's great in a meta narrative, story context where it kind of analyzes both war and it's trivialization and effects on people as well as it's examination between war video games and the player itself. It's a complicated combination that is both really good and hard to explain, and I hope I explained it the best that I can. With that in mind, I'd personally say wait for a sale, but if you're looking for a game to think about, play it cause it's short and good.

[h1][i]Spec Ops: The Line is one of the most unique experiences I have ever had playing videogames. This game's narrative is nothing short of a masterpiece![/i][/h1]

- This game starts off as your standard and generic military shooter game. But as you keep playing, the game continually starts becoming more and more sinister and horror. It slowly starts to present a very strong and mature narrative which was pretty rare to find at the time of this game's release. This is an action shooter game that does not glorify killing.

- You'll go from tacticool and quirky COD-like dialogue while blasting fools to your character slowly going insane and changing the way he talks during gameplay. You'll start to question the morality of your actions and choices, not that they matter anyway. Soldiers slowly start dying in much more gruesome ways as you progress during the game, usually with the horror still frozen on their faces after you kill them.

- This is not a game you play for the gameplay. This is a game you play for the narrative and the small details. Infact the gameplay of this game is utter trash, it's not fun to play and it's a chore to get through. You can't even turn off Mouse Acceleration, making aiming your gun much more harder. I think this was intentional by the developers to help with the narrative even further. Had the narrative not been as strong as it was here, I would've stopped playing.

- This game isn't shy of breaking the 4th wall. During earlier levels, Loading Tips tend to give out useful or lore information when you retry checkpoints. However during later levels, they start to show more sinister "tips" and stuff that's completely unrelated to the game. In the last 2 levels, the tips give up and constantly mock you, the player.

- The game is fairly short but that's not a bad thing. It doesn't overstay it's welcome and every level is well paced. The game gets the job done and knows when to end.

- No matter what choices you make, you are not the hero of the game. Instead, you should just die.

Spec ops the line sends you to hell. I mean Dubai. 
It's a hell so dark you are barely aware of its existence, but it's full of so many guns you'll feel like giving up after ten seconds. The game is an arcade style shooter featuring 100 guns to kill 100 enemies with, and it even includes all the basic weapons you'd expect, plus some more useful ones like knives and lasers. Once you run out of bullets you can still kill enemies by throwing grenades or by targeting weak points (and this would be the part where you'd vomit in your mouth and wipe your eyes so you can focus on the screen). The shooting is simple and fast enough to ensure your brain never thinks about survival, and instead your eye is glued to the screen, dreaming up different scenarios and escape routes that will keep you glued to the screen.

You play as a member of an elite team of soldiers sent to kill terrorists hiding out in the streets. Sounds easy, yes? Nope. Our guys are inexperienced (we are), the terrorist's hideouts are crawling with them (they are), and the entire city has been taken hostage (surprise!). If you can get past all of that, you'll run up against several more hurdles. You and your squad aren't armed with anything special, aside from bullets, grenades and the odd sniper rifle. As long as you have the brains to hold down the fire button you can take the city (and every weapon and item there is) down with you.

Gameplay, as expected, is a fast-paced arcade shooter. You can jump, crawl, crouch, run, aim, shoot, and you can also hurl grenades. The controls are easy to master, and you can even get on the ground and throw your grenades by moving just one controller (the left trigger) forward, causing them to fly straight and finally land right next to their targets. For this review, I'd like to quote the late George Carlin from his 1990 stand up special:

[quote]
There’s a condition in combat. Most people know about it. It’s when a fighting person’s nervous system has been stressed to its absolute peak and maximum, can’t take any more input. The nervous system has either snapped or is about to snap. In the first world war, that condition was called "shell shock". Simple, honest, direct language. Two syllables: shell shock. Almost sounds like the guns themselves. That was seventy years ago.

Then a whole generation went by and the second world war came along, and the very same combat condition was called "battle fatigue". Four syllables now. Takes a little longer to say. Doesn’t seem to hurt as much. Fatigue is a nicer word than shock. Shell shock! [i]Battle fatigue[/i].

Then we had the war in Korea, 1950. Madison Avenue was riding high by that time, and the very same combat condition was called "operational exhaustion". Hey, we’re up to eight syllables now! And the humanity has been squeezed completely out of the phrase. It’s totally sterile now. Operational exhaustion. Sounds like something that might happen to your car.

Then of course came the war in Vietnam, which has only been over for about sixteen or seventeen years, and thanks to the lies and deceits surrounding that war, I guess it’s no surprise that the very same condition was called "post-traumatic stress disorder". Still eight syllables, but we’ve added a hyphen! And the pain is completely buried under jargon. Post-traumatic stress disorder. I’ll bet ya, if we’d have still been calling it shell shock, some of those Vietnam veterans might have gotten the attention they needed at the time. I’ll betcha that. I’ll betcha that.
[/quote]

By turns elegiac, scenic, beautiful, then all of a sudden brutal and barbaric. The Line is a cover shooter couched in a slightly hard-to-swallow morality play: "heroes don't fight wars, they end them." The narrative wedges 3 unwitting Delta operatives into a 3-way struggle between Dubai's dying populace, an AWOL battalion, and the CIA operatives who miss them and desperately want them back...or, at the least, want to prevent them from becoming a permanent fixture in that region.

The game itself is one more entry in the glut of cover-shooters, though certainly a memorable and polished one at that. The Unreal 3 engine is shown off well here with terrific scripted effects, and a grand vision that is well-realized from the concept stage and up. Overall this game features a high level of polish, from sights to sounds. 
The narrative itself flows into a fever dream by the end, giving Dubai an otherworldly and surreal vibe while barely  giving recourse to the player's actions throughout. The moral ground is tread uneasily by the fact the gameplay is consistently gratuitous and exploitative; kind of like Apocalypse Now, but starring The Expendables (cgi-blood spurts and all).
So that's to say, if you're the type to think about the game; it's a real humdinger and I'm not sure it really gets all the way over.
My major gripe with the game came in the form of the frustration emerging from FUBAR difficulty playthrough; i think despite becoming fine-tuned to the game, all and any shortcomings of the gamedesign become quite magnified. Though not enough to stand in the way of some fun, but it will certainly make the veins bulge out of your neck. Most problematic being the unreliable geometry of cover, and second being unreliable pain-states of enemy-npcs. The game forces you to be exceptionally precise while the game-mechanics cannot always keep up lending you or your soldiers to be killed much too frequently. You simply cannot move behind some cover, where even switching directions could expose you to instant death.
 
Friendly-npcs can be ordered to engage particular targets, throw flashbangs, grenades, snipe, and assassinate targets. When and where is all contextual, and more often you will only be able to order them to engage one hostile at time. I think it's a good mechanic, that needed to go further (thinking of Brothers in Arms). Friendly Ai is benign and mostly unhelpful. Sometimes they're completely ineffectual against a target unless ordered.

I think that what's on offer here is a solid game, held afloat by an ambitious narrative. The voice acting is quite good too, with many familiar voices...too familiar...Nolan North sounds like Troy Baker, and between those two you have every 7th gen game hero covered. This would have been a 10/10 if voiced by Bobcat Goldthwait. 
Anyway, it's all about crazy alternate reality Dubai and some weird Bioshock-esque allegory here & a 7.5/10

Of all the games that have graced the hard drive of my PC over the years (a number that I am happy to say is quite high), Spec Ops: The Line is one that impacted me most. Too often throughout the history of video games the idea of war and killing is glorified and the effects it has on those involved are entirely unrealistic.  The most prevalent perpetrator of this is the very popular Call of Duty series. It’s refreshing when a game forgoes this and paints war as what it is, a bloodbath. Soldiers and their commanding officers are forced to make impossible decisions; one’s actions have consequences and the trauma that comes from taking another’s life isn’t shrugged off. Spec Ops: The Line, published by 2K games and developed by Yager Development, is one of the few war-based video game titles that effectively shows this other side.

The Line puts the player in the shoes of Captain Martin Walker, the leader of a three-man Delta Force team sent in to perform reconnaissance in Dubai after the United States Army fails in their evacuation attempt.  As the plot of the story progresses, it becomes clear that the situation in Dubai is far more complicated. A 3-way conflict has been born from the high tension situation. The bulk of the 33rd American Army infantry battalion has split into two factions. The main force is led by Colonel John Konrad and acts as an occupying force while commiting atrocities against the civilians, while the “exiles” are a splinter faction of the 33rd who staged a coup in response to the atrocities. In addition to this, the CIA has organized insurgent forces from the shadows and directed them to attack both the 33rd and the “exiles.”

As Walker leads his troops through the storyline, the player is forced to make terrible choices and commit atrocities of necessity to survive.  Much of the combat in the game consists of fighting and killing fellow American soldiers. Some of the choices the player must make consist of: choosing between saving innocent civilians or a fellow soldier with valuable information, choosing between killing a man who stole water for his family or killing the American soldier who was ordered to kill the former’s family in response to the theft, and choosing to shoot or spare the civilian mob who you find after they have lynched one of your squad mates. These choices influence the story in a way similar to that of hypertext, each one leading to a different outcome to the situation; albeit, all outcomes leave little hope and there is no “right” choice.

The Line also uses the literary strategy of an unreliable narrator. Throughout the story the player character Walker is shown to hallucinate, a result of his PTSD from his former service. These hallucinations grow steadily worse as the plot progresses and Walker is forced to commit greater atrocities. At one point he is forced to fire a white phosphorus mortar when he believes his squad is hopelessly outnumbered only to find that, after the smoke clears, he was firing on a group of the 33rd who were sheltering civilians, civilians that the mortar killed down to the last one. In the end, having lost both of his squadmates, Walker’s mental state has become so unhinged that nothing is as it seems. It turns out that Konrad and some of the 33rd were just hallucinations. After this reveal, the player then chooses how to end the story. One can choose to kill himself (Walker) or attempt to kill Konrad.  If one does kill Konrad, evac will come for Walker and the final decision of the game is presented: go home, tormented by inner demons, or kill the evac squad.

Spec Ops: The Line is one of the strongest examples in recent history for why video games can be viewed as literature. It sparked much debate in gaming society and even lead critic Brendan Keogh to write a book length review of his playthrough. Its story and execution serve as an homage to Joseph Conrad’s Heart of Darkness in a new medium that can accomplish more by putting the audience directly into the character’s shoes instead of witnessing it from the outside.

Spec Ops: The Line comes from a perfect time in story driven videogames in my opinion, where games didn't concern themselves with being long just for the sake of it. The game can be completed in about 5 hours, and its length is perfect for the story it tells, the game plays like a 1.5 hour action war movie with gameplay. 

For those of you that want to play the game on modern hardware and not have it feel like a buggy piece of ♥♥♥♥ with its terribly ported PC controls, download flawless widescreeen even if you are not on a widescreen monitor, as it allows a simple FOV slider and FPS scaling that fix the games performance and input issues instantly.

The gameplay is simple, its a cover third-person over-the-shoulder shooter game, it plays similar to uncharted (and Nolan North is incredibly recognizable as the main character in this one as well as the Uncharted series which is my favorite series of all time.

The story is great, its intriguing and makes you think about the reality of war, it also leaves several questions for the player to think about upon its end, with multiple endings and choices throughout that effect the ending the player will get. This game was way ahead of its time in that regard, while the changes to the story based on your decisions are not incredibly noticeable, it can also not be noticeable that you are even making these decisions, most of them are simple gameplay decisions that happen naturally without a prompt that simply says choose a or b (though there are still a few of these)

Overall I love this game, I think it succeeds at what it trys to be, its not super unique, its not the most incredibly memorable game of the time period, but for a game you can easily pick up for less than $5, its well worth it in my opinion.

On the one hand it's amazing at depicting the sensualization of violence in media, similar to Hotline Miami but different in it's approach. Walker is an amazing portrayal and critique of those generic American hollywood protagonists we see in movies and games who use ethics and morals to justify violence. It starts off just like all the other propaganda films, with the American national anthem and an American flag and Muslim terrorists that don't even speak the correct language (game takes place in Dubai, locals speak Farsi and Turkish), but it uses this stereotypical imagery to both subvert expectations and critique the industry supporting this propaganda ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Real life isn't Rambo, there is no right way to kill a person. It shows how one can delude themselves into committing horrible acts by telling themselves it was the right thing to do or it's for the greater good. And once it becomes too much to bear, the ridiculousness of the horrors in front of you too clear to deny, how we shift the blame on others or try to argue how there was no other choice.

"It takes a strong man to deny what's right in front of him."

...On the other hand, the game is marketed as "A Third-Person modern military Shooter designed to challenge players' morality by putting them in the middle of unspeakable situations.". My morality was never challenged. I never felt like I was doing something wrong, simply because I was not given a choice by the game. When I realized I would be killing civilians with white phosphorus, I tried to avoid firing, but the game forced me to do it in order to progress. I realized how delusional Riggs plan was to leave thousands of people to die of thirst, but the game forced me to do it in order to progress (side note but a theory I love about Riggs' plan was that it was never meant to fail and actually destroy the water. Walker just shifted the blame of his own failure to Riggs and acted like it was Riggs' plan all along). The only part where I felt genuinely bad was when I realized at the start of the game that the 33rd weren't set to kill the civilians and were just helping them out. Like Walker and his squad I made a false presumption without the full story and decided to open fire at them. However, even if I did figure out what was going on, it wouldn't have mattered, because I'd still be forced to kill them to continue the game.

Is my morality really being challenged here? Nope. If it actually gave me a choice like Undertale, then yeah maybe. But all of this makes a lot of sense if you look at it from the perspective of Walker the character and not the player, so I choose to do that, even though that clearly wasn't the intention of the devs as can be seen from the marketing.

Also some scenes were executed flawlessly despite not being cutscenes. The desperation of the first sandstorm scene, the horrifying atmosphere in the white phosphorus scenes, the scared confusion of the mannequin heavy scene, the panic of trying to shoot the burning people rushing towards you in the last chapter, it was all executed flawlessly.

Now to the gameplay. It sucks. I didn't mind it TOO much because I generally like cover shooters but this game isn't it. The controls are clunky, too many actions require the same button, and there's just no depth really. So much of the game is spent fighting hordes of never ending enemies over and over again, it's boring and just pads the play time. If you want to play the game just play on normal or easy because this ♥♥♥♥ isn't worth your time. Some say this is intentional and adds to the narrative, I say it is bad game design pretending like it's good writing. And ♥♥♥♥ heavies dude like how can they survive 2 frags, 2 stickies and 20 417 shots to the head and still proceed to plug walk over to my cover and gun me down like it's a guy in heavy armor not ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ iron man

I had to think about this game for hours after I completed it to figure out what I thought of it. It's one of the most psychologically twisted games I've ever played that messes with your head near constantly. I finished the game in a single sitting and I'm glad I did because there was a lot to mentally unpack.

From a purely mechanical standpoint, it's a third person shooter. I'd go so far as to say it's pretty run-of-the mill in that regard. Enemies a little tougher than you'd expect, like most games of its era, less ammo than you'd expect, and tons of goons to fight. Also, it is a cover based shooter, so expect to spend a lot of time crouching behind walls.

The way that this game is different in who you fight and what that means. I have to speak VERY carefully, otherwise I may give something critical away, as the real charm of the game comes from the mystery that unravels as you play it. Understand that the player takes the role of a Delta Force operator, attempting to discern what is going on in the city of Dubai after a cataclysmic sandstorm enveloped the city. The group is going in blind, and the line between friend and foe is pretty blurry.

The game is short, only 5-6 hours long, depending on how many times you need to restart sections, so I'd recommend you get it on sale, as the playthrough won't last long. I would also recommend that take some time to decompress after you're done playing it. Some of the parts are pretty hard to watch, and the ideas in the game can be down right disturbing. 

I'd recommend this game to people who enjoy shooter games that focus on the storytelling. Something like Call of Duty: Black Ops (the original), as long as you can deal with a gun combat system vaguely like Mass Effect 3. I would not recommend this for someone who wants to play a turn-your-brain-off military shooter, glorifying soldiers and warfare. This game does quite the opposite, and it's a shock it ever made it to release.

A fantastic story with a premise different from the typical games of the genre, Spec Ops: The Line has tried to do something ambitious in a short game. It succeeds to a fair extent, but there are some factors holding it back. The bad control system and extremely janky gameplay are persistent hurdles which consistently obstruct enjoyment. The game is fairly challenging but feels unfair due to the said hurdles, which do not arise as natural gameplay obstacles to be overcome by skill, but rather as hurdles generated unfairly by the poor responses to controls. To a large extent, the story would have been a better fit for an RPG-style game like Mass Effect, as the frantic pace of Spec Ops (although an important element of the story itself) does not seem very conducive to the absorption of a story like this. Overall, a decent short game with a great story but the gameplay is a major issue that any player would need to be willing to overlook to reach the great payoff of the final chapter.

Spec Ops: The Line is just another military shooter on the market. It came out in 2012 the same year as Call of Duty: Black Ops II. [i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i] is really intriguing story told through fairly uninteresting third-person shooter gameplay. To the game's credit, however, it is relatively short at around 5-6 hours, so by the time I started to feel the fatigue of the shallow gameplay, it was already over.

As for the story, if you've ever seen the film [i]Apocalypse Now[/i] (you should still definitely watch it regardless of whether or not you play this), you'll have a good idea of what to expect from this game, though even knowing that, it subverts what you might expect. It's a criticism not only of the military and humanity's capacity for evil, but also the games industry and players themselves for blindly engaging in violent acts in games without ever really thinking about what they're doing. It's not saying that violence in video games is some major societal problem, but simply pointing to the absurdity of being forced to kill countless people in a game such as [i]Call of Duty[/i], and getting treated like a hero for it.

My only real complaint of the story and its message is that it loses some of the impact it may have had back when it released during a time of endless AAA military shooters. It feels like I'm not quite the right audience for this, that it was intended to be played by the people that would pick it up thinking it was just another mindless shooter game to waste time on, only to get... well, this.

It's a mediocre third person military shooter... but with an absurdly well-crafted story and presentation in which nearly every single detail matters. This is the type of game to play for the first time while knowing absolutely nothing about it. Stop reading right now if you haven't already been spoiled and play it for yourself.

Last warning.

I'm serious.

Okay.

The White Phosphorus scene makes No Russian look like Slime Rancher. No Russian is legendary but you don't have to kill any innocent civilians if you so choose. There are zero consequences to just letting Makarov and his friends mow everyone down. You do have to eventually kill the cops but until you exit the airport you can play as a pacifist. That is not the case in this game. You- PERSONALLY- press the button that murders all of the innocent civilians. There is no way around it. You have to do it to progress, every single time. You have plenty of other choices to commit war crimes or stay your hand, to kill or spare people, to frag a literal lynch mob uh I mean a group of "innocent" civilians, etc, but the white phosphorus is THE definitive scene of this game. And what a scene it is. You can't talk about this game without talking about that. But unfortunately it's all anyone really seems to remember, which is a real shame, because the rest of the plot is ALSO REALLY REALLY GOOD!

Without spoiling anything else, it's like Heart Of Darkness (or Apocalypse Now) meets Metal Gear Solid 5: The Phantom Pain, with elements of System Shock 2 (or Bioshock), Jacob's Ladder (or Silent Hill 2), and of all other things, Doki Doki Literature Club. Yes I am being completely 100% dead freaking serious. A lot of love and care went into the story's design and presentation; nearly every single detail is important. Every line of dialogue matters. The animations of your character change over time to reflect how he changes as a person over the course of the game and the choices he- through you- has made. The physical wounds he suffers (in cutscenes) last until the very end, permanently altering his in game model. And I personally classify this game as meta psychological horror because the loading screens emotionally manipulate YOU, the PLAYER.

This game is criminally underrated as an experience, namely because gaming journalists reduced it down to a wannabe Call Of Duty Modern Warfare 2 ripoff back during the period of time where gaming journalists were still somewhat trustworthy in the public's eyes, expressly because people only talk about the willy pete nuke. And that's really unfortunate because this deserved so much better than it got.

If I had one criticism, it's that none of your choices have any meaningful lasting consequences until the very last 5 minutes of the game. But that's not so much a criticism as it is a social commentary on the us military and the policies of foreign martial entities on other nations' soil because the intentions don't matter at all. Only the outcome matters. And the outcome is innocent children burned alive by million dollar weapons. I don't mean to get heavy but this game invites the heavy discussions about actual real-world problems that are still happening today over a decade later.

All the things you have heard about Spec Ops: The Line being a narrative masterpiece are true. It tells a powerful and relevant story in a deeply immersive way and sets a bar for storytelling that no other military shooter has come close to matching. That story is supported by characters that feel real, each of whom has their own arc as the story progresses. The environmental storytelling is rich, the visuals are breathtakingly beautiful, and the soundtrack more than pulls its weight. The shooting itself is nothing special, but the varied level design and focus on verticality force you to think tactically and keep the combat interesting.

spec ops: the line is a 2012 third-person shooter developed by a german studio named yager development and published by 2K. it's a reboot of the spec ops games from the late 90s/early 2000s. the game is critically remembered well despite being considered a commercial failure due to low sales, which sadly effectively ended the series for good. it's developed a cult following since it's release, mostly due to the meaningful story which paints a realistic picture of the horrors of war. the story is definitely the strong point, as the gameplay lacks comparatively. it's less polished compared to other games from the era, the combat can be clunky and has a couple annoying flaws, but nothing major. it plays like a less polished version of gears of war. the graphics and setting itself dubai are both at the very least decent, but overall it's the story and plot you want this game for. it's not just some military propaganda game, it actually has a really important story and is, in my opinion, one of the more underrated video games of the early 2010s. the main story will take you anywhere from probably 4-8 hours depending on difficulty level and what not, but going for a completionist run which requires one play-though on hard which unlocks the extra hard difficulty, meaning you'll probably end up taking again anywhere from 10-20 hours, but not more. this is definitely one of the better third person shooter games i have ever played and it is well worth the money the get this game (on sale especially).

[h1]Where is the Line? What is the Line? [/h1]
Basic premise/Story

Usually, whenever I play a shooting game there are always principles you just can’t do without. Such as: the main cast shooting with guns. Enemies dying. Some sequence in which you kill off a whole wave or more of enemies trying to gun your position. And a story to pull your cast into. Which is usually a rescue, investigation, elimination, etc. Spec Ops: The Line Has all of these qualities… Except with a clever twist. What happens when you twist the narrative into something more psychological? And making the players feel something other than fun? And more along the lines of thought-provoking, the mental consequence of following orders or disobeying them to our very own desires. Still, feel like it’s one of those regular shooters? If not. Well, you’re in for one hell of a welcome party Delta Team. Good luck.

[h1]Find Konrad. With Whatever Means Necessary [/h1]
Unique Gameplay

I want to say the first hour and into the second the game turns from a regular run-of-the-mill shooter into something far more sinister and insidious. When you delve deeper into the game and follow Delta’s team progress into Dubai. Where you’ll find underneath the superficial orders Walker(Your main character) keeps sprouting on and on. Find Colonel Konrad.

Although, finding him can be a bi*** to do when sandstorms come rolling in. And worse you can’t roll innately. So you’ll be running like hell from cover to cover. Speaking of covers can’t turn properly when under the cover system the game employs. So you’ll have to stand up and then run towards the adjacent concrete block for cover. Thankfully, you can vault over covers and even kick enemies if they’re on the other side. A pretty brutal surprise kick to the face never fails to give me a chuckle. Aside from the somewhat troublesome cover system, the game could’ve used a bit more enemy variety to spice up what kinds of enemies you face. Players will often face standard enemy mobs of regular people with guns, snipers, shotguns, and a crazy knife guy who charges you sometimes. Which is pretty illogical when everyone has a gun hah. Some heavily armored dude. And that’s pretty much it. 

These flaws I see in the game aren’t significant in retrospect. However, I feel it's still worth noting to readers. The game isn't perfect. But it does have quite a lot of well-deserved praise that deserved to be mentioned.

[h1]Something White, but Marred with Blood [/h1]
Final thoughts/Ruminations

The graphics still hold up today and the setting of Dubai ravaged by storms and destruction is a compelling place to hold the game’s grounds. There are levels in the game where it’s not just running and shooting enemies all the time. So it's nice to get some highly intense sequences to keep the action moving and make the pacing exciting. This is followed by decisions you can make during downtime moments in the story which can affect the outcome quite a bit. I won’t say more about this. But I think it's a cool mechanic the developers of Yager did. Additionally, I found the level design to be incredible and didn’t feel it was overused. Whereas other games would gleefully copy-paste such level designs and moments. Spec Ops holds the belief if it is done well, do it once. Don’t abuse it. And the level design conveys that belief in practice time and time again. Not to the point of over-saturation, with explosions upon explosions. And nonsensical slaughter everywhere. But here it is done with purpose and innovation to make it feel realistic to the story and narrative. 

The story holds up incredibly well and I feel subverts the shooter trope we often see to convey to the player's something more than the run-of-the-mill shooting game. The voice work is splendid and I felt every raw emotion the Delta team fared throughout the game. More human and not robotic monotone machines all the time. The main cast oozes personality which is contrasted well by the villains who are given the same wonderful voice-acting treatment. Nice pacing and narrative inject some heavy themes like the psychological suffering of war on our soldiers and the mental toll it has not only on soldiers but our enemies and civilians as well. 

Very much appreciate how the game makes full use of the mature rating from the ESRB. There are some scenes in the game which can be hard to stomach. But, the impact/s it has on the Delta team and what they do in the aftermath is pivotal to the game's narrative and structure. These scenes being graphically depicted in their full glory would not have the same impact if it was toned down or censored. 

Also, appreciate a very small detail of how the Delta team suffers through wear, tear, exhaustion, and painful wounds as you progress further in the story. As if detailing to the player how much the team is going through to continue on and that not all victories lead you away unscathed. The clever narrative is also joined by an equally great soundtrack with audio mixing to give off a distorted vibe of something wrong going on under the surface. Rock tracks successfully give off both highly packed action set pieces with adrenaline pumping. Both of these work in tandem to set the mood for cutscenes you encounter during the game. And I think fits very well in each scene. I didn't get bored when the music started to blare rock solid tracks or unsettling tracks.

Honestly, my hours flew by as I progressed further into the story, and aside from the flaws I mentioned above everything else that I praised helped to immerse me into the game’s narrative. Making the gameplay quite satisfying since I didn’t expect what would happen next and allowing me the freedom to continue without major obstacles on normal difficulty(This is labeled as Combat Op). My 5-6 hour playthrough with Spec Ops: The Line, didn’t give me major hurdles throughout on normal difficulty. It felt balanced and fair. 

The story doesn’t overstay its welcome and fully utilizes almost everything above, regarding praises and flaws to the fullest extent. To create a solid third-person shooter game. A must-play for any veteran who loves shooting games and any player with little to no experience with shooting games. I highly recommend the game to anyone looking for something above the average to shoot enemies to get to your objective and the game ends. If you want something unique with a powerful narrative that sticks with you long after the end credits roll. Look no further than Spec Ops: The Line. 

[i]Perhaps at the end. Can you answer what “The Line” means for you?[/i]

This is a good story with some complex plots.  It took me two runs to understand what the story is really talking about.  The game is recommended for any one loves story rich games.

All achievements require at least two runs, with the first on Suicide mission difficulty and Fubar in the second run.

As you likely know, the story is great. If at any point whilst playing you disagree with that then I beg you to push through because you will agree by the end. But the story had me pretty hooked the whole time. It may not live up to the amount of hype it has received but nun the less you will understand why people praise the story.

Notice however, that the story is all that is praised. That's because unfortunately, the game play is a bit poor. Mouse sensitivity doesn't go low enough for me so I played with gamepad (which I got the impression the game wanted me to anyway) And the shooting can be a bit all over the place. One minute you're back to back popping heads like balloons, 1 bullet per bad guy and the next you're laying 50 bullets, multiple of which are in the head, and the target will flinch once before diving back behind his wall, and he'll still hit you first when he pops back up. The guns flip violently between feeling impactful and feeling like laser pointers that the enemy aren't even aware of. And attempting to delegate to friendly ai took two to three business days.

The level design is my biggest gripe however as cover shooters with hard coded cover mechanics require levels that compliment it well. On the whole they do but I found myself in situations more than once where I needed to abandon cover and shoot whilst detached from a wall because of where the enemy were (the game blatantly hates you doing this as it lowers your accuracy when not using cover). Then, in those exciting moments where you're using cover and dug into a firefight, someone will throw a grenade right in your lap whilst you have no where to go and couldn't take a flick to the ear let alone one more bullet when attempting to change cover.

Finally, whilst large chunks of the game aren't hard, when I did die I died multiple times to the same thing and unfortunately in the majority of these scenarios I'd say the clash between level design and mechanics/ai behaviour contributed a large factor to these moments. The levels are on the whole fun until you die and have to do any part again. The best way I can describe it is that a high octane fire fight is only high octane the first time. When repeated they're not. And Spec Ops: The Line needs the octane in it's scenes in order for them to have the right impact.

Over all though it is definitely one to experience for the story alone, and whilst the gameplay can be poor, it still contributes well to the story and needs to be there. The story wouldn't work the same if the player wasn't controlling walker, as the player wouldn't be affected the same way if it were for example a film.

I completed the campaign in 5.4 hours of play time, I paid <£5 and have to say if I'd have paid the £19.99 the game is listed at, I'd still leave it feeling it's worth what I paid. As well as feeling quite shook and depressed from experiencing this story.

When I was in 12th grade I wrote a 2000 word essay in English comparing this game to Apocalypse Now. I got an A. The reason I could was because Spec Ops has that much content to work with.

I think the subcategory of war stories that address our relationship to war as depicted in the media is woefully undernourished. All the subconscious shorthand films and games use to set up their conflicts - race, violence, rhetoric about victory, revenge, ego - all these things we agree are toxic go out the window in an adrenaline-fuelled life or death situation. (It's 9/11, alright? That's the origin.) There are few things that can be more comforting than gliding your way through a seemingly morally justified war without any threat of consequence, and post-COD 4 modern millitary shooters are the perfect place to sink into that. Of course, judging the actions you perform in a video game might ring a little hollow once you remember that they're not actually real, but Spec Ops: The Line, I think, is more interested in questioning the "why" and the "how" than the "what". 

Everything about the game's setting is designed to lure you in to assessing it as the black-and-white morality you find in most other war games - metaphorically and literally. The all-American team, the bantering, the trigger-happy foreign insurgents-who-aren't-actually-foreign-because-they're-in-their-home-country. But in truth, as Captain Martin Walker obstinately refuses to acknowledge, the whole city is on a knife's edge ceasefire between the Damned 33'rd Battalion evac team who declared martial law amidst dwindling food supplies, and those very insurgents who don't aren't a fan of summary executions for stealing bread to live, thank you very much. And into this drops some American Idiot who thinks murdering everyone is going to solve everything. Oh well, no more sandcastles for us.

The core of the story is Walker and therefore the player being powered by all those feelings I mentioned earlier - a desire for justice and heroism being mistaken for an ability to achieve either of those things. A desperate, often pathetic need to live up to the reputation of those he idolises, seemingly given permission to throw morality out the window by those exact reputations. In reality, it's all one great big conga line of enablers trying to feel better about themselves. Walker is partially a product of the the society he lives in, and in becoming a garbage human being, passes the baton down to his subordinates.

Refusing to accept responsibility for his actions, not a bored need for dopamine, is the catalyst for Walker sinking down into that numb shooter mindset where all context is kept as vague as possible. It goes about as well as you might expect.

The gameplay is functional, but the story will keep you hooked to the point that you don't notice. This game deserves all the praise it gets.

[b]CLUNKY CONTROLS[/b] you take cover using the same key you use to sprint... this has lead to many situations where I intended to sprint away from an incoming grenade, only to inadvertently "take cover" right next to it and die because I was trying to un-stick myself from the cover. Seriously, this is going to be a major source of frustration for most of you.

[b]BAD GAME DESIGN:[/b] one example of this is the whole "scarcity of ammo" thing. That's actually pretty cool, I like it, it forces you to be careful with your shots. GoW5 did this wonderfully and it was a lot of fun. The problem with SpecOps' implementation though is that *guns disappear from the ground quickly*.

Say you're in cover and you are methodically taking shots, conserving your ammo, headshotting the enemies one at a time. By the time the fight is over, half of their guns will have despawned, leaving you with no source of new ammo. This "feature" encourages you to aggressively push towards enemies and try to grab their guns for ammo, but on the higher difficulties this is extremely difficult as you'll simply be killed for pushing out of cover.

This lead to a situation where I ended up in a new stage of the level with limited ammo while under heavy fire from a Heavy unit and a mounted machine gunner at the same time. Every time I tried it, I ran out of ammo trying to kill the heavy, and the guns from the enemies had despawned, leaving me with no new source of ammo. I ended up restarting the level entirely and very carefully conserved my ammo to pass that level. It's just frustrating and poorly implemented; I never had this issue with GoW5 on the hardest difficulty.

[b]BUGS:[/b] after completing the prior level, I ended up at the next stage. Finally, alas! I had made it... only to find that I was stopped from proceeding further by an invisible barrier.

I tried reloading the checkpoint, restarting the game, looking online - nothing could help me.

So that's it. I pushed myself through 7 frustrating hours of this game for a plot that honestly, is never really explained very well, only to find myself stuck due to a bug.

Spec Ops: The Line leaves you emotionally scarred. It's tough to write a review that encompasses it's nature without giving it away. "Rule Number One: Don't talk about Spec Ops: The Fight Club."
Yet this game deserves to be talked about. It's the interactive adaptation of "Heart of Darkness" that takes the liberty of not just describing a soldier's hell but goes out of it's way to abstract it's content to beg the question about whom this game truly is: about Cpt. Martin Walker or about you, the player?

SOTL makes you think about the terms "duty", "ambition", "obsession", "morality" and "warcrime" in a very less romanticized light than most other media would want you to, for it is uncomfortable to the highest degree. It takes you on a trip to hell, showing not just the bright, flashy sight of the good guys fighting for what's right, killing the baddies and saving the day; it shows you the full package of mental deterioration paired against an onslaught of violent kill-or-be-killed situations that require heavier and heaver copium overdoses to withstand – but the more Cpt. Walker rationalizes, the more surreal everything becomes and you stark asking yourself: who am I really playing? And what am I doing? 

Also, it still manages to make /v/eddit mad even ten years after it's release, which is probably the biggest testimony for it's quality. 

I recommend it for you, whole-heartedly. 
Just remember: all of this could've been avoided if you had not listened to this recommendation.

Honestly one of the best games from a story telling perspective. It is one of the few  games that remains incredibly impactful, even if the player already knows what is going to happen. While it isn't perfect, the story manages to get it's message across very clearly, and perfectly shows the descent into darkness Captain Walker goes through. The gameplay is the weaker aspect of the game, as it isn't all that unique, and has all the jank of most early 2010's games. Despite this, most of the time the levels are fun and well designed, until you get hit in the face with the jank and are forced to redo it multiple times. There were only a few times this happened to me, but it is incredibly frustrating when the button prompt to do an action doesn't appear so Walker stands there like a statue, and forces you to repeat the entire section. As a result of dead enemies and dropped weapons despawning after you die and reset, you can occasionally be left in a situation where you have to let your AI squad mates dispatch any enemies until you can pick up a weapon. As far as difficulty goes, it is mostly fair (playing on the hardest difficulty offered on a first playthrough.) Most levels are pretty simple but a few interesting mechanics here and there help make them more interesting. Overall, the gameplay is nothing to write home about, but merely serves as a vessel for the excellent story and performance by Nolan North. While not being perfect, the story still manages to hint enough things and have enough subtlety that any twist can be understandable, and nothing feels like it's truly out of left field. 
I'm incredibly glad I picked this up, as it was just as good as all the talk of the game says it is. I would also highly recommend looking at videos analyzing this game, as they help point out some of the less noticeable stuff.
Overall I would say the gameplay is about a 7/10, but the story caries the game so hard that I would give the game a 9/10. Definitely worth playing, and replaying.

Spec Ops: The Line was one of 2012's biggest surprises.

Summary:
With amazing graphics and atmosphere wrapped around tight gameplay and superb voice acting, the game takes you through a dark story by taking control of  Captain Martin Walker, the leader of a small reconnaissance team sent into a war torn Dubai to find and rescue any surviving members of the 33rd (a group of soldiers) and bring home a man of great importance, Colonel John Konrad, head of the 33rd.
 It's not your run-of-the-mill shooter by any means; no, the game digs a lot deeper than just killing people. 
It becomes a half psychological thriller, half third-person shooter. 
There's multiple endings, and each of them is more horrific than the last. 
By today's standards, the gameplay won't shock or really impress but it's good, challenging and it does its job at pushing the narative forward. The controls are a weird mix of Uncharted and Call of Duty and it mostly defines all of the craziness of the shooter genre wars,

Overall:
+ Good Story
+ Fun Shooter Mechanics
+ Emotional
+ Touching Moral Moments
+ Brilliant Post-Disaster Dubai Setting
+ Solid Cover-Based Shooter Gameplay
+ Interactive Environments and Useful Partners
- Weak Multiplayer

Spec Ops: The Line was... a little disappointing to me. Granted, I'd heard a lot of praise for this game over the years, so my expectations may have been unfairly high for the game. No comments on the multiplayer since I only did the campaign.

It's the story in particular that people always gush over. It was kinda unique, sure, but I didn't really feel it -- at least in the way it wanted me to, I think. The overly buggy in-game cutscenes didn't help either. The game's really short too, only taking me around 6-7 hours to beat the campaign.

Very generic gameplay-wise, with average cover combat with some real janky controls. Sprinting is difficult when you have a magnetic sphincter, latching onto anything as you try to run out of harm's way, and being the Goldilocks of cover-based shooters that he is, your character refuses to aim over or around many completely normal chest-high walls. Any weapon with a scope had painfully unresponsive aiming to a point where I had to borderline whip my mouse to actually move it up, though this might have been a result of intentionally lowering the sensitivity in the configs due to the in-game settings being too fast even on 1. By the way, what's up with encrypting the config files while only providing the barest of in-game settings?

Your AI pals are very inept, frequently getting downed out in the open despite their thick skulls absorbing about 8 times more damage than you can. Ordering them to attack an enemy is pointless, since you'll be pointing at the target already and will easily kill them in the 30 seconds it takes for one of them to actually do something about it.

The music and sounds were decent. Visually -- though I realize where the game takes place -- I never much cared for the "everything brown" style. The excessive shakycam in cutscenes was very unnecessary too.

In conclusion, from I gathered, the game is less about making an enjoyable gameplay experience and more trying to convey a thought-provoking message through its story, for better or worse. Considering the short length of the campaign, I may come back to it some day to see if I'll see it in a different light. For now, however, I will have to say I [b]wouldn't recommend[/b] the game, unless it's on sale.

A satisfying slice of anti-war magical realism.

The good
The story that lurches from COD, to the horrors of war to hallucinatory fever dream.
The moment to moment on-rails cover shooter combat is actually pretty satisfying.
The environments are destructible, which can lead to some pretty cool ways to take down enemies.
Voice acting and script is solid.
Finished it in 5 hours, and I was satisfied with that. Didn't overstay its welcome.

The meh
I enjoyed it with keyboard and mouse, though reload and pick up and melee and vault are unfortunately bound to the same keys.
The story wears its Apocalypse Now and Fight Club influences pretty brazenly.

The bad
I'm sure multiplayer is dead as a doornail, so if that's your thing, go elsewhere.

The verdict
It's kind of a must-play classic in gaming history at this point, forcing the player to be complicit in the horrors of a conflict that seem even more a grey area once we realize that our protagonist may be a bit of an unreliable narrator. Far Cry 3 treads similar territory, but The Line is darker and more single-minded.

Spec Ops The Line is a prime example of video games as art. To achieve its desired effect, it utilizes tools that no other form of media is currently able to. Though best played without any previous knowledge, I still highly recommend at least one playthrough even for those who have already seen important parts of the story.
