This was another title that I kept hearing about, that it's worth going through at least for the strong narrative. And yep, they were right. It's got a pretty solid story, althrough inspired by existing works. And it does a few winks at that here and there. But that shouldn't really detract from the appreciation. It's not very often that games have good and solid stories.

Unfortunately, all of that is in the body of a pretty generic and sometimes painfully mediocre third person shooter. One that often feels unpolished, and can sometimes get on your nerves. The save system especially is awful, with some pretty few and far between checkpoints. Which was especially aggravating since for some reason I died quite a bit in very stupid situations, not all of them my fault. And I wasn't even on any high difficulty or anything. Second to easiest, and it still managed to annoy me a few times, making me replay certain parts. One particular moment was when, in usual "quick-time" action setpiece moment, I had to guess exactly what the game wanted me to do, otherwise I kept dying over and over. Quite frustrating. I even turned down the difficulty to easiest in the last 2 missions.

The other issue with the vehicle that carries this story, as is the issue in a lot of games with strong and poignant narratives, is the dissonance caused by what you're doing in the game when playing vs the story it's trying to tell. This game could've really used a more gritty and realistically portrayed campaign, and not just your usual mass murdering escapade that you have in most shooters. I mean, for god sakes, I think you end up killing hundreds if not thousands of enemy soldiers throughout, in a Rambo-style shooting gallery. Last of us part 2 had it's own dissonance, but something like that could've really improved everything. But of course, we have to be sensible, and realize that not every studio will have that kind of astronomic budget and support behind it. With what they had, the team probably did the best they could. But maybe toning everything down, and killing a lot fewer people, wouldn't have cost much. 

But even with its fair share of negatives, the best parts still manage to shine through in the story. There's also quite a few little story touches in the actual gameplay, that I kind of missed myself and was made aware only after watching a pretty good analysis of the whole experience. It's also one of the rare games that focuses on an anti-war, anti-interventionist and anti-american exceptionalism story. And it could also be the only one where the protagonist kills american soldiers, and does so by the boat-load? I'm not sure I ever saw that in any game. Of course, those are deemed soldiers gone rogue, so of course there is that caveat. But still. It was a pleasant surprise that the main enemies weren't middle-easterners.

7/10 due to the strong narrative. With a Last of Us style game behind it, it could've jumped to a 8 or 9, probably.

Spec Ops: The Line is a competent cover shooter, touted for its deeper-than-average story, especially compared to other games of its genre, be it those released around the same time or those released today. 

Gameplay-wise, it's a standard cover shooter. You press a button to snap into cover and then pop out to aim and score headshots. Then you walk, listen to dialogue, and repeat this process until you reach the end. It ticks every box for a military-shooter of this type, including heavily armored, bullet-spongey, MG-wielding minibosses that are in stark contrast to the otherwise pretty realistic shooting, where everyone (including you) goes down pretty quickly.

Graphically it still holds up very well. Sandy, bright Dubai stands out from the gray-brown-drab color palette of many other games of this era. The PC port is fine, and 4K resolution really helps revitalize the game. Some of the more unique setpieces have great lighting and deliver exceptional, haunting atmosphere.

The game's most talked about aspect, its story, is not unique and has been told many times before in other media, but that doesn't change the fact that it's excellently written and acted and still gets its point across really well. Though completely different as far as setting goes, I'd say a more modern example of a game that told a story in such a way would be "Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice".

Great third person story shooter, if you down to get your hands dirty in the bloody sandstorms of Dubai while making complicated choices that can effect you / your squad and your characters stability. Be prepared to see lots and lots of warm sand and an insane madman of a evil enemy.

The storyline is based on the book ''Heart of Darkness'' from Joseph Konrad and it's a showcase of descent into guilt, regret, genocide, and how that affects the mind. It has some psychological themes as well. The game is also a critique to shooter games in my opinion. It questions your morality by breaking the fourth wall, but that fourth wall wouldn't exist if you weren't playing, if you didn't keep going...and for what? To see the end of the story? The end of the line? Disregarding what you need to do to get there?

If you hop into the game thinking of it as another third-person action shooter, killing everything in sight thinking of them as mindless NPCs...you're in for a big surprise.

 It is a very neatly weaved narrative that speaks to you, mostly. 

And remember that there is ALWAYS a choice, but you'll have to look for it. Is it disregarding orders or what the game tells you to do? Is it refusing to do certain actions and closing the game for good because it's too violent? Is it choosing survival over the mission, the mission means survival, what is it?

It's a great game. It is functionally very good, as well. Never encountered any bugs. The graphics are decent, and quite good for 2012. The movement can be clunky sometimes but nothing that will make you frustrated. On the hardest difficulty, there are some levels which can get quite annoying. The soundtrack is on point to how the story progresses, and you'll notice changes in voice acting and animation as you progress, as well.

Overall it's a great game. It's a very good narrative. It is passionately crafted and you can tell. At first a generic shooter for the first 2 hours, then it starts to become a descent into hell. I really wished the developer would've made a sequel or a title in the same lines. 

We don't see these types of games anymore, apparently it is almost 10 years old (damn i'm old), but it is very, very underrated, and totally worth your money, especially on such a cheap sale. 

If you enjoy narrative driven games with epic action moments and that make you question the story, the characters, and even yourself, go for it with no regrets.

I thought was one of the most immersive moments in gaming history was in Spec Ops when you are at the Radioman's tower and you get into the helicopter and you start using the minigun, I was thinking about how good it felt to finally be able to shoot as much as you wanted without worrying about the ammo, the whole game up until that point is an uphill struggle where you are locked into an intense firefight trying to look for an opening to shoot back at your enemies and cringing at every single shot you miss because you know how rare the ammo is and that you might have to ditch your M4 or another good weapon to trade it out for the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ AK47's or shotguns that the enemies use if you run completely out of ammo, and then you find yourself just MOWING down the guys who have been making you their ♥♥♥♥♥ the entire game, the amount of power you feel as the bullets cascade out of the six barrels and into the building, tearing apart concrete and splintering the wood, and not even to mention turning it directly onto the enemy, watching his spine severed by a barrage of tracer fire, his torso literally torn apart, his brain exploding from within his skull and the fragments of bone shredding into the flesh of what remains of his body. The segment only lasts about a minute as you wait for your final squad member to get up the stairs to the waiting helicopter. I remember thinking to myself that I never wanted that part to end. But eventually it does, and Sgt. Lugo climbs aboard, and I was just praying that the level wouldn't end at that point, but I found myself absolutely ecstatic when the helicopter takes off and starts climbing in the air. I was thinking about how good it would feel to watch those some destruction mechanics from earlier apply to the entire skyscraper, how good it would feel to let loose the minigun and the glass tower, how good it would feel to watch it all crash down onto the heads of all those soldiers still alive in the lower levels of the tower
And Cpt. Walker feels the exact same way as you do, he orders the pilot to fly around the helicopter, even though the pilot is practically begging to just fly away and leave the hellhole that is Dubai. He knows you could end it all right now, but Cpt. Walker and the player are both enthralled by the idea of the amount of death and destruction and carnage that the minigun is capable of doing onto the 33rd Infantry, you can finally make them pay and let loose everything you have on the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that got you here in the first place, and the power goes to Cpt. Walker's head as he orders the helicopter to circle around and around again and again until nothing is left of that tower
I think at that moment the player and the character in the game are more connected then anything else I've ever experienced in a video game, hands down

Keeping this short and simple as to not spoil this game, go buy it. I recommend it when it goes on sale and while the game is short, it'll have a lasting effect on you. The graphics are pretty good as well and it ran pretty well on my potato PC. You also get great voice acting and the amazing work of Nolan North. My only flaw with this game is the gameplay.  Don't get me wrong, shooters are fun and I do enjoy most of them. However, after the first 5 or so chapters, it got repetitive and I didn't find it as fun anymore. With all of that, do yourself a favour and play this gem. I give Spec Ops: The Line an 8.5/10 for its great plot but bland gameplay.

This game saved my life.

I am 27.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and adopted our son together. They are now both 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I found myself lost and miserable. I was self destructive. I got so mad one day from everything spiraling out of my control that I punched some concrete in a moment of overwhelming emotion. That caused me to break my 5th metacarpal in my right hand... my working hand... my games hand.. the hand that I held and carried my children to bed with.. The hand I desperately needed to make sure I could continue to provide.

After learning of the severity of my self-inflicted damage, I was borderline suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man with no history of depression or anxiety. I have never had fits of rage, or been one to break down and cry, but I was in a low spot that just really buried me from being able to see the light on the other side.

Having nothing better to do, I searched for a game I could play, ONE HANDED while I recovered. I somehow stumbled upon this game and read some of the reviews. I decided that it had to be worth a shot... I must admit, I didn't beat the game, or play nearly as long as some of you. In fact, I may have only played this game a day or two.. With that being said, after doing so, I had a new found joy and hope for life. I was able to put behind me the pain and suffering that had been cast over me. I was able to experience other peoples joy and happiness. I was able to see the fruits of my "labor". I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ minutes to this music long enough to realize that I was going to be okay.

After coming to that realization, I turned the game off, and I went back to work. It hurt my hand like hell but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so damn sorry for myself, and I became the father I needed to be in that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving as.

Today, I am close friend with my kids mother. We don't fight, or argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents, and friends.

I now have 3 kids. My third child is, wait for it, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my own separation, and we just stumbled in to each others life unexpectedly. We have been in a relationship for a year now, and are very happy together.

Moral of the story, you never know what life holds in store for you, and if I would have given up when all the odds were stacked against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

[i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i] is a cult classic third-person shooter. A military shooter disguised as an anti-war work that's actually a searing critique of the relationship between player and videogame, this title offers a solid campaign to lure players in and an amazing exercise in self-evaluation of the genre by the end. Though the multiplayer mode in this is a waste of time and the squad-based gameplay can sometimes aggravate, [i]Spec Ops[/i] offers an unforgettable journey into the horrors of war and our drive to blindly pursue it. A must-play for any fan of shooters/military games.

You play as Captain Martin Walker, a U.S. soldier leading a three-man squad into the heart of a ruined Dubai. Attempting to locate a Colonel Konrad who went missing in the region while organizing an evacuation effort, you're faced with an onslaught of unlikely resistance and are faced with choices that yield terrible consequences. Who will you come out the other side as once you cross the line?

[i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i] is the latest installment in the older [i]Spec Ops[/i] series of war shooters. This entry bucked the trend of AAA shooters upon its release that began with 2007's [i]Call of Duty: Modern Warfare[/i], which shifted the time and setting of games from WWII to the modern Middle East. In doing so, the games had an effect of desensitizing players by sensationalizing military operations in the MidEast. This game refocuses its critical eye on the horrors of war and man unleashed, fitting alongside pioneers of this genre such as [i]Heart of Darkness[/i] and [i]Apocalypse Now[/i].

As a game, [i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i] offers a fine third-person shooting experience. The crux of the gameplay is squad-based tactical combat: players command two AI-driven squadmates, Lugo and Adams, to perform offensive or diversionary maneuvers while the player performs the brunt of the combat. The AI is intelligent enough to handle itself without orders, allowing players who wish to go it alone to do that too - though at times the computers can cause issue when they expose themselves and put you at risk by being downed, since their deaths are Game Over too. In general, you'll get good gameplay out of this given the standards at the time.

[i]Spec Ops[/i] does include a multiplayer mode, though it is entirely forgettable and barely functional nowadays. Public matches are nigh impossible to come across, and if you do manage to put together a private match you'll find a tedious experience that clashes with the cover system and, moreover, the game's values. It is no surprise to learn that the multiplayer mode was a publisher-demanded inclusion, and as such should be considered a non-factor when purchasing. If you're playing this, you're doing it for the single player campaign.

The depiction of anti-war messaging in war shooters predates [i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i]. [i]Modern Warfare 2[/i]'s infamous "No Russian" mission, for instance, predates this by a few years. But where this game does innovate is by melding the anti-war message with a study on player choice. Atrocities done by the player in the name of - of what? To see what's next? Are you doing the right thing by seeing this story to its conclusion? Later games like [i]Undertale[/i] would expand on this thought experiment on player choice, but this game really did it first - and the context of actual pain and suffering wrought by conflicts in the Middle East makes this game's message all the more potent.

[i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i] is a marvel to witness in the dreadful story it tells, how it so expertly combines narrative and theme to scrutinize its own genre, and all managing to deliver this subtly enough behind a competent third-person shooter to boot. True, the AI can sometimes be a pain and the multiplayer mode is a black eye on an otherwise awesome singleplayer campaign, but this title thrives in showing and telling a story that'll stick with a player. Beware acting without understanding what drives you, soldier. [i]Spec Ops:  The Line[/i] gets an A-.

For a game I haven't heard much about, it exceeded my expectations by a lot. From the little that I had heard about it when the game released it was just like all of the other third person cover shooters of the time. Around two years ago a friend told me to try it after he had watched a video about it. He refused to elaborate on why I should and thankfully he did. This game was outstanding and I definitely would not have enjoyed it as much if i had the main story beats spoiled. 

Before mentioning the story, I should talk about what surrounds it. The gameplay can be clunky at times, but it never ruined the experience for me. It ran super smooth on both my laptop and main pc (granted both are decently strong) but 200fps on ultra was nice to see. I recommend downloading flawless widescreen and using their FOV patch to make the game a little less jarring to play during combat. Besides that, for a game that released in 2012 it looks stunning still. I caught myself looking around at the sandy ruins of Dubai on multiple occasions, especially when i was high up on buildings. The voice actors do an amazing job as well, but that's expected from Nolan North. The soundtrack was also decent and I never felt the need to turn it down and play music from spotify instead like I usually do with games.

Moving onto the story, this game BLEW ME AWAY. I really can't describe how it made me feel without spoiling too much. Funnily enough i'm writing a research paper for my college English course on war media and how it represents certain themes, or periods in time so while playing I was constantly thinking about how this game is trying to convey a theme about American imperialism, and our country's military complex. While doing separate research for my article I noticed a lot of American military advertisements and recruitment media makes you feel like if you enlisted you'd be a "hero" and I think this game tried to somewhat tackle this idea. With the choices Walker (main character) makes throughout the game becoming more erratic and drastic, you see him trying to justify his means by saying that the people in Dubai needed help. Eventually this switches to him needing to stop Konrad (main "villain"). You also see how Walker's choices end up effecting his squadmates Lugo and Adams. In the end the game throws you for a loop and shifts your perspective on Walker, and his "mission" in Dubai

[b] SPOILERS [/b]

When facing Konrad in the end of the story, you realize he's been dead for a while now. It isn't specified when, but his body is shown decayed and lifeless, pistol in hand. It is implied that he took his own life. After Walker comes to his senses, you can see that after the white phosphorous incident he hallucinates walker communicating with him, and even hallucinates a few key parts of the story. One being the choice between killing the man who stole water, or the man who killed the family of the first man while apprehending him. Konrad becomes an extension of Walker throughout the game, justifying his crusade in Dubai. All in all the story conveys that in his quest to become a hero, something Konrad points this out by saying "you're here because you wanted to feel like something you're not: A hero. I'm here because you can't accept what you've done." Konrad is a manifestation of Walker's guilt, taking the face of an enemy he can bring to justice, not realizing the enemy is himself. In his mission to exert this justice, Lugo and Adams die for Walker. In my opinion out of the four ending that you can choose, the one where Walker takes his life next to Konrad's corpse makes the most sense. After getting all four endings it's the only one that really matches his emotions during his final conversation with the fake Konrad he conjured up in his mind. Walker feels guilty as he has most likely doomed Dubai's survivors, and killed his friends in the process. Him going home doesn't make sense, nor does him becoming the new leader of the 33rd or dying fighting off the rescue party sent to get him.

Spec Ops the line is a loose adaption of Heart of Darkness/Apocalypse Now that masks itself as a typical tactical military third person shooter, but is really more like a surrealist psychological/horror/thriller. It is a relatively short (about 4-5 hour) game about a Delta Force team that is sent into Dubai 6 months after a natural disaster cut it off from the world. The overall gameplay of the title is a typical third person shooter with very very light tactical options and clunky mechanics that do not really distinguish it from other titles of the genre during that time period. 

What the game does stand out for is its mind bending and surrealist plot that heavily deconstructs the military shooter genre with a meta commentary about why would someone want to play a game where you just kill scores of people without a thought to the moral consequences while believing you are the hero. You will either come out of this thinking it was a very bold artistic decision that excellently gets its point across and is thought provoking enough to really make you think about the moral ramifications of enjoying violent videogames. Or you will think that it is a hypocritical pretentious critic bait that tells you that you are a garbage person for playing this game and enjoying it and you would be better off turning it off and going outside. 

As a whole I believe that Spec Ops: The Line is worth checking out when it is on sale for $5.00. It is a short title that offers a thought provoking and surreal story with a beautiful setting and haunting visuals. The gameplay is not anything to write home about but the story might be something that sticks with you and make you ponder it years later.

Maybe you have already heard about Spec Ops: The Line. The game that everybody keeps bringing up when talking about hidden gems and games that didn't get the attention they deserved. The definition of "don't judge a book by its cover". A game that stands out as something truly special. A game so daring and real that it's surprising it even exists in the library of one of the big publishers, 2K. Somehow YAGER got a lot of freedom with this project. And better yet, they dared to take this opportunity to create art that will forever be remembered for a story that goes against convention. An actual anti-war game, if you can believe that.

First off, don't expect too much from the game-play. It's your very, very standard cover based third-person shooter. One gimmick it has is the usage of sand. Sometimes you can shoot windows or glass ceilings and let a big heap of sand in that buries enemies. And you can give your two squad mates simple orders but they are usually self sufficient. Other than that, the mechanics are nothing new. The game-play is serviceable.

The environment can be quite the sight. It's Dubai but it got hit by a massive sandstorm and is now swallowed up by the desert. It's a very different take on the "post apocalyptic" scenery and it's as eerie as it is beautiful.

You are greeted with a patriotic menu screen as well as the cliched team of bro-dudes. It all starts simple enough. Investigate the ruins of the city in search for answers as to what is going on. You immediately encounter bad guys and shoot them up. All in a days work.

Then, step by step, comes the part that is so lauded about this game. What starts out as something you have seen a million times takes a harsh and very real turn. Both on a meta level that directly addresses the player and with a story that confronts you with the depths humans fall to under extreme circumstances and pressure. You can witness not only the deconstruction of a genre that usually glorifies war heroism but also of a group of men faced with the nightmarish hell that is a war for survival, where decisions and responsibilities are demanded that humans are not meant to shoulder.

[u]Story:[/u] As Captain Martin Walker, you’ll discover dark and disturbing things about Dubai and the people stuck within it. In your mission to save civilians and make contact with a former commander, you’ll make tough decisions that aren’t like other video game choices. Each ethical dilemma Walker confronts are subtle story beats dealt with by in-game action rather than a separate yes/no mechanism. You project their meaning and importance onto your character without seeing substantial in-game consequences. Deciding which of the bickering, increasingly angry teammates to side with, or who lives and dies, doesn’t affect the outcome of your rescue mission. Game really makes you think about the horrors of war.
[u]Gameplay:[/u] Game is a cover-based shooter. Gameplay does a great job of facilitating that narrative between intense encounters. In fact, the game accomplishes something most shooters don’t bother with: It makes violence meaningful.
[u]Graphics:[/u] Hight amount of bloom and yellow gamma is not really my taste.
[u]Sound/Music/Voice:[/u] Voice over is pretty good.

[u]Optimization:[/u] Good, runs well on low-end PC.
[u]Bugs:[/u] No bugs.

[u]Singleplayer:[/u] Yes.
[u]Multiplayer:[/u] Not worth it (very unpopular).
[u]Pay to Win:[/u] No (no DLC, no lootboxes, no microtransactions).

Spec ops is incredibly narrative focused, I would go as far as saying you should only really play the game for its story and not the gameplay it offers. Spec ops, narrative focus does have a pay off, the story is incredible, utilising themes of guilt, despair, the horrors of war and its effects on the human psyche. There hasn't really been a game that told a war story just like spec ops.
While the story is amazing the campaign is rather short, it took me a little over 6 hours to beat, I think it's a good thing in this case due to the rather terrible gameplay. One last pro is the gunplay, it's rather interesting to see recoil and something resembling spray patterns in a game that isn't multiplayer focused, but spec ops does have a small learning curve when it comes to its firefights. This could be a pro or a con for you, but it was a pro for me so I will keep it in the pro list.

Like I mentioned earlier Spec Ops has rather awful gameplay, the movement of your character is often very frustrating, sprinting is a full charge to cover and shouldn't be used for anything that isn't going from one piece of cover to the next. Speaking of cover, the cover system is a clunky and frustrating mess. Your melee and vault button are bound to the same key (Left Shift on Default) and you can't separate them in the menu, snapping to another piece of cover when you meant to snap out of cover is also quite frustrating. Combat itself can also be summarized as frustrating in itself, Spec Ops's combat loop consists of finding a piece of cover lying there poking your head out and shooting a few enemies, go back in cover if they throw a grenade switch to another piece of cover. This loop would be fine if it wasn't for the clunky cover mechanics and awful mouvement.

My final thoughts on the game are rather simple, if you want a war story that isn't about how America are the heroes of war and tries to portray something realistic, Spec Ops is a good game for you. 8/10 best war story in gaming that was brought down by bad gameplay.

Spec Ops: The Line is a [b]good[/b] game. It's one of those videogames that sticks with you for a while after you beat it. It's a solid third-person shooter with squad mechanics that takes a deep dive into the unpredictability, chaos, and hard choices of warfare. It has a small but fleshed-out cast of memorable characters, and it has some truly jaw-dropping moments that unfold as the story progresses.

Spec Ops is set in the ruins of Dubai after intense sandstorms lay waste to the city. You play as Captain Martin Walker, the leader of a 3-man Delta Force squad as he enters the city to look for survivors. Among those trapped in the city are Colonel John Konrad and his "Damned" 33rd Infantry Battalion, which had been evacuating civilians from Dubai before the storms hit. Venturing deeper into Dubai leads Walker into conflict with local insurgents, a rogue CIA team, and hostile troops with ties to Walker's past in Afghanistan. Walker and his squad are forced to cross moral and personal lines to uncover the truth and survive the nightmare that Dubai has become.

Combat plays out pretty typically for a cover shooter. Walker can carry two guns and three kinds of grenades at once. His squadmates, Adams and Lugo, can be ordered around to fight enemies and pick specific targets. Ammo is fairly scarce, forcing you to pick your shots and scavenge weapons as needed. Wounded enemies can be executed for additional ammo. Sand also plays a major role in combat: explosions in sandy terrain kick up dust clouds that obscure enemies' lines of sight and stun anyone nearby. You can also destroy environmental hazards to bury enemies in mountains of sand. There's also enough enemy variety and level spaces to keep the action fresh.

I enjoyed the way that Spec Ops played with choices. Sometimes Walker is thrust into dilemmas without any prompt or warning, leaving the player to figure out what to do. Some choices pass you by without realization, while others get big moments dedicated to them. They do a good job of showing how harsh and unforgiving war can be while keeping the player on their toes. These pivotal moments also reveal more about the main cast and about the way you play as Walker.

Spec Ops does not have a traditional story co-op mode, though you can do four unique co-op missions alongside another player. It has a multiplayer mode, but the option isn't very good. Power creep is a serious issue among the higher levels of multiplayer, especially with guns like the Vector and Scout Tactical. The initial unlocks are often worse than the guns you start with, forcing you to grind if you want decent weapons. You can rarely find people playing it, though there are Steam Groups dedicated to organizing matches to this day. I didn't enjoy multiplayer, but you might like it.

Even though I went into Spec Ops with two of its major twists spoiled, I still enjoyed it a lot and got surprised by it more than a few times. It's a smart, intense, and fairly fun cover shooter with a gripping story. Its mechanics aren't as refined as Max Payne 3's, but they serve the game well enough and make inventive use of its environment. This is the sort of game you'll probably replay at least once to try things differently or explore earlier moments with more context. It will likely take you 6 hours to do a single run of the campaign, though that depends on whether you rush it or take your time to soak it all in. I would recommend it at 50% off or more - as good as it is, 30 USD is a high price tag for a game that came out in 2012.

Pro:

* Ten years after the release of the game, and the same ten years further into the ongoing climate crisis, the scenario of Dubai, mostly abandoned and half-buried in sand due to colossal, permanently raging sand-storms, is the one bit of this game's story that still holds up and manages to make an impression.

Con:

* The game controls clumsily and lacks everything you would expect from a modern shooter.
* The graphics, animation and playable set-pieces, art-directed purely for realism without any discernible style, would have been fairly impressive in 2007, when the game's development started. By the time of its release, they were already overshadowed by the contemporary competition. Add another ten years onto that and there's not much left to look at. The helicopter-based shooting gallery right at the beginning of the game is probably the part that holds up the best visually.
* The story of the single-player campaign, a war-narrative with a psychological bent, which earned the game considerable praise at the time of its release, is a hilarious mess of tropes and borrowed ideas from various 20th century war and anti-war movies and literature. The ambition seems to have been to write the Apocalypse Now of video games, but in my opinion whatever points it tries to make about actual war fall way short of the achievements of the to-this-day excellent campaign of Call of Duty 4 - Modern Warfare from 2007. There is a bit of a meta-narrative in there as well that tries to make a point about military shooter video games themselves, but it really only lands when applied to the shooters of the first decade of the 2000s, another bit where the game was already outdated by the time of its release. The characterization of the player character and his two AI-controlled sidekicks also has lots of unintended comedy due to virtual over-acting and few relatable traits. Again, COD4 - MW, which doesn't exactly go for super-realistic personalities for its ensemble of characters either, just did a better job all around.

Spec Ops: The Line has an interesting narrative, an interesting lesson, and an interesting campaign. Several months before Hotline Miami had the world questioning what was real and what wasn't and who was actually capable for the bloody mess across PC screens everywhere, Spec Ops: The Line was doing the same in a much more culpable manner. Spec Ops shows gamers everywhere that war is little more than mindless death and destruction... that the enemies that we happily mow down in videogames are in fact an analogue for *human-beings*. The scenes that you see in the game truly bring you to pause, to reflect on your revelry in what in real life would be an unspeakable tragedy. That crappy part is that this lesson is buried in a boring, thoughtless, unoriginal modern military shooter from the beige era of gaming. The graphics are extremely dated and were not awesome even by 2012 standards. The music and sound mixing are unmemorable at best and downright crappy at worst. I believe that all people who enjoy modern FPS titles who have any degree of empathy inside of them would benefit from a playthrough of the game, but only if you can stomach the terrible gameplay and poorly-aged graphics.

In a genre dominating by games who claim to have a message to tell but end up not saying anything at all, Spec Ops: The Line stands out. It shows you the horrors of war and the fact that there are no good or bad guys in a conflict like this. It puts you in the shoes of the soldier, forced to make extremely hard decisions that always leave you questioning how things could have gone differently. Instead of throwing in some morally grey decision in a dialogue sequence or cutscene, you have to make those yourself and see the terrible consequences of it. If you can get past the repetitive, but suitable, third-person cover shooting that was all too common in this era, Spec Ops: The Line will be one of the most defining and thought-provoking experiences in gaming you'll ever have. It's a shame the game never sold too well in its release, as it is one of those games that could have changed the landscape of the industry.

Spec Ops: The Line is a perfect example of a narrative that only a video games games truly convey effectively.

The story fully utilizes the fact that you are acting as the protagonist, from their perspective, to make you feel complicit in the actions taken. It makes you simultaneously want to slam on the brakes because something is off, but also understand why you keep trudging forward.

The game posits surface questions about why war is bad, but unexpectedly demonstrates how insidiously well-meaning people can be sucked in and destroyed by it; desires for honor, survival, or just to help can all lead one to assign themselves dangerous levels of power over others.

Entertainment is the vehicle that brought you here, but in the end it's also what transports you to question the very medium itself. As one loading screen notes, "Killing for yourself is murder. Killing for your government is heroic. Killing for entertainment is harmless."

To me, the game was both a serious portrayal of "Heart of Darkness"-style atrocities, while also being a scathing satire of how unquestioningly we consume vapid narratives glorifying war. 

And to be honest, I often felt like the people working on this game made a war-shooter begrudgingly. The controls (Xbox controller on PC here) can often be frustrating and the gun play is a bit basic, but it's fun enough to usher you through the aspect where the game shines -- narrative.   

After completing the game it will stick with you and make you think. 

Most aptly: "Do you feel like a hero yet?"

In truth I do recommend this game. However, I am posting as a negative in order to draw attention to some issues that many reviews ignore.

Pros:
Everything but the gameplay. Fantastic story about the horrors of war, decent characters, music, etc. Chances are every other review you've seen will praise these, as they should.

Cons:
Gameplay. This is painful to write. It's not broken, the game plays ok. This game, and it is a game, is rough around the edges. AI, both friendly and enemy, occasionally act dumb. Individual enemies may stand with their back to you or facing a wall in combat. Your ai teammates may go out into the middle of a firefight to die, stand in your way(especially when grenades force you to run), take forever to follow your command to kill a target if they can kill it at all, and barely kill when unpromted. Cover may have invisible barriers just slightly bigger than it should be, making it somewhat easy to blow yourself up in cover. Checkpoints are often just BEFORE a cutscene(thankfully skippable if needed), may stick you out of cover to get killed or, in rare cases, switch your guns(happened once near the end in my first playthrough). Repeated deaths may cause a prompt asking if you want to lower the difficulty, which is just annoying frankly. Certain sections were clearly not tested on higher difficulties(ex: a part where you have to run from a helicopter, on hard or higher you have to get lucky to make it out on time, and this wasn't just me, numerous forums showed this was a major issue) which just made the above checkpoint shine more. Melee isn't silent, somehow... ok. The campaign does not inform you that silencers reduce damage and recoil. Enemy flinching is inconsistent, and even damage needed may vary(I've gotten clear headshots with various guns, indicated by blood spatter and bullet lines on sniper rifles, and the number of shots needed vary, especially on beefier targets). I've seen random bits where enemies teleported a couple of feet into cover. And finally, a weird event where if you headshot a helmetless "melee/knife exoert" instead of dying the first time, they roll to the side and resume charging, needing another headshot or several body shots. Just a weird "bug" or design choice.

TLDR: You should buy this game, just don't expect the gameplay to be perfect and don't start on the hard mode.

[h1] This is not your usual Call of Care Bears game [/h1]

If you play Call of Duty for the single player campaign, you need to play this game. It's third-Person but it's good to see the evolution of your character along the story even if you might feel it not as immersive as a fps. Ammo is scarce so you can't go full akimbo everywhere.

The story is the greatest part of this game. It just blows away all the cute, surreal Doom/Quake-like campaigns and provide you with a 6-7 hour story which is closer to Heart of Darkness/Apocalypse Now than Saving Private Ryan. 
It starts relatively simple, you are a squad of Delta Force Super Soldiers (as usual) and go to Dubai which suffered a crazy sandstorm that destroyed and created a humanitarian crisis in the city. A US army battalion is there by chance and instead of leaving the city before the sandstorm, they decided to stay and help the population. So get in there, find survivors and evacuate them, simple enough, no?
I don't want to spoil anything but this game will make you question who you are and above all, what is your [b]real[/b] role as a super soldier. Maybe ask questions first and shoot later? It's like in Planescape: Torment where you don't have swords, you mostly talk instead of fight, the opposite of classic hack&slash RPGs. 
This is a shooter where you will shoot but should you shoot? will you shoot? why are you shooting? What's the greater good? Your good? their good? or are they just all bad? What's self-defense? What's survival? Who is responsible? Me? Them? The trigger? So many questions that will popup in your head as you play and become the main character.

Besides the great and gritty story, the second best thing is the level design. Oh. My. God. Some of the places are so great, so wonderful. You are in a Dubai ravaged by Sand and [spoiler] a civil war [/spoiler]. You get to see various parts of a post-apocalyptic city covered in sand, there are lots of little details to make you feel like people lived/survived in those places.
You can also really note the opulence of the place with incredible apartments, huge shopping mall, marinas, etc. All of those destroyed/looted/reorganized following the Sandstorm. 

Even if it's a 2012 game, the graphics are more than acceptable, as the levels are beautifully designed, the only ugly parts are some cinematic which appeared a bit compressed but other than that like the in-game cut-scenes, there are no issues and it's a beautiful game.

Music is also very well chosen and is the perfect companion during frenetic battles and some dramatic moments! 

To conclude, for any shooter fan that loves epic stories, people who loved the Single Player campaigns of Call of Duty 1/2, Modern Warfare trilogy, will enjoy this game. Especially if bought during a sale!

I just fired this up again having forgotten I even owned it.  I couldn't remember beating it and wanted to see why if I hadn't.  I quickly remembered after a bit of combat.  The game play is... not great.  It's a bit buggy in a few areas and the AI of both your companies and the enemies is overall not very good.  The bugginess primarily manifests in the game's inability to properly recognize and "intelligently" interact with the environment.  The main ways you will interact with your environment is to either take cover using objects or vault over objects.  These often don't work as intended.  The shared keyboard/controller buttons I think are a major contributor to the issues.  Your vault button is also your very rarely necessary melee attack button.  Your take cover button is shared with your run button.  I don't believe I made it through a single firefight without either melee attacking when I should be vaulting or getting stuck in a run animation against something I wanted to take cover behind, which seems to take seconds to stop.  This lead to taking unnecessary damage and leaving me in a situation of risking shooting an enemy while at low health or sit there and wait to heal while the enemies get free time to advance or take up better positions.  Even outside of these issues there is another pretty annoying issue where about 10% of the time when I would be behind cover and I would hit the aim button the game would just have me zoom into the barrier I was hiding behind rather than have me pop up and aim.  This issue wasn't dangerous to me, but that ~1/10 chance of trying to pop my head out and it not working was an aggravation.

The shared actions assigned to keys might make sense on a controller with limited real-estate, but you should have the option to separate these out in the control options for use with a KB and mouse as this is a PC game.  While I did run into these issues often, I haven't personally run into anything game breaking that reloading a save hasn't resolved.

Otherwise the story and voice acting are really good.  When things work the gun play is fun. There were great set pieces and I also appreciate the main menu changing as you progress through the campaign.  I generally feel pretty middling on whether I would recommend this.  I personally like a good story, and the effort to tell this story shows.  I also REALLY like a good FPS, and this didn't feel like it meets that criteria for me.  If you don't mind a game with a few warts and can get this on sale it's almost certainly worth picking up.

This is a prime example of how to subvert expectations in games. The art, screenshots on the store page as well as the first hour of the game lead the player into a false sense of security that it is just another dime a thousand shooter among the market that should be skipped like many modern military shooters, but this is far from the truth. The game holds no punches showing players the consequences and difficult morality choices in war that many of them have been desensitized from the mindless dopamine rushes that modern shooters give. 

The game is detailed to its core and by far my favorite aspect is its slow buildup to heavy drop of the image of the generic military hero shooter, with its main aspect of your player character and squad mates becoming both mentally and physically damaged as the game goes on, with their executions, squad orders and voice lines being once professional and military-like to being replaced permanently as you continue over the course of the game with more and more tired, bloodthirsty and savage alternatives.

The only "flaw" to be found it the game is that in terms of its actual gameplay it is a generic third-person cover shooter with little to no unique mechanics but I assure you, its story, music and overall everything outside of gameplay make up for this "very" minor criticism tenfold.

Summing it up, [b]Spec Ops: The Line[/b] is an awful, boring cover shooter game with an interesting plot, even though the story it's not so original.

[i]Gameplay side:[/i] as said earlier, this 2012 game suffers from the "cover shooter wave" started with the original Gears of War. In that period a lot of games were designed like that, repeating and adding very little changes and variations of that formula. Spec Ops doesn't change that trend, but unfortunately it makes it worse due to cumbersome controls and not so fluid player movement. Especially on PC, played with mouse and keyboard, the keybindings are strange: space to sprint, shift for vaulting over obstacles (and of course no jump button) and so on. At first it takes a while to memorize these bindings (yes I know you can remap them), but the real problem is that movement feels clunky and sometimes it's even difficult to enter in the cover spots for shooting the bad guys. Speaking of which, they're generic bullet-sponge soldiers providing absurd damage to the player on high difficulty. AI is not so good, but in some combat situation they try to flank you and throw some grenade at you, but that's it. Combat it's very average, and it occupies 90% of screen time, which is annoying.

[i]And the plot?[/i]

Well, the plot itself starts as a generic rescue mission in the United Arab Emirates, specifically in Dubai, which has fallen due to violent and huge sandstorms that covered the whole city and its nearby zones with sand. Because of this climate-catastrophic events the whole area it's barely accessible and there are few survivors. As Delta Force captain Martin Walker you command a rescue team in order to search for any survivors and specifically for colonel John Konrad who was in charge of evacuate civilians in Dubai from the natural disaster. What began as a salvage mission will evolve in an unpredictable and sinister experience as the team descends into the collapsed city. 
Spec Ops differs from the traditional military shooter where the protagonist is the traditional american hero facing a conventional enemy, but it tries to capture the horrors and atrocities of war in an emotional and psychological way, leaving the player with making choices during the game. These choices unfortunately do not affect the multiple endings (there's 4 of them) but they serve only for narration purposes. The good news is that it is the player that take decisions and the story do not suggest to take certain paths, leaving this freedom to you. Sometimes these are simple binary options that changes some dialogue, but they do work, considering that is a linear experience. Even if the overall plot is not so deep it has its emotional moments, and the game sometimes plays with the player with some hallucinating moments, questioning the protagonist's reality and morality. Overall, it's an engaging story, sometimes crude even if there are some clichès taken from american war movies such as Apocalypse Now or Black Hack Down, but at least it encourages to finish the game even if the gameplay it's not great.

In conclusion, if you want a mediocre shooting videogame with a mature story it's for you. But I would recommend to play it at lower difficulties, because it becomes frustrating when you seek a harder challenge.

Something clicked for me today. I was looking at the wiki page for Spec Ops: The Line, and I noticed something; it didn't get many awards. Now, I'm not going to proclaim that it's MP was great, or really even good. And sure, the mechanics were a bit dry and generally not all that interesting. But with all that in mind, that seemed to reinforce what the game was trying to say, so in the end, I think it should've gotten a bit more credit for it's single-player narrative. But it didn't. It got some mentions in most reviews as being surprising or well-done, but many reviews seemed to ignore it and focus more on the lackluster mechanics or the weak multiplayer.

Here's the thing about Spec Ops; it's not a nice game. It runs completely contrary to everything that modern military shooters are about. It takes the jingoistic pro-war stance that makes you feel like some sort of be-all last line of defense for freedom against the chaos of evil and completely turns it on it's head, revealing how ridiculous, and in some cases, terrible, so many shooters have become.

I normally don't think of shooting members of the Taliban in Medal of Honor as racist, and hunting drug lords in Ghost Recon was justified because orders were to take that man out. Call of Duty and Battlefield both have used Russians as their enemies, but that's fine, because they're Communists, and we need to be aware of that threat. At least, that's what I thought, until I played Spec Ops, where I spent 6 grueling hours gunning down American soldiers. The whole time, I couldn't help but feel that I was doing something wrong, because I was shooting Americans, and Americans are supposed to be the good guys, right? Well, why is it different with Latinos, African Americans, Arabs, or Russians? Why is it okay for them to be gunned down in droves by me and my comrades, but as soon as I see Americans in my sights, it's wrong? This is where I started to see how racist and lazy other shooters were, throwing non-American groups under the bus as an easy enemy for us to fight.

But Spec Ops goes even farther as far as shock is concerned. They're not content to stop there. I'm sure anyone who's played a modern military shooter is familiar with the level were you're put in a large vehicle and shoot enemies from a distance. Here are some examples: Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 3, Battlefield 3, Medal of Honor. 

You don't need to watch all these in their entirety, as I'm sure you get the idea. Even Saints Row 3 gave you a mission where you used predator missiles, although to be fair, that game was meant to be more of a parody. Moving on though, Spec Ops included it's own mission similar to this one, but they did something significantly different with theirs. Obviously it looks similar to other games gunship missions, but they then force you to face the consequences of what you've done, walking through the corpses you've just bombed, and then finding out you just bombed a civilian refugee camp.

This scene hit me hard, because I felt like it was such a standard scene that I'd done so many time in so many games, but here, I was seeing the consequences up close and personal, and finding out that I had done something truly terrible. This scene was a punch in the gut for me.

There are other moments, but I think I've made my point. Spec Ops stood as a huge criticism of modern military shooters which are currently flooding the gaming markets nowadays, and in my opinion, it was incredibly successful. And I think that the gaming press ignored it because it performed it's task so well.

The mainstream gaming media of today is seems to have become incredibly easy to please, with Call of Duty regularly scoring incredibly well, despite common complaints of it being stale and repetitive. Battlefield 3 was able to get away with a terrible campaign on it's multiplayer component alone. Other games that are largely considered to be merely average or simply well-executed are generally given very good reviews. Spec Ops struggled compared to many other games, however, with metacritic averages around the mid-70's. While some critics praised the single-player narrative, such as Ben Yahtzee or the show Extra Credits, most other sites tossed it aside, forgetting about it. Maybe it's because they're busy and only have so much time to commit to particular games that they couldn't give it the attention they thought it deserved. But I think something else is going on.

If the critics that praise games like Call of Duty and Battlefield were to turn around and give Spec Ops the credit it deserves, there would be some implications. First of all, they would be praising a game that's largely criticizing games like CoD and Battlefield, and they might have to start rethinking their opinions and stances on certain products. If they were to take the game's story seriously, they would have to start looking more critically at games like CoD and Battlefield, and this might shake things up a bit. Beyond that, they'd have to start weighing games more evenly, which while they'd agree is good, would require a lot more work and critical thought on their part, and might occasionally require them to take harder and less popular stances on certain things. To elaborate on this, Battlefield 3 was generally well-received with praise based on it's MP, despite a lacking single-player. Spec Ops, on the other hand, lost a lot of points because it's MP was lacking, although most would likely argue that the single-player was the main draw of the game. The point is, critics are sending the industry (and they've been sending this message for years now) that MP is ultimately more important that single-player. Both these issues are part of a larger problem with a gaming press that isn't willing to shake things up and take the hard stances on certain things. Rab Florence did an excellent piece for Eurogamer that said this better than I can, but to summarize, we have journalists with little integrity who are simply trying to maintain their domination over the gaming press by releasing easy reviews.

One thing I often read about from reviews of games like Bioshock is how great it is to finally have a story that makes the player think about bigger issues, and how great those games are for pushing the medium forward artistically. And yet, it seems that those sorts of stories aren't really missed all that much during the sorts of games that depend on it's audience not thinking. Critics praise story when it's there, but when it's not, no harm done, and they're perfectly willing to check their brains at the door of their next gaming experience. Basically, there's no consistency here, and if gaming journalists were serious about wanting better narratives, they would've taken Spec Ops more seriously. I'm not saying it needed to be showered in GotY awards, but it seems to have largely been ignored, and I see a press that's scared to admit that a large part of that game was pointing at people like them, who've allowed our industry to become dominated by thoughtless and horrific games that make us feel empowered without ever making us grow.

Thanks for reading.

An Incredible experience. This game's story is an absolute masterpiece and unlike anything I've ever played. Certain scenes gave me chills and the whole thing was very David Lynch-esque, which is a good thing. Gameplay is run of the mill cover shooting, but with some basic squad commands and environmental attacks to keep thing interesting. Turret sections galore and a few chopper sequences. But what really makes the gameplay stand out is the grittiness, and how the characters become more desperate as time goes on. There are subtle changes in how Walker and his comrades communicate with each other as the game goes on. Gun SFX are great, enemies scream in pain, make call outs, and bullet feedback is nice. There are also executions, which become more violent as the game progresses. HOWEVER, there are faults. Team mate AI can be atrocious at times (even game breaking every now and then) movement is a bit clunky, and some keys being used for multiple actions can cause problems at times. Graphically, the game is gorgeous and has aged extremely well. Character models look a bit dated, but the environments are downright stunning at time. Textures still look great and the lighting is fantastic. The game has an art style that borders between cartoonish and realistic, and somehow pulls it off convincingly. Multiplayer I have not played, so no comment. But overall, it's an 8/10. 

Final Notes: Clunky controls, spotty AI and some bugs here and there, but one cannot deny the incredible story and thrilling tension the game maintains throughout. Quite honestly a masterpiece, with a few faults holding it back.

Controls aside, the guns all feel decent to use, except the scoped weapons on their high zoom setting. If you've ever heard anything about this game, it's probably the story. I disagree with the way seemingly everyone praises this story so much but I'm waaaay too late to playing this game, so the point of this game has kind of lost its point with how ridiculous military shooters have gotten in the last decade. 

First off: I played the game on normal difficulty. The gameplay is terrible, although it seems like most third-person shooters have this problem. Specifically with this game, the enemies are way too beefy, ammo is very sparse(probably the point), and you die very quickly, to the point I was getting 1/2 hit KO'd near the end of the game. The grenades were actually very useful, which I find uncommon in most shooter games, and overall the guns, aside from sniper rifles, felt very weak. There were also quite a few areas where the difficult shot up and it felt artificial, especially near the end with machine gun spam. There are a couple fights where [spoiler]you fight visions of your teammates and you can die, but the game doesn't show the "you died" screen and just restarts you at the last checkpoint[/spoiler]. I couldn't tell if this was intentional or not.One last point I wanted to make is that you can get ammo and grenades when you execute an enemy, and the game doesn't tell you this.

So, the story is pretty good but I think it's exaggerated as to how good it is. This game is, more or less, a critique and parody of every military shooter protagonist in other games, where in real life those protagonists would be psychopaths. The gist is that you go into Dubai to find out what happened to the evacuation of the city. Spoiler alert, ♥♥♥♥ is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up.

[spoiler]I interpret the story as the majority of what happens being in Walker's head. He's suffering from PTSD and glorifies a fellow soldier, Konrad. There's also a theme throughout the game of Walker trying to be a hero to the point at the end of the game you are asked "do you feel like a hero yet?" after everything you've went through. The really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up stuff that happens in the game does actually happen, including the white phosphorus scene and the scene where you gun down civilians. By the end of the game, you find out that Konrad killed himself and was dead the entire game(or, presumably the entire game, he's been dead a while). The main character, Walker, is having one hell of a PTSD freak out. There's an option post-credits, if you choose not to kill yourself at the end of game, where you are 'shellshocked' and can choose to either shoot the soldiers who came to rescue you or to give up and go home,[/spoiler]. The story is deep, but it's deep if you don't already think that war and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up military history is, y'know, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up and psychotic. To be fair, I missed a lot of the hidden meta-details throughout the game e.g. [spoiler] you can supposedly see Konrad's face through out the game, as well as certain foreshadowing details[/spoiler]. That's on me, to a certain extent, but most of the game is non-stop shooting and there's very little space for stopping and taking in the environment. Overall, the story is pretty short and for a majority of the game it's kind of "eh" until you get the plot twist. I don't know enough about the military and PTSD to give an in-depth analysis of what this story's impact really is.

The music and environment is pretty good. There's several scenes where it feels like you're playing a movie(granted you don't die, which I did a lot so it kind of ruined it for me), and the ending sequence is well done with its music and how everything looks. On the point of dying a lot, I had issues with dialogue skipping or messing up when dying, as well as when listening to intel/collectibles, so the whole "vibe" of the game didn't really click with me.

If you don't like your stereotypical shooter game where the protagonist is always the hero and never seen as a psycho, then this game is a great short experience. It's not too difficult but there are some rough spots, and the story is subtle enough until the end but the end of the game ended up being my favourite part. The rest of it just did not stick with me as much.  Although, in retrospect, there's not much you can do with a game like this. It accomplished what it wanted to do and is a pretty decent experience. As for the price, however, it is WAAAAAY too overpriced. I don't know how much I bought it for myself, but there is not nearly enough replay value or unique concepts here to warrant a $20 price tag, even.

One word comes to mind when I think of this game. [b]Decay.[/b]


The care Yager took to ensure that every imaginable facet of this game is in a perpetual descent the whole way through is staggering. Dubai falls apart around you the moment you step foot on its sands, as does Delta's mission. Delta themselves lose their professionalism as soldiers as the tragedies stack up. Their combat barks change, slowly "sir yes sir" turns into growls of rage. Walker's animations for mercy killing enemy combatants evolves from merciful and professional to bloodthirsty and out of control. Delta's physical condition decays along with their army fatigues, and Walker's mental state. Elia Cmiral created multiple versions of his melodies in the OST, ranging from earthy and atmospheric to mechanical and hellraising. The loading screen tips come to taunt you. Hell, even the sniper in the menu screen goes on a downward spiral of his own. Everything comes together to tell the player, and Walker, just one thing: [b]stop.[/b]

[b]Combat - [/b]

Minor spoilers ahead, blacked out. They are not real spoilers however, just "how things are unfolding in general way".

[h1]Story, you're here for this[/h1]
There aren't many games out there which make you [b]commit war crimes[/b] and reflect on that. Seriously, i'm talking CoD:MW2 "No Russian" scale here. This experience and its aftermaths alone make it worth playing.

The plot itself isn't outstanding or unique, and it doesn't need to be. If you watched classic cult movies [spoiler]Apocalypse Now[/spoiler] and [spoiler]Fight Club[/spoiler], you kinda know where you're descending into. That's also the main drawback of the story and the way it's told: protagonist does what he has to because of circumstances and condition he's in. It works pretty well in movies: you observe and try to understand another person. In games, however, you as the player are forced to [spoiler]do questionable things while being totally sane[/spoiler]. Disagreeing with chosen course of action separates you from in-game character.

He makes bad decisions and you can't deny him that, just follow and see where it gets you both. [b]Understanding this is the key to enjoy the game.[/b]

You know, when Kojima did [spoiler]MGS2 ending[/spoiler], he didn't go full [spoiler]Fight Club[/spoiler] and thus maintained connection between you and game character. Spec Ops The Line explores another direction.

[h1]Visuals are great[/h1]
This game illustrates that [b]artistic style and effort matter more than technology and engine features.[/b] Some textures are poor for today's standards, sure. Reflections and shadows are not popping. Some settings have to be improved manually in a config file. [b]But oh dear, you have to see Dubai covered in sands![/b]

[h1]Gameplay is generic[/h1]
This is not bad, the game is pretty damn short and does not let you get bored. It is like shooting sections in Uncharted, one after another, without much walking or exploring, but with several extra tacticool features like auto/burst fire switching. Optional stealth is here too. Artistic effort shows here as well: in certain places you can use surroundings to kill enemies in creative ways, and this works and looks pretty naturally, not being just "red barrels go boom". Barrels, certainly, do go boom, too.

What was really bad and broken, that's AI: bunches of bots pretty regularly got stuck at their hidden spawn rooms and sometimes they were trying to shoot through unpenetrable walls or floors, making noises but staying out of reach. I don't know why, maybe because i played at 144 FPS?..

Key bindings are.. sort of unconventional, and cover system sometimes failed me. Nothing critical, however. Guides suggest editing configs a bit to make controls feel more familiar, and i recommend doing it.

[h1]Music is fun[/h1]
And refers to movies i mentioned: some psychedelic rock and bits of classic. Main menu plays Jimi Hendrix! Well done post-rock-y (?) stuff during combat and dialogs (i'm not an expert in modern music styles). Credits theme surprised me, going from regular song to full-blown improvisation lasting as long as titles did.

[h1]Attention to details[/h1]
Grenade explosions, if happened on sand, raise it up in the air and create cover like smoke. Main menu changes after every chapter, reflecting how story goes. Reloading with a loaded gun leaves 1 extra bullet since it's already in the chamber. I just love when people get creative and make you pay attention to subtle touches they made.

For the unfamiliar, "Spec Ops: The Line" is an extremely cynical criticism of "well-meaning" military intervention and especially of war games, whose gameplay mechanics are mostly standard if polished third-person fare but whose story lurches closer to disaster as the game goes on.  You start off trying to rescue civilians after a huge sandstorm hits the city of Dubai, but things go sideways, and betrayals mount up.  The reasons for why you're fighting and why you're even involved quickly get called into question even as your character, Captain Walker, continues to believe in his own good intentions.

Walker also has two AI companions, Adams and Lugo, who can be commanded to attack enemies by hovering the mouse over them while holding the middle mouse button.  It's an intuitive and uncomplicated system, though early on my companions seemed to have issues with following orders (outside of situations where they're smart enough to disregard blatantly foolhardy commands), an issue that ironed itself out as the game went on.  The cover system isn't as sophisticated as in other third-person games, so I frequently found myself wanting to wall-hug corners or crouch-sneak to forward positions in ways that the game's mechanics have limited support for when compared to something like Mass Effect 3.  You can only hold two weapons at once, and there aren't a whole lot of them, but weapons generally feel very 'weighty' and usually boast incredible sound effects.  This and the hard mode's remarkably adept, aggressive AI make the game more genuinely fun to play than I think it wanted to be.

Battle pacing sometimes tends to last longer than in comparable games, which I think was intended to bore the player if you play on Normal Mode, but on Hard Mode, this turns every fight into a tightrope act, especially since not all of the battles have checkpoints after them (one of the few things I genuinely disliked about the pacing since screwing up one fight often means having to repeat the one before it, and outside of the remarkably large numbers of "target this enemy at such-and-such location" lines, battle dialogue gets really repetitive).  Weapons usually have alt-fire modes that are easy to switch between, from a grenade launcher to a rifle scope, and the game generally gives you weapons that are well suited for upcoming fights, even as this has the unfortunate issue of telegraphing close-range or long-distance fights a bit too bluntly.

You can revive your allies (Spacebar), but I was usually impressed by their friendly AI and their amount of health (so weapons fire, whether from you or from your enemies, doesn't just instantly take your friends out), as well as by their ability to heal one another with a simple mouse-click.  There's also a mechanic where you can dump sand on some enemies, but this came up so seldom for me that I rarely saw opportunities to use it unless the game felt like reminding me that it was there.

Level designs are generally linear but also have plenty of places for you to be flanked, so the game generally does a very good job of never letting you have a comfortable defensive position, especially toward the end of the story.  If you repeatedly die in the same section, the game politely asks if you want to lower the difficulty.  The art design is gorgeous, chock-full of luxurious Dubai restaurants, skyscrapers, and museums, and the various collapsing-level setpieces look like they took the best lessons from the Uncharted games.  The original soundtrack is incredible, with some of the best rock music I've heard in a war game.  (That stated, there is one battle late in the game where the lights flicker on and off, which I found disorienting and some players might not be able to comfortably deal with.)

The story does a great job at emphasizing its characters' various (usually deteriorating) mental states throughout the game; the plot is generally easy to follow, with little emphasis on outside politics or obscure military jargon, so it feels more approachable than do many entries from its genre, even with its abhorrent context.  You periodically are given choices to make, some of which seem unduly inconsequential (the game says, "you chose that, but I'm going to have this happen anyway," even if you reload and make the other choice) while others have unusual solutions.  I especially enjoyed [spoiler]the large variety of ending choices[/spoiler], whose outcomes were more diverse and less universally nihilistic than I frankly expected.  The game eventually openly criticizes you for continuing to play—even [spoiler]the loading screens[/spoiler] get in on the act—and while I don't think that's the right message for a game (it makes more sense for a movie since movies can proceed to the end on their own without maintaining or respecting viewer interest), the actual gameplay is oddly compelling.  Headshots are rewarded with a gratifying slow-motion effect, which doubles as giving you a breather to scope out the next enemies, though it does seem a weird thing to maintain as the story goes on.

You'll probably see a lot of the twists coming, especially since one of the game's bleakest moments has been spoiled countless times, but it's to the game's credit that I rarely if ever felt like the story ran out of ideas even when I knew going in what was about to happen.  Its ruthlessly graphic content won't appeal to everyone, and rightly so, but mature players who are ready for a very different shooter experience will find something of a gem here.

It's a surprisingly [b]well written game that stays engaging all throughout.[/b] 
A bitingly critical story of military corruption that doesn't waste a minute to make it very clear how many issues it has with US interventionism, as well as the military's dirty hands that it smeared all over the shooter genre, including the Spec Ops franchise.
But even if you aren't interested in the well-known fact that (US) military spends a significant portion of its budget on corrupting all kinds of media, or being reminded of the several atrocities it committed, commits and will commit; the game still has [b]vibrant characters[/b] that aren't overstated, [b]clear storytelling[/b] full of impactful twists, [b]nuance that's hard to find[/b] in most harshly critical stories, and an [b]attention to detail[/b] that brings it to a point of greatness.
There is not much else to say without jumping straight into spoiler territory, so [spoiler]let me just say that the framing of gunning down tens of military dudes screaming desperate tactics at each other, while your squad mates do the same; it's just as impactful as seeing them kill civilians, or being presented with the many amazingly directed sets full of dead bodies and US flags that are about as subtle as your average Banksy piece. [/spoiler] This game knows what it's doing, and it will take it and slam it repeatedly into your head until it's deep inside. And it will continue. [b]Probably into places you didn't quite expect.[/b]

But much more than a barrage of deprecating set pieces, it is a [b]military cover shooter all throughout[/b]. And it's a good one.
I am sure it's far less engaging on lower difficulties, but the time I had with it was one filled with [b]constant action[/b] to rival most in its genre. You need to stick to covers, think fast, shoot faster, and always be aware of who could be off your cone of vision. And your squad will help you out with that, as well as make you worry about them needing healing (but only a few times).
[b]It is still very handholdey[/b], which can get a bit annoying. Its [b]tactical aspects are only really useful in situations that in-game text tells you it is[/b]. And it's definitely not something that requires too much strategizing, until late game. It has plenty of mishaps, like the infamous Freebird segment.
But it is [b]mostly smooth sailing[/b] through a worrying amount of bodies. Very much thanks to [b]great level design that never gets stale[/b]. It's a dizzying, constant, action-packed movement from one tightly designed area to another, that slowly unravels all that the game could do. You are forced to try all weapons, utilize every corner, trudge through sand storms, fire, and shattered glass. In some parts it almost feels like survival horror. 
And it just keeps going. It's a daze of advancing through heavily defended areas and defending the same areas on the enemy's side from the enemies behind you. Of witnessing horrible ♥♥♥♥ and committing it yourself.

It's a full experience. It's hard to imagine it could disappoint.

The story exists to railroad you into "morality challenging" situations of "unimaginable choices", but this is a lie. I get the feeling it was written by a team that watched "Apocalypse Now" too many times, and wanted to do something similar, but without the art, skill, or emotion required. 
The big moment where you realise you have done something bad ([spoiler]The white phosphorous attack[/spoiler]) is forced upon you, with no way to avoid it through skill or planning. It also is utterly undermined by the fact you slaughtered hundreds of people in a mission just 5 minutes earlier, so now the game trying to moralise feels cheap. The major moral situation where you have agency, just after your third party member is affected ([spoiler]The refugee camp lynching[/spoiler]), has no impact on gameplay or dialogue - You can commit whatever deed you want for no plot-relevant punishment. The plot holes are so large you could drive a tanker truck through them - How is a city on the coast running out of water? How has there been no communication in or out, but this is possible as soon as the game finishes?

Arguably the most egregious is the final "twist", which falls back on some of the cheapest story writing hack-job solutions to a problem, and tries to convince you it was true all along ([spoiler]"Konrad was always dead, and you've been hallucinating"[/spoiler]). It doesn't stand up to any inspection when compared to the plot or the actions that have been taking place ([spoiler]For example, the bridge prisoner execution[/spoiler]), and your squad members who have up until now in game been willing to challenge you on your actions, apparently never mentioned your multiple hour long psychological detour into the wilds.

Gameplay wise, it varies between bland and horrible. A very typical of the time cover based shooter, with the usual spectrum of guns available, is a perfectly acceptable basis to tell a story around, but the gameplay is poor. Environments descend into a shooting gallery of idiot enemies running towards you, in such varied locations as "corridor", "corridor with sand in", and "outside area full of chest high walls". The stress and theatre of the storytelling, of an enemy force with limited resources descending to brutality, is undermined by the typical video game ramp-up of enemy types. You start off against insurgents with no armour, and end the game fighting helicopter gunships and super heavily armoured elite troops who can absorb multiple bullets. No clever enemies, just waves of bullet sponges.
Your character model handles appallingly badly, with no fine control for small movements, instead swerving like a drunken farm animal. The cover system is poorly implemented, the HUD inadequate, and the willingness to get in/out/over cover is simply not there - There is a risk you'll die standing up, looking longingly at some sandbags.

In conclusion, this is a game that exists so that people with no experience of anti-war media, or of good storytelling, can pretend to have done something socially virtuous (and thus appear more enlightened that the typical Battlefield-playing gamer), and I'm annoyed that I have ended up being conned into playing it.
