Ladies. Gentlemen. Others. I welcome you to a review of Spec Ops: The Line. And yes, I got this during a sale over at Humble Bundle and thought to myself, yeah, sure, I've been meaning to get this anyway.

So. As I had spoken of in the beginning, this game is designed to punish you for every known atrocity you think you'll be regarded as a hero for. Everything about the story screams out every known war movie you can think of, from the second half of Full Metal Jacket, Platoon, Saving Private Ryan and many others. This game also draws upon inspiration from Apocalypse Now and Heart of Darkness and it wears those inspirations right on its sleeve like it was a badge of honor and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ proud for it. This game shows you the outright horrors of what warfare can to even the strongest of men, and as a matter of fact, I would like to go on record and say that this game is absolutely NOT for the phony tough or the foolhardy brave. No, this game will push you to your absolute mental limits and then some, until you're left as a viciously scarred, flaccid, quivering mess upon the floor, begging for the sweet release of death. But even then, this game will offer up one more surprise, one more twist, one more mind screw until you finally break. Anything more I say regarding this game would be considered a spoiler, but what I will tell you is that you are the unwitting extra in Walker, Lugo and Adams' trek through Dubai with the sole purpose of uncovering the events that transpired there. But along the way, your mettle will be tested time and time again until it becomes an all out war of attrition and your only objective, good sir or madam or whomever you may be is to push on through until the very bitter end, no matter how bleak and how everything has fallen to pieces at your feet, even if there is a small glimmer of hope that everything will be right in the end as long as you keep on going.

I conclude this review stating the following, that if you're looking for a game that makes you feel like a big badass hero or that perhaps you'll right the wrongs and the injustices of the world so that everyone goes home all happy and snuggle up to their loved ones in bed, well lemme just put this out there, this is SO NOT that game, buddy. This game is an emotional and mental punch in the stomach, a kick in the taint and about 10, maybe 15 years of constant psychological torture that will knock all the wind out of your sails. So if you wanna pick this title up, you had best realize that what you're in for is not going to be pretty. But if you get all squicked out or easily offended or whatever, remember. I gave you PLENTY of ample time to just simply walk away. You chose to buy this game, play it through a friend's shared library or however else you do it, therefore, you have no one else to pin the blame on other than yourself.

Now if you were to ask me what I think of the multiplayer, I dunno. Seems like no one's on it these days, so it's kinda hard for me to say offhand. From my understanding of it, though, it seems like maybe they might have screwed it up, but I dunno. Otherwise, yeah, I can recommend this game to the sadomasochists out there that are wanting to subject themselves to this. But if you're squeamish, then yeah. Stay as far the ♥♥♥♥ away from this as possible.

What can I say, I had just finished Ghosts of Tsushima on PS4 and was a bit burnt out on the whole open world 40/50 hour games. I wanted to play a decent linear game that had a great story and not take too long to finish......well Spec Ops - The Line hit the sweet spot.

Story: 
The story in Spec Ops - The Line is fantastic! I don't know what else to say without ruining any possible experiences you may have, the line up of main characters are great and the way the game tells their story over the course of the game is fantastic. This game has choice and test's your own morality and really gets you thinking about difficult choices. Superb. 10/10

Visuals/Sound:
For a game of this age I was highly impressed with the visuals at 4K 60FPS, during game play it is crisp and rather good looking despite the sombre tone of the games theme, downside for me was the cut scenes....they ran at 30FPS and were aged and blurry (There may be mods or patches out there to resolve this but it didn't affect me enough to look for them) it didn't take away from my experience at all. The sound was good with great voice acting and great sounding weapon fire as well as environmental sounds, some fantastic music in this game too especially during the later parts of the game....it really sets the tone of certain situations. 8/10

Gameplay:
The 3rd person over the shoulder view was as good as any other game of this type in my opinion, shooting felt good and my only complaint really could be the cover mechanic felt too sticky, there were times I tried to escape grenades but struggled to come out of cover mode. In general though I really enjoyed the gameplay. 8/10

Overall:
If you too are looking for a quick 10-15 hour game with a good story and enjoy Gears of War style games then Spec Ops - The Line is a must play for you. I can only vouch for the campaign as I didn't try out the multiplayer due to me not being that type of player. For the price it is well worth it for the single player experience alone. 9/10 MUST PLAY

Spec Ops: The Line is a narrative driven cover based third person shooter inspired by a classic film called Apocalypse Now, which in turn was inspired by the novel "Heart of Darkness". If you've seen the movie or read the book, then you somewhat know what to expect, but I still recommend you play this whether you've seen the game's inspiration or not- it not merely a rote retelling of either plot.

Cons-

-Some of the cutscenes are videos rather than being in-engine, and I don't understand why developers do this. I've almost never seen a video cutscene that didn't look like complete dogcrap, and this game is no exception, which is a shame, considering that the in-engine cutscenes, as well as the game itself, still holds up quite admirably in terms of visuals.
-The combat in this game is competently put together, but there's not much to it. It is very standard, so if you're looking for a game you'll be replaying over and over for the combat loop, I'm sorry, but this ain't it chief. It's not bad, and capping someone in the head or blowing them away with an AA-12 is satisfying as all hell, but it's nothing you haven't seen before.
-This game is very short- I completed this game from start to finish in about four and a half hours on standard difficulty. You're looking at maybe... Six hours or so if you decide to crank the difficulty up some. Maybe even eight if you scour the game for every collectible as well.
-The multiplayer component is dead, which may be a mercy, considering it was never all that good even when you could find a match.
-The pricetag is ludicrous for a game that's this short and this old. I didn't buy it for thirty bucks, I bought it for six on sale, and that's the pricetag I recommend for you, as well. Maybe ten bucks max.

You might be thinking to yourself, "Good grief, that's rough. Why are you recommending this game?"

The story and the art direction in this game carries everything. In-engine cutscenes still look phenomenal- the use of color and lighting, the texture fidelity, voice acting, it's all great. Some facial animations and models look a bit rough but quite frankly for a game this old marketed mainly to console players, it's to be expected, and the visuals hold up well enough that it's more of a nitpick. The story, which I am desperately trying not to spoil, is great, with a fair few choices to be made that might change things later on down the line, but a lot of them are really meant to impact you, the Player, rather than the progression of the plot itself. A lot of people really overhype this game as being the most dark, morally complex and emotionally challenging game EVAR, and honestly, they're blowing smoke up your behind. 

No, this game isn't the second coming of Christ, but it absolutely does deliver a solid experience for the player from start to finish, which is ultimately this game's saving grace. Without it's narrative, all you'd have left is a dead multiplayer component plagued with technical issues, some decent presentation, and some stock-standard third person shooting. Instead of being an 8/10, you'd be looking at a 3/10, and I wouldn't be recommending this game to you now- hell, I wouldn't have gone through the fuss of purchasing it again, having already played it via "alternative distributors" way back in the day.

With all that being said, I absolutely recommend Spec Ops: The Line... On sale. That's an order, soldier.

Spec Ops: The Line is a third person shooter that's based around the lives of three American soldiers, and it's got a very, very interesting story. The narrative is gripping, and it kept me playing till the very end, even though some of the other mechanics such as the squad management, seemed to be out of place. 

The game has a satisfying combat system, and the enemies are tough. I played it first on the intermediate difficulty, and it was challenging enough to make you focus on the game. You have to constantly switch between weapons if you don't find the required ammunition, and the enemies get stronger as you progress. No, this doesn't mean there's any satisfying levelling-up system, it's just a challenging way in which the game progresses.

I had a hard time finding some of the important story-related 'treasures' found throughout the game, as my PC isn't high end. As a matter of fact, I actually played this in the lowest resolution, so that the game would run smoothly for my Intel Pentium. The graphics are good (for a game from 2012) , especially if you set it to the highest settings, so don't mind that. Other than that, controls were okay. 

One of the only things which I didn't understand was the horrible squad management - which there really isn't any. I found my two teammates getting into trouble a lot of times, and the loading screen keeps on saying that the squad commands can be used tactically - all I've managed to do, was command them to use a flash-bang, and nothing more. It momentarily appeared at random times, triggerable via the third mouse button. I wonder whether it's just my lack of knowledge over the controls, or just the game having some really bad squad-commands.

Nothing else to mention without spoiling the game, but when you're playing the game, keep your eyes open. Things might not be what they seem!

spec ops: the line is a good game with a lot of flaws.

it's a story based game with a great story and a bit of a shoddy game. it seems like it's trying really hard to be a movie, but a lot of what it does just wouldn't work as a movie, so it is begrudgingly a game.

all of the gameplay is combat, without any of the puzzles or platforming that other games might use to avoid the combat getting too exhausting. there's the occasional token "stealth" section, but it really doesn't count - the gameplay is all combat. the combat is third person cover shooter, which is fleshed out so poorly and filled with so many contextual actions that i can't bind to different keys, that most of my deaths in the game felt like they were due to poor controls instead of me actually making a mistake. the game needs to be a third person shooter so it makes sense, and i respect that, but the execution of that screams 2011 aaa shooter more than anything else. if that wasn't bad enough, the fov is permanently set uncomfortably tight, it shakes the camera like its flatlining grandmother, and there's no borderless windowed option (though that might be a ue3 thing). also it has prerendered cutscenes that look like porridge.

with that out of the way, the good news is that the story is the prodigious half of this story based game. it's heavily inspired by heart of darkness and apocalypse now, and has a strong antiwar sentiment that's almost unheard of in aaa shooters. i won't spoil it, although with those comparisons you pretty much know how it goes. narrative devices such as the unreliable narrator are pulled off incredibly well and this execution is the sole reason spec ops is a game instead of a movie. what also stuck out to me is the colour palette is surprisingly diverse for a game set in a desert, and is almost psychedelic during the more cinematic moments that make use of it. in addition, the game handles combat progression by letting you pick up a maximum of two weapons from fallen enemies, handing you only paltry ammo so you have to switch often, and this is a really clever way to avoid using upgrades or skill trees while encouraging varying playstyles as well as allowing the player to become more powerful as the game goes on, as enemies at the end of the game have way better guns than enemies at the beginning.

overall, spec ops feels more than anything like an indie game that somehow managed to pick up the budget to become a aaa shooter. now the combat certainly doesn't benefit from being out of a aaa game, but it's hard to find another one like spec ops. i don't know how it manages to be so unique as a game, because if it was a movie it wouldn't be nearly as special. maybe there's an untapped niche here, who knows.

Spec Ops: The Line is to Call of Duty and Gears of War (and other games aping Resident Evil 4, for that matter) what Bioshock is to System Shock and Thief.  A jejune and pretentious attempt at a deconstruction and send up.  In the end, it ends up exposing more unfortunate truths about its creators than the thing it is arrayed against.  It's a generic third person cover based shooter that rides the cart of superior art direction and production values.  The voice acting is excellent and Nolan North is particularly haunting as the lead, the artwork in the game is utterly gorgeous, animations are detailed and well above the norm for Unreal Engine 3, etc. - it's the one part of a game that can have more money thrown at it to achieve reliably superior results, and it does.  The problem is that the game itself is not particularly good and it doesn't seem to have nearly as much faith in its premise as its posturing creators crowed in interviews.  One might, perhaps, indulge in the speculative notion that the final product, which is a radical change from the early E3 promo builds which showcased a rather different story and characterization, was the result of relatively late changes as either budget or some other consideration forced their hand into trying something relatively easy to implement to make an otherwise relentlessly average game stand out from a very crowded pack for the 7th gen was lousy with bland third person cover based shooters built in Unreal 3.  This would be speculation, of course.

Even though it starts off as your usual military shooter, little by little it becomes this dark, depressing, violent and insanely twisted journey through the mind and consciousness of a soldier who's seen all kinds of unimaginable horrors way too many times. It explores how being a high ranking official in the military, often tasked with doing and commanding others to do unspeakable things, can mess you up so bad you start to slowly lose your mind. I'd grown accustomed to playing all those "Hell yeah, I'm the American supersoldier!" kinda shooters that this particular game gave me a genuine shock. It's an epiphany which made me realize there's nothing "cool" about winning a war. There's nothing "cool" about humanitarian crises that wars bring. There's nothing "cool" about having to choose between who you're gonna save and who's gonna die. There's nothing "cool" about killing hundreds of enemy soldiers to support your cause. This $hit only grows on you, piles up at the core of your heart and consciousness, and if those emotions are kept inside, they're slowly gonna take the better of you.

The story pushed me further and further, I killed countless "enemies" for the sake of "the mission". And at the end when a loading screen asked me if I even remembered why I'd come here in the first place... I couldn't. Harrowing.

I recommend [i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i] to everyone.

I was disappointed with this story. Maybe if I played it in 2012 when I was 21 (and very impressionable) I would have appreciated it a little more. But really, it's pretty basic. Now with the meaty part out of the way, the sped-up review of gameplay:

-Gameplay is your typical cover-based shooter from 2010s, with the added bonus of being pretty clunky at that - sprinting is stiff, obvious pieces of cover sometimes are very hard to enter.

-Graphics are serviceable. 

-Gunplay is horrible - a mishmash of automatic, semiautomatic and burst-fire weapons with added "features" like scopes, silencers and UGL. 2\3 of all guns feel the same. And the sounds of guns and explosions are pretty bad.

-AI is barely alive - enemies and your allies use pre-defined pathways and sometimes engage in hilarious "indian trail" formations, lining up for you to get headshotted. 

-Your ally AI is somehow even worse and is basically useless - they rarely kill anybody on their own, and it's almost always way faster and easier to shoot baddies yourself than to use a "squad command" feature.

- Single player campaign is very short (thankfully) - I beat it in 6 hours on third difficulty, with fourth being unavailable for the first playthrough. The replayability is questionable - while you get several choices (always a fork between 2 choices) during your playthrough and so there is a potential for a different ending, I didn't bother to go through this slog one more time to watch a different cutscene.

- Multiplayer is dead. Maybe there are enthusiasts that cooperate over Discord to scrape some players for a single match, but considering how poor the gameplay is I didn't bother looking for that.


So, while it's definitely not the most awful mess from the depths of Early Access, I sincerely think that this is not a good buy. Unless you're some weird collector of basic cover - based shooters from 2010s.

I liked the game enough that after completing my first playthrough (about 6 hours on 2nd from highest difficulty), I started up another run. I played again through to a section of the game where I had hoped a choice other than the one I made on my first try would lead to more information, and I'm disappointed it leads to no such thing. A certain character dies anyway, you learn nothing, nothing changes, and another character still has the same temper tantrum even though you DID do as he asked. Immediately after this is a section where the protagonist does a BIG oopsie, so I was hoping I could choose to engage a large enemy camp at a certain gate differently and maybe avoid said BIG oopsie. But no, you have no choice but to do it. This confirms that even the few choices I initially lamented, aren't really much of a choice anyway. Characters die and collateral damage is caused at the same time and mostly in the same way regardless of your "choices." E.g. a certain character is stuck under a truck and is going to die, but you can choose to shoot him or let him burn to death.

This definitely takes the game down a peg from my initial impression. I still view it as worth the time, but somewhat less so than before. The game has exactly one story to tell: driven men who may be generally righteous can still commit horrible acts in the name of duty. It tells this story well enough, it's usually subtle about it, though at times it loses all subtlety, especially on some loading screen messages. 

I do still believe the game is worth playing through at least once, but probably not more than that. And that once will probably be 4-8 hours depending on your difficulty, how quickly you try to bee-line the missions, and how often you die. As such, I would recommend you buy it on sale.

Over the years I have continuously heard this game praised and I decided to pick it up. Ultimately, I feel disappointed. I had heard that the story and plot is what drives the game, and I agree wholeheartedly. The plot is the only thing this game really has going for it.

By now the graphics are slightly dated, but I do appreciate the attention to detail in many areas and the varying environments, even if the various cover-infested arenas are a bit convoluted. I especially like how the main characters change in appearance as they perform their various outrageous stunts.

The gameplay itself is repetitive and a bit of a slog. Few of the guns are satisfying to shoot. Many of them are extremely inaccurate even in short bursts (and there's no fire setting to control this for most guns). This is exacerbated by the tiny off-white aim reticle which invariably gets lost against the bright backgrounds of the desert and more drab-grey interiors along with the soldiers themselves which are brightly colored in many instances. It's a shame that one of the best weapons in the game (IMO) is the desert eagle which secures a kill in one shot on most occasions and is one of the most accurate in the game, even giving sniper rifles a run for their money. Secondly, in the last two thirds of the game, the enemies are absolute bullet sponges (don't even get me started on the trope of big guys wearing EOD armor in battle called "heavies"). The cover system is clunky and hard to maneuver, and I constantly found myself breaking from cover instead of vaulting over because the "Jump-down" button is the same as the cover/sprint button while vaulting is another, which is shared with melee. 

I was only playing on the recommended difficulty because I wanted to enjoy the story, but the one thing this game is centered around just made me not appreciate the snippets of plot the game doles out. Moreover, the [spoiler] choices you make are basically inconsequential, and the game forces you into becoming a war criminal. The only difference is the steam achievements you get for the particular choices you make. Even so, while the plot is quite strong, I feel that using the ploy of the main character imagining so much of his interactions is a cop-out. They never even explained why the 33rd began fighting itself in the first place, so I'm just left confused about why the US soldiers instantly fired on the main characters in the first place.[/spoiler]

Revised and spoiler-free:

So many years later this game feels like a very unique and interesting take on USA's hard-on for war crimes. Pretty much as close as it gets to a Hollywood "war is bad" movie, but even better because it is a video game and it throws you right into the action, holding you directly responsible for the horrible choices of the protagonist. 

There are some very poor (in my opinion) critiques of this game that it falls into a trope of "don't do the cool thing" and it doesn't even bother to present you with a choice so that the line "you always had a choice" could have more impact. I think the people that make the latter argument don't seem to understand the subject matter. This game shows you how much wiggle room you have in the confines of a warzone. This isn't a game where you get to play a random average dude who was just thrown into a random situation and has the profound capacity to experience immediate catharsis out of nowhere and say "hey wait a minute... all of a sudden I no longer believe we have to be here, let's go back". You are in the shoes of a soldier. Someone who is going over to another country armed to the teeth, trained to kill and believing he is doing "the right thing". He even says it in the middle of the game. 

The lack of choice is not there to glorify or justify violence for the player. The lack of choice is there to solidify the emotional impact of a story in which the line between right and wrong is not just blurred, but has completely abandoned us. We are watching the story unfold from the point of view of someone who "survives" the entire thing. We almost see nothing of the motivations the 33rd had to do what they did, or Konrad, or CIA... we just see the protagonist being judged as if Walker is the only one who participates in this war. Someone who clearly walks into a hell that was there long before he arrived. Plenty of other soldiers have already committed the worst things imaginable to Dubai at the beginning of the game. The entire backstory is concealed from us, not just to make it work, but because it shows how little you're in control of when it comes to war. In fact, I think when Walker hears that he has a choice and that he wanted this, the writers just throw that in our face as a joke. To show us that Walker was doomed from the start. 

Incredible writing in this game.

Inspired by 'Heart of Darkness', More akin to 'Apocalypse Now', Spec Ops the line is a stand out narrative driven shooter. Though it shows its age in 2020, it still looks great It's a little clunky by modern standards, but remains a must play title by any metric.

Gentlemen, welcome to Dubai!!
If you love narrative driven experiences, then please do yourself a favor and get this masterpiece already! Before I begin quick Disclaimer: This is a very serious game and depicts the evils of war and bloodshed. Developer Yager successfully managed to create something that actually understands the dark side of war. It deals with real life struggles and serious topics like PTSD without turning these topics into jokes. Not recommended if you’re faint-hearted. I will only review the single player aspect but I won’t be going into characters and plot details to avoid any spoilers.

The Good
-Spec Ops: The Line is a shooter like no other. The story kept me engaged even after the credits rolled up. Despite all seriousness the main cast have a personality. Interaction with your team is very lively and believable. You’ll witness many npcs and you get to see how deep it gets over the course of the action.

-A big shout-out to the developers for adding realistic hard choices that had an impact to the story, the team put in a lot of morally ambiguous split-second choices all in real-time. This helped in building up some tension. They nailed it given the state of the subject matter by blurring the lines between the “good” and “evil”.

-Your squad is very helpful during difficult situations. You can also use the environment to your advantage to bring down heaps on sand over your enemies by shooting over windows and surfaces.

-Collectibles actually matter to the plot in Spec Ops. There are about 22 voice recordings that share important plot details. You can check your progress by simply pressing Escape key so try not to miss any of them.

Minimalistic design and HUD. No stupid mini-maps, navigational arrows or tech guy that yells directions and ruin the immersion.

The Bad & Ugly
-The gameplay is arguably the worst part of the game. I felt the combat was generic and lacked polish compared to other cover-based shooters like Gears of War and Mass Effect trilogy. At times I often found it very boring and repetitive. The cover system and enemy A.I isn’t good at all which is a shame considering this was marketed and sold as cover-based third person shooter. PC controls aren’t well optimized for keyboard and mouse.

-Enemies have a fixed spawning checkpoint area and every combat encounter is scripted. It’s predictable becomes a cake walk when replaying on higher difficulty mode. One can easily exploit this trick after dying because you’re mentally prepared and know exactly where the next enemy spawn point is going to be.

-Extremely linear level design with frequent invisible walls on every level. You’re not expected to explore any areas unless there are hidden collectibles on the way and this might ruin immersion to some players.

-Graphics did not age very well in Spec Ops: The Line. Some textures and character models do look good and benefit from having high polygon count a major portion of in-game assets has very low-quality detail and resolution. This results in overall inferior visual quality. I’ve also noticed a weird glowing effect on flat surfaces and characters that makes the game’s aesthetic look washed out like early smart phone camera. This bloom-like effect seemed to be a quite common problem.

-I’ve experienced a few sound bugs where the audio would remain silent during few cutscenes. Restarting the game fixed these issues.

The Bottom Line
At the end I believe that this game will always have a very special place to the fans. When it was released in 2012 it turned out to be a commercial failure for 2K Games but went on to win several awards and nominations for its storytelling and writing, now considered a “cult classic”.

The developers got me to feel the guilt, misery and regret. Emotions like these seem a bit rare these days in shooters. One of the fine examples of video games as an art if you ask me. The developers break the fourth wall at one point and question your thoughts about treating war in a game as an entertainment.

It takes a while before you could get attached to the story. The ending left me completely speechless! I did not expect how the plot would unfold. By the end you’ll truly feel sorry for the main character. The writers also don't spoon-feed you with every little detail. You might have to play through the whole game twice to fully understand the plot. It was very memorable experience and it’s going to take a few days to get over it lol. Maybe give it a try if you like good stories. Thank you for your time.

Another feature of this section is the existence of humorous dialogues along with shocking scenes. In other words, the game has the capacity to both laugh and regret. [h1]Gentlemen, welcome to Dubai!![/h1]
If you love narrative driven experiences, then please do yourself a favor and get this masterpiece already! Before I begin quick Disclaimer: This is a very serious game and depicts the evils of war and bloodshed. Developer Yager successfully managed to create something that actually understands the dark side of war. It deals with real life struggles and serious topics like PTSD without turning these topics into jokes. Not recommended if you’re faint-hearted. I will only review the single player aspect but I won’t be going into characters and plot details to avoid any spoilers. 

[h1]The Good[/h1]
-Spec Ops: The Line is a shooter like no other. The story kept me engaged even after the credits rolled up. Despite all seriousness the main cast have a personality. Interaction with your team is very lively and believable. You’ll witness many npcs and you get to see how deep it gets over the course of the action.

-A big shout-out to the developers for adding realistic hard choices that had an impact to the story, the team put in a lot of morally ambiguous split-second choices all in real-time. This helped in building up some tension. They nailed it given the state of the subject matter by blurring the lines between the “good” and “evil”.

-Your squad is very helpful during difficult situations. You can also use the environment to your advantage to bring down heaps on sand over your enemies by shooting over windows and surfaces. 

-Collectibles actually matter to the plot in Spec Ops.  There are about 22 voice recordings that share important plot details. You can check your progress by simply pressing Escape key so try not to miss any of them. 

Minimalistic design and HUD. No stupid mini-maps, navigational arrows or tech guy that yells directions and ruin the immersion.  

[h1]The Bad & Ugly[/h1]
-The gameplay is arguably the worst part of the game. I felt the combat was generic and lacked polish compared to other cover-based shooters like Gears of War and Mass Effect trilogy. At times I often found it very boring and repetitive. The cover system and enemy A.I isn’t good at all which is a shame considering this was marketed and sold as cover-based third person shooter. PC controls aren’t well optimized for keyboard and mouse. 

-Enemies have a fixed spawning checkpoint area and every combat encounter is scripted. It’s predictable becomes a cake walk when replaying on higher difficulty mode. One can easily exploit this trick after dying because you’re mentally prepared and know exactly where the next enemy spawn point is going to be.
 
-Extremely linear level design with frequent invisible walls on every level. You’re not expected to explore any areas unless there are hidden collectibles on the way and this might ruin immersion to some players. 

-Graphics did not age very well in Spec Ops: The Line. Some textures and character models do look good and benefit from having high polygon count a major portion of in-game assets has very low-quality detail and resolution. This results in overall inferior visual quality. I’ve also noticed a weird glowing effect on flat surfaces and characters that makes the game’s aesthetic look washed out like early smart phone camera. This bloom-like effect seemed to be a quite common problem.

-I’ve experienced a few sound bugs where the audio would remain silent during few cutscenes. Restarting the game fixed these issues. 

[h1]The Bottom Line[/h1]
At the end I believe that this game will always have a very special place to the fans. When it was released in 2012 it turned out to be a commercial failure for 2K Games but went on to win several awards and nominations for its storytelling and writing, now considered a “cult classic”.

The developers got me to feel the guilt, misery and regret. Emotions like these seem a bit rare these days in shooters. One of the fine examples of video games as an art if you ask me. The developers break the fourth wall at one point and question your thoughts about treating war in a game as an entertainment. 

It takes a while before you could get attached to the story. The ending left me completely speechless! I did not expect how the plot would unfold. By the end you’ll truly feel sorry for the main character. The writers also don't spoon-feed you with every little detail. You might have to play through the whole game twice to fully understand the plot. It was very memorable experience and it’s going to take a few days to get over it lol. Maybe give it a try if you like good stories. Thank you for your time.

[h1]My Rating: 8/10 – Emotional and Soul Crushing Rollercoaster Ride![/h1]

Few stories break boundaries like this one did. I stumbled upon it while browsing youtube and i was impressed so much by it that I wanted to experience the game myself. This game ends up leaving you with questions, often questions about yourself and your morality. For a game that's so under rated, it is still highly popular among the community.

[THE GOOD]

The aesthetics are phenominal and the graphics (for the most part) hold a level of realism that blends well with the art style.

The music really gives a gritty feeling and [spoiler] a truly hopeless and depressing one as well [/spoiler]. 

The story is (without going into much detail) probably one of the best uses of parallels, multiple themes, imagery, foreshadowing, level of detail, and a final message that I have ever seen so far in any game.

The gameplay isn't as bad as many claim it to be, especially on the higher difficulties. Level design really improves towards the end of the game and I can't help but feel that was intentional as well. 

The voice acting is probably the best I've heard and seen in any game and even any movie. Moreover not a single character feels like filler. I still remember even the ones that appeared for only one mission, for each character is truly unique. 

[THE BAD]

There are moments where the graphics didn't fully render and there were a few glitches with the soldiers. [spoiler] There was also a moment during the last mission where Konrad's body suddenly became bright and was visible for a split second before the scene played where he was turned around.  [/spoiler]

Cursing is used throughout towards the end of the game, but at the same time I can understand due to the war scenario. 

As some have pointed out before regarding [spoiler] the white phosphorous scene, it could have been done better, where enemies wouldn't end up spawning immediately. [/spoiler]

Violence is throughout the game [spoiler] but it is good that it tries to show it in a negative light. [/spoiler]

Gameplay wise combat can feel a little clunky every now and then. Sometimes when you want to take cover in a location that looks possible to cover behind, you end up standing out in the open instead. Personally I had few issues but it was annoying when it did happen. Also the range and accuracy on some of your arsenal is too much and too precise. Understand that it's not meant to be a fully realistic game, but there are areas where some reality would be beneficial to have included.

[THE MASTERPIECE]

Few games have left me chills like this one have, chills that keep coming back as i remember the music and the moments throughout the game. It questions the psychological and spiritual stance of one's stance and values, and even questions narratives that are portrayed in games, movies and other forms of media as well. Truly this game was well thought out to the very most intricate detail and it shows well with this game.

Even though it has some issues when it comes to gameplay, it is still one of the best shooter games I have ever played in terms of story. Its immersive story puts you at the center of universe, yet you have no idea what is happening around you and somehow the game manages to put you in vague and messy situations, moral dilemmas that are absolutely the result of your actions. Psychological horror aspects of the story and the thin, blurry lines between good and evil of your actions gives the game an unmatching experience.

Even though game tries to put you as an audience, a witness to this dark story by making it third person, you can't escape from the consequences of your actions. It slaps you in the face with the things you do. It has some of the most shocking scenes I've ever seen in a video game. It feels devastating and on top off all of these, hell/heaven symbolism in desert puts this game to another level. Who would have thought a desert would be such a fertile land for a story.

Level of detail is incredible. From the details in main menu, to arts in the streets, to black/white scene transitions, it makes you play this game a couple of times.

I really enjoyed this game, Couldn't recommend more.
10/10.

It's the first time I'm taking the time to write a legit lengthy review. Not because I think this game is great (this is *just barely* a recommendation from me), but because I have mixed feelings about it.
Things I need to clear up before we start:
I bought this game for 80% off.
Performance was great on my machine, no issues there.
Played it on Suicidal difficulty for 12 chapters until I hit a block too hard for me, where-after I switched over to the "Normal" difficulty.

Now, getting into what the game got right:

The visuals: Really good for such an old game.

The character VA (This is a story based game and character development is a key part): Apart from in-game VA (which is basically just screaming "reloading" and "take cover" all the damn time), the VA during the cinematics was very well executed.

The story: The story was paced very well and I loved every major plot point. The moral issues brought up by the game, showcasing the horrors of war, felt very original, somehow...?

Now, what the game messed up:

The controls: What the ♥♥♥♥?

The controls: Seriously, what the ♥♥♥♥?

The player responsiveness: Walker is braindead. Snapping into cover against a wall is so har—*gets shot*

The gameplay: The materialization of the word "stale" (And I didn't even know such a word existed until now, that's how bad it is.)

The handling of the guns: The guns had weight to them, but holy crap did it shake all over the place.
I don't play that many shooters, but the gunplay still felt out of place compared to the few shooters I have played.

The camera: The number of times the camera flops around/is "unstable" is astounding. I don't know what they wanted to portray, but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ does it stir my stomach. Let's see, what other game did that - Oh that's right, fkn Tomb raider 2013. That game had such terrible cameras I still didnt complete it due to the sheer amount of motion sickness (both of these make me feel like I'm playing half life again.)

The Enemy AI: Literal aimbots with zero spatial awareness (atleast in suicidal). Check out  [u]this screenshot[/u] {now removed} from my playthrough. Just because I increased the difficulty, turning them into aimbots is the wrong move. Give some awareness to 'em. The worst part about my screenshot is that some dudes were screaming at the top of their lungs "LeT's TrY a DiFfErEnT aNgLe!" 
If only they listened to themselves.

I would recommend the game if it's on sale, but that's about it. The unoriginal and repetitive gameplay is enough of a reason to give up on this game. As much as I appreciate a well written and executed story (and they really knocked it out of the park with this one), when I play a game, I expect... well, gameplay, and Spec Ops failed to deliver on that front. The only reason I am recommending this game is the unique concept. That's it.

Spec Ops: The Line has an intriguing plot; certain elements of eeriness, psychotic themes, gritty, and its substance of real-life violence catches the positive setting of a wargame. Certainly not a fringe shooter in story compared to the first Black Ops but the game itself is just shamelessly infuriating, I’ll talk about the flaws later. One of the sequences in this game gives the protagonist an emotional shambles and raw shock by his own gratification of being a hero and a soldier. It lets you understand how a villain can become when a man doesn’t question by their own morality from the orders of Coup and survival. After all, this is just a video game, you can shoot all the civilians and killing your country men as much as you want, but at the end of that, you’ll realize how disgusted you had become from those glorifying kills in survival. You had an actual choice here, but you marched through hell by believing these orders; a choice to leave the game and those atrocities behind. That’s what Konrad stated his message at the ending. A soldier is just dispensable as others. It’s not possible to walk in fine line when you think of doing the right thing in war. Everything there will be questionable at your own actions.

The whole story here is deluded. The real stories is what you'll find in the environments and the intels you had collected from every chapter that explains everything. All of what you had playthrough is all Walker’s purgatory, a constant loop of events at the beginning and the end.  This is perfectly fitting from this theme, “Only the dead have seen the end of war”.

Now that was the summary, I’m here to talk about the game itself. I had several gripes while finishing every chapters until the end in FUBAR difficulty. One of my main crux here is that squad based combat is a punishable and obscure game mechanic. Yager developers didn’t learn anything from the previous resident evil games like four and five by creating repetitive damsel in distress, this was also my biggest complaint either from Conflict series which should be suitable for PVE multiplayer. Lugo and Adams are the most pathetic AIs, a constant deadweight members leading themselves getting killed during the middle of warzone while I’m stuck covering fire and do all the dirty work until it’s clear from getting them back in the field. Squad commands are too conditional in environmental design like narrow spaces such as hallways is a good spot for them to charge with pillars to cover. In a middle of an open area is most likely a bad way for them to assist regardless of the sandbags or coverable objects on display. Lugo can be the most useful at taking out snipers from distant ledges since he is a marksman and I don’t have to use my HK417 or Scout tactical rifle to waste ammo. By latter, two of these men takes 10-20 seconds to kill each enemy which makes it very tedious throughout the whole battle. Second, the cover mechanic has a problem that can’t be pressed one button while sprinting at a same time. It only takes one bind delay to get shot and dead. Covers can lead to another disadvantage also at the very most corners that’s possible way to get shot through. Another, enemy grenades don’t even have trajectories or bounce out on floor, a very rage inducing part that it’s likely a throwable magnet and had to escape from the current position each time and switch back from the spot. Camera position is only dedicated on right side and 1/3 of the screen covered by Walker, no optional way switching sides unless I have to vault on walls- walking through an archway of doors with several enemies inside a room is going to be a huge problem. This is all bad.

The overall experience of outflanking targets here was too horrible and not enjoyable from what I had played. Every fight scene is just way too scripted aside from a player’s decision of attack so not highly ambitious and innovative at all, it is merely a shonky gameplay. This is only worthy from preaching its outstanding story written by Walt Williams but just molded on a disastrous game. Bringing those good things in two sides of the same coin deserves an overwhelming positive approval. 

I’m still glad I bought this even it’s 9 years late ahead, hits me in the feels without suppressing the real state of sadistic tortures. It’s one of best examples of an anti-war experience but it’s definitely a “no” for me as a game.

Spec Ops The Line is an action game that has matured like fine wine since it's release in 2012. The story follows your stereotypical shooter archetype of 'Angry American vs every ♥♥♥♥♥♥ in sight' until about two missions in where ♥♥♥♥♥ hits the fan. 

The graphics are aged, as is to be expected of an almost decade old game, but they serve their purpose very well and the gunplay is satisfying. 

Gameplay is similar to that of other cover to cover shooters such as gears of war, which makes blasting through enemies a breeze.

At the beginning I was disappointed and thought about dropping out of the game. Gameplay is average; a single button is bound to sprint/cover/zipline/drop/heal, and another button to vault/melee/execute, so it's cumbersome to properly operate your character. Third-person view is encumbered by a badly set mouse sensitivity, which often makes confusing to know which direction you're going. The only notable positive thing is the possibility of giving squad commands to your NPC teammates (which have a pretty good AI).
However, I kept playing, and I'm glad I did that. 
Scenarios becomes better as you progress in the game, and more and more immersive and beautifully rendered. The scenery filled by sand is well thought and causes an innovative gameplay. The strong point of this game is its excellent storyline and the very good script and acting during the cutscenes; I felt really immersed in a movie like "Apocalypse Now". The descent of the main character into the madness of the war is masterfully shown, also thanks to several easter eggs cleverly hidden. 
In short, this game is a true work of narrative art, testified also by the awards it received.

Pros:
1. Incredible plot and storytelling. 
The game forces you to face the horrors of war, pushing you as a Delta Force leader to make grisly choices that are understandably sugarcoated over by most games. While the game's starting sections may make it feel like a typical military/special forces shooter, the story steadily grows darker, introducing controversial moments where you have to make difficult choices on the spot. The more you progress through the game, the more you wonder if you are doing the right thing. "No Russian" in CoDMW2 is nothing compared to this. 

2. Fantastic character development
Character development is also arguably one of the best selling points of the game, where you get to see the distinct personalities and attitudes of the 3 protagonists slowly brought out by the game's events. Player models will slowly deteriorate with damage throughout the campaign, showing the toll all the combat is taking on the Delta Operators. These changes also extend to character voicelines and animations, going from calm and professional to violent, emotional and exhausted. Interactions between characters will also change as tensions rise as a result of the above-mentioned controversial choices. These changes really illustrate the physical and mental stress that the characters are suffering. In line with the game's dark themes, you may end up questioning even yourself.

3. Gorgeous presentation. 
*Do take note that the game was released in 2012, and so the graphics obviously cannot match up to modern day AAA titles*. The game takes place in the arid wastes of a destroyed Dubai, and it certainly makes you feel like it. The environment and lighting create a perfect atmosphere to represent a war-torn, sand-buried city in the middle of the desert. The animations are very smooth with a few excusable oversights. Sounds are also good, nailing the warzone feeling. The world detailing is also very intricate, with plenty of foreshadowing and hints at the plot and the conclusion.

4. Decent gameplay
The gameplay is decent, but not exactly excellent. Combat itself is rather one-dimensional with a few exceptions, such as shooting out glass to drop sand onto your enemies or sudden sandstorms changing environmental conditions. The game also makes stringent use of a cover system that must be followed or you will be cut down quickly. Take cover, wait for opportunities to peek out and shoot, regenerate any damage taken and repeat until all the waves of enemies stop coming. It's simple, repetitive and doesn't change much throughout the game and might even be called boring if the weapons didn't feel so good to use. You can also order your two NPC teammates to take out targets, throw flashbangs or heal each other, and they are noticeably better teammates than in other games like CoD. Stealth is offered in very small portions of the game, and I don't know if it was me screwing up, but I could never get it to work properly. To add to the difficulty, ammo can be hard to come by, forcing you to conserve your shots and repeatedly scavenge weapons from enemies. For example, the M4A1 only has a maximum of 5 magazines, and an overwhelming majority of enemies in the first few levels use Uzis, shotguns or Ak47s, forcing you to ditch it quickly.

Cons:
1. Janky movement and cover system
Movement in this game makes it feel like a console port (granted it's also on console). Character movement isn't very precise, sometimes taking cover doesn't do anything even though you're right in front of the sandbags, sometimes you can't shoot out from behind your cover for some reason, sometimes you stand up and shoot over the sandbags you were meant to be peeking out from the side of and get killed as a result. Some controls are also unnecessarily mashed together, such as vaulting and melee attack. It was slightly frustrating at times, but it shouldn't diminish the gameplay too much.

2. Not too much content
I finished the campaign on Normal in about 4 hours, the remaining 0.8 hours was spent going back once to see an alternate ending and reading the collectibles that I had found, so the game can be easily finished within a day, whether that's worth full price is up to you. The campaign offers no real replayability apart from seeing what would happen had you chosen a different option (which can be easily found on YouTube anyway) or wanting to challenge yourself on higher difficulties. However, do note that the events of the first playthrough and plot points might be disturbing enough to discourage you from replaying the game. I never tried the multiplayer, so I can't speak for that. 

3. Slight bugs
Although the game is overall well-polished, there were still a few bugs here and there. Sometimes you could headshot an enemy, blood splatter and all, but they took seemingly no damage. I also encountered one where enemy spawns were somehow messed up, forcing me to restart from the last checkpoint.

Tldr:
Overall fantastic game with its thematically dark and controversial story as its overwhelming selling point, supported by acceptably entertaining gameplay. The engaging narrative is something rarely seen in shooters these days and really makes you think. I would personally recommend waiting for a sale as I don't feel it's worth full price.

I claimed this game on HumbleBundle under the assumption that it was just another shooter. At first, I was sure that I had thought right. Generic third-person game play, cookie cutter action heroes, killing faceless insurgents in some far away wasteland without a second thought. The game really begins after the first hour. As soon as I began to kill American soldiers, I realized that the first hour had been pure bait. This shouldn't be right, Americans are the good guys in every game! That's why I adore this game, you're not killing Soviets or Terrorists, you're killing American Soldiers who are just following orders and trying to survive you and your onslaught of death and destruction. The game challenges your moral compass by frequently putting you into situations where there is no good outcome. Unlike most games where decisions benefit the character in the end, in Spec Ops: The Line there are no good decisions. As you progress in the game, even the loading screen begins to change. In the start, it will display basic tips such as 'changing the fire mode on your weapon will give you a tactical advantage', but as you progress further, the loading screen will being to mock and even insult you with lines such as 'if you were a better person, you wouldn't be here' sending chills down my spine. Even the menu is intended to set the tone of abandonment and the sense that your character should not be in Dubai. This feeling is supported by menu's lone sniper staring into the ruins of Dubai as Jimi Hendrix's Woodstock cover of the Star Spangled Banner is broadcast through a radio. The sniper is accompanied by an upside down American flag, which the loading screen lets you know is a universal sign of distress. Every decision just makes your situation worse, and leads to the main character slowly going insane. I, too, was going insane with the main character, because the later parts of the game surround you with so much pure suffering and death that Dubai begins to feel like hell. I think that was what really stood out to me in the end, the fact that the game slowly becomes hell on earth, and at the end of the game, you really have to ask yourself if your actions as the character were worth anything. There is no good ending to Spec Ops: The Line, and because of that it remains one of my favorite games that I have ever played. To this day I still think about this game and how it has stuck with me, no other games have affected me like this. 9.5/10, a true work of art. Please give this game a try, you will not be disappointed.

If you're even remotely interested in those themes, absolutely give this game a shot, I doubt you'll come away indifferent.

Let's start from the good points. The strongest suit of SOTL is definitely the setting, depicting a climate-torn Dubai on the brink of total collapse, overrun by the desert almost completely. The population is in a state of misery and abandon, the luxurious skyscrapers lie in ruins, while wars are waged on basic necessities like food and water. This amazing premise is further enhanced by the visuals and art direction, not afraid to show even the greatest brutality of war, to make players fully understand the insanity the team has to pass through. The combination of these two factors creates an incredible blend.

Gameplay is as well very good, oriented to combat through a series of firefights and encounters with diverse factions. Using cover, saving ammo and ordering your teammates around to help you are all important factors, while variety is good because of varied situations such as vehicle sections or defense segments. The optimal challenge level for the seasoned player is found on "Suicide Mission", while FUBAR, the highest setting, offers an extreme challenge that will test even TPS veterans.

There isn't much to say on the bad side, except a few things. A specific scripted "chase section" with an helicopter around halfway though the game is really badly designed, not allowing players to take any type of cover but instead having them follow a straight path with no clear indication on how to dodge the hail of bullets - I myself had to try this section over 30 times before randomly surviving. The other bad side is your companion's AI, which especially on FUBAR will not be adequate and be wiped quickly - your companions dying means a game over, if you don't heal them. 

[b]Overall, Spec Ops The Line is an extraordinary game, capable of transporting you in the darkest horrors of war with a gripping story, solid gameplay and brilliant setting all packed together. It took me 6 hours to finish the game, and there is not much replay value after that. A couple more hours if you have someone to play co-op with. For the default price of 20€, but also exceptional quality, in this case I can recommend buying at full price, it's worth every cent.[/b]

[h1]In-Depth Breakdown[/h1]
🎮 [b]Gameplay Analysis[/b]
Gameplay is divided into Exploration and Combat.

[b]Exploration[/b]
Is mostly performed on foot, though during some sections you'll also be able to use ziplines to descend buildings, or vehicles in pre-determined rail sections. While not in combat, exploring every environment is rewarding because grenade canisters, ammo packs and Intelligence lore fragments are hidden around, other than sometimes unusual weapons. Finding all of these things can give you an edge in the next battle, since supplies and ammo are not at all plentiful. Also, the detail and atmosphere of each place while doing so makes it all the more enjoyable.

[b]Combat[/b]
Is the core of SOTL and plays out in a relatively simple but well refined manner. Aiming is generally in third person but certain weapons such as sniper rifles or DMRs have scopes to use in first person mode for better accuracy. In each engagement, enemies will always outnumber you and employ military tactics such as flanking, using grenades, and suppression fire, while also using cover consistently. Generally the enemy forces are competent and deadly especially on higher difficulties.

Both for you and most enemies a few shots is all it takes to die, and headshots are always lethal, also on you and your companions. If you are killed it's game over, while your companions can be revived with an injection by yourself or the other one still standing. Using the environments when possible (explosive canisters, static turrets, blowing up sand to blind enemies...) is fundamental to get an advantage, while saving ammo and the best weapons for difficult enemies is recommended, since you can only hold two weapons with limited ammo each.

Variety is good as combat isn't always simply a shooting gallery but features defense objectives, vehicle sections, and tougher enemies or special units as the game goes on, so it does not become stale with the further addition of different weapons as well.

Preface - [b]IN MY OPINION[/b]

There are certain things etched into the DNA of almost every gamer, and one of them is [i]video game thugs are fun to kill[/i]. No, it's not because we're all psychopaths, it's because developers purposefully make their basic enemies seem like clusters of pixels on a screen. That way it's more fun; it's just shooting grey blobs. If someone made a video game where you shoot properly realistic enemies I'd be willing to bet that it would be more disturbing than fun.

Spec Ops: The Line is a game that makes you shoot properly realistic enemies and it's more disturbing than fun. Nevertheless, it's utterly fantastic, in the same way that [i]12 Years A Slave[/i] is horrific yet brilliant.

First things first: the shooting is nothing spectacular. It's ok, and definitely doesn't take away from the experience, it's just not going to blow you away. What [i]will[/i] is the sheer depth that this game's story has. Every enemy you shoot feels more like you're actually ending a life than just shooting at husks. The two side characters, Adams and Lugo, are actually memorable, which makes a nice change.

As well as one hell of a twist ending, the game gives you plenty of choices throughout its relatively small runtime, and every single choice has an outcome that makes you question whether you did things right. And they're not just 'Press A or B'; many times you're unaware that there was a choice at all, because there are moments where nobody tells you your options and you just have to do what you think is sensible. Every choice adds to the story's realism and horror, which makes the final product that bit more special.

[h1]tl;dr[/h1]
Although the shooting is a little 'meh', the story is spectacularly-written and offers an ending that makes you think for quite a while after the credits roll.

Spec Ops the Line brings you in the mind of a soldier in a slow but steady psychological breakdown. It follows the protagonist's mission and also slowly unveils his deteriorating state of mind, one that was initially a military-driven rescue operation which eventually spiraled to a more rogue-like act of vengeance that was catalyzed by the harsh truths that they discovered through their mission and even by the actions that he felt stifled by. 

Anyone can finish this game in about six hours or less in medium difficulty. The game really fleshes all these hours though so I much prefer it this way as opposed to fruitless fetch-quest sort of deals that break the immersion. The game boasts a good selection of guns and a well-designed, interactive environment, and the difficulty level scales quite nicely given the number of missions condensed in the game. But what sets this game apart from other contemporary FPS games lies in its story-telling and the choices that you have to make which challenges your own morality on difficult situations. Many times there will come painful decisions that you will have to make during chapters, and the game makes you feel the brunt of that decision to the point you'll feel like ♥♥♥♥ after. The characterization is spot on as the soldiers also become less and less level-headed as they come across these grueling situations. Moreover, the loading screens and intel that you spot along the way advance the worldbuilding and speak to you as the player rather than the protagonist - really pushing you to examine the morality of your actions in the game.

There are also many other elements present in the game that separate it from other shooters, appearing in the later chapters of the game. Without delving too deep into spoiler territory, both the mind and the combat will act as a unitary force which is unique and well-designed. This separates it from the hordes of shooter-focused FPS games by introducing a more psychological twist to it, imagined at a frightening level of engagement. If you're a fan of morality-challenging, choices-matter style of gameplay, this one would be the right fit for you. The shooter aspect is done pretty well too and is manageable enough to navigate to have a good challenge.

     First off, the atmosphere incredibly well put together. Though as I said, the graphics are dated, the visuals as a whole are stunning today: with dauntingly huge, beautiful vistas of a half buried Dubai and haunting, meticulously designed abandoned interiors. That overarching design with the reinforcement of the color, lighting, and soundtrack make this games atmosphere and setting truly special. 

     Then there's true pull of the game -- the story. Think Apocalypse Now and Lord of the Flies and you are almost there. You play as the leader of a three-man squad sent to Dubai to search for survivors after a failed evacuation led by a U.S. battalion who volunteered themselves, despite having other orders, after huge sandstorms near completely buried the city and cut it off from the rest of the world. What follows is an intense journey through the ghastly remains of the city, where a chaotic war now rages, in order to regain control and save the survivors. And in most other shooter you would do just that. Go in, mindlessly shoot bad guys until you win the game, and not give it another thought. But this is not any other shooter. It is a shooter about the cost of war and will make you question who and what is right.

      In conclusion, It's an amazing, truly unique experience and you should buy it.

[i]"A Third-Person modern military Shooter designed to challenge players' morality by putting them in the middle of unspeakable situations."[/i]

This game gained so much praise from players and critics. But was it earned? I don't think so. 

For starters, the gameplay is below average for a shooter. This PC port doesn't have mouse sensitivity settings in-game so you are required to change either your mouse DPI or edit settings file if you don't find the default sensitivity comfortable. It's core loop is basically: hide behind cover, wait for a chance, shoot few shots which in most cases doesn't even land you one kill, repeat. If played on harder modes, it becomes really tedious. Some say gameplay was intentionally made that way so take it as you wish. I've played it on hardest available difficulty on start and the challenge wasn't satisfying at all. The progression was really slow as you wait really long either for a pocket of time in which you can shoot safely or because you've been hit for not hiding in cover longer than 2 seconds and need to wait to be healed. Grenades helped but are limited and your companions aren't really that useful.

Onto the story, it's most praised part. If you have never experienced any kind of war (relatives died in war, living in country affected by war, or even read any books or watched movies about it, etc.) or you are young teenager then you most likely will find the story intriguing. It's main point has been done better many times before in other mediums. It implicitly gives you choices to make and later gives you consequences which is to be expected. The game gives you mostly evil and horrible choices yet the worst deed the game judges you on was forced (player doesn't have any say in the matter). And because of that your morality isn't really challenged. While I'm not against playing an evil character, the whole point of the game gets redundant. First: because it's obvious you have committed some heinous war crimes and you don't need the game to guilt you for you to be aware that what you've done was horrible. Second: there really isn't any point in choices as almost everything you do is morally evil and leads you to the same conclusion (Light spoiler:[spoiler]There's one choice most players missed where you can actually resolve the situation peacefully.[/spoiler]). Which leads into only one conclusion: you win if you turn your back at mission 1 and not play it in which case you've spent money to not play the game. The whole advertisement schtick of the game falls apart as a player choice experience. It can be understood as an attempt at educating the Call of Duty crowd but even that is corny.

While the story doesn't work, the presentation side of the game really deserves praise. Visual effects, environments and hidden dynamic changes in the scenery were really well done. For example[spoiler]the trees change appearance from fully blossomed to withered after you pass them and look back to symbolise the delusions of the main character.[/spoiler] Which really makes the experience somewhat surreal.

It's common sense that the war is in fact bad and that horrible things happen. I don't really see the point in spending time/money on below average shooter with a redundant idea despite the amount of hard work and care put into it. Read a book for a stronger, cheaper, shorter and better experience overall.  If you really want to play it, instead of a challenge to player's morality, treat it as a story of Cpt Walker, an "experienced" stereotypical American soldier who learns that war is bad.

Spec Ops: The Line, a compelling and gripping story on the horrors of war. A truly thought-provoking experience that subverts the expectations of the usual generic military shooter. Unfortunately, the gameplay didn't subvert my expectations in a similar fashion.

[h1] Pros: [/h1]
[b]+Amazing story[/b]
An incredibly refreshing experience; the enemies you mercilessly gun down aren't faceless and emotionless terrorists, but soldiers of the US Army. Makes you think twice before blasting everything and everyone.

[b]+Graphics[/b]
Quite solid on max settings, holds up pretty well even to today's standards.

[b]+Supporting Cast[/b]
Your squadmates SSgt Ludo and Lt. Adams express their opinions about your actions, criticize your mistakes, and make you question your sanity as you progress through the campaign, They're not just set pieces that help you kill.

[b]+The Radioman[/b]
Gotta love 'em.

[h1] Cons: [/h1]
[b]-Controls[/b]
God awful. That's all there is to say. I felt like I was controlling a tank the entire game. Many inputs have more than one function. There's no option to rebind multiple input buttons onto separate keys. Button context actions (ie. hit [x] to rappel) were displayed as if I were using a controller despite playing without one. I couldn't find a way to change this in the settings. Also, the mouse sensitivity was ridiculously high for some reason, and I had to manually turn down the DPI on my mouse.

[b]-Cover System[/b]
Abysmal. You can never move into or out of cover smoothly. Want to sprint? Character awkwardly charges forward and never stops. Want to take cover? Character stands there with a vacant look on his face as bullets whiz past. Want to vault your cover? Character stands up, punches wall several times, and is subsequently gunned down. Repeat. (See multiple inputs for same button above).

[b]-Gameplay[/b]
The general gameplay is just a slog, move from point A to point B and murder everything in your path (though sometimes with moral consequences). Mechanically, Spec Ops: The Line doesn't bring anything new to the 3rd Person Shooter genre.

[b]-Game Length[/b]
5 hours??? That's it? I watched all the cutscenes, played on the hardest difficulty I could, and I made an effort to find a few collectibles along the way. Replayability-wise, I don't think there's enough there to make me want to go back and do it again.
 
[b]-Heavies[/b]
I just wanted to add a little rant section about these absolute bastards. F*ck them. They're the worst part of this game. If you don't have grenades or explosives, enjoy dumping hundreds of rounds into their dumb faces. I played entirely on suicide mission so I'm not sure if they are any easier on lower difficulties. 

[h1] TLDR: [/h1]
Plain and simple, Spec Ops: The Line is only worth playing for the story. From a mechanical standpoint this game brings nothing new or interesting to the table. The core gameplay is clunky and often frustrating. I can't complain too much though, I got this game for $1 on Humble Bundle. For that price I'd say give it a go if you're bored, but for anything more than $5 I'd say give it a pass. Honestly, you're better off looking up the story cutscenes on Youtube and watching the game like a movie.

The best forms of art medium force the audience to feel uncomfortable with some element of what they're experiencing, and force that audience to introspectively examine themselves as a reflection of that art.

Spec Ops: The Line achieves this brilliantly. If you want a fun shooter where you feel like a badass, look elsewhere. But if you want to experience something truly artistic, play Spec Ops.

In my ongoing and likely futile effort to write a Steam review for every game in my library (#463 out of 612)... it's time for  Spec Ops: The Line.

If you've heard at all about Spec Ops: The Line, it's probably because of the critical acclaim it received at launch specifically for being a modern military shooter that ultimately subverted the jingoistic tropes that then-defined the genre (and to my knowledge, the genre hasn't changed much since). The reason why Spec Ops landed with such a big place among the critical community at the time, I think, has less to do with The Line's own intrinsic quality as a game than it did with critics expecting another generic, bog-standard shooter... and finding something considerably more interesting, complex and nuanced instead.

But the thing is... what makes The Line so special is really all in its (very unique) setting and the big narrative twist in the final act of the game. To get there, you have to suffer through a great deal of a game that is, still, a bog-standard modern military cover-based shooter. You run from room to room, and while the set-pieces are very cool, you're doing the same thing in each room: fighting an absurdly large number of hostiles while jumping from cover to cover. For much of the game, the most interesting thing going on is the subversion of the usual modern military tropes of gunning down neverending hordes of faceless brown people by pitting you instead against a much more threatening foe: the United States military itself. Yup: this is a modern military shooter where you spend much of your time attacking the US Army itself—never thought I'd see the day.

You can probably tell from my tone here that I'm not coming into this game as a fan of the subgenre, ready to have my mind blown; nor am I a professional critic, being paid to suffer through a game I have little interest in. Clever set-pieces and a unique narrative framing can only get so far when the gameplay I need to wade through to appreciate everything else is so mind-numbingly tedious. So, ultimately, I view Spec Ops as a game that's very interesting to read about, but has very little core appeal to actually play.

Which isn't to say I don't recommend the game, necessarily, -- the shooting mechanics are all very competently executed, if utterly conventional, and the setting (a post-apocalyptic Dubai in the wake of a devastating sandstorm) is much visually interesting than the usual Forever War fare. But at the end of the day, we're still talking about a game that relies on a fairly bland execution modern military shooter mechanics. If you're not already attracted, in at least a minor capacity, to this genre at its most generic (this is me tossing shade at Call of Duty) then Spec Ops: The Line will likely be better enjoyed in the form of analytical blog posts and video essays.

A solid cover shooter elevated to greatness thanks to its story and audio & art design

This game is a decent cover shooter, where you advance from shooting gallery to shooting gallery where you stay behind cover to avoid damage and pop out to shoot enemies, but it becomes much greater than an average cover shooter thanks to the game's story, voice acting, and art design. The game plays simple enough where you have a primary and secondary weapon, can swap either at will, and you also have different grenades you can use. The shooting is satisfactory and simple enough, where you need to stay behind cover on harder difficulties, although it still comes from the era of "regenerating health" so you can pretty much get through any section if you just exercise caution enough. Sometimes the game will throw some curveballs with destructible cover, but most of the time you can find a safe spot and pick off enemies without too much trouble. There's a melee button, too, but I honestly used it maybe once or twice at the beginning of the game, forgot about it, and then used it another time toward the end of the game when I remembered I had a melee option this whole time and hadn't been using it.

The story is a modern riff on Joseph Conrad's [u]Heart of Darkness[/u]. much like [u]Apocalypse Now[/u] was for a different era, and parallel's Conrad's timeless story with excellence while also putting its own spin on the tale. While I was familiar with Conrad's story going in, I managed to avoid spoilers for this game, so even knowing the parallel I was still pleasantly surprised by this game and I recommend anyone looking to play it to do so knowing as little as possible about the story to enjoy it the most. The voice acting and sound design in the game is excellent, as the sounds of NPC's, your allies, and the character you play during skirmishes sound very authentic and effectively convey the hectic situations taking place. The main character is voiced by Nolan North, who is a very talented voice actor, and while from time to time I couldn't shake that it sounded like Nathan Drake (aka the default Nolan North voice), it didn't ruin the experience for me. Technically-speaking the only issues with sound I experienced seem to be problems caused by design and not the exemplary sound team on this game, as when enemies spawn in they immediately begin their battle chatter and so you'll hear enemies screaming from a direction and think you hadn't cleared the area yet when in reality the enemies for the next area had already spawned into the world and are waiting for you to progress before they start moving. The other issue is that because pre-rendered videos are used at times that the audio level of the videos is much quieter than the rest of the game audio, so this can be annoying at times, and is a bit jarring at the end of the game when a sequence cuts between in-game scenes and pre-rendered scenes back and forth while characters talk.

On the visual aspect of the game, for something almost a decade old this game still looks great on modern hardware. It worked for me perfectly out of the box on Windows 10 so that was welcome, and other than some low-res textures used from time to time the game looks stunning. The art design of the various locales you travel through look great, with a wide variety between dusty buildings, destroyed buildings, high rises, colorful places showing off the excess of Dubai, and hellscapes full of ruin. Control-wise the game was a breeze to play through using mouse & keyboard, although there is controller support if you really want that console cover-shooter feel. There's a multiplayer mode for deathmatches if you want that sort of thing, but it really doesn't mesh well with the single player campaign and seems to really miss the point (apparently it was something that 2K, the publisher, forced the developer Yager to include). There's also a co-op mode, but it isn't the campaign and is just another tacked-on mode that doesn't detract from the overall package, but doesn't really add much either.
