As an avid Linux user, I've recently come to understand the importance of having decent games run natively on my OS of choice. As such, I browsed through the (rather impressive) steam catalogue of games that run on Linux, and came across this title. I'd never heard of it, but liked what the reviews said:

This is indeed not your average 3rd person run 'n gun shooter. Sure, it seems to start out that way, but quite soon it becomes obvious that there's a bit more going on than just a bunch of soldiers playing hero. Though the textures betray the age of the game a bit, overall the game still looks good. If not so much the models themselves, the level design (the rooms, the hotels, ... just Dubai in general) looks great.

The main selling point of the game is that you have choices to make, and they each have their impact. While true to some degree (the game has about 3 different endings), some decisions really are forced on you. That's not the worst thing in the world, far from it. Working out what choices I could actually make, and how they translate to the story further down has had me play this game all the way through a couple of times.
Each time I did, I noticed the quality of the voice acting more and more. The main character (Conrad), the DJ, but also your main NPC buddies (Lugo and Adams) do a great job. The players character (Walker) arguably is the most cliché tough  marine type voice, but it fits. Mostly because of how the story develops.

Reading more on what the developers had to say about this game, and what they were trying to convey also somehow added to the experience rather than diminish it. It's the first time I've played through a game and paid close attention to the opening/fade-out screens being black or white, and trying to puzzle it all together.

There's 2 main complaints I'd have about this game: The mechanics/controls feel broken somehow (specifically the dodge/cover mechanic). It took me 2 playthroughs to work out how you had to sprint into cover, for example. The other thing that I found a bit annoying is the weapons. There's not that much to choose between most of them. They're almost all a bit same-y. True, you get a decidedly better gun at the end of the game, but that's just it: only one gun really stands out.

Pro:

* Vastly underrated game
* aged reasonably well, the world still looks great
* Good for several play throughs
* Good story line
* Not your average shooter
* Voice acting is good
* Runs on Linux flawlessly

Con:

* Controls/mechanics are a bit wooden (cover specifically)
* Guns are all a bit same-y
* Multiplayer is dead

TL;DR

Definitely worth a buy, perhaps not its full  price, but add it to your whishlist in case there's a sale on next time.

Imagine Gears of War meets Shutter Island in the desert, but with less refined movement controls. It's a game that takes itself very seriously and yet, or perhaps precisely due to it, somehow managed to make me smile at times with its almost grotesquely brutal sense of humor.

Contrary to popular belief, I don't actually think that this game's selling point is or should be its questionably "difficult" moral choices. Most of them leave barely any impact on the story. Instead, I think that the overall character development within this weirdly mysterious and surreal context is what makes Spec Ops: The Line really shine. And this rhymed. What I mean is that you get to experience how Walker and his obedient squad almost lightheartedly go into Dubai, cracking jokes,  but then eventually turn into broken, filthy creatures that have to go face to face with the reality of war brutality. And this gradual change is carefully illustrated with subtle shifts in character design (more blood with different, harsher dialogues and voices) and environment (dark red sky, omnipresence of death, graffitis, loading screens, etc.). 

Furthermore, what's really fascinating about the game is its attempt to deconstruct the contemporary standard of shooters by breaking the forth wall on multiple occasions to directly address you, the player, in various, borderline provocative ways (loading screens, radioman, déjà-vu, ...). It's in other words a story that you don't fully experience unless you stop to think about what you're doing yourself right there, pressing buttons on your controller or keyboard.

With that being said, I was able to complete everything in this game in only 16.5 hours (all achievements and all endings), meaning that it's not a particularly long game. Also, I'd like to point out that the main technical issues in this game are the clunky AI and movement controls. Otherwise, the shooting is fairly fun and entertaining.

Conclusion:
If you're into complex stories that have plenty of details for you to ponder about even after you're done with the game, it's definitely worth the money. It's not particularly "deep" or anything like that, but, without giving anything away, let's just say it's pretty wild and out there. Though, be warned, the controls feel off at times and the AI isn't all too good, which could lead to some frustration at times.

Personally, I would buy it on sale, but at the same time, I don't think that your money is wasted if you do pay the full price.

There are games that wouldn't be particularly bad, they just go astray and even worse, deceive the player. I'm not thinking about studios advertising their game and trying to sell it as something which it obviously isn't and definitely not about games with a mind-blowing finale with a surprising twist, that no one - or just a very few - expected. No, I mean those games (and movies) that are constantly teasing and playing around with the player (viewer) just to give them a slap in the face, offering a shocking, pretentious, half-baked excuse of an ending. [i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i], this cover using, third-person shooter is unfortunately one of these games.

After a rather hectic helicopter fight in an unrealistically huge sandstorm, we are thrown back a few weeks earlier where a cutscene explains us how Dubai was hit by said sandstorm and how the whole city fell into chaos after that. The US Army, the 33rd Battalion intervenes, trying to help evacuate the locals and foreigners alike who were seemingly abandoned (couldn't they leave on their own?) by the authorities (I kind of understand why this game got banned in the United Arab Emirates). Then the CIA gets involved, since the US doesn't want the presence of the Army within the area and somehow a war ensues between them (meanwhile the civilians get butchered as well, because of... reasons unknown).
This is where we come into play as the leader of a 3 men unit, who were sent to deal with the evil colonel (he was our mentor before - of course), the commander of the battalion and who seems to be responsible for all this mess (since we can't do much about the sandstorm anyway). 
I don't want to spoil the story from this point, but let me say that I had a slight premonition where the story was heading to and I was hoping I'd be wrong... sadly I wasn't. And yes, the plot is quite similar to the 1979 movie [url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0078788/]Apocalypse Now[/url] (which I also deem a bad movie).

The gameplay focuses heavily on cover using, so much, that it gets monotonous fast, since we are basically going to run from cover to cover (especially on harder difficulties where a single bullet can kill us) while trying to overcome often endless (or so it seems) waves of enemies. Moreover the controls are not as fluid as they were in [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/atisz2/recommended/203750/]Binary Domain[/url] (this game being compared to [i]Binary Domain[/i] is actually a disgrace, but still, both are cover using third-person shooters, but this game can't catch up neither in terms of gameplay, fights, nor story).
So basically we're going to spend about 90% of our time hiding behind covers (and wait for the slow automatic regeneration...) while shooting the enemy with various weaponry (we usually have to take and use the guns of our foes, as ammo supply is scarce). While firearms are relatively accurate, shooting isn't that fun, since we basically use those split seconds to shoot, when our enemies are reloading their guns (if we manage to perform a few headshots, we get a little slow-motion bonus). It's not all that easy of course since our opponents are going to use their numerical superiority and charge (melee is clunky: it's not instantaneous and takes a while to be able perfom again) or throw grenades at us. This latter can be quite deadly since we can't just leave our cover like that (we are still under fire) and if we stay, the grenade kills us (if the grenade indicator is red, it means the explosion is lethal). This can make very cheap deaths and since the spawn of enemies is scripted (which I have no probelms with usually) some trial and error gameplay is involved (we'll have to remember in which order we have to kill certain enemies). This also applies to certain situations, the helicopter attack in the plaza for example, where we can only run into a given direction without stopping, even if it seems suicide and even if there are seemingly more logical choices around...
Our 2 teammates (one of them is a heavy machine gunner, the other one is a sniper) can actually make our job much easier (something I noticed late in the game), if we spam-command them to take out some of the opponents. This is the other end though, it almost makes the game too easy.

As the game slowly builds itself up to make the far-fetched ending somewhat more believable or rather acceptable, it's something that just can't be achieved (even if the game tries it, sometimes really hard, especially through certain conversations we have with our squadmates). I never liked those war dramas that portayed brutality for its own sake while hypocritically sending the message to the viewers: "war is bad folks". No, there are excellent anti-war movies that can send a powerful message WITHOUT glorifying needless violence (think of [url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0091763/]Platoon[/url] or [url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0120863/]The Thin Red Line[/url]).
The other main issue is the lack of choices the game seemingly offers us at some points (there's a part where we are surrounded by snipers and we are ordered to kill either of the 2 obviously innocent people in order to stay alive, or the one where we have to choose whether we save an officer or a couple of civilians), these are minor choices that have no effect on the outcome. Meanwhile the major choices are taken out of our hands and the game decides instead of us, putting us into situations we don't feel ourselves repsonsible for. Sure the game has 4 endings, but they can all be done by reloading (which I didn't even bother to do) the given section, they aren't the consequences of the choices we made throughout the game.

There's also a multiplayer section in the game with character classes and plenty of game modes, but no one seems to be playing it anymore. Shame.

The graphics, contrary to what the bleak environment would suggest initially, is amazing. The Unreal Engine 3 once again shows what it's capable of (but of course the bigger credit goes to the game's graphic designers): both the outdoor and indoor environments are astonishing at times. Especially some of the palaces we visit, with all the lavish crystal monuments and giant aquariums inside, all those accessories that characterize some arabian sheiks who don't know what to do with their money anymore.
Cutscenes are numerous which could be a good thing if the game had an exciting plot, but like this, they feel as if they were there just to prolong game time (which isn't very long).
Sound effects are generally good, above average with some especially good wind howling.

If [i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i] stayed at what it originally is, without the pretentious determination of wanting to show the monstrous nature of war, it could have been an all right game (and with a bit less cover action :P). With all the fake messages, the presumable but not really explainable 'psychological' plot and the lack of choices the game seems to be offering, without delivering, it's not something I would recommend.

PROS
+ excellent visuals
+ interesting, unusual setting
+ good sound effects

CONS
- the whole 'psychological' concept is a mistake
- monotonous cover-to-cover gameplay
- the game offers no choices at key points
- pretentious messages about war

RATING
4/10

This game's best played on the easier difficulties because, frankly, the combat isn't really anything to ride home about. This is a story based game, through and through. It just happens to have a lot of "shooting gallery" bits inbetween all the good parts.

I actually went into this game with high hopes, which I guess might of deteriorated some of the experience. The game itself works, kind of. The AI is a bit buggy / slow at times but I guess it's what you get for a 3rd person cover shooter. I've seen certain enemies just stare at a wall for 10 seconds before finally deciding to do something. Movement can be stiff at times and just doesn't work when you want it to, which causes a lot of unnecessary deaths. Whether it's the running, shooting, or the cover system that's wonky, I'm not sure. I've played my fair share of cover based shooters and I feel like this one just doesn't quite hit the mark for me. And on the higher difficulties, it's straight up frustrating. Crank the difficulty as low as possible and just cruise through the game for the best experience.

Story-wise,  this game is pretty alright though. There's a lot going on with a bunch of decisions to make that really question who you are as a person. There's a lot of entertaining cutscenes scattered throughout, and some of the banter between the main cast is downright hilarious. I've got to give them props for trying what they did here, there's a lot of ambitious storywriting techniques that they expanded upon that make this game unique. If it were a movie, it wouldn't have the same effect. It's all the small details which only video games have that are being added up to make this story one heck of a ride.

The gameplay is as derivative as ever. It's a military shooter. Find guns, hide behind cover, shoot things, and if you got shot just sit around until your wounds coagulate. There's lots of Oscars and Mikes and Flank this and that and blah blah blah we've all done this a million times and just thinking about it bores me to tears. Here's a thought: If I'm already pointing at something I can just [i]pull the trigger myself[/i] and cut out the middle man. They're mostly there for generic military banter during the combat and story elements when out of combat.
There's your usual assortment of rifles, shotguns, handguns, sniper rifles and grenades. There's a few on the rail shooter bits and gun turret portions and they are as boring as they sound. I hope you like set pieces with lots of convenient chest-high walls. Nothing changes from the first minute of the game to the last minute of the game.

But people aren't recommending this for the gameplay, they're recommending it for the story. It starts off as a naked copy of Heart of Darkness, going so far as to call the main villain "Conrad", which I guess is slightly more subtle than calling him Brando. The selling point here is as you progress through the story constantly defending yourself from people trying to kill you, you're supposed to feel very, very bad about doing this. That the game forces your hand doesn't help things.
There's a hilarious moment where I am told to [spoiler]firebomb a bunch of bad guys[/spoiler], but I deliberately did everything I could [i]not[/i] to because it would be too boring and easy so I wanted to get through the level conventionally. After 3-4 deaths it became obvious that the game was spawning an infinite number of enemies and wouldn't stop unless I did what it wanted. Grudgingly I did, [i]and the game had the audacity to criticize my decision for doing so[/i]. You can't blame my moral choices when [i]they aren't even my choices[/i]. This trend continues with the game trying to make me care about low-polygon count ones and zeroes and me continuing not to. There's even a cheeky load screen tip that states "The American Military doesn't condone killing of civilians, but this is a video game so what do you care?". 
The game culminates with an obvious [spoiler]Tyler Durdan/Shyamalan[/spoiler] conclusion I could see coming from a mile away. But it's a cop out, the story doesn't make sense with such a contrivance but it feels clever for doing so.

For example, there was a scene where it was obvious it was a group of civilians and even if you avoid bombing them, you still kill them all from a triggered event. The game expects you to feel immersed with the decision making in other times but you learn your decision doesn't matter because nothing changed and there were no consequences for your decisions. You wanted to save that guy, right? Well, you are not allowed to even if we give you the illusion of choice to try. 

Overall, good game as far as campaign goes and full of good surprises and moments. Lots of "oh ♥♥♥♥" moments but some ideas felt experimental or forced in, like giving players choices even though they're not real choices.


The really rough part of the game is the gameplay and its controls. Imagine an intense Third Person Shooter where there are enemies storming you from even your flanks and you desperately need to sprint, but the sprint button is also the cling to wall button so you're often clinging to walls when you're trying to run getting you killed. The controls in the game are really weird, too, like it's primarily made for controller and they half assed the conversion to something more sensible. 


The game also has a lot of difficulty spikes. IT can be a walk in the part, play on hardest difficulty because it's too easy, then there is moments where the game randomly gets so difficult that you will play it on the lowest difficulty. It has an inconsistent pace that's weird, it doesn't feel fair and often you'll notice AI has some aim bots. 


The game tries to push on you squad command leadership but it's kinda mediocre. It feels experimental because there are not a lot of uses for it from its lack of real control over the squad. You can order your squad to kill or pick up their partner, but that's pretty much it. It's one of those "good enough" impression, it does its job but it feels almost unnecessary of an addition. 


Ammo is a mild issue as well, it requires a bit of a learning curve. One frustrating issue is how there might be some situations you have practically none and other times where there's an abundance. In a game where you're fighting so many soldiers, you'd think ammo would be a non issue, just carry the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ammo. It does however serve as a apocalyptic survival type game to an extent, but when you have a huge army I wish it was better balanced. 


So the game overall is far from perfectly, definitely doesn't hold up too well today, but it does its job where its fun and fascinating. I suggest keeping eyes on this one for awhile, get it at a good price.

[h1]HOT SUN, COOLED SAND.[/h1]

I'll keep this review as spoiler-free as I can, because the main force that drives this game to be discussed by both fans and detractors for as long as they have is its gripping story.

Who says shooters can't evoke the sense of guilt, dread, sadness, fear, and trauma that a horror game can? Well, let's be honest: for most shooters, they're probably right. That's what makes Spec Ops: The Line unique. All of Spec Ops: The Line's elements, from its story, its characters, its themes, right down to the tiniest details in its world to the subtle ways some situations make use of its mechanics to drive the player, all of it serve to push its point home for many people who were affected on their first playthrough of this game's campaign mode, and even subsequent playthroughs where many of their questions are answered, while even more start emerging from the sand.

Let's get one big thing out of the way: Spec Ops is a linear game that has one and only one story, and it wouldn't have worked if the player choice people complain about was implemented in such a way that there were two or more completely divergent narrative paths that Captain Walker and his team could take. And that's fine. Tons of great shooters, great games in general, had one story and stuck to it. This is an exploration of Walker's team's descent from just another team of rough and tough soldiers to battered, broken, morally corrupted individuals. And that's not even mentioning this game's derision of the modern military shooter genre at large. How that unfolds, I want you to find out for yourself, hence the thumbs up.

In terms of mechanics, it works. As generic as it is for most gamers and critics, the only real issue I have with the controls is how the melee and vault actions were attached to one button and can't be separated in its option menu. Makes sense for controllers, but there's no reason for this to be a thing when you're playing on mouse and keyboard.

Now, I alluded to the game subtly using its mechanics to drive the player in certain situations. This is very much part of Yager's impressive attention to detail, where even though the only mechanic you have in a game in this genre is to point your gun and shoot, Spec Ops puts the player in situations where even that can make subtle moral choices mean something. Lemme give an example: [spoiler] in the scene where one of Walker's men, Sgt. Lugo, is lynched by an angry mob of civilians retaliating against the team's actions against the 33rd that has caused them suffering, you're boxed in, you don't know what to do, and if you wait too long, the crowd will stone you and Lt. Adams to death right where you stand. The whole situation seems to force the player to take revenge and mow them down. There's no diplomacy option in this game. How then can you restrain yourself, and by extension, Walker, from killing the people you came to Dubai to "save"? Well, it's never indicated, but you can either shoot up in the air, or hit one of the crowd with the butt of your weapon. At this point, Walker and Adams shout for the crowd to run while they still can, with Adams firing his machine gun in the air. [/spoiler] It's these moments where the player actually is given moral choices that show this game's attention to detail. While the choices themselves are of minor consequence to events that follow them, they [i]are[/i] themselves some of the major, impacting moments in the story.

Multiplayer's dead, (and from what I've seen, it's horribly buggy and unbalanced), but then again, it's a tacked-on extra that Yager never wanted given the message of the game. This game should never have had multiplayer, and it shows. That said, the co-op challenge mode could have been such a blast if it wasn't dead. I tried it (alone, sadly), and it's definitely gotten more love than the actual multiplayer mode, and if it had more than just the four solid challenges, could have extended this game's longevity more than it did. It's great that it's there, and I wish there were more maps for it and that more people played it.

Even if you took all of that aside, its presentation of Dubai as a sandblasted post-apocalyptic landscape is gorgeous enough by itself that it's worth seeing the sights, finding pieces of intel that flesh out the mysterious events even further, and appreciating some of the weird, often disturbing "graffiti" artwork that litters the city, some of which change in very subtle ways depending on your actions, giving credence to some of the arguments people have made that Spec Ops' Dubai is less a physical place where a story is set in, and more of a psychological space that both Walker and the player experience first-hand.

It's a shame not more people grabbed this game when it came out. Whether you're a detractor that thinks its exercise of chastising the player for what the game inevitably forces you to do is ineffective and pretentious, or if you're like me and felt its effect years after you've played it, you have to admit: it took balls to get a story like this out into the shooter market. Don't let my Steam stats give the wrong impression, by the time I got the game on Steam, I've already played it a few times, and I still recommend it to friends whenever it crosses my mind. This game, no matter how you look at it, was an important entry for the shooter genre, and, I would argue, for gaming as a whole. Even if it failed to meet its commercial expectations, it's still being talked about for its exploration of PTSD, its criticism of shooters and the people who play them, all the while being a functional, if slightly dated shooter in its own right.

TL;DR: Play it. It's worth your time. Trust me, if you think this game just screams "WAR IS HELL", it's way more than that.

[h1]Spec Ops: The Line[/h1]

[h1]"It takes a strong man to deny what's in front of him. And if the truth is undeniable, you create your own."[/h1]

[h1]Introduction:[/h1]
I gotta say when I first heard of Spec Ops: The Line. I didn't think much of it. It looked like a really fun military third-person shooter and I've always been into these kinds of games since I was a young kid. I played Spec Ops for the first time in my life back when I was still an Xbox gamer. So I picked up for like a couple of bucks in a game shop and went home to play it. It started off good you know. Just your average military third-person shooter. But oh man once you're done with the first 3 chapters. The story will start getting more and more intense. You'll uncover the true message that the game is trying to tell you. You'll be asking for answers because your head will be filled with so many questions. 

[h1]The Story:[/h1]
Six months before the beginning of the main story of Spec Ops. Dubai is hit by the worst series of sandstorms in recorded history. The sandstorm is so huge that the entire city is buried beneath layers and layers of sand. Colonel John Konrad the commander of the "Damned 33rd" Infantry Battalion of the United States Army, was returning home with his unit from Afghanistan when the first sandstorms struck. Konrad alongside his unit volunteered to help evacuate the city. But when the second sandstorms hit. All radio contact with the Colonel and the 33rd was lost. No one knows what happened to them. Whenever the caravan made it to the extraction point or else. Following this failed evacuation. The United Arab Emirates declared Dubai a no-mans-land and barred all travel to the city. Until one day, a looped radio signal managed to penetrate the storm wall. You play as Captain Martin Walker and you're in charge of a three-man Delta Force squad. Your second in command is Lieutenant Alphonso Adams and your Staff Sergeant John Lugo. You're sent to Dubai on a reconnaissance mission to find out if there are any survivors and to find the source of the radio signal. Your story starts here.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
● Fantastic narrative
● Graphics
● Gameplay
● Steam Achievements
● Soundtrack
● Collectables
● Character dialogue
● Great level design
● Performance
● Choices
● Loads of weapons to use
● Astounding landscape

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
● No Steam trading cards
● Sniper rifle scope glitch [b](If I were you. I'd avoid using the snipers in Spec Ops because the scopes are just broken. You can't move it to the position you want with your mouse. Well, you can but you would have to push your mouse off your desk. It's not a sensitivity issue mind you. It's just the scopes. You can't push it up or down it almost feels like it's controlling itself.)[/b]

● Enemy AI [b](Probably the gameplay feature that pi**ed me off the most in the game. Most of the time it's fine but some parts of the level it's just bloody annoying and no I'm not talking about the enemy flanking you and suppressing you. I'm talking about how they deal an s**t ton of damage to you even on the normal difficulty and when you're behind cover. They even have pinpoint laser accuracy and there are able to land every single shot on you even if you just pop out of cover for a second. On multiple occasions, I was even shot and ended up dying because they shot my hand when I was blind throwing a frag grenade. On top of that, some of the enemies end up getting as close to your cover as they can which makes the fights just super annoying because popping out of cover will just get you killed thanks to the absurd amount of damage they do to you.)[/b]

● Mouse acceleration and smoothing [b](It can be thankfully turned off in the .ini files but it's really annoying that it isn't an option in the actual game settings. On top of that, you have to also decrypt the .ini files because they're encrypted by default. Kinda annoying.)[/b]

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Spec Ops: The Line is a game like no other. It may look like a generic military TPS game but the story is the real bread and butter of this game. If I had to compare the story of Spec Ops to a movie that I once watched and really liked. I'd say that Spec Ops is similar to Apocalypse Now. It trades the humid jungles of Vietnam for a scoring hot desert in the Middle East with modern warfare take on whilst at the same time teaching you about events that are most of the time overlooked in military shooters like war crimes, insanity, PTSD and such. If you can find the game for a few bucks then you should buy it. It's seriously a one of a kind military shooter that's available for you to buy. I don't think there is any game out there that is similar to Spec Ops which makes the game just that much more unique and awesome! 

[h1]Overall rating 9/10[/h1]

It's been many years since I first played this back on highschool, looking back at it from now, I can say: Spec Ops was a game of its time. It was made around the time COD was at its peak alongside all the other plethora of militar shooters at the time, and with that said, is more interesting for the context than the game itself.
The discussion that if videogames cause violence is been a long, somewhat still ongoing debate, most of the arguments you'll see throw is either strictly against it or supporting the idea. Spec Ops: The Line is not about that exactly; the game itself mocks the idea of videogames being the cause of violence on it's dialog, but also what it does it shows that "It doesn't affect you" argument is incorrect.

Spec Ops is mean. It's cruel. It will agressively try to opress you to the point you're just asking it to stop, and when you are on the ground, it will start kicking you in the head. It's not only a very well written story, but what I loved about it then and what I love about it now is that Spec Ops is the complete opposite of the modern age mentality: It does affect you, it does matter, NEVER say it doesn't. We are all responsible for our actions, and one of the main focus in the game, is that it can also influence the people around you, it can make them more happy, more distressed, a lot of things really.

With all that said, as much as it's nice very nice written, paced, it plays with your expectations and usually delivers as far plot and characters go, I'll go on ahead and adress what everyone else also adresses besides the story.

I've waited a long time to try and review this game, and I'm still not sure what to say. To start, let me clarify that this is NOT your typical MMS type experience like Call of Duty or the like. The focus is almost 100% on singleplayer narrative and has completely different (and more deeply-cutting) themes than anything in that vein.

If you have the opportunity to come into this game without any previous information, take it. Don't use any walkthroughs or check the wiki, assuming there is one. The gameplay is fairly straightforward anyway. The experience of tuning into what at first feels like a run-of-the-mill cover-based MMS and coming out with a haunting narrative experience is really something else.

That being said, even if the whole thing has been spoiled for you, the game is worth picking up for the firsthand experience of its story and the way it chooses to tell it. In fact, playing through a second time after knowing every twist and turn puts a new perspective on almost every scene. Even after that, further playthroughs will yield more subtle choices. [spoiler]Ever notice that you never go up? You only ever rappel or fall, despite ending up in high places like the tops of skyscrapers. I didn't notice until it was pointed out.[/spoiler]

I hesitate to really elaborate on what makes this game great, but after playing it again for the fourth or fifth time, I'm compelled once again to share it with as many people as I can. If you like a good story that turns everything on its head by the end, this is for you.

This game came out WAAAAY back in 2012, but it still competes with shooters released today. It still looks good too.

You play as Captain Martin Walker. He, along with two others make up a delta force unit who are tasked with rescuing the survivors and refugees of a harsh sandstorm in the city of Dubai. An Army Colonel by the name of John Conrad had volunteered his unit, the 33rd in evacuating the survivors previously. Unfortunately, due to the mother of all sandstorms hitting the city, they had been lost and communications non-existent.

This game is violent. It asks a lot of you as the player, and makes you question just why you do the things that you do. You do a lot of unforgivable things, things that might seem necessary or justifiable, but in the end, you can’t take it back. The game’s story was definitely powerful and left a lasting impression on me. I’d say if you have the luxury of going into the game blind (I sort of did, I only knew that the story was gripping and that you and your squad commit some….” questionable” actions.

The gameplay is solid, and as good as what you can expect from a cover based shooter (Man it’s been a minute since I’ve played one of those. Remember when those were everywhere?). Guns have impact and are visceral. Shooting the guns feel like you are shooting a gun. The sound design and music were also very well done. You and your squad, along with the enemies announce positions, when enemies are flanking, enemies work together as teams like you and your unit does, and the experience is very tight. Unlike many games, I’d say that the game is a good length (Though the difficulty in certain parts seemed to be somewhat overwhelming, especially towards the final mission. In terms of the port, it’s not crazy good but it runs well enough at 60FPS. Only problems I got were when alt tabbing the framerate would tank for several seconds, but that wasn’t really an issue.

The game also has a multiplayer mode, but that is something I didn’t bother with as I have plenty of other games that scratch that first person shooter multiplayer itch. There are people still playing though, so if that interest you, that is there for you.

I heartily recommend this game. But be warned, what the depths it goes to may shock you.

Finally played through it, and I'm glad it's over. I did not like this game. It's a mediocre cover shooter at best. The gameplay is nothing outstanding, and if I want gameplay of this nature, I'll stick to Gears of War. If I want a compelling story? I'll stick to Uncharted.

Sometimes not for that. Who cares if it's linear or has some choices? What is this statement that you're trying to make, game?

By the time I got to the end, I was just done with this game. I was tired of it's preachy nonsense about how you should feel bad for killing people in a video game. This is directed at the main character and towards the player as well since we control him. If you don't see it that way, I can respect that opinion. This is up for debate and maybe wasn't their intention, but that is how it came off to me. Especially with the game forcing certain "choices" upon you.

It starts out good. I like the opening of the story. It was engaging and interesting. I think they had some good ideas. It started to fall apart as the game went on and I cared less about the people I was trying to save and less about my characters. The story, also, wasn't one I'd care to replay despite the ability to make multiple "decisions" in the game. By the end the, "You kill people in games and should feel bad for it" message is shoved down your throat so hard it makes me sick. I'm not gonna feel bad for playing a game and doing what the rules of the game tell me to do. That's why it's a game.

There are some cool moments. The main character suffers from hallucinations at various points, and artistically, these are pretty awesome. I really enjoyed them! Unfortunately they don't ALL make sense. One such drug trip has your character exclaiming, "We've done this before!" referring to the intro sequence to the game. You started in the middle of the story, and then went back in time to build up to that point. But somehow the character knows that? It's more of a meta hallucination, meant to make the player go "whaaaaat?" than have any sort of narrative cohesion. It doesn't play well into the other psychological trips of the main character, though. It's simply a meta reference.

I would also like to say that I really enjoyed the use of colors to differentiate environments. It helps separate areas out and constantly makes you feel like you're in a new location that having everything be the same. It's an underutilized mechanic that I wish more games did.

Overall it was disappointing, had mediocre gameplay, and I wouldn't touch it again. The only impact it left me with is how frustrated I am at the game.

First impressions.
I really like the dialogue and voice acting in this game. The main character’s voice seems familiar. I’ve probably heard him somewhere before. Apparently, a title from 2012, SOTL runs as smooth as silk on my machine. No problems whatsoever, and it even detected my hardware and maxed out the settings accordingly. 
The game’s visuals are bright and colorful. I think it looks pretty damn good, graphically.
Gameplaywise, it’s a standard third person cover shooter, and you’ll probably either love it or hate it based on that, but I’m rather impartial. I can say that they mapped a few too many functions to too few buttons, and the game desperately needs a dodge roll of some kind. 
When an enemy throws a grenade at you, you’ll have to awkwardly unstick yourself from the cover you’re stuck to and then just run in whatever direction you can till the red grenade indicator gets not as red and you’ll survive the explosion. If you take too long choosing directions, you’ll just die, so I found myself often charging off wherever and getting shot to pieces by enemies. 
By and large, enemy AI is pretty stupid. Sometimes they stand out in the open, waiting for you to shoot them, or go charging right into the teeth of your gunfire. Other times they hide behind cover that doesn’t actually cover them and are pretty much waiting for you to put them out of your misery.
Their aim is very sharp though, and I was pleasantly pleased by the difficulty of the game, which I set to ‘suicidal,’ apparently the second hardest difficulty in the game and the maximum I could pick on the first run. 
At this difficulty, you take only a few bullets before going down like a sack of potatoes, and nicely, so does everyone else. Bullets really feel like bullets, instead of everyone using rubber ammo and enemies and allies being bullet sponges. The game is absolutely lethal, so stay behind cover as much as possible, avoid grenades, and hit what you shoot at. This will serve you very well through most of the game, at least until it gets patently unfair at one point where you are separated from your squad with one weapon and little ammo. 
That part sucks.
If a bunch of dudes are shooting at you, you can order your squadmates to throw flash bangs at the enemy to relieve the pressure on you. You can also command them to target specific enemies, most of the time, unless you’re in a sandstorm.
If one of your allies goes down, you have to run over to them and jab them with a needle full o’ magic healing juice to get em back on their feet. Unfortunately, there are no healings for you, no. No health bar, only strawberry jam smeared on the screen and it goes into neato black and white effects if you get shot a bit too much. If that happens, suck your thumb behind cover till the janitor wipes all the jam off and the technician fixes the color on your monitor. 
Then you can pop back up and shoot things again!
Oh, and you can only carry two weapons at a time, cause...reasons.
Honestly, when a three-man squad with regenerating health can clear out hundreds of enemies in an area in a few minutes time, you’ve left realism far, far behind, and you should only concern yourself with what is and is not fun for the player.
These ‘modern shooter’ elements don’t bother me too much. They’re just pet peeves of mine, noticed, but easily ignored since they are so very, very ubiquitous these days.
The shooting is competent, and I generally had very little trouble hitting what I was aiming at. No real complaints there.
I haven’t played far enough into the game to unveil the grand Shakespearean tragedy that apparently lurks within the story mode, but I’m definitely liking what I’ve seen of the story so far.
Plenty of twists.
And a whooole lotta sand.

If you are there for an immersive story, in which you get to make decisions and reflect on them, you will definitely get what you are looking for.

Spec Ops:The Line is a generic third person shooting game, so if you're here for an amazingly fun game, you probably won't find it. The game has a multiplayer which you shouldn't care about at all, and the difficulty can spike oddly or feel impossible to deal with in some sections, example being the helicopter into a hallway you're located in and you have to run through it. On the "Suicide Mission" difficulty, I found it almost impossible to make it through the hallway, and when I finally did I'm not entirely sure how just luck I guess?

As for the narrative, there's alot to say, and alot that can be spoiled so if you want it simple: It's good. But it can be dark. War vet's/people who've been deployed may want to take caution with this game, it may invoke [b]very powerful emotions or memories.[/b]

In more detail however, this game is a well constructed narrative, that starts slow, and will appear very surface level, but will soon burst that impression.After that is where the game really starts to demonstrate it's true colors, which are very dark mind you. For some you may feel unaffected by it's story, or some of the scenes in the game. For others, there will be points where it will make you uncomfortable, and unsettled. As long as it's no determent to your health, then continue the game as this discomfort is a very powerful tool in this game. You'll find it's narrative is [u] soaked [/u] in ambiguity and subtext, and four endings to boot (once finishing the game I recommend loading up the final chapter via chapter select and try to see all four) makes the game open to multiple interpretations with multiple overarching themes.

[i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i] places you in shoes of a Delta Force operative, Captain Martin Walker, sent to the ravaged by the mysterious sandstorm city of Dubai with a simple mission: search and rescue which, within a day of Delta's presence in the city, turns into a slaughter and, in the end, into a mass grave. 

[i]'We cannot escape anguish. It is what we are.'[/i]

[b]Gameplay[/b] is... well... fairly generic and solid. Cover system is great, works every time you need it to, weapons have that 'satisfying' feel in them. When I was downloading the game, I was expecting it to be just some ordinary shooter to keep my head busy for 10-12 hours... But it turned out to be so much more. 

This is no average fun shooting range. If anything this game tells you, and makes you feel, that the war's never a fun place to be at. That the war is first and foremost a responsibility for others' lifes... - but whose? The lifes of your comrades? The lifes of the civilians? Your life? Which do you value the most? And how much can you put on stake to accomplish what you think to be importaint to you?

I was downloading a shooter. I got a great narrative with moral choices, none of which was better than the other. None of which was pleasant to make. I got a great ending that blew my mind. I got a great audio that really hits the right strings in the right moments and makes the experience quite unique. Like, come on, if shooting hostiles while the radioman plays "Hush", or fighting in Collosseum while Mogwai is playing in the background, is not memorable, I don't know what is. Great choice of music, by the way, especially the ending credits. The ending credits is what really gave me chills and gave the game a wonderful aftertaste. Especially the first chords of the song. Even the starting menu is gorgeous and changes as you progress through the game. Also, big props for the intel, which doesn't give you any direct answers, but helps you, through the eyes of the acting characters and oftentimes, through the eyes of other witnesses, to put the picture of what happened in the game together.

You know, even after completing this game for the 5th time, even after finishing it on Fubar mode, there's somethig that holds me in it. Something that doesn't let me say goodbye to it. Maybe it's the music, or the voice acting, idk. Maybe it's thinking about the decisions the main character makes. What goes through his mind when he decides to take a next step? What does he care about the most when he marches knee-deep in death?

I almost forgot to tell how well-developed the characters are in this game! Both Walker and the secondary characters don't feel flat. They feel ALIVE. They have their thoughts, their views, their feelings. They're not some stereotypical rambos, they're living people who do get scared, shocked, relieved, etc. They have their roughnesses, they have different relationships with each other, which also are not static and change throughout the game. Like you can tell that Addams is more friends with Walker and is more often on his side then Lugo, who's more emotional, but also more critical and can see better what Walker leads them to. You do empathise for these people.

And god bless Fubar mode. Some might get frustrated with it, but I think it's as close as this game might get to the real life and only on this difficulty can you truly understand what your main character has to go through, only with this difficulty can you really understand Walker's decisions. Because on this difficulty, you don't have many options: you either shoot your enemy first, or you get shot and die. You don't have that much time to think about the enemies' families or their feelings when the air is stuffed with lead. Fubar makes it clear.

All in all, Spec Ops The Line is a great game that asks and makes you think on very right questions. Moreover, it's a game with a great aftertaste, thanks to the well-done narrative, characters and muisic choice. Totally would recommend it to play even to somebody who's not into shooters. As about me, I'm sure I'm not forgetting this one for a long time.

Before continuing, be warned: this review has minor spoilers. If you don't want anything spoiled, here's the TLDR: If you're the kind of person who enjoys almost pornographic displays of military hardware, shooting brown people, being the good guys, playing as an uber-masculine powerhouse of NRA self-righteousness, then this is the perfect game for you. However, if you're more like me, and enjoy clever, thoughtful narratvies woven together by engaging gameplay, and stories that force you to confront real issues, like the darkest possible depths of the human heart, this is, unexpectedly, also the game for you. 


So here goes. This game almost counts as a parody game. It's a satire of Call of Duty and Battlefield, games wherein a big military beefcake named Austin Stone or Alex Mason or some other generic white-boy name goes about shooting foreigners in the name of American brovado. Now, as games, these almost copy/pasted cover based shooting modern warfare-type games are almost universally fun. They're fun in the same way rewatching "Friends" for the 47000th time is fun. Not really engaging, but at the very least it's something to do. The problem arises when 40% of triple-A games released are just the same thing but with shinier guns and the possibility of shooting a different set of foreigners. So, when I found out that this game was inspired by Apocalypse Now, my favorite piece of media that acts as the very antithesis of the glorification of the military, I couldn't help myself from buying and playing it. I know I called it a parody/satire of generic war shooters, but I don't know if that's totally accurate. Satire and parody usually includes the element of humor, but The Line is jarringly humorless. It's a parody/satire in that it is a pretty clear criticism of modern shooter games, but in pretty much nothing else. 

So let's talk about the story. You play as Captain [strike]Willard[/strike] Walker in his search through [strike]Vietnam[/strike] Dubai for a rogue Colonel named [strike]Kurtz[/strike] [strike]Conrad[/strike] Konrad. The more clever of you readers may have noticed that I'm poking fun at the similarities between The Line and Apocalypse Now, but in more seriousness, I'm not going to claim that the story is a ripoff. In fact, besides the clear parallels of the names, the story is actually incredibly original. Now, the game does a good job of keeping the guise of a generic war shooter for a pretty long time. In fact, so long that I almost forgot what the premist of The Line really is: a cold reminder of our society's tendency to desensitize ourselves to violence by trying to rationalize it with a manichean view of good and evil. So as you progress on, Walker commits acts of violence that aren't too far out of the realm of expectation from a modern war shooter: shooting people's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ heads off, executing them brutally, etc.. However, even though I knew it was coming, the game still suckered me into having fun with it, which made it all the more effective when the game reminds you that you're a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ monster. I remember a particular time when I had just executed someone who definetly wasn't gonna get back up just because I needed his ammo in a hurry. Then, not one minute later, I was sneaking up on a couple of rogue American soldiers. I stopped to listen to their conversation, hoping to hear them talking about how many babies they'd killed, but that wasn't the case. One of them asked for a stick of gum. The other offered his last stick of gum. The first guy refused, saying "Dude, I don't wanna take your last stick of gum". I literally had to pause the game and have a smoke. I literally couldn't handle it. I had had that exact conversation a million times. I almost couldn't bring myself to kill them, they seemed like nice people. But what has to happen has to happen, so I did it. Then, I got killed, had to restart the level, and listen to them talk like normal not-evil people once again. Little bits of polish like that are what makes this game what it is, and what makes it so effective in making you feel actually guilty and genuinely unsettled. the realism with which enemies are portrayed goes a long way in making you feel like the bad guy. The screams aren't hilariously overexaggerated or super masculine, they sound like actual people, actually screaming because they're in actual pain or fear, which works to further the goal of making you feel like you're not killing the monsters that you want to be killing, but the people you don't want to be killing. By the end I literally felt exhausted, and above all, guilty. 

I do have some criticisms of the story, though. I know that this game is meant to blur the line between good and evil, but it blurs it so well that I wasn't even sure what made me the bad guy. Yeah, sure, I shot up the Dubai Shopping Mall, but only because there were a bunch of rogue American soldiers around it, and they were hardly better. See, at the beginning of the game, the story paints you as the good guys and the rogue Americans as the bad guys. Then, the story repaints you as the bad guys. The problem is that they never spin it so that the rogues look like the good guys again, so by the end, I wasn't really sure who  the good guys were, all I knew is that I felt like the planet's biggest ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Maybe that's the point, though. There are no good guys. Just killers killing other killers without realizing that they're all just regular people like you and me. 

That about covers the story, and the story alone is reason enough to buy this game, but I must cover the gameplay anyway. It's squarely medium good. It's cover based, and not all that different to any other game of the type. It controls basically competently, when you put a bullet through someone's head, usually it stops being on their shoulders. However, every now and again, in moments of serious tension, I would find the game seeming much harder to control. You can't just jump. Idk why game designers thought that limiting your freedom of motion by an entire dimension was a good idea, but the lack of a jump button can make the game incredibly awkward. First impressions.
I really like the dialogue and voice acting in this game. The main character’s voice seems familiar. I’ve probably heard him somewhere before. Apparently, a title from 2012, SOTL runs as smooth as silk on my machine. No problems whatsoever, and it even detected my hardware and maxed out the settings accordingly. 
The game’s visuals are bright and colorful. I think it looks pretty damn good, graphically.
Gameplaywise, it’s a standard third person cover shooter, and you’ll probably either love it or hate it based on that, but I’m rather impartial. I can say that they mapped a few too many functions to too few buttons, and the game desperately needs a dodge roll of some kind. 
When an enemy throws a grenade at you, you’ll have to awkwardly unstick yourself from the cover you’re stuck to and then just run in whatever direction you can till the red grenade indicator gets not as red and you’ll survive the explosion. If you take too long choosing directions, you’ll just die, so I found myself often charging off wherever and getting shot to pieces by enemies. 
By and large, enemy AI is pretty stupid. Sometimes they stand out in the open, waiting for you to shoot them, or go charging right into the teeth of your gunfire. Other times they hide behind cover that doesn’t actually cover them and are pretty much waiting for you to put them out of your misery.
Their aim is very sharp though, and I was pleasantly pleased by the difficulty of the game, which I set to ‘suicidal,’ apparently the second hardest difficulty in the game and the maximum I could pick on the first run. 
At this difficulty, you take only a few bullets before going down like a sack of potatoes, and nicely, so does everyone else. Bullets really feel like bullets, instead of everyone using rubber ammo and enemies and allies being bullet sponges. The game is absolutely lethal, so stay behind cover as much as possible, avoid grenades, and hit what you shoot at. This will serve you very well through most of the game, at least until it gets patently unfair at one point where you are separated from your squad with one weapon and little ammo. 
That part sucks.
If a bunch of dudes are shooting at you, you can order your squadmates to throw flash bangs at the enemy to relieve the pressure on you. You can also command them to target specific enemies, most of the time, unless you’re in a sandstorm.
If one of your allies goes down, you have to run over to them and jab them with a needle full o’ magic healing juice to get em back on their feet. Unfortunately, there are no healings for you, no. No health bar, only strawberry jam smeared on the screen and it goes into neato black and white effects if you get shot a bit too much. If that happens, suck your thumb behind cover till the janitor wipes all the jam off and the technician fixes the color on your monitor. 
Then you can pop back up and shoot things again!
Oh, and you can only carry two weapons at a time, cause...reasons.
Honestly, when a three-man squad with regenerating health can clear out hundreds of enemies in an area in a few minutes time, you’ve left realism far, far behind, and you should only concern yourself with what is and is not fun for the player.
These ‘modern shooter’ elements don’t bother me too much. They’re just pet peeves of mine, noticed, but easily ignored since they are so very, very ubiquitous these days.
The shooting is competent, and I generally had very little trouble hitting what I was aiming at. No real complaints there.
I haven’t played far enough into the game to unveil the grand Shakespearean tragedy that apparently lurks within the story mode, but I’m definitely liking what I’ve seen of the story so far.
Plenty of twists.
And a whooole lotta sand.

[u]Gameplay:[/u] It's Call of Duty in third person.

[u]Story:[/u] Let's just say that it's not a story you would expect from a dudebro military shooter.
It's a unique game because it dives into moral ambiguity, but that's about all it has going for it. There is no "deeper" meaning hidden somewhere.

The game gets too much praise by people who think it's the most profound thing they've ever experienced. While in reality the game succeeded if by the time you finish it, you say to yourself "Okay that felt different to what I'm usually used to and I like that".

I researched this game before buying and playing it, so I had a rough idea of what it was about when I started the campaign, though I didn’t know about any of the vital decisions throughout the story yet. I was expecting a game about war being hell, but instead of a story about trying to keep your humanity in the horrors of war, I got a hallucinogen-drugged guilt trip filled with pretentious moral superiority.

It starts before the gameplay even begins: You're part of a delta-force squad on a recon mission in Dubai. Why Dubai? Because Dubai was suddenly surrounded by a supernatural sandstorm and the citizens in there started panicking. Adding to that, there is an entire division of the US Army in there as well, because some stupidly heroic commander, which happens to be the protagonist's idol, decided he would save all the citizens, then noticed he has no way of getting them through the storm.
Meanwhile, your elite Delta Force soldiers walk through that storm by foot and decide to ignore their orders and try to save the aforementioned commander alongside the entire division of soldiers. This process of thought gets even more irrational some chapters later when you start to get the impression that the commander is evil. Then, instead of getting out of Dubai, as you were originally supposed to, or trying to save some civilians, you decide to kill the commander, which leads to a variety of bad decisions, later on, dooming about everyone in the city.
So, with all the options to authentically represent the main motives, ranging from civil wars in the Middle East to dictatorships in Africa, and the people involved in these, they’ve chosen a scenario as unrealistic as possible, with main characters that don’t even have a proper reason to be there in the first place, besides naïve heroism.

The next major flaw to attract my attention is the combat system. The combat is as generic as it gets, I’m not even referring to the gameplay here; I’m referring to three soldiers killing half the population of Dubai and an entire division of US soldiers. It loses a lot of its authenticity by doing this; any situation which could seem threatening loses most of its tension.
One could of course argue that you could play on harder difficulties instead, however, that doesn’t change the fact that a team of three soldiers killing around three hundred soldiers takes away most of the realism from the gameplay.

The biggest flaw in the entire story is the constant guilt-tripping though, which becomes noticeable somewhere around halfway through the game when they start shoving it in your face. Every single loading screen constantly tries to tell you what a monster you are, even though Dubai has been “shoot-or-get-shot” from the very start.
Also, shooting rogue US soldiers trying to kill you is apparently more condemnable than doing so with local guerillas. The same applies to the first vital decision in the game as well, you have the choice between saving an important American soldier or some innocent civilians, no matter what you choose, someone catches a bullet.
This grey morality stuff is way exaggerated throughout the game, as if it was written by someone, who recently discovered that the world isn’t painted in black and white, so to speak. The same goes for the glorifying of war, naturally, as it goes hand in hand with the matter of grey morality. It’s nothing I wouldn’t have known before, but I’m shocked how many people were amazed by this game just by the way it addressed these two topics, like this wasn’t done a thousand times before, even more so in a more realistic and relatable way.
Another important motive is revenge, the driving force in the later chapters, which was done pretty well compared to the other motives; you have the choice to acknowledge your deeds or blame them on somebody else and let them suffer for it. This motive does have a major flaw but said flaw only becomes apparent once you get to know the 4th wall messages the game wants to tell.

Said messages come to show in the water truck and the infamous white phosphorus missions. Unlike other missions, where you had the choice between selflessness and selfishness, these two missions just had you doing straight-up ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
Anyone slightly clever reading the hints could’ve concluded that these won’t end well. This isn’t the case for the protagonist though; he doesn’t know and ends up making everything worse. From the protagonist’s point of view, this is a mistake, but he didn’t know any better. From the player’s point of view, this was unavoidable, as there was no other option to proceed. This would’ve been a terrible decision in design, storytelling-wise, as neither you nor the protagonist feels guilt for what happened. So, to justify this, the game just breaks the 4th wall.

The message behind it: „Well you could’ve just stopped playing”. Not only is this complete nonsense, but the game also throws its entire immersion out of the window, by acknowledging it to be a game. Some say, that that’s how the game attempts to cut out the protagonist, to put the player in his position to blame the player himself.

There are several ways how exactly this is supposed to work: The first one is to make you feel sorry for the ones you killed, but due to the killing being necessary to survive, the deeds of the protagonist seem pretty reasonable. Concerning the water truck and the white phosphorus missions; as you have no choice they also fail to reflect on the player himself, as a real human being would’ve had a choice at this point, while our protagonist hasn’t. While we’re at it, why should I even feel guilty about killing anyone, it’s just a game, right?
Well, this sentence is more or less exactly what is displayed on one of the loading screens later in the campaign, which is an obvious hint at the second way this is supposed to work; you should feel bad for enjoying a game about war. So you’re judged for having these very human feelings, you virtually can’t do anything about. Yet, humans might have these instinctive feelings, but they can choose not to act accordingly to them, which happens to be the very thing that differentiates us from animals. But after all, you do act accordingly to these instinctive feelings, and you like it, right?

Wrong. After all, you might feel good about it and do it to survive, but that doesn’t mean that you can’t consider it wrong and wouldn’t choose an option out of it if it is given. Yet, the very way this game is set up, it only gives you the choices to continue killing, to die, or to give up. As dying isn’t permanent at first and thus doesn’t deliver any conclusion to the story, this isn’t an option to consider. Giving up simply means to stop playing, which whether leads you to acknowledge the story of the game to be meaningless by rejecting every bit of its immersion or to weave your very own version of a conclusion, at which point you rob the game of its sovereignty as a medium, so you could tell yourself that they all lived happily ever after just as well.
And as if all of this wasn’t bad enough already, the end of the game reveals that all of this was actually within the protagonist’s mind. At this point, I couldn’t have given less of a ♥♥♥♥ about what’s happening.

This game wrecked every single device it was supposed to use to give its message the weight it deserves. With all its immersion gone, this isn’t a game to reflect on the players themselves, but a shallow, hypocritical and pretentious game, which only narcissistically reflects on itself. I look at the ideas it was built upon, then I look at the way it ended up, and all I see on my way there is wasted potential.

A modern masterpiece of a shooter

Pros:
- The story is simply astounding. What starts out as a seemingly average special ops plot turns into a spiraling descent into horror, and at times you'll wonder just how much deeper the rabbit hole can still go. 
- Stellar writing and voice acting 
- The game looks gorgeous despite its age, due to detailed animations, convincing physics and surprisingly colourful and varied environments, many of which feel downright dreamlike
- The game uses its medium as a storytelling device to its full potential. The less said about how it does this the better, but suffice to say the game warrants multiple playthroughs
- Astonishingly, for once the collectibles actually warrant collecting, since they give deeper insight into the story.

Average:
- The gameplay is monumentally standard. This isn't a negative, and an intentional choice by the developers, but it still must be said that innovation in gameplay is nowhere to be seen. The weapons, enemies and combat scenarios feel like they could be from any game of the genre.

Cons: 
- The game is rather slim on content for 20€. You'll play through the campaign in 5-7 hours on normal difficulty, and the multiplayer is effectively defunct. 
- Moving between cover effectively and staying out of the line of fire can at times feel more difficult than it should, which makes some scenarios in the game rather frustrating.

Don't let the generic gameplay and scarce content dissuade you: This is one of the greatest videogame stories ever told, right alongside The Last of Us, Undertale, To the Moon and The Witcher 3. Pick it up when it goes on sale next time, and have your heart ripped out.

Spec ops: The Line is an outstanding game in almost every aspect.
The game is a third-person shooter with a cover system. Gameplay and gunplay are made in a very nice and satisfying way. With the passage of time, we get more and more different weapons, each weapon is good in different situations.
AI of the opponents is done correctly, enemies choose the appropriate covers and try to wait for us to open ourselves to take an accurate shot. 
Graphic design has grown old since the release date, but it still fits the story presented, I would risk saying that for the year in which the game has been released graphics are even nice.
Sound design is also flawless, music always fits the situation perfectly, emphasizing its seriousness or tragedy, sounds of weapons give them power, while the shouts of soldiers, whether hostile or allied, intensify the atmosphere in which we will fight. 
Story is the most important thing why you should play Spec ops: The Line. The story begins inconspicuously, we play the role of Captain Martin Walker, commanding a three-man Delta Force unit sent to Dubai covered with sandstorms. The mission is simple; perform a short reconnaissance and call for backup, but how it is finally performed differs from the initial assumptions. I do not want to reveal too much from the story itself because it's great in every aspect, so I will only add that it is an anti-war game, after first few chapters the plot literally changes its form from an ordinary shooter to a post-traumatic stress (PTSD) simulator. Spec ops will show us exactly how the hero turns into an antagonist...
Does this game have flaws? Of course but they are small enough that I don't see the point of mentioning them. In my opinion, this is the perfect game and a must play.

It took me a while to play this, sitting in my library for over a year. Curiosity pushed me to see why people seemed to have such a good opinion of it and after a 7-hours battle over three days, I finally got to the end and ... well, if there's any definitive game about the horrors of war, this might just be it. On the surface, it's just another cover shooter with macho soldiers racking up the body count in the most over-the-top, unrealistic ways possible .... there's a little of that, obviously nowadays you can't have a game about war that stays truly away from Hollywood, but in contrast to today'S popular action flicks, a lot of effort has been put in Spec Ops: The Line's story, a psychologically horrifying tale of a deluded man trying to be a hero in a war-torn, sand-flooded Dubai where civilians live in the constant crossfires between military factions that keep tearing eachother apart. Protagonist Martin Walker fights on, trying to do the right thing when he doesn't even know what is right and what is wrong, denying a truth that doesn't align with his perception of his own morality, flanked by two subordinates who keep following despite arising doubts about their captain's decisions. Whatever happens when Walker finally opens his eyes is up to the player, whose actions in the final chapter determines Walker's fate and how he deals with the delusions he had been following all this time.

On the technical side, more specifically on how the PC version is handled, the game suffers from a few problems. The graphics are still quite beautiful and there's some breathtaking scenery in the sand-choked Dubai but the real problem lie with the controls. Controller users will have no problem whatsoever because the game -and this is problematic- has been made around controllers and every button prompts are marked as Xbox buttons. First-time players will struggle to learn the controls without having to check the keyboard bindings in the options menu as no button prompts will show its keyboard counterpart during gameplay. After setting up your buttons and playing a few hours, though, I managed to do just fine and enjoy the game with the prefered precision of a mouse.

The other problem I noticed with this game is that eventually, during gameplay, pre-rendered cutscenes would have no sound, greatly impacting the strength of the later scenes, especially the ending. I'm unsure if it's because of Alt-Tabbing or if it's a problem with the port but I did wish it didn't happen during the ending scenes.

What else could be said? Well, the games does a swell job of showing the horrors of your actions, especially with the infamous white phosphorus scene, which see the player using a airborn camera to target enemy troops so your allies can fire mortars at them. While you control the aiming, flashes of the people burning and dying appears subtly, showing the impact of your actions and if that wasn't enough to really bring the guilt, walking through the burned grounds littered with bodies, seeing horrifyingly burned soldiers begging for help certainly will hit you in the chest like a battering ram. This is just one scene that will make you question Walker's methods and the validity of his excuses.

In conclusion, Spec Ops: The Line is a gem that is easy to dismiss as another modern military shooter that caters to the dudebros of this world but beneath the shootouts and the loud explosions is an uneasy war story with a troubled protagonist that will leave as big a mark as classic war movies like Saving Private Ryan or Apocalypse Now and doubly as deserving of recognition. I highly recommend it.

The plot of the game is mostly what seems to be heralded as a great work that could hold its own against the likes of Tolstoy, Fitzgerald or Dickens. In reality if you have ever so much as glanced at the blurb of A Heart of Darkness or absentmindedly overheard the advert for Apocalypse Now then you already know the plot cover to cover. However, unlike the book or film Spec Ops attempts to leverage the interactivity of the medium to make the player connect with the characters in ways that aren’t possible through purely written or spoken word. The developers chose to do this by putting the playable character into positions where they frequently have the power of life and death over others. 

The scene that most seems to gravitate towards most is the infamous white phosphorous scene where you may ‘choose’ to bombard an enemy emplacement with white phosphorous to make an engagement trivial. If the player ‘chooses’ to take this option, then it is revealed immediately after that you also accidentally set a large group of innocent civilians alight as well (obviously leading to their quick, and not so painless demise along with the soldiers). This is meant to cause the player to feel guilty for their actions as it is harder to adopt and ‘us or them’ mentality towards a group of unarmed, harmless innocents than it is a large military group that can easily kill you. Now while setting up for this scene you are told by Sergeant Lugo (who often acts as the little angle as the shoulder) that such an action is immoral while the other character (Lieutenant Adams - who is the devil whispering into your other ear all game) that you have little choice. So naturally you would believe that you could choose to forgot the phosphorus and just fight with regular old guns, but in reality this option will just drag out the section for an eternity until eventually a lucky shot on the opposing side kills you and you have to replay the whole segment all over again. Indeed this pattern repeats itself at every major moral choice. Choice presented, Lugo Objects, Adams insist and then you ‘choose’ and time after time you will realise that making the morally right choice will just lead you into a drawn out or instant failure state forcing you to - knowingly - make the immoral choice only for the game to constantly berate you for your ‘choices’ in a constant attempt to force remorse onto you. But it always rings hollow as the lack of any real choice just serves to dissociates you from the characters and the plot as a whole; making you feel at best indifferent.

All in all, the plot is effective only if you pay no real attention until the game decides its time to plaster any subtlety the source material had onto a 100ft billboard and force you to stare down the ‘consequences’ like Alex DeLarge in a Clockwork Orange but its obsession with making you admire it plot caused every other aspect of the game to suffer making every other aspect of the game mediocre at best. So save yourself the money and just got read A Heart of Darkness or watch Apocalypse Now to have the same story told but with a far better, competent execution.

This is one of those games that you play for the story, not the gameplay. The gameplay is a standard 3rd person shooter:
1)	Get to cover
2)	Wait for the enemies to pop out of cover and shoot them
3)	Advance forward

There are some ways the game mixes up the gameplay like having turrets or sniper sections, but don’t go into this game expecting some fresh or innovative gameplay. If you have played a 3rd person shooter with cover mechanics, you can pretty much expect the same here.
