After completing the campaign, I was left with a really empty feeling, and very few games are able to get that kind of a reaction from me through the story. The gameplay in this revolves around being a cover-based shooter with squad orders; nothing that hasn't been delved into before. However, the story delivers a gripping experience that I felt hammered in what PTSD can do and the horrors that soldiers can witness in the field, going into just enough depth to have the story understandable, but still ensuring that the player has things to look into for more information regarding the reality of PTSD. This story is incredibly important and was told very well, showing the player the awful results of war. Very much recommend this game.

It's tempting to give The Line a thumbs down, given that I did not have a good time and it seriously bummed me out. But the thing is, that's pretty much the point of the game. Ever watched Platoon and thought "damn, I wish that was me"? Well, maybe find a good psychiatrist, but also definitely try Spec Ops: The Line because it will scratch that itch without the considerable distress of having to be Charlie Sheen.

So while it initially seems to be yet another piece of Modern Warfare-style hooah military porn, it doesn't take long for a metaphorical nun to enter the room and punish you for vigorously exercising your assault rifle. (That's a metaphor we can all relate to, right? No, just me? Alrighty then.) Turns out The Line is more about the horrors of war than the thrill of whipping out your beefy gleaming weapon in front of a bunch of guys.

[h1]But seriously...[/h1]
Pretend I'm narrating the rest of this review in Al Gore's voice, because from here on out it's super serious. The set-up is that Dubai has been partially evacuated before an apocalyptic sandstorm, leaving the remaining population isolated and starving. A US army battalion disobeys orders and stays in the city to look after its residents, but as supplies dwindle, the colonel institutes martial law and starts executing civilians. You play a Delta Force operative sent in to investigate the city's comms blackout and renegade battalion. You arrive to find a hellscape of bodies, fire, ruination and blinding sand.

And that's the happiest part, before your actions descend the Delta Force team into a pit of trauma and moral degradation. I won't throw any spoilers in here, but The Line forces you to do some pretty horrendous things that made me feel sick. You're usually given some degree of choice, but only enough to feel even worse about it. There's also the fact that the enemies you're gunning down in droves aren't invading aliens, demons, mad cultists or endangered wildlife poachers, they're American soldiers who tried to do the right thing and ended up stuck in the moral pit that you're teetering over. While the shooting dynamic is fine (third-person cover-intensive linear shooter - think Call of Duty crossed with Gears of War), you can never wholly enjoy it because of who you're fighting. In fact, it's often hard to tell if it's your enemies talking or your squadmates.

Like Apocalypse Now, it's loosely inspired by Joseph Conrad's novella Heart of Darkness, and has that film's sense of surreal horror too. It's more like Platoon in terms of the feeling you get, and the way camaraderie can give way to hate. The campaign is short, less than five hours, but the choices you can make along the way add a little variety to things, including a Mass Effect-style final level that allows several different endings (four according to Wikipedia). There's multiplayer and co-op, but given that the game has been out for a while, those are best sampled with friends rather than waiting to hook up with a rando.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Feels bad, man, but it's a unique game that aspires to emulate some of cinema's most powerful projects. I'd much rather hide behind the level of dissociation you get from watching this sort of thing in a movie, but if you [i]really[/i] want to feel that horror on a personal level, here's your game.

This game initially when I played it I thought I was going to be the reviewer that will give a very unpopular opinion base on the story itself, but boy that ending prove me dead wrong and I’m glad I was wrong. This review will be complicate to explain myself because I want to talk about the story with heavy spoiler but also I want to talk about the gameplay aspects, so I will write two separate sections of the review. One focus more on the gameplay review and a bit of a summary of the lore, while at the end is the heavy spoiler section [b] only for those that play the game![/b] Let’s begin!

[h1]Gameplay non-spoiler section [/h1]

I have to say they did an absolute fantastic job on everything about this game despite how short it was. It was one of the most well polish third-person shooter I have ever played, even if it did felt like I was playing Gears of War, the way it played out was excellent. Even if I had some issues in command response by trying to vault and shuffle through walls which it was the only annoying thing I encountered during my gameplay, but other than that the rest is perfect. Firstly, I want to comment the setting of the game; Dubai. I find it interesting that the story begin in an almost realistic scenario of Dubai where huge sand storm cover almost half the city! I say realistic because I think the developers are way ahead of the time since scientists say that when Global warming will come predicted in 2050, the intense heat and increase sandstorm will make Dubai uninhabitable, that is so ominously scary to think about it! 

Which is why you as Delta Force are tasks to evacuate the remaining civilians lead by Protagonist Walker but something during your mission has gone horribly wrong. I will say this game is by far one of the most mature adult game I have ever played, not because of the over used blood or swearing or anything, but the amount of shear imagery of what the game is trying to portray and the horrified graphics of war has become to the civilians and even the soldiers. This I highly recommend to keep an open mind of how you enter the game because there are parts of the game that will make you sick to your stomach which is how actual war is portrayed, it just makes you question things and including how war is by far not as glorious as how propaganda tells you to believe. 
The acting of this game is by far the best parts of the game including the cast of characters especially your squad members. The amount of depth of the voices the animations, the music when there are important moments or even when fighting enemies are incredibly in tune with the gameplay, it is absolutely marvelous. Except the lack of multiplayer in this game which I question why it even exist in the first place and did it ever became popular during its first launch of the game. In any case, this game deserves probably a 9/10 game of the year, the only small glaring issues is how lack of the response time on sometimes when I run, vault or shift walls was the only frustrated part, although I don’t know if people had that problem. The story while the best by far there are some things that doesn’t quite click me which is why the 9/10 comes from, but other than that is still a masterpiece to play.

[h1] Story Analysis SPOILER WARNING!![/h1] [spoiler] Do you feel like a Hero yet?[/spoiler] 

[spoiler]I have got to say once again, in the beginning of the chapters I at first was not impress of the story, because of how the game keeps hinting you “you must be the bad guy the bad guy, America is evil and you look like the bad guy.” I swear I thought this is one of those Jingo push force idea that this game tells you by Walkers action “you are baaaad.” My first initials on this whole antagonist story is “oh, is this going to be like[i]Ghost Recon Wild lands[/i] where American intervention is bad?” I keep question the stupidity of Walker’s action and the crew’s trust on him. It doesn’t make any sense since the game at first gave you the choice the either save the soldier or the civilians making you think “oh it has choices on the game.” Yet the game does not give me a choice to not use the White Phosphorus weapon which is the worse weapon since Agent Orange since it melts your flesh out, but he used it on the soldiers and that lead to the civilians death. This just angers me further when playing the rest of the game as I keep screaming in my head “why Walker! Why you are being such a stupid villain and pretend to keep on caring to save the civilians!”

 Until the ending happen and oh my god that explains almost everything in the game. Walker has hallucinate almost everything happen in Dubai, why? Perhaps the PTSD that has happened around Dubai, the actions around the game made almost no sense to us but made complete sense to him. Even the game made perfect sense of the “illusion” of choice around Walker. You the player are sane enough to try and think about having choices but Walker himself limited the players ability to choose even Adam had said “you didn’t leave us a choice”. Throughout the game you and your crew looked clean and ok, but during those last chapters you and your crew are a complete mess, on cuts, burn marks, and blood on your face, even how aggressive you become when fighting enemies and how the loading screen taunts you of being a hero. The attention to detail is astonishing of the degenerate state of mind of what is happening to Walker. 

However, and I hope you will understand that despite how flawless the story is there are some questionable stuff that I have to address it here. The crew’s loyalty to him, again I find it very hard to believe that they still follow his orders especially Lugo, I understand Adam and I know the two questioned his leadership but it should have ended in the water tank mission. At first I thought maybe he imagined his crew and they died during the helicopter crash but I’m not 100% sure. It would be nice that Lugo would disband his squad, came back fighting you and finally he ran away for cover but the civilians remembered what Delta did and try to hang him. This would have made an absolute kick to the teeth of the relationship of your crew, they did a fantastic job on Adam’s part so no change there, I just think they should bring a bit more sense on the tension it brought to the crew and Lugo just finally quit on him making Walker blame on Konrad even more thinking he brainwashed Lugo.

This one is a nitpick but the game tries to trick you into thinking the 33rd are the bad guys, because they were shooting you which made little sense unless Walker shot them first. Then the DJ acts like a crazy madman gunning you down throughout the game, which just questions me who is more insane, Walker or DJ? He taunts you, made jokes about your killings, your motivations, I get he was supposed to be the good guy but honestly I hate him. At first I thought I liked him but he was starting to get so annoying later on in the chapters where his dialogue just sounds so childish and made him look like this is all a game to him. Which is why I laugh when Lugo tricked him into being friendly with him but he just shot him immediately, despite how Adam got mad at him honestly it was very justified on his actions. The DJ keeps saying you are the villain and he is the good guy even though he can’t even try maybe to reason with him but nope, he will assume you are the bad guy and will try to kill you with no other civil methods.

That is about it the last thing I will say It made us think and interpreted the game about the horrors of war, PTSD, chemical warfare and government. The developers even said that this is a parody of COD where you are supposed to be a big hero doing heroic deeds and save the world, but not every missions you complete is a happy one, even the suppose right calls.

Just watch some Vietnam movies instead.

I started the game, with no prior knowledge; only that it was a "different" kind of military shooting game.

My impressions:
-Visually impressive; setting was completely new to me. A colourful luxury paradise in ruins. I've seen battle torn cities in many games, but Dubai was unlike any I've seen before. Luxury hotel fights. Yachts buried in sand dunes.
-US soldiers vs US soldiers in a foreign land through out the game. With both sides thinking they're doing the right thing. Killing fellow US soldiers left a big impression. (Though I'm Canadian.)
-The game does force you to kill US soldiers & civilians; it would have been nice to have more options, but it's understandable that the writer wanted the story to move in a specific direction.
-The enemy soldiers were overall fun to fight against. Everyone could be killed with head shots. Except, the only one I hated fighting was the heavy armored suits.
-Weapon selection was good. I like sniping weapons, and had a good time. The AA12 was awesome, but introduced far too late in the game.
-You spend most of the fighting hiding behind cover; popping out to shoot in bursts. Most of the time this works great. Occasionally, I got killed when my character ran to an object, but didn't take cover properly.
-It gets a bit weird, with hallucinations, etc. I am really glad they didn't wimp out on the ending. It is not a happy ending, but that not what I would want after killing hundreds of fellow US soldiers.

Overall, this is a memorable game. Very glad I played it.

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
Spec Ops The Line is a 3rd Person shooter publisher by 2K in 2012. Its  a military shooter that takes place in Dubai after a
cataclysmic sandstorm took place and destroyed basically everything. You fight through other rebels and soldiers in order to find out what is happening, and with all that the game gets darker and darker giving a different messenge to the player.

[h1]Review[/h1]
[list]
[*][h1]Gameplay:[/h1]
-As mentioned above the game is a 3rd Person military shooter. Within the game you move from cover to cover as this is the best way to get through missions as freely moving isn't really the best way to handle these situations. The more levels you complete the better weapons you will find/unlock and there is a pretty big variety of weapons going from snipers to shotguns and every weapons feels and behaves different. Ammunation control is a pretty serious feature too as i found myself in multiple situations where i wasted too many bullets and was left dry to fight more enemies. Your Team is actually helpful in this game, obviously not killing the enemies for you but sometimes getting their attention for you to kill them, they do give you cover fire too and overall are pretty helpful! Stealth doesn't exist nearly at all as i cant remember if i meeled someone from behind without noticing which means that this game isn't really meant for the stealthy type.

[*][h1]Story:[/h1]
-The Story is in my opinion the main attraction. At first it might look like it is just another boring war shooter but youre wrong if you think thats what this game is all about. At first you go to Dubai to find survivors etc. where you get attacked by rebels. Later you find out that american soldiers turned against you, from that point you have no idea what is happening and just start killing anything that comes in front of you. After all the killings and bloodshed you are coming into realisation that it was all you and the game basically showed that within War nothing good comes out. That is the messenge this game showed and left everyone with their mouth open. All the characters had deep stories behind them and were constantly taking part in conversation and expressing their feelings for the situations which added to the experience.
I have not much else to say, the story is just amazing.

[*][h1]Graphics/ Audio:[/h1]
-Visuals:
The game was released 6,5 years ago so do not expect this to be a photorealistic game. As i said multiple times, it takes place in Dubai so expect a lot of Sand. When you enter destroyed building the game truly starts to look amazing as there was clearly put a lot of effort to make these destroyed building look as if they had history. Shadows are pretty good too same goes with other effects too. Character movements do look pretty decent too for their Age. Textures are a bit blurry mostly because it is an older console title and consoles back then could not handle that much ( console port ). Faces do look quite good as you can see emotions with every facial reactions the characters make.
-Audio/Soundtrack:
The Audio is pretty solid with realistic sounding weapons and clear to understand voice actors that match with the characters visually.
The Soundtrack is one of the best in my opinion and especially towards the end it just matches perfectly with everything.

On the surface, Spec Ops: The Line is a third-person military shooter. It is one of the many games in its oversaturated genre. What sets it apart from others is its storytelling. From the title screen to loading screen is utilized to establish a narrative. Through its 15 chapters, the tropes of the shooter genre has been turned on its head and moral questions will be tackled. This was done through the main character, his decent into insanity, morally grey choices and situations, squadmates, enemies, visual and audio environment and the dialogue so it didn't feel too preachy. Although the the cover and firing mechanics are clunky, it could easily be overlooked because of the attention to detail in each area. You can observe the physical condition of the characters and their dialogue when getting hit, realoading, needing assistance degenerate as a symbolism to the main character's decent into the abyss. This is truly a work of art in the form of a video game.

Super tough game to review, as the quality of its components is so extremely variable in my opinion. Wish I could give both a thumbs up and a thumbs down... 

To start, definitely there is a great deep narrative (and interesting meta-narrative!) here, like other folks have said. It really is worth experiencing, and beats out most game stories handily. But man is the gameplay on offer here mediocre...

What you get is a console third-person shooter with clunky-as-hell controls, interact and sprint infuriatingly mapped to the same key (killed me so many times in later chapters...), and boring, generic shooting that cannot reasonably be excused with "that's the point bro", as it is nevertheless boring and not fun for your money. 

The few gameplay innovations like sandstorms (and more generally interacting with sand) are infrequent and largely wasted, but again this problem pales to just how clunky and consolized the basic shooting and cover mechanics are. If you're anything like me, you'll constantly be jumping out of cover by accident, or getting snagged on cover you didn't mean to move to, or unexpectedly flipping between cover in an unintended way. And all of these things will get you killed, setting you back to the previous checkpoint. The guns feel largely mediocre to shoot, the game difficulty has random spikes (like running from a copter, or fighting a stupid "heavy" miniboss in a flashing room when you could be low on ammo), and overall if it wasn't for the fantastic narrative, Spec Ops: The Line would be a hard pass for me. I guess the visuals and music are decent too. But being a gameplay-first kind of guy, I can't confidently say I wouldn't have been better served watching the story on Youtube. So an unfortunate (and close) thumbs down from me, if only to balance the currently overrated consensus a tiny bit.

As a game, it was your generic third-person shooter.

As a story, it's perhaps one of the most enthralling standalone video game titles of the 2010s decade. 
The way this game handles PTSD is pretty intriguing, if not excellent. At the peak of the game, it rewards the player with a 'WTF?' or as I would like to call it 'absurdist's check'. This kind of implementation isn't anything new per se; however, Spec Ops did bring it to the stage in the last decade. Spec Ops wasn't the first to bring it back. 

NieR Gestalt/Replicant delivers the player with around the same amount - if not less- of absurdity in its finale and grand finale. The weight of right and wrong became a house of clusterfudges intertwined within a maze. 

While Spec Ops handles the more psychological aspect of it in laymen terms, NieR goes more abstract with it. Nonetheless, they're both amazing cult classic titles which will forever remain a gem within our hearts in the decade of the 2010s.

At first, Spec Ops: The Line seems like another on-rails military shooter with a generic story. But overtime the game slowly turns and shows the horrors of war. 

Let's get the negatives out of the way, because every game has downsides. The gameplay is fairly boring and standard. Combat works like most third person games, you take cover, fire and command squad mates. Overall it does work, but it presents no real challenge and neither does it try to do something new. It would be great if it would lean a bit more towards the realistic side as it first the more realistic theme of the story.

Environments look great and realistic, and so do most of the cut scenes, but unfortunately some of them look horrible. The soundtrack and voice acting on the other hand, is great and can be really immersive.

Now, let's go to the part that makes this game shine, the story. It starts out pretty generic, like any other shooter but the further you play, the more it shows the horrors of real war. Some choices you make may seem quite minor at first, but will set you thinking later on and will make you realize, sometimes there is no correct choice to make. That's what makes this game so great. It's not afraid to show you what war does to people and makes you question your decisions, especially towards the end of the game.

Spec Ops: The Line has choices you make, and multiple endings but because the main story line is quite the same, there is no real replay value.

Spec Ops: The Line is one of those games you don't really expect to be as good as it is. Everything from the trailers to the gameplay in the first few minutes seems to suggest that this will be a bog-standard modern military shooter. 

I went in blind on the suggestion of a friend and I suggest you do the same. What I expected to be a simple, albeit satisfying romp through the desert turned into a nightmare of one bad decision after another. It feels like the developers knowingly made the combat a blast to go through so you would feel even more guilty once you learn what your wanton destruction brought about.

As for the general gameplay and story. You are one Captain Walker; dropped into an apparent deadzone to look for survivors with your two squadmates Lugo and Adams. ♥♥♥♥ goes FUBAR pretty fast as what you expected to be a dead city turns out to be something much more horrific. Do what you must to survive and complete the mission, but don't expect to come out of it as the same man that went in.

Some Pros and Cons as well:

+ Great Story
+ Every choice is a bad one (but in a good way)
+ Excellent characters
+ Fun combat system
+ Hectic combat: Most of the time, you will not know what's coming next. You have to think fast on your feet and make use of every opportunity
+ Great graphics (for the time)
+ Solid voice acting
+ Most exposition done through dialog instead of cutscenes
+ Ammo is scarce, forcing you to use many different weapons and/or tactics to deal with situations

- Under-utilized squad system. Your squadmates are little more than tag-along exposition. They'll throw a grenade or snipe a target, but only if you tell them to
- Under-utilized stealth mechanics. While there are sections where stealth can be utilized, it is mostly irrelevant
- Good weapon variety, but little actual difference in the feel of weapons of the same type
- Campaign a bit on the short side. On the normal difficulty I completed the game in about 4.5h. This includes dying a few times.

I highly recommend this game. Probably the best shooter I've played in years. I picked the game up for 6€ on sale, but knowing what I know now, I would have paid full asking price years ago.

TL;DR
A bog-standard modern military shooter turns out to have a great and heart-wrenching story. Solid combat, solid mechanics. Highly recommend.

Spec Ops: The Line has a lot to say about a lot of topics, and handles all of them in some of the best ways possible. This game is very, very difficult to get into though, and I'll go over all the points and reasons to get this game.

Keep in mind there will be major spoilers for the game that will be kept later on in the review, you've been warned. Play this game before spoiling it for yourself.

So, first things first, there's a key part of the game that you need to be aware of when playing this game, and that would be the controls.
The game's a third person cover shooter that is [b]very[/b] reminiscent of it's time period. Sprinting is locked, controls are very stiff, and half the time you'll find yourself taking cover somewhere you don't want. I've also had plenty of input issues, specifically during minigun sections of the game, where my aim is being dragged down without any input coming from my mouse. Other than this, it isn't too big an issue, but it very much feels like a 2012 console port third person cover shooter.

Now for what splits this game apart from the rest, and the reason you should play it, the narrative. This is where the spoilers come into play, so be cautious. 

So, first things first the narrative is brilliant in the way that it's almost entirely up to interpretation. The game sets itself up so that anyone can take what's told to them and speculate about the story, and there are plenty of theories out there already that have been out there for years about the game, the message, and Walker's team. Let's start with the basics.

You play as Captain Martin Walker, leading a Delta Force team through the washed out, buried landscape of Dubai. This mission is a simple catch-and-go, as you're told, though it ends up becoming much more than that. Instead, it's a mission that changes every person affected by it in all ways. When the game starts, Walker and his men are rather cheery, bright, and joking towards each other, coming across as personable and charismatic. They also look the part, with very clean, tough, soldier-like appearances, and even animations sticking to uniform and professionalism. Once things go south, and you start shooting, everything begins to go downhill. Both literally, and metaphorically.

Over time, the game changes. Walker, Adams, Lugo, and even you as the player begin sliding down the slippery descent into madness as you continue to kill, and are constantly questioning why. The game has multiple possible answers to this. As Walker and his men continue their mission in Dubai, they become more and more rugged, bloodied, and exhausted. Their actions change, their attitudes, and their wills are all crushed eventually under the stress they endure. Any sign of the men they used to be is gone, now replaced by bloodthirsty, savage, and broken individuals.

There are many themes throughout this game, and morals are constantly in question. This game does choice a way most games should, by having it be done subtley. There is no pop-up whenever you make a choice, and there is no multiple choice bulletin you pick. Choices are made directly through gameplay without mention, making it so the player makes a choice consciously, rather than forcibly. As for the messages, the game gives an inner look of PTSD by showing through visual art the ways Walker's mind deteriorates as he witnesses more and more horrors and tragedies. For example, [spoiler]after leaving Riggs to burn, or shooting him in the head, you will see an image on a nearby board reflecting that sight. If you shoot, it's a man with a bullet hole in his head. If you left him, you see what looks to be someone burning alive. Later down, you also see statues, which also vary on choice. If you shoot, one statue is pointing a finger gun at the other's head. If you leave, they're both made of magma with a not-so-faint burning sound emitting from them. Looking at these statues will revert them back to their real figures.[/spoiler] These choices never have positive outcomes. There's bad, and there's worse.
Then, there's the topic of the demographic that shooters in the market tend to attract. You know how most games put you in a position of power, giving you a powerful suit of armor, a massive loadout of amazing weaponry, and let you do anything in the world? Ever wonder about how most of the time those games have you kill hundreds, or thousands of goons to progress, and be the hero? Well, Spec Ops has the killing, but none of the satisfaction. This game doesn't reward you for killing massive hordes of people. Instead, it hates you for it. So much so that the game even directly addresses you through loading screens, and lines of dialogue such as "Do you feel like a hero yet?". It makes you feel bad for relying on the slaughter of tons of virtual people to fill some dumb power fantasy, and it does it very, very well.

All in all, this game has a lot to say. It's not something for the sensitive, and is extremely mature. This is a game that isn't fun, in fact, it's pretty much the opposite. The game makes you feel like garbage, and yet, it's amazing for it. The enjoyment of playing this game comes from the insight that it brings, and just how much it can get you thinking. There's a lot to this game, if you can overlook the massively dated gameplay. It still stands up today, in my opinion.

Before I've started this game, I heard a lot of good things about it, though I didn't believe these comments and reviews. Why? I'm not sure, maybe because of the screenshots and videos of gameplay, looked a lot like Mass Effect with some tactical stuff when it comes to commanding your squadmates, and usually they are so stupid, that it becomes rather a problem in completing game instead of helpful tool in your hands. However, after beating the game, I must say that I'm amazed by the overall approach to the topic of the devs. So, here we go:

Storyline: 10/10

O.M.G! 
No, honestly. Is this really possible to make a military action shooter in this times, that isn't all about brave & heroic american soldiers? We are surrounded by games that present us Yankees as saints and best soldiers in the whole universe. Even in BF1 they are showed as Saviors of the world. But not in here. Trust me, you will not find a better game that shows you the real character of war in such plain way. This isn't about courage, this is about human instincts, disinformation, brutality of war in modern times. The approach to psychological aspects of commanding, obeying orders and fighting on the warfare will simply stun you down. I give this game 10/10 for storyline. It deserves it.

The World: 8/10

Although kinda post-apocalyptic and interesting for the storyline (the World is like an another one narrator in this game, really) it is also booring. I don't really endorse desert enviroment, but what could I espect from Dubay, heh? Anyway, forget about my dislike for sand, high temperature, sandstorms (no jokes about Darude, please) - the city is created in fantastic style, although the games is made in corridor style, you won't feel claustrophobic because of the vast open space that surrounds you. And the Dubay will make you sink into its nightmares and problems. Dubay torn by war. (If you dont' mind sand, add these 2 points, so it will  have 10/10 ;))

Graphics: 7/10

Simply solid, but not astonishing. A good part of work, not done by masters, like story, but by qualified workers. What is the best part of it is the gore. Are you disaapointed by lack of blood and parts of human body flying everywhere after big explosion in BF and CoD? Well, here you go, play some Spec Ops!

Sound: 9/10

The sound is made just as graphics - solid and good, so here's the 7/10. Wait, there is also music! And the dialogues! Soldiers speak like real soldiers, not like heroes from american movies. Citizens of Dubay speak like citizens thrown into the middle of hell. AND THE MUSIC. Hearing [spoiler] Hush by Deep Purple [/spoiler] almost kicked me out of my chair! Really good part of this fantastic game.

Interface: 7/10

Nothing special, some moving mechanics taken from consoles are annoying, but they won't make you abandon the game.

Overall: 9/10

One of the best games that I've played this year. I'm simply astonished by the real-like approach to the nightmares of war showed in this game. If you are bored by CoD & BF singleplayer campaigns and would like to try something else, you should try Spec Ops: The Line.

People seem to be missing that every aspect of this game, including the gameplay, was orientated towards the narrative and thematics above all else. They intentionally wanted the combat to feel repetitive, relentless and fatiguing - not innovative and engaging - because having say bioshock style gamplay would severely interfere with the tone and emotional impact of the game. At first, you think you are above the game, disappointed with its dated gameplay - but you come to realise that was all part of the ruse, a vehicle to drive you into the narrative.

My ending:
"One!" " This is all your fault, Konrad."
"Two!" "I didn't mean to hurt anybody!"
"Three!"
"Fo-" Boom*

What's more important in the game at loading screens, there are messages like:
"Do you feel like a hero, yet?" or "If you were a good person you wouldn't be here" (something along the lines).

The only way to really beat the game is to stop playing. Otherwise you are going in what Walker gone, a little insane and killing for the fun.

I think this is the only game that I almost didn't want to finish or continue. It was a tragedy, it was a shooter tragedy. I didn't want to shoot those people, but I had no other choice.

So you become Walker more and more as you play and feel like a monster.

It's an interesting experience that couldn't work in any other medium, but paradoxically enough, it doesn't work because it's a videogame. The moment I realized the things I was doing were morally wrong and still the game forced me to do them, I started feeling detached, and for good reason — I wasn't playing anymore but being played. I being told a story, preached about what the game wanted to convey. And I realize that's the whole point, that it is satirising war games and the possibility of choice would ruin the story, but at the same time, not being able to choose also ruined the impact this game was supposed to make on me.

It's not simply about linearity, either. Videogames are all about goals. A game with a heavy focus on narrative and no choices like God of War or Uncharted works because the goal of both the player and the developer is the same: to get to the end of the story, and we never get second thoughts about it. Same thing for Gone Home or Edith Finch, in which player's volition take an even further step back. Even Shadow of the Colossus, which is similar in the sense that the players know the character's actions are reprehensible, works better because the game make those actions a compelling challenge to overcome through both gameplay and narrative.

In Spec OPS, however, their goals eventually start to drift apart: the developer wants to keep telling the story, while the player wants it to stop. And that's when it lost me. The degree of interactivity videogames allow when compared to movies and books, in which we are merely consumers that don't take an active part in any moment, makes it hard for me to simply accept moral quandaries whose outcomes are imposed on me. It's one of the reasons I didn't quite enjoy the direction The Last of Us 2 took. It's a interesting story about violence and revenge that would work flawlessly as a movie, but it loses its meaning when it forces us to do bad things and then try to make us feel bad for it. I didn't choose to kill all those people: the game made me do it. Instead of being moved by it, I feel cheated.

Maybe I'm being old-fashioned and I'm just not used to games trying to attain an emotional response this way, but there's gotta be a better way to tell those same stories without completely detaching player's volition from it.

I'll start by just saying that Spec Ops: The Line is an AMAZING game. That doesn't mean it is without its problems. The game suffers from fairly dull gameplay. To me, the gameplay got stale very quickly, so I would encourage you to give yourself a challenge and play at a higher difficulty.

With that said, let's look at where the game really shines. The game's aesthetics are amazing and for a game from 2012, it still holds up well. The levels are very varied and feel dynamic. There's an amazing attention to detail, and you'll notice that as you progress through the game and are exposed to more of the horrors war, your character's behavior changes. In the beginning, your callouts are concise and executions are quick and clean (e.g. the animation will be a shot to the head) and later you will find yourself bashing in peoples faces with the butt of your gun. These sorts of details are what help make the beautifully crafted story really come to life. The story is a (very) loose adaptation of [spoiler]Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness[/spoiler] and manages to, in my opinion, tell the story in a much more captivating way than the novel ever did.

I have played though the entire of the game and so have a decent idea of how the story unfolds, and I have to say that the number of people giving this game praise is ridiculous. I will admit that for a cover shooter of it's time, spec ops is quite well done, the gameplay is smooth and not clumsy. However most people glance over the gameplay and focus on the story, as after all that is what spec ops the line is all about.

-Spoilers Below-

The largest praise that Spec Ops receives is for it's unique and deep story, and while the idea is unique and interesting, the execution is appalling. The game plays out as a group of American soldiers slowly fighting their way though the ruins of Dubai, trying to save the survivors from the ruthless rule of a tyrant. However throughout the game, you have to make various hard decisions in order to survive and complete the mission. And while this all sounds good and cool, the reality is far from it. A good example I find is that of the White phosphorus incident: Early on you discover that the enemy have been using large amounts of this substance to kill their opponents, you are shown the horrid effects and it is established that this is an atrocious weapon that should never be used in combat, then less than an hour of game play later you are presented with an area in front of you that looks like it is a fortified enemy base, upon looking over there you can see less than 10 guards (by this point you have taken on far more that this at once) but upon looking though the thermal imaging camera it becomes apparent that there are far more people are in the trench just behind them, I would like to point out that these people are in extremely cramped conditions that would be useless as a defensive mechanism. You are then informed by one of your team that there is a mortar containing White phosphorus that you could use to clear the way, and while one of your team objects the other states that it is the only way. Now in many games, in situations like this, you would now be given a choice, try and fight your way though, or mortar the defences, and maybe if you choose to fight, then one of your team dies or something. But Nooo, you cannot even go down the ladder, the game forces you into firing the mortar, and then you have to walk though the ruins, while the developers rub in your face what a horrible person you are, before throwing the final insult. You make your way down in to the trench only to discover that it was not a garrison of troops but refugees that you had just burnt alive, aren't you an absolute monster. I would like to point out that though the thermal-imaging camera, anyone with an ounce of common sense would be able, as I did, to work out that the trench was not filled with soldiers, due to a combination of the clusters and size of the heat signatures. Which makes this final bit even more irritating. If I had had no idea that they were not soldiers, then it could have been a horrid realisation, followed quickly by anger that the game would not let me choose a different path, but instead it just makes me feel frustrated and argy at the devs for forcing be down a path, and then ridiculing me for it. As a game design this is once of the worst story telling methods in existence. I can only think of two there examples, both which frustrate me just as much, that being the final DLC of New Vegas (Lonesome Road), where to get to Ulysses you have to launch a nuke, there is literally no other alternative, and you can’t end the story any other way, you are then berated by Ulysses on how you are such an awful person for launching the nuke. The other being Bioshock Infinite, which in general had an awful story, but the this that I am referring to is the wibbly wobbly timey twimey stuff. (spoilers for this as well) You are constantly criticized for stuff that Dewitt did before you even had control, how much of a monster you were and how that is the reason for all that has happened, well Dewitt is a prat and most people should be able to see that so why would I play as such an awful human being.

Right, rant aside, in general if you are just looking for another third person shooter in a very pretty setting then go for it, if however you are looking for the dark and gripping tale about the true horrors of war, read a book because this does not even come close, it rubs it's linear storyline in you're face like it was you fault.

-Even more spoilers for the end-

Finally, the ending. I could not not talk about the twist at the end. Where it is revealed that you have in-fact been hallucinating the entire time, and that there is no bad guy, and that you are the bad guy. as a reveal it is no SW KOTOR for sure but it is OK, however, what causes the whole thing to fall apart is your squad mates, you know the ones that were with you the entire time and did not say anything about any of this. Talking to dead bodies and such. What soldier on this planet would continue to be led by a man who has started speaking to corpse. again, this is rubbed in you face as something that you did wrong and that this is the real world were it is not always a happy ending, well in the real world your squad mates would have had more than one brain cell between them, and would have stepped in and taken control of the situation. 

Anyway, If you have read this far then, I am very surprised, and if you have and don’t hate my guts, then great. Though I imagine most people will rant at me for ranting at the game they so love. I will reiterate what I said earlier though, that if you do not manage to predict the story and are surprised by every turn it takes, then the game is great, however if you do work out what is going on, there is little point in playing the game, as it just becomes tedious and frustrating to be forced down a path that you know is wrong.

This is a good story marred by routine gameplay and glitchy controls. 

Mechanically this doesn't do anything that other cover based shooters don't already do, it's pretty straight forward and functional with nothing notable in evolving the genre. I suppose the "executions" deserve a nod for their gritty realism, but they serve more as punctuation to the story than they do gameplay. (In fact sometimes they get in the way of gameplay as your character decides to execute someone laying on the ground near you while what you were trying to do is smash your barrel into the face of another enemy with a melee attack because they share the same button and the game would rather you stand there locked in an execution animation than save your own life, but I digress…)

It's also occasionally glitchy with the controls, you go to stick yourself to cover and it wobbles between two pieces instead of sticking you to the one you wanted and you end up getting shot because the piece of cover it chose for you (behind or next to you off screen) now makes you face the other way with your back exposed to the enemy ~ but it doesn't happen often enough to make the game unplayable, just enough to make you swear at the screen occasionally during another checkpoint reload. But then there's plenty of checkpoints so you never really lose much of your time, and chances are you would have just gotten yourself killed anyway until you figure out the best approach through any given area.

Tactically it's small map minimalist, but still fun. You have two sidekicks for most of the game and you can direct them to snipe or grenade for you (at their choice, you just pick the targets), and using them to get enemies that are too entrenched in cover for you to get at is functional enough, but again you kind of expect this sort of thing from a squad tactics game. I could slam it for not having more detail in the controls, but it works and it's fun so I guess in this case it didn't need to be any more complex.

Basically the games not trying to win any awards for innovation in gameplay, it shows up, does it's job and let's you kill some stuff, the end.

OR, that would be the end and my review might be negative if that's all there was, instead the focus was almost entirely on storyline and presentation and that's where the game shines. This is a grandiose tale of the horrors of war and the toll it can take on the human mind. 

Whether you see the plot twists coming or not you can still fully appreciate the story telling quality that went into crafting the game, and it's scenery. The graffiti backdrops you wander past along with the executions your character so gleefully takes part in are just visual narrative alongside the audio elements drawing you deeper into your "mission". The subtle changes to how your character behaves along with his squad's attitude are a unique gem in a genre of shooting games where the characters are usually emotionless bricks with guns.

Some people claim the game traumatized them or made them cry. I'm going to tell you I laughed my way through it with gleeful abandon. But you see it doesn't matter what emotion the game bothers to make you feel, the point is it tried to make you feel something, anything.

Whether you ride along the trauma your character experiences or just laugh at the entire escapade, at least it was entertaining along the way and not just another soulless guy with a gun shooting stuff because reasons. (or was it? and maybe that's the point, you decide)

Anyway, if you are indecisive at all just stick this on your Wishlist and snap it up the first time you see a sale for $10 or less, it's worth a few hours for the storyline and if you don't mind the controls and the occasional glitches you might even get some replay value out of it chasing the achievements.

Although short, Spec Ops: The Line delivers one of the best stories in a video game I've ever had the pleasure of playing through. To a newcomer, this may just seem like a standard, by the books and boring Cover-based shooter. While the combat and beginning few chapters of the game slightly reflect this, you won't be waiting long for the excellent story to reveal itself. With (mostly) excellent performances, subtle symbollism spread throughout, and a fantastic ending, I can't help but recommend this game.

The problems mostly come with the bland gameplay. There are neat mechanics here and there, but are never expanded upon beyond surface level. This is certainly a deal breaker for anyone who just wants fun gameplay, but I don't think this game was made with that audience in mind. Also, some may consider the length to be an issue, but I feel it was perfect for the story. Any longer and it would have been bloated.

Overall, as you can imagine, I highly recommend this game for anyone who wants a story. Or, really, someone who wants something different. It isn't a masterpiece, and is very flawed in some senses, but what it tries and achieves heavily outweighs any downsides for me.

Spec Ops:The Line is the most interesting war movie I've seen in a while. This game will make you think of armed conflicts in a very different way. It doesn't make you feel like an immortal, not even like a hero, as opposed to Battlefield, CoD etc. There's a lot of pain, there are choices that you won't like, but you need to get through it to find out what happened. Next good thing about the whole story is fact that there is accentuation to America, you don't feel like antiterrorist dropped in Dubai to kill every terrorist in town, be happy, make jokes, come back to your country and get a medal from El Presidento. Your squad is stuck in city and it's already dead. The capital city of United Arab Emirates is burried after the biggest sandstorm I've ever seen, the skyscrapers are destroyed probably by warfare and there is no sh*t you can do about it.

Now something about the gameplay
Third person shooter. You and your two squadmates, who can be guided to shoot chosen target or heal an ally. The AI is not that stupid as you could think. Enemies can flank you, hide behind cover or even throw grenades to get you out of your own shield. There are not many kinds of weapons, I think 15 types, but you can use some nice sniper rifles, shotguns etc. I didn't really get into this type of aiming. It felt starchy for me. Also I had some problems with running, because my hero enjoyed sticking to random covers when I was sprinting near them. There are some easings for casual players which help you with shooting bad guys. Game is not that hard, I bet everyone will handle it in medium. 
What else? I really liked acting and music in Spec Ops:The Line. It emphasizes the vibe of the whole apocalypse going on there.
Spec Ops:The Line would be a perfect TPS game if they put some time in making the gameplay better. Great story, but put in a very bad, exhausting, boring background. Name: Spec Ops: The Line
Developer/Publisher: Yager/2K Games
Genre: 3rd-person action
Release: June 25, 2012

-----

Based upon Joseph Conrad's seminal work Heart of Darkness, as was the epic 1980s movie Apocalypse Now, Spec Ops: The Line examines what a group of special forces soldiers are made out of when they are isolated from civilization in the midst of a sandstorm-torn Dubai, sent into rescue hostages and ascertain the status of rogue fellow servicemember John Konrad.

It is a harrowing tale that I have no desire to play through again, let alone even start up; it was horrifying in its displays of human baseness and depravity, but everyone should play through it at least once because it's an important story; in the midst of inhumanity you must keep your humanity, or else you become a monster; it's like Nietzsche said. Or maybe it was MGMT at the beginning of their awesome song "Kids."

I don't really have a whole lot to say about it (aside from the usual graphics are great, sounds great, voice acting is compelling (Nolan North does a great job this time) and controls are pretty tight) because its story is so involved that to say anything about it would probably be to spoil the whole thing; I must simply entreat you to play it and put it away. Highly recommended.

Spec Ops: The Line is a weird game to review. With an amazing (albeit flawed) story and narrative but bland cover shooter gameplay, it's really difficult to put it on a scale from 1 to 10, so I won't. Long story short, you should play this game just to experience the story, especially if you got this game free or from a sale.

[h1] Story [/h1]

This game really likes to mess with your head. The story begins with generic looking American soldiers going to a destroyed Dubai to check out what's gone wrong with a division helping civilians over there. Everything seems normal, but after a few chapters, things go south pretty quickly. Who is the enemy? What is going on? Why are you doing this? The deeper you go into the game, the more the game likes to taunt you. The story does have a few major flaws with you not having a choice in some situations, but it didn't detract from the experience enough to change my overall opinion.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]

Like I said, most of the gameplay is basic late 2000s, early 2010s cover shooter stuff: two-weapon limit and all that. The good thing about it is that the cover mechanics are really great: blind firing is useful, turning and aiming from cover is really smooth. The key bindings are really bad though: not even on the PC version can you bind sprint/cover seperately nor melee/vault seperately and it pisses me off to no end. I also had a really annoying bug with aiming where aiming upwards with a scope was really stiff and the sensitivity was sometimes all around the place.

The game does have some nice environmental interactions, such as shooting windows to drop sand over your enemies or throwing grenades to make a huge cloud of sand to blind them. You also have two squad members who can be pretty dumb at times, but they do well on their own mostly and you can command them to target a specific enemy or flashbang a group of enemies. You can also find intel in some levels which explains slightly more about the story. The game has a variety of weapons, but you don't really need anything other than the weapons you start with: rifles are as accurate as snipers and don't even get me started about how regular pistols oneshot everything in the head -- also with sniper accuracy.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

There's not much more to say about the game: you shoot people from cover. Sometimes it can feel like a tedious shooting gallery. The music and the voice acting are both nice, but nothing special.  Everything else about the game feels like "nothing special" except the story. So is it really worth it? Yes -- it doesn't have anything so bad it would make you stop playing, it doesn't stand out with gameplay in any shape or form, but the story alone has potential to make it a memorable experience to you. Especially if you're used to playing cover shooters, you won't mind this one either.

★★★★★

Third person military shooter is a somewhat strange type of games. While most of mastodons of the genre are played with a first-person view, and over-shoulder camera is mostly designed for adventure and stealth games, sometimes you can make a gem by mixing two up. Spec Ops: The Line is a surprisingly great shooter game, with rich single-player campaign, intriguing story and original setting.
 
While being heavily inspired by Conrad’s “Heart of Darkness”, creators have moved time and location even further than “Apocalypse Now”. Game’s story ditches overused existed wars and conflicts by creating original one. Plot unravels in Dubai, UAE, during series of devastating sandstorms, which caused unthinkable level of chaos. You may be used to sand in your military boots but looking on most prosperous and gorgeous Dubai as it lies in ruins, you get goosebumps.
 
Cover-based shooting mechanics is frantic and action packed. Game never lets you to take a break in combat, pumping your adrenaline and trying to force you for a wrong fatal step. Controls and overall feeling is smooth and easy, allowing you to adapt fast and fight your way through. Also, game incorporates some tactical elements, as you are accompanied with two squadmates, but team control is so undercooked, I would prefer it ditched completely.
 
Heaviest and maybe the only noticeable drawback - game cheats to increase its difficulty. While sending waves of enemies - hundreds of them - in any minor skirmish wasn’t enough, and then enemies will require 2 completely perfectly lined up headshots in uncovered face to kill them. Bollocks!
 
And then there is a story. While it would be hard for someone to follow every piece of it under heavy fire, I promise you, the story alone makes this game worthy of your time. I don’t have any moral right to spoil it for you, so I won’t tell more, but praise atmosphere in which it is presented. You can literally feel this zipped in situation, when you are looking for that scarce ammo to continue a fight, but stumble upon clues and evidence depicting  horrors of war.
 
I highly suggest Spec Ops: The Line for everyone, who is a fan of a genre, war movies or books. This title, unlike similar products, is heavily driven by a compelling story. Spec Ops: The Line is polished, aged well, generic shooter, but with so much more on the inside.

Spec Ops: The Line is a unique game that delivers an interesting story about the horrors and the psychological disruption of war, blurring the lines between friend and enemy as the story follows the three-man Delta force team. Although most of the gameplay leaves much to be desired and the graphics can use a slight upgrade, it's an experience that will not disappoint.

Good writing and a fantastic performance by Nolan North are unfortunately marred by bland and, in the late game, super frustrating combat mechanics. Morality choices are always "Choose A or B" and while they do affect gameplay, I never found myself /really/ caring about the outcome. That said, there were a few scenes that managed to get an emotional response out of me, and one late game scene made the prior 5 tedious hours worth it.

Also for some reason half the cutscenes are in-game and the other half are prerendered. The prerendered scenes are in what appear to be 480p which is quite the eyesore.

I'll not spoil a thing to those whom might be unawares of this game's majesty. I'll be vague for safety's sake:
This game. It changes you. You never look at shooters, at War itself, the same way. You'll want to play it more than once, just to see what you missed the first go around. Or perhaps, depending on your affinity and empathetic connections to PTSD, you might not want to play it at all. You'll be harrowed, staring at a wall, lost in thought. Give yourself to the experience, note every detail, every word and inflection, hunt subtleties. You won't be disappointed.

If you're receptive to psychological experiences, this game is [i]absolutely[/i] for you. Play it through at least once, immerse yourself in it.

Quick summary - Spec Ops: The Line is a challenging third person shooter with a couple of computer controlled squad mates, but as usual with this type of game you’re going to be doing most of the heavy work yourself. The biggest selling point of the game is the single player story, which is a great look at the horrors of war through the eyes of hardened combat veterans trying to do the right thing. 

You play the captain of a 3 man Delta Force team investigating the ruins of Dubai months after massive sandstorms swallowed the city. Your mission is to find out what happened to the US army battalion that went in to evacuate the city months ago, but were never heard from again. What you find is chaos caused by the failed evacuation, with the remnants of the US army crushing the locals into submission in an attempt to maintain order and control. It turns out that the American CIA has also attempted to intervene and overthrow the rogue army battalion by arming the civilians, leading to massive violence with both sides shooting at you on sight.

You control Captain Walker in fast paced Third Person Shooter perspective, similar to Mass Effect or Gears of War. There is a simple “cover” system where can hide behind objects and lean out to shoot at enemies, and you have auto-recovering health if you can avoid being shot for a few seconds. If you’re used to Call of Duty games you will find Spec Ops rather difficult, because not only do you have a relatively low amount of life, but you can’t carry that much ammunition either. You carry 2 weapons at a time, and only hold 3-4 extra clips of ammo for each. This means you’ll have to constantly swap with whatever guns your enemies drop, instead of sticking with your “favorite” weapons. 

You should play Spec Ops if:
+A good story is important to you. It will be a slap in the face though.
+You want a short game that you can beat in a couple afternoons. Playing on normal difficulty I beat the campaign in about 6 hours. It would have been shorter except I kept dying and restarting in some of the harder areas.

You should Not play Spec Ops if:
-You’re looking for an easy game. As I mentioned before the game is noticeably difficult, and the enemies can mow you down very quickly even from long range. Running out of ammo is a real danger even though there are guns all over the place left by the hordes of enemies that you slaughter. 
-You’re looking for a co-op or multiplayer experience. Even when I first played the game years ago there was nobody playing online. Just play it for the story campaign. In combat you can issue a couple commands to your 2 computer controlled teammates, but it’s just things like “shoot this guy.” You can’t really order their movements or tactics.

In my opinion, writing a review for a shooter game does not make any sense at all - players are expecting a crazy action, chase, nonstop shooting and fighting. The main things that are really important for the gamers are an accurate rifles and unlimited ammunition. But today, I'm offering something different to you - SpecOps The line.

I actually got acquainted with the game for a long time, but the first time I did not succeed - it was a non-official version that contained a bug, through which you did not have access to one of the missions. I had no hope for it, I thought that developers forgot about the project. Literally until latterly. 
I found the game among the discounts and immediately bought it myself to the collection and, I will say honestly, I did not regret. If you think that it is because of exceptional physical models, graphics or pretentious combat system, sorry, but you are wrong - the plot here is on the first place.

A group of special forces, called "Delta", sent to practically buried under the sand Dubai city in order to find a missing US Army battalion that helped with the evacuation during the storm. Looks like a usual and typical plot? But step by step, a mission after a mission, this feeling just disappears. I will not continue to spoil it, I really recommend to try it yourself, just because it is really impressive and exciting.

By and large, this is an adaptation to Joseph Conrad's novel "The Heart of the Dark," but the actions have moved from the African suburbs to the Middle East. All, what was requsted from the developers, was not to lose key aspects of the book - for example, isolating people from the outside world or what will be with a person who came here - and, I must admit,  they succeeded in it.

[h1]The verdict[/h1]
A history that is worth attention. The game is a representative of its time (2012) so here we will not see something revolutionary in terms of graphics or game design. However, I recommend the game itself because of the cool and unpredictable plot, the main heroes and a series of events through which they will go together.

Got this game for free on Humble Bundle and even then it's 3 hours gone to waste.
TL;DR, this is a terrible game that misadvertises itself as "designed to challenge your morality".

No. You have zero control over the outcome of the story. Literally.
The story is predictable and mediocre at best (hurr durr look at these dumb american soldiers shooting everything, they are so evil, and look at those CIA trying to mess with the middle east). I'll spare you more spoilers in case you do decide to throw away your money on a lousy console port, but you get the jist.

As for the gameplay, it does not deserve to exist in a modern game. That's it. It feels like it's out of the days 3d browser games were a fad. You get a few guns with that all feel the same (even the shotgun has a pretty similar range to the rifles), and some grenades, but no incentive to do anything special. The AI just charges straight at you and a few bullets do their job. You don't need to use your grenades or silencer because they do nothing. Maybe sometimes take cover if there are a lot of enemies, but this leads me to the next point:

The controls are the worst I have ever seen in a shooter, by far. Even the lowest sensitivity has you unable to aim a few pixels sideways consistently since it teleports your cursor, the default buttons make no sense, it's impossible to turn while running (or even stop running until you hit the wall). The guns feel like nerf guns in the sense that their sound is cliche and there is very little recoil. You get the idea.

All in all, not a single redeeming quality for this game, and all the people telling you the plot is great are probably angsty teenage FPS players who are used to gunning everything in sight, and this is the first time they are presented with the idea that not everything needs to be killed. Any sane person playing this will instantly recognize what NOT to morally do, but the game forces you to for the sake of plot, only to be told "SEE? YOU'RE A BAD PERSON! HA! SOAK IN YOUR SHAME, YOU LAZY FIRST WORLD CITIZEN WHO BATHES IN THE BLOOD OF INNOCENT, POOR CIVILLIANS". If you don't mind a small spoiler, read this.

[spoiler]On chapter 8 or so you are confronted with a huge amount of enemies a long way from you, with the option to use some white phosphorus mortars to deal with them. There was a scene 20 minutes earlier showing you how evil that is, in case you didn't know, since it leaves people to slowly burn alive. Okay, you're a sane person so you're ONLY gonna use that in case you will die otherwise. You proceed to try and gun the enemies down, but realize that some of them are too far and you're out of ammo, so you try to find a way down from this area, but nope, no such luck. You try and snipe them with the little ammo you have left to see if the story progresses in case you succeed, but suddenly die to 10 people shooting your face. So you load your save and go  "ok, ill use the phosphorus, but this is obviously self defense". So you shoot the bad guys and notice that there are a ton of civillians in a closed area ahead. There is no flanking and suprising the enemy here; or any form of tactics for that matter.

That was the negative. What this game truly excels in however, is in creating a unique atmosphere. In between the cover strewn landscapes the game takes on a slower pace and creates some truly beautifully orchestrated set pieces that tell a story of their own. From them the story unfolds. At first very lightly, almost gaily, but soon the game decends in complete and utter madness that makes you contemplate on the horrors of war. As other reviewers before have said, the game is worth getting for the story and the experience alone. At the beginning when you kill enemies, the phrases he says almost seems regretful, but later in the game he says things like DIE YOU ♥♥♥♥♥♥ or GOT YOU ♥♥♥♥♥.

Spec Ops: The Line is a game that tries to make me sad but I'm already broken so a little late to the draw on that one, guys. 

You play as Captain Walker, who is sent to Dubai with his squad to find survivors and report back to command. But Walker is a a strong independent Delta Force operative and heads into the city in an attempt to save everyone and also confront John Konrad, the man responsible for all of this. 

Except the sand storm, that was the planet. 

Spec Ops is a third person shoulder with this huge aversion to letting you move around. While the gunplay is acceptable and some of the guns do feel nice to use, you spend most of the game just kind of hiding and killing people.

Enemies will just MELT you if you're not behind cover, which makes sense considering the subject matter. You know, bullets. 

The problem is that the game isn't really set up for using cover to your advantage, there are some parts where its more viable but a lot of areas are set up so you can get closer to your enemy, actually flanking them is a flip of the coin. This mixed with the fact that enemies have pin point hitscan kind of means you're going to spend a lot of time crawling up cover and playing pop and shoot with other idiots who are hiding behind chest high walls. 
Its the formula made popular by Gears of War in its lamest, most basic form. At least you can command your squadmates to attack people you tell them to attack, but sometimes they just kind of...Not do it, and end up getting eaten by enemy gunfire. 

The other big mechanic is melee and executions. Sometimes when you shoot down a baddie they will lie there in a wounded state. From there you can rush them and perform an execution which gives you back some ammo for your current weapons.
Smacking some clown with a melee attack assures that you can perform and execution, you have opportunities to use them when the enemy is focusing your squad or you run into one another, but for the most part you'll be shooting everyone. 

But that's apparently not the point, according to certain video game journalists you aren't supposed to play a game for the gameplay. No sir this is one of those story games apparently. So hows the story?

The thing about Spec Ops is that it starts as a by-the-books military shooter and quickly spirals out of control from there. It deals with issues such as war crimes, self righteous mindsets, war crimes, mental health issues, war crimes, PTSD, war crimes, did I mention war crimes? 

Back in 2012, when this game came out, people went nuts over the sudden change of direction from a generic military shooter to a generic military shooter with a neat story. It became one of those “You gotta play it!” games that year, which kind of conflicted with the whole “You're supposed to turn off the game and stop playing if you were uncomfortable” idea that Cory Davis, the director of Spec Ops, was kind of shilling back then. 

There is a part in the game where Walker nukes the hell out of a big gathering of the 33rd with white phosphorous, and ends up killing a big group of civilians in the process. 

I loved the story, but I liked the story AS a story, you know? It was interesting to see Walker turn from generic grizzled war fighter guy to a messed up, wreck of a man over the course of 7.2 hours.

The game isn't very long, you'll take about 7-8 hours.

Watching Captain Martin Walker change in not only appearance and mental state, but also in actions and wordings is actually a pretty interesting thing to behold. He starts swearing and spitting more venom more often at not just his enemies but also his squad. His executions become more brutal, and his desire to just simply kill “The bad guys” goes to the point of complete fanaticism. 

You also, as a player, start to question what is and isn't real. There are hints here and there pointing out that an event isn't really happening, such as the words of your squadmates and as a story, its pretty good, but the game's director had to go crazy with the “you just don't understand” bit. 

They really wanted to send a message with The Line, to the point that they were shaming people for actually going through with the game. You “could have just turned the game off and walked away.” but you decided to keep on going. Chances are you even bought the game because it was a shooter. 

But should you play it? Hell yes, you should mate.

The game itself isn't anything to write home about, but if you want an actually pretty interesting story to sit through for about 7-8 hours or so, give it a shot. 

This game reminds me of the movie Fury with Brad Pitt, if you didn't watch this movie yet, I highly think you should give this movie a chance.

[i]Only reviewing the single-player campaign.[/i]

I've really loved games that promise morally-complex choice, like Fallout, Mass Effect, etc. I enjoy most first-person and third-person shooters. I [i]loove[/i] games that promise to make me think and say "huh.", like The Last of Us (omg that game though), Gears of War, or actually the original Halo. So when I heard about a game that promised the joys of all of these, I jumped on it (when it was on sale, of course, cuz on Steam who's got time to pay full price?).

What I got was this lump.

From the start, with lines like "after all, I'm a hardened killing machine!", and the near-instant jump to moments of "look, they're doing [b][i]BAD STUFF[/i][/b]", the game wasn't going well. The first line was actually particularly interesting, because it was said by the character (Lugo or Adams, I already can't remember which was which) with irony implying he's more than that, but perhaps the real irony was the game proved they weren't much else. Cue the Alanis Morisette.

I ultimately played through the whole thing, hearing from really-real IRL friends that the ending is craaaazy and it makes up for the rest of the game's downfalls. This turned out to be false.

Anyways, to lighten the mood, I'll start with some positive thoughts about the actual game:
[list]
[*] The game sounded alright. Guns sounded like guns, faraway people sounded kind of far away (although why could I hear their radios?).
[*] The graphics were pretty good. Mostly just good, although some of the shots of the skyscrapers were pretty awesome. There was a shot of the Burj Khalifa with like Sauron's tower-type of flames around which was pretty wicked.
[*] Some great music choices; Jimi Hendrix' "Star-Spangled Banner" for the menu?  Hell yeah!
[*] Some interesting game dynamics were new, like the sandstorm changing how combat plays out. In that particular example though, it pulled me out of the game a bit because your character says something like "they won't see us in the sandstorm!" so I ran out into the sandstorm and promptly got shot to bits by the enemies who could still very-much-kinda see me nonetheless.
[*] That one part with the speaker [spoiler]in the guy's mouth[/spoiler] was legit creepy. It was great.
[/list]

And... some negative thoughts:
[*] Mechanics are mostly a copy of Gears of War (third-person perspective, cover and vaulting over it are first-class concepts, executions, etc.), except they suck more: They pulled from a great game, but they did strictly worse. As noted in various magazine reviews, the controls are awkard (sometimes leaving you meleeing at your cover instead of vaulting over, other times failing to take cover). It's particularly painful having played so much of the game they copied here (having played multiple Gears games fully through on Insane difficulty).
[*] Guns (I used mostly assault rifles) are all pretty interchangeable. Some are somewhat less accurate, some are slightly slower, but all are unbelievably accurate at range. Desert Eagles are basically a one-shot, but you generally only wind up with them after certain cutscenes and can't get more ammo. Kind of leaving you to wonder, where exactly did it come from? Since the closest thing to an explanation was your character losing all his guns.
[*] The death screen (a fade-to-black with the text "You Died!" in the middle) was so corny I thought it was a joke. Maybe that was the ultimate twist?
[*] Character development was nonexistent. One of your companions is immediately the comedian (I think that was Lugo), one is, um... not a joker, and that's basically all you get for characters. No backstories, short of your character idolizing faceless random guy #3 for something that happened in the past but is never seen, explained or really delved into at all.
[*] Choices are freaking stupid, most are meaningless, and all the interesting ones are made by your character (ex: we'll do this mission, we'll kill that guy, we're going right down the middle, etc etc). You don't get to make any choices that actually pertain to the other characters, only random faceless NPCs [spoiler]and at the end, yourself[/spoiler].
[*] [spoiler]And perhaps worst of all, the ending is stolen as well! It's almost note-for-note Fight Club's ending, except it's also less interesting than the original. No crazy love interests or giant bombings to spice this one up.[/spoiler]
[/list]

I can deal with mediocre mechanics, I don't really care whether the guns are that different, but the last three points here really bothered me while playing this game. It was billed as a game with a heavy plot and some soul-crushing choices that would leave you questioning yourself. [spoiler]Oh, and there was a twist at the end. Turns out, the only twist was,[/spoiler] at the end I was questioning my decision to finish plodding through this heap. I think the heft of any moral choice would be better if the first hour wasn't the same gun-ho, testosterone driven slaughter fest of brown-skinned foreigners of every brainless military shooter.

Don't be a hero. This game will give you PTSD. 

The game tells an incredible narrative of Captain Walker and his squad regarding the events around a war in Dubai, as well as the rogue U.S. battalion the "damned 33rd" 

The gameplay feels very similar to Gears of War, so if you've played that you'll feel right at home here. 

This game is also quite hard, I beat it on Suicide Mission which is the 2nd hardest out of 4 difficulties, and I struggled quite a lot. I found myself dying in many sections over and over dozens of times, so it's not for the faint of heart. 

If you are able to go through without dying the game should last you about 7-8 hours.

When the game does come to its conclusion, it's a trip. [spoiler] You'll want to replay the game from the beginning with your brand new perspective to see what's really going on. [/spoiler]

The gameplay is really solid, but it's the story that this game really has going for it. It tells an absolute fantastic story of war, and the horrible things surrounding it. Nobody wins in this game, and that's a really interesting take on storytelling. There are also multiple endings depending on what you choose, which gives it even more replay value. 

I'd give it an 8.5/10. Definitely worth a play!
