This is possibly the worst AAA shooter I've ever played, and just for 2 reasons:
1.  You have no control over save points.  This is far more difficult than it needed to be simply because the timing of autosaves.  Sometimes I would deliberately drop a weapon to pick up later (to conserve ammo), only to find that after I died and re-loaded to the last checkpoint, that gun is now gone.  There was one mission I had to start from the beginning because it was physically impossible for me to move forward without it.
2.  The controls are atrocious.  75% of the time I died, it's because of the controls.  Just about every similar game has a separate control for crouch, melee, sprint, and jump.  Sounds simple, right?  For whatever stupid reason, this game does it differently, in the worst way possible.  For example, why is melee and vaulting the same control?  There are so many times I tried to vault over the wall and I punch it instead, leading to me getting shot.  Sometimes I wanted to punch someone but vaulted a wall instead.  Sometimes I want to sprint to a specific location, but I want to stop running half way in between.  Well, sometimes it doesn't let me, where I end up running around in circles until I get shot to death.  I swear to god, I'd have a better chance surviving a real war with no training.  I may find it annoying how a lot of games need an exclusive button for every obscure action but I think it may be worse when a game combines too many unrelated actions into a single button.

I also found the gameplay itself to be very forgettable.  It offers nothing interesting that hasn't been done before.  I understand the main interest of this game is the story and the concept of the story was cool, but even that had its issues (NOTE: some spoilers ahead):
1.  I didn't find the cause or efforts from anyone (whether they were the main characters or the rebels or whomever) to be all that convincing.
2.  I don't even fully understand why Dubai was the main focus of the game.  At least from my experience, they didn't make it clear why Dubai was war-torn.  Did they just throw a dart at the Middle East assuming all of it is full of conflict?
3.  Maybe I'm wrong, but the weather in the game seems extremely unrealistic, at least for that specific setting.
4.  There are a couple points in the game where you have to make a decision, but it doesn't seem like you actually get to decide anything.  For example, there's a point where you have to decide to save someone, where you're told doing so will result in a lot of people dying.  Well, when you don't save him, a lot of people die anyway.  Shortly after, there's a bunch of soldiers you have to kill and you have the choice to use white phosphorus.  All those people are going to die a painful death anyway, so why not just take the easy way out?  Then the game tries to guilt you into choosing the "less ethical" option (as though gunning people down is SO much better) by showing all these civilians you killed.  Had I known that, I wouldn't have chosen that option.

It is a third-person shooter and a solid one at that. However the story is makes this game an outstanding experience as it is more a depiction of how real wars are, meaning there is no good or bad. That being said it is a really different experience and might not be what you expect from a shooter. However it is worth it. Playing through the story took me 6 hours without collecting stuff.

A  striking piece on the pains of war and a soldier's tormented mind unraveled. Spec Ops: The Line stands out as the most unforgettable first-person military shooter I've played for its powerful narrative throughout the journey and stunning visuals. Its gameplay is quite standard but came across polished.

Spec Ops: The Line is a game that tries to make me sad but I'm already broken so a little late to the draw on that one, guys. 

You play as Captain Walker, who is sent to Dubai with his squad to find survivors and report back to command. But Walker is a a strong independent Delta Force operative and heads into the city in an attempt to save everyone and also confront John Konrad, the man responsible for all of this. 

Except the sand storm, that was the planet. 

Spec Ops is a third person shoulder with this huge aversion to letting you move around. While the gunplay is acceptable and some of the guns do feel nice to use, you spend most of the game just kind of...Hiding. 

Much like my relationship with the police, you hide and get shot at a lot. Enemies will just MELT you if you're not behind cover, which makes sense considering the subject matter. You know, bullets. 
The problem is that the game isn't really set up for using cover to your advantage, there are some parts where its more viable but a lot of areas are set up so you can get closer to your enemy, actually flanking them is a flip of the coin. This mixed with the fact that enemies have pin point hitscan kind of means you're going to spend a lot of time crawling up cover and playing pop and shoot with other idiots who are hiding behind chest high walls. 
Its the formula made popular by Gears of War in its lamest, most basic form. At least you can command your squadmates to attack people you tell them to attack, but sometimes they just kind of...Not do it, and end up getting eaten by enemy gunfire. 

The other big mechanic is melee and executions. Sometimes when you shoot down a baddie they will lie there in a wounded state. From there you can rush them and perform an execution which gives you back some ammo for your current weapons.
Smacking some clown with a melee attack assures that you can perform and execution, you have opportunities to use them when the enemy is focusing your squad or you run into one another, but for the most part you'll be shooting everyone. 

But that's apparently not the point, according to certain video game journalists you aren't supposed to play a game for the gameplay. No sir this is one of those story games apparently. So hows the story?

Ever read Heart of Darkness? Good, me neither. 

The thing about Spec Ops is that it starts as a by-the-books military shooter and quickly spirals out of control from there. It deals with issues such as war crimes, self righteous mindsets, war crimes, mental health issues, war crimes, PTSD, war crimes, did I mention war crimes? 

Back in 2012, when this game came out, people went nuts over the sudden change of direction from a generic military shooter to a generic military shooter with a neat story. It became one of those “You gotta play it!” games that year, which kind of conflicted with the whole “You're supposed to turn off the game and stop playing if you were uncomfortable” idea that Cory Davis, the director of Spec Ops, was kind of shilling back then. 

There is a part in the game where Walker [spoiler]nukes the hell out of a big gathering of the 33rd with white phosphorous, and ends up killing a big group of civilians in the process. [/spoiler]
That was supposed to be the “Its time to stop playing” part of the game where you're supposed to start taking the game more seriously. Jokes on them, I always wanted to commit a war crime. 

I liked the story, but I liked the story AS a story, you know? It was interesting to see Walker turn from generic grizzled war fighter guy to a messed up, wreck of a man over the course of... 
3 hours and 22 minutes.

The game isn't very long. Huh, good thing I got it for free. 

Watching Walker change in not only appearance and mental state, but also in actions and wordings is actually a pretty interesting thing to behold. He starts swearing and spitting more venom more often at not just his enemies but also his squad. His executions become more brutal, and his desire to just simply kill “The bad guys” goes to the point of complete fanaticism. 
You also, as a player, start to question what is and isn't real. There are hints here and there pointing out that an event isn't really happening, such as the words of your squadmates and [spoiler] the fact that the screen fades to white every time something crazy is going to happen. [/spoiler] 

As a story, its pretty good, but the game's director had to go crazy with the “you just don't understaaaand” bit. 

They really wanted to send a message with The Line, to the point that they were shaming people for actually going through with the game. You “could have just turned the game off and walked away.” but you decided to keep on going. Chances are you even bought the game because it was a shooter. 
What were people supposed to do, just not buy your game? Are you advocating piracy of your product, Cory? Are you that guy? 
And what do you mean “Stop playing”? People paid full price for this back in the day, and they're supposed to, what? Leave it on their shelf? 
The game wasn't even that messed up, it wasn't making me lose sleep or anything, the big reveal scene didn't even really affect me all that much. 

I guess I'm the bad guy in this case, because the whole point was that it was criticizing people for dehumanizing human beings through video games. But at the same time, even my Jenkem addled brain could rationalize that, even though they looked human, moved like humans, and sounded like humans, they weren't humans.
The game is fictional, none of it actually happened, I wasn't actually killing people. 
Again, I know that that's the point, but still, kind of going a little hard on the fart sniffing there, Cory. 

But should you play it?

You already did, or if you haven't its sitting in your steam library. Everyone I've talked to has either played the game or knows about the big spooky twist.
It doesn't help that websites like Kotaku and Polygon wouldn't shut up about the themes of the game as soon as they took time out of their busy schedule of doing nothing to watch a lets play of it on Youtube. 

The game itself isn't anything to write home about, but if you want an actually pretty interesting story to sit through for about 3 hours or so, give it a shot. 
Or play the old PS1 games, no one else did, you'll be a pioneer!

Some people rate this game as a forgotten gem...i'm not really among them. 

Let's just be plain honest: the shooting part in this game kind of sucks. You're going to be playing against lots and lots of enemies that spawn from the same places, and for the most part not the smartest kind either. Your team also isn't really contributing much, and you have to literally pick them up from time to time. 

The cover system is bad in a way that really seems to come down to its console-port roots. Some actions feel like they should still be gamepad driven rather than key-driven. The overall responsiveness of the cover system and the way it works close to most kind of obstacles is quite inconsistent. Also, the angle you seem to be able to sneak-peak at has been a pain for me, because you don't get much corner peak as  you should, and while you could move from cover to cover, the system doesn't feel responsive enough to make it reliable for fast and precise shooting.

That gets worse because after a while the game feels very, very repetitive. It gets better by the end, but at that point you're going to be sort of bored, cause the game doesn't really lets you do anything other than shooting and reading short bits of info (Intel). The game could've used some depth in its gameplay.

Graphic wise, the game offers some impressive levels and good looking landscapes...at times you do get the feeling that someone actually tried to some love into the way this game looks. It's just that the scenarios aren't on the same detail level: some feel quite generic, while others have a glimpse or a particular sight that sets an atmosphere or signals a change within the direction you're taking. All of which would be fine, if the overall care for detail and atmosphere was on the same level, which really isn't. 

Overall, the game doesn't suck. It's just that it could've been quite a lot better. Play it for the plot rather than the gameplay itself.

[b] [u] TL;DR [/u] [/b] : A pretty good and original game that feels like Apocalypse now set in Dubai. The gameplay is fun but has quite some flaws. Runs well and still looks good. 

[u]Story / Setting[/u]
Probably the best aspect of this game, very original setting and the story itself was pretty good. It really feels like it could be a movie. 
There's a strong Vietnam war feel to it. The rock music (great choices by the way, Mogwai and Deep Purple being some of my favorite bands), the helicopters, the "white phosphorus" that really feels like agent orange, and some characters going insane make you feel like you're watching apocalypse in another part of the world. 
A big part of the game is also the ethical player choices you will have to make, and that was very well made. Maybe the best game I've played on that side of things, as the game doesn't explicitly tell you the different options you have, you can do something that you would personally do even when it doesn't seem like it's an option at first sight.
Some parts can be a bit cliché. At the beginning of the game there has to be 5 times when you hide right next to a bad guy just has he has an important discussion with someone. 

[u]Gameplay[/u]
Pretty typical 3rd person shooter. Take cover, shoot, move further, take cover... etc. Ammo management is a big deal in this game, there's many times when it's wiser to get a fully loaded weapon when there's a much more powerful one nearby with half the ammo. 
The difficulty I chose (Suicide Mission, the 3rd out of 4) was a bit too hard for me, I had to restart some moments many many times, but I still enjoyed the challenge. There's some parts of the game where you really need to die once so that you can expect what is going to happen in your next try, as you just can't know where the enemies are gonna spawn and you die very fast. Also some missions you need to restart force you to watch a little cinematic every time, which is quite annoying when you have to restart numerous times. 
The FOV is a bit too zoomed in, and there was no way to change it in the settings.  
Many controls aren't that great, the game forces you to use the keys for different actions in the game. For example, jumping over something, melee attack, and sprinting are the same. And sometimes when things get tense its hard to do precisely what you meant to do. 
Took me 7 hours to complete, knowing I restarted some parts quite a lot. 

I tried one game of multiplayer, which was kinda fun. I don't think it's really worth playing as some shooters have much better gameplay mechanics. 

[u]Performance[/u]
Runs very well at 60 fps on max settings (i5 4690 / R9 390). 

[u]Style / Graphics[/u]
Still looks good for today's standards, it could just need some extra anti aliasing.

Back when console ports were still a fairly new thing to PC, I gave Spec Ops a go and got very very frustrated by the third person gameplay that focuses heavily on taking cover and moving between cover. So I stopped playing after a couple of chapters (also: back then I didn't really care too much about story in video games.)

Now, several years (and many console ports) later, I gave the game another chance. It turned out to be pretty good. I already knew that the main goal of the game was to show the horrors of war. But actually having to commit a couple of pretty bad things and having to watch the consequences still stirred up some emotions and kept me playing till the end.

Obviously the game graphics are not exactly up to date, but it has held up pretty well and with everything turned up all the way, it's still pretty good looking for a six year old game (or I have really low standards). And it is obviously not your standard military shooter. In Spec Ops the lines between good and evil are blurred, very very blurred ("Do you feel like a hero yet?")

My biggest gripes with the game are the controls and some of the gameplay mechanics:

- Keyboard/Mouse feels extremely clunky

- The default button mapping (for keyboard/mouse) is awkward and some keys are bound to doing two or three different things, depending on the situation. Having "Reload" and "pick up weapon" bound to the same key can make for some very awkward moments when you try to reload while standing near a dropped gun...

- The cover system can be infuriating: sometimes Walker (the guy you play) simply won't go into cover or won't come out of cover, or switches to the wrong wall, is exposed to enemy fire and dies instantly.

- Playing on medium difficulty still gives you some "instant-death" moments, for instance you are in a sandstorm (with near zero visibility), your AI squad mate shouts "RPG!" and a split second later you are dead (because of an RPG hitting you in the head). Luckily the game has frequent autosave points... just kidding: depending on where you die you have to redo what feels like the entire level (which can be quite frustrating, especially if you die due to clunky controls or multi-mapped buttons).


Bottom line:

If you can handle frustrating controls and average gameplay mechanics, you get a game that can get into your head. And for that reason alone you will want to keep playing, despite its flaws.

If it's at a discount and you're looking for "Apocalypse Now - The Game", give Spec Ops The Line a go.

This game is hard for me to recommend. It tells a very immersive story that, while somewhat generic, has a more direct approach to it than I'm used to. It makes you feel bad about the events that happen and offers some twists and turns. The ending is also very unexpected and great; so story wise this game has a lot to offer, despite being only 6 or 7 hours long.

The gameplay, however, is boring. So boring. It's a cover based 3rd person shooter with about 7 or 8 weapons. Despite the game being rooted in realism, you regularly have to fight and kill armies of several dozen enemies. The way you do this, especially on the higher difficulties, is very fun and immersive: you duck behind cover, pop out and shoot a guy, almost die by the shots of the 14 other guys shooting at you, go back into cover and repeat for a good few minutes. Over. And over. Again. Aside from two or three deviating scenes where you shoot guys while not being behind cover, it's always the same. It's not engaging nor particularly challenging; it's, contrary to the story, unrealistic, frustrating, sometimes even unfair. The gameplay is, sadly, the worst part of the game.

It is still worth going through the game just to experience the story; and if it would be a walking simulator, I would upvote the hell out of it. Sadly, the gameplay tears it down; and since that's all you're doing, I can only not recommend it.

Still, if you get it heavily discounted or for free, get it, choose easy or normal difficulties (cause it takes less arbitrary time) and enjoy the story; it's all it has, but that's damn good.

I'll start off by admitting that I haven't experienced the game fully: I haven't played multiplayer or coop, and I've only played campaign on standard difficulty. A large amount of the reason, however, was that I didn't really enjoy the game much.

It feels like Call of Duty, but third person and somehow even worse and takes itself even more seriously. Combat is a chore, since ammo is scarce (which sounds interesting but translates to ordering your team to kill everyone then running around piles of dead bodies trying to max/min weapons and ammo and finding ammo boxes). Guns despawn with kills, and if you die they're all gone and kind of bone you. What's even the difference between half the guns? There's usually a full gun at the start of each battle, though, so don't worry. Health is your standard regenerating kind, you can't take much but your teammates will never die unless they're in the worst possible place for you to save them. Meanwhile, enemies either go down in a few hits or can take two mags of full auto to the face and be fine (heavies). Throw in the fact that you can't actually move them with your command system, and it makes things really annoying at times. Speaking of, it's extremely bareboned; you can send a teammate out to heal the downed one, make them shoot at/grenade a closer enemy, or snipe a further one, and that's it. At least you see where they are so you don't kill them by mistake. Firefights can get really bad at times, almost impossible; that's when you have to balance taking half an hour ot pick people off and making sure you don't run out of ammo/teammates. Movement I hated the most in the game, it's like Gears of War but baaaad. No jumps, invisible walls everywhere, prompts to "drop/rappel/zipline down" to trap you in the next zone, tap to sprint and never stop until you hit a wall or let go of a movement key, furious button mashing to try and vault over over and get behind another, unclear zones of being able or unable to shoot or get hit from cover, walking and crouching are nearly meaningless, hip shooting is nearly meaningless, stealth is nearly nonexistant...the list goes on and on. There's a few CoD scenes with the "grenade launcher event" and the "helicopter event" and whatnot.

The plot was okay, but lackluster compared to how it was advertised. A quote from the game illustrates it pretty well, it went something like, "There's always a choice." "No, there isn't". There's no real "line" that you cross, and there's barely any "choices" that you make (and when you do it doesn't change anything, the only time it matters is getting achievements and the choices at the ending). The "horrors" get pretty edgy, but a lot of it felt forced and stereotypical at times, and the dynamics and moral grey zone between between all the factions was barely explored. The plot twist at the end is interesting, but upon closer examination makes a lot of the game not make sense. Obviously, the characters are pretty flat, and I can't tell who's talking half the time.

6/10. It's a shooter, it works, had an interesting premise, but just kind of sucks.

Like many a Steam reviewer before me, I will lament the lack of a "neutral" review option. This game most definitely is not bad. Visuals, sounds, setting, idea are all very interesting and well executed. But I think most of the parts people praise are over-hyped. And the gameplay is average.

The big talking point of this game is the moralities it presents. "Deep", "hard", "challenging", "disturbing", etc etc. I understand why people feel these things describe the game well and even agree on most. But its deceptively shallow in all of this. You're railroaded into the most important black and white decisions while suddenly having choice on the more ambiguous ones. It took me out of it and made the obvious reveal at the end have far less impact. That being said, its still well written and an interesting dive into the mess of a war-like situation. The 'shell shock' and going crazy parts were the highlights. I just wish the decisions were either more open or never there to begin with. Either way I could've been more immersed or gotten swept away with the current of the story. Instead I was in limbo, waiting for that moment that sold me.

Gameplay-wise its just a third person 'take cover' game where if you take your time you'll be fine. The most difficult parts are short scripted moments. Some not even involving gunplay. Could've used more polish there. They take the quantity over quality approach to enemies like most shooters while missing a chance to ram that home with the other morals covered. The guns are fairly fun, especially in the late game. And they toss it a very basic squad command of targeting a specific enemy for your inept partners to shoot at.

I'll admit most of my complaints come from my own imagination of what this game had in store for me via the hype but it did indeed come up a little short. I guess my only real message here is lowered expectations on the impact of the story. Plus the game pops up in bundles and free so easy recommendation if you're in the mood to take cover and shoot things.

[h1]I just wrote a review for a 13-year-old, delisted video game that probably nobody is going to see, maybe apart from the last 3 people online owning the game and visiting its community page. And yet I think it’s one of the most important reviews for me. [...][/h1] 

[b]Spec Ops: The Line is a very important game that artistically achieved everything that it wanted. It challenged the industry, it challenged the player, it challenged the form of entertainment that video games are – among all the other things that video essayists talk about to this day. While it fell victim to poor sales and the decay of digital media distribution by getting delisted from stores, we can’t let it be so easily forgotten.[/b]

Dubai is getting hit with severe sandstorms, ruining the city, endangering civilians and cutting the place off from the rest of the world. The 33rd US battalion volunteers to enter the city and extract the civilians. Its last known status was 6 months ago when it was leading a caravan of survivors out of the city. Now, after receiving a mysterious transmission, your squad enters the ruins for a recon mission to see what happened in Dubai.



Playing through the game is very easy, it almost feels natural to get lost in the action. The music goes hard, gameplay is cool and engaging - the story confusing, but you’re too busy with gunfights to care - until sh.it starts to happen and you realize that this ain’t Call of Duty. Everything is chaotic, loud and confusing – but it’s all deliberate. You’re supposed to go too far, cross the point of no return in a way that you don’t even notice. The mindless entertainment absorbs you until it’s too late. Do you remember when enemies shifted from armed local combatants to US soldiers? Do you recall which faction does what? Did you notice how Walker barks orders differently now? How he sees weird stuff? How your teammates never talk to Konrad over the radio, only you do? Do you even remember why you came here?

The narrative focuses on characters, “heroes” going too far, making mistakes which result in innocent lives taken and having to deal with the guilt of it all. However, it’s not just another war movie, Spec Ops: The Line uses its medium to the fullest when it starts to creep out of your screen. When as a video game, an interactive experience, it interrogates not only the main character, but the player themselves. When the loading screen stops being helpful and starts commenting on your actions, it starts being sarcastic and judgmental, mocking you. Or fu.ck it, when you are [b]refused[/b] a loading screen, when it gets replaced with this horrifying scene of a mother and a child about to be burned to a crisp. It’s like all of these little details and hallucinations pour out of the game not to just affect Walker, but also you. 

You are not a hero of this game, you “soldier on” no matter what, even though you weren’t even supposed to be here. By trying to rescue people, then fix your mistakes, then avenge the civilians [b]you’ve[/b] killed, you dig yourself a deeper and deeper hole. All of that could’ve been avoided if you would just have stopped. But we’re gamers, we don’t just... turn off a video game... right?

No matter the choices you make in the game, it will always result in tragedy. There is no way to turn back, leave the city. While the player is judged for everything, there is no real way of stopping. The player’s autonomy in that regard is limited, almost pushing you into some time loop, purgatory theory. I think however, that a secret easter egg of just walking off into a desert and leaving would be nice. 

There are so many scenes, little details, motifs and interpretations of this game speculated to this day. It is deep and meaningful, a piece of art that as of now is not preserved properly. 



The game is a TPP cover shooter done in a really solid manner. The cover system is really good and nicely animated. There are many guns which feel good to shoot, 3 types of grenades to utilize, targeting orders to bark at your teammates and of course obligatory stationary turret sections. Besides the spots with sand that you can shoot to bury your opponents, the game doesn’t innovate a lot gameplaywise, it’s just really solid. The headshots have this satisfying slow-mo lasting just a perfect crumb of time, the aggressive music induces adrenaline, pushing you forward. Action is dynamic, addicting – it resurfaces as fast as it disappears to throw you back into a gunfight after a brief moment of respite. It feels good, it feels [b]too[/b] good. 

The gameplay absorbs you, so you don’t pay attention to what’s actually happening. The narrative screams somewhere in the background, muffled by the action and heavy guitar strings. Until the game shows you something horrible right in your face. The moment you start to care is far too late. 

The game is a really fun and solid shooter, but if it was just that, we wouldn’t be talking about it right now. At the time of its release there were far safer and better alternatives to buy and play soldier in a video game. This game would probably go unnoticed if it was purely a shooter. Instead, a lot of its elements feel more like a psychological horror. The gameplay is addictive, but its main purpose is to actually serve the narrative by distracting you. 



The graphics aged nicely, the bright sand of Dubai serves as a nice aesthetic when it covers the colorful billboards and parks of the city. The artwork painted on various walls as well as visible in the loading screens is equally horrifying as it is cool. 
The audio quality is crisp and the music purposefully loud and hard. There are several licensed songs that although cool and fitting the atmosphere, are probably the sad reason why the game has been delisted. However, the original soundtrack is just brilliant rock – if not for reminding me of the anxiety you feel while experiencing this story, I could headbang to it every day. Put it on Spotify.

[h1]”Gentlemen... welcome to Dubai.”[/h1]

The gameplay hasn't aged very well (movement feels clunky, and the 3rd person gunplay is quite a step back from titles like the division and warframe), and if you already kind of know the jist of the games storyline it kind of ruins the entire experience. I got it for free from the humble bundle, but even that said I kind of feel like I waisted 4 hours for promises of an interesting story.

Spec Ops: The Line is a bold third-person shooter set in the ruins of Dubai. The combat is solid, but the storyline is where this title shines. There aren't a lot of games out there that show you the true horrors of war and the consequences of your decisions, but Spec Ops: The Line delivers. By the end of the last chapter, you will question your morality as you deal with the aftermath of your wild goose chase through the streets of a once thriving city consumed by the grips of war.

Impressive game! Not often does an FPS gets you remembering it for its story. 

Spec Ops: The Line offers you a deep, mature and gut punching storyline, attempting to show you the horrors of war, the choices and decisions that have to be made by those living it and how it can also tear and torn them apart from inside out, as seen through the eyes of a team captain struggling to deal with the conflicts in his mind.

The plot is so well outlined it remains open to many interpretations due to its subtle nuances on how both the character and the world around him change as the game progresses, weighing you down along his path as everything becomes darker and sorrowful while angry and vengeful at the same time. 
Conrad's Heart of Darkness serves as visible inspiration for the main actors  (the antagonist is even called Konrad!) and the music usage gives it a very much Vietnam-movies feel. The whole thing feels very cinematic and dramatic.

The game is also quite (maybe too much?) reliant in combat sequences when driving forward. The player and his team go on a walking journey across Dubai and every few steps music kicks in and combat ensues, only to repeat itself a few meters ahead. Luckily environments are beautiful and varied, including sand and sandstorms as an interesting participant mechanic in combat. Still, I felt combat was tiring me as there was so much of it, especially with ridiculously overwhelming odds.

I will not remember the game for its combat but the story makes it very much worth it. I found Homefront, another story-driven FPS to be not as strong in terms of plot (which was alright though more straightforward) but much more balanced in terms of combat presentation.

In my opinion, do play it to experience a great story. At least on the level of Bioshock or F.E.A.R. in the way it makes you appreciate them for their story. Do not play it hoping to find interesting FPS combat.

[h1] The End Justifies The Means [/h1]

Yeah, not in Yager's Spec Ops: The Line case.
One of the best games I've ever played in terms of story is a disaster in terms of gameplay. A [i] hellhole [/i]

Without futher ado, here's my in-depth review about Spec Ops: The Line.

[h1] "I didn't mean to hurt anybody" [/h1]

I would start with the atrocious gameplay at first, but the story really deserves to be aforementioned.

The action takes place in a post-apocalyptic Dubai, after the worst sandstorm in the history of the UAE. The wealthier people were evacuated in time, leaving many Emiratis and foreigners behind. The "damned 33rd" battalion of the United States of America's Army, under the command of Colonel John Konrad was in transit, going home from a mission in Afghanistan. After seeing the chaos in Dubai, Konrad decided that the 33rd would disobey the Army's orders of abandoning the city and it's population to instead help with the evacution of the helpless people.
After six months without a trace of the 33rd, the US Army picked a transmission. It was from Konrad. The evac was a total fail, leading to many deaths. A Delta Force team, formed by Captain Martin Walker, Lieutenant Alphanso Adams and Sergeant John Lugo, was secretly sent in Dubai in a reconnaissance mission. It turns out that the 33rd turned rogue and the mission turns from a recon one into a rescue one.
Walker's psychical state keeps getting worse when his decisions continue to affect people, turning him into a ruined man, with a mind incapable of understanding what's good, what's bad; the reality, the guilt or the morality.
   
At first sight, the story was mediocre. Yeah yeah, war is bad and stuff, but as the game advanced, the story became better and better, with heart-breaking scenes, from the white phosphorus to [spoiler] Lugo's death [/spoiler] to that ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up ending.

[h1] The Bad Part Now [/h1]

The gameplay. Oh, the gameplay...

The game, in theory, is a cover-based third-person shooter.
Why in theory? Because the mechanics are horrendous.
It is very hard to stop from sprinting or entering in a cover, and that's ruining the game. It may sound like a small problem, but when a [b] cover-based [/b] game is failing in one of the core mechanics, the cover, then it is a hell of a problem.
The AI is not that bad. The friendly NPCs are pretty helpful, in some cases saving me from a loading screen because the cover system failed me. The enemy AI is also pretty smart, knowing when to supress fire, where to shoot or when they should stay in cover. The annoying thing is that any enemy can hit you from the other side of the map, with any kind of weapon. Also, when you tag him with a sticky grenade he tends to run into it's allies, but that's more of a funny thing. When HE throws a grenade near you though, well, God should have mercy on your soul. It's a pain in the arse moving when staying in cover.
The gunplay is also a burden. Your bloom is horror. If you find yourself in a long distance fight with only a P90 and a shotgun (yeah, a shotgun, because the game makes you change weapons after just a wave of enemies. Finding Scar or M16 bullets is kind of a miracle in The Line) then you're pretty much ♥♥♥♥♥♥.

[h1] Graphics and sound [/h1]

There's not much to say about these things so I'll put them in the same chapter.

The graphics are good, though I'm not much of a fan of the art style, but this is strictly subjective. The levels are varied, so the shooting isn't so boring. Here you find yourself in the desert, and here you find yourself in an Emirian hotel.
The game isn't very environmental interaction friendly, only some of the covers can actually be destroyed.
Also, it is very well optimized. I have never lost a single frame throughout the whole game on a middle-ish end PC, playing it on the highest level of details at a 1920x1080 res.

The sound benefits from some pretty good choices. The soundtrack is varied and it is integrated in the actual game,  coming from some improvised speakers, which is a nice kind of a feature.
About the characters' voice actors I can only say that they are amazing, memorable. Nolan North (Captain Walker) and Bruce Boxleitner (Colonel Konrad) are doing incredible jobs. The dialogues are well written and credible. They are also evolving over time, from Walker & co. speaking in military terms in the beginning to shouting and swearing in the late part of the game. 

Lugo's "he turned us into ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ killers" will stay with me for some time.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

I can't speak about the multiplayer because I haven't played it, but I don't see potential in it. Play Battlefield or CoD for multiplayer.

So, if you want a 6 hours adventure in an interactive film, be my guest. It was free a few days ago on HumbleBundle, so you can give it a go.
If you don't want a game with an in-depth story though, it's not worth it.

Spec Ops: The Line stands tall as one of those games that everyone should play.

It’s an award-winning third-person shooter with great graphics, actually quite acceptable gameplay mechanics and sequences, and of course the must lauded story.

I love the story as an in-depth examination of the meaning of truth, the issue of personal choice, and a commentary of war. The player is inexorably drawn into the story of Walker and his squadmates as they descend progressively into the madness of near-future Dubai.

One of the tropes it turns on its head is that the player character - Walker - is always right. In most video games, whenever the player defies the orders of the authority, it is invariable because the protagonist sees something inherently evil or wrong in the authority, or because the player has seen something on the ground that countermands the authority’s viewpoint. But in Spec Ops, Walker is blinkered by half-truths and his own perceptions, and his actions are consequently more and more off-piste.

Another trope is the role of the protagonist as the hero of the story. (I don’t have to give any examples of that.) But Walker and the rest of Delta are interlopers, a team initially unrelated to the rebels, to the CIA, and to the 33rd Battalion. Except for an oblique relation between Walker and John Konrad, the commander of the 33rd, there was no need for Walker to be involved in the conflict. Instead, Walker decided to insert himself in the narrative; as the story progresses, it’s clear that Walker is the one whose actions escalate the conflicts ever upwards.

Walker's squadmates Lugo and Adams are not examined in as much depth, but their responses are quite revealing: in order to reconcile their actions, they place the blame squarely on Walker's soldiers as their commanding officer. Adams is the more interesting of the two: he clearly vacillates between enforcing the chain of command on Lugo, and questioning Walker's decisions.

Many have called the action sequences generic, but I actually though there were some great set pieces too. A mall scene where Walker is separated from his two squadmates and they progressively cover each other as they strive to reunite is a stand-out. I also enjoyed the sequence in the aquarium, where harrowing close-combat mixed with challenging lines of fire from different directions in the main stadium area. It’s a shooter trying to tell a story, but it’s still a good shooter.

Spec Ops: The Line is definitely not a game for the faint of heart. The game is ugly, gory and it puts the player in the middle of the action of a hypothetical war in Dubai. To be completely honest, it's not a fun game at all. It's intense, that's for sure, but that's because you're always in the middle of loud and fast gun action. In that sense, the game doesn't really give the player a lot of quiet moments to reflect. You're always firing at enemies, near and far and you're always looking for the best place to take cover, so you can protect yourself from gunfire and take aim at enemies successfully. Is it a good cover shooter game? I suppose it is. It has the full package, you can order your squad to take out enemies and throw grenades and there are various different kinds of weapons.  

I know not every player liked the cover shooting mechanics, but I found them functional enough. Keep in mind this game came out in 2012. Back then, cover shooter games were everywhere and this game was seen as one of the nails in the coffin of the genre, because of the commentary it provides. I won't spoil anything, but there are some moments in Spec Ops which are deliberately "meta", and the storyline doesn't pull any punches. There are also some references to other games. I am sure everyone will get the reference to MGS3 towards the end. 

Narrative wise, this game has historical impact in the gaming world. It came out when war shooters and cover action were the biggest thing in gaming and it wasn't afraid to make the killing unpleasant, gory and way too real. It can definitely be mentioned in the history of games as a dividing line in the war shooter genre, where it said "hold up" and showed that video games can very much be "grown up" about things and "keep things real".

Gameplay wise, well, it's april 2018 as I am reviewing this and none of the gameplay is exactly cutting edge, but as I mentioned in the beginning, it works. I never really stopped and thought any of the shooting was fun, but the game isn't THAT long, so while it does get old pretty quickly, you're not too far from the ending sequence, which also doubles as an emotional rollercoaster and a final middle finger to war and all the atrocities that always seem to come with it.

Rewriting this review years after playing now that I have a lot of knowledge about it's origins:

Spec Ops the Line is a dark, gritty war game, and critic of both the American Military Entertainment Complex and the subject of warfare overall. 

Acting as a modern retelling for Heart of Darkness, one of the greatest novellas of all time, the game replaces the African and European Imperial setting for a more modern, more relevant. 

The game is set in the city of Dubai post devastating sandstorm. 

Mirroring Heart of Darkness, we see a modern raw take on American imperialism in the Middle East, we see horrid violation of the laws of war, done by our own hand, the game slowly breaks down our "war hero" facade to show us how truly mad, how truly mentally deranged we are. Spec Ops the line is not a game about being a hero, it is not a game about America saving the world. This game shows shooter heroes as they are, it shows the United States of America as it is: A system created to brainwash and turn men into emotionless killing machines for the sole intention of furthering America's foreign interest.

To go into more detail, would require time that I do not have, so instead I make a simple request:

Please read Heart of Darkness

So, how's the story?
Well let me tell you. You, and your squad members so it would be 3 guys, are soldiers with a mission to find survivors and help them out of Dubai. It was sandstorm that makes the town devastated and people trapped inside of the city. The damage of Dubai makes it banned from UAE. Same thing as Modern Warfare 3 in France because of that Eiffel tower destruction. (I just heard it from friend, not reading the news, so I can't confirm). Apparently there was a US Infantry Battalion volunteered to help these poor civillians. It didn't end up pretty well. And what happened next after these trio reached Dubai? Get inside and play the game! I won't spoil the story for you guys and break the fun. But I'm telling you, the story is just... harsh.

Now, the gameplay.
The game is third-person shooter. It's with present day background so you'll see usual weapons that's still being used around Middle-East and the US Army. I can say it's good, but the aiming sometimes is annoying. Is it because of my shaky hands or the mouse is not so comfy, I have no idea. But why don't you just try and get yourself to the field? Also, as a leader of a squad, you can give orders to your teammates. You have a sniper and a heavy. The sniper can kill enemies in long range with his rifle. Yes I said it, because he brings a Steyr Scout and a TAR-21 which he use all the time. And the have can take down enemies with his SAW (not that one belongs to Doom Guy, but squad automatic weapon) and throwing grenades.

"And, the graphics. That's, y'know, that's really what this is all about, and uhh..."
So the motion is kinda stiff. You can see it from running, reloading, talking, that sort of thing. Sometimes you'll see the hand doesn't really grab the mag, but pass through it and the gun. But come on, now, it's a common mistake that even Ubisoft oftenly make. (See Tachanka when coming in with foregrip attached and exfilling when using MG in Outbreak event and believe me, it's worse.) It's also kinda gory. When you kill enemies with explosive, their bodies will be thrown apart like some Treyarch games' bodies. When you headshot someone with a sniper rifle or a shotgun, the head will disappear like in GTA San Andreas. Overall, I think it's pretty good for its year.

So will there be any more updates or more story, perhaps?
Sadly, no. The developer said the game is underrated and lost in competition with bigger titles such as Call of Duty and Battlefield. Some reviews said that the gameplay has similiarities with some other titles like Gears of War, making it lack of special characteristic to differenciate the game with another title. If they keep working on this game, it would be not very profitable so screw it and leave this project. (I think that's how they thought). There's no DLC either, although there's an option for DLC in the main menu.

Is the game difficult? Kinda.
Since the game is third-person shooter, the aiming is not as precise as first-person shooter. Sometimes the enemies are far away and you can't shoot them precisely with your assault rifle or the enemies are very close and you need a lot of ammo to shoot one guy. Don't compare it to PUBG, it's different. You have sticky grenades that you can throw to your enemies' body. If you're lucky, they'll run to their comrades. If not, they'll run to you and kill both of you. Sometimes you'll need 3 sniper rounds to kill one guy. Sometimes you'll die in same spot many time because you're surrounded or grenades or HMG or whatever and you'll have an offer to lower your difficulty which is annoying me many times. But that's okay. You can do more training and sharpen your commando skill. Practice makes perfect, right?

There's a multiplayer and a co-op option. Are they usable?
Don't bother. They're dead. There's nobody in there. But if you guys disagree, maybe we can sort this thing out.

Spec Ops: The Line has turned into one of those games that you either love or hate. There have been a million positive reviews hailing SO:TL as a masterpiece that critiques Military shooter games and game design as a whole, but many of them failed to actually speak on what REALLY makes SO:TL a memorable game to me. Playing Spec Ops: The Line, even knowing going in that things get real, was like watching End of Evangelion. There was this sinking feeling in my chest as chaos began compounding, you're entering a disaster area, killing your own brothers in arms, accidentally killing civilians, and going on a wild goose chase that only makes things more hellish. Spec Ops: The Line being a critique of linear game design and military shooters is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and this take has always fell short due to SO:TL's linear design in itself, and thus to a loud minority of people, SO:TL is a pretentious game that takes a dump all over their favorite shooter games, so a Contrarian reaction was only waiting to happen from those who never even cared to play the game. In reality, Spec Ops: The Line is more like Military Psychological Horror than any of that. It's just a really cool game, and I can't think of any other game that has felt so visceral in its chaos. If you are one of those people who never played this game even when it was free on humble bundle, and are on the fence because you always thought the game sounded pretentious, just let go of your preconceived notions and confirmation bias, and play this game. It's not particularly long, and the cover shooter gameplay really isn't anywhere near as bad as some people make it out to be. It's a unique and horrific experience.

For its time, Spec Ops: The Line was a really innovative approach and a welcomed change to an over-saturated market of shooters and at first glance it looks just like that, yet another installment in multitude of franchises revolving around military shooters, which makes me think it was done on purpose so as to subvert the players' expectations. Although it's not perfect, it has a very mature look at war and conflict as a whole with its gritty approach, moral gray areas, dark undertones and excellent foreshadowing.

Its gameplay, however, is notorious for being clunky and frustrating to work with. The game offers little to no control configuration which is a big problem, as the regular mouse sensitivity is all over the place and multiple actions are bound to a single button, such as sprint and taking cover, that can't be separated meaning that the game often has conflicting inputs, leading to a lot of struggle and death at the hands of faulty mechanics. It's for this that I recommend experiencing the game on a standard or lower difficulty, with anything above for people who like playing with odds stacked against them.

On Suicide and Fubar difficulties, enemies punish you for the slightest of things, even if they don't always make sense. For example; sometimes you'll be out in the open for a few seconds and not get hit once, but other times you'll get one shot before you even get a chance to peek. This is only complicated more with the lack of ammunition to make it more realistic for lower levels, but frustrating on higher ones as it takes you forever to gun down a single enemy and often creates long and grueling stalemates.

Sidenote, its multiplayer is a joke. You can tell it's tacked on just for the sake of having one because, apparently, the game can't be a military shooter without it these days. Even if you manage to get enough players to experience it to its fullest, it's riddled with bugs and poor net code with no consideration for balance whatsoever. Its mechanics are directly ported over from the campaign meaning that you're playing a fast-paced mode with stiff controls and pistols that act like sniper rifles.

Overall, if you're looking for a good single-player story driven experience, I highly suggest going for it, you won't be disappointed.

If Spec Ops had no story, it's doubtful that it'd be destined for anything other than the bargain-bin.

The core gameplay loop revolves around colour-by-numbers, third-person cover-shooting at it's most unremarkable. Worse still, it's a no-frills console port, so chances are, you'll find yourself battling more with the gummy controls than you will with the hordes of suicidal cannon-fodder enemies that hurl themselves at you with reckless abandon.

But the generic gameplay in Spec Ops is elevated by how it's framed; to the surprise of many of early reviewers, Spec Ops' story is an examination of PTSD, the cost of war, and a metacommentary on the nature of choice and consequences in gaming as a whole.

Spec Ops subverts expectations, but like a Shyamalan twist, it doesn't really pack as powerful an emotional punch if you already knew what was coming. This issue is only compounded by the fact that Deus Ex had more-or-less pulled the same sort of bait-and-switch as The Line's most memorable moment twelve years prior, but in a way where the player—due to retaining agency in every potential combat encounter—was actually complicit in the consequences of their avatar's actions.

So while this may have come as a welcome change of pace for some, others may find little of lasting value that hasn't been done before (and done better).

I received the product for free from Humble Bundle's promotion of it a few days ago (played through most of it March 31st, 2018 and finished it on April 1st, 2018) but it has been on my radar of games I've wanted to play since I heard how gripping the story was. I'll try to remain as spoiler free as I can, but will warn in advance if I discuss spoilers.

Gameplay wise it is a very generic cover-based shooter with slightly odd button mapping for some (I got used to the controls and didn't rebind keys personally, but the default choices for sprinting and vaulting over cover are odd to say the least). I played through on the normal/medium difficulty "Combat Ops" and died a good handful (due to health being very low) of times to the enemies since they come out of the woodwork most times and ammo is scarce so picking up new guns is almost always going to happen. There are resupply boxes for the guns you have and they mostly appear after each intense fire fight and your companion AI buddies are fairly competent and will help in combat and if you make them with the ordering command (defaulted to Mouse 3 and moving the mouse to the target). Tl;dr: gameplay is passable if with some odd default keyboard/mouse controls and huge waves of enemies and a relatively low health will offer a decent challenge.

The setting is nothing to get overly excited about, but it takes place in a desert so it works for it in that regard. Voice work is good across the board with particular praise going to the protagonist (voiced by Nolan North) and companion AI characters that tag along with you. Graphics are dated for the current games out on the market, but I think adds charm to the grit that is coming across while you play.

The story is very good. It does an excellent job at subverting the trope most military-based shooters of the day go with ('America is the good guy, the other guys are evil, go in there and win one for the team, rah rah') which is very refreshing. The choices you make during certain points of the game do stick with you and really make you question what it means to be a Hero. Are you the good guy? Were you ever a good guy to begin with? It's very self-reflecting of both yourself and pretty much the whole genre in general.

My playtime clocked in at around 7 hours of playing (with me taking my time to explore the limited areas I could go since it is linear) so for a price at $30 dollars for those who didn't get it from the Humble Bundle free thing I think have a decent chunk of entertainment value for the price.

As an aside I encountered 1 bug that didn't register that I had killed an enemy for my one teammate to go and safely pick up my other downed partner while I was cut off from both of them. Failing that point twice and killing the enemy slower seemed to fix the glitch.

TL;DR: Gameplay has some hiccups with some odd keyboard bindings, enemies come out in waves too much and with a low health pool (even on normal) except some difficulties if low on ammo with no ability to get to a new gun though the checkpoint system is very generous. Story is the shining point in the whole game that is amplified by the stellar voice work on display that can pull you away from the bland desert area you will find yourself in.

I don't know where to begin with this game, to be quite honest. All I do know is that by the end of my first playthrough on Suicidal made me feel as exhuasted as its main character. 
To simply put, Spec Ops: The Line is a third-person cover-shooter with a focus on narrative in the setting of Dubai after a series of sandstorms ravaged the city. The game starts out just as any other third-person cover-shooters, where you're put inside the shoes of Capt. Walker of Delta Force with his team composed of Adams, stereotypical black soldier, and Lugo, stereotypical smartass wizzkid, trying to figure out what happened in the failed evacuation attempt of Dubai. This is what the game wants you to believe and it does a good job at it, in fact, it does its job too well. Throughout the first half of the game, you're thrown into this chaotic world being as cookie-cutter as possible with every trope from the book of "How to design a military shooter in the 7th-gen", all to subvert it and to make its point in regards the horrors of war and what it does to a soldier, or better yet, how it breaks them. I actually enjoyed how it did it, even though you could see it happening a mile away, but the main problem with this is that it does its job too well and it never seems to get away from being just another bog-standard third-person cover-shooter, the world's most tiring combination of words and genre I've had the misfortune to witness.
The gameplay isn't even bad, it's serviceable, but that's just it, it only does the bare-minimum. You move from cover to cover, pop head after head and blow up stuff. It does some interesting things such as different enemy types and blinding them with sand from explosions, however, it's not enough. The reality is that this game is serviceable at best, and frustratingly and boring at its worst. The AI, for both on enemies and your companions are braindead and often seen them either stand around eating lead or running straight for the all-you-can-shoot buffet. For a game that harps up its narrative and story and tries to evolve it beyond from just another military shooter, at its core, it's just another military shooter that makes you feel bad. It would've been amazing if the gameplay evolved alongside with the story, such as the game forcing you to play looser and more chaotic rather than sit around, which could've worked in the game's favor. Unfortunately, what we got just more of the same, but with a better story.
Don't get me wrong, I don't hate this game. I thought I did, at first, but now I just realized that I'm more frustrated with it. It has a good concept, but the execution is simply subpar. It has great visuals, it runs beautifully on my laptop equipped with a 8250u and a MX150 on max settings and at least it tried to have an interesting narrative. However, it's not enough to warrant constant praise, especially when the game had the potential to go above and beyond.
Even though there's a big fat thumbs-down icon on my review, I do recommend playing through this game once, but I personally wouldn't pay for it. Get it for free like how I did on Humble Bundle or play it from a friend steam library to at least experience what this game has to offer firsthand rather than parroting opinions from highly-opinionated jackasses like myself, because then you could understand my frustration I got from playing this game, and the cartharsis I got afterwards. A very conflicting game, to say the least.

Spec-Ops: The Line is not your ordinary military shooter. Sure, it plays like the bastard child of Call of Duty and Gears of War, but the style and story could not be any more different.
This evocative, provocative setting isn't the only thing that sets Spec Ops apart from the globe-trotting, timeline-jumping antics of its militaristic video game peers. The game also tells a bold and often subversive story that is in many ways a deconstruction of the modern war video game.

Wait, really? Well, yeah, really. Spec Ops: The Line is a distinctly, consistently flawed game. But despite the many things it does poorly or with at-best-bland competence, it deserves consideration for the risks that it takes, and for the chutzpah with which it takes them.

Despite the somewhat intriguing story and the great final twist, this game is a complete chore to play.

All of the combat situations play out the exact same way, tediously grinding through waves of enemies, with little to no variation. There are no memorable set pieces or really thrilling moments with the exception of a few moments toward the end. But worst of all the games color pallete is so dull and bleak, that it makes playing for a long time unappealing, and the graphics haven't aged very well.

I get that the ending is unexepected, and that's what this game is known for, but I feel like people are forgetting how bad the rest of the game is.

[i]Now… What to say about this old, classic ‘psychological, PTSD military, third person shooter’ that hasn’t already been said? Its publishers are the famed 2K which has published classics such as Borderlands 2 & 3, MAFIA, Civilisation, XCOM, the BIOSHOCK trilogy, Duke Nukem and my absolute personal favourite… The Darkness II. This should be an indication of the pedigree and quality of Spec Ops: The Line.

Another benefit is the fact its API is DirectX: 9.0 meaning you can completely max out the settings even on a relatively old rig and your CPU & GPU temps remain super low (mine didn’t go past 40c) and graphically its aged remarkably well which is a pleasant surprise. Sure, it’s never going to look as magnificent as the Witcher 3 but it doesn’t need to be.

The total storage needed is only 10GB meaning it obviously won’t need as long to download and it’s not really a game you need to uninstall to free up space for a new game. 
To give you an idea of just how glorious this game looks in 4k, ultra-settings and consistently hitting 60FPS (and often exceeding that) check this video out below:[/i]

[b]STORY (Plus a bit of background):[/b]


[i]The game is set in Dubai, Saudi Arabia, the worst series of sandstorms in recorded history began across Dubai. Six months prior to the start of Spec Ops: The Line the city's politicians and wealthy have downplayed the situation before evacuating secretly, leaving the population behind as the city is engulfed and swallowed by the Rubʿ al-Khali sand desert. Col. (colonel) John Konrad, Commander of the "Damned 33rd" Infantry Battalion, volunteers his 33rd battalion to help relief efforts... He fails and struggling to maintain order amid the winds, riots, and dwindling resources, the 33rd declared martial law and began committing atrocities against the civilian population. 

Fast forward to the start of the game and the US military sends CPT (Captain) Martin Walker, a member of Delta Force (an elite branch of the US military, the equivalent to our SAS here in the UK as they are both airborne special forces). Along with SSG (Staff Sargent) John Lugo & 1LT (First Lieutenant) Alphonso Adams. You play as CPT Martin Walker, the games main protagonist, You and your two squaddies are sent to carry out two mission objectives, firstly, recon (recognisance) to search for any remaining survivors then secondly, radio for an immediate ‘evac’ of any survivors they encounter… 

The ♥♥♥♥ hits the fan straight from the opening scene and as the game progresses the horrific choices you’ve made takes their toil on your characters already fractured state of mind, leading to his PTSD becoming more and more pronounced as the game progresses… I’d recommend you play it at least twice to fully experience the different endings and make different choices. If memory serves, I’m sure Spec Ops has a total of ‘four’ different endings.

The story is fantastic, and is told remarkably well, it is gripping and leaves you wondering what you could have done differently, especially at the end. The story touches on the ‘destructive element war has on the human psyche’. I strongly recommend NOT researching to much about the game as it will ‘give the game away’ (no pun intended lol). You will also pick up on the ‘smaller’ details once you play it for a second (third and fourth) time but will almost definitely miss these small but magnificent details during your first play through as they are beautifully and perfectly integrated with the environment that’s thought provoking and forces you to ask yourself how you could of missed that! It’s the small details, different endings and fully immersive story telling that gives this masterpiece added replay value. There is a particular part in the game that will leave you thinking ‘What the ♥♥♥♥ have I just done, I am a monster’ which is multiplied by Lugo’s outburst but I absolutely won’t spoil that shocking moment for you but you’ll instantly know what I’m talking about once the event unfolds and the results of your actions are laid bare lol.[/i]

[b]The two AI squaddies that accompany you on this mission are: [/b]

[i]SSG (Staff Sargent) John Lugo, He is the squad's designated marksman and medic. Outside of combat, Lugo is depicted as the team's engineer and a translator. His reactions to your orders will make you question your morals and choices throughout the game and

1LT (First Lieutenant) Alphonso Adams, He is the squad’s heavy gunner. Out of combat, he is used as the team's breacher and tracker. Adams feels a lot more loyal (namely at the start of the game) and will try to explain the decisions you make away. 

A huge plus is the voice acting of every character within Spec Ops but namely Walkers character. Cpt Martin Walker is voiced by none other than Nolan North who is the voice actor in FIVE Call of Duty games, Prince of Persia, Star Wars: The Old Republic and its following expansions, Dota 2, Team Fortress 2 and Destiny 2: Forsaken along with a string of animated movies. So… Yeah, the voice acting by every character in Spec Ops: The Line is flawless.[/i]

Spec Ops: The Line is all-in-all a fairly mediocre game. The characters are bland, the story bare-bones, the gameplay about as basic as a third-person tactical cover shooter could possibly get, and the choices are cherry-picked from story-convenient spots.

[b] Spoilers ahead (You've been warned): [/b]


[h1] The characters: [/h1]
[list]
[*] There are essentially only four actual characters in the game: Captain Walker, the protagonist; Lugo, the sniper; Adams, the heavy weapons guy; and the Radioman. Captain Walker is the most fleshed-out, and considering he's literally a cookie-cutter action game protagonist, that's saying something. He attempts to justify every action that the player takes, even when such an action is unjustifiable (for example, out of curiosity, I shot a CIA agent that I was rescuing after he had put down his gun, and yet Captain Walker says that he might have been tricking us with his surrender). He also suffers from pretty severe hallucinations for... some reason? I don't think it's explained at any point.

[*] Lugo and Adams are both pretty much one character. They trade off which one provides the "stay focused on the mission" argument and the "save the civilians" argument, leaving me confused as to what their ideals actually are. They seem written as if the player is already supposed to care about them, and so the game never actually spends time making you invest in their stories, so their deaths end up meaning very little to the player besides "oh, I guess I won't be able to order them to kill people".

[*] Radioman is just annoying. He constantly talks to the player for the first good chunk of the game, and every second that he spoke just made me hate him more. And not in a way that made me want to kill him, which definitely could be argued as a good point, but instead in a way that made me regret spending the thirty seconds it took to get this game from the Humble Bundle Pack.
[/list]


[h1] The story: [/h1]
[list]
[*] The story of Spec Ops: The Line starts off with a red flag. It starts in media res with a rail shooter scene. I'm sure you know the type. Sitting at a minigun in a helicopter, shooting the enemy helicopters flying around. Pretty boring all told, and I'm immediately confused as to why I'm shooting these people in the first place. Timeskip backwards to the point where the protag team is dropped off in Dubai, and I already have a bad feeling about this game. 

[*] As we progress through the story, I feel worse and worse about it. Basically the only thing holding this story up is its gimmick: the whole "making hard decisions that make you into the villain" thing. And, to be honest, it's really not that creative. Sure, it may be new to the video gaming industry, but the idea is so pervasive throughout media elsewhere that it's kind of become a meme in literary circles, often referred to as "hard men making hard decisions while hard". It's not new, and it's tired out at this point.

[*] The whole hallucination element also comes out of nowhere. Like, the whole idea of the plot is that the main antagonist wasn't real, and was instead just a figment of Walker's damaged mind, but that's isn't even hinted at until like halfway through the story. It's introduced in a near-replica of the helicopter scene at the beginning, where Walker starts talking about having done this before (even though this is the first time he's done anything like this). This just came out of nowhere, and twists with no setup are not twists, they are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
[/list]


[h1] The gameplay: [/h1]
[list]
[*] Think of a third-person shooter. Add cover mechanics. Add minimal squad commands. You have Spec Ops: The Line. There's maybe fifteen or twenty guns in the whole game, which wouldn't be bad if the game made up for it in other ways. However, it does not. The cover mechanics are about as bare as they can be. You run into cover, you lean over cover to shoot, you vault over cover, and that's about it. And they aren't even implemented well. They use the same button for Sprint, Get Into/Out Of Cover, and general Use. Not a great system, as there are many times where you will be attempting to run away from an enemy, and magnetically stick to a wall because the game thinks you want to be in cover facing away from the enemy, or where you want to revive a squadmate and instead you just run into the middle of the firefight and die.

[*] The squad commands have literally only two options: Shoot this guy, and Stun Grenade. That's it. There's nothing else. I honestly almost never bothered with squad commands because they already shoot people, and I don't feel like micromanaging in a third-person shooter. Honestly, the squad commands are so extraneous that if you removed them I don't think anyone would notice.
[/list]


[h1] The choices: [/h1]
[list]
[*] You can kill innocent people without warning, but you can't kill villains without warning. Basically sums up my main complaint. Early in the game, you meet a guy who's beating up a CIA agent that you want to rescue. You can't kill the guy, even though you have silenced weapons and the guy is not paying attention to where you are at all, because Walker decides to call out at the last minute. But you CAN kill the CIA agent for no reason (see my example above in the section about Walker himself).

[*] And some of the choices aren't choices at all, really. Like, at the point where you shoot a bunch of civilians to avenge Lugo, you have Adams constantly begging you to let him shoot them, and they attack you and knock you around so you can't even just walk through them without shooting (which I intended to do). Or at the very end, where you have the choice to kill the innocent soldier whose been driving through the ruins of Dubai just to rescue you. Like, why would you do that? Is there any reason? I don't believe there is.
[/list]


[h1] Miscellaneous: [/h1]
[list]
[*] Whenever you need to go to a specific place where a character is waiting, they will constantly call out to you. Like, not exaggerating, every one or two seconds they will play another voiceline, constantly bugging you to go talk to them. And in a game where there's rewards for exploration (like ammo and the intel collectibles), this is a really, really annoying thing.

[*] All of the twists are so predictable its laughable. Like when you get to use the white phosphorous artillery on the military base, when they show a big mass of people in a trench, my very first thought was: "oh, it's gonna be a bunch of civilians, isn't it?" And, of course, you can't exit the artillery menu, for whatever reason, so I was forced to bomb what I knew were civilians with white phosphorous. And, as it turned out, I was right. That didn't really feel like I chose to kill them because of a lack of forsight, that felt like I was held at gunpoint into killing them because I did what the game told me to do (use the artillery).

[*] Finally, and this more of a pet peeve than an actual flaw with the game, but what the hell where the designers thinking when they designed the protagonists? Like, for some reason they're wearing short sleeves and either no or minimal hats in the Arabian desert. While this may seem to make sense because it's hot, just think: would you rather be really sweaty and thirsty, or would you rather have severe, blistering sunburns for the next month? In the desert, you cover up. I think the worst part of this is that most of the enemy soldiers are wearing full combat gear, so clearly the designers knew what the US military wears in the desert, so why are the protagonists dressed like they're going to the beach?
[/list]

A little piece of torture aimed specifically at messing with the minds of the customers who were daring enough to go thru its 18 floors of hell with absolutely horrific and uncomfortable controls. 

Everything about this screams it was made for the controller in mind, in the hopes that PC gamers will suffer as much as possible with a mouse and keyboard. Acceleration and smoothing aside, its sensitivity is on the super upper end of the high spectrum, you'd better wanna get ready to mod the controls for yourself to play this game. 

It tries to copy a cover system from gears of war but the developers seems to have forgotten that they were not epic games and never had the skills to create such a system in the first place, so in the end what you end up with is a half-baked system that feels wholefully incomplete and sometimes raises the question of why you bothered taking cover at all.

However, once you managed to endure thru such an ordeal you will find yourself in the shoes of an unfortunate war victim trying to wrap his around the choices that one has to make in a war. Often you will question yourself whether or not you could have made another choice to avoid the consequences that would follow from your earlier decision. But questioning is all you can do, for the game doesnt allow you to make any other choices than the only one you were allowed to make, which then begs the question; why bother adding in dialogue to make the pretence that the player had a choice in the first place if you werent gonna give em one. Either way the plot and the tale it contains is not nearly as bad as its controls. But the controls were crap enough to overshadow what little goodness there was in the story. 

TL:DR Dont buy this game, unless its super cheap (and im talking 5 bucks or less), unless you really enjoy getting spat on in the face by the devs as pc gamer or fancy a self-bdsm session with your mouse. Best of all, get it when its free on the humble bundle or sth. Even then i wouldnt recommend spending the hours of your life on this game unless u are willing to mod its rubbish controls right right first.
