It's the "♥♥♥♥ you for liking military shooters" military shooter. 

I confess to no experience with earlier games in the Spec Ops series, though I suspect they were nothing quite like The Line. Mechanically, The Line is nothing special. It's just a Third-Person cover shooter from a time when the market was saturated with them- However, I don't doubt that its deceptively generic appearance made its unusually dark and thought-provoking story have more impact. You can carry two guns, three types of grenades, and order your squadmates around. Standard stuff, right? Well, things start to break down. Eventually, you will question your role as a player- and even the loading screen tips will call you out on the proceedings.

If you are familiar with the book Heart of Darkness or the film Apocalypse Now, you might have some idea of what to expect from The Line. Though I would argue the reality is actually worse.

The sandstorm to end them all has descended upon the city of Dubai and buried it alive. An American infantry division, the "Damned" 33rd, was diverted from Afghanistan to try and assist with evacuation efforts, which failed spectacularly. They refused the order to withdraw, and that was the last anyone heard of them for six months, and then- a cryptic call for assistance from the 33rd's leader, Colonel John Konrad.

You take the role of Captain Martin Walker, Delta Force. You and two of your subordinates have been sent in to Dubai to ascertain wether there are any survivors. Get in, make contact, get out, radio back. It should have been simple. 

The Line is an admittedly heavy-handed, but jarringly and I would say necessarily vicious deconstruction of military shooters and of wanting to be a hero by way of shooting a bunch of people. Depending on viewer interpretation, its also going after American military interventionism, acting on one's own impetus without sufficient information, and the very concept of war itself. It's as much psychological horror as military shooter, unsurprising given that one of its co-writers worked on the F.E.A.R. games. The enemies in The Line are not "insurgents" or "terrorists". Remember when the enemies in shooters were demons, invading aliens, hostile robots, zombies, nazis? Things that were ok to hate and justifiable to kill based on their cruelty and murderous actions? Remember when your targets in these games started being Arabs, Africans or Russians, instead? What if your enemies were just desperate survivors?

What if your enemies were your own people?

Dubai has descended into barbarism. There are no heroes here. Mistakes are made, and left unaccounted for. The smart thing to do would have been to run like hell. But you can't just leave it alone, can you? No, that's not what a hero would do, is it?

As a fan of 90s-style, Doom-like types of shooters, I have heard that the Line has appeal for that demographic, and does for me, for its apparent ripping into military shooters and their fans. But it even wants you to question that viewpoint. You might feel better about killing demons then people, but should you feel good about killing at all, in of itself? I've heard that the games Haze and Blacksite: Area 51 simiarly tried to deconstruct shooter violence, but their commercial failure led this aspect to go unnoticed. I've not played Haze, but Blacksite in particular was so mediocre in its gameplay and unsubtle in its writing that I actually completely failed to notice it was meant as a deconstruction, takes I read were also had about Haze.

The Line has coop and versus multiplayer modes, and though I have not partaken of either, I doubt it needed them. In particular, I have read that the multiplayer was farmed out to a different studio and some of the campaign's writers went on record as saying they were against the inclusion of multiplayer at all, as it went against the game's spirit and intended message, to quote lead writer Cory Davis, "rammed onto the disc like a cancerous growth." I'd be inclined to agree. They also objected to the inclusion of achivements, and the ensuing icons are mocking pictures of the developers mocking the obtainers of such. It is a clearer dileniation then is presented in many of the Call of Duty games, for example, which might have morally gray campaign stories that cause the player to ask some questions, while also having the completely and unapologetically violent multiplayer modes, by the same developers that gave us some of the most toxic reprobates in online gaming. Think about the type of person that prefers those games and wether they would for a moment question why they enjoy them. 

There are some that believe that The Line was intended to make you hate yourself for playing it. That the game hates you, and hates you for liking these games in general. I choose to believe it is not an assault, but a lesson. If you are comparitively sane, rational and possess a modicum of sympathy for your fellow apes, The Line asks you some difficult questions and merely wishes that you consider your answers. It does however, want you to question the idea of violence as an escape fantasy and how that cheapens war and what it does to its particpants, willing or otherwise. 

If you are someone as burnt on military shooters and what they represent on a moral level as I am, you should really play Spec Ops: The Line. I can only hope it was eye-opening for genuine fans of the genre. Much like the Bioshock games, it has important messages to give that I fear are lost on the greater public.

And no, it's not a game you get for the multiplayer aspect. I never tried it but I heard that multiplayer is lacking compared to other games. So what does that make this game's worth then? If I could give it one label, I'd call it a self-testing narative.

Many military games try to (mostly unsuccessfuly) emulate what it's like to be a shooter. This is usually done through combat, with the more realistic, gritier and harsher the game is, the generally perceive realism is usally greater. Spec Ops the Line goes with a route that most games forego, the morality aspect, how you as a human react when the entire situation falls apart and you succumb more and more to the stresses of the battle.

That's all nice to be said but let me give you a personal example, up towards the end of the game you are given a choice, I'll be vague about it as not to spoil but basically after suffering a terrible blow you have a choice that basically allows you to maintain what at that point is a small amount of your character's military professionalism or give in to the barbarism and rage at what has happened and hurt and kill "innocents". At that moment I knew I could probably find the more professional solution to that choice that would spare bloodshed, but I was so enraged and engrossed in the scenario that I had let my emotions make a snap call and did the other, morally disgusting choice. Afterwards I literally backed from the keyboard, running my hands over my head just thinking of what I was doing and if this was how I would react in real life.

Now full disclosure, I'm a soldier in real life so the effects this game had on me were mostly amplified. When I started the game, I sympathized with my character, wanting to help the people and accomplish the mission. But the further it progressed, the game, purposely might I add, made me feel worse and worse about what I was doing throughout the game. Even some of the loading screens take jabs at you while you're down with quotes like "Do you even remember why you're here," "Do you feel like a hero yet," or "It's all you're fault".

This game does the exact opposite of almost every other military themed game on the planet. Every other game, intentionally or not, glorifies combat and warfare by putting you into some super soldier and has you kill with your character displaying no outward emotions. This game, through both the combat (mostly the prolonged effect on your character versus the actual fight itself) and the choices you will make (which almost always inevitably lead to a still ♥♥♥♥♥♥ scenario), shows that war and the potential for everything to go awry is truly hell.

"Spec Ops is at its best when it's not trying to be CoD-lite"

Part of the problem with this game is that its filled with drawn-out, CoD-like firefight sequences. It works in those games because its popcorn entertainment, but for Spec Ops it not only feels like it was just added to create padding for the game, but it goes against the narrative nature of the game itself. For starters, it felt unrealistic that you were facing this many soldiers. I know battallions have hundreds of soldiers, but this is set months after the 33rd was deployed to a hostile area and survived a civil war within itself.

Also, unlike CoD, Spec Ops doesn't have a good checkpoint system, meaning if you die you may have to restart from afar. Checkpoints are based less on mission objectives and more on activating the next cutscene.

Biggest problem for me were the "supersoldier" elements of the game. You're an elite soldier, but you and your 2 other teammates are able to mow down trained soldiers like its nothing while taking an infinite # of bullets. There's this one cutscene in particular that was ridiculously OTT (you'll know it when you see it).

Voice acting is a mixed bag. The actual VAs like Nolan North are good, but most of the celebrity VAs like Christopher Reid, Bruce Boxleitner, and Jake Busey were mediocre at best, which sucks since they voice major characters in the game. Did like Omid Abtahi, even if he ironically sounded like a younger Nolan North.

Absolutely terrible music choice during some scenes, particularly the big revelation at the end.

Shooting mechanics are honestly a little mediocre because it plays like a typical cover shooter, meaning difficulty comes from being flanked than being outgunned. Also, your crosshair is hard to see during shooting. I will say I did like that they at least tried to put some enemy variety, but the new types of enemies you encounter (knife soldiers, juggernauts) not only feel borrowed from other games (MW2, Batman: Arkham City), but are also rarely encountered.

One thing I liked was how, if you choose to shoot from a cover without exposing yourself, Walker turns the backwards and shoots, limiting accuracy but protecting you. It was a nice touch.

Liked character animations for reloads.

Because of the limited ammo in the game, you will constantly have to take enemy weapons. There is an obvious commentary on encouraging players to kill to make the game easier (killing a wounded soldier is even labeled "execute" and will give you extra bullets in addition to providing a new gun), but it falters a bit since there are always plenty of dead bodies to take guns from.

Honestly, there are times where I genuinely believe that the game was supposed to be less of a straight-up shooter and more of a stealth game. You have the ability to equip silencers to your gun, for example, but there are only a few times where that is used. You also have the ability to do a crouch walk which silences you, but again its really not used for anything.

Definite CoD influences such as environmental triggers, exploding barrels, and juggernauts.

Spec Ops: The Line takes itself very seriously, making a point that it is DIFFERENT to other Hollywood type shooters, namely Call of Duty. I do agree with this, but at the same time, it contradicts itself.

The campaign of the story tests players real world morals, some scenes, like the part where you have to bomb civilians unknowingly with white phosphorous are unavoidable, but other scenes where Riggs asks you to kill him or after Lugo dies and you have the choice to gun down the civilians that murdered him actually effect the game and your outcome. The more degrading a human being you become, the more your uniform and injuries worsen, as well as you voice lines becoming more aggressive and your executions more brutal.

This is where Spec Ops succeeds, a portrayal of desperation or retribution is decided upon by choices the PLAYER ACTUALLY MAKES. But now we come to my one and only problem with Spec Ops: The Line. Although it portrays war and the acts of those participating, particularly members of the U.S Military, who this seems to be quite critical of, are quite realistic and break the social norm of FPS Games, Spec Ops holds traditions that most FPS games do, over the top fight scenes, an overwhelmed underdog rising through and intense chase scenes that would never take place. 

I believe that through certain choices the player makes, there should have been no way that Walker, Lugo and Adams, three members of Delta Force, massacred the entire 33rd Battallion, composed of about 3000 men. 

Despite the hypocritical acts on behalf of the devs, Spec Ops: The Line gives us an idea of the kinds of conversations we should be having about the way war should actually be portrayed in video games and other mediums.

Spec ops: The line is an incredible game. Not for its gameplay which is a quite generic for an FPS. What makes this game stand out as an incredible experience is its story. While you play an action hero badass with two also badass squad members the game questions your assumptions. Who is good who is evil nothing is for certain as the story twists and turns. The game is about war and war is hell.

There are a lot of military shooter games out there that do a great job of making you feel like a special forces soldier badass; they make you feel like Rambo and able to take on anything. What they don't do is hammer home the reality that this is war and war is inherently evil by its nature and even if you aren't a bad person yourself no one who experiences war comes back unchanged.

At the start of the game I felt like any other action hero from a shooter game (Roach, Snake, Pryce, Soap, Sarge, etc). However what The Line does (unlike most other shooters) makes you feel from the main character in way these other games don't. As the story unfolds you slowly feel yourself slipping further and further away from that heroic ideal we have in our minds of the country's elite soldiers and eventually find ourselves hating what we have become. Once the story is nearing its end that's all you can really think about, just let it end. Give these tortured characters some peace either via an evac chopper or a bullet to the brain.

If you are looking for another run of the mill military shooter, stick with Call of Duty and others of that genre because The Line falls short in terms of multiplayer. If you would like to experience a work of art that is graphically beautiful and demonstrates the effects of war on the human soul then give this one a try.

I finished the game earlier today and I have to say that the ending(s) - at least for me, storyline is subjective - made the experience worth it. This is a game that really makes you think and has a very powerful message, all while managing to avert the cliche'd, "happily ever after" style ending that too many shooters these days have. If it weren't for the fact that changing whether or not you "recommend" the game to other people resets the helpful and funny count, I would say that I recommend Spec Ops: The Line. However, I also feel after re-reading my original review that it still has merit in regards to the unfortunate control issues and less-than-optimal key mapping, so I will leave it in.

---

ORIGINAL REVIEW:

At first glance, don't be fooled by the negative review. This is a game with a great storyline which plays with your emotions. It's a game where the further into it you get, the more you will feel the weight of your actions as your player character, Walker, gets railroaded into a horrible situation that has harrowing consequences. That alone makes it [i]ALMOST[/i] worth playing.

However, this is a thumbs down not for the story, but instead for the gameplay.

Spec Ops: The Line will pit you against an overwhelming number of enemies that, on the hardest difficulty is TOO frigging hard. It will make you restart from your checkpoint over and over again as you die from poorly-designed, dated game mechanics that feel like utter BS. Why play on hard though? Well, you need to play on hard to unlock the final 4th difficulty, which I can't even begin to imagine would be possible playing through. I like to think that I'm a mild-mannered kind of guy who can put up with frustrating games, but there have been countless times playing this where I've gritted my teeth and wanted to throw my monitor out the window. Here's why.

First of all, the controls are garbage. Half the keys have more than one action mapped to them, meaning that in trying to do one thing, you will often do something you don't want to and it will cost you your life and make you start over from a checkpoint that you passed [i]minutes[/i] ago. For instance, reload (default "R") is also used to pick up weapons, spacebar is used for both dashing AND moving into cover as well as "executing" fallen enemies, and shift is a contextual action button that is used mainly for vaulting AND melee attacks. Moving into (and especially out of) cover doesn't feel organic, and most likely any failure of proper input will leave you vulnerable for a crucial second or two that will let your enemies gun you down. All of the actions that share a keybind cannot be individually bound, so in the end it really doesn't matter if you change the keys or not.

Shooting from cover is difficult at best and impossible at worst. Aiming from cover leaves you exposed, so most of the time you have to take out a couple of enemies before hiding behind cover again to regenerate your health. Not all cover protects you equally, and you can often still be sniped pretty easily by enemies on the high ground unless you're totally concealed. At the same time, you can have a heavy machine gun pinning you down while being flanked on multiple sides, and god forbid they decide to throw a grenade at you to flush you out. Grenades will insta-kill you too, at least on hard difficulty, forcing you to run out of the way or die without compromise. Also, good luck running from one source of cover to another and successfully preventing yourself from being shot to death.

The "heavy" enemies that show up in riot armor are absolutely insane. They take a lot of bullets to put down, and once they take aim at you it's basically a death sentence. Unless, of course, you can blind them temporarily with a grenade which you probably don't have at the moment, and proceed to unload an entire magazine into them from whatever gun you're using and switch guns to do it again. That is provided, of course, you have ammo, which is scarce.

You have two squadmates throughout the whole game, whose AI is at least as competent as the AI enemies. You can command them to attack specific targets, like rooftop snipers, to take some heat off of you. However, if they both end up going down and they're not behind cover, there is little chance of reviving them before they bleed out or you get gunned down since you're completely vulnerable in the few seconds that it takes to get them back up. Luckily, you can command them to fairly reliably res each other, but only if one of them is still in the fight.

All of these problems combined make Spec Ops: The Line less than enjoyable. Between every major firefight, there's a shred of story that gives you a feeling of what's happening, piece by piece. But when every firefight is the same formula with increasingly more difficult enemies, it feels hardly worth the effort. I still hope to beat this game to at least see the ending, but even that just seems too darn hard. On that basis, I can't recommend this game in good conscience unless you don't mind playing on an easier difficulty. Even then, I can't say how much easier it will even be.

TL;DR: A game that should be fun is rendered nearly impossible due to BS mechanics and gameplay elements.

It's pretty obvious why this game never became a commercial success and why it will never see a sequel. It's an incredibly buggy, clunky, and mechanically abhorrent third person shooter with the moral depth of a kiddie pool.

The game is completely broken. It shouldn't even qualify as a beta, much less a full release. You will experience a bug pretty much every mission, whether it be spontaneously dying, your squadron getting stuck, resulting in you having to restart at a checkpoint, or dying because of the unbelievably buggy cover system. Enemies have horrible ragdoll effects that look incredibly stupid and can be distracting and annoying at times. I quit at Chapter 11 because there was a part of the game that was so incredibly buggy that I was unable to progress through the game.

I've played my share of games with awful controls, but this one takes the cake. Every single important control is bound to your SPACEBAR. There is no way to change this, because they all fall under one key in the controls. Sprinting, interacting, and getting to cover are all under space, so you're going to find yourself sprinting when you want to take cover, leaving cover when you want to swap positions, taking cover when you want to move forward, and a whole other wild assortments of the game just not doing what you want it do.

The story of the game is what I want to address most, because it's by far the aspect of the game that was most acclaimed as well as the aspect of the game that was the most lacking. While it does have moments that seem to be politically potent, they're few and far between, flat, and insignificant. Any other moment of the game that lacks this potency just feels like thoughtless fodder (kill this guy ... or kill this guy?) that the player will blow through. The story as a whole is a confusing slop that is incredibly difficult to rationalize. The characters seem to lack personality and seem to have virtually no real motivations behind their actions, making it impossible for this game to have any kind of emotional appeal.

Overall, if you're looking for an emotionally deep military shooter, look elsewhere. If you're looking for a style of game similar to this that isn't complete garbage, try Max Payne or Deux Ex.

I think Spec Ops Can be summed up in one moment that happened to me in the game.
I was behind cover, listening to two soldiers talk about gum and sincerely sounding like friends, sharing details about their life back home compared to Dubai. I tried to let them pass without killing them, but they saw me and sent off the alarm, getting me killed. So when I respawned, I had to execute them both silently. It wasn't a choice I wanted to make, but I had to do it. That's essentially the game in a nutshell. 
This isn't the average shooter where you play as a soldier holding two AR-15's,  bare chest free with a bald eagle on your shoulder while screaming "'MERICA!". You don't kill the stock bad guy.png and watch them neatly dissapear. They shout for help to each other, don't die instantly all the time and need you to execute them. This is a game where you can see yourself slowly losing your humanity along with your sanity with every innocent life that is lost with the choices you have to make. 
In terms of story, I would reccomend it on that alone, considering it's actually smart and subtle, making you think about choices that need to be made in harsh situations and their ramifications. The characters are actually relatable, and you do grow close to them and can see them slowly cracking under the pressure of their situation. The premise of explored the destroyed city of Dubai is brilliant, and pulled off fantastically. So in terms of the story, it's absolutely quality and is what seperates the game from others like it.
In terms of gameplay, thats where the game starts to show its age slightly. The act of cover is largely well done, but running to cover to cover can sometimes awkward, and leave you standing in front of the aforementioned cover sadly as the bullets rain down on you. However, this doesn't pull the game down, it's just a minor issue. On the whole, the guns are satisfying to use  and have the appropriate punch to them. Ammo is sparse, and had me foraging more than once. However, it makes it all the better when you kill 6 people with only half a clip of a rifle.  The challenge is solid enough, and forces you to actually think instead of running at them screaming with a shotgun. 
The graphics, when on ultra at least, makes the game look great, and I never thought that something looked poor in terms of quality. However, occasionally the cutscenes with cut to 30fps prerendered, which actually looked worse than the rest of the game. That's the only way you could really tell the game was from 2012. 
The only real issue I had with the campaign was that it only took me 4 hours to finish, but I can't complain that much, considering that those four hours were of such a high quality in terms of storytelling. 
All in all, Spec Ops had me exploding someones head with the lovely 44. Magnum, feeling great for a moment, then really guilty at what I had done before justifying it by saying that "it had to be done". 
10/10 would question what morality is worth again.

[b]Yeah, this one’s going to be spoiler-y.[/b]

Everyone’s favourite game of 2012, [i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i] dangerously straddles the line between not getting a recommendation due to being an admittedly bad game by all standards of design and variation. The saving grace, which has been discussed countless times, is the gut-wrenching 180 that the narrative takes directly into [i]Apocalypse Now[/i] Territory. The story takes place in Dubai, jewel of the United Arab Emirates and now a horrifying wasteland having been all but wiped off the map by a sandstorm of biblical proportions. We play as Martin Walker (Nolan North, doing the most obviously ‘Nolan North’ of his many voices), captain of a small squad of Delta Force soldiers on a mission to confirm the presence of survivors in Dubai, either civilian or members of the 33rd Infantry Battalion, led by Colonel John Konrad (yes it’s a [i]Heart of Darkness[/i] parallel, we get it), who Walker furiously jerks off in the introductory cinematic. Twists and turns ensue, and Delta Force ends up travelling throughout the city, growing more and more rife with infighting and unease as a variety of horrors turn them from a plucky band of would-be heroes into a traumatised pack of murderers. That’s one thing [i]Spec Ops[/i] does really well - deconstructing the concept of heroes and villains by setting up a proper evil maniac only to have him either die unceremoniously with no payoff or turn out to have not been the antagonist you expect, and even come to desire by the end. The game knows having a clear moral bad guy makes things more straightforward, and plays with this and many other audience expectations throughout the trail of guts and gore that is its story.

Like everybody else who first played [i]Spec Ops[/i] more than a week after release, I went in expecting to witness some pretty horrific stuff, but what I didn’t expect was just how introspective it gets. I went in with prior knowledge of the infamous ‘white phosphorous’ debacle, but the big fuss led me to expect that to be the worst of it, which made it even more uncomfortable when it wasn’t by a long shot. White phosphorous - which was a fake moral choice at best (you can’t progress without using it) - looks tame compared to later setpieces which give you an actual choice over whether or not to commit atrocities, but only after forcing you into a position where sometimes gunning down dozens of civilians or taking your loaded revolver and leaving a dying soldier to burn alive don’t seem like terrible ideas. It plays with your emotions, invokes feelings of rage and hate, and then makes you choose without giving those feelings time to wear off. One of the most effective devices is the way choices matter, which is to say that strictly speaking, they don’t. All of [i]Spec Ops[/i]’ multiple endings are left open right up until the end. Whether you choose to do awful, terrible things only affects your own perception of yourself as a player and Walker as a character - after the WP incident early on, it stops feeling like the characters in [i]Spec Ops[/i] are turning Walker into a creature more monster than man and starts feeling like [i]Spec Ops[/i] is turning you, the player into that creature.

It’s not ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fun. And if [i]Spec Ops[/i] was fun, it would totally undermine the message, which is not only that war is bad and makes good people into bad people, but also that everything you (and Walker) do, is pointless. I've played this out of the box on the hardest difficulty available (the true hardest difficulty level is locked behind a completion requirement which I have not played).

The good:

- Themes, story and story-gameplay integration.
- Environment design. One moment you're in gritty desert, the next you're in ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fairyland.
- Sound and music.
- Cool set piece events.
- General difficulty.
- Decent gunplay.
- Graphics.
- Competent cover mechanics. Novel sand mechanics, grenade mechanics, stealth.
- Generally helpful AI.

The bad:

- Controls are odd and might need a rebinding out of the box (and you must bind EVERY action). Even then, they are janky. It comes down to two controls with multiple actions assigned to them: Melee and vaulting over obstacles are one button, sprint and enter/leave cover are both covered by another button. I've been killed by this weird scheme working against my common sense. You'll notice this when there's a downed enemy next to a vaultable barrier, you will likely perform the action you didn't want to do and die because of it.
- Weapon auto-swaps when it completely runs out of ammo. There are so many problems I have with this specific gunplay mechanic as you then have to swap to your empty gun in order to trade it with a weapon on the ground. This is more of a problem than you'd think it should be.
- Friendly AI can be dumb as bricks. Yes, you can order them to do stuff... But more than likely one of them is going to go down and you won't be able to help the AI partner because you'll die in the process. You can send your other AI partner to help pick up the other person before their death timer ends... Which can sometimes lead to both AIs falling. The AI going down will often lead to mission failure as they have to survive. This problem is only prevailent in a couple of sections.
- Some firefights are puzzle-ish in nature, meaning there is one and only one optimal completetion route. Other times, the "obvious" route is a trap (there's one sniping section of the game which is guilty of this). Sometimes the game will give you a not-so-subtle weapon pickup as a hint. As a result, you'll likely die dozens of times before you realize that you are supposed to not push forward... or that you need to push forward... or that you need to aim somewhere else first... et cetera.
- Environmental "traps" where you would expect to be able to vault over an obstacle but you weren't in the exact positioning between two non-vaultable things... Or you are not able to vault over some objectes that you'd normally think you'd be able to.
- Over reliance on cover system and hide 'n' regen gameplay.
- Minor graphical glitches.
- The few novel mechanics are only used on few occasions. Grenades being the exception... Though you'll mostly be using frag grenades.
- Obnoxious "do you want to lower the difficulty?" dialogue that appears after you've died several times in an area.

A third-person cover shooter. Nice to see a game that pushes the boundaries a bit in terms of the usual copy and paste storylines.

The game is worth playing if you haven't come across any spoilers and it's on sale, otherwise I wouldn't really bother.

The first half of Spec Ops: The Line is indistinguishable from any generic shooter that came out in the past decade or so, complete with mediocre cover based shooting mechanics and generic protagonists who I couldn't remember their names despite actually trying while playing the game.
I kept on playing because I heard so much praise for this game's narrative, and I was not disappointed. The narrative starts to escalate and the characters suddenly drop their generic soldier dude attitudes and start sounding like people with conflicts and emotions (and I clearly remembered their names by now). 

The game has plenty of cutscenes that drive on the story, but the things I liked seeing the most were the subtle changes in attidute. For example, the game has a mechanic that allows you to pick targets for squamates to kill. At the begining of the game when you issue an order your character says something like "Lugo, take out that sniper" in a very straightforward professional voice. In the later stages of the game when issuing that same command your character yells with seething hatred "Lugo! I want that f**ker DEAD!".

Your faces gets charred with dust, dirt and wounds. Your cloths are torn to shreds. The battle chatter between you and your squadmates (Reloading ammo, enemy down, etc) starts to sound more tired, out of breath and desperate. Even the loading screens, which up until then showed generic hints like 'this weapon has this type of secondary fire', starts showing messages like 'This is all your fault', or 'Do you feel like a hero yet?', further pushing the escalating narrative.

It's these narrative subtleties that I enjoyed the most with the game. The ending is sort of predictable, but still satisfying. The road to the ending, with the game escalating more and more and the uncomfortable feeling you start having in the back of your head was much more interesting.

In my opinion, this game stands out purely for it's narrative. The gameplay is just tolerable, don't expect any amazing shooting experience. Try to push beyond the second half of the game and you'll see the clear difference between this game and others of its genre.

This is a nice 3rd person cover based shooter

Don't expect a revelation tho. This game is lauded online so often, it's really overhyped.

First, the gameplay mechanics. While shooting is pretty standard, it has a weird control sheme, that nonetheless other 3rd person shooters have too far too often. there's no way to (just) run, no way to jump freely.. if you hold spacebar to run, you automatically get in a cover approaching one.
while that sounds like it was great, often it's more of a hindrance than a help, because the game steers you towards the cover. Want to run down a hallway with some cover spots left and right? well the game will steer you towards them instead of letting you run straight. More than once this killed me in a combat situation as instead of running away from the dangerous spot (around the next corner, away from a grenade etc), he ran towards the cover and stopped.
Also, Sometimes it doesn't react right when you hit it because you recoil from a shot or something, so you tap the spacebar, nothing happens, you let go and hold it again. the game reacts to that in going into sprint for a second and then you leisurly jog instead of run, despite holing down space. Also the reason for at least two deaths.
Both of those are probably because it's a console port. I dunno, but I assume.

The checkpoints are rather crudely selected, and some times they're location based, so you run to a point, get shot down.. and then it loads at that point with all enemies gone. It also doesn't save dropped guns, so if you temporarily changed your weapons, rn in a checkpoint, picked your main weapon up again and then died, upon reload your weapon is gone.

Oh and at times the difficulty is really cheaply done. One enemy class, the heavies, are bullet sponges. Sure, heavy enemies should take more damage, but you can empty a clip into them, lob two frag grenades right at their feet and they're still standing. Or you shoot their face plate so much it breaks, and then you shoot half a clip right into their uncovered face and they still carry on. 

Oh and by the way, the weapons of the enemies vanish. Running out of ammo with your fav weapon, but you just killed a bunch of guys holding it? the game gives you a big nice f you, because once the area is clear and you go from guy to guy, there's just one dropped weapon for every 5th enemy body. I dunno if the game just has an upper limit of guns on the ground or despawns them after a while but it's infuriating.

Then the story. The story is great, all in all. Has some nice twists and things aren't always how they seem.
But.. it forces your hand sometimes, forcing you to do stuff you don't want to do and then laying down the blame for it.
One example, which was not the only one but the one that pissed me off so much that I nearly ragequitted..
(midgame spoiler) [spoiler]At one point you are above a large number of enemies. There's a white phosphorus mortar station right there, and the game has you say "you have to" while one of your budies is against it. I didnt want to use it because it's f*cking white phosphorous. So instead I tried just shooting the guys. I was dead in seconds. Fair enough, it's probably not the best to go gun ho on dozens of enemies, so I tried again, off by the side. There was a rope anchor going down but no rope, that only appears magically after you did what the game forces you to do, but to that later.
So I try from cover, all is going well, I shoot a sniper.. and a second later another one runs to the same spot. I shoot it again and another one comes. Kept that up quite a while and the game kept spawning enemies - turns out it does spawn endless enemy waves if you do not use phosphorous. Thanks game.
So I use the mortar.. It shoots up a camera that slowly descends, or at least it should, but in camera view, it always stays at the same height. you select targets and your guy on the mortar shoots them. The last target was on a bridge and below were many people without guns (you only see a 'ghost image' through the mortar camera). I assumed those were prisoners, so I didn't shoot the last target. I figured I had just found an RPG and could take out the last target with it. There was no way to back out of the camera view, and when the camera "fell to the ground" I instantly died.

So there was no way at all to not torch those..[/spoiler] and later the game decides to lay down heavy blame on you for it.
As far as I understand it, this was the scene people like to rave about, about how good a job this game does to convey how horrible war is. I just felt cheated/mocked by the game.

Spec Ops: The Line is a war story. Not in the "come listen to this old war story of mine, kids" way, but rather in the "this is the reason why I have PTSD" kind of way. Throughout the game it will assault your sense of morality, where hesitation leads to death and hard choices are common place whether you like it or not. Realities of war, as the phrase goes. The story is brilliant; both in how it reflects war by making the characters completely alone, going from conflict to conflict, trying to survive and be as moral as they can be; and how it critiques gaming and the genre itself by emphasising the shaky moral ground of killing countless of people as well as how tiring and confusing combat can be.

I can't stress this enough, as a story this game is truly great to the point where you SHOULD play it, especially if you've played other shooters.

With that said, however, it is still a game with mechanics, and some of them are... rough. The game has been around for a while and that might be the reason, but I truly didn't like the shooting in this game. It's cover-based (which has it's own set of problems, with awkward un-sticking being the worst of them) but the real issue is that your crosshair doesn't appear if you don't aim, and aiming takes you out of cover where you will be riddled with bullets. This wouldn't be so bad, except that being hit affects your aim, making shooting an absolute chore. With the awkward cover system as well, nothing really feels great to operate, with a lot of "fighting the game mechanics" going on. [spoiler]Add to that the Heavy enemy type, which is both unrealistic and frustrating to play against...[/spoiler] You simply get a game that can be pretty awkward to play, making at least me drop it to the easiest difficulty at the last stage because I had gotten so sick of the whole thing.

Spec Ops: The Line is a difficult game to critique, succeeding in being a third person shooter where I loved everything but the third person shooting. At the same time, a lot of the flaws can, and maybe should, be excused by the fact that this is not a game that should feel good to play - it's not supposed to be enjoyable, and a lot of the developers' decisions that I would criticise can also be seen as part of what makes the narrative so great. 

No matter what, this game should be experienced in some way. It's a gaming classic that should be remembered for a long, long time.

[u]An Overview[/u]

Six months prior to the game's events, the worst series of sandstorms in recorded history began across Dubai. The city's politicians and wealthy elite downplayed the situation before evacuating secretly, leaving countless Emiratis and foreign migrant workers behind. Colonel John Konrad, the decorated but PTSD-troubled commander of the "Damned 33rd" Infantry Battalion of the United States Army, was returning home with his unit from Afghanistan when the storms struck. Konrad volunteered the 33rd to help relief efforts, defying orders by the Army to abandon the city and its refugees and deserting with the entire battalion. The storms intensified and a massive storm wall engulfed Dubai, disrupting surveillance, air travel, and all but the strongest of radio broadcasts. Struggling to maintain order amid 80 mph (128 kmh) winds, riots, and dwindling resources, the 33rd declared martial law and began committing atrocities on the civilian population. Aggrieved by this, some members of the 33rd staged a coup d’etat against Konrad but failed and were exiled. The CIA then sent in a black ops unit to investigate, and as part of their plan organized the locals into insurgents to attack the 33rd, eventually resulting in a ceasefire. The last communication from Dubai stated that the 33rd was attempting to lead a caravan out of the city. The caravan never arrived, and soon afterward, the United Arab Emirates declared Dubai a no-man's-land. All travel to the city was barred, the 33rd was publicly disavowed for treason, and no further news left the city.

Two weeks before the start of the story, a looped radio signal finally penetrated the storm wall. Its message was brief: "This is Colonel John Konrad, United States Army. Attempted evacuation of Dubai ended in complete failure. Death toll... too many." The United States military decides to covertly send in an elite three-man Delta Force team to carry out reconnaissance, captained by Martin Walker, who served alongside Konrad in Afghanistan and views him as a hero. Walker, First Lieutenant Alphanso Adams, and Staff Sergeant John Lugo, are ordered to confirm the presence of any survivors, then immediately radio for extraction.

White phosphorus is a material made from a common allotrope of the chemical element phosphorus that is used in smoke, tracer, illumination, and incendiary munitions. Other common names include WP and the slang term "Willie Pete" or "Willie Peter" derived from William Peter, the World War II phonetic alphabet for "WP", which is dated from its use in World War II and Vietnam War and is still sometimes used in military jargon. As an incendiary weapon, white phosphorus is pyrophoric (self-igniting), burns fiercely and can ignite cloth, fuel, ammunition, and other combustibles.

In addition to its offensive capabilities, white phosphorus is a highly efficient smoke-producing agent, which burns quickly and produces an immediate blanket of smoke. As a result, smoke-producing white phosphorus munitions are very common, particularly as smoke grenades for infantry, loaded in grenade launchers on tanks and other armored vehicles, as part of the ammunition allotment for artillery or mortars and as payload of incendiary cluster bombs. These create smoke screens to mask from the enemy movement, position, infrared signatures, or the origin of fire.


White phosphorus can cause injuries and death in three ways: by burning deep into tissue, by being inhaled as a smoke, and by being ingested. Extensive exposure by burning and ingestion may result in death.


Injuries from white phosphorus:

Incandescent particles of WP cast off by a WP weapon's initial explosion can produce extensive, deep second and third degree burns. One reason why this occurs is the tendency of the element to stick to the skin. Phosphorus burns carry a greater risk of mortality than other forms of burns due to the absorption of phosphorus into the body through the burned area, resulting in liver, heart and kidney damage, and in some cases multiple organ failure.[90] These weapons are particularly dangerous to exposed people because white phosphorus continues to burn unless deprived of oxygen or until it is completely consumed. In some cases, burns are limited to areas of exposed skin because the smaller WP particles do not burn completely through personal clothing before being consumed.

Smoke inhalation:

Burning white phosphorus produces a hot, dense, white smoke consisting mostly of phosphorus pentoxide. Exposure to heavy smoke concentrations of any kind for an extended period (particularly if near the source of emission) has the potential to cause illness or death. White phosphorus smoke irritates the eyes, mucous membranes of the nose, and respiratory tract in moderate concentrations, while higher concentrations can produce severe burns. The Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry has set an acute inhalation Minimum Risk Level (MRL) for white phosphorus smoke of 0.02 mg/m3, the same as fuel-oil fumes. By contrast, the chemical weapon mustard gas is 30 times more potent: 0.0007 mg/m3.[91] However, the agency states that the 1935 study used to determine the MRL was insufficient to accurately assess the health risk to humans[92]. No studies have investigated the lethal effects of inhalation of WP by humans[93], however a former US soldier has stated that breathing in smoke close to a shell caused the throat and lungs to blister until the victim suffocated, with the phosphorus continuing to burn them from the inside[94].

Oral ingestion:

The accepted lethal dose when white phosphorus is ingested orally is 1 mg per kg of body weight, although the ingestion of as little as 15 mg has resulted in death.[95] It may also cause liver, heart or kidney damage.[90] There are reports of individuals with a history of oral ingestion who have passed phosphorus-laden stool ("smoking stool syndrome").[95] Its extreme toxicity is due to the generation of free radicals, especially in the liver, where they accumulate and are not easily metabolized.

Fume inhalation:

Long term inhalation of derivative fumes causes a condition called phossy jaw or osteonecrosis of the jaw, which is a painful, debilitating and ultimately lethal condition that afflicted factory workers involved with the manufacture of matches that contained white phosphorus. The mechanism for necrosis is clot formation leading to bone ischaemia or infarction, leading to the putrid rotting of the bone of the lower jaw. For this reason, the Berne Convention (1906) was enacted to forbid the manufacture, sale or purchase of matches containing white phosphorus. This condition may also be caused by high doses of lead, cadmium and bisphosphonate based cancer drugs.

Spec Ops: The Line is a must-play experience of a lifetime. A narrative-driven third-person shooter that challenges the player on multiple fronts as a meta-commentary for the FPS genre, which is still relevant almost a decade later.
The game is absolutely dripping with details. It is enough to fill a book worth of subtleties and easy to miss aspects that could put the entire game in a new perspective. It is also packed with allegories and symbolism that can be talked about for hours. So much is stuffed in a relatively short story of only 6 hours, the game itself is very dense, short but also very (bitter)sweet. This game is without a doubt a masterpiece of storytelling. It is hard to tell why exactly the game's story is so excellent because spoiling this game would be a travesty to newcomers who need to experience it firsthand. Despite the condensed length of the story, this is a game that you can play repeatedly, as you will pick up on new details and new perspectives each time you play.

The story is the shining beacon of the game, but most other things are also up to standard as well. The music is full of classic war music from the Vietnam era and onwards, very classical and catchy tunes such as Deep Purple-Hush, and "Nowhere to Run" by Martha and the Vandellas.
The gameplay passed with flying colours, it is bloody and visceral as the topic of the game is supposed to be a meta-commentary on the horrific nature of war and of the FPS genre. It does a good job of portraying the depravity of man vs man conflict.

This is not a game you should play on a whim. This is a game that will stick with you for a very long time, without a doubt. It is a haunting and memorable experience, and the tragic/depressing tone of the game might turn some people off, but it is a line that I glad I crossed.

The whole story takes place in post apocalyptic Dubai, you play as Captain Martin Walker, who was sent with his Delta team for the recon mission. Straight after the prologue, player'll get a chance to know about the whole game plot - Colonel John Conrad is your main mission. 6 months ago he had a mission to evacuate people, disobeyed and instead of leaving the city, stayed there with his subdivision, trying to evacuate everyone on his own. Nobody ever knew what happened to Conrad next, until they got a week signal from him that now mission is officially failed. That's why you were sent with your Delta squad to Dubai - to literally figure out what the heck happened to Conrad and civilians. But after first meeting with Conrad's guys, Walker realize that it's not a rescue mission anymore, it's a combat mission now. And this is where the real game starts.

[h1] Overall Score: 9/10 [/h1] 
A compelling and powerful story with underwhelming and clunky gameplay mechanics.

[h1] Story [/h1]
The story plunges you in the heart of a war where the you constantly questions your actions and your purpose in this entire conflict. As the game progresses, the story develops the characters marvelously as it reflects the mental and physical toll the war took on the inhabitants and combatants alike. This goes hand in hand with how the story unfolds and affecting the decisions you make. There are no good choices here. Only bad or worse ones. 

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
The adaptation of 'player choice' is very well implemented. It is unlike the typical Mass Effect decision making process where a player selects a response amongst a bunch of options. Frequently, you are thrown decisions you need to make that you might not even be aware of. And of course, continuing your course of action (even unknowingly) is making a decision. Even more realistically, you have to decide what your options are. Sometimes, you think that there are only 2 options. A or B. There are usually more options which requires to think out of the box. E.g Option C - Not do anything at all.

Mechanics wise (movement and firing), it is clunky with many frustrating moments but it is not game breaking. It is definitely not ground breaking either. 

The game keeps you on your toes. Not only with the intense and emotional story, but with the pace of the game. You are constantly under threat and you rarely have any down time. Combat is not only well spread out, it also takes you through many different levels and scenarios that is very refreshing. Most shooters gets old or repetitive after a while, but not Spec Ops. 

[h1] Multiplayer [/h1]
PVP is dead but coop is plenty of fun and it is reasonably easy to find a buddy to team up with. I would think that PVP wouldn't fly anyway with the clunky mechanics which would only be more frustrating and obvious in multiplayer.

Spec Ops: The Line is a diamond in the rough: though it has many virtues, it doesn't enjoy a lot of name recognition or popularity, and that is a shame. On the surface, the game struggles to stand out from it's contemporaries, so it's easy to "judge it by it's cover." The gameplay is solid, but a little generic. The cover-based, 3rd-person combat works well, and comes with a simple mechanic for ordering your two squad-mates to prioritize targets. It's modern setting as American soldiers fighting in the middle east is arguably a bit TOO familiar (though this famliarity arguably serves a greater purpose). The artists do a wonderful job of contrasting a once opulent city with rapid chaos, destruction, and decay, though the graphics aren't technically amazing.

So why recommend it? Because beyond that, it is a profound and haunting experience. Spec Ops is a story rich 3rd-person action-HORROR. The choices and insights it presents will linger with you long after you exit the game. The downward spiral of events imbues what would otherwise be a generic experience with a message that keeps the player pushing forward to see what happens next.

Spec Ops is set apart by its story, and a POWERFUL story it is. Set in Dubai, a huge sandstorm has wrecked the city, and ravaged the populace. Of all the civilian and military aid originally sent to help, only Colonel John Konrad and "The Damned" 33rd Battalion remained through the worst of it, disobeying orders and deserting to do so. The 33rd promised to evacuate the city and get the refugees to safety beyond the Stormwall; the evacuation never came. You play as Captain Martin Walker of Delta Force, sent in with your team to figure out what went wrong. What you find is a situation that mutates from bad to horrifying the deeper into the city you go.

Beyond that isn't for me to say. You have to see the details--and the devil within them--for yourself.

Bottom line: If you like a dark, introspective NARRATIVE, or want to experience a subversion of the typical military shooter story, this game is worth buying. On that basis, I can't recommend it enough.

Spec Ops: The Line is a 3rd person shooter developed by Yager Development. It was released in 2012. I remember watching a review about how this game was better than most of the military shooters released at the time, so I was interested in playing this game for the longest time. I never got to play it at launch, and having just finished it, I am glad I didn't buy it at the time.

It is not a terrible game. Its functional, and thoroughly boring. There is nothing original about the gameplay. I understand that this is supposed to be a narrative driven game, but that does not prevent the game from being boring because of generic the gameplay. Gears of War is a much better cover shooter, and that came out years ago.

The game is built using Unreal 2 engine, and it handles a lot like Mass Effect. What this means is, the game does not have jump, and shooting involves diving behind cover and peaking out, and taking shots at enemies. Just about every single encounter turns into this. Like most console ports at the time, the controls are not optimized for the PC. Spacebar is used for both sprinting and taking cover. I did not enjoy this in Mass Effect, and I did not enjoy this in Spec Ops.

The gunplay is weak, and the weapon variety doesn't add much to the game because other than ammo capacity, all rifles felt the same. I understand that they cannot stray too much from reality because of the military setting, but that is no excuse of the weak weapon handling. The reason I did not like the weapon handling is probably because I am playing this game in 2017, and as a Battlefield player, I find most other shooters to be not as good as Battlefield 3 and Battlefield 4.

The game tries to incorporate squad play, but the system is not very fleshed out, and I felt it was awkward to use. There are few instances where giving orders to your squad is useful, but overall it is possible to play most of the game without ever giving any squad orders. The much talked about environment interaction is basically shooting some objects during combat to take out enemies, such as shooting a window to cause a sand slide etc. Do not expect Red Faction like environment destruction.

The main selling point  of this game was the story. I am playing this game 5 years after its release, and having played other games which attempted something similar, I could see the twist coming well in advance. Like Modern Warfare 2, there is one section in the game that this game is going to be remembered for, and I could see that coming as well. That said, the story itself is not too bad, but I think there are some instances where they left things to interpretation and this doesn't provide closure. Also, the suspension of disbelief required is a little too much for me. The main character and his two friends take on what looks like the entire US army, get thrown off buildings, survive a massive truck crash, and a chopper crash with no broken bones...

It is difficult to achieve the level of engagement they were asking for, because they want to tell a story that is grounded in reality, but the gameplay just does not lend itself to that.

I purchased this game as a part of a Humble Bundle for $1, and for that price, I am not disappointed, but I really would not recommend paying any money for this game because it has no replay value, and there are so many great games out there for cheap.

I got this game for free after voting in the Golden Joystick Awards in 2016. While I'm not particularly into third-person shooters, I quite enjoyed this gift.

PROS
+ The storyline is powerful with some thought-provoking and often harrowing twists. Major decisions are genuinely challenging.
+ Fantastic character development with strong voice acting.
+ Gameplay is good, and the AI provides a reasonable challenge.
+ The Dubai setting and architecture looks great, not to mention realistic. The sandstorm mechanic is done well also.
+ Great soundtrack, featuring a handful of 60s/70s classics.
+ Good variety of weapons, from firearms to grenades.

CONS
- I played through the story twice (on the lowest two difficulty levels) to get the multiple endings. After that, though, the game offers little replayability, and it sounds like multiplayer is to be avoided.
- Speaking of difficulty, I saw little difference between those first two settings when it came to AI strength.
- Cutscenes are rendered very poorly, which is a shame, considering the game itself looks graphically sharp.
- Movement can be clunky, as can the controls.
- If you're the squeamish sort, this is a game to be avoided.

The pros outweigh the cons for me. Even five years after its release, and even though it was a commercial failure, it is still a quality game for fans of TPS games or even just story-driven titles.

Spec Ops: The Line is a mediocre third person cover-based shooter and a spectacular story-driven game where choices matter. Instead of the general war glorification or simple "difficulty to overcome" style that almost all games these days have when dealing with war, the game focuses on the impact of war on the soldiers themselves, and how it can affect them on a mental level.

Pros
 - Amazing and emotional story.
 - Well made and designed levels.
 - Cover mechanic is fluid (doesn't require button press to go into cover).
 - Game still looks good, even if the graphics aren't 4K realism.

Cons
 - Mediocre gunplay, although definitely adequate.
 - There's a multiplayer mode... Why?!

If you like stories in games, buy it! If you don't care for stories in games, then this game may change chat.

Long:
I bought Spec Ops: The Line to satisfy my trigger finger.
Figured it would be a decent shooter. Didn't check any reviews or anything.
I received a solid action game, and a story that got under my skin.
Haven't played it in a long time, but it still rattles around deep in my mind. Coming up to the surface every now and then.
Reminding me of that which I have experienced in this beautiful, broken world.
The line between brave or fool, sane or not. Hero or monster.
The line; "Gentlemen, welcome to Dubai". Keeps repeting whenever I recall this game.

That should say plenty, soon to be 4 years later since finishing the story during something like 6 or 7 hours and I still carry it with me.

Not sure why I decided to review it now, I'm suppose to go to bed but now that I'm sitting here writing it seems impossible to leave without doing my best to convince you to buckle up and dive deep.

But I can't find the words. It's like wanting to tell someone an awesome secret but if you do it would be ruined.
This is not a game where you review the gameplay, or the music, or the voice acting, or the graphics.
They're all great, don't be intimidated, my point is that this is a game you feel.
It's masked as something so very familiar but somewhere along the way you realise it's something different.
Towards the end it beats you down and breaks something deep inside. 
The kind of game that leaves you sitting there with a 1000 yard stare, feeling empty.

So you venture out on the internet looking for others, for answers. Wanting confirmation that you had no choice.
You did what had to be done. Right?
If you're not feeling it by now, you will when you realise that there was always a choice.
"What do you mean you shot them? All you had to do was scare them off!"

Why do I feel shame for the actions I took in a game?
Does it scare me that they reflect what I would have done in real life?
That the decisions came so easily to me in the moment?
How rigid are my morals?

I willingly drank the kool-aid, to be the hero. I had no choice.
But after, I only see a monster. And question all my choices.

[h1] FUBAR: Fouled Up Beyond All Reality [/h1]

What may seem like a generic shooter involving mass genocide on the surface, is actually a well-paced strategic fight for survival that tests your morality. Spec Ops: The Line conveys the truth about why we engage ourselves in this genre of gaming and makes us ask what we would actually do if we were placed in this depressing narrative.

[h1] Story [/h1]

From the start, you are thrown in to explore the new barren geography of a decimated Dubai, where a massive sandstorm has swept through, killing most of the population and leaving survivors with little to no resources to live off of. The plot puts players in the boots of a special forces operative: Captain Walker, who leads his squad to recon for survivors, that is until they encounter a group of hostile refugees. They then get sucked in after receiving a distressed call from surviving American forces of a battalion that has stayed behind to look after the local populace. From there, the gravity of the situation forces you to betray your orders and embark through rough terrain to desperately find answers, even if you have to kill for it. As you traverse through the city with each horrific scene you witness, you notice your own character become progressively more unhinged and violent. The game, through all the characters, speaks to the player and reflect about your recent actions, as if you are Walker yourself. This direct engagement with the player makes it immersive and hooks you in. 

[h1] Presentation [/h1] 

For how much destruction is in the game, the visual presentation is very welcoming as you traverse through nicely textured ruins only to see the beautiful skyline all around you. Although the level design is quite linear, it’s nice to see that there is attention to every corner you pass. 

The environment drives the story, shapes the environment, and changes your approach in completing your mission. From being in a helicopter chase with a minigun chewing up pursuers to various sandstorms that will limit your view and mostly relying on the muzzle flashes from the enemy to know their location. There are buildings stuffed full of sand and if an armored machine gun turret were unlucky enough to be near one, the player could shoot out the glass and crush them, getting Walker out of tight spots. You are not always afforded this though, flanking and team command may be required, making reliable gameplay very important.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1] 

Although the controls take some getting used to, the gameplay is quite mediocre. You will find yourself hitting keys by accident that can expose you and both friendly and enemy AI will inexplicably do the same or sit in cover uselessly. Being cover based, it good to see that this is done flexibly, since you are able to swap cover, peek over and to the side, and destroy other cover. There are 18 weapons to use, most of which are balanced out and I found myself constantly changing weapons to try, considering none were really overpowered. Other gadgets like frag and stun grenades can also be used to help progress further. The types of enemies you encounter will affect your strategic approach. Heavy units may require you to fall back and use explosives while snipers can easily be taken out by your teammates when given the command. Again, this encourages players to take advantage of their surroundings. There is a difficulty setting that accommodates all player skill levels and playing on harder difficulties will demand critical thinking, putting more stress on you but making victory much more rewarding.

[h1] Realism [/h1] 

Some of the logic is flawed, whether its falling out of a building and surviving to having water tankers decimating a full city block. There is a lot of evidence that did not add up with the reality, but it is possible that a lot of what the player sees are the hallucinations that Walker experiences, but it’s never explicitly confirmed. There were some clichés and exaggerated behaviour amongst your team as though the game was trying too hard to generate emotion, but these were rare cases and won’t put you off once the bullets fly again.

[h1] Sound [/h1] 

The sound was invigorating and helped to make up for the gunplay. From a slow breeze walking through a deserted highway and metal cranking from billboards to crisp gunfire flying overhead with a slice of screaming carnage. There are strong metal tracks while also some soft moments where appropriate. The voice acting feels authentic to the situation and gets tense, especially when your team shouts aggressively between a volley of gunfire. Nolan North does an exceptional job in his lines as Walker who sounds real and emotional in all aspects.

[h1] Multiplayer/Co-op [/h1] 

I had only managed to play a few games of both multiplayer and co-op, but I felt I did not miss out on it much. It uses conventions already seen in games like Call of Duty and Counter Strike and there are only a handful of players still playing. That is not to say it is unplayable, but it lacks in innovation leaving players with no motive to continue when there are so many other shooters that do multiplayer much better. Multiplayer involves your standard level progression system which unlocks new weapons and cosmetics and the game modes are heavily inspired from existing shooters, establishing a sense of “I’ll give it a go” to experienced shooters and not "Woah, what's this?". Co-op has you team up with another friend and completing missions that consist of going from point A to B fighting off hordes of enemies much like Left 4 Dead. 

[h1] Longevity [/h1] 

There was never one point that I was not invested in the single-player. I finished the campaign in one play through, since I was so eager to uncover what happened as well as the future complications that came with it. The ending left me thinking afterwards about what soldiers really look for in a mission. That being said, it was also confusing about what actually happened and I think it was wrong to not provide a clear explanation of what was real and not. There are collectibles and intel that help fill some of the holes about the story as well as character history. This, along with the achievements will encourage a second or third playthrough. 

[h1] Verdict [/h1] 

Spec Ops: The Line’s greatest values are its story and presentation. While the controls had a frustratingly unusual layout to get used to, coming to grips and developing experience makes you more of an effective player, giving off a sense that you are really a special operative who needs to take tactical consideration, which the dev’s took care in the level design. As I usually recommend with older games, wait for this to go on sale for about 5 to 10 dollars, especially if you want to host games with your friends. Considering the current online population, I’d recommend this to anyone looking for a single-player decent shooter that, although involves violent gameplay, addresses the repercussions of war which is a fresh take from what we are so used to. Mainly because it was not a sales success, Yager development are not going to make a sequel, making this the second time the series has been put on halt, after the original games that started from 1998 to 2002. I think it is important however that this game is remembered for how it portrays violence which future games should consider and if done correctly, can drive a really beautiful and interesting narrative.

First off: Sorry this review is so long, but I don’t give negative ratings let alone reviews normally. So when I do, I feel like I really need to explain myself. Plus in this case I’m mostly trying to get other people to enjoy this more than I did, because of the high expectations that were set to me by basically everyone else, and I feel like I had to share my experience I had with this game.

TL;DR: Decent story ruined by sloppy gameplay.

So, Spec Ops: The Line, a game that was so highly praised to me by many. With the absurd amount of positive reviews when I bought it and people praising the story on Bioshock-levels, I just had to try it… but man was I disappointed. So first of all let me say this, I don’t hate the game or anything. I’m just trying to lower your expectations, so the same thing doesn’t happen to you IF you decide to buy it. So basically, I’m going to focus heavily on the negative stuff from the game.
Another thing I want to mention is that this was my first true cover based shooter I played, so it could be that some claims I make are general practice among these games.

Now the thing I hated most playing this game was the horrible input layout. Almost every action you do during the game comes from one of two buttons. When only one button is used to sprint, take cover, heal and drop, you’re just asking for trouble. Of course, this can be tolerable in lower difficulties, but if you’re like me and you like to replay some games or hunt for achievements these tiny cracks in the game design can truly ruin the total experience. The most frustrating part may even be just thinking who came up with this design and what superior approved this, thinking this was a good idea? As a game that seems to take pride in its multiple difficulty modes and replayability, make sure the game is still enjoyable at that point. I’m all for challenging gameplay and testing myself. I’m also a pretty patient guy and don’t really get frustrated if I die a lot… if it’s MY fault! But when you die half of the time because 1 button does over 3 actions and it just happens to choose the one you didn’t want, it can get pretty frustrating.
The sprint also is a horrible feature. Once you start going, you basically lose all control. So you better know the right direction to go beforehand, because there’s no way to swiftly change direction when you’re going. In a game where all these features seem critical to the gameplay, I think this is a total failure in the design.

Also the game has times where cooperation with your comrades seems preferable and when an enemy is somewhere unreachable, Lugo just snipes him and this feels pretty satisfactory. BUT whenever an enemy isn’t somewhere unreachable, most of the times your companions just run straight towards that target like they’re trying to melee him. When you play on lower difficulties this isn’t that big of a deal, but when you’re on the highest difficulty and you die by just sticking your head out for less than a second, every action taken is pretty crucial. You would think in this case to just let your partners take out some more enemies while you stay safe under cover, but since the AI is so dense, you’re better off doing all the work yourself. But I guess that’s what to be expected in the first place, it’s just that your AI companions often make things way harder than they actually are. If you actually reach them to heal, the ‘heal’-button is the same as every other action you take so maybe you’re trying to take cover before healing them… NOPE, you heal them and switch positions for the cinematic heal so you end up in plain sight.
And as common practice with AI, they made sure that they’re as much in your way as possible. You’re trying to aim for that sneaky headshot? Let me just stand right in your line of fire and eat some bullets while I’m in plain sight. Oh, you’re trying to run from that grenade? Let me just block the only way out. Most of these things could technically be avoided if you didn’t group up, which is common knowledge even in real life practices. But you can’t do that, because when you go too far away, your teammates just start running in plain sight and seem to forget they’re under fire. So you need to stay as far back as possible at all times and steadily take out enemy by enemy, even if this means you’re grouped up and a single grenade can ruin your day.

Some other things that I kind of missed or noticed in the game: [olist]
[*]	The ability to turn corners while in cover. Instead of getting out of cover, eating some bullets, derpingly turning the corner and get back into cover as quickly as you can. I feel like I was able to do this once or at a specific place during one of my earlier runs, but I didn’t notice anything like this in my last run. 
[*]	You only have 2 types of cover, high or low and your stance is the same in every low one and every high one. But there are some low covers that are lower than others, so your head sticks out a bit or so and you get one-shotted by an enemy while thinking you're under cover. At these times the only thing I can think of is: “Why can’t you just keep your head a bit lower?”
[*]	The morals of Adams and Lugo also seem to be switching during the game. But this I can live with, since a person’s mind and moral isn’t that straightforward as often shown in games or movies.
[*]	Also, during the game Adams gets shot in the leg and refuses to take morphine because he wants to keep his head clean, but whenever they’re downed and you need to heal them, they happily take a shot. Maybe not morphine, but I just thought it was funny.

[/olist] On the other hand, the story is decent… I do have to say that about it. The story isn’t bad, but it’s also way too overpraised in my opinion. It’s not your conventional, everyday story where the heroes save the day. It tries to depict the horror of war and the psychological effect this has. Now I say “tries”, because, this can just be me and I don’t fully get it (very possible), but it just felt too forced to me. The story basically consists of a series of bad choices that just pile up and you have to live with the consequences. As far as a game goes, there really aren’t any choices you make that influence the game in anyway (except for at the ending itself, but I’ll avoid talking about that part). BUT, I feel like this is one of the genius parts in the story itself. Just because you constantly try to make the right decisions and have the best of intentions, does not equal a good outcome. (THIS PART MAY CONTAIN LIGHT SPOILERS) [spoiler] But then the game tries to play it off or make it sound like “his hands were forced”, but at these points you start to feel like "why am I doing this exactly?" and you can actually hear your comrades say this to you. It’s pretty well done how you see the protagonist lose his sanity, however it does lead to a forced feeling of your first playthrough. But then even when everything is revealed and I’m in my second or third playthrough, it still feels a bit forced to me. [/spoiler] I can’t really explain this well, but it feels like the game and the story aren’t up to sync with each other… if that makes any sense.

I've only just completed this game now some five years on from release. Spec Ops seems to strike a chord with everyone I know who has played it, it has to be said that the basis of the game is well written and while visually lacking in this day and age the game does a wonderful job of putting imagery to the points the writers are trying to make.

However. For me all of the things that people applaud this game for; the story it tells, the statements it makes, the well coreographed cutscenes and mental breakdown sequences are all overshadowed by just how aggravating the game is to play. Frankly the whole thing would have been better off being done as a film rather than a videogame.

The cover system is clunky and doesn't allow you to transition from cover to cover smoothly or briskly, the binding of multiple actions to the same keys such as Space and Left shift means that often times you'll be punished by performing an action you didn't even intend to perform such as vaulting when you wanted to deck a fool, there are a couple of scripted sections where the game is just outright infuriating such as a midgame sequence when an enemy Littlebird opens fire on you while you run down a corridor. You will die multiple times in this section if you don't do something which is completely asinine in that situation and that is NOT to run immediately.

The result of this was that I was not able to properly enjoy the game as others have done, I was unable to forgive the game it's technical faults to the point where I got indescriminately angry at ALL the factions in the game; the 33rd Battalion, the CIA, the Insurgents and hell even Adams and Lugo, your squad members.

Frankly if you want to experience Spec Ops at it's best, just watch a playthrough on Youtube or something. You'll be better able to fully experience the nuances of the story like Walker's decscent into insanity, the White Phosphorous scene, Lugo's hazing and so on. If after all of that you enjoy the story, consider buying a copy for the privilige. I don't regret the purchase but I definitely would not recommend the "game" portion of this interactive novel.
