One thing not covered that I think really needs to be talked about more is this game is an incredible shooter. The controls are responsive. Moving to cover works well (usually). Swapping weapons feels right and not clunky like some other games. And squad commands make a LOT of sense without having context sensitivity. For instance, throw on a silencer and creep around to a location. Telling your squad to attack will lead to your character calling for a silent approach. You don't have to specify that they go silent or anything else. And you don't have to fiddle with telling them to take cover. The AI takes care of itself, except for a few instances where they'll jump ahead out of cover and fumble around before coming back. But I've never seen another shooter that handles it so well!

Overall combat is satisfying. At first the experience of a slight moment where time slows down on head shots is jarring, but it quickly becomes a mechanic that draws you in and a small bonus for a well aimed headshot (or maybe a lucky spray and pray). And with the rest of the plot, that ends up REALLY flowing well into the psyche of Captain Walker, the main character. 

It bothers so much that I never noticed this game until it appeared on a top ten list on Youtube that I saw. Spec Ops: The Line is probably the hardest game to play. Not so much because of its difficulty but because the theme it presents to the player.

While many games nowadays tries to dehumanise war, this one pulls no string to show you the consequences of your actions, without trying to do any sort of guilt- tripping. Even more depressing to think that while this may be just a game, in many countries this is an everyday reality.........

Taking control of a 3 man squadron, Capt. Walker, Lugo and Adams are sent into the deep end of Dubai, tasked to find the 33 squad. But the more they go further, the more they realise that the once luxurious city became a living hell, where its every man for himself. There are no heroes, there are are no good or bad choices you need to make: but to sometimes having to decide between the lesser evil. 

The game breaks the fourth wall at many occasions and among other things asks one simple question to the player: "Do you feel like a hero yet?", which never felt as gutt-wrenching and tear-jerking as it did in this game.

I recommend this on sale... While it's a good game it's a bit short. Took me about 7 hours to get through collecting most of the intel and exploring a bit on my own. I really enjoyed the game a lot and I really enjoy the works it takes inspiration from but there are a few issues with it. The game is completely linear. It provides the illusion of choice and that what you do has consequences but unfortunately you aren't actually given any choices (Spoiler: except the ending... kind of). I don't have a problem with linear games really but when they turn out as short as this it's frustrating. I can see what the devs were aiming to do, taking inspiration from Heart of Darkness and more directly in my opinion the film Apocalpyse Now, they didn't want players to cookie cut their way through the game to try to get a certain playthrough and wanted an immersive experience to show the true horrors of actual combat and the effect on the human psyche. The problem with most games that make you take moral choices, for example DIshonored, is that the effects of what you do is shoved in your face immediately and if it's not the result you wanted you'll reload and try to fix it. The nice thing about Spec Ops is that you are forced to live with your illusionary choices and there isn't really a white or black path. Everything is gray area. 

In Short: I enjoyed this game. It made me think about the impact of war on the human psyche and I really recommend it if you're a fan of classic war films it takes inspiration from (Apocalpyse Now, Platoon, FMJ, etc). Just don't expect much replability.

Let me just start off with saying a great majority of the reviews I've read, and watched about it say it's a good game, with great story and the narrative is unique and interesting with a powerful message.

I've played 108 minutes of it on the normal difficulty so far.
I have checked out.

First of all, the controls are different to the standard shooter layout, like Shift being melee, having grenade on Q, using space to sprint, and R to pick things up. This is done for no reason I can think of, it just makes playing so much more awkward.

The story is you're going into destroyed Dubai in search of survivors in this desolate no-man's land that the city has become after <Irrelevant plot>. The point is the city is messed up in a big way and no one wants anything to do with it.

After about being there for about 20 minutes, the player is pushed into countless scenarios where an absurd number of bad-guys just crawl out of the walls, floors, and drop from the sky (They'll come from anwhere you can think of).
So immediately my idea of this sparsely populated city with barely anyone left alive in it is shattered by the abundance of terrorists and evil U.S. military troops (which motivations have yet to make sense 2 hours in).

Reviews say it's a look into the morality of video game protagonists and players.
However, I haven't had to make any choice that's even remotely ethically challenging. So far, I haven’t even had the option of a choice.

In the first encounter with anyone in the game the protagonist, and his squad of generic military stereotypes, Stg. Jokes, and Lt. Serious, stumble upon survivors just of the outskirts of this dead and deserted city (what are the odds) and Stg. Jokes talks with them in Arabic while Capt. Protagonist and Lt. Serious discuss how to murder these people they’ve just met (you know, just in case). Surprise, sur-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥-prise, the locals don’t take kindly to this scheming (or maybe it’s just Stg. Joke’s grating one dimensional character), Capt. Protagonist tries his best to stabilise the situation as the locals get more and more aggravated. 
Then they shoot first. They shoot first, well there goes my agency right there. First of all, it’s self-defence so there’s no ethical quandary about killing these people. Secondly, even if you “choose” not to kill them your squad mates are going to shoot them for you. Thirdly, the game itself will not let you progress until these people are killed. There’s no ethics, there’s no choice.

A few minutes (and several hundred dead natives) later, Capt. Protagonist and his squad stumble across alive U.S. troops (who were there originally to conduct and evacuation of the city). To literally nobody’s surprise the U.S. troops shoot first.
After slogging through a few more minutes of intolerably bad gameplay and some more of Stg. Jokes famous inappropriate-for-a-warzone-because-Lt. Serious-says-so jokes (what a unique and interesting display of character discourse) it is revealed that the U.S. troops are gathering and executing civilians, for no other reason I can deduce than sand-madness (it’s the only logical explanation I can think of). So once again there’s no great ethical debate I’m having with myself about killing these soldiers. Only the dread that I’ll have to go through another area with a stupendous number of enemies appearing out of every possible location all the while fighting with the control scheme.

To summarise my experience so far:
The characters are the generic, bland, stereotypical military shooter guys.
There’s no insightful moral messages or choice.
The gameplay is an absolute struggle to play through.
The story may pick up, and there may well be a powerful moral message at the end of the game, but I’m not going to see it because I cannot force myself to slog through anymore of this drab, samey, and just plain awkward gameplay to see it.

This is one of the most excruciatingly [i]boring[/i] shooters I have ever played, issue number one being storytelling: Sure, we start [i]in medias res[/i], without even a hint of why we're in Dubai, and what we're doing there; I've got nothing against this sort of exposition. The problem starts when you realize that, between a paper-thin plotline about rogue, treacherous U.S. soldiers and not a shred of an attempt to make any sort of emotional connection between the player and the character he controls, the game is formula on top of formula.

The moment I heard the name [strike]Joseph[/strike] John Conrad and listened to those radio broadcasts, the jig was up: this is merely yet another clumsy attempt to rip off [i] Heart of Darkness[/i] by way of [i]Apocalypse Now[/i]. If I were a teenage girl, this is where I'd sardonically roll my eyes all the way out of my skull: Not this again.

Maybe this is an intergenerational issue: I understand not having read the book (it's a hard read—I know, I've had to teach it to four dozen fidgety undergrads one semester), but anyone who's missed the iconic film must be living under a rock...and knowing the film doesn't help any, because anyone familiar with Francis Ford Coppola's uncompromising visual aesthetics and strong storytelling would have to raise a brow or two at this game's clumsy visuals and awkward dialogue.

This brings me to my final point: This game is unpolished in the extreme. The controls and the corresponding characters' movements are clumsy (Why would you want to mess with the proven-and-true sprint action? How the hell do I roll away from a barrage of grenades?). The cover mechanics are ridiculous, and I'm honestly not sure what to make of the all-out idiotic command system (the AI is really, really bad). A lot of work has been put into sound design and voiceover work—I'll give them this much—but the graphics are poor, even for 2012 (this was the year of [i]Dishonored[/i], [i]Mass Effect 3[/i], and [i]Call of Duty: Black Ops II[/i]).

Lastly, let's say you're willing to forgive the game its sub-par graphics and storytelling. What do you do with the extremely repetitive shoot-cover mechanic that the game forces down your throat again, and again, and again? Stop playing, most likely. I did.

Here's a short history lesson

The year was 2012, gaming has been a very shallow and safe year for many triple A companies. Usual genres that were put out were shooters as that is what every company thought what their customers want. But what was believed to be even safer, or more importantly insulting were military shooters. Games that glorified the military and tweaked the mechanics of gameplay to give you a sense of power like, brain dead AI, regenerating health and a black and white story of good and bad. Perhaps it was not intended for these developers to make propaganda games and thought it was what the public wanted, given for where the companies were set up. But never the less, they obviously made a foolish story for more mature and experienced players that the idea that one country is morally better then the other.

Going in the background, a team of developers called Yager who were responsible for the spec ops series in the late 90's and early 100's decided to make a game to not compete with major games like call of duty or battlefield, but still act like one to convey a message. A message that violence was not fun and there is no need for unnecessary conflict. their recent games conveyed respect and the harsh realities that these soldiers go through unlike the other brands. This may have not been a game to make major sales, but maybe as a cult classic and to go down in history as one of the greatest feats in gaming history.

I won't spoil to much of the game because it's best to go in with the expectations of cluelesness. You should definetly play it or if you can find a copy, buy it to perserve it, because the latter is why i brought it, i'll explain later.

[u]gameplay[/u]
For the mechanics of the game its boring. Its a mix of terrible cover based shooting with modern military tropes that make it feel like a bland shooter cashing into the fad, but that the point. It purposely does this to make it look boring at first and assumes that you brought it for shooting [b]all da bad guys with poor life decisions[/b].

Infact, its made to look like it has bad shooting mechanics at first and then it alters its minor details to convey the mental state of Walker, the protagonist throughout the game. These mechanics alter how the enemies die as well, in the first hour your given only two small arms but later on your given high powered and explosive wepons, which may sound exciting, but its not and not in the tedious way. Even the new mechanic, exicutions for ammo, changes differently from what weapon your using or how long you are into the game.

This may sound small, but in truth these are put into the game because alot of military shooters don't show you what actually happens when you shoot someone in the head with a high power weapon or when you blow them up with a rocket launcher. This game bravely shows you how sickening it is to kill someone, and when you see that motar loaded with white phosphorus you will know what its like to truely hurt someone badly.

[u]atmosphere[/u]
This game is chock full of visual metaphors that enforces the idea of an unsettling feeling that something is not right, where there is questions on whats real or not real and as it goes on from the first act to the last act helps us to understand ourselves of what actions we do. Its not a very pretty thing but it helps with the expeience.

The game is also very self aware that you exist, i don't want to spoil anything about how it will do so but it will make you feel bad and it will do so in ways that will make you embarased and disgusted of yourself. You will notice things that only you can see and no one else can.

But the biggest shocker is that you are in control of your actions and when you hear the line "do you feel like a hero", the major characters mocking you for your pretend heroism and the loading screen contributing as well, the true villian will be put out.

[u]conclusion[/u]
Gaming with modern millitary and real countries tropes have basically gone down the plughole. The companies that popularised the genre of war games have turned to historical battles and futuristic/fantasy settings. Any companies that tries to cash in on alternate reaities of our future with real countries taking over the world, is going to be decimated because of a fad no one likes anymore, Homefront the revolution for example.

[h1]The War as It is[/h1]

There is a story that you, as the protagonist, tell yourself, and there is the story as it really is. The tension between both is the greatest feature of [i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i], but it is revealed in a very subtle way.

You are in the path to be a saviour, but as you pass by a tree and look back you may not notice that the tree you saw alive is in fact dead, or that the faces in the walls are with their eyes covered to do not see the horror near them — aren’t you doing the same to keep making so much blood flowing on the ground? “We are soldiers”, you say to your companion after being questioned about the violent path you breached for yourself, all the killing you did must have seemed trivial to you, moreover, the bloodbath you took must have been the necessary step you had to pass through to become a hero — for yourself, you are headed that way, if you crossed the line it was because you needed to do. You might not see this, but even the game load screens remind you that you are not a hero.

Something that seems real but only happens to you, this is hallucination. And the reasons you just give yourself to keep killing, what are they? Of course the game could not explicitly show the hallucinations as such, instead they seem lively as any other experience and there are only a few visual details that can be hints to reveal what they actually are, like the fades being white whenever one is occurring.

All the killing looks fine for you, it seems necessary and what you expect to do while playing a game of this genre. But the end confronts you with the reality, it shows to you the war you fought not anymore through the perspective of a fighting soldier, but as it is. You finally tell yourself that what you are seeing is not happening, or you decide to finish your own spectacle of fire.

Once again I go head to head with Spec Ops: The Line. I think this might be the game that has frustrated me the most as somebody who enjoys a good story based game that leaves an impact on you. Not only did Spec Ops: The Line's story fall completely flat, but the gameplay did it no favours either.

Spec Ops: The Line is a gritty yellow and grey third person cover based shooter where you play as a hoorah military man sent to dubai to attempt and fix a situation that has gone completely south. Things proceed to get worse and worse, leading to a climax where you make a choice that changes your ending.

This sounds like the most generic concept for a shooter ever, and it is. But before we continue on, It's important to note when this game was released. June 2012 was during the period where people were just starting to get tired of these yellowed desert war shooters, similar to how people are slowly getting tired of open world games now. This was a time period where literally everyone and their dog was still talking about Modern Warfare 2 and 3, and every shooter that came out was trying to be them. I think Spec Ops: The Line is partially a frustrated response to these tired shooters, and we should acknowledge that. However, to me, this doesn't excuse any of Spec Ops: The Line's problems.

Spec Ops: The Line is largely bogged down by it's mediocre story, choiceless actions, and absolutely abysmal gameplay. The part where this gets more complicated with all three of these things is that it's very clear that in a way they are deconstructing the genre at that time and it's conventions in those areas.

Spec Ops: The Line's story is often what the game is heralded for. As previously explained, you and a small group of soldiers go knee deep into dubai to clean up somebody else's mess as a bunch of military groups occupying the region have begun infighting. The character development of your team is handled very well- at first they seem like the kind of people you'd stop giving a ♥♥♥♥ about 20 minutes into the game, but when push comes to shove they begin to each grow different arcs that all climax throughout the story. Even the main character, while having potentially offensive interpretations of war related PTSD near the end, has a semi-decent growth and conclusion. It's too bad that all of this completely gets sat on by the message of the game, which is trying it's best to shove itself down your throat.

It's honestly hard to continue from here without spoiling things, but I'll try my best. The main problem with Spec Ops: The Line's storyTELLING (not the story itself) is that it constantly wants to show you how bad a person you are both in the game and past the fourth wall. I'm not entirely sure if this is just because it's aimed at the dudebro audience that loves violence and shooting things or the developers just think you're an idiot for purchasing the game. This leads to the game explaining extremely basic, overdone messages to you like you're four years old and constantly wagging it's finger at you like you were a dog that just crapped on the carpet. You are given choices, but both choices always mean nothing. Either the other choice you didn't choose happens immediately after anyways, or the person/thing you saved/did whatever with just goes "thanks!" and never shows up ever again. But no matter what you choose in these choice segments, expect to be berated for it. Your teammates and the game's tone itself will constantly remind you that you are literally hitler and did a bad thing by choosing the action you chose. This is extremely obvious at probably the most famous scene in the game, in which you have no choice but to do an action. Then for the rest of the game, you are yelled at for doing it. The only thing stopping you from not doing it is an invisible wall, as it's been previously established through past fights that the threat in front of you is no match for your arnold schwarzenegger accuracy and powerful grenade launcher. The game itself is stopping you, not the narrative. This may all be the point and what the game is trying to tell the players- that you have no choice when war is involved and every action you take is a bad one. But is a slightly more complicated message than "war is bad" really worth tanking an entire pretty decent story for?

The storytelling itself is also not done any favours by the absolutely abysmal gameplay. At the very least the gameplay could compliment the story and message by making things more dire and hard to deal with as time goes on, but it doesn't even [b]attempt[/b] to go that far. It is THE most generic third person shooter you might ever play in your life, and plays exactly like those terrible Kane and Lynch games I try and forget about every time I look at my PS3 collection. It's actually even worse than other generic third person shooters: multiple actions are mapped to the same button, the snapping to cover is buggy (sometimes you'll just run past cover into a guy's gun), grenade trajectory is faulty and sometimes acts completely different than expected, and at points cover that should be protecting you randomly fails to do so as a bullet clips through concrete straight into your head. The game advertises "[commanding] an intelligent and powerful squad of Delta-Force soldiers" when realistically you just press a button on your keyboard and one of your dudes eventually decides to shoot the guy you're looking at. Sure, you could say this is all to accentuate the point of third person cover based shooters being boring and terrible and compliment the deconstructivist view of the military genre at a whole, but beyond the gameplay being ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ bad it makes no attempt to match itself to the story. You are in a water starved, sand ravaged dubai, yet everyone has infinite ammo and act livelier than ever. You constantly regenerate health despite being beat to ♥♥♥♥ through cutscenes and having no further medical supplies or water. The city is buried in sand, yet the most that comes into play is three points in the game where you can shoot a window and sand comes out, and a sandstorm part near the end that has barely any bearing on gameplay. Things get more mentally tough for your crew, yet they still scream "♥♥♥♥♥♥ A" and "HOOAH" whenever you kill somebody, and other than a hilarious hallucination part at the end your mental state has no impact on gameplay other than walking segments and a way too "trying to be deep" ending.

I'm running out of space so I'll make it brief: Spec Ops: The Line may be a visually gorgeous game (its ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ beautiful), but has a story that is euthanized by it's own storytelling and gameplay. These two problems gangbeat the whole point of this game down, making what could have been a great timepiece of gaming in 2012 and a decent look at the horrors of war into little more than a dying whimper of a good concept. I appreciate it's attempt, but it just doesn't work.

It is so masterful and deliberate with its story that you can't help but walk out of the experience feeling like every action you took and every person you killed during the campaign took a serious, definite toll on your psyche. [i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i], while not having perhaps the longest single-player campaign, and not exactly having incredibly compulsive or polished shooting mechanics, is still one of the best games I've played.

The game is a criticism of the common themes of many shooter games, which struggle with issues of ludonarrative dissonance, and the glorification of war and pro-American agendas or Western values, while also antagonising those of different races, ethnicities, or ideologies.  The narrative, based off of Joseph Conrad's [i]Heart of Darkness[/i], depicts a protagonist affected by his murderous actions, the trauma of war, and the indiscriminate mass killing he performs.  In this way, [i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i] is one of the first game narratives that overcomes the common problem of ludonarrative dissonance, by presenting a character suffering from the player's actions.

Additionally, the game has a very interesting choice system, where there is no explicit choice mechanic, but instead the choices stem from interaction within the game system.  This works very well, and feels like you are actually making legitimate choices, while an explicit system, at least to me, never feels like I'm making real choices, but just following the directives of the designer.  While both systems have technically been designed, an implicit choice system works amazing at conveying the illusion of control to the player; it greatly rewards players when they're allowed to discover the choices, rather than just choosing them from a list.

I highly recommend checking this game out, I'd say that it's definitely one of the top games of this decade.

I appreciate Spec Ops: The Line for being one of those rare games that actually tries to make you actually think about and feel bad for killing people. It's a bit more heavy-handed than other games that also try to make you feel for those you are killing (for example, the original Deus Ex, and This War of Mine), but the heavy-handedness and extreme situations you are in where you do extreme things seems to be one of the main focuses of the game. The setting is interesting: Dubai after it has been ravaged and isolated by lethal freak sandstorms. The gameplay is that of a typical 3rd person cover-based shooter, but the dialogue and in-game choices make you think more about what you are doing, and the overall story and relatively mature treatment of killing compared to other military shooters definitely make the game worth playing if you are familiar with the genre.

Rating: 8/10
Overview: Cover Based Third Person Shooter 

The Good:

+ The story/premise is the main hook for the game. This game deals with the consequences of your actions and shows the mental, emotional and physical trauma the characters’ face when dealing with their actions. Given that so many games in this industry has you slaughtering people repeatedly, it is somewhat refreshing for a game that deals with the aftermath and consequences with making difficult choices. This is probably the more “realistic” war games out there. 

+ Your AI companions are useful. The can take out enemies, distract enemy fire and give you feedback on the battlefield. Too many games have AI companions that are useless and give the appearance of being helpful so its nice to play a game where I am not constantly frustrated by my AI partners. 

+ Given that the game takes place in Dubai, the developers did a fantastic job of mixing up the environments so it never feels stale or boring. 

+ At some points in the game you can make choices in how the story unfolds. Nothing major but it does add a nice little touch to the game

+ Sound design is excellent 

The Average:

- Main character is the very definition of the ‘average male video game character’. 

- The gameplay itself is nothing new. It controls well enough but for most of the game you will be running into new environments, shooting hordes of enemies and then doing it all over again. I would have liked a few more interesting scenarios thrown into the mix. If you ever played a cover based third person shooter before, this game will offer no surprises with its gameplay.  

The Bad:

- Lack of replayability, no compelling reason to replay the game

- Multiplayer is dead 

Conclusion: 

A fun if not short third person shooter with its main selling point being its story, something you don’t often see with action games.

Wanna know a good argument for games being art? 
This is one of the pieces you should use.
Spec Ops: The Line is like watching the [i]Challenger [/i] explode: It's horrible, people are dying, but you can't look away because you're too awe-stricken to move. Spec Ops has one of the rawest portrayals of war in videogames, and it knows it. Spec Ops is full of symbollism, anti-war sentiments, and morally ambiguous choices that you'll wrack your brain over. The game doesn't shy away from occasional fourth-wall breakage to make fun of modern war games like Call of Duty either, and I can appreciate a game that treats its audience with respect. Multiple endings and consequences for your actions make you want to play through multiple times, assuming you can handle the guilt.

The game is also gorgeous; Dubai is full of scenic backdrops, hellish sandstorms, and Crumbling architecture. You'll even get a full HD picture of a gut-wrenching scene involving phosphorus.

Spec Ops' only noteworthy flaws are, unfortunately, the gameplay. It actually works fine, and it won't glitch/crash on you. But the third-person cover and shoot mechanics are very simple and plebeian, and as a result the strict shooter sequences are nothing to write home about. Similarly, multiplayer is eh. Again, it works, but definitely not the game's selling point.

Spec Ops is not an easy game to play. By the end of it, you WILL hate yourself. You'll rethink why you played it and what could have possibly changed anything, or if it was worth changing at all. You'll feel pain for the characters, and solace in their resolution. And a video game that makes you think like that, as far as I'm concerned, is art.

Spec Ops: The Line is an old game (since I can run it on very high with my potato). On first glance, its main theme centers on shooting, and war. While it is played with 3rd person view, people will group it with other 3rd person view titles, such as Tom Clancy, or the other, more famous AAA titles, like Battlefield and Call of Duty franchises. In general, they have similar game modes i.e. multiplayer, in-game mechanics (although the latter titles are first-person shooters) i.e. vaulting over cover, melee attacks. Nonetheless, I had planned this game to be finished quick, and move on. I was wrong. The game-for some reason-from the moment I start playing it, I can't stop.The only time I stopped, it was to eat dinner, and sleep. Even then, I can't stop thinking about it. D:

The game starts in an aerial fight scene, helicopters buzzing around, shooting other helis down using minigun. Sounds familiar? For people who have played other similar themed games, you would know what I mean. Then, the sandstorm comes in. *̶c̶u̶e̶s̶ ̶f̶o̶r̶ ̶t̶h̶e̶ ̶d̶a̶r̶u̶d̶e̶ ̶-̶ ̶s̶a̶n̶d̶s̶t̶o̶r̶m̶ ̶s̶o̶n̶g̶ ̶a̶n̶d̶ ̶m̶e̶m̶e̶s̶ ̶i̶n̶c̶o̶m̶i̶n̶g̶*̶  Then, a crash.

Then, the game starts. In a desert, one plays as the main character, Captain Walker. Accompanied by his two subordinates, Sergeant Lugo and Lieutenant Adams to Dubai, trying to find Colonel Konrad and the 33rd Batalyon along with survivors. This 'search for survivors' does sound like an over-used plot device utilized by so many game companies, I had consider it to be the most basic 'norm' developers use to start any similar themed games. However, after the first few chapters where I somewhat understands the basic gameplay (cover and shoot, give orders, etc.) I did think that this is similar to Tom Clancy's franchises. However, as the game goes deeper, I start to understand why the game had the reputation which sets itself apart from other titles. The actions; words that the MC, Lugo and Adams used; enemy executions (Yes, there is an option for that); their clothes and wellbeing; the words on screen that appear when you die and restart from the last checkpoint; even the early game backgrounds when the game starts up, REALLY CHANGE as the game goes on. I start to question, what was going on.

Then, at one point, one scene was particularly... unsettling. It was one of that 'What did I just do" moments. Through out the game, I was presented with choices that I have to make in a limited time. However, there are multiple times when one is presented with choices where choosing either of them will lead to bad situations.  In this type of moments, one usually chooses the one which is the lesser evil. Still, how do one knows that the choice IS the lesser evil? At that moment, no one knows. Only later on in the game, one finds out and it is not a pretty one. 

The later stages in the game are a bit frustrating since I failed and died a few times (which even prompted the 'do you want to lower the difficulty' sign). I have to remap the controls since vaulting over cover and melee attack are mapped originally at the same key, which made it difficult. Ammos are also limited, forcing you to drop and switch weapons to deal with certain situations i.e. snipers, juggernauts. Movements are a bit mechanical (which caused several deaths) but I put it down to my ability since I was not accustomized to the playstyle. I have to give props for the AI enemy who are particularly challenging (even on normal difficulty that I was playing) which will force you to get out of your cover by throwing grenades, flanking you and will kill you when they had the chance i̶n̶ ̶t̶h̶e̶ ̶m̶i̶d̶s̶t̶ ̶o̶f̶ ̶r̶o̶c̶k̶ ̶m̶u̶s̶i̶c̶ ̶b̶l̶a̶r̶i̶n̶g̶ ̶o̶v̶e̶r̶ ̶t̶h̶e̶ ̶s̶p̶e̶a̶k̶e̶r̶s̶ ̶a̶s̶ ̶b̶u̶l̶l̶e̶t̶s̶ ̶w̶h̶i̶z̶z̶e̶d̶ ̶p̶a̶s̶t̶ ̶b̶y̶ ̶a̶n̶d̶ ̶g̶r̶e̶n̶a̶d̶e̶s̶ ̶c̶a̶u̶s̶i̶n̶g̶ ̶a̶ ̶m̶o̶m̶e̶n̶t̶a̶r̶y̶ ̶s̶t̶u̶n̶. AI friendlies are surprisingly useful, helping during tough battle scenes, even though sometimes they went down because they just stand there while the enemy shoots at them. :/

Into the 5th or 6th hour, in my mind, I started to think how does this game end? How? Who is Konrad? The earlier chapters I have played is already.... confronting enough. And then I played the last few chapters. Watching everything I hold dear, MC, the other guys, break and fall. Sometimes I don't even know if these guys could've reach this far, considering what they went through. Then, the final chapter, and epilogue came. It was... an emotional rollercoaster. For the first time when I play a game, as the credits roll, I tried to gain some understanding on what had happened up there. For the first time, when I played games of such genre, I feel... mainly upset. However, to call it just upset is not exactly correct.  Of course,  I feel upset that I had played this game, as one starts the game thinking of what was the general norm in such games, and in the end... felt empty inside. There is also a combination of conflicting and mixed feelings of confusion, and relief. Why I put relief? Because, I get the chance to play this game. It was one of those games where you just have to experience it once, without spoilers, and knowing nothing about the game at all. 

I have been particularly late in playing games that are not popular anymore but people still consider it timeless. It has been the case for a few games I own i.e. Bioshock, Bioshock 2, Bioshock Infinite, and Walking Dead: Season 1. I was glad, I had the chance to try a game that invoked such conflicting emotions and thoughts, even after the game have ended.

Spec Ops The Line is a military shooter with a story unlike any other within this category of FPS games. It's sick, it's twisted, and it makes you wonder if you really are playing the hero or if you're playing the villian. But we'll get onto this later, ON TO THE REVIEW!

[h1]GAMEPLAY - 3/10[/h1]
The gameplay in this game was really, REALLY boring. It was such a slog to get through, I ended up having to take tons of breaks just to get through this game because the gameplay was just so bland and repetitive. Even down to the weapons there wasn't a lot of variety with what you could do in terms of playstyle. It all boiled down to do you want to play in close or long range and that's really it. Not much else to say, it just made it really hard to get through this game because the story ended up being really good.

[h1]GRAPHICS - 5/10[/h1]
As per usual we're treated to a lovely palette of brown, brown, and more brown. Thankfully though, this isn't a huge issue since it's used to good effect with the story which we'll get to later. What I really appreciated about this game though is all the little graphical touches that it sprinkles around as you progress through the game to make the world feel more alive and real but also to show just how much Captain Walker (the guy you play as) has changed as the war rages on. Even during combat when you get more and more damaged you see Walker's face get more and more distressed, and it's these little things that make me get that little bit more immersed in the game.

[h1]SOUND - 4/10[/h1]
The music in this game is a real mixed bag. It can't decide whether it wants to be appropriate for the setting and mood of the current scene or whether it wants to be a song chosen at random on the sound designer's iPod. It's really jarring and rips you out of the experience which I hate in a game that is already hard enough to get into and enjoy. The sound effects were nothing special, the voice acting got a bit off at times, but overall it was very okay.

[h1]STORY - 6/10[/h1]
The story was touted as being one of the most well told war stories in games, esploring war and it's affects on people which don't get me wrong, it did very well. It starts off romanticising war like other games of this type do, but slowly it begins to peel away layers of this glorification and you begin to see what affect war has on these people. The only issue is, it took far too long to get to the pinch point of the story where we get to see everything go south for these soldiers. I ended up playing around 4-5 hours before getting there and I was seriously considering dropping this game because it was just too hard to play through. I am glad I played through this game, but I do wish that they could have cut down on the horrible slog at the start of the game so we could get to the meat of this story.

[h1]OVERALL - 4/10[/h1]
This game was really hard to play through and for most people I would say you probably don't want to play this unless you really value story in your games. It's a long and hard game to get through but the payoff at the end was worth it for me.

Gameplay wise the game is a fairly standard shooter. Hide behind cover, shoot enemies, proceed. That kinda thing.
However, the characters, the story, and the overall experience are phenomenal.

The game is short, as indicated by my play time of it, but it's absolutely worth it. Quality over quantity, every time.
If you are patient and manage to snag this on sale, it's some of the best bang for your buck you can find on steam.

Spec Ops: The Line occupies a believably precarious world that deserves a bit more exploration and when the game gets itself together enough to know when to shut the hell up, it can offer up one of modern gaming's most unique dramatic experiences. Oh, boy. I really want to dive right into this. So here it is, why you should play Spec Ops: The Line. 

First, the story:
You play as Captain Martin Walker. He has two squadmates, First Lieutenant Alphanso Adams and Staff Sergeant John Lugo. Together, you form Delta Force. You venture into a war-torn Dubai on a mission to rescue the civilians and find out what happened to the 33rd Infantry Battalion. That's really all I can say about this without going knee deep into spoiler territory. 

The story is what this game is about. This game isn't your typical Call of Duty or Battlefield game. It's a realistic, brutal game. This game is gonna mess with your head. 

Now, the gameplay:

The gameplay is a third person cover-based military shooter. The mechanics aren't that amazing for the shooting. The cover system can be something you need to be careful with. Many times, I found myself running to a piece of cover, only to find that Walker wouldn't get behind it for some reason, and I'd get very close to dying. 

The shooting is alright. It's not the best, but the best way to describe it is very similar to Uncharted. Mostly, that is done for a reason in relation to the story. If you play this game, you'll know exactly what I'm talking about. 

And the performance: 

Nolan North stars as Captain Walker, and he does an amazing job. If an actor can make you forget about the actor and get into the character, they've done a good job. Nolan North was Captain Walker. Christopher Reid and Omid Abtahi do outstanding jobs as First Lieutenant Adams and Staff Sergeant Lugo, respectively. 


Finally, the graphics: 

This game isn't the most amazing looking game, but by god does it look gritty. It looks great if you turn up the graphics to the maximum settings. My computer isn't the greatest, and it handled it fine. I found zero glitches throughout the entire game. 

Verdict: 

This game was designed to make people remember it. I certainly will. I don't think I'll ever forget it even if I wanted to. With all the mechanics coming together, this game delivered in what it was trying to do. Please, don't think this game is a standard military shooter, because it is not. It's not a game. It's an experience. 

With all these aspects, my final verdict for this game is a solid 9.8/10. 

I loved this game. I can't praise this game more. Buy it. Play it.

A superb game which takes heavy inspiration from the novel ‘Heart of Darkness’ by Joseph Conrad. No other game has delved so deeply into the moral minefield that is war. Whilst shooting people in a game may traditionally be easy, it is not easy on the psyche, especially in a game like Spec Ops: The Line. 

The player is dragged kicking and screaming through the war torn streets of Dubai as they witness horrific war crimes, leaving the memories of screaming mothers and their children engraved in their minds.


The game follows Delta Squad. A group of three soldiers sent into Dubai to gather Intel and hopefully save an entire city of civilians. The city is trapped by a storm wall, an impenetrable wall of sand that often rips across the city, destroying buildings and tearing the landscape apart. The three soldiers have great chemistry and listening to them interact throughout the story is simply amazing. The developers did an amazing job to not only place the player into world, but also into the mind of the protagonist Captain Walker. The actual gameplay is solid. There is nothing amazingly innovative, but the cover system works great, with certain walls being destructible. Gunplay is also fun, with a wide variety of weapons to choose from, each with their own attributes, such as weight making you move slower. 

All in all I would highly recommend this game to anyone. It is not only an impressive third person shooter. But also an amazing story driven experience that is sure to make you question the morality of war, and the durability of the human psyche. A great game, which should really be made into a movie so more people can experience this masterpiece.

[h1] DISCLAIMER: This is a full review, and NOT a first impressions review like all my other reviews, if you want a better full review, then please read better reviews then mine [/h1]

Spec Ops: The Line is a game developed by Yager Development and published by 2K Games. Dubai was hit by a devastating sandstorm. The 33rd infantry battalion, on their way out of Afghanistan, was volunteered by their leader Colonel John Konrad, to assist the evacuation of the citizens

However, when the storm wall hit Dubai, evacuation became impossible. Months later, they attempted to convoy out of Dubai. However, the evacuation failed horribly, resulting the loss of “too many” soldiers and civilians, and there wasn’t any word about them ever since

Spec Ops: The Line is a third-person shooter set in the modern day post-catastrophe Dubai. You will follow as Captain Martin Walker as he and his team of Delta Force operatives are sent on a reconnaissance mission to Dubai. Their objective was to locate any survivors and radio for evac

I originally played the first few chapters of Spec Ops: The Line and I thought it was just a generic and bland third-person shooter. However, later on, I decided to give it another try, and boy I was wrong about the game

The gameplay is comparable to other third-person shooters, you can use covers, sprint, pickup items like any other third-person shooters. Your squad members can be ordered to focus their fire on a targeted enemy, snipe far away enemies, and even throw flashbang or grenades at the enemy

The AI for your squad members are quite smart, so they won’t get in your way as they can move on their own as you progress, find covers by themselves, and you only need to issue those commands at certain situation

Some weapons have special abilities such as having a grenade launcher attachment, laser sights, scopes, and more that you can toggle depending on your needs. Sometimes you can eliminate your enemies by using the environment to take the fight at your advantage, such as shooting gas cans or even shooting glass walls to bury your enemies with sand

And speaking of enemies, the enemy will always try to find a way to flank you, thus you need to be aware of the position of the enemies and stay mobile. Some covers can be destroyed so you must be wary of what you are using as cover. 

The single-player consists of fifteen chapters in Spec Ops: The Line, with four different difficulty levels to choose from. There’s also a multiplayer mode and a cooperative mode

There are a lot of things I like about Spec Ops: The Line, one of them is the atmosphere. The city of Dubai looks beautiful with its ruins of tall skyscrapers, combine that with amazing graphics and you will end up with a game that looks breathtaking. The lighting, particle effects, and textures for a game of that time looks amazing

What a lot of people praise about this game is the storyline, which I myself agree. It really escalated from being a cheesy cliché into an intense and unforgettable story. It’s really unlike any other military shooters which glorifies war, instead game focuses on the horrible things that happen in wars. It really makes you think about what is right and what is necessary

One of the things that I don’t enjoy is the finicky controls. The cover system is quite unreliable sometimes and would often get you killed. The combat gameplay alone is quite lackluster in my opinion
 
To wrap it up, Spec Ops: The Line is truly a fantastic game. The smart enemy AI and the great level design make up for the lackluster combat, and the finicky controls. However, I can honestly say that the story and the visuals are the ones that make this game great for me, as it really hooked me to finish the game. The story was unlike any other war games I’ve ever played, it was very dark and grim and it truly captures the horrors of war

I highly recommend this game!

Spec Ops: The Line may not look like something out of the ordinary, but at the end of the singleplayer story you will be left asking yourself several questions. A few of them answered, but most of them left to be answered by yourself.

The choice of music is spot on throughout the game, further amplifying the overall tone and atmosphere, so in this regard there is nothing to complain about.
Gameplay is just like what you would expect from a Third-Person-Cover-Based-Shooter, nothing special there... sadly.
Do not make the mistake and consider the game to be a realistic depiction of combat, for it clearly drops a lot of realism (at least at some points) in favor of atmosphere, serving as a good way to establish a little bit of distance between your actions and yourself (which you are going to need). 

In conclusion Spec Ops: The Line is an outstanding action game which might look rather generic, but has much to offer, once you let yourself be taken in by its dark and grim atmosphere. Even though a single playthough does not take long and combat is rather simplistic, the replay value is pretty high (for reasons you really should discover for yourself).
I really recommend to play at higher difficulties though.

The story in this game is the shining gem in SO: The Line and it's definitely not one you would want to experience secondhand. You want that gun to be controlled by YOUR mouse when it comes to what dehumanizing choice you'll be dragged into making. While it does railroad you into many decisions, and the results of some of those decisions can be nihilistically inconsequential in the grand scheme of things, your intial run in this game will weigh heavily on you when you're later informed that there were more choices available than you thought possible, especially if you THOUGHT you only had one or two options. With no binary 'right or wrong' morality, you're pushed into making decisions that are too grey to decipher.

So many people have talked about this game, and so few can do so without hard spoiling memes, but even being set up to know a lot about how the game would proceed before I even played, never would I have thought it could still get to me by telling me the mere idea that there was always options, oftentimes several, and one that was always present was the idea that everything I was going through wouldn't have come to pass if I had just stopped playing. And that's true. It sounds like a cop out when you first hear it, but nothing stood between me and just shutting the game down, loading up Youtube and just watching someone else make those decisions for me. The game never takes too much control out of your hands when it comes to the important parts, even when it feels like there's only one way forward. If I wanted to stop feeling responsible for committing digital atrocities, I could have just relegated that task to a random Let's Player and hid from myself.

But I think it's important to press on. Even knowing that you're not going to come out of the experience with warm fuzzy feelings, it's important to challenge yourself, whether it's your skills as a gamer, or just self-examination, so you know where you stand and see if you can make the choice to change that or the industry and genre that this game heavily criticizes. With that, you can use the thoughts that this game may provoke in you to a good purpose knowing that:

What happens in this game is all your fault, but even after you're long done with it, you're still a good person.

Gameplay-wise it's a typical cover-based shooter which plays very similar to Mass Effect 2; however, even though I enjoyed the shooting mechanics and different environments, I believe some may find the gameplay elements generic and at times even tedious. I recommend [b]Spec Ops: The Line[/b] to those who want to play a third person shooter (a genre not so popular on PC) and/or a story-driven game.

[h1]Do You Feel Like a Hero Yet?[/h1]

Dubai was hit by a devastating sandstorm. The 33rd infantry battalion, on their way out of Afghanistan, was volunteered by their leader Colonel John Konrad, to assist the evacuation of the citizens. However, when the storm wall hit Dubai, evacuation became impossible. Months later, they attempted to convoy out of Dubai. However, the evacuation failed horribly, resulting the loss of “too many” soldiers and civilians, and there wasn’t any word about them ever since.
Spec Ops: The Line is a third-person shooter set in the modern day post-catastrophe Dubai. It was developed by Yager Development and published by 2K Games in 2012. In-game, you will follow as Captain Martin Walker as he and his team of Delta Force operatives are sent on a reconnaissance mission to Dubai. Their objective was to locate any survivors and radio for evac. 

When researching about this game, I was surprised that this is the eight title of the Spec Ops series. This is apparently a reboot title, and the last Spec Ops title was released in 2002 for the Sony PlayStation. I bought this game from playfire.com as a promotion for the 34th Golden Joystick Awards in October 2016. It was bundled with two other games, Sid Meier’s Pirates! along with a random game. So essentially, I only paid $0.33 for Spec Ops: The Line.
I didn’t know much about this game before playing it. In late October, I played the first few chapters and I thought it was just a generic and bland third-person shooter. However, in late November, I decided to give it another try, and boy I was wrong about the game.

[h1]GAMEPLAY[/h1]
The gameplay is comparable to other third-person shooters, you can use covers, sprint, pickup items like any other third-person shooters. However, what makes Spec Ops: The Line gameplay stands out is that you can issue orders to your squad. Your squad members can be ordered to focus their fire on a targeted enemy, snipe far away enemies, and even throw flashbang or grenades at the enemy. The AI for your squad members are quite smart, so they won’t get in your way as they can move on their own as you progress, find covers by themselves, and you only need to issue those commands at certain situation. 

Some weapons have special abilities such as having a grenade launcher attachment, laser sights, scopes, and more that you can toggle depending on your needs. There are three types of grenades, frag grenades, sticky grenades and flashbangs. Sometimes you can eliminate your enemies by using the environment to take the fight at your advantage, such as shooting gas cans or even shooting glass walls to bury your enemies with sand.

And speaking of enemies, there are several types of them that you will encounter as you progress. Aside from regular enemies with guns, there are the fast-moving melee specialists, and the heavy armored troopers. The enemy will always try to find a way to flank you, thus you need to be aware of the position of the enemies and stay mobile. Some covers can be destroyed so you must be wary of what you are using as cover. There are also collectibles that you could find throughout the game, and each collectible you find will tell some story elements of the game.

The single-player consists of fifteen chapters in Spec Ops: The Line, with 4 different difficulty levels to choose from. It should take you up to 6 hours to finish the game. There’s also a multiplayer mode and a cooperative mode. The multiplayer is class-based, with all sorts of game modes. You can also level up your character and unlock new weapons that you can use in the multiplayer games. You can connect to both cooperative and multiplayer mode via Steamworks and LAN.

[h1]POSITIVES[/h1]
There are a lot of things I like about Spec Ops: The Line, one of them is the atmosphere. The city of Dubai looks beautiful with its ruins of tall skyscrapers, combine that with amazing graphics and you will end up with a game that looks breathtaking. The lighting, particle effects, and textures for a game of that time looks amazing. I would consider Spec Ops: The Line as a very optimized game, as I have never encountered any FPS drops and it could run quite nicely on a slower system. The music really fits the atmosphere of the game, and the voice acting is very genuine and believable.

The developers put a lot of details into the game, such as when you land a sticky grenade on an enemy, he will immediately run for help to his nearest mate to remove it. Sometimes it ends up with blowing them into chunks together, or the mate would just run and abandon him. Ammunitions are very scarce, so you are forced to use your weapon effectively and switch weapons from time to time. I also like how the main menu changes as the game progress. The enemy AI is fantastic as they will always try to flank you. The level design is excellent in my opinion and the weapon’s special ability also adds more depth to the gameplay.

What a lot of people praise about this game is the storyline, which I myself agree. It really escalated from being a cheesy cliché into an intense and unforgettable story. It’s really unlike any other military shooters which glorifies war, instead game focuses on the horrible things that happen in wars. It really makes you think about what is right and what is necessary. The story really impacts the player, and accompanied with a great character development makes Spec Ops: The Line’s story a masterpiece.

[h1]NEGATIVES[/h1]
One of the things that I don’t enjoy is the finicky controls. The cover system is quite unreliable sometimes and would often get you killed. Such as the time when an enemy throws a grenade at me, I sprint away, but I ended up latching on the cover behind me and died from the blast. It is also hard when using a sniper rifle or a scoped gun as the mouse acceleration is too fast. The combat gameplay alone is quite lackluster in my opinion.

Some people will find the story to be too short, as it only takes 6 hours to complete the game. I tried to play the multiplayer via Steamworks, but there isn’t seem to be anyone playing it. However, all achievements can be obtained from the single-player campaign, so it’s possible to get all of them. There are some minor issues such as lack of Steam Trading Cards which I would prefer for a game like this. I also wish some special units, such as the melee specialist would appear more often as they only appear a few times in the game.
 
[h1]SUMMARY[/h1]
To wrap it up, Spec Ops: The Line is truly a fantastic game. The smart enemy AI and the great level design make up for the lackluster combat, and the finicky controls. The multiplayer is just there, so it’s primarily a single-player game. However, I can honestly say that the story and the visuals are the ones that make this game great for me, as it really hooked me to finish the game. The story was unlike any other war games I’ve ever played, it was very dark and grim and it truly captures the horrors of war. I highly recommend this game.

The combat sections are restricted and rushed, and most notably, the few choices you have in-game are not really impactful in the story whatsoever, except for an achievement or two.

Aside from that, everything else in the game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ amazing. The story on itself is great and showcases a lot of horrible ♥♥♥♥, especially what an armed conflict can turn into. How much can you handle before you lose your head? What is the right thing to do? Are you capable of sacrificing lives for the greater good? What is the greater good? The intel files are a joy to listen to and help you understand what the hell is going on. And the ending...while somewhat predictable if you bother to find the intel pieces, still manages to throw a curve ball your way.

But there is one part in the entire game that had me stop, take a good look and almost quit it because it made me feel like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ monster. I'm not going to spoil what happens in that part, but it happens in chapter 8.

Spec Ops: The Line is the latest installment in the until-release relatively obscure Spec Ops series, and on the surface looks, sounds and plays like your incredibly generic Gears of War game, with a hint of tactical shooter. However, it is a [i]very[/i] plot heavy game. The game's premise is set around the attempted reconnaissance and rescue of Dubai's remaining citizens, after vicious sandstorms have all but razed the city to the ground.

Everything is presented as a generic shooter. [b]Everything.[/b] You have achievements and awards, multiplayer, co-op, difficulty selection, and a trio of military grunts fitting the charismatic leader, wisecrack cold sniper and big scary black dude tropes to the letter.

Graphically, it is decent. A selection of "filters" let you play the game with vibrant and saturated colours, the standard settings or the overused "real is brown". Main character textures and models are good, though the facial animations occasionally look odd, and their details clash with the otherwise technically unremarkable world and enemies. That isn't to say a destroyed Dubai isn't something to stop and gawk at - it's a sight to behold no matter where you're from.

Voice acting is superb, an essential part of character development. Sound effects are on point. The music is pretty banging when it kicks in.

Gameplay, again, is your bog standard cover shooter. Hug that chest high wall like your life depends on it, because more than likely it does. Sandstorms are an occasional gameplay element, which ruin your accuracy and your mobility whilst allegedly doing the same to enemies. They still hit you pretty often. The tactical gameplay extends to ordering your squadmates to focus fire on a single target, which may or may not simply make them run into the open and get themselves incapacitated by the other 200 enemies.

Past this point, dissecting the motifs, the game's design and characters, will be marked as a large block of spoilers, so you're free to skip it towards the conclusion.

[spoiler]Before gameplay ever happens, Dubai is ravaged by sandstorms, and the United States moves in to organise an evacuation and rescue the survivors. The 33rd Batallion moves in. The initial evacuations turn into a disaster, so they're forced to hunker down and instate a draconian martial law on the remaining survivors, to ration their dwindling supplies. They act as the only law in an otherwise chaotic region. The CIA is tasked with wiping out the 33rd and any survivors, to ensure no hostilities break out between the United States and the Middle East.

Months pass. After a lone transmission from the 33rd reaches the US, Delta Force is sent in to [b]investigate, recon and call for support.[/b] Very shortly, hostilities engage with the local insurgents, who were likely afraid Delta Force was part of the CIA. They push forth to uncover the truth behind the hostilities and to investigate on their captured American comrades. In no time flat, twisted fate has them now shooting at American forces, the Damned 33rd. Delta Force continue pushing deeper into Dubai to find the truth about Col. Konrad's motives for the 33rd's actions, and to attempt a civilian evacuation. 

They go past the point of being able to safely leave the city. They're faced with lose-lose decisions. They begin commiting attrocities without intending to. The single most controversial moment in the whole game happens halfway through the campaign, the aftermath of which Delta Force's confidence is visibly shaken as they're "turned into f-ing killers". They thought they had no choice otherwise. They, shortly afterwards, unwittingly take part in the CIA's plan to kill off the remaining Dubai citizens by destroying the last remaining water supplies. They become the mockery and scourge of Dubai.

Captain Martin Walker, the leader of Delta and the player character, continues putting the blame on Col. Konrad and intends to get revenge on him. The truth is, Delta has already caused more death and destruction than the 33rd under Konrad's leadership, and Walker tries coping with the crushing guilt of his actions by using the 33rd as a scapegoat. 
He hallucinates Konrad everywhere. The unfolding devastation mirrors his degrading mental state, manifesting through gameplay on more than one occasion. Walker's leadership is questioned by his squadmates, who revolt at his decisions and his plans despite having gone through the same ordeal as he has.

The finale is the turning point, the "Wham Episode" where all of Walker's actions were meaningless, his pursuit for revenge: pointless. It is up to the player, now, to judge Walker and decide his fate.

This is a shooter game that viciously deconstructs the "America Saves the Day" mentality; the moral choice system from other games; the heroic, altruistic, "go the extra mile" attitude; and the player's gleeful, oblivious enjoyment of the torment caused to (admittedly virtual) soldiers and civilians caught on the battlefield. You can even say the monotonous, uninspired, "seen-it-a-million-times" gameplay is done on purpose to detract from any satisfaction. It has a pretty potent anti-war message (despite the developers clarifying that this wasn't their intended statement), but it is especially designed, overall, to make the player question their decisions in other shooter games, why and how they derive enjoyment from inflicting pain and destruction. The player is instead punished as they continue playing the game, both in the form of greater damage done to Dubai, and as literal mockery on the loading screens and even as a subtle part of dialogue.

There are plenty of advocates in favour of the game's meaning, theme and execution thereof.. and just as many who oppose it, based on its overly pretentious premise. Its linear story structure works as either replicating the protagonists' despair and lack of real alternatives, or as an act of severe railroading that you get punished for following through. There's also the hypocrisy of playing the exact kind of game that is being heavily deconstructed through the story. While the developers have anticipated the kinds of responses usually garnered from players, it is still odd that a game, which costs money, is asking the player to stop playing it.

It is heavily divisive, but what it can be applauded for is having the balls to attempt delivering such a controversial message, when several other games have tried but failed.[/spoiler]

The story is short, around 5 hours max from start to finish on Normal difficulty. 

While it is flawed and extremely divisive, Spec Ops: The Line is nonetheless a unique experience and a fresh take on a tired genre. Its message and execution have sparked numerous discussions and essays that analyze its story, motifs, symbolism and so on. It is best you go in as "blind" as possible, though - it is a very plot heavy game. And if you do buy it - and I suggest you do, if only for its unique approach to the shooter genre - play only the campaign. You may replay it once or twice to see some previously unseen details, but you can't go back and experience it like it was the first time playing it any other time.

The setting is essentially a post-apocalyptic Dubai. Not the world being so, just that one city that we all know and adore for its beauty. The city was absolutely and horrifically demolished by a monstrous sandstorm that would have Mars getting jealous, and they still pop up in the game from time to time and make for some hellacious tense gameplay. The US Army sent in a ranger battallion to the city in hopes of relief effort, but they had fallen and become rogue as a civil war broke out inside that battallion. The CIA gets involved, the locals take up arms in rioting, and resistence, and your squad gets caught all in the middle of it, and are forced to fire back on US Soldiers and locals alike. There are no allies except your other two men, and even that gets put through many tests, and test you this game will. There are decisions to be made in this game, but unlike other games, there is no right or wrong, no branching path, no ultimate change in story, and it tests your morality and makes you think on just what you might do in the absolute hell that is now Dubai. On the surface in this review, that may seem like a bit of an overstatement, but play the game and see just how much it gets to you in the heat of the moment. There are *very* few games that will have the impact that this one carries, and this game is very gruesome and dark in that aspect. 

To wrap it up, this is WITHOUT A MODICUM OF DOUBT, a game that you absolutely need to play and experience. Inspired heavily by Joseph Conrad's "Heart of Darkness" (same book that inspired "Apocalypse Now") this game tackles war, jingoism, and choice in a way that takes advantage of the videogame medium.

It's a very competent third-person cover-based shooter. You have the weapon types you know to expect, the well-known enemy types, the strategically placed turret sections. As the game starts you find yourself as the leader of a three-man squad sent to the heart of Dubai, after first a natural disaster and second a whole US military company going silent. Your squad starts as a bunch of by the numbers badass types. A small "band of brothers." They are "professional." They are there for "humanitarian reasons." It's not surprising that 10 minutes in you are mowing down brown people by the dozens. It is surprising though, when a couple hours later you find yourself mowing down US soldiers by the hundreds. And that's the first hint this game is here to subvert your expectations and face you with a giant mirror.

And as the game advances it all devolves more and more for the characters, emotionally and physically. It devolves for the game menu. It devolves for the loading screen tips. You are behind the wheel fot it all and hopefully will learn something about war and yourself too.

It's also important to note how the game handles choice. As in war, there are many times when you as a player have no choice and are being railroaded by the developers. There are times when the game telegraphs you clear choices (Hey, you can stealth this section or go in guns blazing! Hey, you can choose to save this character or that character!). But then the game has several points where the choice is entirely up to you, it's up to you to even think there is a choice, and this includes the multiple endings for your character.
I would recommend this as required reading in schools. Screw Scarlet Letter and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn - this is the thought-provoking and decidedly dark story they should be exposed to.

Holy hell this game was depressing. Like most people these days I imagine, I went into this game already knowing it was a deconstruction of the modern military shooter. Hell, knowing that is the only reason I even bothered, since it's not normally my genre. But I don't think I was quite prepared for just how dark this game gets. Everyone knows the now-infamous White Phosphorus Incident, but that's really only the tip of the iceberg, the moment you're first made aware of the road you're going down. This game is one long domino sequence of poor decisions and horrible acts in which Captain Walker - a man who looks like a cross between Stephen Amell and a hawk - slowly loses himself in a desperate scramble to rationalize the increasingly ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up scenario he's put himself into.

Gameplay-wise, Spec Ops: The Line is unremarkable. A perfectly adequate cover-based third-person shooter that mostly just serves as a vehicle for the emotional ride. A few petty criticisms (the heavy troops that can tank multiple grenades are a bit incongruous, for example) are all I can really muster against it. The game gets a fair bit harder in the final act, but given it's building up to the climax that's kind of to be expected. I might be inclined to argue that there's a bit too much shooting in this shooter if that made any sense at all, as by the end you've mowed down literally hundreds of rogue American soldiers and practically every scene is bridged between firefights with fifty opponents or more. I mostly take it as a symptom of the genre, even if I'd personally prefer harder fights against fewer enemies than take on constant swarms of Clown Car Soldiers.

Not much else to say, the game is a fairly basic package containing an emotionally intense story. Pick it up if you want to feel like a complete bastard for a few hours.

If you choose to kill, there are consequences. While, at times, there isn't much of a player choice in whether to mass murder or not, and while this might feel unfair, it does this to make a point, and by George, does it make a heck of a statement. I found myself drained, and exhausted by the end of the game, but I wasn't disappointed. Everything that I did- everything that I didn't do- it really showed me the horrors of war, and brought about a new question in my mind: Is he who kills thousands, and has lost few of his own, the hero, or is he the villain?

Many of the guns feel very similar to use, and the game is rather easy if you stick to cover (although I only played on medium difficulty). There is a lot of big action sequences in this game that while really cool, are not very realistic. I think that perhaps a different approach to gameplay could have helped convey the story better.

I was recommended this game because of its story, but I found this to be its biggest let down. The story just isn't believable and player character is annoying.
I'll try to avoid spoilers.

Spec Ops is advertised as a game that will "challenge players' morality by putting them in the middle of unspeakable situations," however this never really happens, because in these 'unspeakable situations' you have no choice at all. Failure to perform whatever horrible action will cause the mission to fail, and you must load a checkpoint. I think this idea would me much better executed if instead the player was forced to choose between two bad options, rather than being simply forced to do something or the mission fails.

The player characters scripted decisions further detract from the believability of the story with him very quickly disregarding his original mission, and instead deciding to try and fix everything himself. His two companions realise that he is making bad decisions and comment on it, but for some reason never actually do anything about it and just follow along.

However there are some pretty cool action movie bad guys in this game, however their placement is what is meant to be a realistic war just makes the story less believable.

Perhaps I just don't see what everyone else does, but this game just didn't do it for me.
Spec Ops: The Line isn't a bad game, it's just not anything special. If shooters are really your then, then you might want to pick this one up when it's on sale, but if you're looking for a deep and harrowing story then you had best look elsewhere.

A competent third person shooter that stands out by delivering a story that will engage and shock you like no other. If you enjoyed Heart of Darkness or Apocalypse now or like amazing storytelling, this game is a must buy when it is on sale.

It's not often that I can play a game that has some pretty gameplay elements, and yet still be completley enthralled in its grips. Spec Ops: The Line is one of those games.

Spec Ops puts you in the shoes of a Captain leading his team into the middle of worn torn Dubai to find a Commander who has gone AWOL. What sounds like a typical war game is anything but.

Man this game takes you places other AAA gmaes wouldn't dare take you. If you enjoy storytelling with depth or games that are different from the standard crop, check out Spec Ops.

A Gripping and Unforgettable Journey Through the Darkness

Spec Ops: The Line is an emotionally charged, military shooter with an incredible story that will stick with you long after the credits roll. While the narrative is a bit on the shorter side, its impact is undeniable. It’s a tale of moral ambiguity, survival, and the horrors of war, and it takes you to places you wouldn’t expect in a shooter. The twists and turns of the story are truly something special, offering a rare depth that makes you question the very nature of conflict.

The game offers a wide variety of weapons to choose from, giving you the firepower needed to tackle the intense combat situations. However, prepare yourself—this is not a walk in the park! If you find yourself dying repeatedly (like I did, crying and cursing my way through), don’t rage quit—stick with it, because the payoff is worth it.

It’s a shame that Spec Ops: The Line is no longer available on Steam, but if you can find it on sale elsewhere, don’t hesitate. This is one game you won’t regret playing. Highly recommend giving it a try if you enjoy a gripping story paired with intense action.

Despite the underwhelming gameplay, especially considering the refinements this genre had already made on this game's release, Spec Ops: The Line redeems itself by telling an incredibly intriguing story that forces you into situations that you'd never expect to find yourself in, whether in this life or the next five or so.

I definitely recommend this game. However, there are some things you ought to know about it. 

First, about the gameplay. It's your typical third person shooter, but it is well done. It is challenging, but generally not unfair. If you enjoy third person shooters, this should satisfy that desire. 

However, I don't recommend this game because of the gameplay. The real reason to play this game is the story - an unfortunately rare case for military shooters. I don't want to spoil it, if you've somehow come across this game without knowing about the story, but it has much more depth and consideration than you might expect, that is much more befitting of the violence it contains.

Overall, this is a really incredible game - but it won't really make you feel good. If you want a mindless shooter - which can be a good release - there are better choices. But if you want a substantive story to accompany strong gameplay, Spec Ops is a great choice.

It's difficult to explain why this game is so good without spoilering it, since its best feature is how the story subverts your expectations in several key moments. To make it brief: Dubai has been isolated from the world because of terrible sandstorms. The only thing that's sure is that the military forces that were trying to keep order have failed, and the situation in the city has degenerated into anarchy.

Luckily there's you, a good old American soldier, and your two companions. You managed to get past the sandstorms and into the city. Now your mission WOULD be to simply transmit your position via radio and to wait for orders and reinforcements. But when you discover that the situation in the city is worse than you thought, that other American soldiers are killing and being killed in a civil war, you decide you can't just stand there, waiting for orders, and let things happen. You're there to SOLVE things. What could possibly go wrong?

Spec Ops: The Line was not what I was expecting when I first bought and played this game. It is easily one of the best, if not the best, games I have played in the genre of "Military Shooter" in the past fifteen years. The story is rich and deep, and the characters are memorable and worthy of attachment throughout the story. The game is unique, but does not deviate too far from what it is, which often would make a game like this feel "Mary Sue" and clunky.
