Spec Ops: The Line is a third person shooter which delves into the psychology of being a soldier who is forced to face post traumatic stress disorder and the horrible crimes of war they commit throughout their lives and the game.

The story starts off simple, you and your squad of two other men are sent into Dubai after the city has been buffeted by horrific sandstorms, effectively crippling the entire city and cutting it off from the rest of the world. Your mission is to find the source of a signal and report back to HQ, but you quickly find that the american army unit that stayed behind, disobeying orders in order to protect the people, have taken over and fully intend to kill you. As the game progresses, your characters get more and more stressed to the point where they mentally and physically break, and you are forced to question everything you have done and are doing in the game 

The gameplay is your standard third person shooting romp, complete with a nice selection of guns and only being allowed to carry two at any given time along with a choice selection of games. But, the game also has a large amount of enviromental interactivity, allowing you to turn the very ground against your enemies, or in some cases, them exploiting it to ♥♥♥♥ you over. As you progress, difficulty increases drastically, what was once a simple romp becomes a military themed hellscape with walls of bullets flying at you from all sides, requiring you to time every shot and knowing when to use your few granades. Its punishing, difficult and at the same time, satisfying. 

Visually, its a pretty outdated looking game, the textures on everything were once impressive, now old and a bit off putting. However, the further you progress in the game, this becomes less noticable as the game makes fantastic use of particle effects (smoke, fire, sandstorms, etc) to mask these textures and really helps smooth things out, while adding to the atmosphere of the levels and overall game. The soundtrack is a combination of old school music pieces, ranging from bad boyz to songs from deep purple and the black angels. There is only one original score within the game, which is just as good as all the rest. It was strange at first, listening to all these old school bands while blowing the ♥♥♥♥ out of "bad guys", but it really does grow on you, and if you pay attention to the songs they use, each one really does belong.

Now, the meat of the game is its theme. The game starts as your generic third person shooter, similar to gears of war, but gradually slips down into an exploration of morality, psychological effects of conflict and the ethical gray areas of war and peace. The decent is slow, and if you did what i did and play the entire game in about two sessions, you yourself might struggle to notice just how far you have fallen. Everything, from the way the levels look and the choices you are forced to make, to the loading screens messages reinforce this sense of psychological trauma. this disconnect from reality that happens so gradually that when you step back and look at the trail you've blazed, you don't see a heroic campaign by a team of good guys, you see blood, suffering and in the end, death. I noticed how much chaos i had caused when one of the loading screens asked me a simple question. "how many americans have you killed today?" 

Spec Ops: The Line is not the greatest shooter mechanically speaking, but it is a fantastic introspective look into the shooter genre. It is well worth the price, and i would recommend it to a vet of shooter games. If you are thinking of buying this game as your first shooter, i'd almost tell you not to, and play through several others first before approaching this in order to fully appreciate it. On its own, Spec Ops: The Line is great, and is one of my personal favourite shooters of all time, and is worth your time.

tl;dr : Not bad but not as good as it could have been. Choices don't have the impact they should have and are advertised to have.

I will start with a few thoughts to explain what I mean when I say the choices don't make you feel bad as they should (and as it has been advertised) :
 - If someone attacks you and you "choose" to defend yourself, and later you realise they attacked you by mistake, you have no reason to feel bad about your choice, since THEY still attacked YOU, so defending yourself was still the right (and logical) thing to do.
 - If you have no information and still have to make a choice, you don't feel bad about it because you just couldn't know, you had to pick an option randomly.
 - If you can't choose what you actually want to (and what would realistically be possible in real life, but just isn't an option in the game), you don't feel bad about the choice because it was forced onto you.
 - When it's obvious that there is no "good" choice, you don't feel bad because you know for a fact that the other alternatives were as bad or worse.

Maybe I'm being too rational about it, but I can't feel bad about a choice I made if I feel like I did nothing wrong. To me the decisions should have involved having enough information to make an educated choice, but not enough to predict every possible outcome, and also a good reason for options to be unavailable (because it's very frustrating to wonder "Why on earth can I not do that ? It just makes no sense !").

You're supposed to be put in "unspeakable situations", but you're not. You just have to choose "do I kill that guy or not ?", "do I strike that area or not ?" and that's basically it. No sick twisted horrible psychopathic situation you would expect when you're told about "unspeakable situations".

You're supposed to make important choices, and feel bad about them, but you dont.

There are not so many story-changing choices, and in some cases there are obvious alternatives that you cannot choose (you just have to go with one of the two possibilities the game forces on you).

Most of the time they don't really make you feel bad or hesitant since you "don't really have a choice" : there are a lot of choices where you have no information whatsoever about the situation, so you don't make a decision, you just pick randomly, and other situations where it's obvious from the start that both possibilities will have the same kind of bad consequences so it doesn't really matter what you chose. There are very few nuanced situations where you have information to make your choice but you can't predict the consequences, either you just pick whatever because you have no info or you just pick whatever because it won't make a difference. And when you realise the consequences you're like "Meh, whatever...".

Only a few choices are actually made (with information to help you make your decision) and have unpredictable consequences. And some of them are cases where the game just wouldn't let you choose an obvious alternative.

The game is not bad. But it's just a generic warfare shooter. Not worth the price (maybe get it on sale), and certainly not worth the hype.

Just to start this review off : I have payed 1$ for 3pack of games including this one (Got a discount by voting in Golden Joystick Awards 2016)
[h1]Introduction[/h1]
Spec Ops : The Line is a interesting mix of serious war story and dynamic action, all perfectly mixed. Game puts us in a boots of Martin Walker, a Delta Force Operator with 2 companions by his side, Lugo - A highly trained sniper and Adams - M249 wielding support guy equipped with grenades. 
[h1]Squad[/h1]
One of the most important mechanics of the game is commanding the said two. There are 3 types of commands :
-Stun (Orders to throw a flashbang into crowd of enemies)
-Attack (Orders squad to attack selected target, usually also suppresses enemies close to the target, effective but forces your allies to be more exposed to enemy fire which can end in them being injured)
-Heal (Availabe only if ethier Lugo or Adams happens to get shot too much, then you order the other one to heal the downed one, if both are down you need to come close to revive your allies, its quick tho)
Its not a spoiler, your squad wont be at your disposal all the time, there are a some parts when you are ethier separated or need to cover them, but you can rely on them for most part.
[h1]Plot[/h1]
We are being sent to Dubai to investigate a lost 33rd Infantry Division sent there to evac the city after the giant sandstorm which cut the city off and totally ruined it by burying it under tons of sand. Thats all i have to say in department of explaining storyline, cant say more without spoilering, and please dont play this game if you already watched playthrough of it, its not worth it just due knowing more than you should. [spoiler]Also, game has some choices through it, always think before you act. There is a line that man sometimes need to cross to do whats right. [/spoiler]
[h1]Movement and Camera[/h1]
Game is in 3rd person view, very similar to GoW in many aspects, not in a bad way! Movement mechanics are very similar to said Gears Of War, you need to rely on taking cover by pressing space by obstacles and you have an option to vault over them, it may seem awkward to PC gamers, but trust me it really suits the game. Only flaw with this system is sometimes not taking cover right after leaving a cover by "Slip Out" option (Sprinting out of cover) You need to stop before trying to take another cover because otherwise it is likely to dont do anything. Thats just flaw of the whole system, that issue was even in GoW :P
[h1]Weapons[/h1]
Game offers us a wide array of guns Pistols, Assault rilfes, SMG's, LMG, Shotguns, Snipers, Damn even Rocket Launchers and Drum Grenade Launchers. Most of the guns have additional feature activated by pressing C by default it can be a underbarrel GL, Silencer, Scope, Fire mode etc... Gunplay feels really fun and smooth, Ammo is Scarce in this game because most of the time you end up trading you weapon out because enemies use a diffrent weapon and you are out of ammo, one sure way to get ammo for any gun from any enemy are Executions, just walk to a bleeding out enemy and press melee button , animation will play and you will get some ammo, regardless if its RPG or a pistol. Other way is of course an ocassional ammo box.
[h1]AI and Difficulty[/h1]
Game has 4 difficulty levels, i personally played on 2nd lvl its like normal in most games, yet it was fairly difficult, enemies  dealt significant dmg and took a bit of dmg themselves, especially later on ingame. I did not seen any major flaws with it, they reacted fast, flanked, used nades and did their best to bring you down, If you like challenge play on 3rd one, that one is really hectic :P 
[h1]SUMMARY[/h1]
This game delivers one of the best single player experiences in shooter genere at least if we are speaking about modern times semi-realistic war setting. I would strongly reccomend getting this game, multiplayer is still playable but i didnt personally played much of it, not my jam. The real treat of this game is SP experience ;D

Spec Ops: The line is a third-person military shooter developed by Yager Development and published by 2K Games in 2012. As someone that does not play shooters often, I was quite impressed by Spec Ops despite its age and the rough graphics.
One of my highest highlights in the game was the movement and covering system in the game which was similar to the Mass Effect series. The player could hide behind a wall or object to gain protection from the shots as well as getting calibration while using the sniper rifle. This type of interaction makes the shooter extremely enjoyable and seems to have been quite advanced at the time.
The plot of the game is not extraordinary but it can be touching for quite a few of the players and it will decently break some individuals. The plot is filled with grim and sad moments which makes the player discover the horror of war as well as a nice moral dilemma when it comes to decisions and facing the consequences. Spec Ops is excellent when it comes to demonstrating the extreme actions soldiers take while put in difficult situations when no matter what option is picked, someone will get hurt.
The devs made an excellent job when it came to the characters. Some memorable individuals are you, commander Walker, Lugo and Adams, your two companions following you all the time, commander Konrad the war hero and the Radioman of the 33rd Squad. The beauty of the game is the ability to make all the people have real personalities. In fact, in the whole game no one is good or bad, but rather they are open to interpretations which sometimes makes you question the moral decisions you took and if you did the right choice. The beginning of the game shows this example by starting with an FBI agent torturing a member of the 33rd squad but later seeing this same squad using a radio to attract your team with the recording of a tortured FBI agent.
One of the features that I loved in the game is the squad system. The only teammates you have in the game are Lugo and Adams, two extremely competent soldiers. The targeting system helps you in difficult situation given orders to your squad to focus a specific soldier in the game. Lugo is the master of sniping while Adams is known for using explosives often. The system is a nice touch to the game and a unique system which I wish would get adapted by more games (and not just shooters).
The sound in the game is also good and adds quite a bit to the immersion. Civilians screaming, squad teammates as well as people getting tortured makes some scenes hard to bear.
In terms of graphics the game looks very outdated, although it is understandable for a game from 2012. The imagery on the other hand is extremely well and the immersion is great when you see the surroundings in Dubai. 
One of my big gripes with the game was the fact multiplayer is essentially non-existent, although this is understandable since the game is quite old. This issue combined with the non-existent ability to co-op makes the game 100% single-player.
Overall, Spec Ops: The line is an excellent shooter even for a 2012 game and I would recommend it any day to shooter fans even if it is just for the single-player. The game deserves a nice 8/10.

Spec Ops: The Line is a solid modern military cover third person shooter set in Dubai.  The game is on the somewhat shorter side, taking about a dozen hours at higher difficulties to finish.  For the most satisfying experience do not try to blitz through it at difficulties below Suicide Mission.  Playing on FUBAR difficulty is something else altogether.  It will be frustrating, and you will play some parts of the game maybe a dozen times in a row before you finally manage to stay alive through it, but the frustration only adds to the experience.  This is not your cookie cutter shooter about a western soldier putting evil eastern villains to the gun in heroic fashion. It's a game about a soldier having to kill fellow soldiers and worse.  It's about getting frustrated with having to kill until you literally have no choice but stop giving a ♥♥♥♥ altogether.  The storytelling is nothing short of genius and by the time it all comes together it will leave you with a twisted satisfaction and a feeling that you've experienced a new narrative standard in video games.  This is the best game I played in half a decade, maybe even longer.  Buy it, play it and keep asking yourself if you feel like a hero yet.

[b]Spec Ops: The line[/b] is a third-person shooter, with a strong storyline that's worth of Hollywood attention. However, that's not where the game really shines.

You have to be a fan of action games to truly appreciate Spec Ops: The line, and if you played on FUBAR difficulty, you know what I mean. The developers made sure everyone could enjoy it, but once you play on the hardest difficulty, small details start to make even more sense.
The aiming, the blind-fire, the cover locations, the level's details on positions and even diversity make this one of my favorite action games.
Adams and Lugo team up with our main character to take Dubai to its righteous path, under heavy fire from the rebels, U.S troops and even private military. Although there is no online co-op, the campaign is pretty much intensive. But if that's not good enough, then killing heavies on the hardest difficulty will make you feel happy!

The design team worked extensively to make sure this wouldn't be forgotten, and they nail'd it. Dubai under a crisis is perfect, with the sunsets far away on the horizon... The afternoon desert storms, the despair reflected in the abandoned luxury cars... A city in despair, and with a backstory to make you go wild.

In [b]Spec Ops: The line[/b] you make decisions that don't really matter, but they tried it, and that's halfway through. Speaking of things that could be better, we also have the stealth, that could have been away more improved, but still... Playing an extreme action game, would you go quiet? :)

I really love this game, I love how tough it is, and how well it works under pressure! Of course we all hate when our teammates die because of the stupid AI, but they have a pace of movement, and I learn it while playing on FUBAR. Once I did, I start having so much fun.
If is there any negative feelings, they are towards some areas, where playing on the hardest difficulty, become annoying. Two in particular; Last part on the Chapter 6 "[i]The Pit[/i]", where the player needs to escape, and the entire thing is based on luck. No skill, no strategy, nothing. Just luck.
The other is the famous last part in Chapter 10, where protecting the water truck can be awful due to the lack of checkpoints.

I wish everyone could have the same excitement I had with this game, and either if you're playing for the story line, or for some extreme action I highly recommend that you try it.

Spec Ops: The Line: Late To The Game.

There was a shining year this game was the ♥♥♥♥. One single year. From June of 2012 to June 2013, everyone gave this game all the brownie points, all the extra apples from the cafeteria line, everybody LOVED Spec Ops: The Line. And, at the time, after half a decade of Modern Wahfare clones, that makes sense. It's interesting of a concept, taking the basic formula of the Generic Military Shooter and twisting it's feature set to change up and critique it and the overall themes of it. It's how I got into the game, as much as anyone else buoyed in by the constant media buzz. And I played it.

And I got to the section at the "camp", realized what the game was going to do, and realized it wasn't going to let me opt out of it whatsoever. All of the choice and interest the game had just sucked out in a second.

In a modern era, SO:TL is to video games what Super Size Me was to the Obesity Epidemic. At the time of release, it was the big thing, media fanfare out the wazoo and once people realized issues behind it's points, they vacated. I've rarely heard the game mentioned in recent years, and that's not surprising. While it aims to poke fun at the issues thematically of the modern military shooter, SO:TL falls into a lot of the same pitfalls and it combined with the overall flaws of the writing make the game one of the shortest slogs I've ever gone through. The playtime I have is almost a 25/75 split between the pre-WP scene and the late game. This game at the end is a death march of spongy enemies, annoying turret sections and constant babysitting defense missions. 

You can call that a parody, and I call it lazy game design using that as a cope. A shame as the gameplay is the stellar point of this game, a fun version of a standard third person cover shooter. The graphics do still hold up fairly well as well. But the story is a flat note. If you've played Far Cry 2, you know how this ends. If you've read Heart of Darkness you know how this ends. If you've seen Apocaly-, you get the point. This game tries it's hardest to twist on that formula, and it almost succeeds. But it doesn't. The illusions of choice make you realize there's no chance to change, no attempt to break away, only follow the path. And then have the game swat at you with a ruler for doing so. 

You WILL hit those refugees with white phosphorus. You WILL follow along with a CIA official. You WILL follow The Line. Not only the literal one, but the metaphysical written one. And you'll follow a parody of a formula that Activision had dropped two years prior to this game's release with Black Ops, and which was summarily killed off with MW3 and BOII. Once people stopped caring about Iraq, they stopped caring about critiquing it. Once people stopped caring about Modern Warfare, they stopped constantly pointing out the obvious. So now this game remains as a ghost of an era that's more faded than MW2 Limited Edition Night Vision goggles.

Surprisingly good. Spec Ops: The Line is not just another shooter set in the modern day. It's very story-focused, putting you into the shoes of Captain Walker and his squadmates, and making you live through the harrowing events they had to face when deployed in war-torn Dubai. 

The game has a very cinematic feel to it. The scenes build up gradually to big climaxes, and the squadmates discussing what's going on and arguing with one another the entire time, making them seem like real people and not just mindless NPCs. In addition, the game presents you with some moral choices at times, making you think twice on your decisions and putting you in situations where neither choice can be considered good. Without giving away any spoilers, the game concludes on a mindblowing ending, or more precisely - endings, whilst leaving some ambiguity behind to let the players interpret the rest. I would highly suggest to play the game to the end and then to check the Youtube videos to see all the endings and their interpretations. 

Story aside, the gameplay is pretty fun as well. The combat is fun and for the most part consists of your typical third-person cover-based gunfights. There is some variety in the environments where you fight, ranging from desert outposts to insides of malls and other semi-broken buildings, as well as rooftops. This in turn presents some interesting challenges from time to time, such as defence sections and the like. It could get a bit repetitive, however, and some of the bigger gunfights do feel a bit messy at times. Additionally, the squadmates and the enemies wear similar-coloured uniforms, so it's very easy to mistake a fellow ally for an enemy during a heated combat. The crosshairs of some weapons turn red when on the enemy, but this isn't the case for all weapons, so it's easy to accidentally hurt your allies.

Overall I've enjoyed my time with this game. Although the combat started to get repetitive and a bit frustrating towards the end, the story makes it well worth playing the game through from start to finish. Recommended.

Post-traumatic Stress Disorder can occur following a life-threatening event like military combat, natural disasters, terrorist incidents, serious accidents, or violent personal assaults like rape. Most survivors of trauma return to normal given a little time. However, some people have stress reactions that don't go away on their own, or may even get worse over time. These individuals may develop PTSD.

People who suffer from PTSD often suffer from nightmares, flashbacks, difficulty sleeping, and feeling emotionally numb. These symptoms can significantly impair a person's daily life.

PTSD is marked by clear physical and psychological symptoms. It often has symptoms like depression, substance abuse, problems of memory and cognition, and other physical and mental health problems. The disorder is also associated with difficulties in social or family life, including occupational instability, marital problems, family discord, and difficulties in parenting.

If you are suffering from PTSD, or know someone who is, the following list of resources and information will help you find help in dealing with PTSD and related conditions.

Each VA medical center has PTSD specialists who provide treatment for Veterans with PTSD. Plus, the VA provides nearly 200 specialized PTSD treatment programs. A referral is usually needed to access the specialty programs. You can use this VA PTSD Program Locator to see if there is a specialized program near you.

NOTE: If you are in crisis dial 911 or 800-273-TALK (1-800-273-8255).

Spec Ops: The Line really wants to be the gaming industry's Apocalypse Now or Heart of Darkness. The developers want to give the player an unflinching look at the horrors and murky, moral grayness of modern warfare.  It's a subject that few developers want to tackle.  It's not fun or empowering, but it's honest and thought-provoking.  Few games have brought the subject fully to the player's attention while film has examined the futility of warfare several times over.  Spec-Ops wants to bring that same message, spoken through a game, in a genre that is overrun with games that want to make you feel like Rambo in First Blood or Dutch in Predator.  And while Spec-Ops's story certainly invokes a lot of emotion, it feels like one of those games that would rather be a movie.
	The gameplay is boiled down to moving from Point A to Point B while killing wave after wave of blank-faced enemies.  There are one of two deviations from this formula, but player agency is reduced to walking down linear hallways, hiding behind cover, and killing anyone that isn't in your squad.  That's all you'll ever be doing in a story that, although provocative, lacks in-depth characters and a plot worth following.  Everything else, from the out-dated graphics to the clunky controls, is disappointingly sub-par.  Spec-Ops: The Line rests alongside the Gears of War series and Uncharted series as games with little to no merit, better watched than played.

Sometimes I would stand up and get myself killed by accident because melee and vault over cover are mapped to the same button for whatever brilliant reason. Going into cover, as well as leaving it, requires you to sprint, which often times sent me bolting forward when I really just wanted to stand up. Would it be so hard to create a designated cover button like nearly every other cover based third person shooter? 

The story, the only thing anybody ever praises this game for, is completely linear; player decision plays a nonexistant part in it. It's main method of eliciting an emotional response from the player is by forcing you to commit senseless, atrocious warcrimes and then showing you how awful you are. It desperately wanted me to feel bad for what I had done, but failed to do so because I cant feel bad for doing something that I had literally no choice but to do. I like great storytelling in games.  I like moral choice systems in games.  I like well polished shooty action.  Spec Ops: The Line has one of these.  Just one.  But it does it so incredibly well while giving the illusion of having 2 and the third is good enough to pull through.  So I'll go a bit more in depth on these 3 elements.

Spec Ops has absolutely great storytelling.  This isn't a war game where you go to another country and shoot foreigners from behind chest high walls with the most advanced technology on offer.  This is a war game where you go to another country and shoot rogue American soldiers from behind chest high walls with adequate technology.  Rogue American soldiers have much more room for excellent storytelling because it gives the impression that you're killing men that don't deserve death and are only fighting for survival and the right thing, just like you are.  Everyone, including your character Captain Walker, is rogue and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ in the head, just trying to do something right in the wrong place at the wrong time.  You see things through his eyes, but seeing things through the eyes of a man with a fractured mind is different from what reality would be.  You make choices you think would reflect your personal decisions at the time, but after they are made, they're an outcome you hate.  It tells the story that in war, there is no good outcome, only death and horror and misery.  And that is a good story about the evils of war, the terrible things man does to fellow man.

I'll stop you right now if you haven't played the game and don't want a simple spoiler at all, because what I'm about to say could be considered a spoiler.  So go forward to the next paragraph if you don't want to know about it.  You gone?  Good.  The moral choice system is fake.  It's meant to be fake.  It's designed to give you the illusion of choices that affect the story but all outcomes are the same, this is a linear story with all choices being the same outcome.  But this is fine in this situation because it adds to the storytelling.  This isn't a moral choice system that you feel is empty and faulty, this is one that gives depth to the story because you realize it's a core part of Captain Walker's insanity and disconnection to reality.  It is an illusion, but the best kind of illusion that is welcome in the mind of a crazy man just trying to do some good in a world that is 110% ♥♥♥♥♥♥.  So despite not having an actual moral choice system, I give this game a pass on it for adding it in to enhance the story and give more meaning where they could have just left it out.

Finally, the shooting.  I play a lot of shooters.  Destiny is currently my absolute favorite for the best shooting mechanics, guns are responsive and feel powerful, bullets go where you aim, ranges, damage drop off, aim assist, and weapon stability all feel well done and polished and necessary.  Spec Ops does not have the best shooting mechanics.  Simple as that.  However, that doesn't make it bad.  You pick up a gun, you fire bullets into enemies, they die.  It gets the job done.  Some guns are incredibly inaccurate and you tend to use those only as a last resort.  Since weapon ammo is actually quite scarce, the game pushes you into these kinds of situations, forcing you to be challenged.  This game has balls, it doesn't hand you everything you could want or need and then hold your hand through the level afterwards, this system is in place to make you feel helpless and alone.  Sometimes you find a fully loaded (insert weapon of choice here) lying on a box somewhere and you feel rewarded and safer, but you can count on that ammo type to be incredibly scarce as you move through the level and you're left with the choice of leaving your favorite gun behind in favor of having enough ammo to get through the next section, or winging it with one weapon that you don't like but can count on enough ammo lying around if you don't get ♥♥♥♥♥♥.  I found meaning in this system, another choice you get to make to try to ensure survival.  The bullets don't always go where you want them to go, but it feels well done enough to get through the game and also add to the atmosphere of helplessness and difficulty in surviving in a land that actively wants you dead.

I recommend this game very highly, it leaves you feeling fulfilled but sad.  This is more of a horror game, meant to scare you and confront a darkened heart from the horrors of war.  It will not scare you in a way that traditional horror games and movies would do, but in a way where you have to confront your own opinions of war, which could be that you want to see more war or less war, it doesn't matter, but either way it teaches you that war is not something to take lightly, it is absolutely destructive to men and women who have to fight it and who simply just get caught up in it unwillingly.  And for that, I give this game high marks for being decently functional and telling a story that gives us something important to discuss that otherwise would just get ignored.

[spoiler]...Have they left? Do I have to worry anymore about spoiling the game? No? Okay. Let's get into the actual review.

Where to begin with this game? It's been a few months since I last played but I still remember this game and the effect it had on me. I see many people joking that this game should be called "PTSD simulator" but surprisingly it is a very accurate title. Make no mistake, this game will break you. 

The game follows Captain Walker and his crew consisting of a Lieutenant Adams and a Sergeant Lugo. Your mission is to go find a officer in Dubai by the name of Colonel Konrad. It is here that your descent into hell begins. At first, you're following a breadcrumb trail, trying to put together what happened here and what caused the place to get so insane. After a while everything starts spiralling out of control. 

As you go further and further into the game Walker starts making much more questionable decisions, and the unity of his team begins to fall apart. There are points throughout the game where you must make a choice, and far more often they involve choosing between two evils. By the time the game ends, you are left battered, broken, and psychologically damaged. This doesn't just happen to the characters it happens to the player as well.

No other game that I have played has made me feel like this game does. I could feel myself slipping along with Captain Walker and by the end it leaves you, the player, feeling like you have just stepped out of a warzone. There were times throughout this game when I instantly regretted the decisions I had made. Decisions that were made at the spur of the moment. Decisions that I questioned if they were the right thing to do. Here's the thing, pretty much every single decision the game has you make in this game could possibly be justified. Very few games have that.

Spec Ops: The Line is a game rife with contrast. In the sandstorm-wracked city of Dubai, refugees huddle in crude shanties erected in the opulent atriums of luxury hotels, and soldiers construct rough outposts in swanky rooftop clubs. On these makeshift battlefields, most of your time is spent casually gunning down hundreds of enemy combatants, but your squadmates still argue passionately over the value of one anonymous virtual life. Mechanically, Spec Ops is an utterly commonplace third-person shooter, but narratively, it strives to raise philosophical questions and put you outside of your comfort zone. These contrasts create some intriguing moments, but they are too often muddled by mediocre execution.

The environmental design is one of the highlights. A fierce sandstorm has left Dubai with an entirely new geography, one defined by sliding dunes and sandy canyons. Trapped by the swirling debris, the citizens are forced to create makeshift shelters amid the towering skyscrapers, carving out settlements in the luxurious wreckage. Walk just past the glittering peacock statues and extravagant mosaics to find rickety cots, shabby walls, and dirty sheets.

A battalion of American soldiers have taken up residence here too, following their failed evacuation attempt, and their military outposts add an ominous air of conflict to the landscape. The artifacts of the aborted exodus tell a story too; cars are abandoned, belongings have been left behind in a hurry, and desperate pleas for help adorn the walls.

These striking scenes are punctuated by the politically charged graffiti that some stranded artist has created around the city, anonymous accusations that target the suffering of the people (smiling images of hotel guests with their eyes hollowed out) and those who helped exacerbate an already bad situation (a skeletal news anchor holding a smiling yellow puppet). The disparate architectural and artistic threads intertwine to create a fascinating landscape, one that is a pleasure to explore. The sights are even more captivating on the PC, as the higher resolutions make for more detailed textures and richer lighting effects.

Unfortunately, no such creativity is found in the actual combat. Gunplay in Spec Ops: The Line is a simple matter of taking cover, popping out to shoot enemies, and advancing to more cover from where you will shoot more enemies. The guns you fire are a fine military array of assault rifles, shotguns, sidearms, and heavy weaponry. The enemies you fire them at return the favor vigorously but lack the kind of artificial intelligence that can liven up a firefight. There are a few neat opportunities to destroy barriers or ceilings and let the environment kill your foes, but the bulk of the time you're serving up headshots to anything that moves (and getting a nice slow-motion flourish for your troubles).

This humdrum gunplay is paired with slightly clunky movement mechanics, which might see you failing to sprint on cue or melee attacking a low barrier instead of vaulting over it. Spec Ops does not compare favorably to its genre peers when it comes to maneuvering around the battlefield, but these shortcomings are rarely an issue in the single-player campaign. In the competitive multiplayer modes, however, they become a hindrance exacerbated by your relative fragility. Some interesting map layouts, a light class system, and a nice array of objective-based modes can create some fun conflicts, but the creaky locomotion makes it unlikely you'll feel invested enough to make a significant dent in the bevy of unlockable weapons, perks, and gear options.

The campaign itself can be completed in under seven hours, and the journey you undertake is inspired by the novel Heart of Darkness, in which a man journeys upriver into the jungle to seek a powerful and enigmatic character who may or may not have gone off the deep end. In Spec Ops, you play as Walker, one of three Delta Force soldiers who arrive in search of Colonel Konrad, an American commander who took his battalion to Dubai against orders in hopes of saving the people trapped therein. It quickly becomes clear that the situation in the city has deteriorated drastically, and there are numerous factions struggling for survival.

Though your mission is to rescue survivors, the first humans you encounter are hostile. A failed attempt at communication leaves you no choice but to fight back, and this pattern repeats throughout much of the campaign, establishing one of the main narrative contrasts of Spec Ops. You're there on a rescue mission, but you just can't seem to stop killing people.

Sometimes, you are given a choice. Try to rescue the potentially friendly operative, or save two innocent civilians? Who is guilty, the man who stole water for his family, or the soldier who administered harsh justice? There are no right or wrong decisions, just a difference in who dies and how. These moments shine a spotlight on your squad chatter as Lugo and Adams chime in on the situation you are presented with. They generally argue different sides and react strongly to what you do, but your character's response is almost always to bully them with talk of "doing what's right" or "doing what you had to do." Then it's back shooting the guys who are shooting at you and exchanging profanity-laden victory shouts. The moments meant to encourage reflection fade to the background, drowned out by the overriding narrative justification of self-defense.

There are some story moments that make an impression, however. There's a humorous homage to the similarly inspired movie Apocalypse Now, and a number of licensed songs are piped in to the battlefield to set an appealing fatalistic tone. Both of these examples are the work of the mysterious Radio Man, a disembodied and incongruously jocular voice emanating from speakers rigged throughout the city. Other moments force you to look at the horrors you've wrought, but these often feel cheap because you so rarely have a choice in your action. It's not until late in the campaign that Spec Ops gets more daring and disruptive with its storytelling, but by then it feels like too little, too late.

The disconnect between the gameplay and the narrative elements of Spec Ops: The Line is numbing, which makes it more difficult to contemplate the murky morality of war in the way the game wants you to. There are some intriguing things to be teased out of your adventure through the lovely ruins of Dubai, but the contrast between ambition and execution makes the experience as unsteady as the shifting sands.

[b]THE GOOD:[/b]

+ Engrossing amalgam of art and architecture
+ Memorable moments, both humorous and shocking

[b]THE BAD:[/b]

- Stiff movement mechanics
- Relentless killing overrides moral dilemmas

[h1]Spec Ops: The Line, Hopefully Helpful Review (Also spoiler free)[/h1]
TLDR below

I'll just call it Spec Ops in this review.
Spec Ops starts with an introduction on the situation of Dubai. You play as the commander of Delta Recon Squad, Captain Walker. After an introduction to just how bad the situation is, you get into combat, and the story really begins.

This is a game about choices. When I say that, I do not mean it is open world and I do not mean you can do anything. This is a game with a pre-crafted story, and there are limitations. That being said, the game delivers the choices you can make very well, with some being extreamly obvious and some not. There are portions of the game that you will really feel should be a choice(those of you who have played through the game know the point I'm talking about), but part of the game is also NOT having a choice.

The game plays as a third-person cover shooter. Cover is your friend. Use it. Really, you may regen health but you can easily die.

My recommendation for playing this game is to play through it all at once. The campaign is ~6 hours so this is easy to do. Do not play this game with a meta mindset. This game is one that you throw yourself into, immurse yourself into the story and play it. Get into the game and let it toss your emotions and thoughts around, and I promise you will love this game.

This is a weird f#cking game. Feels like the Anti-COD of Doody, and I must say I f#cking love it. However it does have issues that you should know, and that’s where I’ll start:

First and foremost, the gameplay. It’s a third person shooter and sticking to cover is a must, however sh#t doesn’t always work as it’s meant to work. At times you try to stick to one cover and end up sticking to another. At times you try to do something simple, and end up doing something else entirely, and probably end up dying stupidly. There are also a few bugs on it, although not game-breaking at all.

The only other problem the game has is the multiplayer, and this one must be explained as it’s actually quite interesting: The devs didn’t actually wanted to add it, the publishers however though that a military shooter HAD TO HAVE IT and asked the devs for it. When they refused, the publishers hired ANOTHER TEAM OF DEVELOPERS to make the multiplayer, even against the wish of the original devs. And what happened? The multiplayers sucks balls at sucking balls. The coop is decent if you have a  friend to go through it and have a laugh or two, but I wouldn’t really recommend playing this game’s multiplayer AT ALL. The devs didn’t want it there to begin with, so ignore it as if it didn’t exist. If anything, just insult the publishers for trying to force this game to follow the sh#tty standards of this sh#tty gaming generation.

Ignoring that though, what do we have left? Hell, that’s what we have. The game takes a rather serious look at how war actually is, rather than the classic “HELLO, YOU’RE MERRICAN WHICH MEANS YOU’RE A GOOD GUY AND PRACTICALLY INVINCIBLE, NOW GO OUT THERE AND SHOOT DEMOCRACY AND FREEDOM TO ANYTHING THAT MOVES” kind of games. It’s a heavy story-driven game, and you gotta get deeply involved into it to like it, but seriously, 9 times out of 10 you’ll like it every time.

The music is also something I liked about this game quite a lot. Not only the licensed music that plays and quite seriously fits in, but the original themes made for the game, especially as it goes on and on.

The characters themselves are also worth mention. All the important characters of the game are seriously well written and truly feel real, even if some characters on the story don’t develop too much. The writing is also spot-on with the story and the meaning behind it, and might even make you feel bad once you actually do SEE what they meant.

Is it a good game? It is. And it’s quite the experience. However, it’s more like a movie than an actual game, and you should seriously play it for it’s story rather than the gameplay. On a sale, this is quite the steal. Do you feel like a hero yet? 

TL;DR Edition: It’s a big “F#CK YOU” to games such as CoD, which show that war is all fun and shooting chickens in the head. Really, seriously good story and average gameplay, the multiplayer should be ignored entirely as the devs didn’t even want it and the publishers forced it there. A good purchase on a sale.

Before I review this game, I have to make a very important note: This is not a good representation of real events or a representation of the army in general. This is a fictional story. By playing this game, you're walking into a "War is bad" propaganda campaign with some unrealistic consequences. I am reviewing this game for what it is, a game, and nothing more.

So basically, you're playing Captain Walker, a Commander Shepard lookalike who leads a 3 man squad (including himself) through Dubai in order to evecuate the city. What follows is a series of bad choices and some action scenes taken directly from a Michael Bay movie. Without revealing too much, I'll let you know, the game is quite thrilling. The combat is somewhat enjoyable, it's challenging (on suicide mission difficulty, at least), the overall feel is very hurt-lockerish and the voice acting is solid.

As I was mentioning before, the plot is completely bonkers and serves one purpose only: to shove anti war agenda up your ass by forcing choices down your throat, that basically, doesn't really matter. We get it, "War is bad", "Killing innocents is bad". Why do you have to spell it out for us? at one point the game clearly mocks you for events occuring in the game and asks you if "You're a feeling like a hero yet?", or tells you that "It's just a game, you shouldn't really care". Mixed signals, game! Mixed signals. You're making everything so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ dramatic, but then tells us nothing matters, so which is it?

Other than this pretentious plot, I recommend playing the game if you're into cover shooters. It doesn't offer anything new, it isn't mind-blowing or anything, but it does provide a challenge, and most probably it's also fun in multiplayer (but I'll have to say almost anything is better with a multiplayer).

I wish I could give this a mixed rating, and at this point I still am unsure of whether I should recommend it or not... 
I guess I'll have to say, play it, but only if you get it in a deal.

Lets look at spec ops: the line and see if it is a good. I will go over the game in a pro con style while trying to provid as much detail as i can to get my point across.

   Enjoyable story. At times the game will throw you a curve ball making the player reaccess what is going on through the game. You might think you know the story but with twist thrown in making the player keep thinking about actions or choices they have done.

That isnt in this game.

    Ai support orders are a unique mechanic to this game since if the player is stuck in a heavy fire the game would sometimes say press the squad button to throw a flash bang or used the squad button to mark out a sniper to be taken out by the ai.

    Some environment hazzards. The player can shoot some objects like explosive barrels but that is really casual for shooter games to have that. Here you can shoot glass that has trapped sand. So what some might say but what is cool is that this is one of the ways to kill off your enemies. Yes this is pressent is very few locations but it is a mechanic worth mentioning allowing players to save ammo and have an alternative to killing enemies with bullets.

Con:
   Poor Ai. The ai do some really stupid things like moving forward while under heavy fire or moving out of cover to apply suppressive fire. These moments will cause the ai to go into bleed out. What sucks is when the ai's bleed out timer runs out then its game over. Most of the time you will get a game over from the ai rather than you dying personally.

   Enemys throw gernades like mad at times and really accurate at it too. This is very apparent on the hardest difficulty called FUBAR (♥♥♥♥♥♥ Up Beyond All Repair). The enemies would toss gernades right at you many times, what would be nice is if we had the ability to toss the gernades back. Another thing gernades are very weird on how they work. Conclusion:

I would reccomend this game to all who are interested in shooting games and i offer one advice you cover. This isnt like call of duty where you can rush into combat with no real worries here you need to use cover to survive and take enemies one by one making a safer passage to move up to the next cover.

Spec Ops: The Line is an excellent example of why I no longer trust video game reviewers. Somewhere along The Line between entertainment and art, curators and plebs alike decided that a game with a point was somehow exempt from basic rules of gaming. It’s like if Mona Lisa spat on everyone who looked at it we’d still consider it genre-breaking. Except, Spec Ops isn’t Mona Lisa, it’s a trite piece of undercooked antiwar masturbation that appears to fear rupturing an aneurism if it avoids a cliché. Admittedly, I am comparing it to my larger recollections of war stories, not the current state of the subject within games. Compare Spec Ops to Stanley Kubrick’s Paths of Glory and the chasm between entertainment and pacifism Spec Ops apparently thinks unavoidable appears more of an artificial border. That is to say, Paths of Glory is every bit as cynical as Spec Ops but with half the tedium.
I am not the first to point out that Spec Ops is a horrible game. Its benefactors admit this with the caveat that it somehow lends credence to its message. The Cynical Brit said it “isn’t a good game per se, it’s deliberately mundane 3rd person shooter which makes you think about the horrors of war.” It’s the “deliberately mundane” that irritates me. A deliberately mundane game is often indistinguishable from an incompetently mundane one. Cover-based gunfights that can be best described as soggy could be a statement about the stupidity of war, or a testament to how hard it is to make crisp-feeling third-person firefights. Considering that Gears of War is the only successful such attempt in recent memory, it’s all too convenient to say the gameplay was supposed to be bland. The blurb from its Steam store page describes this allegedly meaningful mediocrity as “tactical squad-based Delta Force gameplay throughout a horizontally and vertically oriented world”. Perhaps I expect too much, but anyone who pens prose such as this should not be trusted to make any adaptation of the Heart of Darkness. The memorable part of the gameplay is being constantly overwhelmed by hugely boring enemies who appear to be completely fungible with the exception of a single heavy type, who by describing as ‘heavy’ I have already imparted more information about their humanity than the game ever bothers to. Which is another issue with the deliberately mundane hypothesis. The storyline meshes with the gameplay precisely not at all. As I stand knee-deep in American soliders I shot to death because they stood between me and the next cutscene I’m expected to find my accidental shelling of a few dozen civilians the moral low point and story high point of the entire affair. Why? Ten minutes ago I intentionally killed men whose principal crime was proximity, and now I’m expected to feel remorse over the ones I offed on accident? Perhaps the convenience of intentionality ran dry by this point in the plot, because apparently designing mundane gameplay does matter yet designing to murder does not. Who’s ever heard of manslaughter anyway?
While I’m worrying about intentions, this game does an impressively bad job of concerning itself with mine. Sometimes, I was killed by the nameless faceless ‘baddies’ because I was too bored to be bothered to think about any kind of tactics. The rest of the time, I was killed because the game figures “run headlong into the enemy” and “cower beneath chest-high wall” are basically synonymous. Neither was any quick recovery possible, because unlike in Gears of War, the far superior gameplay progenitor of Spec Ops, I could not reverse my inertia with the tap of the ‘don’t-get-killed’ button. Instead, I stood to my full height, rearing my all-American chest to their all-American steel, slowly reoriented myself to our homeland and attempted to correct the game’s mistake.
But allow me to judge this “Story Rich” and “Political” game by its story and politics. Besides the name Conrad, the only feature Spec Ops retains from the Heart of Darkness is inexplicable motivations. And I don’t particularly appreciate that in the original text. Why does the protagonist continue on? That his unwilling companions constantly question him only compounds the issue by making it apparent. The complete lack of confusion on his part lulls the player into a blind acceptance of the plot, as we are presumably supposed to feel about the soldier’s acceptance of their mission drift. If you’re wondering where the plot holes are, just list the plot points. Why does he continue on into the city despite his orders about the retaining wall? To save the soldiers he watched die? What about the rebels who kill those soldiers; why do they vanish? Why does he accept the CIA so readily, while accepting that his fellow soldiers must die? And at no point do his Delta force underlings question him. These are men who are better educated and generally older than the average soldier: Men who are trained to question things normal soldiers aren’t. Even at the end, the last underling can’t bring himself to actually defy the protagonist. He merely won’t go with him any longer. Apparently, Conrad’s existence is enough to throw the protagonist into a fit of vengeance but his murdering of fellow soldiers, disregard of common sense, morality, and orders isn’t enough to inspire anything but words from his compatriots. I suppose they made the mistake of not being player-controlled characters.
The Heart of Darkness doesn’t work without xenophobia. Chinua Achebe was right to point out that the text portrays Africans as inhuman, but it’s a necessary literary move for the text to work as a whole. It may be wrong, but you can’t just take the xenophobia out and expect the story to survive. Unless you’re Spec Ops. There are no foils for “good” Europeans to be compared to within the game. No “savages” on the shore to provide a visceral reminder of what the main characters are pretending not to be. All that’s left is people acting strangely. The ideology of imperialism cannot even be mocked if there are no apparent victims to it. And the handful of quivering refugees are as easily regarded the victims of the sandstorms as they are of the American military industrial complex.
My principal emotions from playing the entirety of this quagmire of a game were frustration, confusion, and apathy. Frustration with the gameplay which clearly hated itself, confusion as to why any of the characters were doing almost anything they did, and apathy at the results of the decisions I didn’t understand. If this game is political, what political views should I take away from it? That we should be careful before dropping mortars on thermal signatures? That Delta Force commanders should not have total jurisdiction over places at which they just arrived? There is no political message here that is any less tedious or obvious than the game itself. Unless you need an eight-hour reminder that killing is bad (m’kay), stick to Bioshock for literature-inspired gaming.

I'll start this review by saying that i purely played this game's campaign. That being said, the campaign's story is excellent. It forces you to make tough descisons and makes you witness the result, which is usually horrifying. This game really made me feel like a cold blooded killer sometimes. The gameplay, however, was not as pleasing. It was just your average cover shooter, which was slightly excuseable, since it was kept realistic for the story. Also, it was really short. Overall, if you want a refreshing take on the story of military shooters, this ones for you.

Although on the surface this looks like your average third person war shooter, that couldn't be farther from the truth. Underneath that thin layer of average shooter game fluff is a dark message about the PTSD, the horrors of war, and the civillians caught in between it all.

Overall, this game was actually pretty good. In fact, I was fooled into the predictability of the game. What do I mean by that? This game almost from Chapter One leads you to believe there is one man behind all the chaos and destruction in Dubai when in fact we come to find out in the last chapter that is not true at all. The game leads you down a path, the same one Walker is taking, and in the end, both your character and YOU find out that path was never real. It was of your own creation. In that sense, the game roped me in, which made it feel predicatble until the end when I realized even I had been fooled. In that sense, the game gets my thumbs up.

In addition, the horror of Dubai and the internal war within the city are also well portrayed, from the mistakes you make on your journey to do good to the multi-front war being waged by citizens, soldiers, and insurgents. 

Overall, the story itself was actually pretty good. That being said, I don't feel like the game really ever challenged my morality. The "choices" you must make never really pulled at me or made me question my squad's integrity. Maybe I'm just a monster, Who knows?

The combat system was another pit to the game. I did like the constant lack of ammo (relatively speaking), but the combat itself was the same every time. Once you figure out how the enemy works, you can pretty much guarantee victory every time. It was pretty predictable to me. That being said, I did like the different enemies. I also liked how easy it was to die because it made me realize I couldn't pull some Call of Duty bulls**t and hero charge every enemy while taking minimal damage like I was the Master Chief warring with infant soldiers.

The squad command system in this game sucked. I'm sorry, well actually I'm not, but it really did. The static command system rarely benefitted your squad or you often enough to really impact the game. I wish there were a diversity of commands like flank or clear or something. I also wish the commands could have been individual commands instead of two stock squad commands, only one of which could be used freely while the other required you to be "pinned down" to use it. 

In conclusion, the game was pretty good, and I'd venture to say that I hope these developers come out with a new game similar by comparison but more immersive than this title. All in all, this game gets a 7.5/10. Not bad, pretty good, but not great. I'd recommend this game to someone looking for something different, like a legitimate story behind the rifle instead of the rifle palooza most shooters have become.

P.S. Don't take my earlier Call of Duty comparison to mean I am one of those die-hard Call of Duty players who runs around no-scoping dual wielding bazookas. I am a man who appreciates a good story behind my games.

Honestly it seemed like Yager Development wanted to tell a story and put it out there in the most familiar, comfortable and easy to sell format possible: a chest high wall cover based shooter set in the Middle-East where white dudes with guns shoot up some stuff.  But folks, look beyond the chest-high walls and mediocre gameplay we've all seen a million times and you'll find a military based shooter set in the Middle-East that DOESN'T glorify war or congratulate you on shooting up a million people from some other country.

[h1]Quick Intro (spoiler free)[/h1]
Walker, a squad leader of a Delta Special Forces unit, and his squad-mates, Adams the heavy weapons operator and Lugo the sniper and technician, get deployed into a sand-storm stricken Dubai undergoing a crisis. When the game begins, Walker mentions that his orders are to find survivors and evac the city with his squad and presumably head to safety. He decides to stay around because he recently picked up an emergency broadcast from John Konrad, leader of the 33rd battalion of the U.S armed forces. Walker really admires Konrad for his bravery and heroism. Last anyone knew of Konrad, he was trying to save some civilians evacuate Dubai safely. Walker decides to look for Konrad and save him and the civilians with his squad, and the events of the game unfold from there.

This game brings nothing new to the table in terms of gameplay, but here are some things it was really good at:

[h1]Strengths[/h1]
[list]
[*] Story. It has you asking questions and every answer leads to more confusion about what it all means. The ending may or may not answer all your answers. It had twists and turns and even if you've thought you'd seen it all before, it may still get you. Even now as I try to recall good details from the game I think of the overall story in retrospect and have one of those moments where another thing suddenly makes sense. In my experience, only good stories make you do that. Also, the loading screens start off by giving you tips about gameplay and when it thinks you've known enough about the mechanics and the story at some point, it just starts taunting you and making you question yourself. Nice little touch there.
[*] Character building. Walker and his mates fly in with a cool head, ready to be heroes and save the day. By the end of it, quite the opposite. Walker and his squad mates get more jaded over the course of the game, they not only look visually more tired and beaten up, Walker's executions on enemies get more brutal, his voice and speech get harsher etc. Other key characters don't feel crowbarred in, they all have a role to play and are vital to the story one way or another. You start liking some, you start hating the guts of others, and for others, both. While WASD moves Walker and left click makes him shoot the gun, from a story perspective you'll start questioning whether or not you really are controlling Walker or if he just starts making his own decisions you're not necessarily on board with. Play the game, then go over all the decisions you would have personally made instead, you'll see what I mean.
[*] Command gameplay. Cover based shooters are as easy as it gets. No part of the game was all "that" hard, even on the second-hardest difficulty (hardest is locked off the get-go). That said, commanding the team proved useful in tight situations and after a while it felt like the game would be much more challenging without them, be it them providing cover fire, sniping a hard to hit target, or just tanking shots while the enemies' heads exploded via Deagle.
[/list]
Briefly, the story and narrative was good. It's worth the money just for that, and if you like cover based brown sandy shooters then go for it.

That's not to say it's a perfect game.

[h1]Weaknesses[/h1]
[list]
[*] Cover based shooting. It's overdone and boring. This game did not try to innovate the shooter gameplay, let alone innovate cover based shooting.
[*] Terrible controls. Good lord the controls are terrible and bad. Can't count how many times I've died because I wanted Walker to take cover behind a wall, only for him to walk over to another one a few feet further and crouch in front of a whole bunch of enemies' direct fire. Then you start spamming shift so he'd try to vault over the wall to safety, but those seem to be random. That just didn't work for me half the time. Weapon pickup is garbage and in the heat of battle could be confusing, squadmates tend to get in the way sometimes, and really getting "cover based" shooting wrong in a cover based shooter is hard to fogive. Again, terrible controls..
[*] Not the best graphics I've seen, even for a 2012 title. It was a really late xbox 360/ps3 release and looked like it. Not the end of the world but the graphics annoyed me until the story got a hold of me.
[*] There's a gimmick they try to introduce where you can shoot surfaces holding back sand, so the sand can flood in and give you cover or bury enemies. Problem is, it was rarely there and even then not that useful unless it was required to progress the story.
[*] Kind of a weakness of the plot, but also one of the main twists of the plot. Big spoiler, so mouse-over at your own risk: [spoiler]Walker is going crazy and starting to imagine and hear stuff that leads to bad things. Walker was doing the right thing in his head since the beginning by going into Dubai and trying to find Konrad. About halfway through the game he starts "hearing" Konrad over the radio, whereas it's just his imagination. Where does his delirious state take the best of him which eventually leads to him napalming 47 civillians? Was the whole plot hinged on Walker just going nuts at some vague point near the beginning of the game? Was some guy going psycho the only reason the only hope for Dubai gets screwed? Nothing really quite scratched that itch for me. Also, when did he get seperated from his squadmates and get on top of the tower? At what point does that happen if he gets comfy enough to paint a giant picture of the napalmed civilian scene? Or was that supposed to be his imagination? [/spoiler]
[*] Also spoilery: [spoiler]I might me missing something here, it's very likely that I am. But if the Radioman takes orders from someone above him, and Konrad was dead since the storm hit, and Walker wasn't taking his place if that somehow makes sense, who was the radioman taking orders from? One of those questions I'm guessing the whole "Walker is going cray cray" thing is supposed to answer but that only excuses so many things.[/spoiler]
[*] Grenades were scarce and not too effective. The mechanic could have used some work, like making them easier to find or giving them more of an impact. I rarely bothered with mine.
[*] Is it me or was the M249 SAW the best gun in the game? First shot accurate with fair damage means 1-2 quick headshots kills almost anything, and that thing has ammo for days. A secondary Deagle and you're all set, no need to change weapons at all.
[*] [spoiler] And yes I'll go for the low hanging fruit because no one else will. That room with the flashing lights and the LITERALLY teleporting armored heavy was stupid and made little sense. Yes you could blame it on Walker going nuts especially since his squad mates weren't close by but even from a gameplay perspective, it was plain annoying.[/spoiler]
[/list]

If the Call of Duty franchise is a well-oiled machine, Black Ops III is the replacement part that keeps the wheels moving into yet another year. It introduces minor changes to an established formula, and in some aspects, this is developer Treyarch near its peak. But in other areas, Call of Duty: Black Ops 3 lacks inspiration.

Treyarch has set a high bar with its contributions to the Call of Duty series. The first Black Ops introduced a twisting, engaging campaign with vivid characters and historical conspiracies. Black Ops II revamped multiplayer customization, lending deeper player choice to a fine-tuned competitive experience. And now there's Call of Duty: Black Ops III, a shooter reaching in several different directions with vastly different results.

The rare AAA game that manages to grasp for the vaunted (phantom?) classification of "art", Spec Ops the Line is mechanically simple, but its presentation and narrative elevate it to something greater. On paper a straight forward 3rd person cover shooter bringing little new to the table, Spec Ops manages to build an identity by masterfully subverting one of action gaming's sacred cows: the lionization of the military, and of heroic adventurism in particular. Although there is a meta-commentary running through on the player's implicit guilt in the entire affair that doesn't always hit the mark, the in-world narrative has more than enough meat to provide a refreshing take on armed conflict in games, and the reliability of narrators in an interactive medium.

Spec Ops: The Line is best described by a metaphor. It is an AKM in the hands of a first-year philosophy student at UCLA. The shooting is serviceable and fine for what it is, but unpolished because no amount of polish will shine that particular turd up. The story hates itself for what it's doing, hates you because you're in this situation too, and hates the society that has made doing these things normal because if we all just put the gun down and talked none of this would be necessary.

"If we could all just stop being self-interested, stop being selfish and angry and thinking only about what we want," says Spec Ops: The Line, "maybe the world would be a better place and you wouldn't have to listen to me preach at you about ethics and how your choices don't matter, you filthy murderer."

This was actually a very surpising game. I really did not think I would have liked it as much as I did since I am not a huge fan of modern military shooters. The main reason why I tried it was because I kept hearing great things about the way the narrative was handled and I was not let down. It does not glorify war or the military and it actually felt like the developers put a lot of time into developing the story. In this game, story came first, and the multiplayer aspect came second, and that is something that is a bit rare in shooters nowadays. So without further ado,  here's my review.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1] 

The game is a third person shooter and has all the stuff that is considered standard in third person shooters nowadays: cover system, grenade projectory, blind shooting, etc. In terms of shooting, the game really brings nothing new to the table. It is all pretty standard shooting and the enemies provide a decent enough challenge. The player does have a squad that they can order around, but it pretty much boils down to the player telling them to just focus on a specific target or throw the occasional flashbang. A fun little mechanic, but nothing that is very innovative for the genre.

At times the controls can be a bit clunky and I have died a few times because my character got stuck in cover, but it doesn't detract that much from the main game. Since the shooting is a bit standard and the controls are a bit clunky, the multiplayer really is not that great, so if that's what you're looking for, don't get this game.

 In terms of gameplay, it really isn't anything revolutionary.

[h1] Story [/h1]

This is where the game really shines, and people who have played the game would probably tend to agree with me. It actually does a great job at providing a mystery for the player to figure out and the reveal is very well done.  The main idea of it is that sometimes it is not always clear what decision is the right one, especially in times of war. It shows a much different "war" than we are used to seeing in video games. One where not all the player's actions are not necessarilly the right or wrong choice. They are choices where, at the time, you thought for sure they were the right decision. (Or you thought for sure they were the wrong decision, if you're a bit sadistic.) 

The characters are actually pretty well developed too. I'll be honest, when I first started the game, I thought the characters were going to be the typical military charracter that we find in lots of media. You know the trope I am talking about, the "I aint got time to bleed" guys. I was pleasantly surprised to see that while the characters were tough, it wasn't their defining trait. The interactions they have after some of the situations they get into are quite believable and the player's squadmates have pretty distinct characteristics. When they disagree with the player, they let it be known. I like how the developers handled this in particular because in the beginning of the game when they disagree with the player, they just give you a certain look or something subtle. As the game progresses and the squad starts to see more and more horrible things, that subtle look of contempt turns into more obvious displays of their dissatisfaction. 

The strongest part of the story have to be both the main character (the player) and the villain. The trauma that a soldier experiences in times of war is depicted very well in the mental state of the main character. The way they depict how the main character starts to question the morality of his actions and why he is even fighting is just something that you don't typically see in games that are centered around the military. And that's really all I can safely say without completely spoiling anything.

A fictional war game where the carrot of choice is dangled in front of the player frequently. The graphics and setting, to me, were the best part of this game. The attention to detail is great and lends a real element of immersion to the world. However, the gameplay, which is where I'd put the most emphasis, I found to be incredibly lackluster. I found myself fighting the controls more than the enemies in the game. This game relies heavily on a cover mechanic (that is also mapped to two other functions) and often times is unresponsive or downright broken. More times than I would have liked to count, I was in cover, was moving along cover, and then all of a sudden would be out of cover and get shot to death. A GAME WITH A COVER FEATURE SHOULD ONLY UNCOVER WHEN I PRESS A BUTTON. OTHERWISE, DON'T FORCE COVER. It could honestly only be a problem with the PC version if the game was designed around consoles, but regardless, it happened enough times to sour my taste to it by the end. The next gripe about gameplay is the ammo system. The devs clearly didn't program this aspect of the game well at all. If 30 enemies are bearing down on you with automatic weapons nonstop, you'd think they'd have a few magazines worth of ammo on them, eh? But no, if you fight 30 guys and go to collect ammo after a fight, they will have like 4 different varieties of guns amongst them and if you are lucky, you will find about 20 rounds of ammo for a gun that suits your current needs. All the immersion the graphics and attention to world-detail that were brought really just collapsed under this awful system. To sort of strengthen this point, the ammo cap for all weapons is ridiculously low for the amount of enemies per section. So, the game is really designed around keeping you low on ammo the whole time for arbitrary reasons. The gunplay by itself, though, is fine and actually enjoyed it a fair amount. The story is nothing to write home about, although it's what everyone who plays this game talks about. They were going for a Fight Club vibe where everything you do makes sense in a sane and insane context. Otherwise, it's obvious early on you have a soldier going rogue that you can't do anything about (oreders at the outset were to radio for more troops. They get disobeyed like 30 minutes into the game) unless you just quit the game. The main protag's name is Walker, too, which I find highly ironic considering how many cinematic, slow walking scenes are incorporated throughout the gameplay. It didn't add anything to the story for me and could have just as easily been achieved by a cutscene. I think my overall impression of this game is that it should have a been a decent movie, but instead they made a mediocre game out of it. I would personally not recommend anyone I know to play this game, hence the score, but if you are absolutely dead set on playing this, it's worth maybe one playthrough with Flawless Widescreen on PC to bump up the FOV. I also wouldn't pay the full $30+ asking price; definitely check it out on sale if you must.

Spec Ops: The Line is trying to tell an emotional story about the tragedy of warfare, mixed with third-person shooter combat.

I appreciate what it was trying to be, but ultimately I think it largely missed the marks, falls flat, and is just kinda bad. 

From a gameplay perspective, its actually really bad. The controls are floaty, movement is sluggish and unresponsive, getting into or out of cover is very finicky. All weapons are innacurate with way too much bullet spread, ammo capacity is low, and enemies will soak up bullets like sponges sometimes even surviving multiple headshots.

But what about the story, the main focus of the game and the thing people like about it?

The story is meant to be this dramatic rollercoaster where the rug keeps being pulled out from under you, so you don't know what to think, but when analyzed as a whole it actually just doesn't make any sense. You're initially told that your goal is to just radio for evacuation for civilians and the 33rd army, and leave, but you get sucked in by trying to reach the character "Konrad". 

You're given false "choices" like.. shoot the guy or don't shoot the guy. But either way, the same consequence happens, making the choices irrelevant. 

Apparently, the CIA is evil and killing people. The 33rd army is evil and killing people. We, the good guys, are killing literally everyone. Just kidding, the CIA doesn't matter and the 33rd are actually good guys, and we keep killing everyone. 

After this second playthrough I went and researched the game to make sure I wasn't somehow missing something huge, and I wasn't. After having watched a story analysis video and a video of the various endings, im not missing anything.

The game tries so hard to confuse the player and surprise them with horrific story twists, that it completely loses it's own plot, and the gameplay feels largely tacked on as an afterthought. I usually can get into firefights no problem, but I found it so... sluggish, like it was a chore I had to get through, and then i started feeling that way about the whole game.

I kinda feel bad for saying it, but, Spec Ops: The Line is just a really bad version of Gears of War. I couldn't help but think, almost the entire game, that everything feels worse than Gears 1 and 2 which came out around the same time. 

The story is nonsense and ultimately un-impactful, they had a good concept but bad execution. Story: 3/10

The gameplay was overall lackluster, buggy, and feels bad in every case, other games from the same era did it better. Combat: 4/10

Voice acting, sound effects, graphics. Compared to the rest of the game, 9/10

Overall it was pretty disappointing. I did not have fun, and can't recommend anyone to play it themselves for all the reasons stated above. I guess its fine that you can't buy it on steam anymore. 

Overall Rating: 4/10
