First and foremost I must note that I own this game both on PC and Xbox360.

On Xbox, I enjoyed it thoroughly because of its storytelling and the welcome balance it provides when compared to games like Call of Duty's single player campaign, which are basically just glorifying the slaughter of faceless enemy soldiers. You're a hero. They're the bad guys. Easy as that. If that's your kind of game, you probably shouldn't play The Line. If you choose to anyway, prepare to be dissapointed.

The Line will not reward you for the kills you make. Instead, it will constantly make you doubt yourself and the decisions you've made. Your enemies aren't necessarily bad guys. You're not a hero. Are you shooting the right people? Is their aggression justified? Your duty is to get your squad through the horror-filled city state of Dubai, and that's what the single player campaign is all about.

In essence, The Line starts out the same as any other third person shooter. You command a squad of two Delta Operators, an Assault- and CQB-specialist and a Sniper. You are their superior officer, and as such, you call the shots. A nifty one-button function lets you command them to either stun a group of enemies with a flashbang, snipe an enemy over long distances or focus their fire on a single enemy so you can circle around and flank. This is the base of The Line's combat mechanics.

There's a reasonable arsenal of weapons, including assault rifles, sniper rifles, pistols, shotguns and submachine guns, even light machine guns. Enough tools to work with, I'd say. Each weapon has its own feel and specialty. Assault rifles work well on mid-range, SMG's work best up close and machine guns quickly paint an area with lead.

As I said before, this game was a blast to play on the Xbox 360. It's obviously made for the consoles. This is important to note, because on the PC it feels like a lazy port. Which would've been fine, if that didn't make it completely unplayable with a mouse and keyboard. There's a bug in the settings that sets your mouse sensitivty to >800. I don't think have to explain to anybody what that does to your game experience.

It really breaks my heart to give this game a negative recommendation because I honestly loved the story and how it's told. If you're willing to play it with a controller, I'm sure you'll have a very compelling, cinematic experience. If you're anything like me and you want to have the option to play with a mouse and keyboard, forget it. Not going to work. Even after trying to revisit this game two years after purchasing it the bug has not, and most likely never will be, fixed.
There are fixes available online which you could try, but personally? If I pay 40 bucks for a piece of software, I want it to work, out of the proverbial box. If I, the end user, have to edit the game's INI's (using a converting tool because they are encrypted) to make it the least bit playable, then in my opinion the developer has failed.

An unfortunate mixture of a 'realistic' approach in design and a severe lack of control in combat. I quit just before the last level after dying multiple times for the stupidest reasons, reasons I cannot condone :/ Figured I'd write a review before uninstalling. I'll list some appreciated pros and then why I can't personally recommend it. (minor editting done)

[h1]Pros[/h1]
+Interesting narrative (the ♥♥♥♥ that swayed me into buying it...)
+AI Alies make your game livelier and not so lonely, and can be commanded (only focus target or heal ally)
+Highly destructible environment; the game makes great use of the setting (Dubai & sand) and the frequent sandstorms make for some epic scenarios
+Great sound effects; maneuvering terrain, breaking structures and walking through sandtorms sound great (if it doesn't 'cause some eargasm - don't leave it too loud))
+/- AI is quite challenging (Suicide Mission difficulty~), you can't run at them from the front or stick your head out of cover for more than a few seconds and expect to be okay.
+/- There are a few choices in the storyline - what course of action to take - but they mostly don't seem to have any lasting effects or matter at all.

[h1]But eff all that[/h1]
[b]MAPS[/b]: As a cover-based third-person shooter the game has some really bad level design, and combat (more on that below). One could argue that being pretty open is rather realistic compared to very conveniently placed covers, but having a single safe cover in the area and then having multiple enemies throw grenades at you (which you can't throw back, veeery realistic~), an enemy shooting RPGs at you, and everyone else firing unlimitted bullets at you in this barren land where bullets are so scarce is NOT (mainly describing the levels around which I quit...).

[b]COMBAT/CONTROLS[/b]: a few incredibly stupid implementation choices. One is that, as mentioned above, you CANNOT throw grenades back at enemies, a grenade means awkwardly detach from cover and run (i.e. sprint uncontrollably) and possibly die or stay and die - someone said your allies will sometimes throw a grenade at an enemy directly in front of both of you, I didn't see this. 
Second is that uncontrollable sprint. When you sprint, Walker (our unfortunate hero) behaves like the Tank in Left4Dead; he becomes extremely difficult to steer or stop and you can essentially only go in a straight line until you stop moving completely. 
Melee is limitted to wacking people with your gun which isn't all that stealthy but from behind it kills enemies (headshot).

[b]Additional Notes[/b]: The game tells u bullets are scarce, and it's reflected in the fact that I can't go past one area/level without changing weapons; this is pretty counterintuitive considering I'm sometimes presented with the opportunity for a stealth attack for example and I don't have my 1 pistol with the silencer, so there goes that. Even stranger is how enemies have unlimitted bullets and can spray them all day long. Another thing is the HEAVY enemy, that one arsewhole that I feel almost all devs don't think rationally about when they include them in the game. It takes 2 grenades (your full load) and several shotgun hits or more than your full load of rifle bullets to take one down, and he just keeps walking up to you spraying bullets until he reaches your cover and then there's an invisible barrier preventing him from going any further - that's when you can more easily kill him.

Anyway, I'm not even glad I got it on discount. Maybe it'll be more playable in easy mode though.

This game makes you do what is says in the title; walk a very thin, and eventually cross, a proverbial line.

I have the utmost respect for any soldier; they are beyond politics, they're doing their duty, and in situations where you never know whether the next civilian could be a potential hostile, when you live on the edge all the time, I do believe black and white turn into grey at best.

I have never served in the military, but based on what I know, what friends in the armed forces told me, and what I've seen in documentaries, this game gets very close to reality.

There is nothing glorious about combat, it's survival. Sure, there is a mission to complete, whatever that may be, but ultimately it's about making quick decisions and living to tell about them.

The game shows that it's not about being a hero, it's at best about respect; respect that, in my opinion, every soldier who has ever been through a combat situation deserves.

They will see things that no news report, no photo, no movie can show. Approximate perhaps, but no more. This game puts you one step closer by giving you the choices. And unlike other military shooters where you hardly ever see the aftermath, here you will. You make a call and the game will slap you in the face with the often harsh reality of that choice. It will show you what you did, and tell you to live with it. Welcome to the suck.

I guess the only thing we, the gamers, can take away as a good thing is, that, in this case, it IS just a game. Your decisions won't change the world, or someone's life, or end it. Based on how the game shows you what's going on, that is, however, not easy to keep in mind while playing, and maybe some part of your soul will end up paying regardless.

Beautiful surroundings are in stark contrast to the atrocities that await around the next corner. You want to know war without actually having to physically live through it?

Go ahead. Walk "The Line"...

Easily one of the best things to happen to video game narrative in years. The game is short, anything but sweet, and brutal. It veers away from current triple A games industry practice of glorifying war in shooters, and instead uses the genre to further the story to explore themes such as war exhaustion, devastation and the impact on civilians that we do not commonly see. It has moral ambiguity as one of its core concepts, and one which I applaud with great enthusiasm; decisions actually have an emotional impact and there is no wrong decision. In one section it took me a long time where I just sat there, simply to decide what the right decision to make was (to me at least)- I had the luxury of time, whereas in war you do not always have that luxury. The characters are believable and have strong development, even with unseen characters. The collectables also further the story, allowing you to see another side to things and give you an incentive to find them besides just being another statistic for the perfectionist. The gameplay is decent, I never felt overpowered or had the option to rush into things carelessly to progress. Likewise, the difficulty never spiked unrealistically at any point- it remained a reasonable challenge throughout. It isn't revolutionary in that regard, but nor was that the intended purpose. In conclusion, if you are ready for an emotional rollercoaster, looking for one of the most satisfying endings in a video game that is heavily story focused and DO NOT accidentally spoil sections of the story to yourself then this will be one of the most gratifying (and emotionally draining) experiences you can immerse yourself into in gaming.

And so ends
The Line. But what did it all mean? Well, I don’t ﬁnd that a particularly interesting question. Many people think
The Line is about how horrible war is, or how horrible military shooters are. I don’t think that is so. For me, The Line isn’t about statements or answers, but about questions.

Its theme is not one of criticising the military shooter, but simply critiquing it, asking questions about its nature. What is actually going on in these games that some of us play with reckless abandon, and which some of us dismiss outright? What do these games contribute to a broader culture of disassociated violence and dehumanised others? What does it mean that as these games increasingly depict war with more realism, reality itself increasingly begins to look like a videogame?Tese are not the questions that The Line answers; they are the questions that The Line left me with. Trough my complicity in Walker’s descent into madness, I learned things about myself. Once I stood before Andrew Ryan in Bioshock and realised I had never before made a choice in a videogame, and absolved myself of all my sins. Now, I stood before my own reﬂection and realised that just because I had no choice, that didn’t mean I had no responsibility over my actions. My sins are my own. Maybe it seems like a copout to conclude 50,000 words with “it’s complicated,” but war, violence, videogames, humanity, everything truly is complex. And that is the beauty of The Line: it is complicated. Too many games—not to mention other media forms, critics, journalists, politicians, everybody and everything—want to ﬁnd the nice and easy dichotomies. The good and the evil. The human and the other. The start and the end. The right and the wrong. The Line stubbornly refuses such dichotomies. There is good and evil in everyone. Every start is an ending, and every ending is a start. Every human is monstrous. Every right is a wrong.
The Line refuses to give us a simple answer. Instead, it embraces contradictions to expose just how fraudulent simple answers are.

This is a very generic (though competent) 3rd person cover shooter (with very, very basic squad mechanics) with a striking story. Especially the ending will probably keep you thinking for a while (and/or make you watch Youtube videos about the (multiple!) endings). The graphics and sound are also quite awesome and support the setting in the middle of the desert. Also all the hidden "intelligence" pickups in this game are actually worth it, as they are all voice acted, interesting and fit into the story.

My main problem with this game is that in between the iconic story moments of the game, the generic shooter part can become quite boring. Shoot at enemies, stay in cover until health regenerates, repeat until everyone his dead, proceed to next cover or segment of the game, repeat. There are some badass moments but also a lot of dull moments. At some point in the middle of the game I just wanted to finish the game to finally delete it. But the ending is really worth it! If they had put this story on a good shooter, that would have been one of the best shooters out there. And the fact that ammo is actually scarce, you have to switch weapons regularly and that all weapons are useful in one situation or the other distinguishes this game at least a bit gameplay-wise from other cover shooters.

If you crank up the difficulty the game will be quite challenging as you are not able to take many hits (enemies will still die after 1 (most enemies) or 2 headshots). And there is also a coop mode which makes every game better. ;)

But who the **** came up with these heavies? That was the worst design decision of the game. These are some heavy armored enemies, that take WAY too many hits to kill. Like I said before, all the the other enemies in this game die after at least 2 headshots but this guy takes several grenades and/or 10-40 (depending on your weapon) headhots while shooting at you with an LMG or shotgun. I know that he has a very tough armor and therefore moves very slowly but this enemy just don't fit into the game and is just annoying as an enemy. Also his visor cracks after the first headshots but you still need many more headshots RIGHT INTO HIS FACE before killing him...

Anyway, after finishing the game I would definitely recommend this game if you can get it cheap (it's only ~6 hours of gameplay on the highest difficulty (so with quite a few deaths)). The story is worth it but nevertheless, the game is quite short and I see no replay value as the story (any maybe the coop mode, which I did not play) is the only thing that keeps you playing.

By now you're probably aware of the game's gimmick. It's an emotionally punishing morality based knock off of Dark Heart (Apocalypse Now) masquerading as a generic FPS. The game aims to put you into a series of morally conflicting positions. Situations you would likely have faced in many other FPS's but it tries to humanise your opponents and confront you with the ramifications of your actions. Cute. If you want to get a better idea of what the themes are and how they're implemented Extra Credits has two good videos about it on YT (one with, one without spoilers), if you can put up with the pretentious high-morality fapping to the game.

So let's look at this one three levels: the morality mechanic, the themes of morality and PTSD from a narrative perspective, and the actual quality of the game play otherwise

[h1]The Morality Mechanic[/h1]
The themes of morality manifest themselves as game mechanics when you periodically come across “moral” situations and have to make a decision about how to proceed. Here's how they've utterly ♥♥♥♥♥♥ it up: 
* At times, and one scene in particular everyone keeps raving about, you're presented the illusion of choice but no actual choice. You do the one thing the game lets you do, and are treated to what I assume was meant to be an emotional cut-scene to punish you for it. I cannot feel bad for doing the thing the game required. This isn't console players blubbering into their controllers, this is the PC master race. We've been dropping chemical weapons on civilians since Postal. You gotta bring something better than that.

* The majority of the time the game misleads you about your options. There are hidden “high morality” alternatives in a lot of cases. Sure it's nice for the game to put explicit and hidden alternatives in, but the thing is you can just play the game the way the game tells you to and it still works fine. There's no reason to look for alternatives. In fact I'd've been more morally invested had I seen the high-morality option and still felt I needed to take the low morality choice.

* And finally, and probably most egregiously: the moral choices you make seem so to have [b]absolutely no impact on the game[/b]. Why would I make the moral choice here? I'm trying to get from this level to the next one and I will shoot a civilian in the head if that's what the game says I need to do to progress the story. I absolutely loathe ending changes based on a morality meter (à la Bioshock, Dishonored) but if you implement a morality mechanic it needs to at least change the game-play somehow. The entire game seems to assume that everyone who plays a game like BF or CoD must spend their entire time vacillating over how they could solve each problem in a moral way. I, like I think most normal PC gamers, just did what the game said I should do. I'm not interested in the lives of NPC's who don't even get a name tag. I don't care. It's a game, it's a challenge to get from A to B. You need either REALLY good storytelling or something particularly special to make me feel things, or harder still, to make my feelings factor into my game play style. 

[h1]The Narrative Themes[/h1]
The terrible implementation into the game-play not withstanding, the artistic value here is pretty high. The story is kind of interesting, despite its obvious plot-holes, the way they represent constant descent, the psychosis colour schemes, loading screen accusations, the 4th wall breaking. They're not all immediately obvious, but they're there and they're pretty well thought out and it'll give you plenty to mull over and wonder about on a second play-through. While we're at it, the general visuals are pretty sweet actually, so good job there.

[h1]The Actual Game-play[/h1]
I won't say that graphics [i]don't[/i] matter, or that narrative [i]doesn't[/i] matter, but I will say and I will defend this to the hilt, they matter [b]less[/b] than mechanics. A game with a pretty poor delivery can still be good if its mechanics are solid. But the opposite is rarely true. Spec Ops: The Line does [b]not[/b] have good mechanics. I mean yes it's so so agonisingly obvious that this is a port from a console game, and it has what are pretty standard mechanics for a console game I guess so fine, but I'm sitting on PC, wondering why I spend half my time hiding behind a bench or wall or ornamental plant pot, taking turns to fire at enemies who are also hiding behind whatever debris magically happened to be there. The most tactical thing in the game is blowing up explosive barrels or taking advantage of the ridiculously contrived breaking-glass-to-unleash-an-avalanche-of-sand mechanic the whole handful of times the game remembered it wanted that to be a thing. A fortunately all the miniguns scattered around shopping centres can be turned around and used to mow down waves of suicidal enemies. 

[h1]Your NPC's[/h1]
But the worst, the absolute worst, and this I cannot forgive a game, are your NPC's. In theory you have a sniper and a heavy and you can light up a target for them to take out. Yeah good luck with that. They're useless as all hell, they get in your way a LOT, by the time they eliminate a target for you, you could just have done it yourself since you need to have the reticle on the target anyway to tag them. But to top it off, if they get shot, you need to run in and revive them. And they have no idea of how to not get shot. ♥♥♥♥ stealth, these guys assume that not only are you going to speed-run-n-gun this game, but that you will somehow provide much better cover for them than mere concrete or sandbags ever could, so eschew both in favour of just sitting out in plain sight. Possibly the worst example of NPC's ruining any hope you have of making good tactical choices is one scene where you see a yacht in the desert. Plenty of openings, no aerial cover, and a reasonable amount of open ground between you and it. Open ground which has an inbound truck load of enemies. I wanted to stay put in my indestructible aircraft hull, with a box of nades, a box or ammo, high ground advantage, and crucially, one small controllable entrance. But my highly trained delta force sidekicks thought our only hope for survival would be to run like idiots for the yacht and then stay put half way when I didn't run with them. Needless to say they got mowed down and I lost the game for not reviving them fast enough. If the game had let me I'd've shot them in the first 5 minutes and gone on alone but alas the point of the game seems less about killing the enemies and staying alive than it does basically babysitting two idiots with the survival instincts of a screamapillar through a war zone dodging bullets to shoot them full of adrenalin.

[h1]Final Thoughts[/h1]

This game is a masterpiece. It's one of the best games I've ever played, and it's one of the rare games that I know I'll still be remembering in 10+ years. I've played it when it came out (2012) and I still shiver whenever I read about it or hear the soundtrack.

A few things to consider just so you're not disappointed :

1) You're buying this for the SP campaign. MP isn't great.
2) The campaign is maybe 7 hours long. It's the perfect length for this kind of game.
3) Since the game is "short", I HIGHLY recommend trying to beat the game in a short period of time. Ideally in 2-3 sessions, unless you're willing to clear it in a single sitting which I'd recommend if you can. The story is intense and can be quite confusing, so waiting weeks between 2 gaming sessions could have a negative impact on your appreciation.
4) Don't read anything / watch anything about the story or pretty much anything about this game before playing (even some reviews). Spoilers would ruin it.
5) Don't give up on it too early because the first hour or so is average at best.
6) Should be obvious but anyway, make sure to play with sound on (music, sound effects, voice acting). It's not a game you want to play while the TV is on or while talking on Skype.
7) Pay attention to the little details. Hints : Title screen, voice acting, flow of the game, etc. This is part of why it's a masterpiece in my opinion.
8) If you're not great at shooters, don't hesitate to play at an easier difficulty. Seriously you're not playing this for the challenge / gameplay. Some parts near the end can be annoying, and there's no real point in playing this at a difficulty where you'll have to restart often. Just make sure you're comfortable for the ride and enjoy it.

"The truth, Walker, is... that you are here because you wanted to feel like something you're not: A hero." 

Everyone who played and finished the game will probably have that sentence stuck in your head for weeks, I know that I did. This game is in my top 10 favorite games of ALL TIME. I finished the game a while ago, because it's ending, or should I say endings (which I won't spoil, don't worry) was just... mindblowing, to say the least. It still haunts me to this day, and that is very weird for me, as it's only happened a few times in my life. Anyway, if you happen to stumble to my review, here's what I think of it.

So the story starts six months after a huge sandstorm hit Dubai... A ton of people died and American soldiers that were sent to evacuate Dubai also died. However, a mysterious radio signal is being picked up and a Delta Squad (being lead by Walker, the main character) is sent to locate survivors (the most important being Col. John Konrad, who was leading the evacuation before the sandstorm hit) and then radio for evac. So that's basically all you need to know about the game's story when heading into it. Now comes the gameplay...

Okay, so when I first saw this game, it was in the PSN Store back in 2012, back when I had a crappy computer that could barely run an 8-bit game.., I downloaded it's demo and I found the gameplay to be very good. I was sort of more into FPS games at the time, but this game was still awesome. I didn't buy the game, because I have a terrible experience when it comes to playing demos first and then buying the full game... The full game almost always disappoints me, Anyway, back to Spec Ops... I bought it on May this year, after seeing it being on sale. So, I'm not very used to play shooters on the PC, but this game was suprisingly easy to control. I would say it's your standard third-person-shooting games. You have to squadmates with you, and you can give them commands, like target who they should and send them to heal the other squad member if he's done. Also, sometimes you can shoot a glass roof, for example, and sand will drop onto your enemies, stunning them for a bit. Neat feature, it beats the old "shoot a gas tank to blow everything up" which is cool and all, but there's too much of that in the other "war simulator" games. Ammo in Dubai is very limited, so watch where you shoot and how much you shoot. There's your standard pack of weapons in Spec Ops: The Line: pistols, assault rifles, heavy rifles, etc. All are easy to aim and shoot, but you still get the feeling you're the one holding the gun. Some weapons have alternate fire modes, so you can just fire one bullet at a time instead of having a burst. The graphics look great for a game made in 2012, it makes you really feel as you're actually in Dubai with the Delta Squad. There's multiplayer, but it's the standard... Finally, we reach the most important part of Spec Ops: The Line... The story.

Okay... I literally can't explain anything without spoiling it all... So I just have hints for you:  Get some tissue paper if it's easy to make you cry... I didn't do that, but after finishing the game, I just had a moment where I was like in total disbelief. Every emotion that you could feel went through me all at the same time. Yeah, the story is THAT GOOD.

It's not by luck that 94% of the reviews for Spec Ops: The Line are positive... The developers did a fantastic job. The voice acting is excellent. When you head to this game, don't think it's like CoD or Battlefield... This game is a true war simulator, it isn't just shoot, shoot, shoot, kill, kill, kill.... It actually has a story, and I know I said it a lot throughout this review... But it's damn good.

This might just be the best game I've played to date, if not one of the best. This game sort of came and went during 2012, and nobody noticed it too much. IGN gave it a 7/10, and GameSpot gave it a 6/10, and the world moved on. But not me. I was fixated on my favorite game reviewer, Yahtzee Croshaw, who proclaimed this was the best games of 2012 and one of his personal favorites. And I thought to myself while looking up the info on Spec Ops, "What's so special about this? It looks like a samey third-person cover-shooter." And I have never been so wrong in my life.

To lay things down simply, don't go into Spec Ops: The Line to feel like a badass or a hero. Just don't. While 99% of games make you feel like you can take on the whole world, Spec Ops is part of the 1%, making you feel like a horrible piece of crap- and manages to tell the story of you, as a piece of crap, in the immerse and beautiful, yet ugly, Dubai. As you navigate this storm of sand and insanity with your crew, you start to realize how things aren't just getting more complicated with the situation in Dubai... but also in your own head. 

The game handles controversial issues like fighting Americans (Seriously! No Russians or Muslims, but your own men!), the usage of White Phosphorous, and PTSD, all of which the game sheds in it's horrifying light. The game even goes beyond the actual gameplay mechanics to ask you things like, "Do you remember why you came here?", and "This isn't real, so why should you care?". And people chastise the game on this front saying, "Well, I did it because the game made me do it!", which is completely missing the point of Spec Ops. You are actively taking away peoples lives in this games, if you want to believe it or not. And Spec Ops goes out of its way to make sure you know the weight of death and how these people are living and breathing- not just programs.

A great example was a mundane moment, where my squad and I were about to enter this tower, and I raised my gun to these two guards- unaware of my presence. I held my finger, because the first guard said, "Would you like some gum?", which led to a horrible conversation involving the two opening up to each other, and feeling depressed of how the whole world has gone to hell. And I shot them.

The funniest thing is, people glanced over this game, not giving it the time of day, then the very next year showered praise all over The Last of Us. I love The Last of Us, don't get me wrong, but Spec Ops: The Line is far superior to it's message than I think The Last of Us was to theirs. I view The Last of Us, like The Godfather- the one everyone loves and talks about and I love just as much. But Spec Ops: The Line is like Barton Fink. If you bring it up, people will react with, "What is that? I've never heard of it." but I think it's superior to the former. 

Don't play Spec Ops expecting to play another Call of Duty game or Battlefield- go into Spec Ops like a normal human being, and realize just how horrible of a human being you are.

There are stories out there (be it movies, books, or in this case, video games) where it is highly encouraged to experience with 0 prior knowledge.  I would suggest doing so with this game, but let's be honest, you most likely know that this game leaves you with some heavy emotional baggage.  With that said, I will do my best to avoid any plot-specific details, and instead, mention their presence.

This falls into shooter subgenre, the 'Modern Military Shooter'.  The subgenre is classified by solely focusing on Multiplayer, with short, linear campaigns, because making a game that's multiplayer only isn't worth 60$ (though the Single Player isn't valuable). The gameplay itself relies on hitscan weapons (weapons where bullet travel is instant, and explosives travel about as fast), very low damage threshold, and regenerating health.  I bring this up because Spec Ops dumps their eggs into single player, and only added multiplayer because 2K requested it.  Without getting into finer details, the gameplay doesn't derive itself very far.

The story is more than serviceable; it's good.  The story is based around the special operatives Walker, Lugo, and Adams going into a post-apocalyptic Dubai to find signs of life, and if so, leave and signal for a rescue team.  It takes you less than a tutorial level to find out a bunch of anti-American zealots  have taken a marine trooper hostage and plan to execute him.  So, instead of finding out about survivors and leaving, you go after the hostage.  Along the way of killing survivors in self defense, you run into a splinter group of marines who you trade bullets with.  So now, you are killing marines who survived the apocalyptic sandstorms, and the citizens of Dubai.  This is counter-intuitive to saving the city and its people.  The events that transpire end up getting to our three generic grumps, who end up going crazy and stricken with PTSD the more the game goes on.  The descent into trauma is the best part of this game.  At the start of the game, you're talking with your squad using terms like "tango down" or "target down", and as the game goes along, slowly degrades into Nolan North shouting incoherently.  

The problem is that the whole game, you're told that you're responsible for all the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ problems that you experience, while the player is disempowered from being responsible for the situation.  The developers say that your power as the player is to whether or not you quit the game or keep playing, and even incited this mid-way through the game.  I don't think I need to point out how juvenile of an excuse that is.  The only option is option A, I took option A, and now the game is telling me I'm a monster for taking option A.  I don't mind that the characters start to slowly lose their sanity, because they are empowered as human beings, and do debatably evil things.  I, as a player, am coerced into doing debatably evil things.  There's a plot twist at the end which I'm not going to spoil, because, you know, you're reading this to debate whether or not to buy this game, but do know that it almost ruined the entire experience, because it was so bad.

The gameplay is vanilla with a cherry on top; a bland, but competent formula with a topping that is in and of itself bland.  You have a cover shooting system, weapons that do a lot of damage, recoil, but are samey.  You have a heavy assault partner, and a sniper.  You can make them focus on killing certain people, and, if you're pinned, they can throw a flashbang grenade to save your ass.  Between Elizabeth in Bioshock Infite and Ashley in Resident Evil 4, their AI is closer to Elizabeth, while not being absolute game breakers.  I played on Hard, and it definitely kicked my ass.  I'd recommend playing on Hard because you're supposed to be playing a game that makes you feel like ♥♥♥♥, and making it difficult on top of that helps.  The game does get more difficult as it goes on, because your cover options become less and less suitable, though they do throw a meat shield or two your way, and your only option is to kill them before they kill you.

For a game with the words "Spec Ops", I don't really feel like a special forces agent.  If I were a heavily trained soldier, with a focus on saving lives, I would imagine being more like Naked Snake or Adam Jensen where, while I can fight in open combat, prefer to not be caught.  You're given silencers on your base guns, but those silencers don't matter when the level designs don't permit this gameplay.  Instead, the levels cater to set piece battles (a real problem with cover shooters, sadly).  I do think that the game's story would have been damaged though, if you managed to get through almost all of the game without getting caught, and are then told by the game that you're a horrible dude because you killed all those guys.  

I do have legitimate problems with this game.  It does have a good story that does throw some legitimate sucker punches at the players, with what is most likely the best story of any modern military shooter in a superb environment.  However, the gameplay detracts from the whole experience, because you have no choice (or illusion of choice at points), and are treated like you did.  I leave it with a recommendation, because I can tell people to play this game comfortably, but you might find the game's hollow gameplay and disgusting plot twist detract too far from the game.

I played from 11pm to 4am, expecting that the game was some sort of quick-play game that I could put down easily at any time, like, say, call of duty (oh good grief, even the comparison makes me cringe). I was so driven to finish the game [spoiler](the mission, as it were) much like Walker was[/spoiler]. This revelation made me hate myself beyond belief, as I realized the very same determination, the self-same urge to commit to a goal made me ignore warning signs all over the place. This game makes you truly explore yourself, the deepest darkest recesses of your psyche where the hidden threads of psychopathy lie. 

When I finally finished the game at 4am, I was unable to sleep. I stayed awake, tormented by what I had done [spoiler]and the face of the white phosphorus burnt mother and child[/spoiler]. I kept telling myself: "This is a game. Get over it and get to sleep.", but I just couldn't get over the fact that at the heart of every human is the capability to take things to an extreme in order to pursue a perceived greater good. It is the very thing that drives the best of humanity and the worst of humanity. Medical scientists pursuing a cure, versus the extremists ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ up Syria as I type this. This game revealed an inner heart of darkness that needs to be understood, addressed and controlled. If only every one of us could think about it with the due weight and clarity that is needed in such a discussion.

Play the game, and finish it, please. Do yourself a favour and finish it. Understand how dangerous it is to be unaware of your own actions, and bloody well learn from it.

The fact that an anti-COD even exists makes this game somewhat interesting. As a story and as a videogame, however, it comes off pretentious and a bit juvenile. That said, you may appreciate your time with Spec Ops if you're a bonafide fan of military shooters. This is because the stinger at the end will have a positive effect on you.

Gameplay is fine. Shooting is inaccurate, it's really hard to score grenade kills, and you die extremely quickly. You can carry only very limited amounts of ammo, so you'll be swapping your empty weapon for a new one on the ground very often (I earnestly found that bit interesting). You have squad commands, but they're limited to "shoot that guy" and, when the game prompts you, "flashbang those guys."

The story is where a clever idea suffers from pretentious, juvenile storytelling. A literal read is impossible, because it's complete nonsense. For example, progress always moves in a downward direction, even when the laws of physics would normally prevent it (you drop through the sand, then fight through a hotel, then drop through the floor, then end up on a terrace overlooking the entire city of Dubai, then you drop down to a lower level...). Presumably that downward progress is symbolic. 

Your mission never really makes sense, but that's to make a point that the game spells out for you right before it ends.

And on and on. That this game is nonsense when read literally is what makes this story pretentious. The story wants to be clever food for thought, but the ony way the writers knew how to tell it is a nonsensical sequence of metaphors and other symbols.

Then, at the end, it chastises you for playing a military shooter. But, if you're not the type who normally plays military shooters, it'll sound like a boss at work making you go to a training about something you learned at your last company, all the while acting like he or she is really giving you an important learning opportunity.

Play everything you want to play, then, if you still want to play a video game, give this one a go. 5-6 hours turns out to be just the right length, and the brevity actually makes the story a little less pretentious than it otherwise would be.

Spec Ops wants very badly to be the thinking man's Gears of War (or Binary Domain), and now you know exactly where I'm going with this review. I can't really talk my way around it, this game lives and dies on its story because everything else it does has been done before, and spoiler alert, the story ain't gonna save it. You and your two gruff, snarky squadmates trek into Dubai after a biblical sandstorm annihilates the city on the lookout for survivors. What you find are rebels and remnants of the US Army regiment sent to aid the populace engaged in an endless shootout, which you of course join. It's third person action with sticky cover, two weapon slots, and thankfully enough guns to give variety to the 6 hours or so (I guess, I think I'm like 2/3 of the way through) of shooting hundreds and hundreds of dudes. Levels are pretty short and fights are pretty challenging on the upper difficulty levels. The graphics are pretty good but it really just looks like a very sandy over-saturated Divide from Fallout: New Vegas to me.

So that's it, it plays like Binary Domain, but with none of the clever characters or entertaining story to prop it up. It's very much Apocalypse Now with an extra dose of "no YOU are the monsters", and honestly that's where the whole thing falls apart for me. I've never liked this trend in shooters to make the player character question the morality of their actions, because that moment of self-doubt always comes after murdering like a hundred other people. The whole thing hinges on clear good guy/bad guy labels to conveniently absolve the player of inconvenient guilt, and it's honestly pretty gross. In Spec Ops you get a few chapters of grizzled "This is ♥♥♥♥♥♥" as you mow down rebels and fellow US soldiers, and then the thing happens and all of a sudden you're supposed to feel like a REAL murderer. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ really? No game has really pulled this off well; the best example I can think of is Modern Warfare 2 and that was because it came very early in the game and they dialed the atrocity up to 11 for shock factor.

Well, I was about to give this game a bad review. I was at the second to last chapter and convinced that this game was nothing special, the story hype was wrong, and it was just another boring shooter that tried to be edgy.

I've never been so wrong about a game in my life.

That's the problem with this game, though. You have to play it through all the way to the VERY end, and then, you'll want to play it again. And that's something I never thought I'd say before I reached the final chapter.

Graphics: Technically, they're nothing special. The game runs pretty well and looks decent for being released in 2012. The design of the graphics is pretty good, though. The landscapes and the whole Dubai scene is gorgeous and has some wonderful views from tall buildings. 

Gameplay: This is definitely the worst part of the game. The unfortunate part is that the gameplay is so generic, boring, frustrating, and clunky that I nearly stopped playing it. It's a typical third-person shooter where you're killing lots of people and using cover. The cover system is terrible, especially since the cover button and sprint button are the same. I'll be trying to take cover and instead sprint out in front of the cover, get shot, and die. Movement in general just feels clunky. Like I said, I nearly stopped playing because I got so frustrated. But trust me, you HAVE to push through.

Story: Believe the hype, and don't read spoilers. This game is on another level when it comes to twist endings. Leading up to the big reveal, I was just HOPING that there was gonna be some sort of crazy twist, but I had no idea that it would be what it was. It really hit me hard and turned my opinion of the game all the way around. I really don't want to give anything away because it's the only saving grace for this game, but I will say that the tediousness and the horrific killing is the whole point. You're supposed to feel like you're excessively killing people, you're not supposed to enjoy what you're doing. This game is MADE to piss people off, that's the whole purpose, and the whole reason that the ending works so well. 

Overall, the game itself is generic, but the story, the message, and the twist make it worth it. Plus, it's only 6 hours long, which is just short enough to get people through the tedious gameplay. Trust me, it's worth it. 8/10

The Civilians are under the protection of the 33rd whether they like it or not. The 33rd are still trying to save everyone from an admittingly hopeless situation.
It's unclear whether or not the insurgents existed before the CIA arrived and stoke the flames. But in any case, the Insurgents want the Americans out. They see this as another case of classic American interventionism in a country they don't belong in. Vietnam, Afghanistan, Iraq, you name it. They want them out. This is their home and they will fight them to do it. The 33rd's violence against civilians during riots and martial law only fan the flames.
Ok so that is all before Delta shows up. This is where things get complicated.
Delta arrives and runs into rebel forces. They attempt to have a conversation. Interestingly enough in Dubai, the local population speaks Arabic, Lugo talks to them in Farsi. In any case, they try to talk, Walkers and Adams discuss how to kill the rebels in case things go bad. The rebels notice them talking and say "they're plotting to kill us". And they're right, technically. The rebels shoot at you because they think you're the 33rd coming to take them back to the Nest. So you start killing them because you think they're bad guys.
Then you get to the plane and shoot at more rebels who're fighting the 33rd. The 33rd, at this point, are actually fighting against the CIA trying to prevent the cover-up/destruction of Dubai.
You run off to rescue the soldier taken by the rebels, and find out it's the CIA running the rebels. You now think well if the CIA is fighting the 33rd, the 33rd must be the bad guys, right? Why would the US Government fight the 33rd unless they went off the reservation and turned traitor? So now you side with the CIA against the traitorous 33rd. The first sequence where you shoot Americans is more or less started by you. If you let the soldier go, he warns his friends some CIA goons are coming. You're met with resistance and you shoot. You kill because you think you know what you're doing. Similarly, in the market where the 33rd are shooting at civilians? They're not shooting at them. They're trying to evacuate the civilians and take them back to the Nest.
By the time you figure out that the CIA is just trying to kill everyone, it's too late. You've already massacred freedom fighters, civilians, and American troops. You've already doomed everyone.
The 33rd keep fighting you because they have to. You're killing them! Walker and Delta are like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ meat grinder, everything they run into is reduced to quivering slabs of meat. The 33rd also think you're part of the CIA, at least initially. But the most telling scene is near the end when you make your run at the tower. Even after everything you've done, after all the soldiers you've slaughtered, even after the white phosphorus attack... the 33rd have you surrounded and they ask you to surrender. The 33rd are willing to let you give up! They weren't trying to kill you, they were defending themselves!
Delta constantly thinks they're the good guys, but they're not. They make decisions when they think they have all the facts, but they only ever know a fraction of the story. They have good intentions, but it leads to death, destruction, and despair at every turn.
The story is unclear because it has to be. Walker has to make his decisions with partial facts and half-truths. If you know more than Walker, the effect is lost. You have to be just as blind as Walker for the story to have any impact. 

There are also four different endings to this game:

The first is that Walker commits suicide after not being able to cope with the crushing reality of his actions in Dubai. (Medium ending, not too sad and horrible but not to happy)

The second is that he is killed by Falcon One, the army squad sent to rescue him, when he chooses to retaliate against them. (A little sadder then the previous one because it shows how ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ crazy Walker really is)

The third is that he kills all of Falcon One, and continues to live in the ruined city of Dubai. (By far the saddest and most horrible ending. Shows that you're an insane killer that doesn't care about anything anymore.)

The last is that he surrenders to Falcon One and is safely returned home, albeit mentally scarred. (Probably the best ending, if that makes any sense)

The way the levels are crafted is truly mindblowing. They had a system in which you had to perfect a level to earn a key, and you would use that key to earn more levels. In layman's terms, to earn more levels, you had to perfect current levels. They ditched that and added an XP system in which you gain more XP to earn a key the more levels you play and perfect. I'm very glad they added this system and was skeptical about buying it. But now that I did buy it, I do not regret it even for a second. One thing I really love about this game is how you don't have to unlock base levels. In a sense, this game is open world. That sense is that many levels are available to you, and you can choose whether you want to advance into more challenging levels, or stay where you're at. To get an S in completion, you have to sweep up EVERY leaf, and to get an S in Finesse, you have to maintain your combo throughout an entire level. 

Another thing I absolutely enjoy about Dustforce is its expasive community. There are lots of Community Workshop maps for you to sharpen your skills on, and lots of people who can set a good example. I'm sure most of the people who get best times on all the levels have a Youtube channel, so you can probably catch them there. The community may or not be active, but it sure is good and friendly.

Overall, in terms of gameplay, music, artstyle, animation, and difficulty (it's not an easy game, but it's not that hard of a game either. It just depends on how much you want to play it), I rate this game:

For me, this game doesn't live up to its praise. 

What I will praise the developers for, however, is the interesting art direction. I like the color choices made; they successfully captured the clashing beauty and chaos of the war-torn desert environment. Although I appreciated the visuals and great voice acting, the campaign is short and lacks replay value other than going back to collect achievements. Gameplay is average and mostly involves blasting enemies head-on.

Most importantly, the actual story wasn't as gripping, guilt-inducing, and thought provoking as the developers had purported. They wanted to show players that their actions had consequences, but... they really didn't. The game was linear, and pivotal choices simply amounted to earning an achievement whether you went with Option A or B. I was expecting to be forced to make decisions between different, but equally horrible, options.  In my opinion, this would have been more impactful in providing a tacit explanation of Walker's psychological breakdown than the cliche representation that was later revealed. To be fair, I did feel horrible at two points in the game after some "bad" decisions you are FORCED to take at two points in the game. I'm not talking about the moments where there is Choice A vs Choice B, but you can actually create your own Choice C; I did that. 

I'm talking about the unavoidable, plot-driving actions such as the **MAJOR SPOILER** [spoiler]white phosphorous[/spoiler] scene: These should have just been made into cutscenes. I won't accept "but you always have the choice to stop playing!" as an acceptable option. I'm looking for a game that can back up the hype that it's putting out. I expected consequences to be at the level of Fallout, Witcher, Dragon Age, etc.

Consequently, the reveal of Walker's downward spiral seemed stereotypical and unnecessarily "artsy" to me. It severely detracted from my understanding of the chronological events of the game and made me impatient to get to the end. I knew what angle they were going for, but it gave me an unsatisfactory grasp of what actually happened in the time I invested into this game.

If you can check your brain at the door and just "go with it"...a relatively fun, though standard third person cover shooter that swings for the fences on its story and, despite falling short, is commendable for making the attempt.

In Spec Ops: The Line, you play as the leader of a Special Forces team (of three) being sent into a desert city, ravaged by sand storms, to investigate the apparent desertion of a respected career officer and the troops under his command. **NO SPOILERS** The story of his (and his mens') desertion slowly unfolds throughout the course of the game while your actions are supposed to impact the story as it unfolds from there. I say "supposed to" because the story is very linear with no real choice given to the player with even those choices given being cosmetic in actuality.  This is where the earlier "turn the brain off" comment comes in since if you can just "enjoy the ride" and try not to pick apart the plot you can have some fun. The problem comes in that even if you do give the  story its chance, it fails to deliver in specific ways that are obvious, if not always immediately. In the end, the story isn't bad, but its noticably deficient in areas and in a game that is obviously trying to focus on this aspect of game-making its especially disappointing.

The rest of the game, is pretty generic. Weapons are standard military weapons of the day and the two other characters are interesting enough, but definately fall into stereotypes. The combat, as mentioned earlier, is standard third person cover shooter. They do introduce a mildly interesting gameplay mechanic in that since much of the city was made of glass and there was just a massive sand storm, you can shoot out pains  of glass to unleash avalanches of sand to take out teams of attackers. In the end that is fun, but kind of gimicky. As for enemies...AI is adequate, but fairly mindless and they use the "Bullet Sponge" mentality of increasing difficulty. Personally, I hate when developers just increase the health/armor to ludicrous levels as it seems such a cop-out...especially when you try to play the game on harder levels and you get bored of having to head shot some enemies 10 times (it seemed like) to get them to die.

One last thing, when I first tried to play this game it was horribly bugged. So much so I couldn not continue as the game would reliably crash to desktop at a specific encounter. I must have gotten a patch update as after a couple months of sitting I came back and was able to play through the game in its entirety with no more issues. So be warned, you may or may not have problems.

In any case, if you like the genre (or can over look this game's generic implementation of them), want to see some very pretty desert city environments, and want a really intriguing story that isn't as well executed as it could have been. Try this game out.

It's short, only took me 6 hours to complete my first playthrough, though it does have some replay value with it's multiple choices throughout the story and an extra unlockable difficulty setting.
Multiplayer seems pretty dead, but this game didn't really focus on it to begin with.
It makes you feel like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ person and hate yourself.

But besides those three(ish) cons, the game is well worth the 20 Euro (at time of writting) price tag, buy it for yourself (or for a friend if you already have it and need to spend some money quickly), play it to the end.

The other plus with the length is that it is the perfect length to tell the story it is trying to tell without dragging itself out with nothing to show.  There is one event where it all begins to spiral out of control, and neither you nor the characters can get it back under control.

This is a game you play for the narrative and for character arcs driving the events.  And if you reach a point and find yourself unable to press on, you may be a better person than the character you play as, or players who do press on.  I'm not quite sure.  I'm still not sure what I should be thinking or feeling, but right now, as I write this, I feel slightly physically ill and emotionally dead inside.  The player and the character will share in a declining mental and emotional state, gradually unable to quite tell what's real and what isn't.

You can tell even from the opening line, "Konrad is a hero....", and the dialog between the squadmates, that this game is well written and well thought-out.

As you progress through the game, it messes with your emotions, questions your sense of morality and forces you to make tough choices.  It these regards, this game pushes forward video game as a medium, and is incomparable to any other game, shooters or otherwise.

However, all this goodness is wrapped up in a conventional shooter with mechanics that are less refined than other shooters.  You have the annoying 2-weapons inventory.  You have the cover system, that isn't as useful and feels less fluid than cover systems in other games.  You have also the obligatory half-baked stealth elements that do not have the mechanics to support it, as it is contextual and merely devolves into ordering a squadmate to use a silencer.

Your squadmates, thankfully, are competent enough most of the time, which unfortunately hightlights the few instances when they misbehave.  They may meander to an open area without cover.  Or they may shoot away errantly without an apparent target.  And on the other end of the spectrum, they will wipe out all enemies without your help,  Not a huge issue, but the variability in the competency of your squadmates does detract from the immersion of the experience.

The environment and set-pieces are well done and creative enough.  The destruction, devastation, and despair of the city and its inhabitants is conveyed convincingly.  The occassional intel items do fill in the gaps as well.  There are constant scripted events that keeps the plot moving.

Overall, despite its flaws, I would highly recommend every gamer to play this game, especially those who mindlessly wade through violence in other games.

Spec Ops: The Line is something of a highly underrated masterpiece that, I don't believe, was ever given the recognition it deserved.  The multiplayer is pretty bad, but from multiple sources, the games developers originally were against the idea and 2K (the publishers) forced the concept to push sales and stick with the multiplayer trend in the market.  But in terms of single-player story, this game is a marvel, something I honestly never expected from any military video game.  

Firstly, I'll address the issues people have with the actual gameplay.  I personally find nothing wrong with the gameplay at all really.  The actual firefights and action sequences are what we've come to expect from shooters these days and is therefore nothing special, but it's what fills the moments between these action-filled firefights that really make this game.  The controls and mechanics are smooth and feel great, damn me for saying, they are comparable to Gears of War in feel.  The shooting is superb and the movement is a bit sluggish at times, but overall, still a good shooter from this perspective.

Where Spec Ops: The Line really shines is it's absolutely shameless telling of the truths and atrocities of war in the modern age.  Nothing about it is good, nothing about it will make you a hero, no one really is in those situations, and this game will really make you realize that.  This game takes the stereotypical shooters "heroic" stories, and tosses them in the trash.  Then burns the can.  Then shoots it into space where a black hole swallows it.  This game does away with Hollywoods interpretation of modern age warfare and digs deep and dark, where many are too scared to go.  This game will completely destroy the image of war that most games would have you believe in and instead deals with depression, self-loathing, Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder, and the grittiness of war that no game has mentioned.

Buy this game.  Experience the story.  I'll meet you on the other side of The Line.

The Standford Prison Experiment, conducted in 1971 and led by Phillip Zimbardo, showed that anyone can be a villain.  Innocents were divided into two categories, the "prisoners" and the "guards".  The mission was simple: keep the prisoners in check.  When the prisoners rebelled against the injustice of the guards tyranny, they were punished.  The guards thought they were the heroes, punishing and delivering "justice" to these "criminals".

In Spec Ops: The Line, you play as Martin Walker, a "guard".  Your mission is simple, save Dubai from its "criminals".

Amazing narrative and pacing, though the controls were often sticky and could be frustrating at times throughout the game.  I found the gameplay to be quite enjoyable and much less of a slog than what others have claimed it to be, though admittedly I haven't had much experience with third-person shooters in the past.  The story is truly where it's at though, and if more mainstream shooters could introduce this level of immersion to their campaigns, I'd be all over them.  It pretty much felt like I was playing an interactive version of Apocalypse Now, and the frustration and challenge of playing on Suicide Mission difficulty really made it that much easier to "become" Walker and put yourself in his shoes.  Traversing the roads, tunnels, and rooftops of a post-apocalyptic Dubai was absolutely gorgeous too--hauntingly so--and it reminded me of the breathtaking beauty of games like Mirror's Edge at times.

That being said, I did have issues with certain areas of the game such as the Ride of the Valkyries helicopter sequence, which honestly should have been a cutscene and in which I had to pray to RNG Jesus to survive.  Raiding the yacht in Chapter 13 was incredibly frustrating as well as you were swarmed with enemies from all sides, had limited cover to utilize (and which you frequently had to abandon with all the grenade and RPG-happy assailants), and when the storm sets in you seriously have no idea what's going on or from which direction enemies will be attacking.  I think I died at least 20 times in that segment alone.  The other issue I had was with the sprinting system that was unusually sticky and which caused me to run past cover and get killed on numerous occasions.  Still an enjoyable experience overall--I didn't buy into the whole thing with the game trying to guilt you over your characters' choices or criticizing the conventions of the genre--was fun to think about though!

This game...where do I start? I played it through all in one sitting, not because of it being short (it really isn't), but because of how the game grabbed me right from the start and begun my slow spiral into insanity.

You play as Captain Walker, an experienced soldier, who leads two of his men, Lugo and Adams, into a simple recon mission in search of Colonel Konrad, a soldier who went missing 6 months ago leading a group of survivors from the desolate wasteland that is now Dubai. Dubai has turned into a kill-or-be-killed world due to the constant amount of sandstorms, forcing most of its citizens out, but keeping those who couldn't leave trapped. The soldiers start off comical and optimistic, but that quickly changes. Fights amongst each other, accusations fly across the room, and you're just trying to keep your head straight. As the storyline unfolds, you will end up blaming everything from a company of soldiers, to a deejay, to the CIA, a veteran soldier, and even yourself for the events that occur. 

There are decisions to be made in this game. Real decisions. Not just a simple "Go left or go right". You choose who lives and who dies. This game has the most difficult decisions I've ever made, with neither choice being "the good one". There is no such thing as a good choice in this game.

Spec Ops: The Line poses many moral questions: How far will you go to do your mission? How many lives will you save? What's an innocent man's life worth to you? Do you even remember why you're here? This game will make you find out, and you won't like the answers. This game has shown me just how far us as humans will go to find a scapegoat, blame it on something else, because we can't be that evil. We're too good for that. We're just trying to help, right?

Or so I thought.

Spec-Ops: The Line is highly regarded for its unconventional narrative that attempts to criticize other games in similarly-themed games for the "power fantasy" that they give players by having them act as a gung-ho hero with no question for the actions they take. It is largely inspired by the Joseph Conrad novel "Heart of Darkness", most well-known as also being the inspiration for the Francis F. Coppola magnum opus "Apocalypse Now"; the story of how prolonged exposure to war and violence can warp anyone, a theme that holds true in this game as well.

I personally found the lofty narrative to be less impresive than I was expecting going in. Yes, the game does attempt to chastise the player by having them perform objectives then showing them the consequences of it but a problem lies with the fact the game is trying to be bleak anyway. Seldom do you get a chance to choose your route and no matter what you do, it ends up being really crummy anyway. The protagonist is torn between his objectives and what is right yet you can never lead him down a positive road. The game's linear structure basically demands you do what other games such as Call of Duty have asked but then admonishes you for doing it, despite the fact it never let you have your say in the first place.

However, that considered, the rest of the game, I thought, was better than most critics had to say. A common complaint is the game is wholly generic and any reason to play is primarily held up by its unique plot but I personally found the gameplay solid and uncompromising. It's definitely rote but as a third-person shooter, it checks all the boxes and does them well. Your team members are also not of the braindead A.I. that you have to be joined to the hip to like most shooting games. They will actively help position you if you use them right and have helpful skills like flashbangs and sniping. The only real complaint I have about the gameplay is some of the animations are too stiff-looking (enemies just pop up from behind cover with no semblance of finesse or human-like movement).

So, ultimately, while the narrative fails to deliver on its intended message for me, I still say play Spec-Ops if you're looking for a fun, albeit by-the-books third-person shooter. And, hey, if you're not as jaded as me then you might even see the message the game was intending to leave too.

A brutal storyline that shows how dark and sadistic human nature can be if that separates survival from death, or just greed and comfort from sharing. Paired up with a relatively short but compared to today's standards completely normal playtime and the well known generic TPS gameplay, it's a masterpiece where you won't even notice that the gameplay feels like the 1000th same TPS, because the atmosphere and the narrative is what gets you hooked on Spec Ops: The Line until you finish it. With all it's horrors and misleading delusions, it could be among the best fictional war movies with a perspective that slowly blurs reality with losing your mind to all the terror happening around you, with you, with your loved ones up to and beyond a point where you can't make a difference of what really happens and what is a delusion, and who is responsibile for all the death and suffering shown in shockingly real instead of overdramatizing and coloring it like the rest 99% of games do. It really is a masterpiece of psychological themed games. It makes YOU, the real person do horrific things and question your own morality, MAKES you want to find a twisted way to justify your decisions and depending on your choices, it possibly makes you feel like a monster.

Other games tried it too but it was either too black and white or overly dramatized, almost cartoon-ish to keep the player reminded about this is fiction, and always gave a reason not to worry or feel like you are doing good in some way, even if that requires doing bad things.

You'll question yourself here eventually, where were the line you shouldn't have crossed, and how long ago.
And this is unprecedented in the gaming history.

Throw in all this to the postapocaliptic feeling of Dubai being swallowed by the desert, with the people there being isolated from the world and are starving to survive any way neccessary.

And the greatest thing is, that this isn't a selfish way of the developers to make their sick gore fantasy (partially) come to reality, everything you see is part of a greater puzzle, and once you see the whole picture it just blows your mind and leaves you in shock for minutes.

TL,DR: It's pure genius worth mentioning (and being recommended) among the top games, even looking back more than two decades in the genre.

Spec Ops the Line at first seems quite carelessly executed FPS, a match for last Medal of Honor. But it is only an envelope which brings you emotionally affluent, strong message. Message about soldiers, war exhaustion and very basic one - about role of destruction in our system of values.

For a gameplay Yager offers you a railroad shooter with a bit of squad support. If you seek a glorious, challenging gunplay - look the other way, that's not about Spec Ops the Line. For some reason, the most of the action feels like you were shell-shocked from the start of the game. Shooting part not really engaging. Two big notes about AI: 
1) your companions are not that bad, as you can expect, playing in games like Bureau: XCom Declassified or Battlefield3. They scoring kills, and it feels like in normal difficulty setting they can bend opposers almost without your support. If only they were not rushing forward before it's clear sometimes, I'd say they are a perfect team.
2) Quite opposite, behavior of your enemies usually is quite weak from the point of battle effectiveness. Even in the hardest difficulty setting where they shoot very precisely, and you dying alot being both outnumbered and outgunned... Still they a prey, and you are the hunter. You mow them, in dozens and hundreds.

Being quite a mundane FPS, Spec Ops the Line offers a rather spanning visual experience, though. Sights of Dubai, all those sand and weather features are gorgeous. Impression when you destroying something to let another portion of sand, symbolizing chaos, gets even more space over a once-a-great-city... Can't buy it with the mastercard, obviously.

And music! Music part is fabulous. Maybe the best part of the whole game.

Overall, an artwork, audio and visual feast, all of this combined - is what keeping your interest, where the rush for gunplay challenge leaving you.

But again, all of that - gunplay, visuals and one of a kind soundtrack - still just a cover for the story with guaranteed catharsis in the end. For that Spec Ops the Line is taking such inordinanar reviews, like "take a PTSD in 6 hours. 10/10!" That game Will Be Remembered.
Story what starts like "Only the dead have seen the end of war", and goes with "I destroy therefore I endure". What we observe as happening with the protagonist, Erich Fromm called "splendid isolation". This philosopher was describing destructiveness as a defence mechanism to preserve a human integrity, which is offended by some unexpected trials. That mechanism is never working like you think it should. See the game for it.

Apart from the regular enemies, you only really have snipers and heavies. They aren't too unfair though and there is little artificial difficulty in this game so it's mostly your own skill you'll have to worry about. Your teammates AI, on the other hand, is a different story. You only have one button/key you can use to order them, which is simply "kill this guy". You don't have any advanced commands which would certainly be welcome considering they can and will rush out in front of enemies to kill them and you have little control on where they go and when they do, they will likely go down and if both of them go down you will have to rescue them.

Having played through the entire game on Xbox 360, Windows and Linux, I can say that this game plays well no matter what platform you choose and plays well with both a controller and a keyboard and mouse.

The multiplayer, on the other hand, is terrible and not worth playing even once. It has a tacked-on feel and look to it, like it's simply there to be there. It's modes are as generic as they come and with terrible balance issues and a dead community, you'd be lucky to make past one match if you even get one.

The graphics are reasonably good, especially for a game released in 2012. The background and setting is particularly well done, well able to convey a sense of a city tearing itself apart, and also the issues that have arisen from a city cut off from the rest of the world. It is a pretty brutal Dubai that you find yourself in, and the game conveys the sense of horror that has descended on the city very well.

The soundtrack is fantastic. Both it, and the storyline, short it may be, are probably the standout features of the game for me. Evoking imagery of Apocalypse Now, Spec Ops: The Line shows just how nightmarish and hellish war really is, apart from the glorified imagery that certain media has portrayed it as. Offering a look at the damage that can be done to a soldier's psyche from tours of duty, it also offers a look at the chain of command, something that is explored comparatively rarely. Offering questions regarding morality and cause and effect, while short, Spec Ops: The Line is well worth playing through.

[b][u]PREMISE[/u]

[i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i] starts off as any run-of-the-mill modern military shooter. Coming out in the middle of 2012, these things were a dime a dozen; go to the middle east and shoot non-white people because they have a nuke or they are terrorists or something, right? We've all heard it before.
[i]The Line[/i] in particular is about a squad of soldiers sent into the city of Dubai to help evacuate the civilians of the city after the world's biggest sandstorm has swept through. There are also reports of a rogue infantry battalion in the city, being led by one Colonel John Konrad, an old friend of our main character.
You play as Captain Martin Walker, the leader of the squad, voice acted by the legendary Nolan North.

I wish I could go into details about how the story unfolds, but to spoil any bit of it would do a complete disservice to anyone who hasn't played it. Go into this game as blind as possible.


[b][u]PRESENTATION[/u]
[/b]

Gameplay-wise, [i]The Line[/i] is rather generic. Third person shooting, nice selection of weapons, the cover system works. Occasionally you'll get a turret section, nothing out of the ordinary. The combat itself can feel very intense at times. I played through on "Combat Op" difficulty, which since it was the second-to-lowest of the four options, you could consider it the medium option. You have to aggressively use cover and be very careful you don't get flanked. The AI isn't smart enough to do it themselves, but sometimes they'll spawn on your sides, and if you can't deal with them quickly, you're screwed. You will almost consistently run out of ammo with weapons, so you have to keep switching it up and scrounging around for ammo/weapons dropped by enemies.
During these intense shooting sections you'll hear some pretty generic hard rock playing in the background, but it fits perfectly. You keep up this vibe of being a badass even if the game is trying to strip you of it.

It's interesting to note how many of the games are made by 2k when we asked the various gaming groups to nominate games with the best story. This particular one entitled 'Spec Ops: The line' is actually the 8th one in this particular series though it shares nothing in common with its former installments of the games with the same namesake.

(Spoiler Alert)

The story basically follows a soldiers personal journey through limbo. You take control of a captain Walker who is in charge of a 2 man delta squad. The three of them are on a rescue mission to find the 33rd battalion and their captain Konrad who is someone considered to be of noble rank since he saved your life in a previous battle.

Dubai has become somewhat apocalyptic thanks to huge never ending sandstorms requiring that the whole city to be evacuated. The politicians and the elite downplayed the situation while at the same time evacuating it themselves in secret leaving countless thousands of refugees behind. The 33rd battalion coming home from a war in Afghanistan volunteered their services to help with the relief efforts.

The United States government however ordered the 33rd to abandon the city and its refugees, but the 33rd led by Captain Konrad ignored the command and insisted upon their wishes of leading a caravan of 1,000 people out of the city. However the sandstorms grew worse and the caravan promised never arrived at the proposed time given. Future communication and travelling was severed and the 33rd was publicly disavowed for treason.

After significant time a looped radio signal could be heard coming from the city again. It was a brief one from Captain Konrad. It basically stated that the attempted evacuation was a complete failure and the death toll was too many. The US military then decide to send a covert 3 man delta team in to locate any survivors and then radio for extraction.

Problem is as you guide this 3 man crew into Dubai, things begin to seriously not add up. The refugees are trying to kill you, the 33rd battalion wants to kill you and so does the CIA operatives. As you begin to hallucinate voices and visions, you also begin to witness some atrocities that each splintering faction of the city has done to each other. The game unfortunately forces you to make some of those atrocities yourself in order to push on and find answers and hopefully in the vain attempt to nobly save someone. Somewhere at the end of the game you will be haunted by the dead faces of those that you have killed asking you why you committed such acts and for what purpose? Eventually you will realize that your character is suffering with severe effects of PTSD.

There are 18 campaign chapters to play through with a somewhat highly decorated abstract version of Dubai buried in the sand. These chapters are spasmodically broken up with several morale choices placed throughout the game. The importance of these morale choices and the effects they will have on the game are purely there for illusion. None of your choices will really matter. No matter what you choose or how you go about things your character will be haunted by the people he has killed. There is no pleasant way out of this. The game literally forces you to make a decision which unknowingly at the time will kill thousands. It will then show you the consequence of that decision regardless of the fact that you had no choice about it and it will ask you why did you do it?

Here's where the nobility of the story fails immensely and does not have the same power or punch to a story where your choice really does matter. Any morale judgments are quickly dismissed under a rigged gaming framework. While it does get you to think about things and it has moved and inspired countless people to think about the consequence of actions, I personally think it could have been delivered better to make more of an impact on gamer's than what it already has.
