I was very positively surprised by this game.

The story starts out in Dubai, where most of the population have been evacuated due to heavy sandstorms. Your team is sent on a recon mission, and when discovering dead American soldiers, you continue further in to the city to investigate and look for survivors.
http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=482770326
The basic mechanics of the game are those found in most third person cover based shooters. Most of the time you're behind cover, returning fire at any enemies present. You also have grenades at your disposal, and you can issue simple commands to your squad members (target certain enemies, and in some situations order one of them to throw a flashbang).

The game mechanics themselves are good enough to make the game worth it, but as the game unfolds, you discover that there is more to it than most other modern action games. You are faced with some difficult choices, and have to live with the consequences of your actions in the game.
http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=482770499
The choices are few and far between, and don't really change the storyline, this is not a role playing game, it's more of a cinematic experience (the player is even credited as a "special guest star" in the credits) where you take control over the action. The level design is quite linear, but this isn't necessarily a bad thing.

I don't want to reveal too much about the story, but when you in other games kill hundreds of enemy soldiers and don't think much of it, this game makes you think about what you're doing. You experience the trauma through the main protagonist, and chances are, you won't feel great about what you've done after playing through the game.

While this game is by no means a masterpiece, if you are tired of generic, unimpactful shooters that have all the depth of a poorly written soap opera, then you should, by all means, buy it.  It leaves a huge impact on you from the first few decisions you make.  After one section that I cannot elaborate upon because of massive spoilers, I became physically ill watching the fruits of my actions; I've played several shooters before, and this is one of the first that really made me think, "Wow...I really am a horrible person for doing this", even though that particular part of the game forces you do make that specific action.  It is a military shooter that is highly critical of the military and of war in general, which is quite the oddity in video games in general.  Unfortunately, the singleplayer and its message are undermined by the tacked-on multiplayer, which 2K apparently insisted on.  Don't blame Yager for this, however; 2K had another developer, Darkside Game Studios, make the multiplayer.  It was completely out of Yager's hands.  That said, I have not played it, so I cannot comment on the quality of the multiplayer.  Anyway...the story is, overall, quite good.  It suffers from a bit of the normal ridiculousness that many modern AAA games have in them, but aside from that, I don't remember any problems in the story.  The gunplay is smooth, or at least what I can remember of it.  I'm planning on replaying it in the near future, so I'll update this part of the review when I get to it.  It can be said, though, that ultimately, the gameplay doesn't matter that much, except for a few main points, like using the mortar while assaulting The Gate and making one of the many choices in the campaign.  The main draw of this game is the story, without a doubt.

If you try the demo before playing the full game, please note that it's incredibly misleading.  It does not show what the game is really about, and to be fair, it was intended to be that way.  It was most likely designed to lure in CoD and other typical shooter fans; it does not showcase even a bit of the game's true essence.

I never had any problems with crashes or bugs (except for getting physically stuck in a few areas and having to restart at checkpoints), and it runs quite well on my GTX 770 and i5-4670K.  I felt no need to remap the controls, but that will obviously vary depending on your preferred setup.  As I didn't have a 360 controller when I played this game, I cannot comment on the controller support.  The graphics, while not mindblowing, are quite good on the highest settings, and I do not recall encountering any framerate issues.  All in all, it is quite a good PC port, in my experience.

TL;DR: If you like singleplayer games with intense stories and want a new shooter experience that will leave you hating yourself and questioning your own morality, pick this game up.  It's not one you'll forget about anytime soon.

Or it's an exercise in irony to have an FPS game take every opportunity to say "oooh look at that, you monster. That's the sixth head you've exploded in as many minutes. Ohh did you really have to turn that guy's head into chunky gazpacho? He was already down. Your teammates told you to stop but noooooo. Isn't war terrible? Well, I recently played and finished this game, and I must say it hasn't aged well. The things the developers tried to do with this game are similar to many other games that do them better.

The story is weirdly heavy-handed and disjointed, with your two supporting characters inconsistently swapping roles of being your conscience or urging you to brutality. There's a "twist" at the end, which either doesn't make sense or is just trivial. For "moral choices" and emotional gut-punch storylines in gaming, Walking Dead or Papers Please do a much better job.

Combat is jannnnkkkkyyyyyy as heck. For FPS games, there's a lot of getting surrounded by enemy mobs and getting pounded, while your AI companions stand around not killing things. I must have reloaded some battles dozens of times while getting just the right kills in the right order (or having my AI buddies do so by accident), in order to advance. A far cry from Gears of War, Call of Duty, or Far Cry. Figuring out which object provide cover or can be vaulted over is also super confusing.

The desert setting of a ruined Dubai is unique and gorgeous, and is probably the best part of the game. If someone wanted to make a Dune FPS with this team, it would probably look fantastic.

Some critics praised this game as a bold step in morally dark storytelling in shooters. I'd say some of that praise is exaggerated, and there are certainly enough other games that do it better.

Spec Ops: The Line does for games what Heart of Darkness did for books and Apocalypse Now did for films. I do not write a lot of reviews, but this one deserves it for being a great game, showing war from a unique view in modern gaming.

This is a game that really shines on it's story and narrative. It pulls no punches and unflinchingly shows you every aspect of war that most other games brush over. This game provokes emotional responses that other games try to avoid and involves the player with the decisions faced in conflict situations, and sometimes those choices are not good, or have no good answer at all, but you are still forced to make the hard decision.

It starts off drawing you in as another 3rd person cover shooter, but changes as the game progresses so that you are less interested in the action and more interested in the story, which is masterfully done. It reveals just enough as you are going through so when you get to the end, you remember all those hints that were tugging at the corners of your mind, and catch yourself saying, 'I knew it!' On a replay, there are a lot of those subtle hints that you see that you miss on the first play, and it has been very well written that way. (Think Sixth Sense for this). The twist at the end is pretty clever and makes this game stand out from a lot, but it is not completely unexpected.

The action set pieces are done well in the desert city environment and this comes into play in the game a lot, though it can feel a little bit forced sometimes. The whole 'My Squad vs the World' gets a bit tiring towards the end, as you take on just about every living person in the city with a gun. As I said above though, the importance of the action at that point should have faded away.

Positives:
[list]
  [*] The narrative is the best in the business.
  [*] Involves the player.
  [*] The environment is cleverly realised and used in game well.
  [*] The achievements are fun to chase down.
[/list]
Negatives:
[list]
  [*] Short campaign.
  [*] Simple control system that is clunky.
  [*] Difficulty does not scale up as the game progresses.
  [*] Very linear story, given the emphasis on choice.
  [*] Pointless Multiplayer aspect.
[/list]
Conclusion:

A well crafted and engaging piece of work. Worth the effort you put into it as you walk away from it with more than just the simple amusement. If you want just a piece of gung-ho action, avoid it, but if you want more from games, dont hesitate, buy it, and enjoy.

Spec Ops: The Line takes a very, VERY hard look at war, breaking most of the modern tropes that games like Call of Duty follow (glorifying war as some sort of patriotic action) and instead follows classic war movies, such as Full Metal Jacket, Apocalypse Now, Platoon, and to a lesser extent modern war movies like The Hurt Locker and Zero Dark Thirty. The plot starts off the way most modern shooters start off, with a dessert, and a joking Delta Force operative making jokes about sand in his crack. This is a false starter, as the mood quickly darkens, and only gets worse as you go down the rabbit hole... 

There are two potential turnoffs for players who like games like Call of Duty. First, the controls and gun-play itself is fairly standard. Second, is the game itself is VERY dark, and there are a number of scenes that are very, VERY graphic (harrowing is an accurate description) that will stun and disturb even hardened gamers (myself included) upon their first encounter. This game is not for those who are easily triggered or weak-willed, and as such, consider yourself warned. 

This game is well worth a look, however, particularly for those who want an experience and a hell of a story.

[h1]VERDICT[/h1] [b]Buy (8.2/10)[/b]
Completion Time: 5-7 hours
My Purchase Price: $12.49
Bottom Line: "[i]It's a story worth experiencing, and upon its conclusion, you will reflect on Spec Ops more than any other game you've played.[/i]"

[h1]PROS[/h1]
+Narrative driven game
+Pretty crazy ending
+Unique and gorgeous setting
+Insane set-pieces
+High-throttle action

[h1]CONS[/h1]
-Repetitive game mechanics
-Fairly short
-This game will make you feel bad

[h1]REVIEW[/h1]

This game has left me with some deep seeded inner conflicts. It's a story that delves in to the choices soliders make in the heat of war, and presses the player to choose between life and death in difficult situations. This is not a game about gameplay. It is the running and gunning that is used as a mechanism to continue the plot. It's a story worth experiencing, and upon its conclusion, you will reflect on Spec Ops more than any other game you've played.

You are Commander Walker, a member of the three man squad "Delta Force" who has been sent to Dubai on a reconnaissance mission. Just months earlier Dubai was on the brink of experiencing life-threating sand storms that would destroy the city. The army was sent in to attempt an evacuation, but was soon ordered to abort the mission. The troops in Dubai refused to abort, and deserted the army to stay in the city. Six months later, after the US army intercepted a radio transmission from Dubai, Delta Force is sent in to figure out the situation. It's safe to say that things get really hairy really quick.

It's this story that drives the game. From hallucinations, to some really tough decisions, I found myself wading through the gunplay just so I could advance the story. And let me tell you, it's a good one. Trying to understand how the Dubai situation unfolded is a trip. There are so many different factions at play, and as a play you fell swept up in a war larger than you can imagine. Your choices only minorly affect the ending, but it's very easily for individual players to have different paths to get there based on the decisions you make.

The gameplay is incredibly straight forward. It's the third-person run and gun action we're all used to. I would say it is most similar to Gears of War in that it's largely predicated on the shoot-and-cover mechanic, with vehicular sections interspersed. You really aren't going to see anything you haven't seen before. In all honesty, the gameplay got tiresome after a while. There wasn't enough diversification to keep me too engaged with taking down baddies. To get the most out of it I would recommend making things explode, getting headshots, and most of all taking advantage of squad commands.

My favorite part of the gameplay is the city. You will be traversing the tops of insanely tall buildings, navigating the catacombs that lie at the city's base, exploring the deserts on the outskirts, and shooting your way through some beautiful landmarks and hotels. The developers nailed the setting, and it made the experience much more enjoyable.

So should you buy this game? Well as a whole it is quite the blockbuster experience. It's characterized by an immersive story, some crazy action, and heartbreaking choices. While the gameplay may get tiresome, and the story may be stressful, if you can get it for a fair price I would recommending taking some time to explore Dubai.

This was a pretty incredible experience. As long as you go in knowing that the plot is supposed to an examination how the psyche deals with making irreversible mistakes, rather than a condemnation of violence or argument for pacifism, I think this would be a pleasant change from the usual run-and-gun third-person shooters. 

STORY - Sadistic yet realistic

The story develops from a rescue mission into a much more engrossing tale of redemption and revenge. Prepare to feel very crappy when loading screen prompts change from gameplay hints into taunts, such as:

"Do you feel like a hero yet?"
"Do you even remember why you came here?"
"This is all your fault."

Just like the character in the story, I could feel myself rationalizing my poor judgements. "Yes, those civilians ended up dying, but ... oh, maybe they were going to die anyway. Oh, and other civilians were shooting at us too earlier, so maybe they would have turned on us too. Yeah, that's right, that's why it was okay to burn those women and children alive... right?"

In the end, the story leaves you feeling very empty, but you definitely want to play it a second time to fill in the gaps and make sense of the timeline.

CHARACTERS - Believable and likeable

Your squadmates Lugo and Adams are very likeable. The dialogues do a good job of making you care about them. They will bicker, crack jokes, and think up plans together. 

The squad order system is also very handy, using the Middle Mouse Button to designate targets. Lugo will snipe from a distance, while Adams will lay down heavy fire using a MG or throw grenades.

GAMEPLAY - So-so

The cover system is fantastic. The way you slide into cover, and swap between covers that are side-by-side is pretty awesome.

The shooting mechanics feel very weak though. It is a third-person shooter, so the accuracy always feels wonky. The weapons also SOUND weak and flat. 

There are definitely some scenes that require dozens of tries because of distant checkpoints and hordes of enemies.

There's also the infamous "Freebird" sprinting scene, which is very buggy, and you'll die many times even when you're sprinting as instructed.

GRAPHICS - Fairly good

Texture detail is very good, especially for the characters. 

My main complaint is the overuse of Orange and Blue color grading. Just as it applies to many Hollywood movies, such as Transformers, this is way too prominent and conspicuous. It's not major, but it did distract me from the game when it's too noticeable.

OVERALL - Very Good

Definitely worth a playthrough, although it might be more fitting for people with masochist personalities. 

Buy it at around $15.

Spec Ops: The Line is 3rd person action shooter with elements of squad control. You take control of Captain Walker and his squad of Lugo and Adams, through a desolate Dubai.

Story: The story of this game is its strong point. It starts off as a simple search and rescue mission, however, as you progress through the game the tale gets more and more intriguing. You find out that everything is not as it seems as you must make choices that affect your morality and ultimately, the ending that is presented (which are numerous). It is well-told, has good dialogue and is entertaining and even thought-provoking at times.

Graphics: The graphics of Spec Ops is great. The game engine does a good job of representing Dubai in all its glory, ranging from vast landscapes of sands, to the wealthy and often over-the-top indoor landscapes of the richest in the city. The visuals are crisp and each character are animated very well.

Gameplay: It takes various elements from shooters such as Gears of War (with its cover system) and small parts of Brothers in Arms (squad control) and meshes them into something enjoyable. Shooting weapons and landing hits are satisfying and general movement of characters is fun. You can also issue orders to your squad mates such as, ordering to hit specific targets or to throw stun grenades, and these work well and add to the enjoyment of the game.

Overall, Spec Ops is an underrated game and hidden gem amongst a crowd of 3rd person shooters. With an interesting story and decent gameplay, it is worth playing for all fans of action games.

In Spec Ops: the Line, you play as a military commander with your two squad mates (a sniper and a heavy arms specialist) amidst some really messed up situation in a post-apocalyptic sandstorm setting of Dubai. Here's how a typical scene in this game looks like.

Your helicopter has been hit down. You find yourself alive after the crash and cut down from your teammates. With nothing but a Desert Eagle and a single mag you manage to carefully rush through enemy troops and reconnect with your wounded squad mate, who is sitting by the helo wreck. The next enemy wave is approaching. You're outnumbered atleast by 2:20. You slide into the cover. You have left few bullets in your pistol, but fortunately there's an assault rifle and 2 frag grenades next to you. You throw a frag grenade and it creates a sand cloud. While the enemies are disorganised and blinded, you quickly manage to make three headshots. The enemies start suppresing fire and you're back behind the cover. The enemies try to frag you and you quickly run to the next cover, as the enemy bullets are flying across your head. You wait for the moment when one of them is reloading. Bang! Confirmed kill. Back to cover. Another frag grenade. Another cover change. Meanwhile the enemies are trying to flank you. A shotgunner is approaching from the left side. Bang! Your wounded teammate shoots his head off. That was close. Using the tight windows of opportunity in the constant supressing fire you manage to shoot down two more waves of enemies. After the last enemy soldier is killed, you hear that a "heavy" is approaching. You retreat to the cover further behind you. You have just enough bullets left for this tough guy. You can't afford to miss. He is persistently firing from his light machine gun and you are waiting behind the cover for him to reload. Bang, bang, bang – you shoot at him while he is reloading. It doesn't help as he has heavy armor. He restarts his fire and you get down behind the cover again. If only you had grenades – you think, but you used the last one on the elite troopers. With each second the "heavy" is getting closer and you have nowhere to run. Soon he'll get you. But luckily he needs to reload and with your last bullets you manage to put him down. You save your wounded teammate, salvage whatever the ammo there is left and continue to find your other teammate who has barricaded somewhere further – behind that sandstorm that is approaching.

This scene shows both what is good and wrong with this game: intense, realistic action at the cost of scripts and almost impossible odds.

Due to messy controls and camera angles, lengthy periods between the checkpoints and suicidal, tactically incorrect team member behaviour, there were moments when I cursed the developers, but the grim, engaging storyline and satisfying weapons and enemy kills kept me going until the end.

Completing this game on suicide difficulty was very hard and very satisfying, but it also left a weird aftertaste, almost a psychological trauma, as this game depicts the horrors of war very vividly and realistically.

The graphics are also very beautiful and voice acting is excellent.

There are many fantastic moments in this game, as well as many annoying ones. Despite messy controls and heavily scripted gameplay, I recommend this game for its realistic and deep depiction of war, gradual, seamless progress and challenging, fast-paced action that requires constant adaption and fast reaction.

My overall rating 7/10.

p.s. Few words about the CoOp: great, but only 4 maps.
Multiplayer: almost dead; the experience itself is so-so; beautiful, complex, but unbalanced maps, awkward camera rotation. Your kills are matter of luck and weapon (rank dependent)

After watching the trailer, I wasn't going to play Spec Ops: The Line - it looked like just another war-glorifying soldier hero game, Battlefield of Duty 26. Then I read some of the reviews, many of which rave about the game's plot exploring the horrors of armed conflict, etc. On the strength of the reviews, I decided to give it a try.

Having just finished the single-player campaign, I can't bring myself to go farther than a solid [i]meh[/i]. The plot, while slightly more involved than I had feared, was still fairly shallow. Additionally, it wasn't supported by the gameplay. For a game that tries so hard to make the player consider the ethics of his actions, it gives the player remarkably few choices, and the ones it does give only highlight the lack of the others. [spoiler]For example, there are multiple occasions throughout the game where the player is unable to advance without committing a war crime, so it seems a bit petty in contrast that the biggest of maybe five actual choices given the player is whether to fail to rescue another soldier or whether to fail to rescue a group of captive civilians.[/spoiler]

The gameplay is also fairly bland and repetitive. Most of the game is spent crouching behind sandbags and shooting dudes in the face. Advance to next area, find more sandbags, shoot more dudes in the face. There's very little opportunity to involve stealth, strategy, or anything but frontal assault. There are a couple of sequences where you get to do something different, like cover your squad's escape or act as a helicopter's gunner, but those are few and far between. The enemy forces are very monotone - the entirety of the game is populated with Basic Soldier™, who carries one of a handful of weapons, maybe a dozen Edged Weapon Experts, each of whom can inflict more damage with a single stab than Basic Soldier can with fifteen bullets to the face, and another dozen Heavy Troopers, who are to absorbing damage what Edged Weapon Experts are to dealing it.

I played through the game on Ubuntu 15.04 - it seems to be a solid port, although [b]holy loading hitches, Batman![/b] I took about 7 hours to finish the single-player campaign.

Overall, I have to say that, unless you [i]really[/i] love shooting dudes in the face or have always wanted to see what it's like to blow up postapocalyptic Dubai [spoiler]or rain down white phosphorus onto hundreds of helpless refugees[/spoiler], it's probably best to pass on Spec Ops: The Line.

You play as the golden boy leader of a three man recon squad, with a somewhat murky past, and you're on the outskirts of the ruins of the former city of Dubai, one of the richest cities in the world. Things get real, feelings are felt, and even the loading screen begins judging you. You'll wonder who the bad guys really are. To start off I'll say that this is probably the most unexpected success of the year 2012 and probably one of the ridiculous ones'. Now to the actual game.
I'll start with [b] pros[/b] :
1. [u] Graphics[/u]: Now here there isn't much to explain. Astonishing views from the tall sky scrapers of Dubai and the sandy color were on the high level. It makes you believe you are in Dubai on the war zone, and not in your half broken apartment with neighbours drilling walls. Also worth noting that the demands for such beauty aren't high.
2. [u] Difficulty level[/u]: This one is very balanced. Like in some games of this types, you are playing a role of one man army, and fighting against huge huge huge amounts of enemies. Unlike in most of the games, and this is very important, you have very frequent checkpoints. So even if you die, you will not be thrown back to the beginning of      10-20 min fight as often it might happen, but rather 1-5.
3. [u] Music[/u]: During the tense fights you might not even notice it, but the music that's playing is very good, at least to my taste. Some hardcore rock really does it during the fight. Bands like Deep Purple, Alice in Chains, Bjork and others are featured in the game.
4. [u]Plot[/u]: And here comes the beast - the reason this game is worth all of the fuss. Mainly, the aim of the plot was to show the tough job of the soldier, and the decision making, but also criticise the fact of the war itself, and the way we make war in general. Some touchy issues were shown like use of chemical weapons such as white phosphorus, and the unpleasant consequences that it can bring. You can accidentally vaporize a whole camp of civilians... And then you will have to deal with it. 
One of the other touchy issues, although only if dug deep enough, is the USA "invasion" in the middle east countries and their interference in the local conflicts often in order to protect their own interests which brings more victims. But this discussion will not occur here.
In conclusion the plot really makes this game a big deal with very unexpected twist in the end of the game. If you play the game the second time, you will feel as if you would watch say Fight Club for the second time. You know the big twist and you can see how the game slowly leads you into it.

Regarding [u]cons[/u], this game doesn't have too many of them. The big one is movement, and controls in general. Sometimes when you want to get behind cover the character disagrees with you, running is also a bit weird. 
Another big con, and I really really really hate this one, is when one of your crew members goes down, you have to pick him up, and if not, you'll have to start over... This is the most annoying part of the game, especially on the higher difficulty levels, where you'd run towards him and die, or you just won't be quick enough. Other than that...
Enjoy the game.

Now this is one of those games that tear me apart. On one hand it is good yet on the other hand I feel like the developers should be publicly flogged for all those sins they committed when porting this to PC (I don't know if this was developed for PC side by side with the console versions, but feels like a generic console port).

Now this might contain some spoilers though I at least try to avoid them. You have been warned.

[b]The good:[/b]
The story of the game was amazing. At first it seemed like yet another Call of Duty -ish (or Medal of Honor) game with all-American patriotic attitude and story ("Oh hey... relax. USA ie. The Good Guys are here to save the day from evil terrorists"). But then it just turned... strange. No longer the morals were black and white, but grey, grey and another shade of grey. The player is no longer necessary The One coming to save people from evil. Things go south and it is made clear to the player. Little by little the sanity of the main character is called into question.

[b]The bad:[/b]
Now... the console origin or target is clearly visible in this one. This is not the worst out there, but neither it is one of the best ones. I could bash the game for low quality textures and if I really want to please certain type of people in the internet, I could say things like "It doesn't even have tesselation or <insert new graphical fx here>", but frankly my dear... I don't give a damn about it if the game has decent story or fun mechanics. Yes, the graphics are not that great necessarily, but at least it is not like some ports are: subpar graphics AND requires lots of power to run well.

The level design is also quite boring. While some places and events do look quite nice, they do follow the modern military fps rulebook and are quite linear in design.

[b]The ugly:[/b]
Here is the most infuriating thing I encountered. The controls. I get it, they aimed for consoles as well, but it is not a good enough excuse not to polish the PC controls and make them well customizable. It is not all right to bind several actions to a single key (ok... there are exceptions but generally one action per key). Many times I got really annoyed when I wanted to do something (like going into cover) but there was some interactable item near and game thought I wanted to use that item. In addition, I play some games with gamepad (there I said it though it is a curse word for most PC gamers) so I have gamepad connected most of the time. In Spec Ops this resulted in having all the tooltips (press X) showing gamepad controls though I was playing with keyboard and mouse.

The AI is also rather questionable. Enemies seem to be attracted to the player and pin him down while NPC allies are trembling in cover out of fear, only sometimes doing something actually useful. The allies also seem to be the accuracy of a storm trooper (and no, not the ones who attacked Uncle Lars' homestead but the latter ones who apparently also wore a red shirt under the white "armor").

[b] The Answer [/b]
In conclusion, can I recommend this game after this little rant with more negative than positive? Yes, I think I can. While the mechanics and the design is nothing special and the developers are guilty to all seven deadly sins of console porting (I might exaggerate this a little bit), the story and events themselves are enough to draw the game back to positive side. I really liked the story of this game and would like to see more like this.

Okay, here's the summary; this game is BORING. The shooting mechanics are very basic, with absolutely nothing new or interesting. You do have a squad, but there are a grand total of 3 commands you can give, 2 of them situational, so all you really do is mark targets for them to shoot. The weapons are very generic, but frustrating, because ammo is limited and there is just enough weapon variety to run low or out of ammo regularly, because enemies simply won't use gun X for a while. Grenades are common but very under-whelming, best saved to dump on heavies and turrets. Enemy AI isn't bad, but again, nothing special, with the main difficulty coming from enemies spawning at different places and running onto the map with little to no warning, so you can't intelligently use cover until you learn their spawn patterns. Really, the game is mostly just holding back enemies in clear, distinct waves a couple of times at every checkpoint. Over and over. I guess this isn't that unusual or bad compared to similar games, but it's also why everyone gets those other games for MP, because the SP gameplay is so boring! There's no unique enemies or visceral combat or anything this game can call it's own, and ends up being completely unmemorable.

And I honestly don't understand the praise this story gets. Your characters are three dudes you know nothing about, at all. They don't act intelligently, they are not consistent, and the "big choices" you make don't much matter. And those choices...okay, this is the laziest kind of "choice" writing; completely unexpected, impossible-to-know things happen, meaning, your CHOICES don't matter, it's just dumb luck. It's like choosing to shoot a guy in the leg to NOT kill him, but you happen to shoot his lighter and he erupts in flame. Umm...okay. You tried to do the right thing, moving on. But no, the game tries to make this kind of random chance into a morality play. The overall plot is riddled with holes and is made VERY DRAMATIC only because PEOPLE keep YELLING and CURSING constantly! Stripped of that, it's actually not intelligent or clever; it may "make you think", but as soon as you do, you'll see how idiotic everything is. Basic questions are not even asked in game; we are just supposed to not think about the blatant contradictions and not wonder why our heroes are doing what they are doing.

Yeah, this is not fundamentally different from every other brown/grey modern shooter. All they did was take the very basic stock story, and add hamfisted guilt, a few trippy scenes, and the theme of "your choices matter!" while not allowing your choices to matter and delivered with the subtlety of a 2X4 to the neck. I LIKE good stories, but honestly, I would have preferred a simple but well-written story versus this failed attempt to do better, because instead of being "out of the way" and forgetable, it's instead a headache that makes me go "What? Why?!" every 10 minutes. Don't buy this game unless you just need another dime-a-dozen over-the-shoulder shooter, and you don't mind someone desperately trying to Oliver Stone you over the head with plot you don't care about.

I’m not a “VIDEO games” person but a “video GAMES” one. You won’t see me praising a game like Heavy Rain because of its dull gameplay mechanics, neither over-crediting it for its TV movie-quality plot, what you would read from me about Telltale’s The Walking Dead series is that they are good interactive movies, perhaps calling them good “games” would be hard for me. But this one, this one it’s a bold act of rebellion, even when the game itself is nothing impressive, it is one of those few cases where I'm inclined to recommend a game I didn't enjoyed a lot playing to.

Spec Ops: The Line should be played, it deserves to be played, at least to experience what it does well and how it was a failed but respectable attempt to make a AAA game with an actually adult narrative and distancing itself from the cheap “play this to feel more mature” trend on gaming narrative that started more or less a couple of years after the 7th generation of consoles. 

The GAME

In Spec Ops: The Line you won’t find a hidden gem with terrific mechanics, in fact, the game feels like a tasteless Gears of War clone, it feels like the genre of the game was chosen just to appeal to a bigger audience, if they had developed a top-down shooter or a strategy game a la “XCOM: Enemy Unknown” they would had saved a considerable amount of money, and even been able to invest more on its gameplay and get more or less the same sales they got (roughly 1.13M according to VGChartz).

This doesn’t mean the game is horrible, in fact, It’s decent, and even good at times, it isn’t boring and it’s A.I. isn’t bad, for example, in the hardest difficulty (which is the only one I played), it also has a fresh level design which helps to bring variety to the experience, using verticality pretty more often than third and first person shooters regularly do.
So, in short, the game is not painful to play, but it isn’t also memorable gameplay-wise and you will feel no need to replay it. 

The Portrait

One of the three things this game does right, and the first of them you will notice, is its environment, the ashes of Dubai are real, and not because the game is ridiculously photorealistic (which is not), but because it’s meant to communicate something, not a feeling, not a direct message, but a story, you know something more than a sandstorm happened there. The devastation and helplessness, the man-made disaster over the implacable overtaking of nature against a metropolis turning it into a no man’s land are tangible. 

The designers did a good job (most of the time) trying to immerse the player by mixing the “COVER HERE PLOX” structures among the rest of the environment and they try to constantly draw the players towards what is left of the civilization to give us a break from the sand. The people designing its environment probable spent most of the time guessing: What would people do if “this” happened? The environment results believable and satisfying to watch too.

The Chant

The sound effects are decent and the voice acting accomplishes what it’s meant for. What the game does well is the music, instead of using an over the top generic film soundtrack, the game uses a soundtrack of rock music and its specter of derived genres, constantly portraying what is happening in front of you, sometimes even with some bit of irony, most of it has heavy feelings and a couple of tracks which could be considered as portraying an "angry" or "desperate" feeling, it counts with names as Nine Inch Nails, Deep Purple and Jimmy Hendrix.

The music also lets the sound effects of the sandstorms, broken glasses and guns take the main role when it’s needed. The radio signals also play an important role in the immersion and are a nice way of telling us what’s happening instead of leaving such task in its entirety to the cut-scenes.

Another interesting part related to the story is what I would consider as a "cliche" being used many, many times in games to tell us the "background" of the story, is the way of letting us get into the story by finding some intel recordings through the map, which may I say there is nothing bad with it, mostly because it's related to an already interesting story, but it's just another "checklist" type of feature, similar to its completely unnecessary multiplayer.

The Book

The story of Spec Ops: The Line is based in a classic war novel called “Hearth of Darkness” written by the Polish Author Joseph Conrad (something the writers of this game don't try to hide) and they let you know that in the first moments of the game (I highly recommend the book, ONCE you have played the game).

The story revolves around the 33rd Battalion, a combat unit sent to help Dubai’s citizens to evacuate after a series of sandstorms downplayed or ignored  by the high class and politicians of the city turned it into remnants of what it was. The 33rd was thought lost, but suddenly the US Government gets a looped message from the Colonel John Konrad about the situation of the city and the failure of its mission. 

The game starts with the three-man operative from the Special Forces Delta conformed Martin Walker, John Lugo and Alphanso Adams entering to Dubai and trying to find what happened to the 33rd. The game has some twists, moral decisions, and many hard moments, it portrays war as what it is: murder, and a side trying to conquer the other, while its portrayal of the “occupation” is way lighter than how the book is based on portrays colonization, it’s very admirable to have people getting out of the safe-zone of bro-patriotic-BS found in most AAA war games, with silly “good vs. bad” plots. While it doesn’t goes deep about the political causes of a conflict, it’s a reminder of how distorted a leader’s mind can be and/or how harmful can people be by justifying their narcissistic needs by making up “the enemy” as “the evil” as an excuse for the urge to fight that “evil” which isn’t more than a result of our a need to rationalize the actions we commit or condone, probably our only scapegoat as simple mortals in one of the sides; a way of finding inner peace, perhaps full of emptiness, but enough to let us believe our own lie. First let’s take action; justification can come later as corpses can’t reply anyway. We are all heroes.

Score: 60/100.

The cover system is done fairly well, although i found myself fighting with the controls in many instances because it's just a few slight changes from what standard shooters bring you to expect.

I have run into some instances where invisible barriers would block my shots and they threw in the generic heavily armored (Commonly known as bulldozer) type unit who can be frustrating to an extreme when most enemies react appropriately, a sticky grenade or an RPG on his facemask will do little more than break the mask off and stun him.  The bare face of his still requires significant amounts of shots to kill him with any weapon despite being unarmored which means damage is based on body parts and not types of armored cover. Read a lot of the negative reviews before I decided to add my thumbs up. They seem to fall into a few categories, optimization, gameplay, and multiplayer/co-op complaints. So I'll address all three.

1. Multiplayer - Was forced on the dev, is horrible. Don't buy this for multiplayer, and don't bother trying it if you haven't.

2. Optimization - this is a thorny one. I have never had a problem with frame rate on either of my two rigs, but I have a pretty nice setup, and I have no idea how common the problems are. Do some research on the requirements before you spend any money on the game.

3. Gameplay. Yes the game is repetitive, yes it uses many extremely common tropes of cover-based shooters.
However in the context of the meta-narrative I consider that working as intended. I have done several playthroughs (despite my recorded hours) and taken copious notes of how responsive the mechanics are. They degrade as the game goes on. Meaning - I never had trouble sticking to cover, controlling sprint, or reloading in the first part of the game on any playthrough. I had trouble with all of them in the final act on every playthrough. This indicates intent to me. It fits with the scaling difficulty and brutality of the final act of the game. Walker/You break down as you go, and it is reflected in every single aspect of the experience.

The game is aware of the artifice. If that sounds like something that would piss you off rather than pique your interest, I recommend grabbing the game. I would also check out "Killing is Harmless" which is a critical analysis of the game. It covers a lot of stuff I don't have time to write about here. 

I consider this game to be one of the greatest games ever made, but a recommendation comes with some caveats other than those mentioned above. Some experience with shooters will be necessary to fully appreciate the deconstruction taking place here. Without that, it may simply appear to be an example of, rather than a response to the genre. In my opinion, it also requires a straight playthrough. Meaning - set aside a full day or so, and just play the whole game. Don't break it into chunks, take time off between sessions, or fracture the experience. 

Outside of that narrow band of specifications I wouldn't recommend this game to be honest, even as one of my favorites.

War is not always as simple as we would like it to be; the bad guy against the good guy, sometimes the lines blur.

Overall, I recommend the game to anyone that wants an experience that they will likely never forget.

The only reason this game has good reviews is because the Spec Ops community suppresses negative ratings by downvoting them into oblivion. I had to use a custom launcher because it kept crashing on startup. This review will cover the mechanics first, then the plot.

This game is so linear its basically a 5 hour movie that pauses itself every minute or so for you to unpause it with a quicktime event or pressing a button to climb over something. The guns feel awful, never run out of ammo, and you'll never use anything the enemy isn't carrying at the time. Everything consists of setpieces with less thought put into them than MoH Warfighter. You will shoot enemies in a linear environment from cover for about 3 rooms, have yet another encounter with a turret that lasts all of about 5 seconds, then predict perfectly that you will be ambushed by infinite waves of enemies. In these ambushes you have to simply rely on trial and error and waiting. In every ambush there is a special spot you're supposed to be or you will be killed. For example, in the first ambush you have to run across an open field of sand to a broken building and get behind one of two pieces of cover. Lets say you picked the left, you'll be blown up with a rocket launcher setpiece and killed instantly. You restart, try to fight back and get killed within seconds because you want to have a good time, I guess. Eventually, after a few retrys, you'll find the magic position that won't get you killed, sit there for about 3 minutes until another setpiece is activated and you somehow all get away unscathed. You will look around and suddenly realize that you are now conveniently at the exact location you were heading to in the first place. 

This game introduces nothing innovative whatsoever other than the option of shooting a window about every 30 minutes to drop sand on enemies. It seems like more of a gimmick to me than anything else. The movement couldn't even be spared, either. Imagine if Gears of War and Army of Two had a crippled child that was put on the indie games section of XBOX 360. Spec Ops just a step above that. It also doesn't help that the friendly AI is constantly in your way and consistently fails to understand orders outside the context of linear setpieces, which is always a "press M3 to continue this game" resulting in your teammates actually doing their jobs.

Since everyone regards this game so highly due to its story and 99% of the plot is driven by cutscenes, I'm going to look at as a movie. If this was submitted for a film class, I'd give it an A-. I enjoyed the dramatic shift in tone and the twist endings, but that's all that really stuck out. It feels a bit shoehorned at times but I pushed through the generic cliches of modern shooters that is spec ops to reach the ending and the finale was great. However, it didn't make up for the lack of intuitive gameplay. My only qualm for the plot is the poor character development for everyone other than the main character and his squad. There weren't any memorable enemies and the leaders of the various factions you fight are basically just "guys." They don't have anything special to them and I'm bound to forget them within a week or two from now.

In a world where everyone's a hero when they launch a shooter, Spec Ops: The Line crushed that stereotype. Never had a game make me question my morality as much as Spec Ops: The line. This game surpassed the level of a game, bringing to me what I can only described as "a very real experience".

The strong emotions of the graphics and voice acting emersed me into a setting where I ponder over every decision I made while playing as the protagonist. I can still vividly remember the very first time I was shown the repercussions after I made a "mistake". Without revealing spoilers, I can only say I regretted so hard I did not make a save before making that decision and it "haunted" me for the rest of the game, quite literally.

Together with This War of Mine, I'm pretty sure Spec Ops: The Line can be arguably the next most realistic war game ever scripted. It introduces as a shooter, but jolts you back up and shake you vigorously, reminding you that every single round that connects with an "enemy", someone out there lost their loved one.

I have been late in picking up Spec Ops: The Line, and I regret letting it grow dust in my collection and not playing it sooner. The experience of this game is as good as reading a great novel. Kudos to the screenwriters for writing such an outstanding story.

A long time ago, I read Joseph Conrad's The Heart of Darkness. That book featured Marlow's journey down the Congo river in search of a man named Kurtz. As Marlow and his crew descended down this river on their boat, they discended into darkness and saw unfathomable savagery. They witnessed the true brutality of man and discovered horrors that can drive a man insane. I was pleasantly surprised to discover that Specs Ops was based off of Heart of Darkness. 

Like the film adaption of Heart of Darkness, Apocalypse Now, Specs Ops attempts to modernize the story of Heart of Darkness and add a military element. However, instead of the setting being in Vietnam like Apocalpyse Now, Specs Ops takes place in the Middle East. I enjoyed seeing all the little parallels to Apocalpyse Now and Heart of Darkness. A big theme in The Heart of Darkness was one man not being worth all the danger and inevitable carnage, but the main character dragging the crew along anyway because of obsession and mental instablity. Specs Ops offers parallels to Heart of Darkness and offers its own little unique spin to this internal conflict. 

The game is also very fun to play. However, I did have a few problems. There are a few instances where the game is frustrating. Sometimes I'll be taking cover from fire, my health will be low, and an enemy will throw a grenade. This leads to either two choices: die from the grenade or die sprinting into gunfire. These levels are very small, many of them have limited places to take cover from gunfire. It's a tedious experience to die over and over because the cramped level design leaves you nowhere to take cover when a grenade happens to fly in your direction. It doesn't leave players feeling like they died because of an honest mistake. I also encountered glitches where the sniper rifles wouldn't register a lot of headshots. Incidentally, the stealth mechanics and tactical commands feel bare bones and leave much to be desired. 

Despite all my problems, I would recommend this game. There are a few problems, but it doesn't ruin the experience entirely. The game is a little short (under seven hours), but the story and atmosphere are absolutely chilling. It's a well directed game. If you ever see this game on sale, be sure to buy it!

Spec Ops: The Line, was a breath of fresh air in the FPS genre for me. The interactive terrain was enjoyable and the use of it could have a dramatic impact on how many of the firefights turned out. The Suicide Mode was suitably hard and challenging - and the game play mechancs were smooth and made the game fluid and fun to play.

The biggest pro of the game is the story. It is an enjoyable story with elements that many FPS  games don't touch on and this was the best part about the game in my opinion. When you hit the end of the game, those final moments, it really makes you reflect on what you did earlier in the game and wonder - did I make that choice? I also enjoyed the fact that there was no best weapon that could be picked up and used the rest of the game. That different weapons and your own stock of ammunition, called and sometime required switching up. I think the toughest  choice I had to make was do I keep the AR that I had finally fully loaded with extra ammo - or swap to the much needed RPG to take out hardened targets? These choices matter.

Lastly, another big pro is the AI teammates you have aren't stupid. Their kills matter and they will kill things. It was great to see that.

The biggest con I had of the game was that even on max settings it was still sometimes hard to spot enemies in medium range locations. And there was some wall clipping that AI bullets seemed to do that were inexplicable. This could be because of terrain design with the levels. But it happened enough that it caused me moments of intense frustration.

Overall, I'd recommend Spec Ops: The Line as a cheap buy and a great game  for a play through.

Yes, the majority of the time you are going to be playing a console-style checkpoint-based linear shooter where you walk through beautifully-rendered warzones mowing down waves of enemies. The shallow gameplay and gratuitous violence is exactly the reason i personally don't tend to enjoy this style of game. But what makes Spec Ops interesting is that instead of letting the player come to that conclusion on his own, it pushes the main character into situations where you, as a player, are forced to consider how messed up it really is. There are strong parallels with Apocalypse Now, especially in the great music and over-the-top violent imagery, but i ultimately found myself more reminded of The Stanley Parable, another game that makes you think about why we, as players, play the games we do. The highlight of the whole experience is an insanely good "hallucination" toward the end that just punches you in the face with meta, especially if you have played the whole game in one sitting (highly recommended). Very, very clever.

This just gives you that feeling of "Nothing can really happen to you", which makes you stop caring. Now, this would be fine, other video games are like this too, but there is one difference: the characters. 

I couldn't care about any of them because they seemed to have the personalities of cardboard cut-outs, there is nearly no work at all put into establishing characters, and here lies my problem with the game. None of the characters are humanized, we don't care about them, so when the game shows us terrible things happening to them, trying to make us sympathize with them, it just doesn't work. Ambitious and with a fresh look at US-Middle Eastern conflict, this game could have been something awesome if the designers did their job.  The game assigns you objectives without telling you, leaving you to die endlessly without ever knowing what you were supposed to do to progress the story.  Weapons are portrayed horrifyingly inaccurately - if you're going to use real life forces and real life weapons, get the capacities right.  Remember Mass Effect 3's signature screw up, the "omnikey"?  This game's controls are so wonky and counterintuitive, I find myself wishing for the omnikey.  Now, I'll admit, there seems to be a common belief that failure is fun - but that's not the only way to play games, and if you are going to design a game only to appeal to those who enjoy failure, you're doing it wrong.  Spec Ops: The Line is a classic example of why shooters have a limited appeal even as gaming becomes mainstream.  Teenagers and the unemployed may have the time to fail every checkpoint over and over, but it's been decades since those were the primary demographics playing games.  Don't pay full price for this - it isn't worth it.  For $5, I can see it being money well spent, assuming you actually enjoy frustration.

Specs Ops: The Line has received much praise in weaving a horrific tale of an op gone wrong and the horrors of war. The game expertly puts you in the shoes of the main character as he teeters on the edge of sanity as his PTSD nightmare slowly consumes him. But in the end, the game's greatest strength is also its greatest weakness.

The game not only encourages, but actively pushes you towards making crazy "gamer" decisions that leads to the story spiraling out of control. Executing a downed enemy is a common video game mechanic that players have come to expect. Executing a downed enemy also gives you ammo for both weapons. However, should you choose to simply double-tap them with your gun, you will not spiral into madness at the same rate as a normal playthrough. Although there are many hidden third options to most of your choices, the game doesn't let you make any key decisions that sidestep everything.

Spec Ops: The Line does a great job of telling one story but fails to give you the other option of not succumbing to monstrosity. The gameplay is very tiresome and rather boring. Some would say that this is in part of the game trying to parody the meaninglessness of your generic modern First-Person-Shooters, but was this honestly the best way of going about this? Couldn't we have some fun going down this hellish slide?

I only wish that there were more choices that we could make that would better simulate PTSD/anxiety/paranoia. Why was there no choice to interact with the civillian NPCs in a way that would test our distrust of the local populace? Why was there no option to deal with groups that were obviously armed and cutious, yet not overtly hostile?

Overall, Spec Ops: The Line is a good game to experience but not necessarily to play. I would definitely recommend this game if you enjoy storytelling experiences.

Spec Ops The Line is a game I wanted to play for a while now, since it was getting a lot of praise for its themes and portrayal of war.  Is it a masterpiece? Not sure. But it is a great experience. While the game itself is quite story and character driven, it had quite a few cutscenes, mostly just a short intro and ending to a chapter, with ocassional dialogues between characters. Most of the time you were shooting people.

The gameplay was basically a typical third person cover shooter. You get to a new section, take cover, shoot until you clear the area, proceed and listen to some dialogues between your mates, take cover and repeat. It doesn't bring anything new to the table, although shooting glass and killing enemies with falling sand was a great feature, which wasn't implemented often enough.  While I'm not that much of a shooter person, I haven't played enough games to get bored by the genre, so this game felt fresh to me and I never felt bored, nor did the game feel tedious. I was always glued to the screen, waiting to clear the next wave and continue the story.

Through the whole game you're accompanied by your two subordinates, Adams and Lugo, who were surprisingly useful on their own. A lot of games usually have terrible AI partners that rarely kill any of the enemies (notable in Call of Duty and Battlefield), but in Spec Ops The Line, the AI was really useful, and I knew I would have a safe back with them behind me. Even without ordering them to take out a target, they still do great work. It really helped me enjoy the gameplay, since it never felt like I was doing the entire work. Though I still did kill 99% of the enemy in the end, but that 1% still matters, that enemy could have easily flanked me!

The story is where this game shines. At first it seems like your typical Call of Duty/Battlefield game, you go and bring freedom to people. That's what the game initially is, until the plot expands and you aren't even sure WHO you're killing. Even at the end of the game I wasn't even sure whom I'm shooting. Am I shooting the guys that started the mess? Am I shooting the guys that are protecting the people? It was either shoot or die. 

Now, a lot of people mention how they felt bad for killing people in the game, felt the weight of it etc. I could see Walker get traumatised and change because of all the deaths, but I never felt anything, aside from initially not wanting to shoot the civilian crowd (which the game forces you to do, so you don't even get an option). You are usually shooting armed people, mostly soldiers. Not really something that would make me feel bad for killing people. Or maybe it's just because I'm not American, so it's the same if I'm shooting Arabs or Americans in the game. Another thing is the soundtrack, it's just so awesome that it makes shooting people actually fun. 
 
The game is pretty graphic, with a lot of graphic visuals of burned and killed people, showing the true colors of wars, which lots of military shooters don't show. It felt a bit overdone at times, with people hanging almost at every single map later on. I usually don't care about violence and graphic content in games, but this game really used it well to set up the story and the war. Literally the first thing you see in the game are dead bodies. And slowly you see more and more dead and rotten bodies. All of that was nothing compared to watching people get burned by phosphorus (which is often used during wars, and is a really inhumane way of killing people). The first phosphorus scene, and later the one done by you, are probably the scenes that hit me the most.

As long as you don't absolutely despise the shooting genre or story driven games, this worth playing. Buy it or pirate it, it doesn't matter, what matters is the one time experience of it's messed up story and visuals.

"You are still a good person", the game reminds me in a loading screen. It may seem strange or pretentious if you haven't played Spec Ops: The Line, but trust me, it helps you get through the game. Spec Ops: The Line is NOT a fun experience, and it's not meant to be, and that's exactly what makes it the single best war-based video game in history. Hiding its true nature under an ad campaign that marketed the game as just another war-shooter power-trip for the typical CoD-fanboy, only one trailer even hinted at the horrors of the game (look up the trailer for the game titled "The Journey"). Based on Heart of Darkness and by proxy Apocalypse Now, SO:TL follows Capt. Walker as he and his comrades Lugo and Adams enter a ravaged Dubai to rescue survivors of a sandstorm, along with the mysterious Col. Konrad. What starts as a war-fighter game quickly clues the player in on the fact that something is VERY VERY WRONG, and not all is as it seems. I won't spoil anything because this game deserves to be experienced unspoiled by all gamers, but the nationalistic power-fantasy all comes crashing down around the player when they unwittingly commit A VERY BAD THING, and the game rears its ugly head as a brutal deconstruction of warfare, the culture of military video games, and leaves the player haunted and changed by the experience. While many a game has mastered the art of manipulating your emotions, none can ever touch the bleakness and harrowing, nightmarish vision that is Spec Ops: The Line

I found myself rationalising the protagonist's choices as if they were my own. Even as events started to spiral out of control, I found myself trying to think about what I would do if it were my boots in the sand. I couldn't ever question Walker's decisions because they were always based on a truth he had compiled from an incomplete understanding of the situation, which was something I shared with him. 

It's a three dimensional look at war, imaged in breathtaking scenes and with commendable voice-acting. Oftentimes, war is not as we traditionally define it. Decisions are not always based on what is good or bad, heroic or cowardly. They are often driven by interpretation of orders and gut-feel. And when dreadful things happen, do we really fully appreciate the toll on those that felt they had to pull the trigger, squinting though the fog of war? 

This is a visceral and engaging experience which I highly recommend to gamers looking for something a bit different.

Spec Ops: The Line is one of the darkest, most disturbing, and yet artisticly astounding games I have ever played. Every step along the way makes you question all that you have done and how you've gotten to where you are, while being filled with a general atmosphere of psychological tension. This game is truly comparable to Apocalypse Now, the movie it is so often compared to. There are few ways I could recommend this more.

You are still a good person; this is not your fault; you did not have a choice. Well you really don't, at least gameplay wise, but the point of this game is to deliver a story and it ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ delivers it with flying colours.
It took me 3 tries to finally finish it. It was repetitive, buggy, often boring, irrational, filled with typical war hero cliché moments. As it turned out, everything had a reason and the game masterfully appeared shallow on purpose. All you have to do is accept the way it is and enjoy the view. Literally, the graphics is quite a joy to the eye and very refreshing with its desert-post-apocalyptic environment.
Would you please pay attention, because clues about the actual story are all around you.

I thought this game would start off on a high note; one that would get me fired up and ready to take on the challenge set before me. I thought I would enter the world of post-apocalyptic Dubai ready for anything. But I didn't.

I thought that I would feel satisfied every time I landed a well-aimed headshot, like in CSGO. But I didn't.

I thouht I would save the civilians and kill only those who stood in the way of what was truly right. But I didn't.

I dropped white phosphorus on the civilians I was trying to save. Those men I killed with a well-aimed headshot were the true heroes. I was the villian. Anyone who wants to know what the world of war which video games have created is really like: play this game. Next to Portal 2, this is the second game to ever make me shed a tear. But this time it was for the complete opposite reason. The story was incredible.

Issues with the gameplay only lie in the fact that they were unorthodox and strange, but after an hour or two I had mastered them. Still a bit fiddly at times, though. 

The graphics and visuals were great. I truly believed I was in a ruined Dubai. Even when it's destroyed and uninhabitable, the place still blew my mind. Occasionally some of the player textures would sporatically change resolution; they would look life-like one second and then potato the next, all having to do with the angle at which they were viewed. The anisotropic filtering became a noticable annoyance in some cutscenes. But even then, it was a beyond passable overall experience. Someone poured a lot of time in making it as good as possible; this much is evident, even with a few minor hiccups.

[b][u]-Quick Review-[/u][/b]
Spec Ops: The Line is a third person shooter who takes a warfare story telling aspect, and mixes in gritty realism, coupled with very solid cover-based-game play.

[b][u]-Detailed breakdown review-[/u][/b]
[b]Story:[/b]  How do you talk about the story in this game without giving away any great details? The story goes in a very unorthodox direction from most Shooter games I've played. Additionally there are choices that you make throughout the game, and it's not just "go right or go left" as the saying goes "indecision is a choice".
In the words of William T. Sherman we hear the well known quote "War is Hell" To be quite honest not very many shooter games run with that concept, in Spec Ops: The Line, you will see far more gritty details of consequences of warfare... and the people effected.
[i]As a final note regarding the story length, I after playing through the game my first time I put in 5.5 hours. I generally play slower trying to find extra items and do restarts for achievements, so that should be longer then a standard player will take to get through the game.[/i]

[b]Game Play:[/b] Spec Ops: the line is a cover-based third person shooter, meaning while you're being shot at you will move from cover to cover, most of the mechanics are quite straight forward, but do take some getting used too, you can jump over cover, change cover quickly by looking or pressing a movement key in that direction THEN pressing Space, there is a fair bit of learning to be had.
It should be noted that the controls will take some getting used too, I had already played a few third person shooters so those old controls were messing me up while I was trying to learn the new ones. Once you learn the controls the rest of the game is quite enjoyable to play through.
Even if you're unfamiliar with cover-based-shooters the starting difficulty is friendly enough that you can get the hang of it while gunning down your foes. (I would still recommend getting used to hiding behind cover)

[b]Achievements:[/b] There are 50 Achievements in Spec Ops: The Line, after my first play through I had 33 of those achievements, there are four achievement category types: Find the lintel (collection), Get kills or special kills with weapons, Make this choice in the story, and standard story quests.

[b]Price[/b] Spec Ops: The Line is priced at $29.99, by this point most people should be used to games (especially shooters) being priced there, as I always say "I recommend waiting for a sale". 

[b]Conclusion:[/b] Spec Ops: The line will appeal most to people who enjoy the two qualities of "Third person shooter", and "story telling". If you just want a shooter where you run in and pew pew pew, this isn't the right game for you. If you like playing games with meaningful stories, making hard ethical decisions while gaming or just looking for a change of pace this game will provide it.
To quickly recap: Story - Outstanding story telling methods. Game Play - Controls might be a bit tricky at first, but the cover based combat is very good. Achievements - Pretty Standard, there are a few tricky looking achievements though. Price - Standard, wait for a sale.

This review is only for the single player campaign on normal difficulty.  

Pretty well everything about this game was exactly what I would want out of a FPS campaign.  There was a decent variety of guns, some of them had secondary fire options, a few gernade choices and a melee option.  The best thing about the guns was that there wasn't one or two that were obviously the ones you had to take with you, you had the choice to pick whatever two you liked and make your way through the game.  Of course there were times that one gun was much more useful than another but for the rest of the time you could run with what you want, till you ran out of ammo anyways.  

Enemies were not to difficult for the most part outside of a few areas that were tricky.  Later game enemies did start presenting a bit more of a challenge.  They used cover surprisingly well and did attempt flanks and the like.

The setting, enviroment, graphics, etc... were all top notch, there is pretty well nothing that I could complain about in that department.  From the beauty of the open spaces in destroyed dubia to the smaller areas were unspeakable horrors abounded, everything was just so well presented.

And the story.  Without getting into spoilers because this is a game that should be experienced spoiler free.  I loved the story, I'm still not sure I entirely got everything that there was to get from the story, but thats the great part.  The game did leave some choices to make, as to what exactly those choices decided at the end of the day, well thats why I want to play the game more than once, and I can't really think of any FPS single player campaings that made me want to come back for more.  

The only big gripe that I had with this game was with your AI teammates and their use of cover, or well lack of cover I guess.  The two AI teamates that you travel the game with are better than a lot of other AI teamates other games have stuck you with, these guys actually can kill an enemy or two but they tend to walk stupidly out of cover every now and then.  They would end up dying foolishly and you'd have to break cover to revive them or mission failure.

But to sum it all up.  This is exactly what I've wanted out of a FPS single player campaign.  Everything was presented beautifully.  There was a decent selection of weapons to keep the shooting interesting and a story that above all else makes the game stand out far above a lot of other FPS campaigns and is something that I would whole heartedly recommend to almost any FPS fan.

Developed by Yager and published by 2K Games, Spec Ops: The Line is one the most-discussed video games in recent years.

Edge Magazine calls it "one of the most subversive shooters yet made" and notes: “It may not be subtle, but it engages with problems that the bellicose ilk of Modern Warfare and Medal of Honor have yet to acknowledge."

Despite mixed critical response and moderate sales for the third-person tactical shooter, the game inspired a 50,000 word ebook entitled Killing is Harmless as well as an accompanying online bibliography at the site Critical Distance, which highlights over 50 articles, videos, and other responses to the game.

Its narrative references Francis Ford Coppola’s Apocalypse Now (and to a lesser degree Joseph Conrad’s Heart of Darkness) but transposes its setting from the jungles of Vietnam to a ruined, dystopian version of modern Dubai.

The plot ostensibly follows the exploits of a three-man Delta Force team made up of Captain Martin Walker (voiced by Uncharted’s Nolan North), Lieutenant Alphonse Adams, and Staff Sergeant John Lugo as they seek to uncover what has become of the rogue 33rd U.S. Army Battalion led by the elusive Lieutenant Colonel Joseph Konrad.

The game mechanics are typical of a third-person tactical shooter, but as players delve deeper into the heart of Dubai, the sands begin to shift and the objectives of the mission becomes less and less clear. Addressing the idea of player agency (explored in other titles such as Bioshock and Portal) as well as examining traditional tropes of war-themed video games, Spec Ops: The Line rushes the player towards a brutal, unhinged, and final confrontation with the self.

This game. This game! This is how a shooter is supposed to be made. Engaging characters and story, excellent gun-fighting and gameplay, and a twist that made me sick with disgust at myself and Captain Walker. I loved it!
After the half-way point, things go to $#!t. A spiral of madness and death opens up that you walk to the end. Even the loading screens after Chapter 10 or so start to take the piss out of you by passive-agressively insulting all you've done in the game when you're reloading after being killed. Plus, unlike most shooters, it has multiple endings depending on the choices you make! 
This game is a must for fans of shooters, horror, and war games. At only $20, this game is a better deal than any CoD or Modern Warfare game out on the market. It has replay value, fun gameplay such as zip-lining, commanding your troops to snipe or bomb enemies, and interesting enviroment kills such as the standard "shooting fuel tanks to make them explode" but also a new "shoot out glass to drop sand and stun enemies." It has numerous weapons, and while ammo is sometimes hard to come across, the enemies drop weapons with each one you kill, so you can their bodies. You can only carry 2 guns at a time, but this doesn't take much away from the game, giving you incentive to try out the various firearms and find the ones you like best. My only real complaint gameplay wise is that the Sticky Grenade can be more trouble than it's worth, as it has a smaller explosion range and distance to be thrown than a Flash Bang or Frag, and no bounce. It is fun to stick them onto a foe and watch them flail around, though.
As for the characters, Spec Ops makes you sympathise with all of them. Even the villains have understandable motivations, and you wonder if you'd act any differently in this situation. Captain Walker, Lieutenant Adams, and Sergeant Lugo are people, with feelings and emotions that they display through both cutscenes and in-game banter. They are far superior to the burly, no-name, buzz-cut scrubs of the current FPS. 
This game gripped me like no other. I got it (from a friend) on March 1st. It is now March 4th, and I have been playing almost non-stop to finish it. I had to see the ending. I had to experience what was the culmination of Captain Walker's actions and struggles. I had to. This game is the most engaging thing I've played all year, and I'd argue it is going to be an all-time favorite, right up there with the other games of my childhood I remember fondly.
With FPS's pedalling boring stories, gameplay and characters that are little more than cardboard cutouts, Spec Ops: The Line makes me hopeful for the future of gaming, and sick to my stomach for the in-game atrocities I witnessed and committed. You want a good game? Buy this one.

[i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i] is a third-person cover shooter/military shooter that actually had a writing team behind it; a game that deliberately seems to get worse and worse in more ways than one, you push these characters through an environment which somehow doesn't look like it's going to be a plethora of unicorns flying out of giant cakes. 

[i]The Line[/i] will scream at you to turn it off in multiple ways, be its means through deliberately repetive gameplay, shaming the player/voyeur, gruesome imagery or it's measured plot development. You continue on what you think is another mundane and linear foray into a Hollywood-style action game, you keep telling yourself it's going to get better—for yourself at least, then at a certain point [i]The Line[/i] becomes something else altogether; it rapidly becomes engrossing instead of entertaining.

The game itself is generic, a little short and a relatively easy blast-through with various horrifying ways to kill and maim your fellow man (if that turns you on), but "breaking the fourth wall" in military shooters is an elusive narrative device along with the commentary it tries to make here, so if you want story more than yet-another-explosive-orgy-of-machismo trying to fetishize hurting other people as a perfectly justifiable and fun act, then this is for you.

[h1] Story [/h1]
Captain Walker, sergeant Lugo and lieutenant Adams go to the destroyed city of Dubai to rescue any survivors that they are able to find. At least, that is what they think they are doing here. Upon arriving in Dubai the Damned 33d is in a war with the CIA over control of the destroyed city. Many civilians are still alive and breathing, but know no rescue is coming for them. Walker and his comrades walked straight into hell and need to get out, even if this means doing some of the most inhumane things. The story is the best aspect of the game, everybody who likes third person shooters should've experienced this story.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
Spec Ops: The Line is a simple third person shooter, with fair third person shooting mechanics. You, Captain Walker, can take two weapons with you everywhere you go, but these weapons can go out of ammo fast so you'll have to pick up weapons from your dead enemies. sergeant Lugo and lieutenant Adams are some very helpful friends. You can order them to kill a specific enemy, which is very handy from time to time. Sergeant Lugo is able to make long ranged shots with his sniper rifle and lieutenant Adams is able to flash your enemies if they're standing in a small group. They gameplay may be a bit clunky, but fun for the duration of the game.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
A solid third person shooter with an amazing storyline, every chapter has its own setting and never really gets boring. The game has multiple endings and choices to make, so a there is some replayability. Spec Ops: The Line is a game everyone should at least played once purely for it's amazing story. The gameplay does have some hiccups, but can be forgiven.
