It's hard to comment on this game without spoilers, but I'm trying my best to avoid them. Also note that I didn't try the multiplayer and I'm only going to comment on the single player campaign.

The game presents a well-crafted story that starts out as a mission to scout the city of Dubai as it suffers from the destruction caused by a gigantic sand storm. Civilians are trapped inside mile high dunes of sands after the military lost contact to a former evacuation squad and they send Martin Walker and two companions to investigate after they received a distress signal. The deeper the squad dives into the city, the more gruesome events get. You witness atrocities done by American soldiers who lost track of their goal as the horrible story of the fallen Dubai unfolds with your discoveries and the game doesn't hesitate to shock you when it wants you to see what terrifying things people can do in a struggle for survival. (if you don't have a thick skin, you might want to plan to take breaks)

If it weren't for the story, the game would be forgettable, and that is the biggest danger if you don't know it yet - those who don't know what to expect will easily lose interest. The shooting itself plays well enough to work - there's cover-based shooting with various real-life weapons, there are melee attacks and finishers, a small selection of squad commands, you can sometimes destroy terrain to take out clusters of foes with sand dunes. There's not much traditional gameplay evolution, except that the selection of weapons grows as some weapons only appear later in the game.

If you ONLY come for the shooting, you will most likely be disappointed or even confused through the first couple of chapters. If you want to give this game a fair chance, keep on playing until the end of Chapter 8 at least. If you get there and still only come for the shooting, but want to give the game a chance nevertheless, start over again and pay close attention to the dialog and try to think about the twists that happen in the beginning of the game, which are admittedly a little hard to follow the first time around.

A word about the length of the game: The play time is rather short (I beat the game in 6 hours on easiest difficulty.. there is a reason you don't want to turn up the difficulty in the late game, which I leave up to you to find out), but if you get into it, it probably won't let you go for a while, especially since many discussions on the internet send you away with spoiler warnings right away. Once you've played through the game and see the revelations, you will want to play it again to see things in a different light. If you find yourself in an obsession about the meaning of the game, a good reading after you finish it is "Killing is Harmless" by Brendan Keogh. It's an affordable eBook that expands on a lot of details that you will easily miss on a casual playthrough. It links a good amount of articles on the internet, some of which include stances by the developers and lead writer. My Steam profile says I've played this game for only 16 hours, but I spent well over 30 hours reading up and watching on YouTube on what others thought about it.

Spec Ops: The Line deserves more attention for the sheer courage the developer showed for demonstrating such a cruelly honest truth through a video game, and I recommend it wholeheartedly to everyone who likes unconventional games. It made me think for long, and it pulled something off that is impossible to do with a book or a movie.   Spec Ops: The Line. What can be said about it? Well quite a lot actually. You start the game off as Captain Martin Walker, leading a three-man team into an almost post-apocalyptic Dubai. What starts off as exactly the kind of game you'd THINK yourself getting into, is a third-person cover shooter with plenty of brown to spare, designed the lure in the exact kinds of people who play such games. From a gameplay standpoint, Spec Ops fails to break any new ground, playing like how you'd expect a game to play from ten years ago, but the shine isn't from the game itself surprisingly enough, but from the story. As you progress through the game, traversing the ruins of Dubai fighting various baddies, the story really picks up. You go from fighting the locals for the first few missions to actually fighting rogue US soldiers.

 Every encounter leaves you a little more worn, both physically and mentally, as well as your own soldiers, degrading as the game drags on. Dealing with the more serious, personal aspects of war such as PTSD to the very morality of what you're doing, a subject not often touched in war games where you kill five or six dozen people in a level and don't give it a second thought. Your two comrades begin to question your every choice and action, voicing their (sometimes conflicting) opinions after firefights and during decision making periods. The choices don't often matter, sometimes forcing you into situations where there's only one choice to pick, but still lays the burden of its actions on your shoulders as in the end, you are the one who did it.

 The game degrades further as you play, at times breaking the fourth wall and speaking directly to YOU; the player, often through the almost subliminal nature of the environment, even to the very loading screens, where the gameplay tips often found at the bottom begin to say such things as "Can you even remember why you came here?" and "You're still a good person." to the later "If you were a better person, you wouldn't be here." making every level dredge up regret from the more sound-minded players.

 Overall, Spec Ops has grown to be one of my favorite games, having already beaten it several times on another system and twice now on PC. I rather enjoyed the bitter-[strike] sweet [/strike] story, the simple (and sometimes annoying) gameplay, and down-right misery and regret my first playthrough brought me… I don’t know, maybe I’m just a masochist. But then again, if I was a better person, I wouldn’t be here.

Spec Ops: The Line gameplay is standard or mediocre for a third-person shooter game, you'll find shooter game with better gameplay out there, but that's not what Spec Ops: The Line is trying to sell.
It's the story.
Most shooter game have a linear story, or non-linear story but centered on a larger view of the conflict.
Spec Ops: The Line have a large story centered on how our character will define himself during all his 'brutal' mission in Dubai.
Surprisingly the larger story of how the conflict in Spec Ops: The Line happen are told only by collected Intel that are miss-able.

Upon playing to a certain degree, you'll be faced with a choice, that will make effect on your squad impression on you as their leader and your sanity that tread the thin line of soldier that obey order or a human being trying to survive on Dubai's Apocalyptic vision of hell.
A minus factor is that all the choices you made will not result in a different ending. Ending will be determined only by 2 choices, and all the choices you made previously will be presented in a flasback momentarily at the ending choice.

All in all, why should you get Spec Ops: The Line?
Because of the deep story, and how the main character develop it's character. In the end of the story 1 likely thought that the main character will have, is the recurring loading screen message: "Do you feel like a hero yet?" after all you have done in Spec Ops: The Line.
Getting this for the gameplay, and you will have a bad time.

Don't expect amazing gameplay. Gunplay is clunky when I first played, but after a time I got used to it and ended up getting headshots with my pistol and whatever easy peasy. Gosh, but the sniping is difficult. Some of the guns in this game are a real pain, but I guess that's what's unique about the selection. Each gun is a little different from the next in various ways. After the initial awkwardness, shooting did get satisfiying, but also tired easily. No boss battles of any sort. No real challenges, just...A few obstacles that require just a little more effort than usual. You can spend a fair amount of time searching for hidden journals, which I highly suggest if you want to understand the story completely, but they're very few of these anyway.

I actually found myself taking advantage of melee kills moreso than shooting; nothing like Rambo'in down the hallway and elbowing people's faces in. ♥♥♥♥ was waay funnn and much more rewarding than shooting. Oh, there are some other glaring problems. For example, there is this one feature where you can apparently command your buddies to shoot something for you...That feature don't work. Plain and simple. Cover system is wonky at best. Stealth? What the hell is the point? But you know, it's all small kinks. It really doesn't matter. It's still functional, enjoyable gameplay.

Other than that...Well, you shoot baddies to progress to the next point in the story, and that's about it. No rewards system. Very straightforward get-from-point-A-to-point-B linear play, but that's okay for what this game is because...

The game's selling point has to be its story. And this story has some serious DEPTH. The fantastic pacing, the storytelling, the relatable characters...All this coupled with amazing voice acting. I just love hearing Walker's battle cries. Really, talent at its finest. While you actually don't make many tough decisions much like you would in Mass Effect or whatever (in fact you hardly choose at all), the few times that you do, you quickly come to realize just how highly or how little you regard Walker, the MC, and his buddies. That's just how well this game builds you up towards the climax. 

I don't want to say too much for the story, else I risk spoiling it...Just play it and see for yourself! 7/10, damn well good and one for the records.

[h1] REPLAYABILITY [/h1]
There are a few choices that change a little bit the game, you can replay the chapters with such choices for the achievements and see the little nuances of the story. If you like some challenge you have 2 higher-than-Normal difficulties, personally I was satisfied enough with completing the main story and seeing the little twists that came when you made different choices in the 3 or 4 chapters that your choices mattered (you have up to 3  different endings too).
  
[h1] GAMEPLAY [/h1]
Nice shooting and good difficulty levels, good cover mechanics although sometimes it was slightly frustrating that some big structures haven't a cover area or that you instantly cover instead of keep running. The weapon selection is good and it adapts to your preferences (shotguns, ARs, SMGs, snipers, RPGs, grenades, etc).

[h1] AESTHETIC [/h1]
Great visuals, the world is very polished and it truly shines in some mirage sequences and at the radio tower, you also have some pretty memorable moments, including a Lord of the Rings reference. Also a thing I loved is that you do notice the main characters wear and tear during the game, you see them bruised and you see them bleed, that makes them human and not Rambo-like.

[h1] STORY [/h1]
The game is a masterpiece regarding story, what seemed like another military shooter takes quite some twists and turns and by the end of the game *SPOILERS ALERT*[spoiler]  you look back and see the horrors of war and the havoc you brought upon the city in which you were fighting for, very few military shooter that I have played manage to deliver such a perfect climax and also put american soldiers killing other american soldiers, [/spoiler] which makes you question a little bit about the nature of war instead of just playing the same old "Freedom Police vs Terrorists".

[h1] MUSIC [/h1]
I loved this game score, it did immerse me pretty well into it and also have great sounds, the gun shooting, bullet impacts and wind effects are remarkable. In a few chapters you listen to some pretty great funky music that blends really well with the story (yeah, I was surprised too), the voice acting is pretty solid and make the characters believable to the point you care about their fates.

Gameplay-wise, this game is extremely similar to Gears of War, including elements such as run-and-cover system, grenade lobbing, squad-based combat, and hell even the animations look similar. Just swap in a modern setting and there goes a "modern warfare" version of GoW. If GoW is fun, then this game should also be entertaining. So what's different here? 

The story makes all the difference. As a player you will pass judgment on the "enemies" through various events, but as you carry on, you will begin to feel uneasy and doubt whether you are doing the right thing. This game then thrusts you into situations where hard decisions must be made. The character you play will also gradually change his tone from neutral to violent, adding to your feeling of frustration, anxiety, and, perhaps, madness. At the end when truth is revealed, I was dumbfounded and began questioning all my actions before. Replaying the campaign will make them all the clearer.

On the surface Spec Ops: The Line appears to be just another Call of Duty clone. Once you get started, the story comes alive. It is very captivating and will hold your interest until the end, and quite possibly for another play through.

Every part of me wanted to enjoy THE LINE, and occasionnally, while blasting enemy defenses with rock'n'roll music in the apocalyptic Dubai I did, but mostly, playing through the game was a chore. A straight look at the horrors of war with horrendous gameplay mechanics (this one reminds why I hate third person shooters) and rather lousy controls (you use the same button to jump or melee, the spacebar to run or cover). It basically plays like 'Frontline commando', yes the free app, and although the scenery is beautiful and many levels feature a lot of verticality within the broken buildings, it's repetitive as hell, and the mac version is a little glitched with weird performance issues and mouse lag.

The game had great press and reviews, hailed as the mature alternative to 'Call of Duty', but besides one great moment around the middle of the game, SPEC OPS is totally streamlined and would play exactly like COD if it was first person (and it would probably be a better game thanks to more reactive controls). The game plays on rails and there are no important choices to be made as advertised. You will be forced to commit atrocities and deep down the story (although inspired by Apocalypse Now) doesn't make much sense and the soldiers are rather flat, with no specific characteristics. There are other games out there that bring criticism to the genre itself and a much more subtle ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (like Bioshock Infinite) with better gameplay, so I suggest you only get this if it's on sell or just watch the youtube movie that compiles all the cinematics so that you know what the fuss is all about.

PS: Coop and MP are virtually unplayable thanks to the controls (the same button does several actions so half the time it won't work, you'll hit an obstacle when you want to jump or execute a soldier when you want to melee the one next to him) and almost no players are online. Also the game is very sentitive to the hot corners on the mac so you have to deactivate them with a script or work around by adding an extra input key if you don't want to force pause the game when aiming through the barrel, breaking down the action and causing many unnecessary deaths.

The description "bad or worse choices" may have you thinking you have choices in this game.  You do not.  It is a heavy handed moralizing storyline that forces you to make bad choices, then punishes you for them.

SPOILER

There is a point in the game where you are forced to use phospherous mortar shells on civilians.  It is so stark, I kept trying to figure out what the other "choice" was.  One of your squad actually says "there's always another way".  No, there really isn't.  They position snipers to halt your advance until you use the mortar against overwhelming numbers.  If you kill the snipers with gunfire, they get replaced immediately.  If you use the phospherous you cannot exit the interface until you have bombed both the enemies and civilians with it - as in target the group of civilians *specifically* and bomb them.  "Choices" were made by their "creative" team and are not something you find in this game.

As a shooter, it is mediocre.  You are effectively in a long tunnel of cover, killing successive waves of bad guys.  Your squadmates have unlimited ammo and can only be incapacitated.  There are a few near-scripted actions like shooting out windows but the game basically says "aim at that thing and shoot it", then plays the canned animation sequence.

End note: the developer implied the only way to win was to not play.  I disagree.  The only way to win is to not buy this game.

Dubai. An oasis of technology and lust in the middle of desert. Magnificent buildings in a developed city. But nature is always more ruthless than our ability to oppose. Destroyed by intense sandstorms, a city in ruins. The 33rd Battalion of the American army is sent to town for a rescue and extraction operation of the survivors. You are Captain Martin Walker, leader of an elite team of Delta Force of the Army of the United States of America, leading his fellow Lieutenant Alphanso Adams, heavy gunner and Sergeant John Lugo, sniper. Sent to Dubai after a transmission captured after six months without contact, his mission is to locate, reunite and rescue possible survivors.

Dubai is at war. And war... war never changes. The horrors of war are not shown as simple digital polygons falling to the ground with AI off. You will really feel them. You will hesitate. You will have anger and and will be thrilled. And maybe you even cry. You'll be confused. Do not stop. Go straight. Reflect, try to understand. Do not come to this game to play. Come to this story to live it. And so, you will not regret it.

Gentlemen, welcome to Dubai.

Spec Ops: The Line is a third-person shooter with an emphasis on story and tough decisions (which affect how the story plays out/ends).  The storyline sets Spec Ops apart from other shooters; it doesn't glorify war or violence, rather it shows a gruesome side of war not often seen.  I wouldn't go so far as to say this game made me cry or feel depressed, but the mood is definitely dark and macabre at times.  

The mechanics and gameplay are much like Gears of War or any other duck and cover third-person shooter.  The AI is fairly good and will present a stiff challenge.  All this being said, the game is very short (the single player missions can be completed in less than 6 hrs).  As far as replay value goes, the only reason to replay the game is to see the different endings/outcomes of your decisions in game.  

The bottom line is this game has an interesting story but overall bland mechanics and a very short single player story.  There is no reason to replay this game in my opinion, so I wouldn't recommend buying Spec Ops unless it's on sale (the full $30 price tag is definitely way too much for a game that only takes 6 hrs to complete).

The game that puts everything else in perspective. It's all you want from a FPS and action game, but it is also so much more. So much more. It should be in everyone's catalogue. An experience unlike all others. Just buy, play, and prepare for one of the best gaming experiences you will ever have. Bravo.

The Synopsis

There's so much to say about this game. So I'll be descriptive and actually post a thoughtful, in-depth review.

Let me start off by saying that Spec Ops: The Line is an absolute gem. I'd like to say that it's probably the pinnacle of modern shooters in the gaming industry today, although, I won't shun out the other decent shooters that came after this one. Spec Ops: The Line is the result of splicing together fluent game design and a riveting narrative, which blends into a well-thought out, intricate piece of priceless art.

To begin, I'll discuss the story, which was deeply influenced by several various novellas, Joseph Conrad's 'Heart of Darkness' being the most prominent source for influence and inspiration. Spec Ops: The Line sets in Dubai, within the UAE. It is described that Dubai has suffered through the largest sand storm in recorded history, nearly submerging all of Dubai into a pile of rubble and sand. The game's main protagonists are three Delta Force operatives sent on a recon mission into Dubai, the player assuming the role as Captain Martin Walker, the squad leader. Under Walker's command is Sgt. Lugo and Lieutenant Adams, who prove to be an effective, tight knit team. The game does an extremely good job presenting each character's personalities and traits during the many hardships that follow. Each character is unique and displays their own opinions and thoughts on the situations that surround them, and it's up to Walker (the player) to act upon these many decisions. Each decision you make has their own consequences and it will impact upon how the squad looks towards Walker, one way or another. I won't ruin the story for any of you, but I will say that this game will truly make you think afterwards. It does a great job of doing that, believe me. Every scene and every conversation holds it's own weight and it never fails to bore the player. You 'can' skip cutscenes, but I recommend that you don't, as you'll miss out on the nice voice acting and acting the game presents.

Gameplay wise, the player won't have a hard time working out the kinks involved with the cover system, as it's surprisingly easy to maneuver. Beyond that, combat is very fluent for a third person shooter, as the ballistics are almost completely spot on, and for the most part, so is the enemy AI. Commanding your squad in-combat may seem a little difficult to work out at first, but it proves to be extremely effective when picking targets. Enemies *will* swarm you during points, so it's important to stick with your team and to pay attention to their observations on the field. Your squad members will call out units that deviate from your average cannon-fodder, such as shotgun units, snipers, knife bearers, and heavy units. Furthermore, Spec Ops: The Line utilizes not only strategic assault tactics, such as sniping or silently taking out sentries to thin out the numbers of a superior force before an assault, but the game also uses it's superior level design for environmental hazards that the player may use as an advantage over their enemies. There are many other utilities such as the sand storms, the squad's degrading appearance as the game progresses, and the many cinematics and points of interest that make this game truly stand out, making the player's experience with the game one to remember.

The soundtrack... Spec Ops: The Line offers a fantastic soundtrack that truly matches and punctuates the mood of the game itself. From Mogwai and Alice in Chains to the game's own masterfully crafted soundtrack, the game's soundtrack itself never fails to impress and aspires to keep the player entertained during their trek across Dubai. In fact, I still find myself listening to the soundtrack on and off both before and after I played the game.

Whatever you may have heard about this game, it's probably true. It's truly an underrated piece of work and deserves way more praise then it has already recieved. There isn't much that I have to complain about with this game, other than the disappointment I had when I finished the game in one sitting, which took about six hours. I wouldn't say the game offers much in terms of replay value for other than the choices and multiple endings the game has. However, I still found myself playing the game again about a day later, and it was still damn fun. As for other features? I know the game has a multiplayer option that I have yet to try out, which I will get to with a friend of mine when we both have the time.

So to conclude on whether or not you should buy this game? Yes. Hell yes. I bought this game while it was on sale for $5. I can honestly say that it was the best $5 investment that I've ever made. Sale or no sale, this game is worth every cent you put into it. Spec Ops: The Line is a fantastic modern shooter that combines expert game design and a fantastic narrative that is truly a unique experience for every player who touches this game.

Words can't do this game justice. So I'll leave you with this: Buy this game if you want a truly rememberable experience that most videogames these days just can't do.  Also, Walker is voiced by Nolan North, man. Nolan North. Everyone loves Nolan North. So not only will you be buying a stellar videogame, but you'll also be supporting Nolan North's rise to ultimate power. And being me? I usually don't write reviews for games unless they've deeply inspired me on a deeper level.

Cheers, everyone. Happy gaming. :)

About halfway through Yager's third-person-shooter [b]Spec Ops: The Line[/b], in one of the game's most controversial moments, I found myself disgusted and infuriated. Not at the scene I'd just witnessed, or at the game's statement as a whole, but rather that it even needs to be said at all. Two of the ten bestselling video games of all time are [url=http://store.steampowered.com/app/271590/][b]Grand Theft Auto V[/b][/url] and [url=http://store.steampowered.com/app/10180/][b]Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2[/b][/url]. The "military shooter" is one of the most successful genres of the last ten years, and the objective of these games is to kill people. [i]Lots[/i] of people. We eat it up non-stop, and always, always ask for [strike]sequels[/strike] seconds. In order to keep the profit margins wide, we are encouraged to never think about it, to never stop and look at ourselves with a critical, compassionate, clear eye. Of course, it's not only Hollywood that benefits from the blinders we've all put on, since only the desperate and crazy would fight our wars for us if it weren't for the glorification of war peddled by the governments of this strange, sad world upon which we find ourselves spinning through the abyss.

In an ideal world, these things wouldn't need to be said and all of this would be a moot point. Games like [b]The Line[/b] would be seen as a gratuitous miserywank, and people would rightly ask, "Why do we need something like this?" But we don't live in an ideal world, and as gamers, we inhabit a very flashy and seductive yet still a very small and confined space where, ever since John Carmack created [b]Wolfenstein 3D[/b] and [b]Doom[/b] and ushered in the era of the ultraviolent shooter genre, there is an elephant in the room covered in blood and gore. As such, [b]The Line[/b] is a game that needed to be made, its message one that we need to listen to.

The plot, involving a small group of elite U.S. soldiers sent to Dubai on a rescue mission in the midst of a freak sandstorm that all but destroys the city, is adapted from the novella [url=http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_of_Darkness][i]Heart of Darkness[/i][/url] by Joseph Conrad, which also inspired the movie [url=http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apocalypse_Now][i]Apocalypse Now[/i][/url]. The themes of both are intact here -- the horrors of war, the darkness that lives in the soul, and the lengths to which the human mind will go to rationalize its own nature -- but I would argue that they are made much more effective by the vicarious immediacy of the video game medium, and because so much of gaming involves visiting death on whole populations of pixellated AI effigies. Here, the formula is largely unchanged; indeed, you mow down an impressive number of folks with a variety of well-represented handguns, rifles and heavy weapons, but unlike your regular military shooter, [b]The Line[/b] invites and occasionally straight-up forces you to think about the enemy soldiers: who they are, what their motivations are, and of course, how they die. The writers at Yager accomplish this in several ways, some with all the subtlety of a sledgehammer to the face, but others which surprised the sheer hell out of me with their deft use of the medium's voyeuristic and user-participation elements. Spoiler: There's one such moment available in the demo after you use a zipline to reach a building where you sneak up on a pair of soldiers overlooking the ruined city. Their quiet, wistful conversation together is human, poignant, and, because you have no choice but to kill them to proceed with the mission, painfully affecting.

[url=http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spec_Ops:_The_Line#Themes]A lot has been written about this game[/url] and I doubt I'm saying anything new. It is well-deserving of its praise. It's mature and uncompromising. The characters are believable, sometimes heartbreakingly so. At one point I questioned Yager's decision to use the third-person perspective instead of first-person; it seemed to me that the latter would have been much more powerful. But when you stop to wheel the camera around and look at your character, you don't see your typical hardcore BAMF with the obligatory, almost muscular, furrowed brow, the thin, tight, all-business lips, the hard eyes, etc. You see a soldier scared for his life, scared for his soul. His eyes dart everywhere like a cornered animal, he breathes unsteadily, he looks like he feels: horrified, nauseated and on the edge of tears.

The devs say that the story is open to interpretation, but for me, the game is at its heart an honest illustration of post-traumatic stress disorder, or as George Carlin would say, "shellshock":

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hSp8IyaKCs0

If George were still around and had been a gamer, he probably would've approved of [b]Spec Ops: The Line[/b]. He was first and foremost an observer of life, a philosopher who just happened to be funny as hell. This is not a funny game. One of the characters starts off as the typical comic relief character that all shooters seem to require, but like Pvt. Joker in [url=http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full_Metal_Jacket][i]Full Metal Jacket[/i][/url], he sobers up fast and his wisecracks dry up completely during the events of the game. It's almost a shame the cover-based shooting mechanics are so well done, because I find myself torn between wanting to do another playthrough and not wanting to feel the way this game makes me feel. Because this is where [b]The Line[/b] lives: the duality of our chosen brand of entertainment, where we "play" at the deadly game of simulated mortal conflict, and never stop to ask ourselves: what does my kill/death ratio mean for my soul? Does blood still stain if it only exists in my head? Should I even care?

It's a shame that Yager have publicly stated that there won't be a Spec Ops sequel as there is enough evidence in this game to hint at rich promises.

In Spec Ops: The Line you are Captain Walker in charge of an elite Delta squad consisting of Staff Sergeant Lugo, the sniper, and Liutenant Adams, the heavy gunner. The premise is simple, your mission is to enter Dubai, confirm the statuses of Colonel John Konrad; who with his squad, the Damned 33rd, attempted to lead a rescue effort for the storm ravaged city of Dubai, and any remaining survivors of the storm, then radio for extraction. What follows however is anything but simple as you find yourself led deeper into the heart of the city, coming directly into contact with the conflict between the 33rd, the civilians and the CIA.

In an ever shifting narrative where the lines between good and evil are constantly evolving yet becoming increasingly blurred , it is without a doubt that the story is the work of breathtaking brilliance. The game does not shy away from showing the ravages of war and how it can take its toll on individuals. Playing through the game, there are evocative and poignant moments which causes one to pause, think and consider. Even the collectibles in the game demand to be sought after as they genuinely add further to the story, providing additional layers to the narrative and helping to provide some enlightening backstories to some of the characters in the game.

Unsurprisingly there are certain parts in the game where you are given a decision to make, whether it be to save a few civilians here or rescue a potentially valuable informat there. Whilst this adds a bit of variety proceedings, it is disappointing to see that the consequences of these decisions have little bearing in the grander scheme of the story so there is little in the way of replayability. 

Furthermore the gamplay itself is rather subpar. There is little to excite the player with the now standard 'on-the-rails' vehicle section making its way into the game to inspire a change of pace. The shooting itself can prove clunky at times and your team are largely annonymous in a gunfight. However the subpar gameplay is never too intrusive as to ruin the experience. Indeed it may be appropriate for it complements the story. It feels restrained, modest and bare. This way, the gameplay perfectly chimes with the wider subdued tone of the game where the horrors of war unfold. As such your focus remains firmly on the narrative.

Visually speaking, Yager have achieved that sun-kissed perished paradise look that suggests a ruined landscape shorn of its riches. A neat metaphor for Captain Walker's mission. There are memorably evocative passages in the game which arouse a number of emotions in the player. 

The behaviour of the waves of sand as they bury enemies underneath is also believable. Yet the sand really comes into its own element in online multiplayer where the shifting terrain can alter and shift the balance of matches, offering greater tactical depth and encouraging careful planning.

Overall Spec Ops: The Line is a welcome addition to the bloated shooting genre. It stands out on its own with its daring original story, distinctive setting and complex characters. Whilst it does not offer the brash, over-the-top, adrenaline filled fun of other shooters, enjoyment can still be had from this slow-burning, emotionally affecting, multi-faceted adventure.
It's absolutely worth a playthrough based on the thoughtprovoking story but if you don't care about that then this is not a game you want to play since the rest is just a mediocre 3rd person shooter.

I don't usually review games that I play, no matter how exceptional or horrible they are, but this game changed the way I think about games, and as many people as possible need to play it.

This is a game that made me think, for once, about what I did in video games. This game puts weight behind everything the player does and makes the player realize that what he has done in other games in the past, say Call of Duty or Battlefield, is so horrible and evil that the player feels awful about themselves. And, that is amazing. I have never played another game that has effected me this much emotionally.

Lets break down the game into sections to review:

Graphics: The game is gorgeous. It is actually stunningly gorgeous. It has color where you wouldn't expect, wonderful lighting, the sand looks amazing and the destruction and dynamism of the world looks fabulous.

Sound: The sound is very well done. The soundtrack sets the moody tone fantastically, and plays at the exact right volume without adjusting the options at all. Effects sound meaty and full, and voice acting is fantastic.

Gameplay: The game is boring to play. Normally, that would be a fault. However, in this case, it is GENIUS. It makes the player ask, why am I playing this game? What am I doing? And that is integral to how this game knocks down all precedents that the player has from worse, emotionless games. This is not to say the gameplay is bad. The cover system works very well and the weapons are nice and easy to control. There is nothing wrong with the gameplay that makes the game hard to work with.

Presentation: The UI and menus are very nice, minimalistic, and unobtrusive. The main menu is a gorgeous dynamic menu that changes throughout the game.

Note: The game comes with coop and noncoop multiplayer. Both of these are dead and should only be considered if you have a group of friends you want to play with. Otherwise, discount them entirely. This game is about the campaign.

This game made all of it's characters feel like genuine human beings who were going through the campaign's awful situation, and you feel just as connected to what they are going through as to what you are going through playing it. The game is a triumph of storytelling and is a masterful piece of interactive art. The game will make you question everything you do without thinking in other games and will make you put more stock into story rather than gameplay for the first time ever (second time ever if you have played Shadow of the Colossus). Everyone who plays games needs to play this, and anyone who questions whether or not games can really be art/literature just need to be pointed this way. It is one of the greatest games of all time and will stick with you forever.

Spec Ops: The Line.  Oh, where to begin...

If you are a hardcore CoD 'leet quickscoping FAZE member, who goes through the campaign slamming the "skip cutscene" button, go back to your clan.  This game will chew you up, spit you out, chew you up a bit more, spit you out again, and take a p*ss on whatever's left over*.  (*On the easiest difficulty)  This is a TACTICAL 3rd person shooter, where moving out of cover at the wrong time will get you killed, every time.  Now that we have that out of the way, let's talk about the game!

It is beautifully designed in the ruins of Dubai, with shiny skyscrapers and amazing sunglint and lots of sand.  In the first cutscene, you meet the 3 main characters.  A hardcore squad leader, some campy white guy who carries a sniper and cracks a few jokes, and the quintissential black guy with a SAW LMG.  But do NOT be influenced by the first scene.  This is one of the few games that gets it's Mature rating for something more than a few naughty words and marijuana references.  It gets it's Mature rating because it would seriously screw up any 12 year old who plays it.  

Normally, you get into a helicopter, or an AC-130, or whatever to blow some sh*t up, while you have absolutely no chance of dying.  And once you're done, you get a pat on the back and a shout of "Look what you did!  You REKT them Ruskies/Nazi's/Cubans/generic-bad-guys-who-deserved-to-die-and-definitely-didn't-have-a-family-or-wife-or-kids-or-a-puppy-or-dreams-of-opening-a-flower-shop-on-Martha's-Vineyard.  And you get the feeling of acomplishment, the feeling of success, and you want to keep playing to feel that way again.  
This game takes this standard and rips it's d*ck off.  You will get to shoot-em-up with all the big guns, but when you're done you don't poof away to the next spot.  You get to SEE what you did.  And let me tell you, it is the opposite of what you're used to feeling.  I don't want to spoil the game here, but there was one point where my eyes got watery.  If you are looking for a "realistic" experience, then buy this game now and find out what war is really like.  

The pros of this game?  Unbelievable story.  You go into this game expecting some "this guy with a Deagle is a jerk and you must kill him at any costs" kinda story, then get knocked out of your socks. The character development is also great, as well as a very big joke around the middle of the story(if you pay close attention).  The graphics are great for it's age, and it has a dynamic start screen that represents what is going on in your campaign (very cool).  And if the game chews you up one too many times, it gives you the option to tone down the difficulty!  That was very kind of them, but a little necessary...
Cons.  Controls are ugly.  More than one time I am sitting behind cover and randomly vault over to meet the incoming sniper round, or crazed knife rusher, or shotgun soldier just before reaching a checkpoint.  Friendly AI is also atrocious.  Rushing across 70 feet of open ground to get to some cover, and having your squadmate take it when you are about 5 feet away is the worst feeling. [h1][b]Welcome to Dubai![/b][/h1]

[h1][b]Full Review at [url=http://gamedragons.net/viewtopic.php?f=6&t=118]GameDragons.Net[/url][/b][/h1]

[b]Presentation[/b]
Ten years after the release of Spec Ops: Airborne Commando for the PlayStation 2, the franchise reboots with Spec Ops: Line for the current generation of consoles, bringing the classical shooting experience of the 90's to the current generation, changing lots of things to the Spec Ops formula in order to keep up with the current technology and the needs of the market. The story of Spec Ops: The Line follows the Delta Force team formed by Captain Martin Walker, Lieutenant Alphonse Adams and Staff Sergeant John Lugo in their reconnaissance mission in Dubai, after the city was constantly hit by major dust storms in the past six months, killing thousands and leaving those who are still alive in a constant battle for survival. 

As the city was believed to be abandoned when your team arrived in Dubai, your mission was mainly to confirm the fact that everyone inside the city is dead. As you'll find out from the very first moments of the game, that isn't the case as the 33rd Battalion commanded by Lieutenant Colonel John Konrad made a stop in Dubai on their way back home from Afghanistan. The story is profound and different from what you're used to in modern military shooters, and features multiple moments of tragedy, regret and life changing decisions, keeping you constantly on the edge of what's happening in Dubai and reminding you that lives are at stake. Sometimes the game gives you the opportunity to change how the events will unroll in a situation, making the difference between life and death and also the way your crew will appeal to you. The game does feature four different endings, and even though the decisions you take along the story will impact the way you look upon what happened and what role you played in the entire scheme, they won't affect the ending itself, as you can see all endings by reloading the final chapter. 

In addition to the amazing story, the game features a multiplayer mode similar to what other games like Uncharted or Call of Duty have already done in the past, but apart from that there isn't much more to it. There are different game modes and maps you can try out, the most unique and entertaining experience probably being provided by the Buried mode, which tasks two teams of four to sabotage the enemy headquarters while defending their own, a great experience enjoyed with a couple of friends or online with all slots filled.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
The gameplay is exactly what you would expect from a third person shooter, yet there are a few features that make this experience different from the others. The inventory of weapons is large, including everything from pistols, to SMGs and heavy artillery, and even more the game awards you with achievements for using all of them and killing enemies in unique ways. In addition to those, you have grenades, sticky grenades and flashbangs, which serve as an important tactical maneuver, as you'll often run out of ammo, being forced to use a flashbang to stun your enemies while you make a run to grab another gun or find some extra ammo. One thing that is different in Spec Ops: The Line however, is the fact that you can use the environment to your advantage, from shooting the roof on which an enemy is standing, to exploding barrels and breaking the barrier keeping the sand away from an encampment, there are plenty of ways to use the environment to your advantage and save some ammo. 

The game features three difficulty levels, plus the FUBAR difficulty level that is unlocked after you've completed the game on the Suicide Mission level of difficulty. Each level of difficulty is nicely optimized depending on your needs for challenge, and combined with the different story outcome, there are lots of reasons the play the game all over again on a higher difficulty level. You are also allowed to give orders to your crew, a feature that will prove quite handy when you're low on ammo or surrounded by groups of enemies that you can't handle by yourself. The enemies are quite diversified, from snipers to shotgunners and heavy armored shooters the game offers enough variety in the terms of combat, while still maintaining the level of realism and logical equipment for those troops in the middle of a desert. 

On the multiplayer side, the game features many modes, although most of them have the same twists that have been done many times before; in the addition to the classic death match, the game has additional modes such as Rally Point which requires your team to hold the target point for as long as possible, Buried, which serves as a VIP escort mode with a few objectives before getting to that, or Uplink which requires each team to make a rush for the center objective, but only after they've secured their own mini team uplink.

[b]Graphics[/b]
The landscapes of Dubai are simply astonishing, with tall buildings destroyed by the sand, all of it designed by adding the even the smallest detail. The world around you is full of items and equipment, exactly how you would imagine an abandoned luxury city to look like. From the expensive hotels turned upside down by the civilians running for their lives when the storm hit, to the swimming pools filled with sand from the previous storms, everything looks amazing. The visual effects are nice, especially the ones involving sand, dust storms and everything related to that; the lightning effects are awesome and different from a place to another, providing a quality rarely seen in such an area. The characters look okay and detailed enough to actually see the marks left by the combat on the faces of your team from a chapter to another, yet the facial animations could use some improvements.

[b]Audio[/b]
The sound effects are nice and synchronized with the action on the screen and the quality is standard high definition audio. The soundtrack is okay, yet limited and sometimes unneeded, but it does help you get in the mood for what's coming next, so I'd say it does the job just fine. The voice acting features the legendary Nolan North, known for his great acting in the gaming industry in franchises like Assassin's Creed, Call of Duty and Uncharted, things that made him an obvious choice for the role of Martin Walker. Other roles are played by not so known actors like Christopher Reid in the role of Lieutenant Alphonse Adams or Bruce Boxleitner as Lieutenant Colonel John Konrad, yet they managed to delivered their lines in an outstanding manner, making the entire voice cast for The Line one that gives personality to those characters creating this amazing story around your actions.

[b]Extras[/b]
There are plenty of reasons to replay the campaign all over again, or at least parts of it as you can choose to play individual chapters after you've completed the game once, plus the achievements are fun to do and trying new things as you progress through the campaign is always a boredom killer. In addition to that you have the multiplayer mode that offers more hours of gameplay depending on how much you're digging it, but don't expect to be a game changer as most of it has been done before in the exact same manner.

[b]Verdict[/b]
This game isn't your typical modern combat shooter, as it doesn't follow the events of any war or your quest to killing an evil treat, instead it focuses on your actions and the way things can change drastically in just a few hours. The game successfully created a great atmosphere and an even better story, making you the center of attention by the moment you arrive in Dubai, as you'll change the entire city with your decisions and dedication to your service.

As a passionate gamer for over fifteen years, Spec Ops: The line has some of the most emotionally gripping gameplay I have ever seen. The game starts as any other generic shooter does, you have your proto-typical "small team vs. a big army", with your standard AI classes-the grunts, the guys with knives that run at you, the big heavy guys with machineguns, etc. You think to yourself "So what's the big deal? In no time I'll be mowing through them like a superhero badass." It tricks you into believing it is something totally familiar, then hits you like a cannon shell. While other games have featured "the horrors of war" as a thematic element, this game is one of the few that manages to transcend the boundary from simply affecting the CHARACTER to fully affecting you as a PLAYER. Without spoiling anything, the situations you face during the game will not leave you feeling like a hero. You will not feel invincible. You will not feel the same. By the time the game was over, I felt emotionally distraught. That's the only way I can describe it.

         There is, however, one bone I have to pick with this game. The controls are at times unresponsive, and I died numerous times simply because I had difficulty ordering my squad around or performing mission-critical actions. Because, by default, the "take cover" and "sprint" keys are the same, your character will often do the opposite of what you need to do to survive a particularly difficult encounter (run straight towards an enemy instead of hide behind a wall, etc) and attempting take cover near the corner of an object will often see you taking cover on the wrong side, getting you shot in the back. The checkpoint system at times also feels a little inconsistent, sometimes autosaving after every small fight, and sometimes throwing you back to the beginning of a long section of gameplay, creating a few frustrating moments. However, the merits of this game more than compensate for its faults, and honestly, for anyone who's ever played a generic shooter in the history of forever, these are not problems which leave us shocked and totally blindsided, unlike the wonderful story.

Spec Ops: The Line is a terrible game. As a person who shuns the big budget FPS and TPS copouts of today, I never expected it to be so bad. It grabbed me from the very beginning, and took me on one of the worst experiences I’ve ever had as a gamer. As I ventured through, I couldn’t help but keep shaking my head at what was going on. You know what? Terrible doesn’t even work. NOTHING fits as a description for what I went through in Spec Ops: The Line. And for that sole reason, it’s one of the best games I’ve ever played……..oh, what, you thought I was gonna say it sucked? As if.

The campaign puts us in the role of Captain Martin Walker. He and his two squadmates, Lieutenant Alphonse Adams and Sergeant John Lugo, are sent on a rescue mission to Dubai; a Dubai that took a devastating hit from a record-breaking number of sandstorms. It seemed as if it was going to be simple: go in, get the survivors, and get out. However, part-way in, they find dead American soldiers. Now their goal is to get survivors and find out what happened here. 

Because I had known what the story was about beforehand, I knew exactly where it was going to go: ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I’m not going to spoil anything (at least, not yet), but these men go through some tough, TOUGH stuff throughout the campaign. All kinds of bad decisions of made, and all kinds of consequences happen as of a result. It made me feel something I’ve never felt when playing a game like this: guilt. 

I honestly wish I couldn’t reversed some of the things I did in the game, but the thing is, it was the game telling you what to do, not you. With a few exceptions, you were forced to comply with what the game wanted you to do. You were not in control, the game was. Any shooter that tries to evoke this kind of emotion *cough* Modern Warfare 2 *cough* doesn’t have anything on Spec Ops’ story. I’ve had the honor of reading through some of the best video game tales of all time, but Spec Ops is definitely gunning for the top. 

And a good thing, too, because the rest of the game is rather unmemorable. Spec Ops’ is a third person shooter, and a cover-based one, at that. Most of the gameplay boils down to, “Run here, shoot, run here, shoot, run here, shoot, keep shooting, you’re almost there!”, and it’s exciting, but doing that over and over again during the six hours you’ll spend in it gets dull. The fact you can command your squadmates to do certain things during battle, like healing a downed partner or sniping an enemy from far away, is a nice addition, but because the game says it makes the shooting tactical, it comes off as shallow. 

It also doesn’t help that the game is hard as hard can be. I’ll admit, it’s mainly because I’m not into games like this and for that I have no skill, but I’m pretty sure that even veterans of the series and genre would find this difficult. Many of the enemies take more than a few bullets to go down, and because there’s a wide variety of guns and weapons, ammo can get scarce. You, on the other hand, are not quite the bullet sponge your foes are. If you stay out of cover for more than three seconds, you immediately get the sensation of the colorblind, and any more time out in the open brings death. Still, even when the game asked if I wanted to change difficulty, I didn’t switch to an easier mode. I dread what the hardest mode is like: you probably die after one bullet and everyone else takes 50 bullets to even flinch. 

I do have a few other complaints. The game does looks really, really good, even if it’s running on an extremely outdated engine that people still use for some reason, but the pre-rendered cutscenes look surprisingly bad, with compression up the wazoo and a really bad framerate. The other problem involves a few spoilers, so head on down to the last paragraph if you don’t wanna listen. The story is very, very, very, very good, but for some reason, I felt that the multiple endings at the end dulled the impact a touch. They all suck, in the sense that you’re still a bad person, which is good, but I believe a story like this should have a definite conclusion. It’s not necessary, and again, the four endings they outlined are perfect for what the player feels when they play, but I would’ve appreciated it.

Nonetheless, Spec Ops: The Line is still worth playing because of its engrossing tale of the human being. Even when I died or got tired of the monotonous shooting, I kept going because the story was so freaking good. This has never happened whenever I played any other FPS or TPS campaign. Usually, I slug through half of those campaigns and then stop. Thankfully, that’s not the case for Spec Ops. 

- Even Luck

Were it to be judged purely on its design and mechanics, Spec Ops: The Line would be pretty forgettable, but it has an ace in the hole. And it's a bigg'un: a story so out of the blue in its direction and message that it's a miracle, a major publisher put this game out at all. What you think you're getting- particularly if you only play the demo- is another gung-ho gun-wielding slice of Americans saving the day by killing all the brown people. What you actually get is a slow, spiralling descent into madness of one man, that wears its Heart of Darkness/Apocalypse Now inspirations proudly and uses them to forge a modern-day commentary on the type of video game you thought you were going to play. 

Captain Walker is no tiantic Call of Duty avatar who can murder a thousand people and walk away- he falls apart mentally, visually and audibly as the game continues, his professionalism is stripped away and raw ego left exposed. "Tango down" becomes a more chilling, "Kill is ♥♥♥♥ing confirmed" as the game confronts you with issues of culpability and responsibility. It's incredibly unsettling and so out of the ordinary for the modern gamer that to most people, this might be thrown aside in disgust.

This is probably one of the best games I've ever played.

Why?

The gameplay is pretty standard fare for the shooter genre, with some somewhat interesting squad dynamics thrown in. I've heard the multiplayer is terrible, if you can find anyone still playing it at all. 

So why is this game so amazing? The story in the campaign. It plays on your psyche, messes with your head, and makes you question why you even play games like this. It's a critique of the entire genre, one that desperately needed to be made. Why do we, as gamers, typically like to shoot things for fun? Is killing people in a video game truly harmless? If so, should we still enjoy it as much as we do?

The story draws from some classics for inspiration (most notably Heart of Darkness, by Joseph Conrad), but it takes what it needs and expands on the rest. It takes some classic conventions, and finds a way to use that to tell its own story, and tell a completely new and fresh message.

"To kill for yourself is murder. To kill for your government is heroic. To kill for entertainment is harmless."

This is a cover based regenerating health over-the-shoulder shooter that has you roaming the desert city of Dubai with 2 other soldiers under your command. The game has a lot going for it, gorgeous vistas, licensed music, a villain that blurs the line of who is the villain, story choices, but the real thing Spec Ops: The Line can hang its hat on is the engrossing story. I'm not a story person, but this would make a great movie watching the story unfold. There are brief cut scenes here and there, but nothing that gets in the way of the action. You are even given choices, so there is some interactivity to the story, but the choices don't have any real impact on the story.

The story is simple, subtle and deep all at the same time, you are sent in to find what happened to a group of soldiers in the 33rd and you quickly discover in the first 10 minutes they've gone rogue. You're not just fighting inhabitants of Dubai, but US soldiers and other factions that I can't name since spoilers. Dubai itself is in a post-apocalyptic state, because it has been hit by a major sandstorm destroying the city except for pockets of civilians and soldiers. You'll come across both. There are elements where you can use the sand to defeat your enemies, such as destroying glass will send sand oceans burying enemies. There are blinding sandstorms. The game makes good use of the environment and city. You'll be in the sand oceans full of wrecked yachts, on top of towering skyscrapers, inside falling buildings and junkyards, this game has a great variety of areas. Each area is gorgeous, no matter how depressing and shambled they are. When you execute enemies at close range, you'll see the detail on their faces. A lot of detail was put into this game beyond the gorgeous scenery.

Since this is a cover based over-the-shoulder shooter, it feels extremely familiar to others especially Uncharted, especially when the main character is voiced by Nolan North who played Nathan Drake in the Uncharted series. Left stick to run, right stick to aim, left trigger to aim, right trigger to fire, left button to throw something, left and right on the D-pad to cycle through your grenades, Y to change weapons (between two, but you can pick up others), X to reload, B to melee, execute downed enemies and leap over cover. Up on the D-pad will let you alt fire weapons, but its mostly forgotten about. The only unique touch to this game is the right button will command your followers. Tap the right button and Lugo will send out a flash bang that on the PC seems virtually useless. I rarely see it even effect people. Holding the right button and aiming at an enemy will have your sniper take out a long range foe, but really when I'm aiming with the right button I can literally just shoot someone myself if I'm aimed at him. On top of that, it seems like commanding your sniper doesn't work on PC when it does on PS3. The final button is of course the all purpose A button that tap it to run, hold it to run and slide to cover, standing next to cover will make you stick to cover, but really this needs a lot of work. I find my character running in and out of cover or sticking to the cover behind me instead of in front of me. It is quite frustrating and results in most of the deaths I had while playing.

The enemy AI seems smart enough and they will flank you, just like you can flank them with your squad. The enemies are similar for the most part, but with AI so good, that means every enemy can kill you. They boil down to standard soldiers, snipers, shotgunners that come to you, bladers that will run at you to knife you and heavy soldiers that walk slowly at you and take a lot of bullets to kill. Its a lot like playing the Uncharted series. You and your allies get put into big open areas with a lot of cover and you need to stay there until everyone dies. Your allies feel competent enough and will take out enemies on their own and call out things to warn you.  They will need to be resuscitated if they take too much damage, but that rarely happens and you can command the other one to bring the fallen back to life. Your teammates serve as guides without seeming too overbearing. The voice acting in the game is great and its probably an unseen high point in a game full of amazing highs.

For the most part this feels like a fun game with an incredible story, despite frustrating cover and run buttons being the same. I can't say the game is worth $30 and I'm really surprised that its not $20 yet. Get it on sale. Its worth it for the single player.

Playing this game is rather like watching the proverbial train wreck: you'll be horrified, but you can't look away. This is in no way a bad thing. Spec Ops wants to tell a story about soldiers in war. It wants you to see the terrible toll that combat can exact on those who experience it. And above all, it wants you to see that in real conflict, there are no "good guys" and "bad guys," and the world is full of gray areas. I don't mean to criticize Spec Ops so harshly, but I have to when it's setting itself up as such an ambitious, philosophical, game. Trying to raise the bar in any industry is hard enough as it is, but the developers obviously had a tight production budget which shows when actually playing the game.

Which brings me to my next gripe, gameplay and controls. It plays out like any other cover-based shooter, which isn't a genre you can particularly build upon, just look at the Gears series, but you can refine it. And refinement is something this game lacks. You move your character forward, he does so with a rigid animation. You want to sprint efficiently around the battlefield? Too bad you'll be stuck with this robotic, gears inspired, camera wobbling, ♥♥♥♥ animation. That's mapped to holdin down the "A" button on a 360 gamepad and has horrible amounts of sensitivity. It's like trying to guide a raging bull towards a specific area. Then there's your a.i. partners who are suppost to add a level of tactical options in order to outsmart your opponent, but they're dumber than a bag of bricks, and you frequently have to go save their ass's after they've been downed.

The one redeeming value of this game has to be it's ending which wasn't unexpected after the 6 hour acid trip of a campaign but welcome nonetheless. The amount of variations is just enough to place you into the shoes of the main protaginist, and sell the illusion of, "I made those decisions, and this is my Walker." 

Ultimately if you want a standard cover based third person shooter, but are feeling a bit brave that day, then this game is worth the money for the shock value alone. If you happen to find any life changing virtue's from its story that you weren't already aware of from common sense, then I suggest you book into an insane asylum.

I did not like this game. Let me tell you why.

[b]Graphics/sounds[/b]
Nice graphics, but the lack of options is too bad. For isntance, the game would benefit from antialiasing greatly. Also you have to note that there is no FOV option to change it.
For the sounds, well, if you have 5.1 and a headset, then sometimes you won't be hearing jack since the wrong output is used. It is the case during some cinematics (they are video files). Other than that noises spacialization and stuff are great, but speeches are often only heard from the rear speakers. Weird. Voices are okay, but dialogs sucks. It is basic military stuff and has no depth. Don't expect much humour either.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
A basic linear TPS that plays pretty much like a FPS. Move to area, waste tangos, take cover, move to next area, repeat. Your health regenerates, and combat is all about cover. Run, and hide behind a crate, low wall, whatever. Then aim, so your dude raises above the cover, shoot quick, and release aim to get back behind cover. Now, wait safely for your health to recover.
Lame. No tactics, nothing.

[b]Controls[/b]
Mouse sensitivity is super high even when setting the stuff to zero. I had to lower my mouse DPI in order to play. Keybindings now. Well, it must be a console port: keys are screwed.
To take cover your have one key. To jump over stuff another key. To sprint, it is the same cover key. Uhg... how many time did I die, holding shift to sprint... but no, it was space. And rebinding space to shift is no good since it makes you take cover as well when near an object. Also, sprinting continues when you release the button.
Awkward game to play that's for sure, but not impossbile.

[b]AI[/b]
The AI is half scripted. Some tangos will always go to the same spot, other will react to your actions.
Same for your buddies that will go to the same initial cover. You can command your grunts, and tell them to focus on a specific target. It worked well at the beginning of the game. A far away tango will get sniped by Lugos, and a close one will be taken care of by the support dude.
But near the end, the map is not as open as previously. So issuing an order will make your goons move out of their cover and have a little stroll on the battlefield, not dodging lead of course. They will end up incapped near a swarm of tangos.
You cannot issue moving or throwing a flash orders. The throwing a flash command seems to be scripted when certain tangos spawn in groups. Not cool.
Also, your buddies have infinite ammo, and pretty much never die. If they 'die' you can revive them with what it seems to be an adrenaline shot.

[b]Story[/b]
Actually, the best part of the game. At first, it looks like total generic crap. But listen, I realized it was not total shït at the end of the game. Pay attention to details, I mean it, it will increase this game's story awesomeness.
Now, some scenes during the game are horrible on purpose. There were no controversies, and that is surprising since some stuff are much worse than in the CoD airport mission. You will have to kill civilians and US soldiers. Even though choices are offered to you, the outcome will always be the same. The story will try to put the blame on you, and make you realize how horrible war is.
But unfortunately, these gruesome scenes are there for the violence/18+ rating only, they do not IMHO deepen the game's story nor the main character's mindset. It is weak and not subtle.
Life is not black and white.
There is a twist though, you will feel it coming, but you won't know what exactly. It is not bad, but not great either.

[b]Weapons[/b]
You can pick weapons from dead enemy. SMGs, rifles, snipers, and handguns.
You also have an alternate fire button that will do special action depending on the weapon you are carrying. For exemple, the SCAR will switch to nade mode. Some rifles like the AK47 or FAMAS will switch fire mode. However this is not done well, like a hint comes and tells you the burst fire is recommended for stable sniping... WTF.
3-Burst fire is used in CQB, that is what it has been designed for. None of the weapons have a single shot mode suitable for stable firing, except for sniper weapons and a HK417.
Also the AKs are full-auto and 3-burst shot while in real life burst shot doesn't exist on AKs. I would totally prefer to have single shot instead of burst; most areas are open you see.
Aside from these minors innacuracies, ammo is weapon specific. You would expect some weapon to share their ammo since they have the same caliber. But instead it is magazine specific.
Accuracy is decent and correct. Handguns are too accurate though, like the .44 that can snipe tangos and put them down in one single shot :/

[b]Conclusion[/b]
Not my kinda game. I am more of a tactical dude, and this game plays like CoD: it is very arcade style and quite easy. Some areas are however insanely hard though. I played on Suicidal on the first playthrough.

It is a very generic TPS and has not much to offer.

Spec Ops: The Line Review 

-------

Story: 9.5/10

Among the sea of silent protagonists and countless shooters, there lies one that can actually tell a story. Even though it is incredibly disturbing at times, it really showcases just how awful war can be. Post Traumatic Stress Disorder is the primary reason why soliders get taken off of the battefield. Something like PTSD can only be understood if you have it yourself, which is why it (among other mental illnesses) are rarely taken seriously; especially once an affected solider returns home. Playing through Spec Ops: The Line shows you what it takes to break a battle-hardened warrior, leaving him completely raving mad in a journey that goes from bad to worse. The story of The Line is definitely the forefront reason to play this game, giving you an overlook on all the things you never really hear about in war. Regardless of its' fiction, the message is raw truth: war is hell.

-------

Gameplay: 7/10

The gameplay for Spec Ops: The Line is decent. It's much better when you actually take the time to observe your surroundings and strategize your attacks instead of rushing in, guns blazing. The game also plays better on higher difficulties, as you must be exceptionally careful in practically every combat setting in order to overcome your enemies. There is always a way out that is rather obvious in most situations, although, and sometimes the game gives away the challenge. Enemy AI is wonky to say the least. Most of the time they are ruthless and smart and can screw up your day, but sometimes they just stick to some cover and wait for you to come kill them. Movement is very shaky too. Sometimes you wanna slide to some cover, but you end up just sprinting past it, which can earn you a frustrating death. Since it's a third-person shooter, I admire the fluidity of combat that this game offers, but it does not always execute.

-------

Graphics: 8.5/10

The graphics are good...there's no doubt about it. This game has beautiful scenic shots and gorgeous sand storm visuals, as well as spot on interpretation of the architectural beauty that is Dubai (even though it's also ravaged by sand and war). Some of the lighting is confusing though, especially in combat situations. You can tell that the goal was to use the weather and lighting elements to affect combat, which is both a good thing and a bad thing. The frequent sand storms are brilliant and are incredibly unique even though they are seen in other games. They really tie into feeling choked and helpless when you've got 20 bad guys on you and you can't do anything other than just hide behind a cracking wall of a beached yacht, waiting for the storm to subside so you can take your shots. That's awesome. But the lighting can really screw you up because they try to do the HD light glare thing on your screen, but it can be a bit much at times, forcing you to move around until you can get clear shots. It's simply annoying gameplay due to the graphics. This only happens a few times, and the lighting is usually done very well to accentuate set pieces and events that are pretty good.

-------

Overall: 8/10

Spec Ops: The Line is a 3rd person shooter based upon the post apocalyptic ruins of Dubai. It follows a squad of 3 Deltaforce soldiers on a rescue mission into the vast yet empty city - or is it?

After completing this game within the space of 24 hours it is hard not to admit that I thoroughly enjoyed the storyline of this game. Everything about this game is spectacular. The storyline (though dark and gritty at times juxtaposing to the vibrance of the desert atmosphere) the graphics. Wow, the graphics. This game was great for its time. Although it was only 2 years ago, it looks next generation - plain and simple. And the action side of it was amazing too. With many different weapons to choose from in combat with a pretty good melee and execution system. Though my only gripe would be being stuck in a firefight with no ammo and having to beat the crap out of a dude with your fists in the middle of a gunfight. But it adds a sense of realism to the game given the fact it is based heavily off of the feral survivors of the sandstorm upon Dubai, meaning ammo and any resources would be scarce.

Spec Ops: The Line is a 2012 third-person shooter video game developed by Yager Development and published by 2K Games. It was released on 26 June 2012 in North America and 29 June 2012 internationally for Microsoft Windows, and the Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3 consoles.
n Spec Ops: The Line, the player controls Captain Martin Walker, who is sent into a post-catastrophe Dubai with an elite Delta Force team on a reconnaissance mission, where they find dead American soldiers. Upon the finding, Walker declares that the team's mission has changed, and that they will search Dubai for survivors

Spec Ops: does so many good things right, but falls short from a masterpiece. While the game is a brilliant set-piece of PTSD and the true horrors of war, it falls short as a game in whole. While the story, soundtrack, voice acting, visuals and overall quality is amazing, it's gameplay is just so generic and boring. Nothing new will be seen here, unfourtunately. The game is a third-person cover shooter game, with no originality. The cover system and gunplay are mediocre at best, and this is a real drawback from it being an amazing experience in all sectors. But, I really don't want to get too much into such details, it's just something you've played in a hundred other games, let's focus on what's so amazing about this underrated game.

The story. It may sounds like something trivial, because people have high standards these days, amazing gameplay, amazing graphics, amazing this amazing that, you get my point. This game is narative driven game, and that's it. Multiplayer is shallow and unstatisfying, but this isn't the point of Spec Ops. It's a game that sets one goal, and one goal only. To trully showcase the [b]Horror[/b] of war. War is a gruesome experience that really scars the human mind, and while me and you won't probably fight in one, this game has a trully shocking way of showing us just how brutal things can get between the gunfire. It will surely have a last impact on you, it did on me at least. The game starts pretty standard, a turret section that's pretty [i]bland[/i] and [i]boring[/i], nothing too over the top here. But once the game kick off, things start to get heated. We start in the shoes of Cpt. Martin Walker, voiced by Nolan North. The game starts off with you and your squad mates being sent to the new destroyed Dubai, to investigate and search for survivor, call for reinforcements and get back home. Those are your only orders, nothing more. But things get out of hand once Walker gives to order to [i] open fire on the enemy[/i]. This thing will become more relevant down the line, since this game has set out to question one simple thing, [i]Who is the enemy?[/i]. And it will teach you that thing, once you complete it.

Being developed on the Unreal 3 Engine, the games shines mostly. Dubai is a super showcase of glowing sand, vibrant interiors and a feel of depth and complexity. But it's all just a shell to hide all of the horros that lay ahead of your journey to destruction. The game will soon present to you the brutal, and extremely graphic violence of when [i]things get ouf of hand[/i] when people mentally breakdown and can't tell the difference between good or evil. It's amazing, especially since this game breaks once and for all the trope that all enemy's in video games must be shot down immediatly without question, and because they are [i]different[/i] or russian/middle eastern. It's superb, to be honest. 

In the end, since I could talk about this game for hours and hours, even though it's a short, but it's an intense ride, and filled with guilt. Never, ever I have felt such guild after playing a videogame. Like, really. Videogames that make you feel guilty? [i]How is that?[/i] One might ask. Well, it's quite easy. This game does not reward you for shooting everyone in a 100km radius at the speed of Clint Eastwood, it will break you down as fast as the protagonists. It's amazing how well the story is crafter, considering at the end of the day, it makes you feel human, it makes you question so many things. Superb. Honestly, superb.

There is one basic and important thing to know about Spec Ops: The Line, and that's that it is at the same time a deeply satisfying and a deeply frustrating experience. Gameplay-wise, it's a fairly competent shooter marred by some very poor design decisions- checkpoints often come before cutscenes and are too far apart, which, combined with the surprisingly unforgiving difficulty (even on Normal you can find yourself gunned down in seconds) can be teeth-grindingly annoying. The range of guns you can pick up is unremarkable and there are nice secondary functions to a lot of them; you can carry three kinds of grenades; the cover mechanic is just flawed enough to be irritating but functions tolerably for the most part.

This is not a game about gameplay, however.

Were it to be judged purely on its design and mechanics, Spec Ops: The Line would be pretty forgettable, but it has an ace in the hole: a story so out of the blue in its direction and message that it's a miracle a major publisher put this game out at all. What you think you're getting- particularly if you only play the demo- is another gung-ho gun-wielding slice of Americans saving the day by killing all the brown people. What you [i]actually[/i] get is a slow, spiralling descent into madness that wears its Heart of Darkness/Apocalypse Now inspirations proudly and uses them to forge a modern-day commentary on the type of video game you thought you were going to play. Captain Walker is no godly Call of Duty avatar who can murder a thousand people and walk away- he falls apart mentally, visually and audibly as the game continues, his professionalism is stripped away and raw ego left exposed. "Tango down" becomes a more chilling, "Kill is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ confirmed" as the game confronts you with issues of culpability and responsibility. It's incredibly unsettling.

If you don't come away from Spec Ops: The Line with questions and doubts about shooters, I have serious concerns about whether you're dead inside. Do your best to ignore the sometimes-frustrating controls and systems and try and appreciate just how important this game is in the history of, and commentary on, shooters.
