You played CoD campaigns because they are fun? Heck yeah, they are.
You were pissed because the campaigns never last for more than 4-5 hours? Damn, we're soul brothers!

And now you stumble upon this game, and you think about buying it for about 5 bucks? DO IT.

What CoD campaigns made fun, this game makes it intense. The story is superb, I ♥♥♥♥ you not. It's a bit futuristic: Dubai is covered in sand, since a gigantic sandstorm got there and still rages on. A platoon of the US Army has been sent there to help civilians get out of this sandy hell-hole, but communication has been interrupted ever since they went in. Now you and your two SEAL buddies are sent in to find out what happened. But sure enough, what you find is way more than you bargained for.

Now, what is really intriguing about this game is its style. The game system itself is fun enough, but nothing new; you can duck behind cover, shoot from it, you throw grenades, yadda yadda. The mechanics are pretty much the same as e.g. CoDs. BUT, and this is the funny point, you get to choose. From time to time, you as the leader of your little pack will have to make a (often-times) moral decision and live with its consequences. And this is when the game overcomes CoD and becomse pure awesomeness.

Because no, the game won't have a different ending based on your decisions. No, there are no NPCs around you who could react to you differently based on what you did. Instead, you keep pushing towards your goal, remembering what you did, thinking about it, being reminded of it from time to time, and more and more you ask yourself:

Did I do the right thing?

And you go down into a moral dilemma. Of course you did the right thing, there was no other option. But wait, THERE WAS. No CoD ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ à la "Do this, do that, and of course we are the good guys, what we do we have to do, and lets not think about it." YOU have chosen the path you go, and you have to live with it. YOU are the guy responsible for YOUR actions, and YOU will have to look at what that caused. YOU will see the bodies of innocent and people who just were in the wrong place at the wrong time, that is, being where YOU are.

So, is this a war-game shooter? Hell yeah, it is. But unlike CoD, you won't emerge from it as the sparkling war hero who did everything right just as his commanding superior told him to.

No, my friend. You are alone out there. Your decisions. Your responsibility. Your faults.

Welcome to Dubai.

This is probably one of the best games I 've ever played. Not because of gameplay, nor graphics, but the sheer impact of the storytelling. You will feel like a piece of ♥♥♥♥.

This should not be classed as a game, but more an interactive work of art. It tells a story of a squad of American soldiers fighting their way through Dubai to try and free the citizens from the evil John Konrad. The game portrays the effects that PTSD has on soldiers and how a simple rescue mission can turn into a mass graveyard.

This game is not "FUN" it is a serious story-based game which would be best played over a weekend as it can be beaten in roughly 8-9 hours. 

Final thoughts:
This game is amazing and you should buy it once on sale because it is a short story, but great none the less. Also do not read anything about it until you finish it because the game will be ruined as there are too many spoilers.
Also the game mechanics are awful, so play it on normal difficulty because the gameplay isn't fantastic and you can easily get killed out of the blue by things.

Now if you're reading this, I suggest you stop doing so and just buy the game. Now I will recommend buying it during a sale, or finding it for cheaper, but I'm telling you that it's worth it. This game was over-hyped, and frankly it fell short of my expectations by a couple of miles. There is literally nothing good I have to say about this game. 

BAD THINGS ABOUT THE PLOT:

When you first get shot at by the 33rd US Army, your character yells a few things about "friendly fire" and "stop shooting" which is what normal people do. Then, when they don't stop shooting, you and your squad just mow them all down and continue butchering your way through your own side for the rest of the game. A highly trained Delta operative would and could shoot to incapacitate and or minimise loss of life when shooting at people on the same side.
When you get to the bit when you use the white phosphorous, in the thermal imager you see the humvees that you "have" to blow up, and the soldiers shooting at you that you "have" to blow up. Then, after destroying all of the military targets, I found myself stuck and unable to exit the mortar shooting section. Right in the corner, is this little blob of white. I can tell that it's people, they're not shooting at me, they don't have humvees; but the game won't let me progress until I've blown them up as well............SURPRISE THEY'RE INNOCENT PEOPLE!!! AAAARGH HOW COULD YOU DO THAT YOU EVIL PERSON SITTING BEHIND A COMPUTER SCREEN!!!! AAAARGH, THIS WILL PLAGUE YOUR CONSCIENCE FOREVER!!!!!!
No, game, you made me do it, and you executed that little moral section really poorly.
Now, Conrad has a little bit of an argument with his team, and then the mindless slaughter of American soldiers continues. At some point, both your team members die and I don't even remember when and I don't care because they had no human characteristics, they were just one dimensional distractions. Skipping to the next 'moral' point is when there are two people tied up and snipers point their guns at the two of them. Then, you "have" to make the choice over which one to kill. I just shot the snipers, and I think the two people just automatically die, or maybe they still live; either way you don't have to choose which one lives, you can just shoot the snipers. The whole plot point where you blow up all the water and cause some death isn't a choice, it's how the plot progresses so I'm not going to lose any sleep over that. Skipping over some utterly stupid next sections of the game, I'll rant and rave about the multiple endings of the game. "Hmm, should I shoot the mirror or let the mirror shoot me?" What kind of stupid choice is that? The whole point of a video game is to live and shoot everyone else and then in some games a cutscene makes you die for some reason. "Hmm, should I shoot the friendly soldiers come to rescue me?"   If you shoot the soldiers and then go back inside, then how are you going to survive? You blew up all the water remember?   If you put the gun down, then you get to go home and live happily ever after, THE END!

BAD THINGS ABOUT THE GAMEPLAY

I played it on the hardest difficulty, and yet I could still blind fire with perfect accuracy? Who can get headshots crouching with a pistol upside down over the top of their head and hit someone that they can't see in the head? STUPID!
Why could I only get extra ammo by 'executing' fellow American soldiers? Why was I executing fellow American soldiers anyway? (see rage up above)
Why didn't the guns jam all of the time if you're constantly in sandstorms?
Why after your support gunner gets shot in the leg as part of a plot point does he make a big deal of it and when in gameplay he gets shot all of the time and doesn't notice?

OVERALL SUMMARY

Bad gameplay, bad plot, stupid choices, and whoopdedoo nobody has done "morals" in a game before, lets make the rest of the game bad and base our entire selling point on a flimsly poorly executed moral thing to draw people into buying the game. I know that's me suckd in right there, I payed $7.50 for this game, and I regret parting with every single cent.

If you have high or even medium expectations for this game, then don't buy it.

I brought this on the recommendation of the story; the premise being that the largest sandstorm has engulfed the entirety of Dubai. You control Walker from Delta Squad, who is sent in, to recon the situation after an entire US Army battalion went to save civilians over a month ago and didn't come back. It obviously doesn't turn out well else you'd not be sent in the first place.

The setting is sublime - a post apocalyptic-like mess, it stands out heads and shoulders as the most intriguing part of the game - much more so then the army personnel and your squad are.

However I was both fascinated and frustrated by the game; on one hand the story unfolds at quite a pace (with no spoilers here, but just go with the flow even with the plot holes, it's interesting, although I'd have loved more backstory with such a setting), on the other hand the game is frustrating gameplay wise - with constant dying and not the best cover mechanics with the same tired "two weapons, limited ammo for you but not everyone else", and a lack of gameplay choices - even if some of them are "the point" and "making me think", bah to most of the forced choices!

However due to the short length of the game I eventually succeeded past the waves of "You've died too many times, want to lower the difficulty?" messages. Even if some of it wasn't enjoyable I almost took it to heart that the game, as a whole, was better for being that bit more rough then I had expected; war isn't nice after all and it led some gravity to it. I'd say it's well worth a play, especially if it can be nabbed for a fiver or under.

Depending on your tastes, this shooter is awesome. If you ever wished you could play a game that had an "Apocalypse Now" feeling to it, then this title is worth it. While it is linear, it is still fun. I think I'm gonna play it now!

This game is what every military shooter that tries to focus on war attempts to be but doesn't reach it.  The gameplay is solid, sticking to being a TPS with cover mechanics. But while the gameplay doesn't offer too much, the story more than makes up for it. The painful choices of war, the violence you're forced to witness in times of desperation, all become in sync with each other, making you realize what war truly is. As you progress through the story, you (not the character, but the player) will question why you are forced to do such things. Why must you kill all these people? Then it hits you, sometimes you truly have no choice. As the game progresses, the executions and killings you perform become more gruesome, reflecting on the leading character's declining sanity.

If you're looking for a brand new style of gameplay, don't expect anything new. But, if you're tired of a typical military shooter story, this is worth everything. Hell, if you want a real story, get this game. There is also replayability due to the multiple endings that are based on your choices. Not as cryptic as Silent Hill but still very strong choices.

This game has ruined the "Modern Military Shooter" subgenre for me.

This is not because it is by any means a bad game, or does a bad job of presenting the subgenre. Rather, it is because Spec Ops: The Line does what Don Quixote did to the chivalric ballads of old, or School of Rock did to inspirational films about schoolteachers: it eviscerates the subgenre so thoroughly that it will be impossible for me to take any earnest attempts seriously ever again.

At first glance, Spec Ops: The Line comes across as generic shovelware, and the name certainly doesn't help. But it only takes an hour before the plot starts to twist, the line starts to blur, and the black and white starts to become a uniform grey. (Until a certain scene which I dare not spoil, at which point the grey starts to take on a much darker shade.)

This is not a "rah-rah, America saves the day again" video game. This is a game with content that you really should expect after seeing a character named "J. Konrad". This is a game that pulls no punches in its depiction of the horrors of war, or your participation in them.

This is a game that shines like a giant red beacon, burning forever in the night, proclaiming for all to see that videogames can indeed be art.

More games should have stories like this. Feels the right amount of gritty with some humor on the side. The combat can be a little unfair in some portions but overall a solid 3rd person shooter. Check it out since its always so cheap, you wont regret it.

The voice-acting is fine, and the visuals are OK as well. Not the best visuals ever (even for a 2012 game), but they do a good job depicting a war-ravaged Dubai. Performance is great, and the controls are good. Expect 5 - 7 hours of gameplay.

This game was a pretty good experience overall. A great story and enjoyable shooting made for a nice experience, and the moral choices the game presents you with made me question my own morality as well as further immerse me in the story. It is certain that the main reason you should buy this game is to experience the story, with its interesting plot, immersive setting and well-written dialogue. This game also reminded me of Gears Of War, and not just because they are both third person shooters. This game gave me the same experience of being powerless in the face of impossible odds - and it certainly is impossible on the highest difficulty. Throughout the game I also felt a constant sense that what I was doing was wrong. I was fighting for my life - and yet I didn't want to. This was only because I was mercilessly slaughtering U.S. soldiers - my allies. At times I found it difficult to shoot people. One striking moment was when my squad had sneaked up behind two soliders who were chatting together. The dialogue reminded me of their humanity, and made me pause before putting bullets through their heads. 

In terms of gameplay, the game is a fairly solid third-person shooter. Shooting feels good, and the gore is well done. Blowing up several soliders at once with a grenade launcher and watching their disintegrated bodies coat the floor is far more rewarding than it should be. The cover system however feels very clunky, and I often found myself moving in a way I didn't want to, and being quickly killed afterwards. This may be down to the fact that the game uses a one-button cover system, so control is lost as the game has to guess what you want to do. However, you have the ability to hold down spacebar and slide into cover from a couple of metres away. This feels very slick and polished, and it works very well. Not only does it feel good, it is also very useful to evade enemy fire. Without it, I feel that the cover system would be a nightmarish experience. Overall, the game plays well, with some enjoyable moments, but the gameplay is nothing special. This game is saved from bad reviews by its story.

One extreme irritation I have with this game is the lack of gameplay options. There is a good graphics menu with lots of options, and rebindable keys (although not as rebindable as I would have liked; many of the buttons do multiple actions clearly designed with a console in mind. For example, left shift both melees and vaults over cover. This is extremely annoying and there is no way to change it). However, there is also noticeable mouse acceleration and motion blur, neither of which can be turned off in the options menu. FoV also cannot be changed in options, although the 65-70° angle that it is locked at is reasonable for a TPS. In order to change these things, you have to somehow get into the encrypted INI files for the game. I was fortunate enough to find a decrypter online, and it was simple enough to disable  motion blur and mouse acceleration. However, the fact that these were unchangeable in the options menu is unacceptable for PC. 

In summary, this game is a fairly solid third-person shooter. It is worth buying this game for the experience, but the short (6 hours on the second-highest difficulty) campaign has little replayability because the major strength of this game is the story. Do not buy this game if you are playing for the gameplay. The multiplayer is uninspired and dull, the only original aspect being the sandstorms that occur randomly in multiplayer games and make it harder to shoot. The real problem with the multiplayer is that you die so quickly that kills and deaths are mostly down to luck and positioning. However, the fun in this game lies with the story, and I recommend it for that alone. For me this game scores 7/10.

Spec Ops does not reinvent the wheel in any way in terms of game mechanics, graphic engine nor brings up action sequences never seen before in the history of gaming. The gameplay is pretty much your usual shooter. The controls are good, the graphics are decent, but it does nothing different tech-wise from other action games, really. So how can I think so highly of such a "generic" game?

Well, there's the game's plot and what it stands for. It is a reimagination of Josephs Conrad's 1899 short novel "Heart of Darkness". Don't worry, I won't spoil anything. While the game kicks off as a standard "military squad vs the world", as the game progresses it gets darker and darker and what appeared to be just a shalow story turns into a very deep critique of violence, human mental health and even the own game industry tendencies. There's TONS of articles out there the discuss the importance of this game's plot, but you'll have to play first.

TL;DR: the game "disguises" itself as a generic game (and in its mechanics, it really is) but there is so much more stuff going on in this plot that turns Spec Ops in one bizarre phenomenon of the game industry. I dropped the game a few times because he was just "OK" but I'm glad one day I had the motivation to finish. It really is worth it if you're into good stories and some grim stuff.

Dear lord, I just finished Spec Ops: The Line. A masterpiece of a game. It is a military third person shooter, but if the gameplay doesn't chase you off, don't assume anything else. The story is a major deconstruction of the standard views, and deciding what is right, what is necessary, and are they really either of those things. It also has rather excellent use of color, balancing against the common browns and grays.
Now it's not perfect, the game tends to increase the challenge by simply adding a lot of enemies, and they can (even early on) shred through you pretty quickly if you are in the open. Coupled with infrequent checkpoints this can easily ruin the narrative and flow of sections. In addition while stealth is sometimes suggested, it is intensely difficult to do in practice.
However I can't tell you how important of a game this is, both for the general plot, and the emotions it leaves you with. If you can stomach the gameplay and theming, PLEASE give it a shot.

+ Gorgeous crumbling urban/desert environments
+ Excellent visuals
+ Well-written story
+ Takes an unflinching approach to disturbing themes, particularly those of war crimes
+ Solid gameplay mechanics, if a bit simplistic
+ Fitting soundtrack that helped to set the mood
+ The choices you make in this game really take a toll
+ Excellent use of destructible environments while in-combat (ie. Shooting out windows and burying enemies in sand)

- Default controls were an odd choice, and felt counterintutive; I recommend changing them
- Sprint function was poorly implement, and sometimes won't behave, leaving you out in the open trying to get a handle on your character's movement

I haven't been a big fan of shooters. BL and I think Call of Juarez were the last couple I've played. Also, "on rails" games (which this is) aren't my favorite. But, at a friend's suggestion, I picked this up during a sale.

The mechanics are a bit clunky for the controls, but you do get team-based commands and the overall action is pretty well laid out. It takes some getting used to as far as how the combat scenes will take place. If you're looking for an amazing combat system, I'd say look elsewhere. But it is decent, and playable.

I've seen other reviews talk about choices you make in this game, but let's be clear, 100% clear, you don't really get a choice on most things, and the choices you do get are pretty minor (in the grand scheme of things). So don't expect arcing story paths, fifteen playthroughs, and multiple ways to solve things. The "choices" are made for you - and yes, while it's between "terrible" and "reprehensible", there is no way to "make a call" - you're forced into the decision to continue the game.

Now, I'll go onto why someone should buy this game: The story. 

Yes, it's on rails. 

Yes, your choices are pretty light. 

But I can safely say that if you can play this game without a single twinge of conscience, without feeling (not just thinking the words) "that's messed up - truly messed up", and if you don't learn at least a little bit you didn't know about the horrors of war, either you've been through it (and I feel truly sorry for you), or you're a sociopath.

I don't get disturbed and almost never moved by video games. I immerse myself in thier worlds, but I don't get emotionally involved. This one did a pretty good job of breaking that streak. I was... disturbed by the content. War isn't glorious, no one is a hero when stuff goes down and gets real, and certainly in this day and age, not everything is what it seems - "good" and "bad" are pretty subjective.

Even knowing about this, and expecting some pretty labrynthine plot once the CIA showed up and stuff wasn't making sense, this game took me by surprise.

And you know what? 

That's fracking rare in this day and age. 

So even with some mediocre mechanics, buy this game. Play it. And, should you feel no twinge of upset, remorse or empathy, you might just be a sociopath.

First I just want to explain the "have not yet played the game much" part that might show up over this review. I have played through this entire game on the xbox 360 several times, so this review is legitimate. I have experienced this game to its fullest and am therefore qualified to review it. I have only played it for the short time now so that I could see how well it ran on my computer compared to the Xbox 360. It runs very smoothly. I was using an Xbox controller and it was responsive but I am nto sure that it would as good with the keyboard and mouse as I have not yet tried it. Now, let us get on with the review.  

You are Captain Martin Walker, with your team you are being sent on a rescue mission where things end up going south really fast. It seems like everything is just spiraling down to very dark matters very quickly where you end up having to kill the people you came to save. 

If you are looking for a game like the COD or Battlefield series, this is not what you are looking for. The creators of this game knew that they did not have the budget for such a production so they therefore worked more on the games story and mechanics which was truly worth it. On the surface this game seems like a generic 3'rd person shooter. The gameplay mostly consists of lining up headshots on your enemies to preserve ammunition, which in the long run on its own would be boring. What they do right is putting out branching paths, without specifically telling you that you have choices to choose from. I'm going to try to explain one of these as spoiler free as possible, but I will put the notice *SPOILER* in case you want to know none of the things happening in the game before playing it. (Skip to the next paragraph from here if that is the case). There is a part of the game where you are surrounded by civilians who seem to be quite agressive. you can not move on if you do not choose to fire your weapon. On the first playthrough, I shot at the crowd. Making them run away in horror. On my second playthrough I thought that I might be able to scare them off if I just shot into the air, and I was delighted to find out that it worked, but the game has a lot of these.

As I played the game for a while I started to realize that I started to dislike myself more and more while playing it. When the loading screens were loading, it said some things in the place where there are usually hints in games that resonated within me. An example being "How many people have you killed today?" It seemed as the game was directly talking to me, not the character I was playing in the game. It made me think for a while, why was I doing what I was doing? I of course justified it to myself, saying that I had to do those things, if not I could not progress with the game, but I was yet not satisfied with my reasoning. It was clear for me that it was a bad excuse as I just felt uneasy while playing the game, which became abundantly clear in the end of the game (Which I will not at all spoil for you, but I will say that it has all to do with why we play games. If you read this review before you complete the game, just remember that the last level is directly speaking to you, the player). You actually end up regretting the things you have done. 

When you first meet your character, your mind will probably go to the place of "Oh, here we go again. A very clichè, testosterone filled Soldier with problems, who cares*, but after a while you will maybe dislike your character. The fact that I didn't like my main character might be something that made me enjoy the game more(I have heard different things, this is only my experience with the character, while others have said that they started to sympathize with him.)

All in all, it was one of my favorite games of 2012. If the things I've written in this review(my first review) captures your interest, I would tell you to get the game. I do not want you to get into the game with the wrong idèa, so I felt like putting out my thoughts on this one. Remember, this is my own experiences with the game. All have their own thoughts about this. I am just glad I was able to share mine.

Spec Ops: The Line, is most certainly, without a doubt, THE hidden gem of 2012. Here's why:


Gameplay: 6.5/10 - This is probably the weakest part of this game. However, it was still enjoyable enough to keep me occupied during the whole single-player campaign. This game is a cover-based third-person shooter. While there are some neat little gimmicks here and there, Spec Ops doesn't really do much to innovate, and stands as basically being an average shooter when it comes to the core mechanics. You will move from cover to cover, shooting blankly, or pushing yourself out and aiming, using your fairly average assortment of modern-military shooter weapons. 

You also have two squad members that you can direct to either attack enemies or to paralyze them. This is rather useful, and the A.I. is fairly decent and can actually help you out quite a bit when you're in a pickle. Another thing to mention would have to be using the environment to kill your enemies. However, this is nothing too special and just looks pretty for show. 

Now, if you're expecting a non-linear experience from Spec Ops: The Line, then you should look elsewhere. Spec Ops: The Line is an extremely linear game, in which you will go through corridor after corridor of enemy encounters as the story and character progression grows. There are collectibles to find in the game, but are fairly easy to find for the most part, and won't lead you off the beaten trail.

Spec Ops: The Line also has the cinematic setpieces you would expect from modern-military shooters, but they actually compliment the story for the most part.
 
When it comes to multiplayer, it really should just be avoided. It's nothing special and may even ruin the atmosphere of the game itself for you. 

Presentation: 9.0/10 - Spec Ops: The Line isn't exactly set in the most original place when it comes to modern-military shooters (Dubai), but the art-style is fantastic and compliments the game's overall atmosphere greatly. Everything is very bright and colorful, as the lighting and particle effects are excellent. The whole city of Dubai feels very surreal and liely, though the whole game is extremely dark in tone. This actually creates a rather disturbing and disjointed feeling throughout the entire game, which is great. When it comes to textures, there's nothing really special here. The game looks average, with character models especially having seemingly low resolution textures. 

Cutscenes are decent, except for the pre-rendered ones, which are locked at thirty frames per second, and don't even look much better than the ones that aren't. However, many cutscenes are very emotional and well voice-acted, just as the rest of the game. 

What I do have to mention is that anti-aliasing does not work for the most part, which is a shame.

Spec Ops: The Line is the hidden gem of 2012. FTL would be my "hidden gem," but after the whole massive Kickstarter success thing, it was obvious FTL was going to be good in my point of view. Honestly, I used to play Call of Duty and Halo. There. I said it. However, after Black Ops 1, I quit the Call of Duty series and haven't played any of the games since MW3. Halo Reach was the Halo that I played the most, and was the only Halo game (Halo 3 and Wars were good though) that I loved and played often. However, above all of these games, Spec Ops: The Line has one of the best stories of all time. It isn't like Call of Duty how you're fighting as some American soldier running around solo armed to the teeth with weapons and murdering terrorists and in the end "saving the world." Not at all. Some people believe there are "good guys" and "bad guys," but this game is solid evidence that war is just opinions being decided to the death, sometimes costing one's sanity, social health, emotional health, and physical health. Spec Ops: The Line proves war in no way is enjoyable, cool, or humorous in any kind of way. War is horrific, and this game is enough to prove that.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]

The visuals are absolutely outstanding. The environments look beautiful, and the atmosphere is bright on the outside, but dark and horrific on the inside. The characters look amazing, and it's rare you can actually see the sweat of a character in the middle of combat. This game is able to do that. If I were to compare these visuals to The Last of Us, Spec Ops: The Line would win by a mile. These graphics are extremely realistic, but the only con to this is that the facial animations can look weird. For example, when Walker is talking to Lugo or Adams when it isn't a cutscene, it looks like he's gaping every time, like he's shocked at everything for some reason. During cutscenes though, Walker looks fine and doesn't gape like that when he speaks.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

The gameplay is suprisingly the weak point to the game. Although this game is a shooter, Spec Ops is more for people who want a story based game, rather than a gameplay based one. The AI is suicidally bad and the difficulty spikes at times and the awful gunplay ruins it even more. My squadmates keep bumping into me and I die, one enemy shot 3 RPG rockets in a row without reloading for some reason (He had an RPG, I saw him with the weapon, I swear!) and the AI prefer running toward me like overconfident barbarians. However, the game understands the meaning of "limited" unlike other games *cough* Call of Duty *cough* *cough* and makes ammo a bit more difficult to get, so that's something few games did that aren't in the zombie survival genre. 

[h1]Story[/h1]

The story is the reason Spec Ops is highly praised. Like I said before, it proves that war is a terrible thing and (quoted from Fallout 3) "never changes." Lugo, Adams, and Walker's bond with each other was strong, like they were old friends, then all of a sudden, Lugo and Adams part away from Walker, realizing that he's gone insane, but Adams is still merely following orders, while Lugo wants to make a stand. You realize that Walker is in no way a hero, but calling him a villain is illogical. The plot twist around the midst of the game was amazing and blew my mind. I'm going to do another quote, but this time from one of my favorite songs: "This ain't no place for no hero, this ain't no place for no- better man, this ain't no place for no hero, to call home." -"Short Change Hero" by The Heavy. It perfectly describes the story, mixed with the atmosphere, and how the characters develop over time in the destroyed and now insane city of Dubai. I assure you, this game has one of the finest stories in gaming. It seems like 2012 was the year for gaming, since games like this and The Walking Dead came out and wowed us with their storytelling. In the end, the story for this game is simply outstanding.

[h1]Audio[/h1]

The audio is also amazing for this game. The voice actors did an amazing job with their roles, and all showed personality. They  weren't androids and were kind of like the Mass Effect characters, in a way you grow attached to them because they feel like real, breathing humans. But you still gotta hate Walker. Then, hate yourself while you're at it for doing all the harsh decisions. Name me a few other games that truly make you want to hate yourself that much. The music is similar to those found in a zombie apocalypse game, like the recent ones State of Decay and The Last of Us. It's usually a guitar backed up by a few other instruments or the guitar playing solo. It sounds beautiful and fits in perfectly. The audio in this game is some of the finest in recent gaming.

[h1]Replayability[/h1]

It's a bit more difficult to provide replayability to a game like this, unfortunately. However, you could go back and get all the endings. The multiplayer is pretty dead, so I haven't had any chance to try it yet. Either way, I suppose the replayability in this game is determinant. 

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

In conclusion, Spec Ops: The Line proves war is terrifying and that it's not fun at all. However, the horrible gameplay holds it down significantly, along with a dead multiplayer and the jaw drops that happen when Walker talks while playing (Not in a cutscene) hold it back. Either way, Spec Ops: The Line is a must have for any story based game buyer. I highly recommend this gem.

SO:TL is at its heart a tactical military cover shooter, simlar to games like Rainbow Six: New Vegas 2 and Brothers in Arms.  Perspective is 3rd person and you have two squadmates who can receive simple orders like "focus attack here"... generally they will advance as enemies are cleared.  Levels are mostly confined space, although later in the game the field opens up giving you a few path choices.  The setting is something unique to this genre: Dubai, following a series of catastrophoc sand storms that have decimated the city.  The US military has moved in to assist with the evacuation... however something has gone wrong and your small team has been sent in to investigate.  The story feels predictable at the outset but then becomes very surreal as you progress... with a fantastic ending.

As a shooter the game is challenging in spots without being oppressive and provides the standard occasional over the top action sequences.  The control system takes some getting used to, but is easily customized to suite your style.  Graphically the game uses the Unreal engine which is quite responsive but somewhat dated.  Weapon assortment is typical... you have 2 weapon slots and can freely pick up those dropped by enemies.

What really stands out here though is the story, which explores the impact of killing on the mind of the killer.  Having played through the game I can say that there are parts of the game where decisions seem murky at best leaving you feel a bit unnerved.  You can only imagine how our soldiers must deal with these decisions in the field and through the rest of their lives.  An eye opener.

8/10

DISCLAIMER: This is a long review, but I've tried to cover setting, story and gameplay. If you read the whole thing, that probably confirms that you need to play this game.

This game. Oh man, this effing game.
I heard about this title a while back, noted for it's solid story and setting. I popped it on my wishlist and eventually I managed to get it at a good price (2K Humble Bundle, thanks guys!).

It was worth the wait.
Long have I dreamed of a military-themed title that forces you to confront the more horrific aspects of war, and this game does it beautifully. There is very little in the way of clear-cut, waypointed binary 'moral choices', but choose you will, because most of these decisions are organic, and because this is war, none of the outcomes will be pretty.

The setting is incredible. Dubai is a freakish juxtaposition between limitless luxury and hellish desolation; and that's just in the real world. Throw 2K's incredible vision of a city abandoned by authority, beset by brutality, and drowned in the desert itself over the top and you have possibly the best location for a game I've seen in almost a decade. They didn't just make it look good, either - much of the environment is destructible, and if you've ever wondered what crushing your enemies with a thousand tonnes of sand might look like, now you can find out.

I deeply enjoyed the story, and if you've invested any time in military/conspiracy literature or cinema you will see immediately that much of the overarching plot arc is a direct nod to the legendary film Apocalypse Now (to the point that the main antagonist's name (Konrad) is a variation on that of John Conrad, author of the film's inspirational text, Heart of Darkness). The story contains many well-known and frequently used elements of military and warfare media, but by no means does that make it formulaic. The characters are well-written and the voice acting is excellent. Your squadmates, through their words and actions, will elicit within you feelings of compassion, pride, fear, mistrust and guilt.

At times the plot twists sharply enough to make you uncertain of the details, and by extension yourself, but this really only serves to further immerse you in the chaos that almost constantly surrounds you. Factions within the game are unpredictable and rarely what they seem, their motives shrouded in blood and the chain of command; to the point where you wonder if they can be regarded as factions at all. Cutscenes are frequent, appropriately expository, and provide the right mixture of closure on the last scene and motive for the next one. The conclusion really, genuinely deserves to be discovered - but only by those who survive their way through to it, those who /earned/ it.

In terms of gameplay, the title is also top-tier. Very rarely did I feel hampered by game mechanics, although I will acknowledge that I found the default keybinds a little clunky - remapping them may be advisable. (The best example of this is the use of 'Q' to throw a grenade and 'E' to switch weapons. If you've played Source engine games much, you'll occasionally have your muscle memory revert to 'Q' for weapon switch, which results in comically lobbing a grenade without aiming, usually onto your own feet or the wall in front of you).

Weapons are similar enough to be reliable when picked up on the run and different enough to be useful in the right situation. Alternate fire is not something you'll use often, but it works well when you do. Iron Sights are absolutely essential and I didn't find a weapon that didn't do them well. The extra level of thought regarding stationary weapons, like being able to flip a fixed MG turret in the opposite direction, or crouch down and blind-fire it (inaccurate, but out of harm's way) are extra details that make such fixtures infinitely more useful.

Your NPC squadmates are well characterised and are actually useful in a firefight. Squad commands come in handy, laying down suppressing fire to cover their movements (or vice versa) is a useful tactic, combat speech is all business but absolutely an asset in a fight. Thankfully your guys won't run blindly into opposing fire, and being able to recover them if they do manage to fall in battle is no small mercy.

Combat environments are varied, or as much as they can be in a battle-scarred city of sand, glass and steel. There is some element of vertical combat as you engage with enemy combatants rappelling in from the upper levels of the building you're fighting in, snipers on rooftops, and making your way up/down staircases in towers and shopping precints. Some cover can be degraded by heavy fire and there are explosive props that can be used to help dispatch your enemies, but they are not heavily advertised, and spotting one and using it effectively to take down an opponent feels like a victory in perception and adaptation under fire. Additionally, enemies do not automatically spawn and stand mindlessly next to the red crate or barrel, waiting for you to shoot it - you'll need to flush them out or lure them in if that's how you want to obtain your kills.

The only environmental gripe I could come up with was that some static props seem to have a hitbox slightly larger than expected - leaning out to loose few shots would at times result in the bullets harmlessly striking the edge of whatever I, or my enemy, was hiding beside. This seemed to happen more often with scoped weapons, I noticed.


Ultimately I found this game to be one of the best I've played in recent memory. Tense, terse, immersive and explosive. I found myself hungry for answers, but apprehensive of what they'd be. I scrambled for ammo and lunged for cover. I grit my teeth, swore, dug in, and expended brass and blood in equal amounts. I travelled from mindless bloodlust to gut-wrenching grief, and back again, and I loved every minute of it. When you finish this game you'll be left, in a way, unsatisfied. Not because the game was lacking, far from it - but because you'll be asking yourself, over and over;

"..what if I'd done something different?"

[h1]A disturbing, surreal take on war and PTSD, Spec Ops: The Line delves into the dark corners of the human mind.[/h1]

To say that Spec Ops: The Line is a great game falls dismally short of its mark: it is a [i]majestic[/i] game, that deserved more praise upon release and even today. It is a story that portrays the sinister, visceral reality that goes hand in hand with waging a war: collateral losses, vicious brutality and trauma are served in reckless, unapologetic fashion in a story that the more we delve into it, the more we lose ourselves.

Set in a sandstorm-ridden Dubai, the game puts you in the shoes of captain Martin Walker, officer in charge of a Delta Force squad comprising three soldiers: himself, First Lieutenant Alphonso Adams and Staff Sergeant John Lugo. His mission? Make contact with Walker’s former superior in Afghanistan: John Konrad, a charismatic US colonel who went rogue along with his 33rd Battalion to help Dubai’s civilians with relief efforts and to provide the city with some semblance of law and order in the wake of the sandstorms’ path of inexorable destruction. What begins as a simple extraction mission soon degenerates in an unexpected and unwanted meddling in what seems to be a factional war among local militia, deserters of Konrad’s forces and the remnant of the loyalist soldiers faithful to the colonel, all vying for power in a city made up of empty, rotting carcasses of barren, towering skyscrapers.

It is hard to speak of the story without revealing anything, and thus I will refrain from mentioning specific bits, but I will say this: As the plot gets more complex and the various plotlines’ intricate interweaving starts to unravel, so does the candidness of the story, getting darker by the level, delving deep into the darkest depths of human consciousness and psyche and how we deal with trauma and guilt. More than once you will feet shivers down your spine and there is a specific time where you will be hard-pressed to avert your gaze from the screen. Often we see that games are unfairly rated for a mature audience; not this: Spec Ops does not shy away from depicting the horrors of man in the most brutal ways I have ever seen in gaming, exploring the sinister nature of war and how it inexorably ravages the human mind, ushering in maladies that our generation knows all-too-well, such as PTSD. Whereas other games sugarcoat the nature of war and vindicate the role of the military -when not outright glorifying violence- Spec Ops: the Line makes sure that we should never forget the twisted nature of war.

For a game with such a complex story, the gameplay is surprisingly pretty straightforward: it is a 3rd person shooter that sports some of the most solid cover mechanics ever seen in gaming. It feels real, intuitive and fun -even if tremendously challenging!- There is a plethora of weapons to choose from that adapt to our needs as we traverse streets, buildings and roofs filled with enemies bent on bringing our journey to an untimely end. Being the sand a pivotal element of the game, it should come as no surprise that there are dozens of environmental interactions and traps you can exploit to gain the upper hand on your foes, most iconic of which are cracked glasses that hold at bay massive mounds of sand, which will make short work of your enemies in probably one of the most agonising deaths in all of gaming. The execution, as such, befits the story perfectly.

But for a story to be properly told, the technical department must be on par. And this game delivers, and it delivers brilliantly: sandstorm-ridden Dubai is beautifully brought to life with the Unreal Engine, delivering beautiful textures and effects that have remarkably stood the test of time. The sand's physics, in particular, feel as powerful as they felt back when the game was released, and the aesthetics of Dubai are so credibly and realistically crafted that it will bgrin memories to any of us who have had the pleasure of visiting the Middle East. The sound and music in the game is also state-of-the-art, not only in terms of sound quality and fidelity -which exists abundantly ranging from the ominous sounds of bullets and explosions raging about, to the horrific whoosh that accompanies the unleashing of a sand torrent upon unsuspecting enemies and their nerve-racking wailing that precludes their inexorable burial- but also in the artistic deparment, bringing about one of the most memorable scenes in the game (if not in gaming altogether) where we get pounded by the relentless cacophony of the cannoning of an enemy helicopter as Verdi’s Dies Irae bombastically sounds on the speakers, This is precisely what Spec Ops is: a testament to art and quality, a testament that never shies away from going the extra mile to deliver the ultimate experience gaming has to offer.

Spec Ops: The Line is an ode to peace as Requiem for a Dream is an ode to sobriety: in portraying the sinister and despicable effects of war on the human mind, it delivers an implacable, unrelenting assault on the wickedness of the former, seldom seen on any given medium. And for that, the game deserves the highest of praises. 

In the end you will probably look at your hands and wonder: “what have I done?”

Spec Ops: The Line is an incredible game. It's also an incredibly gory, horrifying game. The story is phenomenally well done, and if you're alright with gore (not typical video-gamey "fun" gore - there's a lot of really gross realistic gore (and a lot of the worst is your character's fault) and feeling horrible about your character (Captain Walker) then I highly recommend it. But if you're particularly sensitive to... pretty much any sort of violence and gore, I'd steer clear.
All aspects of the game have been done well. The scenery looks beautiful, the guns feel powerful, and there's actually a good reason to have all of that cover (you can die REALLY easily, and I played it on normal mode). Your two AI companions (Adams and Lugo) do end up coming in handy, especially once the game gets really difficult. The gameplay itself isn't anything new (it's very Gears of War-esque), but it's enough to serve the game, and it's been put together splendidly. Basically, the story drives the game, and the gameplay includes you in the story, just as any story-driven game should do.
This game is truly proof that video games can be art in the same way movies and books have been - not just "oooh pretty" art (though games can do that and have definitely done that too (look at Journey)), but the kind of art that makes you think, poses questions, and makes commentary. It's based around Heart of Darkness, though it takes many different twists and turns, and it does manage to show the sides of one of the victims of actual war that tends to get ignored: the citizens in war-torn places. Though there isn't much direct commentary on that, it's pretty clear the way these people feel, and the game does much to show the horror of your actions. 
The game is very linear, but it's alright here because it serves the story, displaying your character's descent into the heart of Dubai, ruined by great sand storms and violence - as well as his descent into the darkest places of the human heart. In this way, it's hard to say the game doesn't make you feel horribly guilty - either for yourself or for Captain Walker. It's rather clear by the linear nature of this game that Captain Walker is his own character, not you - his decisions are his decisions. However, it is you who end up carrying out his decisions - just following orders. Whether you like it or not, you are part of the story.
I highly recommend you play this game. It is not for the faint of heart, but it shows a lot of depth that video games (particularly modern war shooters) really need to get behind. This is by far the most mature game I have ever played.

[h1] Heart of Darkness	[/h1]

A series of dust storms has destroyed much of Dubai, leaving countless civilians stranded. The 33rd Battalion, a United States infantry unit, is sent to provide aid but soon disappears. In a last ditch effort, a three-man Delta Force team is sent in to find out what happened and rescue survivors. As captain of this reconnaissance team it is up to you and your teammates to fight your way across the city and find answers.

[b] Gameplay	[/b]

Spec Ops: The Line is a third person shooter where you will find that you are heavily reliant on cover. You have the ability to command your teammates in battle, telling them who to target. Combat is fast paced and fun, albeit a bit generic. My main complaint with combat would be that the AI sometimes feels a bit clumsy, but nothing bad enough to be game breaking. 

[b] A Story Worth Experiencing	[/b]

The game is very story rich and is definitely worth paying attention to. Occasionally you will be forced to make some very difficult decisions. What I liked about this is that there is never really a “right” or “wrong” answer. Unlike some military shooters, this game does not glorify war. Instead it touches on the horrors of war and the profound psychological impact it often has on those who experience it.

[b] Beautiful Environment	[/b]

The environment is absolutely breathtaking, by far my favorite in any game ever. They did a wonderful job at making Dubai look so ruined yet beautiful, resulting in a few areas where you have to stop just to admire your surroundings. 

[b] Music	[/b]

I realize that this can vary quite a bit from person to person but I was pleasantly surprised by the music used in the game. Quite a few classics including Hendrix and Deep Purple, as well as some more modern but worthwhile bands such as the Black Angels. If that’s not your thing, it’s still worth mentioning that the original score is pretty solid.  

[b] My Verdict	[/b]

I’m normally extremely skeptical of military shooters, but this game is something else entirely and is now considered among my favorite games.  A bit shorter than I would have liked it to be, but still one that I would highly recommend.

At the start of the game, you may be thinking this is just another modern shooter...
By the end of the game, you'll be proven wrong. The story-telling in this game is unmatched.  If you want a game that shows the true, grim side of war, this is that game.

Spec Ops: The Line is a hidden jem in my opinion. From the steam page, not much is known about the true nature of the game, although, I believe anyone who does play the game will be in for a beautiful but tragic ride. At first the game seems like a normal 3rd person shooter, a decent combat system and beautiful environment makes it almost seem like a battlefield game. But things quickly take a turn when your squad transitions from soldiers to survivors. You slowly realize this isn't just another army game, the things you and your men have to do to stay alive are terrible, and both you and the characters will question the meaning of their lives and choices. The walk to insanity is a slow one, and you and your men will suffer through it.The game is tragic, dark, saddening, and lonely. Mix that in with beautiful environment, graphics, and excellent voice acting, and you have a gripping, adrenaline pumping, and tear jerking experience. It defies the rules laid out by most games. There are no right choices, there is no redemption, and you will feel the regret and pain from the repercussions. Final summary: 8.5/10, a great experience for someone who wants a psychological and deeply emotional game.

Writing this review is difficult, because there are two kinds of games Spec Ops: the Line can be. From one point of view, it's a generic, linear shooter, in a land filled with waist-high walls and conveniently placed guns. On the other hand, the story and choices the player is forced to endure are so investing that it forces you to think and... to some extent, even feel guilt. 

You play as the captain of a small task force, entering the city of Dubai following a massive sandstorm that has all but destroyed the city. As you explore and attempt to rescue civilians, and the lost 33rd platoon who was previous sent it, you start to discover a destitute war-zone akin to Lord of the Flies. The story digs deeper as you see the kind of person who would be willing to perform these atrocities, and you start to realize you might need to become that way yourself, just to help save everyone else.

Despite the chaos and gore, the setting and environment for this game are gorgeous, and the attention to detail is fantastic for a game this price. There are a number of moments the game leads you through that are really meant to etch into your skull. I think that's really what the game has going for it, though. You're playing this almost generic shooter, and the game starts to question your motives --and even taunt your poor decisions, when they do occur. Don't expect a happy ending walking into this game, but whatever route you choose, it's a satisfying, justified one.

The game play gets repetitive and I wouldn't say it is the greatest shooter I've ever played, but anything it lacks in gameplay it will make up for in the story that unfolds. If nothing else play for the story, it will not dissappoint.

There's moments that blur the lines between right and wrong and survival and completing the mission. The lines really blur when you fight American troops because they shoot at you first. Do you like movies like Platoon or Apocalypse now and all other movies about what war will do with soldiers mind, just going a bit deep than "killing is a simple, just pull the trigger"? And do you like shooters? Consider playing this game.

I picked this up based on Yahtzee's [url=http://www.escapistmagazine.com/videos/view/zero-punctuation/6677-Top-5-of-2012]best game of 2012[/url] recommendation, and it was everything he said it would be. Incredibly well written and thought-provoking, this is the first game I've ever played that actually [i]does[/i] hold a mirror up to the medium, the genre, society, players, even the developers themselves. I have never been so morally challenged by a game, and I didn't think I could be more shocked or emotionally distraught over the events in a game than the first time I saw the sword erupt from Aerith's chest. But when you get to [spoiler]the white phosphorous event[/spoiler], you'll understand why I put this game down for nine months before charging back through it.

When you finish the game (and you really should attempt to get at least two of the endings), I suggest you also read up about [url=http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spec_Ops:_The_Line#Development]its development process[/url] as well. It's unfortunate that the necessary evil of the video game distribution model forced Yager to acquiesce to 2K's demands and dilute [spoiler](if not betray)[/spoiler] the themes of the single-player campaign through the inclusion of a multiplayer mode. In the current climate of cynical knockoffs and safe, bland sequels, the ambition shown by the developers at Yager is amazing. Their willingness to explore unpleasant topics and themes in the pursuit of their message is worthy of high praise.

The only caveat I would offer is that the game play can feel unbalanced in a handful of places. There are a few sections that are punishingly difficult to get through, where your squad mates are more a curse than a blessing. While I'd like to think this was also intentional by Yager, it felt more like the product of unfortunate choices in event and checkpoint scripting.

[b]TL;DR:[/b] This game is impressive, important even. Everyone who enjoys the FPS genre (even though this is technically a third-person shooter) should play this. It will make you level up as a gamer... and as a human being.

Spec Ops: The Line seems like any other shooter at its beginning, but it turns out to be much more.  Set in post-apocalyptic Dubai, the brown, lifeless landscapes that are present in many other shooters are replaced by colorful citiscapes and opulent urban backdrops.  Bullets are scarce, so the game encourages intelligent approaches to conflicts through environmental destruction as well as your standard conveniently placed explosive barrels.

Most of all, the game succeeds in being fun to play while also possessing uncommon emotional weight.  As your character is affected by his actions, so, too, is the player.  Intelligence pickups function similarly to Bioshock's audiologs, providing additional information to flesh out the narrative and provide deeper looks into the player character's perceptions.

It's a relatively short game (~6 hours per playthrough), but it accomplishes more over its short duration than most games do over any length.  If you're a fan of exposition and don't mind breaking a few heads along the way, Spec Ops: The Line is very worthy of your consideration.  It's an experience I won't soon forget.

I didn't like the game too much. I got to chapter 7 (of 15) and uninstalled because I needed disk space for other games.

First of all, controls are very unintuitive for PC players, and your muscle memory will keep you tripping over defaults. While you can redefine the keyboard bindings, they are *grouped* awkwardly (for example same key must be used for run and cover so when running or trying to find better cover your character "sticks" to all kinds of wrong cover constantly). Additionally if you have a controller plugged in (but not using it) game will keep displaying controller keys in all context popups which is very confusing.

Gameplay itself is okay, nothing especially good, it plays and feels like a generic "on rails" linear-levels console port with added inconvenience of terrible controls on which you'll either have to get used to or suffer. Also notable thing is that it is very easy to die and get in inescapable situations. Gameplay protip: default pistol is fantastic for whatever-range headshots - which you'll need because ammo is not plentiful (unlike deadly enemies).

Level design is absolutely linear and you can only go and do what the script says. Enemies spawn at predefined time, position and distance as you pass trigger points. For such "on-rails" linear game as is Spec Ops: The Line, scarcity of ammo really hinders game flow.

I won't comment on the story too much because I only endured until chapter 7 until I gave up due to unrewarding gameplay and awkward controls, but so far the story was basically a proverbial "junk food", and I'm not saying this as a bad thing.

*** CONCLUSION ***

I don't recommend the game at full price, even if you are just interested in the story.

Because I got it on sale for €4.99 I don't feel I wasted my money for what I played + I avoided wasting my time when game got sufficiently unrewarding to play.

So I just finised this game today and after playing, decided to write a review.

A modern military 3rd person shooter, putting the player in the middle of unspeakable situations.

Yes, I can agree with that. 

My take on the game is this: Its a modern version of Apocalypse Now. I see so many things in common with that film. The background is that the large city of Dubai was destroyed by a sandstorm and then a large amount of troops were sent in to rescue them. Nobody escapes and all contact with the city has been lost. It has been left to rot. 

Enter a 3 man elite Delta Force squad searching for answers. Once entering the city and being attacked, they decide to find the rouge Colonel (ala Apocalypse Now) and find out what exactly happend. 

Not going to ruin the game by what entails, but it is sick and horrifying. Choices are presented to you, but it feels like it makes little difference because the choices are so horrible. 

The game is short. I tend to play my games on easier difficutly and I completed the game in about 5 hours.  

A good selection of weapons. You can only carry 2 weapons at a time, and some ammo is scarce for certain weapons, so I found that I swapped weapons quite a bit. 

Pretty straightforward game. No puzzles or backtracking. Kill the guys, move into the next area, cutscene, repeat. I did enjoy some parts that allow you to cover your other 2 guys when you get separated or shooting the minigun on the helicopter. No vehicles for you to drive, this game is all on foot. You are able to issue some limited commands to your members as well. 

The AI for the squad members, I must admit is great. Instead of some games that AI units just follow you around and take some cover, firing every now and then at an enemy. In this game, my AI squad took cover, and KILLED units. They covered me when I moved. They moved ahead of me on the map and engaged and killed units. 

The audio is ok. I actually got a little tired of some of the phrases they shout. I wish they couldve included a few different lines because every firefight I got into, it always sounded the same. But whats there is good and sets the mood. Music is ok, nothing really major to speak about. Gun sounds are decent as well.

Graphics are pretty decent as well. The unreal engine 3 is starting to show its age a little, and even though I had the graphics at max, some textures were blurry, but still decent. Large landscapes and sprawling desolate city was nice. I really enjoyed the sandstorms. Every once in a while during the game, a sandstorm would come through. Wind, low visibility and all was pretty decent and felt intense when one hit in the middle of a gun fight. 

I think my biggest gripe with this game is the controls. For me being almost strictly a PC gamer and have played other 3rd person shooters, the controls felt a little wonky. You hit space to run, and once you start running, do not have to hold down space. You also use space to take cover behind anything you can, be it a wall, destroyed vehicle or side of a building. The control key is used to duck/croutch. However, since the spacebar is used to take cover behind something, I felt this wasnt needed at all in game since when your being shot at, will use the spacebar to take cover, not croutch behind something. I kept mixing them in game and died a few times because of it. 

So over all, I give the game a 7.5/10. A good, if some what short game that will make you think about the morality of being a soldier.

While the gameplay is decent, it's nothing very innovative or fun. Finally the game's message of "You always have a choice" is rendered moot in a game where no real choices are given that will change the course of the game. This might have worked with a movie, but it feels strange to have choice be one of the central themes, while giving the player no choices.

HOLY. CRUD.

This game makes a beautifully horrific (those who've played know what I mean) transformation from seemingly generic shooter to a highly psychological shooter. You kill and kill and kill in most shooters, but in this game...in this game...after playing for a while longer, by the time I finished it...I was just thinking, "THAT was heavy. Hit me right in my morals."

The writing is brilliant and the story hooks you deep. The gameplay is shallow, but it's a good shallow in my opinion since the game is supposed to project an overall point in its story so I can forgive shallow gameplay in exchange for focusing on story.

Overall, I give this game a straight up: 10/10. For those who want a game that plays with your head (I won't spoil anything), GET THIS GAME (it goes on sale pretty often on Steam).

All I ever heard about this game was how amazing it was and how it had a great story for a shooter. Well, I am was impressed. The controls are not great. I died quite a few times to grenades because my character would not run when breaking from cover. I didn't like the over-the-shoulder shooter style. This style may work in games like Mass Effect, but here it made me feel lopsided disconnected from my character. The scenery/environments were interesting, and I thought the game looked pretty good for when it came out. 
However, the biggest drawback for this game was the story. Let me say first that I love surreal, complex, and philosophical stories. Although the game's story does pull you in on some amazing levels by getting you to hate your enemies so much that you make choices that you wouldn't have at the beginning of the game (mirroring your character's moral descent), I ultimately felt that the ending was hollow and made the entire game seem pointless. 
An example of where this game succeeds spectacularly is a case where I was forced to make a split-second decision and made a choice that left me shocked and disturbed. I reloaded, determined not repeat this incident, only to make the same disturbing decision in the situation. The story's ability to coax you into letting go of your morals/ethics in very short amount of time was astonishing. 
However, any emotional capital that was built up throughout the game's ethics shredder was evaporated by an ambiguous ending that left me feeling like I needed to play the game several more times to understand what really happened (if there even is anything to understand). This is not something you want to hear after firing on civilians and executing wounded soldiers for 6 hours. Only the worst kind of psycho bred in Dubai's moral ruins would want to start down that path again.
If you want a game that will make you question your very sanity and question every decision you make, then this is the game for you. Plus you will feel bad for everything you do in this game.

After letting the heavy-handed ending set in, I had to really think about how to end this review. Should I recomend it, or not? As I'm sure you're picking up on, Spec ops has some really nice touches and some pretty glaring flaws. Well not necessarily flaws, but just some mechanics that aren't spectacular or polished. 

Let me start with the mehs of the game. First of all, Spec ops is a third person shooter that operates as a TPS should - it has a functional cover system that is fluid in that it allows your character to vault over walls, swap between pillars, and slide into cover, but it isn't really deeper than that. Furthermore, your character is far from bullet proof, meaning you'll be stuck in the gride of HOP OUT OF COVER, SHOOT UNTIL SCREEN IS RED, DUCK DOWN AGAIN AND WAIT FOR HEALTH REGEN, etc. You really can't rush or try any strategtic manuevers, you just shoot until dead. The game also rarely includes objectives outside of go here, there are some moments that involve you protecting a water truck or shooting from a helicopter, but they have all been done before. As far as gameplay goes, Spec ops gets the job done, and doesn't bother working overtime. 

If I were to leave it at that, Spec ops would probably get a thumbs down just because the gameplay isn't particularly innovative, and is a little boring if you aren't new to cover-based shooters. However, Spec ops REALLY excels at its story and enviroments, and the depth in how it explores a soldier with PTSD. Yeah, try naming the games that actually make you re-consider mowing down legions of troops. As a trooper, you are sent in with a 3 man squad to "evacuate" dubai, which was ravaged by sandstorms and is currently under martial law. The downside? The 33rd division has different plans. Without giving too much away about this fantastic setup, the story will make you question the morality of your decisions (and you can make a few as the game goes on), and you never really know who the bad guy is. I mean, sure, you have opponets, but are their motives THAT BAD? It is truly thought-provoking, and the ending is so heavy handed, I had to sit there and ponder it for about half an hour before I could even formulate an opinion on it. 

Buuuuut, to go back to the cons, the game is short, clocking in at about 8 hours. This isn't bad, but for a single player focused game with virtually no one playing its multiplayer or co op modes (shocker), it can be jarring to have the game lose all value so quickly. But, at the same time, if you are a sucker for good story and convincing atmosphere, this game actually can be pretty fun, and does make you think. But if you buy it for the gameplay... you might wanna look somewhere a little more non-routine.

This game is a fantastic story inside of a god awful game. If you've read a review of this game, it probably praises the story more than anything else, and rightfully so. Nolan North is his usual fantastic self, and the voice work of Bruce Boxleitner is always top notch. This game explores the psychology of the average military shooter protagonist and flips it on its ear and shows us how truly psychotic these people actually would be. It starts off fairly generic, but becomes something unique and special.

 Unfortunately, poorly designed gameplay mars the experience. There are bugs that will cause progression events to not trigger. The cover system sometimes doesn't work. Moving out of cover is dangerous because it puts you in to a sprint. Vaulting over cover requires pressing the same button that you use to melee, so you'll occassionally punch at the air above a chest high wall instead of going over it. On and on, I would run in to situations where the basic mechanics wouldn't work. I could forgive all of that if the actual shooting weren't so monotonous and boring.  The most intense fire fights become are pace killing once you realize that your best strategy is to move at a snails pace. Pop out, shoot, wait for health to regen. It's basically modern whackamole. This is a problem that these cover shooters have had for a while now, but the best games find a way to circumvent that inherent flaw. Not in this game. 

In some cases it takes one second to almost die, and nearly 15 seconds to get all of your health back. So slow progression and unspired game play put together means that the actual game is boring. I honestly just wanted it to end. 

 If you do buy this, it is the story that will get you to finish it. However, I don't believe story is enough to save a game. Novels exist. I'm judging this purely as a game, and as a game I don't recommend it.

I remember when this game first came out, and I completely over looked it. Looking back on it now, I find myself wanting to go back, and buy it upon it's release date. Spec Ops: The Line is easily one of the darkest, and most harrowing games that I have ever played. 

The choices you make in the game are extremely important, and with almost every choice you need to choose between two negatives. That being said; some of the options are just downright disturbing, and make you feel like a bad person afterwards. This game makes other war games look like a joke. While games like Call of Duty and Battlefield make you feel like some extremely overpowered bad ass soldier, this game does the opposite; it makes you feel like a monster, and not in a good way. This game shows that real war isn't so simple.

The only negative thing I can say about this game, is that it is very, very short. Only taking about 8 hours to beat, Spec Ops is still one of the best stories I've ever experienced while playing a game. While the gameplay, and arsenal of guns are nothing too special from a standard 3rd person shooter, you'll find yourself wanting more, and more to know what exactly is happening in Dubai. 

If you like dark, and twisted stories, then this game is definitely for you. Do yourself a favor, and just buy this game. It's a great story, and it only takes about 8 hours of your time.

First off, I have to say that I was not expecting to play this game all in one sitting. The story may be short, but what I mean by this is that this game captured my attention throughout the entire ride. I will provide an in-depth review of each aspect from a critical point of view, and a tl;dr of each aspect at the end with personal opinions.

STORY (no spoilers): After I fired up this game, through the first 10 minutes of playing I expected a low(ish) budget military shooter with a simple and forgettable storyline... boy was I wrong. Spec Ops: The Line doesn't do a fairly good job at capturing the players attention right away -- no, it's real strength is progressing the player through an increasingly maturing storyline focused on 3 soldiers who end up in the wrong place, at the wrong time. Surprisingly, I found the characters to be highly relatable and believable (personality-wise, not the fact that they can take 20 bullets without a hitch). You feel connected to them the entire way through, seeing as you will never play through the campaign without them (besides some small exceptions). There were many, many moments throughout the story that really made me think, or put me in awe; one part in-particular was so heavy, I literally had to pause the game and walk around for a minute to regain my composure. Spec Ops: The Line provides a seriously twisted, mature story that suggests consideration for every action you take (there are some sick  choices that must be made, and even when the game forces you into some situations you may hesitate before doing so). Overall, the story is the strongest aspect of this game and is completely worth $30, though to some of you more critical gamers i'd suggest you pick it up on sale. And when I say the story is mature, I really mean mature. If you're a younger gamer then I really stress the fact that you will be faced with some scenes that are very hard to take in. 

GUNPLAY/FIGHTING: Not much to say here. If you're playing with keyboard/mouse it will feel plastic-y, but you will hit targets much easier and end the fightings scenes much quicker (which can be a good thing since you'll mostly find yourself sticking around for the story); with a gamepad and vibration it will feel a bit more authentic, and obviously you'll want to have auto-aim on since the enemies are a bit hard to hit, even with K/M. There isn't much depth to the gunplay. There is a reasonable amount of different weapons to change things up a bit as the game progresses, but it lacks any unique or interesting mechanics. The one thing supporting the gunplay, doing so very well I might add, is the cover system and locations - the perspective is 3rd person the whole game and somewhat resembles a cross between the Gears of War gunplay and the Splinter Cell: Conviction cover system. Though the gunplay may feel repetetive after a while, you'll still be engaged with the environments -- which leads to my next point. 

GRAPHICS/ENVIRONMENTS: Graphics are okay, no anti-ailiasing so you'll have to put up with jaggies. While it isn't the best looking game, boy-oh-boy does it have an interesting style. The amount of detail and variety that is put into the environment, the amount of color and contrast is quite amazing -- really, the lead visual designer for this game needs a raise. If you're expecting "next-gen" from this game, you'll be disappointed. BUT, you will without a doubt get lost in the stunning detail and visuals of weather-torn Dubai. 

OVERALL/ TL;DR: If you're thinking about getting this game for the story, you will be in for a real, grotesque, gritty, shocking, heart-wrenching, plot-twisting treat. I should mention, I did NOT see that plot-twist coming. If you say you did you're lying and I'll throw sand in your face. Seriously I can't stress that enough, the story was easily this game's strongest factor and it is well worth full price imo (coming from someone who is very picky about good sorytelling, trust me on this). Gunplay will leave you wishing for more depth, but overall it keeps you well enough entertained in-between the major story-based bits and supporting cutscenes. Graphics aren't spectacular, but the visuals are really quite astounding and the detail of weather-torn Dubai is quite a sight to behold. Also, excellent color contrast, very pretty game.
