This is a game that, the moment I completed it, I sat down to write a review. I was conflicted about the storyline and content, as it's a game that it's nearly possible to complete in good conscience. Spec Ops : The Line is a common 3rd person military shooter in a lot of ways, save one : Its narrative. Some will find this game to be overly preachy, but having completed the campaign I think I know what the developers were going for. 

Military games of the last few years have shown players a lot of things. New graphics, firearms, and storylines that encompass many historical geopolitical campaigns. Spec Ops intends to show players something they've never been forced to confront. Themselves. In many ways, it's incredibly difficult to put a rating on this game as it's mediocre gameplay is carried by the narrative and (more importantly) the narrative's intent. It's also difficult to avoid spoiling as this is a game you will only experience the first time once. (duh) But the first time will be a troubling journey. During this game you will do horrific things simply because the objectives say so. The developers prod at you by saying "Just because the objectives dictate you should, doesn't mean you have to. You could simply turn the game off." In this way, Spec Ops is more of a mirror than anything. It puts a storyline in place which makes you angry, frustrated, and saddened by what transpires. It then steps back and allows you your chance at revenge. Sure, you're railroaded from a gameplay standpoint but as the Colonel says near the middle of the story, "This could have all been avoided if you just stopped." 

He's right. I could have stopped at any point. Spec Ops features imagery that is horrifying; war crimes are committed and witnessed in plenty. Yet you keep playing simply to make it all justified, to somehow convince yourself that the ends will justify the means and that everything will come out ok. It's not your fault. You were forced. In the end Spec Ops : The Line was the first game I've ever completed that I didn't feel happy about finishing.  Not because the gameplay was bad, but simply because no one with a conscience can finish this game without feeling dirty. I should have stopped somewhere in the middle of the game, and said, "Nope, this objective has gone too far. ♥♥♥♥ this game." But I didn't. 

My impressions of this game are almost the same as though I were reviewing A Clockwork Orange or Inglorious Basterds. You're not supposed to feel comfortable while you watch. Spec Ops is a bit different though, as you're in control of the "ultra violence" that's taking place. Maybe it's because I grew up in a violent neighborhood, where actions were always justified by their ends that this game hit me so deeply, maybe I'm just soft. In any case, if you've been on the fence about Spec Ops I'd strongly recommend a purchase based solely on its interperative value as it stands apart simply by having something to say about combat and war. I've been scratching my head about the ending all evening. 

9/10

This game very much disagrees with what it's trying to be, in a good way. It's trying to be a standard fun shooter, but every action you do makes you feel more and more horrible inside. It is the only game I know that properly depicts the horror of war. Or, at least how horrible I'd imagine it to be. The strong point in this game is the storytelling. I personally don't value that aspect of games that much, so me saying that means that there is something remarkable here. The gameplay is average, and I don't think praising games for what they don't have is appropriate. That said, I'm just going to mention the total absence of QTEs, and the lack of near-infinite ammo that modern shooters have. Those problems don't exist. Cutscenes are cutscenes, and resource management is a real thing.

There are some objective problems though. Even though the vast majority of PC players play with their eyes close to a desktop display, the game runs in a console-like couch distance FOV of 72°, when it should be 90°, to keep central visual feedback from falling in the human peripheral vision. And that setting can't be changed. Secondly, some completely unrelated actions such as sprinting and jumping down from ledges, and melee and vaulting obstacles, are filed under the same contextual key. The PC keyboard has 105 buttons, so why do we need to have the same button for unrelated actions? Thirdly, the game has built-in mouse acceleration that can't be toggled off, so basically someone spent real, paid work hours to make the mouse control worse than it could have been if someone just left it in raw input.

But while those objective faults made me stop playing Mass Effect 2, for some reason they didn't stop me from finishing Spec-Ops. I guess every moment I spent in the average gunplay was properly decorated with the sheer disgusting horror that I couldn't get enough of. The gameplay mechanics are simple, with some competently streamlined special mechanics such as giving orders to your squad mates with the press of a single button. Enemies are very good at keeping you pinned down, and you do need your buddies to survive. There are some environmental hazards that you can use against your enemies, but they are too few and far between, so you might not even realize they're there. The underuse of the setting in this way makes it a failed gimmick.

So it's a decent game with a few minor problems, that isn't as good on PC as it could have been with better PC-specific features, lacking in many modern negative game tropes, and finally, the story is hauntingly amazing. It isn't a game that you want to keep playing. It is a game you will want to finish, and then throw up afterwards, while crying conflicted tears of agony and joy. Nobody is perfect, but Spec-Ops: The Line is a one of a kind masterpiece of horrific beauty.

Spec Ops: The Line changed me as a person and it is a game that I recommend to just about everybody I know, and though it has gained some good attention for its story, I have never felt it received the full attention that it rightly deserves.

 As far as the gameplay goes it is a bog-standard 3rd person cover-based shooter, and as odd as it is to say I think that it benefits from the average quality gameplay (more on that later). The variety of weapons and maps throughout the campaign for the era of gaming this was made in is satisfactory and the use of environment as a weapon at times is very well done. Perhaps the worst part of the game mechanically is that the AI for your squad mates is suicidal at times; however, for better or worse, the enemy AI is less than perfect as well. It also does feel like the controls fight you a bit as well, but I found myself getting used to it at some point in the middle of the game. The top difficulty of the game with these issues can be pretty brutal but unless you are a huge fan of this game like I am you can get the full story on any difficulty you would like. It can be a bit difficult to recommend this game on its gameplay alone, but it really is the story that takes the show.

There is only so much I can say about the story, but I will let you know now that I could probably write a short novel analyzing and gushing about it. The basis of the story is you and your two squad mates have been assigned to find survivors and get them out of the sand-flooded city of Dubai after contact with the leader of the Battalion that went in to help the city during this environmental crisis sends a single message after months without contact. Beyond that I do not want to spoil anything else, it is a game best experienced specifically as a player. You can see the whole story through a let’s play, but the game loses a lot of its impact if you aren’t participating in the story. There are some central themes and thoughts that I have that aren’t spoilers, but may hint too much at what is going on so I will spoiler them, but it is worth discussing, so perhaps come back to this review after playing the game. [spoiler] The core concepts the story explores are things like PTSD, suicide, how we perceive reality, the nature of war, the idea of the end justifying the means, American global interference, who are the real heroes in war, and your ability to choose your fate. The writers for Spec Ops: The Line were not afraid to ask hard questions and they do so masterfully, and because it is like so many games of the era and fits in the middle of them all it sits as a strong critique of the messages they often tried to convey. I think one of the reasons many game writers started to choose more morally grey and nuanced stories is because of this game and others like it that challenged the thinking of overly patriotic games of the post-9/11 years. There is a place for those kinds of stories certainly, but for people who are willing to engage more fully with the reality and suffering that war causes, experiences like Spec Ops: The Line are extremely valuable and far more engaging in my opinion. [/spoiler] Though I don’t want to reveal more than that, I want to note that this game changed me and the way that I think about conflict and video games as a whole. The medium of video games is so powerful because you become part of what happens, it is not just happening in front of you, what is happening is because of you. I played this as a teenager hyped up on my youthful testosterone and hormones dedicated to becoming part of the US military and it made me think about things differently. It never changed my path in life, I never joined the military for medical reasons in the end, but it was still impactful on the way I thought about the world. As I have gotten older I have often thought back to Spec Ops: The Line, few games do that to me, and even fewer do so as powerfully as Spec Ops: The Line. So I will put it in no uncertain terms, this game has one of the best stories I have ever played, it is nothing short of phenomenal. It is a bit of a slow burn, but by the midway point in the story you will likely become hooked. I think just about everyone should play it (this specifically excludes those with PTSD from conflicts and war as it may be harmful to their mental health). 

The sound design for the game is great in my opinion. Sound effects like the rushing sand, the desert winds, the sound of gunfire and explosions, movement, and machinery all are very well designed. The music is solid as well, though beyond a few key songs for story moments, most of it fell into the background pretty easily. The stand out is the main cast of characters’ voice acting. The emotion behind all of it is strong, it is always properly mixed to be well understood at all times, and the casting decisions of voices to match the characters is perfect in my opinion. It is just a great-sounding game and it adds to the whole experience.

Graphically the game has aged, and quite noticeably too. It came from that era when everything started looking good enough that you could represent just about anything you wanted to in a 3D space, but textures have a noticeably lower resolution than many are used to nowadays, some animations (specifically facial animations) lack full expressiveness, and the models are less smooth and rounded than is now commonly standard. It really isn’t noticeable in gameplay, but it is in the cutscenes. Although trying to go for a realistic style makes games generally age worse, this game had to be that way in order to ground it to the other shooters of the era that were also trying to look as realistic as possible, and without that grounding the game would separate itself from the very games it is trying to analyze more deeply. Maybe not everyone will agree, but I do think that the lighting in this game is above standard for the era. Overall, for the era it was in a pretty decent spot, but it is clearly a product of its time.

If you're looking for an exciting run-and-gun experience like Call of Duty, you'll be utterly disappointed. If you're looking for something new in the FPS genre, you won't find it here. But if you're looking for something different that goes beyond mere game mechanics, this game will pull you in. Although this game is a third-person action shooter, the whole experience of a shooter is vastly different in this game. You take on the role of the leader of a 3-man Delta Force team sent to the devastated landscape of Dubai. Your mission is simple; locate survivors and get them out. The initial level pits you against individuals who are bent on killing you and for the moment, they are clearly the enemy. As you delve deeper into the game, horiffic scenarios unfold that chip away at the morality of the protagonist you control and his team. You are FUBAR'd for much of the game with brief bouts of conflict between the protagonist and his team as a reprieve. Along the way, the player is presented with choices that affect the game in varying degrees. Some of the choices allow you all the time in the world to think them over while others require a split second decision. This game is more about psychological warfare than actual combat. Now, this introduction perfectly fits (more or less) into the message of the game. Are violent games really just games, you play and get an achievement for your 50th headshot? Is it okay to sit back and enjoy war, while you are the hero, kicking the ass of all the terrorist scum that threatens to destroy the world? I can't really compare Spec Ops: The Line to Battlefield, Call of Duty setting-wise or Gears of War and Mass Effect gameplay-wise, as I've never played them. But what I can say is, that, in my humble opinion, Spec Ops: The Line is a masterpiece. Not without its flaws, but a masterpiece nonetheless.

Gameplaywise, you get the typical brown modern war 3rd person shooter thingy. What do you expect? You play a badass dude to murder tons of evil dudes. Simple as that. But storywise, you are encountered by some moral questions, you might not have asked you yet. And suddenly, all the dull gameplay makes sense in a more complex way.

I don't want to spoil too much here, so I'll keep it short: If you are expecting a breakthrough in modern warfare gameplay and gunfights, this game is nothing for you. Spec Ops: The Line is a solid 3rd person shooter that focuses on the horrors of war. It's kind of like "Apocalypse Now!" with Dubai as the setting but that comparison is giving it a little too much credit.  It's more like an ultraviolent summer blockbuster war movie. The story and dialogue come off hamfisted and silly at times. The voice acting is decent for the most part and the sound design is good.

 I would've liked the guns to be louder and bullet snaps would be great for immersion. The shooting mechanics are satisfying and the intensity of the combat is what kept me coming back to 100% this game. It's no "Red Orchestra" immersion wise, but I think it illustrates the horrors of war well in some ways. Enemies collapse and some suffer while clutching wounds or crawl away. They cough and whimper as blood pools around them. One thing they never do is surrender, which is an annoying trope of modern shooters. At least there are unarmed civilians on some levels, which goes against convention. The game also forces you into some bad situations with civilians which is a great way to show the ugliness of war.

The game looks fantastic, even years later and it's surreal to see Dubai turned into a wartorn blood soaked ruin. Every firefight is fun and challenging if played on the harder difficulty levels. It would've been nice to have stealth be more viable. It's also a little funny that a 3 man squad kills off thousands of enemies. I know it's supposed to be somewhat of a satire on the modern military shooter but I would've rather had "Rainbow Six" style squad selection/commands and losses than 2 invulnerable baby sitters. I hope more games try to execute a "military shooter gone horror" vibe. I really like that the game is a train wreck of bad events and it tries to make you feel responsible and bad for it, kind of like the Kane & Lynch series. It was just a little too hamfisted, on rails and "gamey" for that feeling to hit me, but I enjoyed the horrific descent into madness nonetheless. If you are looking for a solid 3rd person shooter with an intense atmosphere, definitely grab this game.

Spec Ops: The Line, is a great game. It combines one of the best stories I have ever seen in a game with some excellent gameplay moments. It is a nice change from the almost boring, modern military shooters. It is a great third person shooter and well worth the money.

Spec Ops is a game that tries to move itself away of the tradition of linear military shooters by using a more dark/grim (not gonna use "mature", sorry) story to talk about the horrors of war, and how ludicrous other military shooter's stories are.

But there is a stroong feeling that the developers were too focused on the history to realize that they were doing a videogame, and not a movie.

First, gameplay wise the game is as average as any other linear cover-based shooter can be: Scripted scenes, only one, defined, path, you can "blind fire" while in cover with such good accuracy is a joke, regenerative health, useless squad commands (Well, useless until you start to find the heavy weapons soldiers, then you use 'em to order "attack that guy". And that's all), machine guns that in the moment you man them a stream of enemies appear... the covers have that "magnetic surface" syndrome, meaning that you can't run near a cover without getting automatically attached to it. Really fun in a cover-based shooter in which ALL the maps are casually covered in makeshift parapets.
There's only one original mechanic: The sand deposits you can shoot to bury alive your enemies but there are only over 5 deposits on the whole game.

Don't get me wrong: Average does not really means "bad": The shooting is as fun as it can get, there are plenty of different weapons, and very remarkable moments (Like when defending your teammates through a mall with a machinegun). But still there's nothing specially interesting, nor a really good challenge even in the hard difficulty.

But, second, and more important: The story.
All Spec Ops is about the story. An interesting story about Dubai being blocked by, eh, ok, let's believe that, sandstorms, and about a delta force squad going in to see what the hell's going on.

Spec Ops has a movie story. Is a really good one, but is not a good story for a videogame. Or at least is not told as it should have in a videogame.
Starting with plot holes and unexplained details that are shielded in the "we don't know what's going on, we will understand later" excuse, the game makes the player go through several "war is hell" moments which can be summarized with "civilians being slaughtered, soldiers being slaughtered" all in an intent to make the player feel bad about what's going on around him and what is he doing, as a soldier, in Dubai.

But the concept failure, the main problem, is that you can't make me feel bad about kill people (Civilians or "good" soldiers) in an action game whose main point is, well, kill people. It's all about contradiction, as the main message the game seems to be sending is "You should feel bad for what the script and the core gameplay mechanic is telling you you have to do."
And that's a big "no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ way". I can't feel empathy for the main character (As I would in a more open game) or feel that "I'm" the Main Character because the story is telling HIS story and making me just move him around from one cutscene to the next one. The game is so linear that even the "moral choices" only affect in which achievement you get. There is no way to try to avoid the more conflicting moments of the plot, even though you are seeing what its leading to ("Hey, let's kill all those orphanages." "Ok, but we are going with you because you didn't shoot us"). Some people say that not having choice is "part of the message", and I call ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on this: You can give different choices to the player which will end in bad/worst results, and they will feel much better than forcing the player into a bad designed bombing scene (Floating parachute, if you play the game maybe you'll get it) so the plot can trigger its main element.

Spec Ops tried to move forward the military/cinematic shooter. It tried to make a more crude story, but it forgot that it is still a cinematic military shooter with nothing new to show. It forgot that what it is and what it tries to tell are oppossite things. If Spec Ops were a survival horror (With few killing and more puzzling), or a Fallout-esque RPG, allowing you to join any of the factions, the result could have been better and everything would have made much more sense.

A few reasons factor into this; including, but not limited to: A cleverly written and highly entertaining plot, with just the right amount of twists and turns to keep things interesting. Fluent combat, the game-play is satisfying and fun - cover systems and weapons are fluid, enemies keep you on your toes. The visuals aren't ground breaking, but this is an especially beautiful game - I think mainly given the locale, it is a wonderful sight to behold the once towering city of Dubai now gasping for air as it is swallowed whole by an enormous sea of sand. Spec Ops: The Line will take that and toss it out of the window, hitting you hard with everything to the point where you have no idea what you just did to stay alive, but you did it.  To stay alive.  Then, once the toxic dust settles, you see the monster you've become.  I remember asking myself over and over as I played this game, "Wait, did I have a choice there?  How was I supposed to know that those were civilians?  That was all scripted right?"  RIGHT?!

Spec Ops: The Line is really nothing at first glance. Any passerby would glance at this online and assume it to be a pseudo rip-off of Joseph Conrad’s Heart of Darkness and subsequently Francis Ford Coppola’s Apocalypse Now, complete with a generic third person shooter element and cover system.

And thus the game has already tricked you, the first of many narrative and visual tricks The Line will pull. Maybe as a gamer you don’t want to be tricked. You want to be entertained or praised. But there is none of that here. So why play this game? Because quite simply, love it or hate it, there is simply nothing quite like this.

story

Spec Ops: The Line opens generically enough. Nolan North voicing the gruff captain Martin Walker, leading a Delta team consisting of Lieutenant Adams and Staff Sergeant Lugo, ordered by the US Army to do recon and bring in John Konrad (one of many nods to Hearts of Darkness), commander of the 33rd Battalion, lost in Dubai after sandstorms destroyed the city. As Walker and his team traverse the desert, it soon becomes clear that not all is clear, and the lines of good and evil are blurred to a point where you, the player, will be questioning whether you’re doing the right thing.

narrative

It’s clear that the dark narrative mixed with sensational sound and voice acting meant that Yager Development (the developers) took an extra step in ensuring that the player was giving a harrowing and memorable experience that would leave you talking about it for years to come. Special props must be given to head writer Walt Williams, who provides a sensational story with huge mature undertones. If anything, The Line must be experienced for the story alone.

graphics

In terms of graphics, the sand-covered Dubai is quite a stunning vista. The towering skyscrapers all half buried in sand, the gorgeous backdrop that makes you feel like a tiny ant in a huge (linear) world and the graphic depictions of violence all lend a hand to the amount of immersion you would feel. In terms of violence, the game goes all in and really makes you question how much fun you’re really having, as you sickeningly pop another head in a cloud of red.

For a graphics comparison, the PC version remains the slight winner, with sharper graphics all around, along with the standard freedom of tweaking for your personal rig. But the differences are honestly quite small and on any platform of your choice you’ll end up with the same experience.

gameplay

In terms of gameplay, The Line remains painfully average, though this, like everything in the game, is for a reason. It’s an unremarkable third person shooter that you would have played in dozens of past games (Gears of War comes to mind immediately), complete with wonky cover system. The game gives you different weapons from rifles and pistols to shotguns and launchers to dispatch your foes in appropriately gruesome ways, as you slowly make your way through the corpses of the Damned 33rd.

There is a ‘sand’ mechanic that honestly feels a little like a missed opportunity, where the sand of Dubai plays a big part in firefights. This comes in the form of sandstorms and sinkholes that change the dynamic of the battlefield, but these happen very rarely and in a strictly linear and scripted sense. It would’ve been nice to see a bit more random events thrown in.

shooting

There are also random ‘moral’ choice events that come up every now and then that throw up an interesting thought. For fear of spoiling, they aren’t as black and white as you’d assume in normal games (Mass Effect or Bioshock comes to mind), but really just shades of dark and death, and they are never what they same. It’s a relief to see that acknowledgements were made to the gamer for thinking outside of the box, as there is always a ‘hidden’ option to choose, if you did not want to choose between two face options.

The soundtrack lends a huge hand in The Line’s final presentation. The orchestral score blaring in the background as you conduct firefights is spectacular and the choices of classic rock songs gives off a sense of atmosphere and feeling that you are in a war. The music that accompanies the final few minutes in particular will send shivers up your spine and result in an ending that you will never forget.

conclusion

Spec Ops: The Line is really an unremarkable game on the surface, but below the surface is one of the best narratives you could ever experience. The Line is one of the most exciting things to happen to a ‘modern military shooter’ game in a very, very long time, and it is something that should be experienced, whether or not you’ll end up liking it. The Line is one of the best games of 2012, from a year of winners, and deserves to be played, even once.

Have you ever played a Modern Military Shooter, such as games from franchises like Call Of Duty, Medal Of Honor, and Battlefield?  Did they leave you feeling vaguely uncomfortable, for reasons you couldn't quite define?  Maybe you are tired of the constant portrayal of the western protagonists as a technologically superior force for truth and justice in the face of a ragtag army of foreign soldiers that despite being outclassed in every way by the heroes are still built up as a overwhelming and faceless threat to all that is good and right in the world?

If so, then Spec Ops: The Line is the game for you.  In purely gameplay terms, it functions as an adequate cover shooter; enemies pop up, you hide behind stuff, you shoot at each other.  Maybe you order your AI squadmates to throw a flashbang, or snipe a specific target, or shoot an environmental object to hamper your enemies.  Pretty basic stuff, but it handles well.

What makes Spec Ops: The Line special is it's scathing critique of every cliche that has been fuelling the Modern Military Shooter genre for the past ten years.  Set in Dubai, following a sandstorm that leaves the city in ruins, a team of operatives is sent in to investigate a distress signal, apparently sent by a US Infantry Battalion caught in the storm during the relief efforts.

Without being too specific and risking spoilers, the situation quickly spirals out of control, and your squad struggles to resolve it, through the application of force against foes as desperate for survival as you are .  The protagonists behave as characters in these game normally do, assessing the situation, coming up with plans, and acting accordingly, which doesn't always work out how you'd expect.  Not only that, but they also suffer from the emotional impact of their situation and the actions they are often forced to take, that often manifest in subtle an interesting ways.  This is rare in a genre dominated by the type of stoic action heroes that do whatever is necessary to complete the mission, without suffering any mental scars that any normal person would have after massacring hundreds of people.
To give you a hint, one of the characters your squad is attempting to track down is called Konrad.  This illustrates the kind of literary influences this game is drawing from.

So if you are in the the market for a competent cover shooter that features a deep and interesting plot that provides commentary on the genre it emulates, you could do worse than Spec Ops: The Line.

This game is tedious, annoying, frustrating and simply not much fun.

And that's what makes it so great.

"What?" You might be asking yourself. What makes a tedious, unfun game so great? Is it some kind of "So bad it's good" kind of thing? Absolutely not, it was made this way intentionally, and for very good reasons. Spec Ops: The Line is very much like Schindler's List. You're not supposed to feel good about it once you've gone throught he story.

The real problem with reviewing a game like this is that, without giving out spoilers, it's impossible to find a way to say, "Ya, play it guys, seriously!" Without some kind of attempt to list out what makes this game special, all I can say is, "The gameplay is lackluster, there are obvious monster closets, the AI is horrid and the multiplayer should have just been ignored entirely. I totally recommend this, 8/10." And that comes off as just strange.

So, to try and do this without spoiling too much (and if I do, I apologize for the unintentional spoil), Spec Ops is less a game and more a thematic deconstruction and criticism of modern military shooters. And by deconstruction, I mean a total, across the board deconstruction. The game goes all-in on many gaming tropes and points out various areas that could easily use improvement or development into a generally quality mechanic and also makes it a point to deconstruct the players who play military shooters themselves.

The following topics are given a deep insight:

- The player's relationship with the main character
- Who really controls who? Does the player control the character or is the game controlling the player?
- The effects of dehumanizing the enemy on a person and, by extension, the player
- Tedious gameplay that highlights the effects and shock of what people experience in combat
- Moral ambiguity and a lack of any real clear "good" or "evil" in the game
- Demonstratably real effects of cognitive dissonance experienced by returning soldiers suffering PTSD
- The illusion of choice in video games
- How easy it is to convince people to blame others for "forcing" them into choices they don't have to make

A particular poignant point takes part in the final acts of the game where the game questions if you, the player, are beyond help and are incapable of seeing what's beyond Call of Duty and its clones and pre-emptively telling anyone that scores the game low due to monster closets and tedious third person cover shooting mechanics that they completely missed the point and are beyond help.

Everything about the game is designed as intentional and develops a deep experience that's difficult to find in gaming. While games like The Stanley Parable do a good job parodying the insanity of player choice, it fails to truly get the player to stop and think about it, let alone cast a wide net over the entire first person shooter genre and intelligently question nearly every gameplay mechanic, enemy AI complexity, faceless enemy syndrome, plot decisions and concept of legitimate choice.

If it wasn't for the deliberate end-game reveal, various load screen quotes and even the changing menu screen graphic, I would have simply thrown this game to the side as some kind of boring, derivitive shooter trying to be macho. But everything about this game is lovingly intentional, from the three man squad with token black man explosive expert and wisecracking white guy to wave after endless wave of idiot enemy. The whole game exists as a critique of the FPS genre, the games industry and the players themselves. And it's not a caustic, nasty critique, but one that asks us to think why we suffer through these mechanics and why we don't demand improvement or something better. Even using the fact that this game can be called "Spec Ops 11" is deep in and of itself since using a brand new IP would have missed out on critically adressing the excessive sequelitis that the gaming industry is stuck in.

Spec Ops: The Line is a bad and tedious game, but it's meant to be, and with the plot and decisions made within the game itself turns it into a brilliant commentary on what has happened to the games industry and the modern games consumer. I highly recommend you experience it in full to understand for yourself what's happening. It's a game that needs to be played since those Let's Play videos will do it a disservice as your active participation is necessary to get the complete experience as to what Yaeger is attempting to tell us all.

This is my first time writing an intelligent review rather than a first impressions, so bear with me please.

I'd just like to start out by stating that Spec Ops: The Line is really rather good. It's a third person military action shooter set in a near future Dubai, where the city has been almost wiped out by cataclysmic sandstorms. Taking control of Captain Walker, you make your way through the city, moving between outdoor and indoor engagements with enemy soldiers, using cover and squad commands to gain the edge over your opponents. The game runs on Unreal 3, one of my favourite game engines, and as a result the mechanics are rock solid for the majority of the time.

As you might expect from a military action shooter, you do a lot of shooting, and the game would not be fun if the shooting was not fun. Thankfully, the shooting is very enjoyable. The guns have a satisfying amount of bite to them and sound like military grade firearms, as they should. Most guns also have their own secondary fire mode; the standard pistol and assault rifle can be equipped with silencers and the AK47 can be switched between full auto and burst firing, for example. They also have different effective ranges and aiming properties. Short range weapons such as pistols and shotguns become weaker with distance, while sniper rifles have no cursor and can only be aimed while scoped. This keeps the shooting tactical and also encourages regular switching with weapons dropped by fallen soldiers. Grenades come in three flavours: frag, sticky and stun. They are scarce, but they can turn the tide of a difficult battle. If you are struggling with a nest of enemies, or a heavy, a well placed frag will more than take care of your problem. The system of making grenades rare but effective encourages rationing and prevents the player from becoming overly reliant on them.

The AI, for the most part, is very good all round. Enemies will constantly try to flank you and your squadmates, some will attempt to flush you out of cover and some will charge your position, providing an easy target but potentially distracting you from an incoming wave of reinforcements. Your squadmates, Adams and Lugo, are remarkably competent for AI companions in a military shooter. They can do their fair share of killing on their own, and they react to the squad command system in a helpful and, dare I say it, realistic manner. Lugo will snipe distant targets while Adams can use grenades to blast out enemy nests. It's a shame you can't give directions for them to move to cover, because they have a tendency to wander out into the middle of a firefight and get themselves shot down. While you can revive a downed squadmate (or order one to revive the other) before they bleed out, it is often not possible to do without getting yourself killed, which is frustrating. There is also the rare instance of an enemy just standing out in the open, not doing anything, which is strange.

While I'm not one to get overly fussed about graphics, I would like to make special mention to how the game looks. My dad used to work in Dubai, and I lived there for a year. While there were not very many places or buildings I recognised, the architecture of Dubai has been nailed to a tee, and the lighting outside makes the place seem like the hot, dry and dusty desert that it is. Indoor areas are dark and gloomy, offering a break from the harshness of the desert sunlight (though I doubt the air conditioning is working anymore, so it is probably not that cool inside) as well as welcome splashes of colour to the game's otherwise brown and grey palette. Though brownness and greyness are seen as a bugbear in modern shooters, Dubai as a city is very brown and grey, so you can't fault the art team for accuracy. 

Animation and texture quality are also very high throughout. Characters move in a convincing manner and react appropriately to given situations. For example, if a grenade explodes near Walker, he will duck and cover his head. The facial modelling is also impressive, with Walker talking in real time and grimacing when shot. Sweat plasters his forehead and as the game rolls along, he sustains injuries that leave him burned and bleeding. These wounds are shown in all their wet, bloody glory, and sand gathers in his hair as he struggles through the devastated city. Fire, enhanced by the game's strong lighting mechanic, glows and flickers dangerously, and explosions have a nice feeling of power, heat and spontaneity to them. My PC is an entry level build with components that are a couple of years out of date, but the game ran quite smoothly with the settings on high, with a minimal amount of stuttering (and only one crash). The only really noticable stuttering happened in the cutscenes, which are otherwise nice to look at and help to advance the story.

Going into Spec Ops: The Line, I half expected a typical military shooter "story" of 'Murican soldiers saving the world from the Russian terrorist menace (seriously, since when have Russia ever engaged in terrorism?), but I was pleasantly surprised. This is very much a character-driven story, with some genuinely chilling moments and not a hint of schmaltziness to be seen. I'm not going to spoil the story, but I will say that it kept me hooked throughout my playthrough. I blasted through the whole campaign in a single night, just to see what happens next. The voice work in this game is also worth mentioning. Walker and his squadmates communicate in a reactive manner, as do the enemy soldiers, and Walker gives specific commands depending on the enemy you highlight for your squadmates to attack. As the story progresses, the voice samples of Walker and his squadmates change, which I thought was a very nice touch. Again, I won't spoil it for you.

To play through the entire campaign took me about six hours on normal difficulty, which is more or less what I expected. While some may consider this game short, the game's fifty achievements, hidden intel pickups and unlockable 'FUBAR' difficulty should keep completionists coming back for more. Then again, I got twenty-nine of the fifty achievements on my first playthrough, so whether or not you think this game has very much replay value is up to you. I personally feel that I will make a point of clearing this game 100%.

Now on to my major problem with the game: the cover system. The idea is solid enough. You hit spacebar to duck behind cover, then you can move along it and pop out to fire at the enemy. You can also blind fire from behind cover, which is safer but much less accurate (there is even an achievement for killing five enemies with blind fire). Pressing left shift will let you vault over low cover, and holding spacebar while sprinting (also achieved with the spacebar, weirdly) will let you slide into cover on the fly. The main problem I have with the cover system is that not all pieces of scenary can be used as cover, and the pieces you can use look just like the pieces you can't use. In other games such as, say, Deus Ex: Human Revolution, you can use almost anything in the level as cover, and it is obvious what you can and can't use. This is not the case in Spec Ops: The Line, in which breaking from cover (with spacebar) and moving to a new position in the middle of an engagement more often than not involves guess work, and caused several unfair deaths for me. There were one or two instances in which Walker did not even sprint after breaking from cover, leaving me vulnerable to a pasting from the enemy soldiers.

Overall, despite some problems, Spec Ops: The Line is a highly enjoyable game. The shooting, atmosphere and voice acting are spot-on, and the sound design is arresting. The cover system and AI could have done with just a little bit more fine-tuning, but the rest of the game is so solid that it is easy to forgive. And it is definitely worth a try.

The gameplay is essentially that of a fairly simple, linear, third person, cover-based shooter. However it is fun to play. There's a variety of weapons to play with which are all quite fun to use. The main reason to switch between them is the limited ammo - it is very rare in a game that I have to switch to my side-arm because I've run out. Your two mates never get in the way and really feel like a valuable part of your squad. I genuinely felt a sense of desperation when one of them was out of action and I needed to get over to him to heal him. 

The main thrust of this game is the story. It actually managed to get me involved emotionally. Throughout, one has the niggling feeling that we don't really know what's going on and, without spoiling anything, it turns out there's a good reason for that. It conveys a sense of increasing confusion on the part of the characters. The dialogue is well-acted, with Bruce Boxleitner fitting well as Konrad. It's arguable that more complicated gameplay would detract from the story-telling and I find that that this can often be a difficult balance to achieve. Soldiers tend to be simple creatures though and I think the right balance has, more or less, been achieved.

The game has a few features that made me smile. For example, kicking an enemy in the face by vaulting over a barricade. The sand effects are unique in my experience and add to the game both in terms of visual spectacle and putting you into the story which is set in a place ravaged by sandstorms.

Overall, whilst this isn't a long game - it took me seven hours to complete - I would definitely recommend it. The gameplay is relatively generic but fun, and the story - which I feel is the main reason for playing - is strong.

Its a MUST PLAY for anyone who has the mental strength and maturity to finish it and understand it.

You continue slip after slip, enjoying it more and more. And then, at one point, the wine is gone. And you are left there, standing like an idiot, an empty glass in your hand, wondering what happened, trying to understand this strange feeling you've had. But the more you try, the less you can remember this bittersweet sensation in your mouth. This game will do that to you. It will bring you to strange, powerfull sensations and will suddenly leave you, feeling more alone, ashamed of what you are, wanting more, willing to understand. It is a must have for every player, as it will show you that videogames still can make you feel, and that sometimes, they are real art masterpieces.

Two years after its release, Spec Ops: The Line remains as the most mature presentation of War in video gaming. Comparing it to CoD and Battlefield, the two hype train every year, Spec Ops tell deep narratives about the horrors / attrocities of war while also presenting the player with decisions that provide no black and white outcome, as it should. 

Spec Ops graphics greatly beats Battle Field graphics, its not really about the engine, due to the things that they show. Take a frag grenade. Dust from Frags in Battlefield and CoD dissipate in about 1-3 seconds; while in Spec Ops, they remain for up to 5-7 seconds, completely blinding the players to the features of the enemy AI. THAT IS A GUD THING. War is chaotic and the lack of clear vision adds to this element because you shouldn't be looking at it from a looking glass point of view. New Cryengine that Battlefield sports shows lot of thing in "HD" but nothing you really want to look at. Nothing with meat. Do your human eyes see a difference between a leaf at 720p compare to 480p or 360p really? Clarity of sight is all in the contrast, and Spec Ops does it well with its gritty environement done with darker palet of colors and bright environment has bright palet and light.

Spec Ops the line narrative is great... 


[SPOILER] You pretty much be killing people you set out to save. 

Unlike CoD, where you are a bad ass commando that takes like 5-10 bullets, depending on difficulty, in Spec Ops, you'll die in about 3-5, on normal, just as much as your AI enemy. This adds alot to the gameplay as it humanize the player and make engagements compelling because you're not a bloody bullet sponge.

I could go on but a final note is one thing about the control. It must be a bug on the PC port but you basically dont have control of your sprint exiting or entering cover. Watch out for that and the sort of delay you have when peeking out of cover.

Wow..... That about sums it up. As far as gameplay goes this game gives me hope for the modern shooter. This is the best third person shooter I have played so far and one of the best shooters. Brilliant game, wonderful and insightful commentary on the tropes of first person shooters and the morality of conflict as a whole. By the end of the game, I was hating myself for what had simply seemed natural at the time.
Let me qualify this, however, by saying that the game does box you into some of the "choices" you make. Where the game's intended plotline does not coincide with your actual wishes, there's a distinct dissonance that can lead to blaming the game rather than yourself, as I think was probably intended.

Addionally, the gameplay was rather frustrating and not very well designed. I would often end up repeating certain segments again and again simply because of lack of cover, clunky controls, or unclear sources of damage. One segment, in which there was a helicopter shooting in through a window that had to be avoided, I ended up repeating over and over simply because I couldn't tell where it was shooting (where I could run) and nothing seemed to be working. In the end, I got through by pure chance. Also, these sections would frequently be in the vicinity of a cutscene (which would have to be rewatched every time), or at least take a rather large amount of time to reload, which contributed to an overall feeling of extreme frustration at times.

Overall, do play this game, and do try to play it through to completion, but perhaps choose one of the easier difficulties to avoid the experience being ruined by poor gameplay design.

If you like videogames such as [i]COD[/i], [i]Battlefield[/i] or [i]Gears of War[/i] this game is for you. [i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i] tells you how the war actually is by following the story of three Deltas who go to Dubai in a rescue mission, something that the games I have mentioned before and other military shooters didn't do.  What you feel while playing this game can't be described in any way. 

In my opinion, many videogames should follow the example of this great videogame.

As a story, Spec Ops: The Line is very deep on an emotional level. Character development is superb, and the story flows very nicely with exciting plot twists.

As a game however, its very skippy and laggy and the cutscenes dont always play right. The AI is extremely buggy, and it is often difficult to quickly control your hero. Furthermore, without rebinds, many of the controls are in awkward positions and don't make much sense.

6/10 Stars

There's no glorification in war. A conflict of ethics and code of conduct. What's the importance between one's conscious and one's choice just to survive. Spec Ops: The Line define such philosophies. The game's narrative is one of the most memorable in video game history as modern first-person shooters are too mainstream and cliche. There are certain scenes in the game that might or will make you pause, reflect, or even quit the game just to remind yourself on what war is. However, Spec Ops: The Line is NOT an anti-war game. It just tell what war is like. Many people and gamers can compare this game to Apocalypse Now. Sure, that's comparable but the game can be interpret to many literatures and certain documentaries like Waltz of Bashir. The gameplay is decent and typical but I believe that the developers strongly focused a lot more on the story and its message rather than gameplay. Spec Ops: The Line is a memorable game, but its more of the "one-time play" game mainly because of its heavy subject matter. Would I recommend this game to others? Yes, but it is up to you if you can handle the game's content. Best purchase this game on a steep discount.
Excellent FPS with a variety of game play you'd expect. Story is very good and I found myself emersed ... "Ohh .. go on then ... just one more section before bed" LOL

Spec Ops: the Line gives the average gamer a gritty view of the psychological effects of war. As you shoot, bomb and even melee kill your way through hundreds of enemies, you begin to question if you are really doing the right thing. As your once loyal squadmates begin to question and refuse your orders, you wonder if they shouldn't be making the decisions. 
9/10 because it shows the players that war is not fun, war is gritty, scary, and brutal.

So first off do you play games for the story or gameplay? If you play it for gameplay alone, you aren't in so much luck.

The gameplay is a generic 3rd person shooter but the story, Oh sweet jesus on a cracker the story is like eaing a new slice of cheese pizza fresh out of the oven and having the melting cheese fall into your mouth. It's delicious, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ god like! This is one of the best stories of a game I've played and it has multiple endings. Now I am not going to spoil it because that would be a ♥♥♥♥ move but the story is depressing AF.

Good gaming guys!
Amazing story; picture a modern version of apacalypse now, and that's this game. Gameplay is pretty good too, feels like a revamped gears of war. I'd give it an 8.5 out of 10, do recomend.

Spec Ops: The Line is one of the best games for story I have ever played. The multiplayer is average, but the campaign is probably the best i have played in any "modern military shooter". Some complain about a broken cover mechanic, but I have never had issues with it.

This is the way that art and videogames are supposed to bend together in order to create something unique and special, it is clear from the beginning that this game it's different than the usual run and gun mindless modern military shooter game, it has charm, it's characters and dialog are there, they are perculiar and dislikable while at the same time being the only ones that you can be familiarized with going along the ride.
The game it's particular with it's attention to detail, from the beginning there's just countless upon hundreds of things to take note of, aside the experience and the nightmare that goes in it's side it's perfect and breaks completely into creating an actual terrifying atmosphere that would make you keep playing only to get slapped by a wonderful and one of the most powerful endings in video games.

This game it's just simply a masterpiece, and my game of the year for 2012.

Brilliant game that really blurs the line between good and evil. The popularized American good guy dominance of other modern shooters just isn't relevant as this "war" is completely morally grey. By the end you will be questioning your own character's morality over the decisions you've had to make.

In some reviews this game was highly grated for its 'unique gameplay', honestly doh its just another shooter. And the campaign only lasted 5 hours which is short so if you can buy it for 5 euro's like I did then its a good price and you will have a little bit of fun.

For anyone looking for a shooter that evolves the mechanics for the genre don't look for it in Spec Ops: The Line. However the Story, characters and setting are really what the game has going for. I dont want to give too much away but the story in this is worth the price alone and in my opinion one the most emotional and unforgettable storytelling experiences ever put into a video game.

I was very skeptical when I first came to purchase Spec Ops: The Line as I had read a number of negative comments pertaining to the game's mechanics.  When I saw it on sale for £5, I figured I would give it a shot - I was not disapointed.  Other then occassionally dodgy controls and a relatively short campaign, this game is totally enjoyable.  

What really makes it worth-while though is the message it conveys.  You have to play it to really understand the strong emotions it elicits.  War is hell.

It's your bog-standard third-person military shooter for the first hour or so, an ohh-rah romp into a sandstorm-trashed Dubai on a recce op.  Then the game's designers start to ask you: do you -- the player -- like what you're doing?  Do you enjoy the carnage and the suffering you're causing?  If not, why aren't you just turning the game off?  Can you think outside of the box, or are you just following quest arrows on a map? Spec Ops is one of the few games out there that manages (for the most part) to send a message without rubbing your nose in the wet spot in the carpet. 

Unreliable narration and mind games galore make Spec Ops a unique experience.

What can i say about Spec Ops: The Line. Well its a fantastic 1st person shooter! Graphics, Controls, Story are all Amazing! I got it on sale and to be fair i didn't expect to be this good. The story telling in this game is top notch. Id recommend this it to any FPS fan!
While the gameplay is average at best, the story is impressively engaging and take the player into the heart of their own insanity. A great game for those looking for a decent story

Pleasantly surprised by the game's story and game play. Even though it looks like just another modern shooter, this game shows you that you can make a good, thoughtful, provoking and realistic war story, where you end up not knowing who's good, and who's bad anymore.

I totally recommend this game, if you are tired of playing stereotypic shooters like CoD or Battlefield.
At the end of this game, I have to think about the story in contrast to the "real" history and personalities. 
In this game, there is not a single person who is a "complete" "good guy". 
In this game, black and white are mixed up, an the main character is either villian or hero.
I cannot say anything more to the story, otherwise I would spoiler a great constructed plot which is totally recommendable.
I enjoyed playing this game, at the same time I did not. 

Now to the few negative aspects of the game: mainly the gameplay, which can be a bit monotonous. You often have to search cover, and just firing as long as anyone is standing. The areas are also quite small, and you only have small room for acting individual. A small sound bug in the cutscenes annoyed me sometimes, but I do not think this is a general problem.
So a small suggestion for the developers is to bring a bit more "space" for the Player to act.
All these criticism are quite small arguments against buying the game, because for me the story was the best thing about it. But... just take a look by yourself, download the demo, it provides a quite good view.

To put it in a nutshell: this game shows the uglyness of the human factor in combination with a target, which cannot been reached as easily as thought. I did not played this kind of games often, and I would buy it again!

This is a great game and in my view has one of the most memorable stories in all of the games i have played. It's one of the games that even after playing it you still think about it, the story stuck in your head for a number of reasons. It is a game that tries to show another side of war. Not the side that other games show where you kill and kill, but the side that shows consequences for your killing and the impact it has.

This game feels like a successor to the Rainbox Six: Vegas line, employing many of the same 3-man, cover-based strategies. A great blend of action and decent storytelling, Spec Ops: The Line suffers from one crippling failure, that the "cover" and "sprint" buttons are blended into one, making both actions clunky and HIGHLY prone to failure. A better control scheme would make this one of the more exciting shooters available, but as it is the game is frustrating and a perfect example of a dev team failing to understand one of the core elements of their own genre. If the devs ever patch this dumbfounding oversight I'd recommend this game 100%. Until then, save your money and just pick up R6 Vegas and Vegas II instead.

As most other reviews say this is not your yearly "Call of Duty", the game puts you in front to a more serious approach to the morale of war and a "closer" relationship with your team, the fact that its story comes from a book says a lot with regards of the deepness of the narrative and characters involved in it. Fights are always challenging but not impossible (there are no boss if not for some heavier equipped units) nor fights on vehicles except for the introductory scene. 

The game isn't long, in 10 hours you should be able to finish without rushing, however it is a rich experience and a game that I would suggest to try as it really deserves it. 

Under a technical point of view the game excel with great graphics, character design (to me the main character looks like Shepard from Mass Effect), great voice acting and a sad (in a good way in this case) Dubai.

Give it a try you won't regret it.

This game is a rare gem. Created by the back then rather unknown Indie game studio Yager it was meant to continue the line of 8 previous "Spec Ops" titles, a series of tactical shooter games, but managed to become so much more than a reboot of yet another interchangeable shooter.

As nine to five this game appears to start with its third person shooter graphics and arcade style gameplay and as weak as a console port it might seem, don't be dettered by it. This games dark story explores the morality and psychological consequences of war and with it the shooter genre itself. 

If you ever wondered how a portrayal of the insanity of war and a farewell to the "war is so cool"-depiction, Call of Duty stands for, could look like in one game.. Here you've got it.

This game isn´t for everyone. A potential reason why it turned out a commercial failure and the last title of the Spec Ops licence. You will gaze deep into the abyss of war and it will also gaze back into you. It will take you on an immersive journey where you question what you're actually doing on every step you take as much as you're unable to stop with it. You'll face decisions that will inhibit fears of only making things horribly worse. And you fight the beast you might become yourself to the climax of a finale that's nothing less but a magnificent ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

Well i was simply apalled when i noticed that not one of my around 30 friends owned this masterpiece of a game, even
Ben "Yahtzee" Croshaw had his dark emotionless heart moved by the masterfully written story in this game. First it makes you feel like utter ♥♥♥♥ after something you did was not as super awesome as you thought and towards the end one character i genuinely liked got hung (as in he choked to death, he didn't randomly generate a large penis.), after this i just drew the conclusion that the civilians who were cheering at his death were the ones who caused this, i didn't even understand the language they were speaking. Nonetheless i heartlessly mowed down as many as i could with my machine gun while the rest were running away screaming from this senseless murderer, i then realized that the game didn't ever force me to kill these people, it just told me to get away from there, but, it gave me the possibility and as a huge bellend i took it. Later on the choice didn't feel quite so good. I wholeheartedly recommend paying full 60€ for this but since it's dropped in price considerably since launch you probably have to look around to spend 60€ on it. My point is, just buy it allready.

An amazing game. You play as Captain Walker, who's leading a 3-man team on a search and rescue mission to Dubai, which has been destroyed by devastating sandstorms. The mission turns into much more than a S&R and you have to fight to get through the hell that Dubai has become.

With a thrilling storyline, showing what a commander has to face during battle and when things go to hell. It's a challenging game, even a bit irritating at times, but in a good way. And with a good multiplayer and co-op it's one of the most interesting games I've played in a long time.

An 8/10 from me.

Absolutly the WORST mouse control ever!!! I'm trying to find a fix but so far no luck. Great looking game but the controls make playing almost impossible.

I've managed to turn off the mouse acceleration which was part of the problem (google it) but the cursor is still so unstady that aming a weapon is nearly impossible. The game has great graphics with good sound and voice overs but untill the fix the mouse problems, don't waste your money.

one of the problems with a game being remembered for its stand-out story is that people forget that it was actually a really good game too. if you miss cover shooters & never got around to trying this, let me maybe be the first to tell you that this game was also very fun to play.
it's a bit on the simple side so at the time it came out a lot of people wrote it off because it doesn't have any gimmicks to artificially complicate the gameplay the way a lot of competitors did at the time, but they don't really make these kinds of games anymore so it can be a breath of fresh air to just get some solid & fairly simple cover shooting in.
(its also way more polished than i remember it being -- more polished than any other game in the genre has been since as far as im aware)

This is, by far, one of my favorite military shooters to date. While it has some issues, I think the story more than makes up for it.

The bad parts will be much easier to get out of the way...
The controls. I'm not going to lie, they are pretty horrible. They're clunky and at times unresponsive. I can't tell you how many times I died because of these issues.
Next would be the typical fight, wash, repeat set up to battles. It's all worth it in the end, but it really can try your patience getting through the game.

Now for the good part, and honestly it's just one thing for me...
The story. The story in this game is amazing. It's something that actually makes you think. It's not your typical, "OH NOES THE RUSSIANS ARE ATTACKING! We're the good guys and we must protect everything!" All of this while you are mowing down countless people without second thought and blowing everything up in your wake. This makes you think about what the soldiers are actually doing, the decisions they have to make, the repercussions of those choices, how they have to deal with it. It's honestly amazing. I feel like I'm one of the few people that could care less about multiplayer in a game, just give me a game that has a good story that I can sink some time into and I will be happy. Don't devote everything to making a good multiplayer experience.

Another plus, the game looks really good. I was honestly surprised to see it was running on Unreal. The majority of the time with games on the Unreal engine, the characters look like steroid induced monsters. These people look normal and the environment is beautiful.

If you haven't bought this game already, do it. You won't be disappointed. Especially if you're a person who enjoys a game with story instead of just mindless destruction and killing.

It is a great combination of a third person shooter and storyline I wont spoil the surprises the game holds, but if you love a detailed and amazing storyline as well as a good firefight this game is for you. Its not a mindless shooter like Call of Duty with a bit of detail in the story. ITS THE BEST GAME I HAVE PLAYED and I have played most games and consoles from PS1 (2) and (3) to Xbox 360 including the PSP 3000 through to Vita.
This game is amazing. I usually dont like third person shooters but the story line is this game has me hooked. Good graphics and an addictive game play makes this game deffinitly worth the money.

Unlike the other reviews, i'll make mine's short. This game is amazing in always, and is about/the same/ better/  quality as next gen. It makes you.it makes pychologically think. Now as i am writing this, i think, how would i/you feel if you were illing peopel who were citizens of the same country your from, killing fellow americans. This is a great game, every CoD player should play this for a change. Every BF player should play this for a change, EVERYONE SHOULD PLAY THIS AMAZING GAME. Thanks for reading

Wow. I just beat this game and loved it! There aren't too many games that have made me feel this much emotion while playing them. The game isn't perfect but is well balanced and fun to play. Where this game really shines is it's storytelling. Definitely recommended.

♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I'm not usually a fan of campaigns as i usually find them boring and play the multiplayer right off the bat. This game however is one exception as its campaign is really one of a kind. Even if you dont like single player campaigns, get this game, its amazing.

A highly over looked game.

You have to play this gem. This is by far one of thee' best TPS campaigns I've ever played, next to Uncharted. I think what may steer people away from this game is the title. The game's title kind of sounds like some crappy html flash game.

What makes this game a gem is the story. It is not your average military plot line where you're the 'Murican badass hero here to come save the day from the Russian invasion or a terroist group, thus making the world a happy plus. Spec Ops: The Line? HELL NO. You are no hero. You are simply a soldier, following his orders, not saving the day or rescuing civillians. You make gigantic f**k ups that make you feel like uber sh**. This game shows the other side that most military campaigns don't, This game doens't glorify the killing of enemies like most stories. Instead, it makes you feel wrong for it. Very wrong. And you have to deal with it. What makes the game soo good is how much of a piece of sh** it makes you fee like for your actions. I don't want to spoil anything, but there's this one part of the game involving the use of white phosphorus on your enemies. Boy, does the aftermath make you feel so f'ing depressed. Just play this game. The depressing story is sooooooooo damn good! I know it sounds weird, but trust me. It kind of opens your eyes in a way...
with a story that sucks you in for the entirety of the game and always makes you want to know what is going on throughout the game. I say buy this game now the less you know about it the better.

Starts as your average shooter, ends as a venture through the mind of a soldier ripped apart by the choices he must make. The gameplay itself is your typical shooter spiced up with new weapons you encounter and breakable windows to let sand crash into your battlefield. It the story that makes this game good, the characters in the begginning are stereotype but that vanishes 1/3 way through the game, they fight morale conflicts in different ways creating tensoin in the squad. Spec ops: the line really hits home on creating a dark and horrifying war experience. This game will change your mindset on how to aproach situations completely by the end of this experience, be prepared to question your morales as the bodies start piling.

This game is an underrated gem.  The story is so rich and the environment of a decaying Dubai is surprisingly refreshing compared to other shooters.  The gameplay feels very much like a GOW game, but a bit clunkier and not as refined.  Things like running out of cover or even getting into cover can be problems at times.  I'd also HIGHLY recommend using a gamepad.  There is a nice selection on weapons to choose from and they all feel different.  While many games out there claim to choices you'll have to live with, this one really does.  You will make them, and you will hate yourself for making them.

Ok.I'M CRYING, THIS GAME IS SO MUCH FEELS.

Like the history is awesome, not boring like most shooters and graphics are good.
But the multiplayer is empty :/
Still worth my money.

Probably one of my all time favorite games. I haven't finished it yet but the gameplay and graphics are pretty nice and the story is pretty nice too. This is also one of the only games that actually makes you feel terrible about killing people even though you know they arent real.
Not only is this truly one of the most transgressive upsetting games of the last decade or so, being such in a genre that sells like hot cakes today is nothing short of courageous.

Wow. Awesome game. Really great story. Gunplay is fine but standard for this genre. But my god the story and the ending. There's so much to think about, and this game is truly an awesome experience. I would recommend this to everyone, just for the experience alone.

Spec Ops The Line...oh man, I put off playing this game for a long time. It looked just like any other ordinary and generic Army based shooter to me, Where the story is nothing more than just doing the missions you've been sent to do. But I couldn't be more wrong. Because you see, this game isn't just a game, It's both an intense and breath taking expirience. It opened my eyes, left me speechless and made me genuinely feel empty inside. This work of art manages to visually leave a message inside your mind that reads, There is no Good Side or Bad Side to a war, Any So Called Hero can change into the most vicious of all villians within the blink of an eye. The gameplay itself is a typical thirdperson shooter, But the true beauty of this gem outshines all negativity bought by it. I would suggest anybody with a saturday to kill, pick up a controller and play this from start to finish, And the next day when you wake up, you'll be waking up a changed person.

8/10 - Minor Flaws, Story really makes up for them though.

Spec Ops: The Line was not fun. It wasn't even remotely fun. And thats the entire point. If this game was fun it would lose all of its meaning. It leads you into agreeing with decisions and then realizing how wrong you were. Its a criticism of the incredibly violent nature of videogames, and our callousness to it, all wrapped up in a Heart of Darkness type storyline set in ruins of Dubai.

The gameplay may be very generic and unremarkable, but the story (loosely inspired by 'Heart of Darkness' and 'Apocolypse Now') is an absolute masterpiece, with many disturbing and shocking events and decisions throughout the game. Heavily recommended to anyone that wants a really great story, cause game storylines really don't get much better than this.

This game is a game that you will remember. I would reccommend it to anyone who is a fan of huge, immersive stories. The story this game tells is one of the best, so it is a must buy in my opinion. However, there are a few drawbacks. 

The beginning of the game is somewhat poorly done. Now, completing the game gives it more meaning, but it just seems too generic. The early parts of the game offer little to no story and is overall not that great. The controls are REALLY hard to get used to at first as well. The combat overall isn't anything to brag about either. However, if you can make it past that, you are in for a treat.

This game offers stunning environments, incredible characters, and an amazing story. It depresses you, makes you feel like a badass, and also makes you think all at the same time. The setting in Dubai and all the buildings really make this place feel lively, while the people and story contrast it with a dark and depressing tone.

If you have the money to spend on this game, I reccommend you get this game. It is one of those games you will not forget.
This game is stupid. The shooting system is a crap. The only highlight is Dubai. I would rather to play Call of Duty, which can be much better than this game for being a shooting game.

HOLY HELL!!!!!

This game's story takes you everywhere. at first i was like "all this hype about it making you feel horrible is fairly minor stuff" then i started playing again on the day of this review and it just got deeper and darker as you make morally testing descisions and at some parts i actually felt EMOTION inside me. like i felt really freakin horrible about myself. sad, really. so if you like story, get it. once it started getting darker the rest of my day was dedicated to it. couldnt stop.

now the way the story progresses kinda sucks. it's like if call of duty was thirdperson and had a really well thought out story. pretty much gunning through most parts and if not that you're on an HMG escorting your squad. not necessarily a bad thing, just wished it was more advanced than constantly shooting. so i guess if you enjoy the constant gunning kind of campaigns everywhere, this is also for you. honestly this game covers alot of bases for people of all game groups to join. 

campaign took me about 6 1/2 hours. this game definitly isnt here for the nultiplayer. pretty much deserted but if you could get in a full game i bet it could work out good. 

so basing around the short campaign time (which is okay since i binged played this it was good enough), bad MP (blame the playerbase), but astonishing campaign this is a good 9/10. freaking get it.
